Uniform Title: Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī, Volume 2 Author: Abhinavagupta Editor: Śāstrī, M. K.

Description: Text extracted from Volume 62 of the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies, *The Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī* by Abhinavagupta, Volume 2 of a three-volume set. Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark Dyczkowski. Revision 0: 19/11/2005. Publisher: Research Department, Jammu and Kashmir State.
Publication year: 1941 Publication city: Bombay Publication country: India
Now begins the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī* [The Investigation into the Commentary on the Recognition of the Lord],
by the venerable Mahāmāheśvara teacher, the illustrious...
Composed by Bhinavaguptapāda.
Now begins the fourth reflection (*vimarśa*).
I perpetually salute the Lord, who allays every suffering and is the liquid nectar of immortality.
[He is] one whose head bears the moon, resting in an unimpeded expansion according to his own will.

Although the sequence is such that there is first knowledge, then memory, and within those two, the power of exclusion (*apohana*) residing in living beings; nevertheless, when experience has perished, memory... (1.2.3).
Thus, while the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that [memory is not perception], the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) states:
"But memory-cognition... (1.1.3).
By means of the incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*) formulated in the sūtra, it is shown that memory itself is what was previously introduced under the condition "if it is not [perception]."
Since the self and the Lord are established through the reversal of the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga-viparyaya) indicated [previously], there is a superior form of direct knowledge (abhijñāna).
For this very reason, that same [knowledge] was taken up first in the Gītā. Therefore, its logical justification within our own philosophical system (svadarśana) is now stated.
"For he is the perceiver of objects previously experienced...
and so forth;
thus, by these [words], the two objects appear within the cognizer.

By these eight verses ending thus, [the author addresses this]. Otherwise, someone might say: "Granted that memory is established in the systems of others, but how is it established even in your own system? To that, the establishment of it is stated by one verse; by another, the capacity of memory to manifest an experienced object is stated.

(Page 2) Through another [state], there is an absorption reaching the limit of oneness with both the experience and its object. Through the fourth [state], in memory, the experience does not appear as something separate from the object. This is also the case with the cognition of a yogin.

By the fifth [verse], which states that the experience of another is not manifested as something separate from the object itself, that very point is reinforced. By the other [verse], it is stated that the apprehension of cognition as a separate object through memory—which might otherwise be suspected—is merely conceptual and not real. This is discussed in connection with the topic of memory.
The identity of even conceptual construction with [pure] experience is stated by the seventh verse.

By the final [verse], it is shown—by way of an incidental discussion—that the objects of memory, the act of remembering, and the rememberer, as well as the perceived object, the act of seeing, and the seer, find their ultimate rest in the single reality of consciousness (*saṃvit*). This is the intended meaning. In that regard:
With the intention that the first section is an introduction (*upoddhāta*) which serves as the foundational framework for the entire meaning of the treatise, he says in the introduction:

"Now, by means of the section on knowledge (*jñānaprakaraṇa*). This refers to the fact that knowledge—in the form of memory and so forth—is consistent with his own philosophical system, and thus it is the subject to be investigated.

"In this [work], it is processed (prakriyate) or undertaken (adhikriyate) by means of that. Regarding the phrase "intending to describe" (*nirūpayiṣyan*), the suffix *lṛṭ* (the future tense marker) is applied because another action is the purpose for the first action. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: having resolved in his heart, "I shall describe the essential nature of all [authoritative sources] such as the Smṛtis and so forth," [he says] "of the Smṛti alone," etc.

Desiring to demonstrate that this very [power], which was previously introduced, is indeed the nature of the Lord's power (*īśvara-śakti*), and wishing to declare its absolute impossibility according to other philosophical systems (*paradarśana*),
the author first states its prior possibility with this verse.

Or rather, the verse is non-different from the author himself, its very nature being the vibration of that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). The inclusion of the word "first" (*tāvat*) indicates the sequence, signifying that the essential nature of cognition, exclusion (*apohana*), and so forth, will be examined immediately thereafter. Now, one might ask: whence does such a sequence arise? He replies:
Since memory serves as the cause for establishing the self (*ātman*) whose nature is that of the Lord (*īśvara*), this sequence follows. How is it made perfectly clear? He says:
"pervading all times," meaning from the time of the prior experience up until the time of recollection, by means of consciousness (*bodha*).

If it is not all-pervasive, how can there be recollection? Furthermore, since those two [the object and the cognition] are not restricted [to a single moment], their persistence throughout all time follows by way of that [recollection]; thus, it is established that the reality of the Self is that consciousness whose nature is eternal luminosity. And even so, if [it exists] as inseparable from that...

If it were not possible for [consciousness] to arise from an experienced object, how could there be memory? Thus, sovereignty is described as having the characteristic of being "all-aspected" (*sarvākāratā*).
As Bhaṭṭa Divākara has said:
"If all experienced objects were not well-protected by being assimilated into your own self,
then that which is called 'memory'— which consists in the non-deprivation of the form of the known object— would not be possible at all."
Thus it is said. And this is not all: even in the state of having the form of the entire universe (*viśvākāratā*), there is no loss of its nature as pure luminosity (*prakāśarūpatva*).
Whether certain portions of existence emerge while others submerge, within this manifold variety of many branches, there remains the self whose essential nature is eternal consciousness.
This sovereignty, which is freedom, must be established as having infinite branches;
it is logical that its clarity is achieved through the power of memory (*smṛtiśakti*),
for he is the perceiver of objects previously experienced, even at a later time.
Reflecting thus, he who is independent is designated as "one who remembers. || 1 ||

And here, the half-verse beginning with "pūrvānubhūta" has been introduced by the phrase "svatantrāvabodha" and so forth, through a concise definition of its meaning by means of the expression "aśeṣakālānugata. That Great Lord (Maheśvara), manifesting his own nature as the inner self within himself, will be the subject of the forthcoming exposition.
"Indeed, it belongs to the Lord who consists of consciousness. Here, in the state of the inner self (*pratyagātman*),
that which is metaphorically attributed as existing across multiple times—
even from a time subsequent to the time of a prior experience, at another time such as the present moment of recollection— [is perceived].

Since the apprehension of an object previously experienced occurs within the locus of the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), and its status as the perceiver of that prior object is not severed— therefore, by virtue of this very existence and because it is appropriate for it to grasp both the prior and subsequent times, it is characterized by the reflective awareness "that [is it]."

He reflects upon that object. One should not ask why it is he alone who experiences those infinite states, for he is *svairī*, independent. Indeed, even such things as similarity, past experience, and focused intention (*praṇidhāna*) are merely the unfolding of necessity (*niyati*) through his own sovereignty. The preceding and succeeding moments of this reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—[are of him].
Although the two times have slipped away from one another and, while remaining within the nature of consciousness, have not yet merged into it,
they nevertheless merge into one another and into that very nature of consciousness; and this is the meaning.

For one who perceives that which vibrates within the nature of consciousness as if it were something additional, and though not external, as if it were external—the very sovereignty of the Supreme Lord is his life; this is indeed the state of being a master. For the power of recollection (*smaraṇa-śakti*) alone is the supreme sovereignty. As Divākaravatsa said regarding the state of meditation and so forth: [The text continues: "From meditation..."

"Memory itself, having obtained [the power of] the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), manifests your glory. The particle *hi* indicates that the entire section on memory serves as the reason; for it is the independent Great Lord (Maheśvara) who, being such as he is, remembers according to the logic that will be stated and is now being stated.

This positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is thus established: "this [is] the locus of conventional usage. Therefore, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) stated in the preceding sūtra as "if not" is appropriate by way of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*). Otherwise, how could it be that the absence of those [functions] such as memory and so forth is necessitated by the absence of the self?

For it is not the case that from the absence of a jar there follows the absence of a sprout. Therefore, this negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is rightly established in the form of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*). By the word "for" (*hi*), [the author] indicates that the entire meaning of this section serves as the reason, thereby connecting it with the preceding section.
The meaning of the aphorism is that it brings about a unification of the context; for that single [object],
which is a recognition (*pratyavamarśa*) due to having been previously experienced, is here in contact with both times,
belonging to one who is contracted within the vital breath, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), the physical body, and so forth.

The connection [of the words] is as follows: *smṛti* (memory) is an activity (*vyāpāra*) whose nature consists in the non-forgetting of an object previously experienced. For, because it is unitary, it touches upon both times. Furthermore, its agency itself is its omnipresence and its sovereignty; such is the application of the commentary. Now, one might object: for that which is eternal and of the nature of consciousness, there is no connection with time.

Since this conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) exists even after [the cognition], and that which is projected by it also existed previously, how could those two exist within the nature of consciousness (*bodhātman*), such that the Sūtra says "existing even after" and its commentary says "even later"? Now, it might be argued: "[It is] the perceiver of the object previously experienced."

Thus, when the linguistic usage "it exists after this" (parato 'sti) is applied to a qualified object, it cannot logically apply to the qualified subject itself and therefore adheres to the aspect of the qualifier; just as [the river] is designated by its constant flow,
so too on this earth, even though it is constant, this [river] is described as a great wonder because it flows continuously.
"The world-system exists with the legal and social practices appropriate for the Kṛta Yuga. This might indeed be so, if [the world] were also perceived in its true form.
(Page 5)

A qualifier ought to tolerate a temporal distinction; yet it does not tolerate it, precisely because it is non-different from consciousness. Anticipating this objection, [the author] offers a rebuttal and explains the word "object" (*artha*) from the Sūtra. The word "also" (*api*) indicates that the locative case, which is being restated, functions as the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). And regarding that which is being restated...

Although the permanence of the self (*ātman*) has not been explicitly stated as a reason, it must be understood as being implied by implication for the sake of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). Otherwise, how could the worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), which resides in both [the self and the cognition], be established through the two particles *ca* and *iti* from the prima facie position regarding the experience of objects, even though that experience is of the single nature of consciousness?

One should establish this in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). And this is logical, because the conventional usage of time, which is observed even in the case of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) in the world, must necessarily be accounted for.
Therefore, having explained the two particles as indicating impossibility and so forth, [it follows that] it is indeed the experience of the object itself...
One should not be deluded into thinking that this is merely a justification for the conventional usage of time. By the word "tena" (by that), it means by consciousness;

by "te" (those), it refers to those things being experienced; and by "tathā" (thus), it means that although they are non-different from their own essential nature, they have been brought—as it were—to a state of differentiation produced through the mode of the sovereignty of consciousness. For this very reason...

Having become manifold and differentiated both from the awakening and from one another, there arises a coloring (uparāga) caused by those objects which, through their specific qualities of space and time, manifest themselves; by that cause, just as there is the "I" through inwardness as the cognizer of blue, so too does the outwardness [of the "I"] occur.
It appears; and its very nature is an outward-turned experience, namely, the cognition of blue.

In this regard, due to the sovereignty of consciousness, there is first an internal mental construction—“I shall perceive blue”—preceded by which the external blue appears. And that internal construction is preceded by [the appearance]; thus, this is like the relationship between a seed and a sprout.

Consequently, when there is the cognition of an object due to its coloring [of consciousness], both space and time as well as the cognizer and the experience are perceived as entering into that [cognition]. In this regard, all three—“I,” “the blue,” and “at that time”—appear as permeated by it, such that one thinks, “I saw the blue at that time. For this very reason, the aforementioned objection was raised regarding the inclusion of the word "object" (artha).

It subsists by being the cause [of cognition]. Now, one might ask: since those two (the object and the cognition) exist, they must embrace the consciousness that serves as their witness; what is the meaning of this? He replies: "having the object as its domain.
Furthermore, although immediately following this, the object is the domain of the cognizer, nevertheless, that very state of being an object remains.

How can that which is called "manifestness" (prakāśamānatā)— being itself non-existent— belong to that which does not enter into manifestation? Thus, manifestation [occurs] by means of this [manifestness].
It must be accepted that she does not appear by looking toward him with a form suited to pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*),
whereby she might seem to abandon the deceptive illusion (*śambara*) appropriate to time and place; rather, she appears like a courtesan,
by means of the power of illusion (*māyā*), making him look toward her own face.

He shows that even he [the opponent] cannot deny the pretext of place and time, by stating "the form of the object" (*arthākāra*); the meaning is that one should not suspect that the object has the nature of a cognizer. Furthermore, although a compound (*samāsa*) is prohibited here, it has been employed out of faith in the subject matter to be discussed; for in a compound, the meaning of the constituent members...

Just as dust, when mixed with water for the sake of its function, manifests there a turbidity consisting of that very impurity; yet this word is not entirely devoid of defining characteristics (alakṣaṇika), such that—on account of being an ungrammatical corruption (apaśabda)—it would be non-expressive, and one would have to speak of its deficiency in conveying the intended meaning. Thus he says:

"From an indicator" (*jñāpakāt*) refers to the requirement of a specific rule, such as "the agent who causes that [action] is called *hetu* because he denotes a genus" (*tatprayojako hetuśca*, Pāṇini 1.4.55). "In some cases" (*kvacit*) means in the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). "Universal" (*sārvatrika*) means that if this were universal, the prohibition in the rule "by means of *tṛc* and *aka*" (*tṛjakābhyām*, Pāṇini 2.2.15) would be rendered without scope. Now, how is it certain that this is used by the learned?

Anticipating this objection, he says: "Or [it may be] with a word ending in the suffix *tṛn*. For by means of the suffix *tṛn*, which denotes habituality (*tācchīlya*) and so forth, the term *māyāpada* would be more clearly illuminated. However, the master Īśvarācārya, in his *Vākyavārttika*, established that there is no prohibition against a genitive compound of the *śeṣa* type. This is because [the meaning] is superimposed upon the object.
The phrase "the linguistic usage of time" (*kālavyavahāra*) introduces the objection that this [notion] is to be overturned by the word "nanu" [in the following verse].
It will be stated: "Sequence depends on difference; difference, too, [arises] from the existence or non-existence of appearances" (2.1.4).
And in that context, the meaning is as follows: regarding the cases "the jar stands," "it will stand," and "it stood."

The non-interruption of manifestation within the conventional usage of time is the cause for the interruption of [the notion of] possibility; and manifestation is experience. Here, that experience is the gateway.
As long as that very [experience] is not touched by time, it remains [unified], even if it is connected with another action.

The conventional usage of time does not occur [in that case]. But here, in the act of experiencing, it is directly employed—as in "the object was previously experienced"—referring precisely to that experience itself.
(Page 7)

The primary contact with time must be stated, and through that, [the contact] of the object; however, the reverse is not logical. Time manifests as resting within the verbal suffix (tiṅanta), which expresses the action that is the very nature of the *sādhya* (that which is to be accomplished). Accepting this, he supports it by saying "it is true. Now, if...

"What has been said by us is true; however, how is it that you said: 'In cognition produced by the coloring of an object, [the factors are] place and time'? Anticipating this objection, he says "But... This is not all; there is also another distinction, which is worthy of inquiry. He shows that [distinction] with the words "of that which is without beginning or end," even though...

Experience alone is the seed for the manifestation of time; nevertheless, it is not [manifested] by means of its inward-turned nature, which is of the single form of consciousness, because in that state there is an absence of such diversity. And its outward-turned form prioritizes only the object itself, in the forms of what is to be desired, what is to be known, or what is to be done.

This is the intended meaning (*tātparya*). As for the meaning of the words (*padārtha*): for that which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), whose sole form is pure luminosity (*prakāśamātraikarūpa*), the conventional usage of "beginning" and "end" is not tenable; for if there were an absence of luminosity, such [consciousness] could not be established, and if it were established, an absence of luminosity would be impossible. As it has been said:
"But that inward-turned state which is the locus of the quality of omniscience—could its loss ever occur? No, because nothing else is perceived. (Spanda-kārikā 16).
For if that [state] were lost, perception would be impossible as it would be without an agent; therefore, its loss is indeed impossible.

If it is asked, "How can there be linguistic usage [of it], since it will be used as something other than the nature of consciousness (cittattva)?"—if it were of the nature of consciousness, how could it be other than that?

Or, if it were other, because it would not be luminous, from where would its perception proceed as having that [consciousness] as its agent? This very point he expresses by the word "eka" (one). [Objection: But surely, "I..."

It is true that there is the cognition, "I did not exist previously. However, since the body and so forth—other than the principle of consciousness (cittattva)—are not perceived [as existing independently], how could one establish the beginningless and endless nature of the principle of consciousness? Furthermore, it is not logical that the nature of consciousness should be as if indifferent, as it is in the Sāṃkhya system.
Because, by virtue of having a limited manifestation, it would follow that it is of the nature of the insentient (*jaḍa*), like blue and other such objects. As I have stated myself:
"Limited manifestation is indeed the defining characteristic of the insentient."

"Since consciousness, which is distinct from the insentient, is not measured [by anything else]" (Bodhicaryāvatāra-pañjikā 8). Thus, the state of being an unlimited light is the sovereignty in the act of shining, which is "I."
Deliberation (*vimarśa*) consists of a great intensity that is devoid of obstruction;

this alone constitutes its possession of all powers (*sarvaśaktitva*). Precisely because of this possession of all powers, the multitude of entities—which, though established within, consist of pure consciousness—becomes composed of the expansion of its own powers.

"Let it appear as if divided—both from itself and from one another—preceded by the manifestation of the contraction of its own nature. Even while manifesting in this form, because its sovereignty is unimpeded, it is called "the creator of the differentiation of entities. This is its state of being a creator.

Māyā is a power (śakti). Its domain (pada), its object (viṣaya), characterized by that which is to be fashioned, is the transmigratory world (saṃsāra) consisting of the aggregate of subjects and objects. Within that—that is, within the domain of Māyā—there is the operation of the Lord’s agency-power (kartṛśakti), which consists in the manifestation of the succession of time.

However, that manifestation does not occur within pure consciousness alone; for instance, there is a sequence of time established in worldly practice— such as "this has appeared," "it does not appear," "it appears as a single essence," or "it will appear"—
which consists of past and other states, characterized by the mutual non-coexistence of entities.
The state of being perceived is the manifestation of reality;

it is that unimpeded reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) of consciousness, and that activity consisting in the thought, "I shall manifest in this way even through this form," which constitutes its duty (*kartavya*).

Of the Supreme Lord’s power of absolute freedom, that [power] is called the Lord’s "power of time" (kāla-śakti) because it brings about the emergence of time; it is by relying upon his power of time, whose creative capacity is unimpeded, that [the universe arises].
In such passages as these, that very power of absolute freedom (svātantrya-śakti), descending by means of the series of steps on the staircase,
assumes the form "I am manifest" through this non-simultaneous manifestation consisting of the mass of subjects and objects; thus,
having established its foothold upon the mass of objects as its domain of action, it causes them to appear.

It manifests as the very nature of action in such forms as "he remembers. And that nature of action, appearing primarily, shines forth as necessarily permeated by its prior form consisting of the power of time, even when there is a clear manifestation of a subsequent form; for the prior form, which is like the life-force [of the action], must necessarily persist.

Because of its vibration; it is merely manifested as non-primary, and thus possesses the status of a qualifier due to its subordination. Therefore, that which has been brought forth by the power called Time (*kāla*) is the non-simultaneity within manifestation.

This is the sequence called "Name" (*nāmakrama*); by it, action—characterized by manifestation—is made variegated, permeated by time beginning with the primary elements (*bhūta*). Now, is it not the case that manifestation is emission (*sṛṣṭi*), the act of creation?

And how could the power of the agent be an action following a sequence of creation? This is not to be doubted, because the power of the agent itself is manifestation. For it is solely through the Lord’s absolute freedom (*svātantrya*) that entities appear. And this [power] is present in the perception of the subject under *māyā*, in instruction, and so forth.

Action is said to be that which is defined by a necessarily occurring sequence. For it is in this way that its sovereignty is defined: through the power of will (*icchāśakti*) of the Lord, who is the inner nature of the conscious self as "I," [objects] existing as things to be sought are indeed [perceived] through contemplation (*bhāvanā*).

In the venerable state of Sadāśiva, because they are clearly perceived, He desires to manifest those categories denoted by the word "That" (*tat*) as external forms, distinct from the Light itself, as "this" (*idam*).
And this desire of His is not obstructed; rather, He manifests them in that very way.

Thus, because the manifestation occurs sequentially due to the revelation of the internal and external forms as being non-simultaneous, it is called "action" (*kriyā*) at the time of its determination. And for the potter as well, this very thing is the making of the pot—namely, its manifestation as something new; and that too belongs solely to the power of the agent (*kartṛśakti*).

The manifestation of succession occurs because [the world] proceeds from a desire [to manifest] and culminates in an unimpeded external appearance. Thus he says, "nothing else," meaning that [the world appears] in this way or that way as the self of the universe consisting of the appearances of jars, cloths, and so forth. This will be explained further on.
"For one who wishes to remain [in this state], it is precisely this will that constitutes causality, agency, and action" (2.4.21). Furthermore,

even for a potter and others, this alone is the instrument— that is, the Supreme Lord’s abiding in such a manner as the nature of consciousness— and nothing else, not even the consciousness of the potter himself.

Because it is non-different from the Blessed Lord; not only does the manifestation of the characteristic of the transformation of experience occur through the power of the Supreme Lord’s consciousness as an uninterrupted "this-ness" (idantā) consisting of the cognition of the essence of ultimate "I-ness" (paramārthāhaṃtā), but even that which takes the form of memory does so.
The act of recollection (*smṛti-kriyā*) also follows this same nature; thus, "of this very [Self]" means precisely the reality of consciousness (*citta-tattva*) which possesses all powers.
Furthermore, within this [reality], both agency and the state of being an action exist through succession; he demonstrates this by saying "situated within" (*antaḥ-sthita*).

Thus, as if covered by a veil of darkness, [he remains] within— that is, established in the principle of consciousness (saṃvittattva) which is the nature of the inner self (pratyagātman), delimited by the body, the vital breath, the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), and the void—
and which was previously experienced through the "this-ness" (idantā) consisting of the prior reflection upon manifestation.

The "object" (artha) is that which is perceived; its "investigation" (vimarśa) is the clarification [of it] by dispelling darkness. The desire for that very thing is the "commencement" (upakrama), the beginning, of that which is "external. Thus, from that very contracted form of consciousness, as the knower, [the object appears] through a state of separation as a clearly perceptible object.

Since this present reflective awareness is conjoined with the reflective awareness belonging to the prior time— which is animated by the light whose nature consists of manifestation and experience— it is therefore permeated by the word "that" (sa-), even while it touches upon both times.

It manifests as having the primary character of contact with a previous time, yet its nature is not such that it does not manifest; that [manifestation] is the "conclusion" or limit of which, and thus even the act of recollection has the Blessed Lord as its agent. Therefore, with respect to the inner self (pratyagātman), the distinction between internal and external should be understood here.

But this is not with respect to Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śiva. In that regard, how could there be memory—which has a restricted object—concerning the manifestation of the universe as something externalized through the predominance of *ahantā* (I-consciousness)? That would rather be a creative emanation (*nirmāṇa*), not recollection. [Memory is] that which [pertains to] an object previously experienced...
The light is indeed primordial; it is the outward-turned nature of consciousness directed toward its object.

Even though that [light] has been obscured—as if covered by darkness—it is not "non-forgetting" (asaṃpramoṣa) in the sense of being completely lost or utterly destroyed, but rather its non-robbery through being perfectly rooted out. Now, what is this "non-forgetting"?
In this regard, having set aside the *ghañ* suffix employed by the venerable Anantabhaṭṭāraka and others, what regard is there for the *lyuṭ* suffix?

He says: "it is the operation of the agent. For this very reason, even when it is joined with the property of being established (*siddhatā*), its neuter gender is maintained because it does not discard its nature as something to be accomplished (*sādhyarūpa*).

Because it rests upon the middle term, like a word functioning as an adverb. But [an objection may be raised]: "In the general statement 'that which is its established state' (*siddhatā*), from what does this particularity of his arise? [The answer is: "From conventional usage" (*rūḍheḥ*). For even when applied to the agent, the verbal suffix—just like the suffix *-tṛ* and others—while being prescribed, [denotes] the aspect of being in the process of accomplishment (*sādhyamānatā*).

It makes [the object] predominant due to the diversity of expressive power (*śakti*). For instance, because the aspect of the action to be accomplished (*sādhyāṃśa*) is predominant in the case of indeclinable formations (*avyayakṛt*), the Supreme Teacher Patañjali has determined that when such forms are used, the object (*karma*) is expressed by the accusative case (*dvitīyā*), and so forth.

And likewise, regarding the statement "expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix," this must be analyzed as being like a substance (*dravya*) and like an action (*kriyā*), possessing a manifold variety resulting from the friction of many qualities; so, enough with these intermediate details. Now, [one might object]: [Page 11] And thus, concerning the expression "denoted by a *kṛt* suffix," this must be analyzed as being both like a substance and like an action, characterized by a manifold variety arising from the friction of numerous qualities; so, enough with these intermediate matters. Now, however—

"I remember being thin, hungry, and suffering, as well as my stout body once blessed with the enjoyments of Kashmir, my satisfaction from curd-rice, and the happiness of freedom from fear"— in such cases, it is the body and so forth that appear to be the rememberer; how then can this belong to the Blessed One according to the Sūtra and its Commentary?
The state of being a knower has been stated, and it is according to that [principle] that it is also presented in the *Ṭīkā*. He says, "For [it belongs] to the one consisting of consciousness alone.

The word "for" (*hi*) indicates that this matter serves as the reason, showing that what was previously stated is the probandum (*sādhya*), thereby highlighting the doubt of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). And the matter previously stated is as follows:
The passage beginning with "the act of recollection" (*smṛti-kriyā*) and ending with "concludes" (*avasānā*) is the remainder of the commentary on the verse.

Regarding the phrase "of that which consists of consciousness" (*cinmayasya*): even in the body and so forth, which are objects of knowledge (*vedya*), insentient (*jaḍa*), and devoid of autonomy (*svātantrya*), what kind of subjectivity (*smartṛtā*) could there be?
However, the aspect of consciousness (*cidaṃśa*) is not distinct from the Lord; this is why the word "only" (*eva*) is used. Now, [one might ask]: "Is the nature of consciousness..."

It has the nature of universal illumination and encompasses all objects; even so, how can there be recollection? For if the reality of the object consists solely in its essence being illumination, how could it be that [the object] was experienced, then concealed, and then awakened? It is said: "when autonomy is superimposed."

Because the body is absolutely distinct [from the self] due to its transformation through states, its maturation by cooking, and so forth, it cannot be the material cause by way of being the rememberer. Furthermore, even for the Void (śūnya), which transcends worldly transaction, the status of being a rememberer does not manifest;
for in the world, that [Void] is not conceived as a cognizer (pramātṛ). As for the vital breath and the city-of-eight (puryaṣṭaka), however...
Because it is indivisible from that which cannot be conceptualized (*asaṃcetya*), its continuity makes it appropriate for it to be the rememberer;

however, due to its connection with that [consciousness], even the body and so forth may appear as such a rememberer. Wherever there is superimposed autonomy—such as in the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold subtle body)—therein, while that [autonomy] exists, one assumes the nature of that [rememberer] within oneself.

By accepting [these], one brings about experience (*anubhava*), memory (*smaraṇa*), and conceptualization (*vikalpanā*), which are denoted by the terms "cognition" (*jñāna*), "recollection" (*smṛti*), and "exclusion" (*apohana*); thus, the word *vṛtti* is explained here through the use of the locative case (*saptamī*).
As for the first reading, however, it is to be disregarded because it is not the work of the Sage (*anārṣatvāt*). Now, let it be that [the body] and so forth...
He says "but not" because the states of being a rememberer, experience, latent impression (*saṃskāra*), and memory would merely be a succession of cognitions related as material cause and effect,
[and] because things exist as particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

(Page 12) This means [of those things] that are devoid of contact with objects characterized by mutual forms. By the phrase "by which," the distinction of the object was previously asserted on the basis of the relationship between cause and effect.
"Perception is indeed its own manifestation... (1.3.2).

Thus, this objection does not apply here. Therefore, the meaning is that [the author] has kept in mind precisely this absence of any occasion for raising an objection regarding a difference in objects.

"By its own [power] it moves," "by which its own [power] moves," or "its own [power] is its movement"—these expressions exclude any dependence on something external. For if the subject of Māyā were to remember, why would he not sometimes remember even that which was unconscious, and why would he remember anything else? Furthermore, [this applies to] focused attention, desire, and so forth as well.

It follows that this [cognition] is without an object; furthermore, the perception of its similarity to that [object] would not belong to it if that [object] were not remembered. And if there is no remembrance, then since everything would be similar to everything else, the restriction [that a specific cognition corresponds to a specific object] is untenable.
Thus, even in cases involving relations such as conjunction and so forth, if the object is not obtained, there can be no perception of that [relation].

It must be stated that if the object were obtained through memory alone, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). If the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) were the regulator, then the application of effort such as focused attention (*praṇidhāna*) would be useless. If it is argued that the unseen force exists only within the midst of visible causes and not independently, let it be so; nevertheless, even in the theory of difference (*bhedavāda*), [the same problem remains].
The Lord, whose nature is the principle of consciousness (*cit-tattva*), has indeed been accepted as the presiding controller of the unseen and insentient;
for it is proclaimed:
"This ignorant creature is not its own master over its own pleasure and pain."
Impelled by God, one may go either to heaven or indeed into a pit.

Thus, there is no distinction of space, time, or form within the essence of consciousness (*cittattva*); therefore, it is that Supreme Self alone which is the cause of memory. However, the manifestation [of memory] has seen and unseen causes as revealed by the power of its own necessity (*niyati*). For this very reason, its occasional irregularity is also logically established. And at the moment when one desires to remember...

He indeed knows the entry into the interior of the consciousness-principle (cittattva), which is uncontracted from the body onwards; for by this means, turning away from the region of the senses and their objects, he considers himself as having entered into a cave. Having thus entered that cave, he becomes nothing other than the nature of the Supreme Self.

Established in the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), he causes the power of sovereignty (*svātantrya-śakti*) rooted therein to shine forth and dwells in the state of the fourth (*turya*). Thence, he occupies the stage of the seed (*bīja-bhūmi*), which consists of deep sleep (*suṣupta*) and is characterized by the manifestation of objects that are completely veiled. Thence...

The manifestation of the object from the seed is its unique [function], which consists precisely of its state of existence (*sattā*); its externalized form occurs right there, within the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*) and so forth.

When, in the state of dreaming, one reflects upon that which was manifesting itself in dependence on the consciousness of the vital breath, intellect, and so forth, that is said to be "remembering. Now, an objection is raised: since that very object does not persist in the state of the seed (the latent impression), how can there be the recollection of a fixed thing? It is replied: for even there, there exists a form consisting of the desire to remember (*susmūrṣā*).
Sovereignty, which is characterized precisely by the power of will, descends [into manifestation],
because it does not transgress its own essential nature,
just as one who is entreated according to his will [acts]. (Spandakārikā 33)

Thus it has been said; likewise, will (*icchā*) is also the very sovereignty (*svātantrya*) of that [Lord]. This very point was stated by Bhaṭṭa Divākaravatsa when he sent his mind to your presence, O Great Knower (*mahājñāna*), for the sake of making known the object that had been lost: "O Great Knower, my mind has been sent into your presence so that the object may be made known."
When you demonstrate through reasoning that which is within, the Knower of Reality perceives it as your own unfolding manifestation.

Thus, the state of autonomy (*svairitva*) is observed in the case of the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*) when recollection is preceded by a consciously experienced resolve; however, even when the resolve is not consciously experienced—as in the case of [recollection] based on habitual concomitance and so forth—it must be understood as belonging to the illusory subject alone. It belongs to that very one.

And there is the designation by the word "agent" (kartṛ) in the commentary; and its oneness [is established] because it alone pervades both times. Thus, autonomy, oneness, and agency, although appearing in the primary subject of Māyā who is contracted consciousness, [belong to that same reality].
"Because they consist of the non-contracting ultimate reality-consciousness, they culminate in the nature of the Supreme Lord"—

this is what is shown in the Sūtra by the word *sahi* (for he), which refers back to the previous Sūtra [by the term] *maheśvaraḥ*, and in the Vṛtti by the word *vibhoḥ* (of the All-pervading One). Regarding this, the author of the Vivṛti says:
[This is explained] by the passage beginning with "kartṛtvaiva ca" and so forth. *Vibhutva* (pervasiveness) means existing after having become manifold;
however, here it does not mean omnipresence (*vyāpakatva*), because there is no difference in location and such [omnipresence] is useless in this context.
Now, even that which has gone to another place is remembered by means of this [present] location; how then [is this not] pervasiveness?

Non-application [of the self] occurs here. True; however, that [non-application] is a spatial distinction consisting of the self’s entry into the body and other objects of cognition. But surely, temporal distinction is likewise the same; what then is the difference? This too is true, but—
It was introduced that memory is not possible if cognitions are momentary.

And momentariness is simply a difference in time consisting of distinct moments; the Buddhist does not assert a distinction among cognitions by way of spatial extension, as one might do for a whole (*avayavin*). With this intention, he says:

The distinction between time alone has been refuted; in reality, however, space and time have entered into the body of the object of knowledge and are embraced by the memory whose object is that which is known. Even though memory appears only in the place of the body and only at the time of the body, as they say:
"...because the mind functions within the body.

Even so, for consciousness, there is in reality neither space nor even time. When there is contact with time by way of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), contact with space is likewise the same; for that very reason, [consciousness] touches all places.
The establishment of its pervasiveness is not difficult to achieve, as stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Divākara Vatsa;
for we know it precisely through the external manifestation of the sun, moon, stars, and so forth, located at distant and near places.
Having realized You, the all-pervading Lord who dwells pervading this entire universe, through the destruction of the delusion that consists in the sense of separation from one's own body;

Thus, this omnipresence (*vibhutva*) is indeed already accepted through sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). For one who is obstructed—whether by place, time, or essential nature—cannot possess the quality of being habitually, by nature, or effectively capable of ruling (*īśana*). But surely, [this belongs] to experience alone...
If memory is the non-forgetting of an object, then it would be nothing but direct experience (*anubhava*), not memory;
for a jar whose covering has been removed does not thereby become a cow. This [objection] is inconsistent.
For the very life of a cow consists in its being a distinct entity from a jar. But is this not so?

Remembrance is something entirely distinct from direct experience; rather, it is simply the re-emergence of that very experience. Even when there is such a re-emergence, why is it that one does not employ the linguistic expression "I am experiencing"?
It is said: "only [in the case of remembrance]," because for those [cognitions] in which the manifestation of that object, such as blue, has already ceased.
Of other subjects, from the omniscient one down to a mere worm, together with them,
in that [consciousness] which consists solely of the aspect of the manifestation of blue, and not in the mutual manifestations of the "I-ness" of bodies and so forth.
(page 15)

That which is oneness is the state of having the nature of mere manifestation as the appearance of blue; since that [oneness] was previously absent during the stage of perceiving yellow, its "construction" or "accomplishment" occurs by means of the prior withdrawal into unity with the subject who perceives that yellow. That itself is the "mouth," the "door," or the "means"; by that means—
When that cognizer Caitra,

by means of the cognizers Maitra and others who consist of the manifestation of the appearance of blue, [perceives] within the portion of light contracted by blue in the form: "I manifest blue," or "Blue appears to me."

One enters precisely through *sāyujya*— characterized by identity— into the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is the subject of cognition (*anubhavitṛ*) marked by the experience of blue and is the subject of *māyā*; this occurs only at that very moment,
and not into the aspect of the manifestation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and so forth, even though these too are marked by experience.

[The self] persists through prior and subsequent times. For there is no consciousness of it there [in those states] as a cognizer, nor [is it conscious] in its aspect as the Supreme Self, because that would entail the consequence of the non-appearance of duality. And this will be explained later:
"Thus, even in worldly transaction, the Lord, entering the body and so forth..."
"In this regard [it is said]: 'One may manifest externally, by will, the mass of objects already shining within' (1.6.7).

This entry of the cognizer—which consists in the manifestation of that [object] as a mere appearance—is of the nature of a novel revelation, even while his own body, vital breaths, and so forth remain stable."

Because it did not exist previously, even though it shines as a manifestation like one who has just emerged from the womb and is now born, it is not of the nature of a mere creation; for it existed previously in the form of another subject.
The word "here" (iha) indicates that this is the conceit of the experiencer. Even when there is unification with the manifestation, [it remains so].

That cognizer becomes indifferent [to worldly objects] through a forceful entry into the state of Sadāśiva and others, which is free of conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*) and perceives all manifestations without exception; thus, since the suitability for *māyā* does not arise, there occurs for the cognizer— who is intensely absorbed in bliss— the abandonment and so forth,
as well as the communication to others, by means of an object that is non-different from himself.

To that extent, there is perfection. Thus, like a rustic man wishing to depart from a hall of dance, he is favored by the doorkeeper through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), who casts him into the courtyard of *māyā*.
For therein, doubt is produced regarding something other than the desired blue—something that does not possess its nature.
Rejecting superimposition (*samāropa*) and yet esteeming only the difference (*bheda*) projected by that very rejection, he—
through a certainty whose life-breath is exclusion (*apohana*), both himself and others— by means of his own appropriate [means]...
(page 16)

Engaging in worldly discourse, one considers oneself to have accomplished one's purpose. And although that determination, which consists of the process of exclusion (*apohana*), occurs entirely subsequent to the time of direct experience (*anubhava*), nevertheless, by disregarding a slight difference in time, it manifests as if identical to that very experience, whereby—

This experience, too, is the conceit that the object is indeed distinct—namely, "I am experiencing this right now. Otherwise, every conceptual construction would be nothing but memory. If it is argued that it is thus [a memory], then when the experience has already been engaged in worldly transaction (*vyavahṛta*), the very nature of the experience to be established would not have been firmly established.

How could there be a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of this [experience] as something already accomplished, such as "I experienced"? Nor is there error in the absence of a reflective awareness of a difference in time, because a difference in time is unreal.
For we shall explain that the reality of a thing corresponds exactly to its reflective awareness. Therefore, as for what he said:
Bhaṭṭa Śaṅkaranandana, in order to refute Dharmottara’s claim that "conceptual constructions are experienced as [direct] perceptions," states:
"An established object is to be determined as being established; it is not so [determined] by that [conceptual construction]."

Thus, he shows that [the opponent's position] is outside the scope of one's own experience and is not to be accepted. One who maintains the doctrine of a continuous stream of self-luminous consciousness (*saṃvedana*) is unable to establish that it is experienced as something distinct; therefore, such a person is to be favored by this [argument], which relies on mere straw.
Let it be so. However, when one considers that experience to have been interrupted by concealment in the interim,

and then awakened again through focused concentration (*praṇidhāna*) and other means, then— due to the absence of a difference in time— one manifests a temporal diversity even though both the subject (*pramātṛ*) and the object (*prameya*) are simultaneous.

For, considering that at the time of the experience the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is centered on the object, one primarily touches upon the fact that the reflective awareness of this present time is centered on the subject, thinking: "Just as it is for you now, so too did I have the experience of blue. This very thing is called the reflective awareness "that" (*sa iti*).

The yogi, however, superimposes only the former time upon the object within his knowledge of the past, not upon the experience itself; for that [knowledge] of his touches only the time of the subject existing at that moment. But when he unites these two and conceptualizes them, then there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in the form "this is that. And in that case:

There are two types of distinction based on the restatement of one thing and the injunction of another, and two types of distinction based on the simultaneous restatement and simultaneous injunction; enough of this prolixity. It is not the case there that...

The experience of that [newly created object] is said to occur through the yoga of unprecedented creation; however, when an experience belonging to a period of creation touches upon a prior time, it is called memory. Although, in reality, the subject is characterized solely by the sovereignty consisting of the powers of experiencing, ascertaining, remembering, recognizing, and conceptualizing, [it is nevertheless designated differently according to these functions].
Nevertheless, there is no difficulty in the fact that it is designated by various names in its respective parts.

Furthermore, the word *api* (also/even) and the word *ca* (and) indicate a mutual expectancy between each successive term, suggesting that the single essence of consciousness (*cittattva*) is a continuous flow that is never exhausted. The word *tu* (but/however) [indicates a distinction].

By means of the preceding and following [statements], he illuminates the specific distinction that serves as the cause for the recollection of the middle reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). While explaining this entire commentary (*vṛtti*), he concludes with the word "that" (*tat*):
that which has been thus explained as the non-forgetting of the manifestation of what was experienced.

The connection is that he says "iti" (thus) in order to make this manifest. Here, "iti" refers to the subject of Māyā. If, however, the word "sa" (he/that) does not refer back to the preceding space and time when accepting [an object], but rather refers only to "blue" or "yellow," then that is a specific instance such as ascertainment, recollection, or recognition.

Because it is impossible for there to be a basis for designation and because there is no manifestation of anything previously unknown, it is said that conceptualization is indeed pure. Regarding the phrase "later on," [it refers to] the long, circular, vertical... (2.3.4).
For we shall establish in such passages that an entity is merely an appearance. || 1 ||

But surely, conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are without objects, because the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), being non-universal and non-productive, does not appear therein; because universals (*sāmānya*) and the like are unreal;
and because the form of the apprehended (*grāhyākāra*), which rests solely within the cognition, cannot be conceptually constructed, just like the form of the apprehender (*grāhakākāra*).

And since memory is nothing other than a specific type of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it too is devoid of an object. Furthermore, it is intended here to establish that the essence of consciousness is one, by virtue of having a single object;
for experience and memory possess a single nature of self-awareness because they are perceived as having a single object. Were they of different natures of awareness, [they would not be so].

For it is contradictory for the apprehension of a single object to have the nature of being merely distinct and self-luminous; thus, by the perception of a property incompatible with its own nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*), [the subject] is excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) because it would possess the nature of distinct cognitions.

Since that which is excluded is itself pervaded by the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) once the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established. Anticipating the objection that this [reason] is absolutely unestablished (*atyantāsiddha*) if there were no object, the Sūtra states:
"And it would manifest its own time while reflecting upon the object manifested previously."
The specific characteristic [is perceived] either as a mere appearance of a jar or in its entirety.

The word "sahi" [is taken] from the preceding sūtra; thus, it must be accepted that the Blessed Lord Maheśvara, whose nature is consciousness (cidātman), first perceives the object previously manifested and then reflects upon and conceptualizes it within memory. And when this is accepted, regarding that object—

It follows that [the cognition] refers to that object which consists of the *svalakṣaṇa*, because the *svalakṣaṇa* itself is characterized by being delimited by prior space and time, and because its essence consists in the contraction of space and time.
Furthermore, this act of referring (*parāmarśana*) is inseparable from manifestation (*prakāśana*). For if it were not manifest, what [could there be]?
It would be something grasped; for "not manifest" and "reflected upon" are contradictory terms.
Furthermore, since reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of manifestation, if that which possesses the nature were non-existent, of what could it be the nature?
[The existence of manifestation] is established either by the reason of reflective awareness or by its indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*).

The manifestation of the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is necessarily present; by implication— that is, by the force of the fact that otherwise reflective awareness (parāmarśana) would be impossible— the manifestation of the jar alone appears as manifold, either as solitary or through its association with multiple manifestations such as earthenness, height, and so forth.
Or, it is perceived as merged with all previous appearances;
and this [object] is a particular (svalakṣaṇa) due to its merger with the appearances of space and time. The word "atha" (now/then) indicates conceptual construction (vikalpa).
But if that object shines forth, what is the difference from direct experience? Who says this?

"It shines forth"—indeed, it shines forth. For that past time is the cause of its specific individuality (*svālakṣaṇya*) in the aspect of manifestation (*avabhāsāṃśa*), which accepts the object as something to be known;
and the present time, residing in the body, vital breath, and so forth of the rememberer, is the cause in the aspect of reflective awareness (*vimarśabhāga*).

This very "it-is" (*sa iti*) constitutes the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that touches upon both times. Therefore, there is no occasion for the reflective awareness of recollection by a rememberer—such as "I am," like the Blessed Lord; or "this is I," like Sadāśiva; or "this is it," in the sphere of direct experience—with respect to an object of knowledge, because [the object] has emerged as something separate.
And because it belongs to a prior time— as he said, "at its own time"— it is that which was previously manifested,
and by relinquishing its own time and its own location, it is apprehended merely as the appearance of a jar.

The word "atha" (now/then) implies that even a mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*)—distinct from memory—manifests an object whose nature is universal (*sāmānyātmaka*), while possessing the appearance of limitation (*saṃkocābhāsavān*). Thus, conceptual construction is indeed accepted in the *Avatāriṇī*. Therefore, [the object is grasped] either by way of its distinctness (*vailakṣaṇyena*) or by way of its universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇena*).

Since the state of having an object (*saviṣayatva*) exists precisely in memory, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and so forth, the reason—that it is not established that [the cognition] is without an object—remains valid:
"because of the perception of a single object. This is the meaning of the Sūtra. He introduces this briefly with the word "memory" (*smṛti*):
in the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) which is the nature of memory, that object, delimited by prior time, place, and so forth, is internal.

Even though he stands outside, having transcended the level of the senses, he is nonetheless divided from the "I" (ahantā) by virtue of being distinct from the aspect of consciousness; therefore, the object which is to be grasped through the form of "that" (tad) becomes manifest solely through its own power— that is, precisely because it would otherwise be impossible for such a reflective awareness to occur.

Furthermore, at the moment of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) regarding the form of a pure conceptualization, there is the indication "this" (*idam*) of that which is to be pointed out, without being delimited by previous space and time;
and by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," this applies accordingly even to conceptualizations such as recognition, imagination, and determination, where there is the [awareness] "that" and "this."

The state of being demonstrable—as "this is that," "that is like this," or "this is indeed that"—should be understood as existing on both sides; moreover, the delimitations of space and time are diverse, having those two as their primary aspects. The phrase "by way of a fixed form" means by way of necessity; for in memory, the connection with the previous place and time necessarily flashes forth.

Otherwise, that would be a mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and not memory. Furthermore, in the manifestation of that [object], whether it be a single appearance or a cluster of appearances, there is nothing other than the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); thus, it is established that in memory there is indeed a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the particular characteristic itself. For [memory] is [of the form] "that."

In the commentary (*vṛtti*), it is stated "by the power of memory" (*smṛtiśaktyā*) to indicate that the state of being a rememberer (*smartṛtā*) from the preceding sūtra is carried over (*anuvṛtta*). To establish the manifestation of the object by means of the cause, which is the established reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), he says "and [it] has the nature of light" (*prakāśasvabhāvaśca*). Here, the word "and" (*ca*) functions as a conjunction (*samuccaya*).

By indicating the invariable concomitance (*nāntarīyakatā*) of the probandum with respect to the reason, [the statement] rests upon the relationship of cause and effect. Whatever object is the content of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), that necessarily has manifestation (*prakāśa*). For that reflective awareness is a property whose very nature consists in manifestation; in the absence of manifestation, it would not exist.
How could it be without support? For just as the impermanence of that which is produced is its very nature, so it is with impermanence.

When that which appears is manifest, it does not occur [to one] that "the appearance is fabricated"; likewise, when there is reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), the light (*prakāśa*) is manifest. For if the possessor of the nature were absent, how could it be said that "this is the nature of this"? Consequently, the state of being without nature (*asvabhāvatva*), which is contradictory to the state of having the form of a nature, would ensue.

Out of fear of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving what is contradictory to its own nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*), the property of being that very nature (*svabhāvatva*)—which is excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) where that nature does not appear—is pervasive of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). When this [nature] enters into the appearance of that nature, it causes the reflective awareness, which is pervaded by itself, to enter into that very same [appearance]. And it is not...

It would be more logical to say that reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is the very nature of non-awareness itself; for in that case, memory, conceptual construction, and so forth, would—like blue and other objects—be non-self-luminous (*asvaprakāśa*). Therefore, reflective awareness is the nature of awareness alone, and awareness is essentially luminosity (*prakāśātman*). Thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) regarding the object.
Apprehension (*parāmarśa*) is of the nature of light (*prakāśa*), because its essence is that very [light]. "For this very reason" means because there is no dispute [on this point].

Although verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) denote objects such as the state of being (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), the agent (*kartṛ*), number, and so forth, nevertheless, by the rule "one expresses the state of being (*bhāva*) through the verb," the meaning of the root possesses the character of something to be accomplished (*sādhyarūpatā*).

By predominating and becoming intensified, they [the suffixes] become thus; therefore, for them, action alone is the primary denotation. Furthermore, in the case of an injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) being prescribed makes known the injunction and other such factors which serve as adjuncts (*upādhi*) to the meaning of the verbal root.

Even their status as conditions (upādhi) such as the object of a suffix, the agent, or the object of an action occurs only by way of being conditions for the meaning of the verbal root, because they are connected to the causal power (kāraka-śakti); however, for a substance that is entirely partless, a connection with other attributes such as knowledge and so forth is not possible in itself. Therefore—

He shows that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is the predominance of the state of being accomplished, which belongs to the meaning of the verbal root as conditioned by an injunction, in the phrase "characterized by the instrumentality of the mandate" (*niyogakaraṇalakṣaṇa*).

That is to say, its definition or essential nature is that state of being accomplished (*sādhyamānatva*) which is brought about through the mandate—that is, through the necessary constraint (*niyama*). This applies even to that which takes the form of a command (*ājñā*).
The very essence of an injunction (*niyoga*) consists in making known the intention to exclude the possibility of acting otherwise, precisely by way of its restrictive nature (*niyama-rūpatā*).
For knowledge (*ājñāna*) is indeed the communication of a boundary (*maryādā*); one who knows the boundary oneself [communicates it] to another.

One who, for the sake of another, brings about the cognition of that [object] is said to "command. For in the case of the injunction, "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra*," this [cognition] belongs to the one desiring heaven.
(Page 21)
The restriction is that one must indeed perform the oblation; for otherwise, he would not truly be one who desires heaven.
Indeed, a capable person who does not employ the prescribed regimen, even if excluded by the scripture, is not in reality one who desires health. This applies to desire as well.

The meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is that one who desires that sequence of effects— beginning with the performance of effort and so forth, each succeeding one following the previous— must necessarily come to be, should indeed employ what is wholesome. Even in the case of the phrase "as long as life lasts," if the meaning were merely that "one performs the oblation," there would be no one desiring the avoidance of sin (*pratyavāya*).

Even on the view that the mandate (niyoga) does not suffer the wretchedness of requiring a result, its very nature as a Brāhmaṇa qualified by lifelong [performance] would be lost if he were not to sacrifice; therefore,
the essence of the mandate consists precisely in the communication of the restriction itself, namely, "he must indeed sacrifice."
And although the optative suffix (*liṅ*) lacks the capacity to manifest a specific time, nevertheless,
because an injunction cannot be joined with [past or future] time due to the action, and because it is not expressed through a distinction of agent or place,
it appears as having contact with the eternally occurring present. Nor does this much imply that it is beyond the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In the case of the pervasion expressed as "where there is smoke, there is fire," even though it begins without qualification and does not touch upon a difference in time, the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) arising from perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) is manifested. In exactly the same way,
one perceives someone desiring health who is engaged in the consumption of wholesome diet, [observing] the manifestation of place, time, and agent—

One understands the causal relationship between the desire for that [object] and its necessary accomplishment by means of the exclusion of other specific alternatives; enough with this digression. Now, if that object indeed manifests in memory, then it must be a direct experience (*anubhava*) itself, and not memory.

Not so; for at that time it is the Light itself that shines, while the expression "it shines" belongs to the empirical experience. Although there is no connection with time within the Light, nevertheless, that Light, when infused into the objects of knowledge, the body, and so forth, appears in the realm of Māyā as if conforming to them.

Because it coexists with past and present bodies and so forth, it partakes in the status of being an object of the conventional designations "past" and "present. This light, which consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) pertaining to the remembered object and coexisted with the previous body and so forth, appears as indistinct to those who identify with the body as the subject (*pramātṛ*).

It attains the status of being an object of conceit; however, because it exists with clarity, resting upon the adjunct of the present body, it is the second present reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and for this reason it is designated by that very term.
(Page 22)
"Memory is conceptualization (vikalpa). For it will be stated that conceptualization is indeed a specific kind of reflective awareness (vimarśa).

This very point he expresses with the words "merely," and so forth. Words such as "mere" (*kevala*) and "supreme" (*para*), by means of this restrictive property (*niyamadharmena*)—namely, that "this much more must necessarily be accepted here"—[function] within the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) which has become a substantive entity (*sattvabhūta*).

Those things which attain the status of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇatām*)— being subject to the usage of gender, number, pronouns, the neuter, and the singular— should be understood as standing in the nominative case (*prathamāntā*); or else, even the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārthaḥ*) is indeed an action (*kriyā*), [since it is characterized] by qualifiers such as the factors of action (*kāraka*).

In the expression *rūṣita-śarīra* ("one whose body is smeared"), even when the action (*kriyā*) is either explicitly heard or merely supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhṛta*), the words ending in the accusative case function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). This is because the action is established by its very power (*śakti*) as that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Furthermore, even in the case of [the action being expressed as] an object (*karman*), it is impossible for there to be any grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of that [object] within the verb (*ākhyāta*).

When the qualifiers themselves express an entity that has become a sentient being (*sattvabhūta*), the second case ending occurs because the linguistic impression (*saṃskāra*) of that [sentient being] is transferred to them. Furthermore, the connection with number, gender, and pronouns occurs when the referent is a sentient being.
However, speech was initiated by the wise who maintain that the resting point (*viśrānti*) of a referent that has become a sentient being is logically established.
Regarding the rule that adverbs possess the status of an object (*karmatva*), and so forth: he says this;

that which was explained—that there is necessarily a manifestation (*prakāśa*) of what has been experienced, and that manifestation occurs precisely as having been previously manifested—is stated by the author of the *Vṛtti* through this passage, otherwise...

Thus, there would be no manifestation. Since it has already been manifested previously, how could there be a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that is not attached to that manifestation? And if there were no reflective awareness by way of its having been manifested previously, then the reflective awareness of a past manifestation as "that" (*saḥ*) would not exist. Therefore...

Regarding the phrase "of that which has been manifested" (*prakāśitasya*) in the commentary (*vṛtti*), emphasis must be placed on both the meaning of the base word (*prakṛtyartha*) and the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*). Furthermore, the fact that the past object is appropriated by the suffix and exists only at the time of its own manifestation has been made clear in the commentary by the statement, "and only at the very time of its own existence. Therefore, the construction of the commentary is: "it causes [the object] to appear precisely at the time of recollection. Now, one might object:
Anticipating the objection that this has not been stated by ancient masters such as the venerable Patañjali and others, he says:

"And this very [consciousness]... That which was established as the internal light within present reflective awareness (*vimarśana*), precisely because it has already been previously manifested and examined, is that very same [light] of the experienced object.
Non-forgetfulness is said to be non-deprivation. For here, past experience is described as the manifestation of the object, and non-forgetfulness is that which pertains to the present.
Likewise, there is no re-apprehension [of it]. Now, since manifestation is devoid of connection with time, how can there be "pastness"?
To this he says: "and the state of having been manifested previously. For in that place, yesterday, being thirsty, I saw this jar—along with that friend—in its unrefined form.
Thus, by means of limiting adjuncts such as space and so forth, light is delimited through the states of being aggregated or separated.

And in the realm of *māyā*, there is no functioning of memory. Indeed, the very contraction of the form of light due to limiting adjuncts constitutes the realm of *māyā*. This stated meaning is expressed by the word "by that" (*tena*) in the commentary regarding the matter to be explained.

First, it establishes [the preceding] as the reason (*hetutām*). He explains the word "by that" (*tena*) with the phrase "therefore" (*tadevam*); the meaning is: "for that reason," namely, for what was stated.

He clarifies what was stated by saying "otherwise" (*anyathā*), which refers to the fruitlessness of the investigation due to its lack of utility. In that case, the establishment [of the point] is the reason, and the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) is the reason for the establishment.

Regarding the phrase "as a cause": for indeed, there is no fault in memory with respect to destruction by virtue of its object, nor is there any deficiency with respect to its existence—this is the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of both the *Vṛtti* and the *Ṭīkā*. Having thus stated the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of memory, he clarifies that very nature with the words "by this much" (*etāvatā*). Therefore, there is not even the slightest deficiency in the object of cognition (*prameya*).
This means that its status as memory is logically established. When the previous manifestation of the object does not re-emerge—

that is, when there is no reflective awareness (*aparāmarśa*) of it as having been previously illumined— then that specific cognition which pertains to the mere object as delimited by a past experience is indeed a fresh experience.
This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: "What is this 'yoga'? It is that whose [subject] possesses yoga with the ultimate subject (*paramārthapramātṛ*).

They maintain that yoga is the oneness [of the individual] with the state of being submerged in the reality of the ultimate subject, wherein the portion of the *māyā*-subject has ceased to exist. (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra 4.4)

Thus is the yogin described in the scripture. For him, all objects, being identical with his own self which is untouched by time, are such that they are either manifested as "I" alone, or are fit to appear as "I am this. In that case, how is there the manifestation of only some [objects], and how...

Anticipating the objection that it [the object] is qualified by a prior time, he says "yasya" (of which). The word *hi* indicates the reason and suggests the doubt; for in its absence, there would be no one to provide the justification, and thus the supporting reason would result in being useless. Therefore, in this context, sequence itself consists of both the appearance and the non-appearance.
Time. In that regard, there is the manifestation and non-manifestation of the body through its difference at every moment.
(Page 24)
And it flows incessantly at every moment, bestowing a constant differentiation of time. Therefore,
for those who identify as embodied subjects, and whose acts of perception depend primarily on the external senses attached to that [body], [the sense of time] becomes exceedingly firm.

"By the principle that for those bound by the chains of time, only what is connected and present is perceived... there is not even the slightest capacity to perceive past and future time. But when..."

Due to the appearance of a specific instruction regarding higher discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), one attenuates the conceit of being a limited subject (*pramātṛtābhimāna*) within the body; at that time,
although there is necessarily an absolute temporal distinction of the body because its distinctness is incessantly manifest, even so—

Although this [consciousness] flows forth, nevertheless, because it still possesses the nature of an object of cognition (*vedyarūpatva*), its identification with the subject (*pramātṛtābhimāna*) remains clearly manifest within the *puryaṣṭaka*, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), or the void (*śūnya*), all of which are composed of *māyā* and dominated by non-recognition (*akhyāti*). And although, in that state,
a distinction of stages produced by time cannot occur as clearly as it does in the case of the body, nevertheless—
Due to the uninterrupted persistence of the conceit (*abhimāna*) that identifies with the body and its adjuncts (*sahakārin*), a certain conditioned (*aupādhika*) differentiation manifests.
Consequently, there arises in this [self] the recollection of objects previously experienced;
yet, this [recollection] is rendered difficult by the conceit of a dense veil consisting of the identification with the body as the self.

By the power— that is, the capacity— of that yoga which consists of meditation (dhyāna) preceded by concentration (dhāraṇā), directed toward some specific aspect [of consciousness], [consciousness] which resides within the coverings of the body, senses, vital breath, intellect, and the void, like the light of the sun obscured by pure autumn clouds, [is made manifest].

The manifestation of one's own nature— which is characterized by the state of being free from obscuration and which attains illumination through the stage of meditative absorption— experiences that object as a truly unprecedented appearance; and because it is associated with what was previously remembered, it experiences it precisely as "prior," even though for that very reason it is not subject to recollection.
[The opponent argues: "By means of the direct realization of *saṃskāra*s and so forth, one [remembers] previous births.

But surely this counter-example is deficient in a limb regarding memory, because the factor of the awakening of the previous experience is absent. For the nature of memory is its being permeated by verbal expression (*śabdārūṣitatva*)."
And that [memory] is not present here, because the yogic perception is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*). True;

however, even though the coloring by words (*śabdārūṣaṇa*) exists, there is an absence of memory-character in independent conceptualization (*svatantra-vikalpa*) precisely because the previous experience does not appear. Therefore, it is likewise logical even when the object has been mentioned.
