"It determines the previous experience," and so forth. "By its own will" means that which arises spontaneously from the mind because distraction is its very essence. (Page 25)

According to this principle, there is no recollection of a prior experience in that case. And when his father is indeed a king in reality, and this is not merely understood through scripture— [rather] arising by chance (*kākatālīyena*) from among false conceptualizations due to the force of distraction— even while within the midst of conceptualization, then:
This example is complete; however, if [the object] is understood through scripture (*āgama*), it is merely a case of recollection (*smaraṇa*).

Furthermore, if the object were non-existent, how could its connection with other omniscient cognizers existing at that time—such as their possession of existence and so forth—be logically established? Thus, he refutes the status of recollection regarding the two aforementioned examples.

At that time, for those cognizers— whether they be omniscient or even worldly beings— who perceive and reflect upon that object as something unprecedented through other means of knowledge such as inference or scripture, there exists, in that particular aspect, a manifestation of their cognition along with that [object].

By the will of the Blessed One, he becomes one. However, the distinction is this: in the case of recollection, that manifestation of knowledge belonging to previous subjects—which had become merged with the recollector’s own prior experience—now emerges. He concludes this with the words "therefore," [referring to] its non-emergence.

Because the absence of memory has already been demonstrated: in the case of memory, where there is the reawakening of a prior experience, it would follow as an absurd consequence that it takes the form of direct perception or independent conceptualization— states which are pervaded by the absence of memory, being the opposite of memory.

By the perception of the pervasion of the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), the reason is excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) and is pervaded by the probandum, which is the state of possessing that manifestation; thus, in the establishment of the pervasion, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Having thus explained the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the verse up to the words "it is not thus faulty."
He explains the commentary on the portion of the sūtra ending with "merely by the appearance of the jar" (ghaṭābhāsamātreṇa), which extends up to the word "manifestation" (avabhāsa),

in the passage beginning with "and because of desire" (arthitvācca). "Complete enjoyment" (ā-samantād bhogaḥ) belongs to the state of consciousness (cidbhāva) which is submerged in the midst of the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of infinite objects that have been swallowed up within other acts of perception.
The operation of chewing, which consists of preservation and has the nature of opening [the eyes], is essentially seeking;

while "fullness" (ābhoga) is the application of attention characterized by a continuous stream of thought. To the extent that one possesses desire for an object, to that same extent one remembers it, just as one who desires to fetch water with an earthen jar [remembers its utility].
Even a golden jar, which was easy to find in the royal palace and had been seen since childhood, now [seems like] its maker merely by virtue of its broad base and belly-shaped form.
He remembers; just as a scholar who has completed his studies,
disregarding the endless grammatical derivations taught by his teacher Khaṇḍika, remembers only the correctness (*sādhutva*) of the word "brāhmaṇa" by that much alone.

Because it ensures the successful accomplishment of the intended application; whereas, on the contrary, resorting to the recollection of something else would only serve as an obstacle to the composition of continuous Sanskrit speech refined by the constant flow of the Ganges that one had intended. Thus he says: "according to its utility. And the universal (sāmānya) has the nature of a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).

By casting aside its pervasiveness and eternity, it is extended through space and time alone; thus, because a single manifestation— being a mere superimposition— is devoid of contact with other manifestations,
it is said to be "indistinct" due to its deficiency in accomplishing full purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), as follows:

In deep darkness, [one perceives] "this is something" from afar; this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which is conceived through the principle of memory (*smṛtitattva*), is indicated in the Sūtra by the word *atha*. He now explains it in this very context, in connection with the discussion on the limitation of manifestation (*ābhāsapārimitya*), as "the previous place, time, and so forth."
By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), he also indicates the absence of delimitation by present or future space and time.

With the intention that such a distinction between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not established elsewhere, he provides the reason here with the words "for the universals themselves" (*sāmānyānyeva hi*). [The phrase] "having come together" (*saṃbhūya*)...

Having become mutually intermingled; and not by way of the principle of coordinate terms in a *dvandva* compound—that is, with equal status—but rather through a reciprocal relationship of qualifier and qualified, meaning by way of alternating primary and subordinate status. For instance, when there is a desire for concealment, it is "cloth-ness" [that functions as the primary].

The primary element is [the substance], while whiteness and so forth are the delimiters (*avacchedaka*). When the desire for clarity of mind is intended, whiteness is the delimited (*avacchedya*), while the other [qualities] are qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*);

thus, although there is a mutual delimitation through these synonyms, the expression "mutual delimitation" is used with the intention of referring to that collection as a whole. Furthermore, there is simultaneous delimitation.
The helper [states]: Even though "jar" and "redness" are pervasive, they are restricted by space and time through mutual exclusion.
Thus it has been said that a single particular (svalakṣaṇa) is composed of many universals combined.
Regarding this, someone objects: "But in that case, the *dhava*, the *khadira*, and the *palāśa* would indeed be distinct [entities]."
Regarding the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), [the question is]: "How is there a single cognition (*ekabuddhi*) such as 'tree' in that regard? In response to that, he says: "Even so...
By the mention of color and shape, he indicates [the inclusion of] taste, potency, touch, and so forth.
(Page 27)
The essential nature of the *dhava* tree and so forth has been stated, and their internal distinctions have also been indicated. Now, an objection may be raised:

"An object is nothing but a manifestation (*ābhāsa*). And that manifestation strives for the state of being manifest (*prakāśamattva*). Furthermore, manifestation has reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) as its very life. And in the realm of *māyā*, reflective awareness consists of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) with respect to each individual manifestation."
Because sound has speech alone as its sole body, it rests upon every individual manifestation through the application of linguistic convention.

Therefore, how could that which is called a "particular" (*svalakṣaṇa*) ever manifest? True; this is indeed a refutation of other systems, for even the manifestation of non-conceptual [perception] is made an object of practical activity only by means of conceptualization.

Because [in other systems] there is such an approach, but here it is not so, he shows by means of the words "by itself" (*svayam*) and so forth. It is the universals (*sāmānya*) themselves that attain the state of infinite particularities (*ananta-svalakṣaṇa*). And the reason for this is their mutual difference and, alternatively, their mutual exclusion (*anyonyāvaccheda*). For instance, existence (*sattā*) itself is substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karma*); for existence is...

It is distinct from substance-ness and the rest, and they [substance-ness, etc. are distinct from it; there is mutual delimitation such that "existent" is substance and "existent" is quality. Furthermore, the appearances of space and time are not the essential nature of an entity, as the Buddhists maintain—that an entity is merely contracted in nature—but on the contrary, its very nature is expanded.

An entity is expressed through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). However, limitation (*saṃkoca*) is manifested by the union of another commonality of spatial appearance and a commonality of temporal appearance. Furthermore, because those two—spatial and temporal appearances—are delimited by that [entity], they constitute limitation; thus it is brought about by the six flavors (*ṣaḍrasa*).

Just as in a beverage, through the mutual restriction of their potencies, there arises a flavor such as the unprecedented *ṣāḍava* and others, so too here, the arising of the appearance of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) occurs; thus, even through simultaneity, mutual delimitation is beneficial. And just as in the case of flavor, the activity of a skilled cook is primarily instrumental, [so too is the activity of the senses].
Likewise, O Blessed One, when a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) arises, there is a power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) which governs everything.

For if that were transgressed, everything would indeed be full from every perspective; let that suffice for now. In this same way, one should also consider such cases as "the jar is a substance," "the cloth is a substance," and "the jar is gross. In that regard:
And indeed, manifestation—which consists of synthesis—is alive only through the reflective awareness of the sentence regarding the particular (svalakṣaṇa). Now, one might object:
"In that case, how is it that the two universals—the appearance as 'jar' and the appearance as 'cloth'—do not, when combined, give rise to a single particular? He replies:

(Page 28) "Precisely by way of conformity" means that it is indeed the majesty of the Supreme Lord’s power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) that operates in the merging of appearances, and not its own inherent majesty. And this is just as in the case of "being a *dhava* tree" and "being a tree."

"The mutual blending [of two things] does not occur between the properties of being a *dhava* tree and being a *khadira* tree; thus, O Blessed One, destiny (*niyati*) manifests even in what is purposeless. Likewise, there is also a rule of non-deviation in certain cases," he says with the words "and something else.
This refers to another manifestation (*ābhāsāntara*) that is perceived as distinct from the other.

Even though it is not specified as such, it is clearly a universal (*sāmānya*) because it manifests in its own pure form; for its nature, although it is a single essence consisting of the form of a universal,
is composed of multiple universals and does not deviate from being multiple universals, just as follows:
The generality of *dhava*-ness does not deviate from existence (*sattva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), earthiness (*pārthivatva*), and tree-ness (*vṛkṣatva*);

therefore, it should be understood that in relation to those [higher generalities], existence and the others are indeed more manifest, each preceding one being less manifest than the succeeding one. But if this is so, then...
It would indeed be the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) because of its clarity. He says, "But [it is] generality" (*sāmānyatām tu*).

This word *sāmānya* is an unanalyzed term meaning "common," and not one ending in an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). [Reply: An abstract suffix is indeed appropriate here. And by means of the abstract suffix, in its own...

Regarding the object to be expressed, the ground for the application of a general term is that single characteristic of universals which consists in being the cause of a single cognition across multiple instances; even though this inheres in many, that which is impossible [for other things] to produce such a cognition is said to be "inhering in the general terms for the many."

Alternatively, it is the genus of word (*śabdajāti*), characterized by being a general term, which—by coloring the word itself—also colors its denoted object; for that object denoted by the word is made to assume its own form (*svarūpīkriyate*) by looking toward the face of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and not otherwise. This is also the case with genera (*jāti*).

When universals are created as distinct and independent entities, another universal certainly exists within them, just as there is a further internal distinction within conceptual constructs such as the "self" (*ātman*). Thus said the venerable [author]:
"Or, a universal may be a property of recurrence (*anupravṛtti-dharma*) among all universals" (Vākyapadīya 3.14).
Thus, it is said:
"In that which is a part of a genus-word, that [genus] is intended as the genus of genera" (Vākyapadīya 3.9).

(Page 29) Even when there is the denotation of a meaning-genus (*arthajāti*), all [words] denote a genus, because word-meanings are established as being characterized by activity (*vyāpāra*). (Vākya-padīya 2.11)

And thus: the reason for generality is space and time. Here, even that single manifestation which is grasped as "now" is called a particular (svalakṣaṇa) because it is contracted through the exclusion of the characteristics of generality—namely, its nature as pervasive and eternal; [it is thought] "this is existent here. And yet, by that much alone...

It will be stated that purposeful action, such as the avoidance of the heart's breaking [from grief], certainly occurs; likewise, regarding the "substance of a real jar" (*saddhaṭadravya*)... [as stated] in [verse] 2.3.5.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the term "jar-appearance" (*ghaṭābhāsa*) in the aphorism (*sūtra*) is intended to indicate all appearances in general.

The rest has been explained by one [of the] words. In the sūtra, "by the whole self" (*akhilātmanā*), there is an indication of many appearances. Whether the appearance is incomplete or complete, the commentary states "but at other times" (*anyadā tu*) in order to explain that state of incomplete appearance. He explains that [statement].

Regarding the phrase "But when": the commentary states that "excellence" (*atiśaya*) refers to the manifestation of the totality of appearances. He explains this with the words "at times": when an object was previously manifested in its fullness through as many appearances as were present at the moment of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*), it is remembered by means of exactly those same [appearances]. What need is there for further elaboration?

The thought, "I am now seeing this and reflecting upon it"— this appearance as well is included among the qualifiers; by that [appearance] also, at that time, [the object] exists right before the perceiver (*puraḥ*) in the present space and time, precisely as having that [present] space and time.

That object flashes forth precisely as it was touched upon (*ācchurita*) and as it existed at that particular place and time, such that the realization arises: "Right now, right here, I am seeing this very thing. By this, "making present" (*pratyakṣīkāra*) is explained.
For that which is not directly perceived but is being remembered, there is a semblance of direct perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*) because it has been touched upon.

This means that there is a suppression of the state of being remembered, even though that state exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*). For this very reason, the Blessed Patañjali stated that memory is "to be recollected" (*smartavyā*); it is "cultivated" (*bhāvita*)—meaning it has been brought into being—and it is "to be recollected."

"An object, even though it does not exist [in the present], is said to be 'in this' because it is capable of being remembered. It "interposes" (*antarayati*), meaning it makes something "with an interval" (*sāntara*).

Here, "interval" (*antara*) refers to a heterogeneous element, namely impurity (*mala*); the absence of that is "continuity" (*nairantarya*). Now, at that time— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "nanu tadānīṃ sa-". The translation reflects the available portion.)

To the question, "How can there be the nature of memory (*smṛti*) in the absence of such reflective awareness (*avimarśa*? he says: "At that time, not [as a new perception], but precisely as previously seen.

For this [memory] is not an illumination of a new object like the knowledge of a yogi, because of the absence of identification with the nature of the present subject (*pramātṛ*). It is precisely [an awareness] of what was previously seen.

Being accompanied by reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it has now descended to the plane of present reflective awareness and is thus said to be "with" (*sa-iti*) reflective awareness; therefore, its presence here is indeed necessary. However, because it is intensified through the process of creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*), only the aspect of luminosity (*prakāśa*) is clearly manifest here, while the reflective awareness, though existing, remains suppressed. Therefore, it is said:
"When the memory of linguistic conventions is purified, [the state] in which there is only the object, as if devoid of its own form, is *nirvitarka* (Yoga Sūtra 1.43).

Therefore, when a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises from spontaneous self-reflection (*sahajavimarśa*), there is the reflective awareness "this" (*sa-iti*). This is all the more so [in the case of the higher states].
The meaning is that even the aspect of experience (anubhavāṃśa) is designated as "seen" because it is not lost due to its manifestation (sphuraṇa).
For in that case, although memory and experience share a single self-reflexive awareness, memory [arises] because the aspect of experience is predominant. Now, as indicated by the Sūtra:

In order to explain clarity even within independent conceptualization (*svatantra-vikalpa*), he applies this very commentary [beginning with] "even in the independent" (*svatantre 'pi*). That which is purified by whatever means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— whether mixed or solitary— that has as its object various properties (*dharma*) and property-bearers (*dharmin*), such as inference, scripture, and so forth, as being true...

Having entered the heart, [the yogin] is not like an objective appearance (arthābhāsa) characterized by many qualifiers— which is grasped by conceptual constructions (vikalpa) produced by desire, grief, and so forth— but is rather directed toward Brahman and the like, solely intent upon making it manifest.

By this, the term *dṛṣṭārtha* (perceived object) has been explained. This was stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa in his commentaries on the *Śivasūtras*, namely the *Madhuvāhinī* and the *Tattvārthacintāmaṇi*. Now, it has been said that the perception of a yogin is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpaka*).
"...that clear conceptual cognition (*kalpadhī*) is the fruit.

To the question, "How then is it said to be conceptual (*vikalpatā*)," he says: "And then," [meaning] it is *savitarka* (accompanied by deliberation), being intermingled with conceptualizations of words, objects, and cognitions; [this occurs] when memory is purified.
"Non-discursive [samādhi] is that which is devoid of its own form and consists of the object alone" (Yoga Sūtra 1.42).
According to this principle, the word "or" (*vā*) here does not denote doubt, but rather an alternative possibility. Now, when...

If [it is argued that] there is non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpakatā*), then how could even an independent conceptualization (*svatantra-vikalpa*) be expressed? To this he says: "It is intensely cultivated in the prior state. Since the possibility of conceptualization exists in this [state], which is the fruit of the perfection of cultivation (*bhāvanā-pariniṣpatti*), there is no fault. But [an objection may be raised]: "However..."

Having raised the doubt—namely, how it is that the manifestation of objects, which was established by the statement in the Sūtra "one who reflects" (*parāmṛśan*)—is justified through the necessity of reflection (*parāmarśa*) since non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpakatva*) is absent—he says:
"But [there would be] a voidness of reflection. For reflection...

It will be stated that when there is a connection with the cause for dispelling the suspicion of a counter-correlate, there is a specific nature consisting of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); [this is] the appearance of that and not-that... (1.6.3).

In such passages [as these], there is no absence of the universal when there is no absence of the particular. But if it does exist, what then is the proof for it? He says: "Because of identity" (*tādātmyāt*).
They know that the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of manifestation; otherwise, [it would be nothing]. (1.5.11)
For this will indeed be explained in detail later. Now, one might object: "It should be stated in both the Sūtra and the Vṛtti that 'the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) appears through memory';
why then employ the causative suffix (ṇic), which creates verbal prolixity, and the resulting forms such as *ābhāsitam*?"

Anticipating the objection that this is merely an effort to explain the meaning of the causal suffix (*ṇic*), he says: "And everywhere... The sovereignty of the *cittattva* itself—which consists of internal self-awareness—manifests in the concealment of one form, the assumption of another form, and in the joining and separating thereof. As for that which [arises] from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)...

The view of those who maintain a dry (i.e., purely mechanical) theory of cause and effect— that a subsequent cognition arises from a preceding one assisted by an object or its latent impression (*vāsanā*)— is untenable, as has been demonstrated by the use of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Furthermore, because it is a portion of the sūtra phrase "pūrvābhāsitaṃ" (manifested by the preceding), the meaning of the causative suffix must also be explained.

The [root] was recited previously; thereafter, that which is formed with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) by the author of the *Vṛtti* was given. Since the usage of the Vedic (*sautra*) *ṇic* is explained by that very same [causative form], it was not recited separately. However, because it serves to explain the meaning of the *ṇic* found in the *Vṛtti*, it was recited as a distinct section in the form "of that which has been manifested" (*prakāśitasya*). || 2 ||
(Page 32) Now,

lest the act of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) be like "blind men’s guesses," it is admitted that even in memory there is a manifestation of the object; and therefore, the remembered object is [manifest] just as if it were being directly experienced.

One might object: "Why can this [external object] not be treated as external? For the cause for its treatment as such is the manifestation of that object, and that [manifestation] exists in its entirety. Anticipating this, he says:
"And it is not logical that the remembered object should appear [as if present] when there is a difference from the memory."
Therefore, he is that cognizer who unifies cognitions occurring at different times. (3)

The manifestation of the object being remembered does not belong to the present; rather, it is precisely that which is prior. Furthermore, that prior manifestation is subordinated within the conscious experience characterized as memory by making the present form of reflective awareness (vimarśa) primary.

It appears as nothing other than non-differentiated manifestation, not as differentiated. Consequently, in memory, the light (*prakāśa*) regarding its own subjective aspect (*svātmāṃśa*) is accompanied by reflective awareness (*savimarśa*) and is indeed unconditioned by time. However, regarding the objective aspect (*arthāṃśa*), the light is precisely that which was previously [perceived]. As for the subsequent reflective awareness, it is accompanied by the reflective awareness that is inseparable from that [original perception].

[The object] is present [to consciousness] now. Thus, that which is being remembered appears by means of the manifestation of its prior experience; otherwise, its appearance would be appropriate as something being experienced independently, rather than as something being remembered. Therefore, just as in the cognition of an experience...

Although an object is not separate from the Light, by the power of *māyā* it appears as if separate to the subject under the influence of *māyā*; this is not the case in the cognition of memory, for there that very former conceit of separate existence and manifestation persists. Therefore, there is a distinct manifestation.
One should not raise the objection, "Why does this not apply to memory?

For, as an incidental corollary to the removal of that very fault, the present subject is also established by way of an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (a conclusion established by the context); thus he says, "Therefore. As it was stated:

In memory, the manifestation of the experience exists as its permeating factor, and the object exists through its non-difference from that manifestation of the experience; for this reason, the following is also established:
[the distinction] between the manifestations of the body, vital breath, and so forth, according to whether they are clear or unclear.

And because it possesses a manifest nature that is fully realized, consciousness (*saṃvit*)— which, through its association with the limitations of those adjuncts (*upādhi*), assumes the forms of present, past, and future— is likewise metaphorically attributed with distinctions of time such as the present and so forth.

Furthermore, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is indeed only oneness. And even though this oneness exists everywhere, to whatever extent that cognizer (*pramātṛ*) perceives oneness through the majesty of his own innate freedom (*svātantrya*), to that same extent does it manifest, just as in the case of memory and direct experience. For this alone constitutes the state of being a knower (*saṃveditṛtva*) which exceeds mere consciousness (*saṃvedana*).
"Freedom (*svācchandyam*) in the conjunction and disjunction of cognitions.

That very sovereignty (*svātantrya*), which consists of the unifying synthesis (*anusandhāna*) of such [cognitions], is what bestows distinctness upon the Self; therefore, that alone is the Self. While it could be called "the one Self," [it is described thus].

When an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is used, the predominance of that property (*taddharmaprādhānyam*) is indicated, as in the *Śrīśivasūtra*: "Consciousness is the Self" (*caitanyam ātmā*). For it is said by the Noble One [Dignāga]:
"In those two cases [of the abstract suffix and the nominal suffix], there is the exclusion or non-exclusion of other properties."
The fruit of the distinction of conventions is that which conforms to the desire of the cognizer.

Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is that by the statement "He is this," which expresses the clear essential nature (*svarūpa*) of that very one whose form was concealed, it indicates recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) through an utterance imbued with wonder. He introduces that [Sūtra] in brief with the words "And at the time of recollection" (*smṛtikāle ca*). The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a doubt. That [doubt]...

It was shown at the beginning of the commentary on the Sūtra. Regarding the phrase "showing," the connection is that by showing [this], he establishes the logical proof of the Self, which is Maheśvara in nature and characterized by the sovereignty of knowledge and action.
By this, two intended meanings of the half-verse have been demonstrated.

There is no difference whatsoever between memory and experience, whether in terms of the subjective aspect (*grāhakāṃśa*) or the objective aspect (*grāhyāṃśa*). And this [point] is useful for establishing the subject matter under discussion. As for the phrase "like the cognition of a yogi," if there were only the manifestation of the object, then like the cognition of a yogi, it would be merely a novel experience (*apūrvānubhava*), and not memory.
Regarding the statement "memory is the state of having passed [into the past]," which is defined as "the non-forgetting of an experienced object":
although in all cases the substance’s contact with time occurs only by way of action, nevertheless,
the state of having been (bhūtatva) indicates the non-existence of the thing by way of its invariably present action, such as "being" (bhavana), and not otherwise.

"By way of the activity of experience. Here, "in this" refers to the definition of memory. To avoid the objection that "what is distinct from the light [of consciousness] might not possess luminosity, but how could memory—which is distinct—not exist? the author stated "in the manifestation of memory" (*smṛtiprakāśe*) in the *Vṛtti*. He explains that as follows:

"Consisting of cognition alone" (*jñānarūpaiva*). The meaning is that they were "introduced" (*upakṣiptāḥ*), that is, indicated at the very time of explaining the first half-verse. According to the commentary (*vṛtti*), the object is non-different from the recollection because it is accompanied by experience.

The two intended meanings of the Sūtra have been explained. Regarding the Sūtra phrase "of that which is being remembered" (*smaryamāṇasya*), it was stated that the manifestation characterized by the non-effacement of what was previously experienced is "cognition" (*vedanā*); by means of this, both the subjective and objective aspects attain a state of unification within the act of remembrance.

Regarding this, the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) states the reason: "of that which is distinct from the manifestation" (*prakāśāt bhinnasya*). Now, one might object: "Is this property not found only in an object that is being remembered? For the same situation applies even to an object that is being experienced. True; however, the intention is as follows: having superposed [the property] onto memory, he speaks thus—[namely,] with respect to that which is being experienced.

Through the power of *māyā*, there exists a separate sense of egoity (*abhimāna*) regarding external objects; however, in this case, even that is absent. For this very reason, there is no causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) from what is being remembered. It is for this same reason that Bhaṭṭa [Umbeka] also rejected the view that the manifestation of light possesses the nature of an object only by way of the entity appearing in memory.
"The object does not appear in error or memory...
[and] "...in memory, however, it has as its object a thing that has been consumed by fire."
That entity does not move, nor would it manifest in this way...

And thus: "purastāt" refers to the *ādisiddha* sūtras and others; "and it will be stated" refers to the sense of "prāgiva" in sūtras such as (1.4.58) *prāgivāt kaḥ*. And in that regard, although [it is stated] in a general sense...

This has been stated as being common to all forms of knowledge; nevertheless, just like other specific [objections], memory (*smṛti*) is also refuted here. On the contrary, it has already been demonstrated that by means of that very [refutation], it cannot be established that manifestation (*prakāśa*) is a property of the object. Furthermore, if the object were manifested in memory as something distinct [from the subject], it would not even be a case of remembering.

Previously there would have been only direct experience. Therefore, that manifestation of the object which occurs in memory embraces the object even more intensely; however, the notion of its separateness here exists merely as a shadow—this is all there is to it.

(Page 35) It is said that [the manifestation of whiteness] arises from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of experience. For it is precisely in the case of recollection (*smaraṇa*)—and not in the case of direct experience (*anubhava*)—that the penetration of the object by whiteness is observed as an example; because in that [case of recollection], the appearance of identity [between the object and its quality] is logically established.

Even when there is perception of the inherence of the quality white, its manifestation as being identical [to the substance] must be admitted. As the venerable one said: "By means of which another self appears as if it were that very self."
And because the reality of unity and plurality is not determined.
"...that power called inherence... (Vākyapadīya 3.10).

However, the statement that there is a difference in nature according to the actual state of things is not at all appropriate at the occasion of defining the essential nature of objects, whose core consists in their manifestation. And thus:
"The discernment of the lord of men is itself a palace, neither white nor non-white"—
this is the statement of one who lacks authoritative knowledge; for it is not possible for two properties of a thing to exist through mutual exclusion [in this manner].
Between two things situated in opposition, one or the other must necessarily be the case. Furthermore, it is said:
"Whether it be a portion of a location, or a determination from another [perspective], or the opposite, or non-existence—it is conventional discourse that follows."
Thus it is said: in that regard, if [the object] is the ultimate, indefinable form; or a mere collection of those [atoms];
or a composite substance; or a substance non-different from Brahman; or a particular (svalakṣaṇa) excluded from everything else—when this has been stated...
How can it be understood that "the nature of an entity is such and such," when the Noble One establishes entities by means of a self-nature that is indeed not determined?

"Entities are established as their own [nature]. Thus, it has been rightly said: that which does not possess a certain nature does not manifest in that form, just as blue does not manifest as yellow; yet [consciousness] does manifest in its nature as light.

(36) [The object] exists in memory, but it is not of that nature [of the original perception]. If that which is not of that nature were to appear in such a way, then that very thing would appear exactly as it was in its uncontradicted form; thus, there would be no restriction in either case. And this lack of restriction [would follow].

Because it would entail the consequence of perceiving what is contradictory to the pervader— that is, a rule that is observed to be pervasive— it follows that non-manifestation is excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) due to its not being of that nature; for it is pervaded by being of that very nature, and thus [the presence of manifestation] is contradictory to that [non-manifestation].

The negation of non-identity [of the probans] occurs through the perception of what is pervaded by its opposite. Having thus explained half of the verse, [the author] states— by way of a summary of what was previously said— the commentary beginning with "evam ca" and so forth, in order to apply the status of that meaning as a logical reason (*hetu*) elsewhere, namely to the Sūtra passage beginning with "tena" and so forth.

And that very [point] is expressed by the words "and so forth" (*tadeva ca iti*). In the phrase "poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) also includes recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), mental construction (*saṃkalpanā*), and the like.

However, conceptualization (*vikalpana*) is not mentioned separately because it is already included within the category of "appearing as experience" (*anubhavāyamānatva*). It consists of the unification of the present and the future.
Poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) has been illustrated; it also characterizes the fancy that consists in the unification of what has been and what will be, as in my thought:
"that which I shall experience. Now, [one might object]: "The oneness of consciousness is its uniformity;
how can it be said that the Self is the nature of a single consciousness, when memory and other such states are its attributes?"

This is the view of those who maintain the existence of a self (*ātmavādin*). [The author] shows that while this is true, the underlying intention (*ākūta*) there is as follows: by the word "only" (*kevalam*), he indicates that the cause for the conceptualization of *dharmatā* is its manifoldness; even within that, the manifoldness of objects is conventionally designated, so this distinction is merely conventional (*sāṃvyavahārika*) and not experiential (*ānubhavika*), whereby...
It would be ultimate reality. By this, the delusion of the Vaiśeṣika is pacified. For he asserts:
"Difference is real, but non-difference exists through the power of inherence (*samavāya*). And that contradicts experience, since the proof of the conscious subject (*pramātṛ*) is established.

"Even that which is inherent in cognition and the like is not established simply because it is not manifest" (19). The meaning is: how could both the manifestation as past—at the time of the experience—and the manifestation as present—which has become an object of memory—be the form of a single object?
With the intention that there is no difference whatsoever between experience and memory, he says: "To this it is replied" (p.
"For the prior experience does not appear in memory separately, as the object does. (1.4.4)

Thus [it is said]. By this, one should apply the following passage in order to explain how, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), the phrase "for instance" (*tathā hi*) indicates that the subsequent section serves as a support for the subject at hand.
And the intention [of the phrase] "of cognitions" is that [this applies] even when they appear as distinct. This will be explained [later].

"Only due to conformity with different perceived places and times do cognition, memory, determination, and so forth appear as sequential" (1.5.21). Now, one might object: "Is not the temporal distinction that is metaphorically attributed [to these states] based on the difference in their objects? This refers to the experience and the memory.

"Where has it gone? He replies: "And thus. Even so, that conventional usage of "prior" and "posterior" which is suspected to be metaphorical based on the object does not exist, because there is no differentiation in the object itself. By the word "only" (*tāvat*).
This indicates that the nature of this linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) will be established otherwise. As it will be stated:

"That which is this intuition (*pratibhā*), colored by the sequence of those various objects, is the Great Lord (*maheśvara*), the cognizer whose nature is non-sequential and infinite consciousness. (1.7.1)
In such enumerations as these, one might object: "Surely this sequence of prior and posterior between cognition (*bodha*) and memory (*smṛti*) appears.
True; however, that [sequence] does not arise from a difference in objects. From what, then?
He says, "But of that very [cognition]," meaning it arises from the difference of the subject (*pramātṛ*) constructed through *māyā*. It is not due to a difference in the objects themselves.
The conventional usage of "prior" and "posterior" does not, however, occur in this manner; rather, it serves to illuminate a specific distinction.

The Self alone, by virtue of being the Lord, possesses all powers. Among these, that power which brings forth time—characterized by its capacity to produce diverse manifestations—is [determined] through the variety of the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of those manifestations.
The capacity for sequential emergence— by means of which, acting as the cause,

the processes of rising and setting of the sun and other celestial bodies are characterized through clear experience— is that which constitutes the existence and non-existence, or presence and absence, of the form of manifestation grounded in consciousness.

In the continuous flow [of manifestation], because the difference between appearances such as jars and the variety of their activities are revealed by those two, the manifestation of succession occurs; thus,
at the occasion of reflecting on time, this succession is observed to be logical.
(page 38) Regarding the statement, "Sequence is based on differentiation" (2.1.4), and in this manifestation of sequence, even the body, vital breath, intellect, and so forth—

The sequence of appearances of states— such as childhood, youth, weakness, firmness, acuity, and dullness— belonging to the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*), is merely attributed (*upacaryate*) to these two, namely experience and memory, by means of the cognition that is inward-turned in nature; and this is done even though there is no actual difference between them, for they possess only an imputed distinction.

"Even though their object is one and the same, it appears as if divided. Thus, the sequential order attributed to the referent is not contradicted by its actual non-difference, just as the qualities of fire-ness and cow-ness do not contradict the boy's nature as a boy. For a figurative distinction does not enter into the real entity.

Because that [contradiction] resides in the cognition of the cognizer, the state of having a common object (*tulyaviṣayatva*) is what constitutes the contradiction between two contradictory properties; otherwise, the entire universe would be in contradiction with everything else. Therefore, by means of that which is incompatible with the state of having a common object—which is the cause of contradiction—...
Since figurative usage is pervaded by having distinct objects, it negates contradiction, which is the effect of that which is incompatible with its own pervader;
thus, this is the "perception of what is pervaded by the incompatible cause" (*kāraṇaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). In this way, there is no contradiction at least in the case of mere figurative usage.
How much more so here, in this succession of metaphorical designations? For here, in the ultimate sense, there is no differentiation whatsoever;

rather, it is solely the sovereign power of the Supreme Lord that shines forth through a continuous stream of appearances and non-appearances—just as in dreams, volitions, or the will of a yogi—and thus, what could exist by what means?
The intended meaning is that there is a contradiction. Now, one might object: "Let there be a contradiction here because of the difference in objects;

however, since [the contradiction] arises from the clarity or lack of clarity regarding that very same object, those two [states] indeed exist within a non-different object—namely, in the case of what is being experienced and what is being remembered—and thus a contradiction produced by them would still occur. To this, it is replied once more:

He negates the doubt as to how there can be unity of the object with the words "and not" (*na ca*). Nor does that object differ even due to a difference in manifestation; he characterizes that difference in manifestation through a single approach by means of the passage beginning with "in memory" (*smṛtau*) and so forth. Now, if a difference in manifestation is indeed admitted, then—

How then is there no difference [between them] caused by that? Since the very life of an appearance consists in its reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), the establishment of the difference or non-difference of things is based precisely on the difference or non-difference of that awareness. And here, reflective awareness exists as a unity.
Even by the Buddhists, indistinct apprehension is [admitted], such as [the perception of] a cloud of dust...

(Page 39) It has been determined in the *Prāmāṇyaparīkṣā* and other works that there is indeed the apprehension of the association with other objects such as "l" and so forth, whereas the object itself possesses unity due to the oneness of its determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*). This will be explained [later].
Thus, regarding the remoteness or proximity of objects...
[as stated] in such introductory sections as (2.3.10). Now, is there not a coexistence of the object being remembered with its prior experience?
How is it stated in the *Vṛtti*? For that [memory] does not appear as something separate. Therefore, what is the meaning of "together" (*saha*)? True;
however, when one determines that very same memory through another conceptualization (*vikalpa*), thinking "I remember what was experienced," then...

"By the principle that 'one who is liberated through sovereignty...'," [it is said] because of the conceit that "this experience shines clearly as an object of cognition on the surface of that [reality]. He shows that this was stated with that intention by saying, "even though."

"Consisting of the object" (*arthamaya*) means that in which the object under discussion is the primary qualificand. Now, one might object: "In this way, even experience possesses manifestation as a distinct entity; however, by the force of its being manifest, that non-difference from consciousness—which is of the nature of light—belongs to the object as well. So what is the distinction, such that..."
By means of the identity of consciousness, this is the introduction to non-duality:
"All this is indeed the Person" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.15);
"All this is indeed Brahman" (Nṛsiṃha Upaniṣad 6).
Thus, it is said that [the relationship] is based on a distinction from those things which are of such a nature—namely, those characterized by non-differentiation and lack of distinction.

He says "thus" (*evam*). Although this distinction has been shown through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) characterized by the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyatā*), nevertheless, even though the ultimate unity (*aikya*) of the object exists within the sphere of *māyā*, [it remains so].

It does not depend on the state of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), but rather on experience itself. Therefore, by means of that causal mode of reflective awareness which consists in the non-differentiation from the ultimate subject, there occurs the manifestation of the experience as it has ascended into the subject in the form: "I experienced this previously."

This is logical. For that reason, just as in the state of illusion (*māyā*), the experience does not appear as something separate from the object in memory, but rather as non-separate; for that reason, the point stated in the preceding aphorism—that there is unity with consciousness (*saṃvidaikya*)—is established as being distinct from the doctrine of the partless non-dual (*nirviśeṣādvaya-vāda*). This is the meaning of the aphorism.
Let it be seen by first directing the mind toward that which is to come— namely, by means of causing the application of attention in the form of thinking, "This is indeed thus.
(Page 40)

This has been shown in the commentary (*vṛtti*). By the word *hi*, which occurs in the forthcoming sūtra, it is stated that the meaning of the present sūtra serves as the reason for the justification of the opening statement regarding the unity of consciousness (*saṃvidaikya*); thus, it is demonstrated that the unity of consciousness—like a cow in the case of the milk of a royal cow—is connected with both the preceding and the subsequent meanings. || 3 ||
For the prior experience does not appear in memory as something separate from the object, like the object itself;
this is because it appears as superimposed upon the self in the form "I experienced [it] previously."
He introduces this with the concise statement "and not... (*na ca*). Regarding the phrase "in the cognition of recollection" (*smaraṇajñāne*), the meaning is as follows:

although it may appear as something distinct, created as a qualifier within another determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) that consists in the linguistic usage of the cognition of memory, let it be so. [Objection: But let there be a connection with the agent in the case of "I experienced" (*anvabhūvam*).
"But how can that [subjectivity] exist when experience is attached to an object? He replies: "It is the object itself.

Even though actions residing in the agent are clearly attached to an object, they do not abandon their support in that agent; thus, the fact that experience resides in the agent is not undermined. Therefore...

Thus, its status as a subordinate element (*upasarjanatā*) is appropriate. For if it were to be distinguished as "this is such-and-such," it would indeed possess the status of a qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) by virtue of having the nature of a distinct substance; however, in the case of "the brave man" (*vīraḥ puruṣaḥ*), its status as a subordinate element does not arise from the direct application of the word (*śrauta-vṛtti*), but rather from the syntactical context (*vākyīya*). This will be examined in the investigation of relations (*saṃbandha-vimarśa*). Now, when...

Experience (*anubhava*) is referred to by virtue of its non-subordinate status, whereas the object (*artha*) is [referred to] by virtue of its subordination—that experience [is such that one says], "A clear [experience] of blue occurred for me. At that time, there is its manifestation separately [from the object].
Therefore, he says, "But of that" (*tasya tu*). By the word "only" (*mātra*), it is meant that [the cognition] rests solely upon the primary perception.
He states that the reality of conventional cognitions is as follows: "It will be said" [in the verse] "That which was seen by me while sitting, that very thing is thus... (1.4.6).
And he confirms that this alone is logical with the words "I am thus," etc. Nor is it the Self...

The intention is that it has indeed been stated: "The object of knowledge (*vedya*) alone [is established], because there would otherwise be an infinite regress of further knowers (*vedakāntara*). And regarding those qualities of the subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*)—such as happiness, suffering, and delusion—which are cognized by the intellect (*buddhi*) and consist of the nature of the object of knowledge (*vedyarūpa*), their "awakening" (*bodha*) is spoken of metaphorically (*upacāreṇa*), due to the conceit of duality (*bhedābhimāna*) produced therein.
The meaning is that this "imposition" (*āropaṇā*) is what is to be known; and by the commentary passage beginning with "yaśca" (on page 41),
the meaning of this sūtra [is explained].

The particle *hi* in the Sūtra has been explained as indicating that [the self] is the cause for the unity of consciousness. He elucidates this with the words beginning "This which... and explains "I" as "the object of knowledge. By the mention of the "stage," he shows that the Supreme Lord, whose essence is light, possesses forms such as these—just like an actor—and thus possesses the state of being an object of knowledge.

He says that [this state] consists merely of self-conceit (*abhimāna*), without abandoning one's own firm support. Now, since consciousness has no contact with time at all, how can there be a "function" (*vṛtti*) that extends across multiple times? It is simply because of the orientation toward objects of knowledge (*vedya*) existing in multiple times that that very awareness is said to be "of multiple times."
It is taught by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). [Objection: But surely even the objects of knowledge (*vedya*) are indeed non-different from consciousness (*bodha*).

To this he says: "the nature of the inner self" (*pratyagātmatā*). That which moves toward—i.e., knows—each individual person (*pratipuruṣam*) in a manner directed inwardly (*ābhimukhyena*), as the mere form of its own self-awareness unmixed with anything else; that is the inner self.

The group of individual subjects (pratyagātman), whose nature is that of the subject under the influence of *māyā*, possesses as its vital essence the differentiation from objects of knowledge and from one another; in that state, because the objects of knowledge are differentiated, there arises a temporal sequence produced by the presence and absence of appearances, resulting in their being situated at different times.

And that single self-luminous cognizer (*svasaṃvedanapramātṛ*), being oriented toward that [object], is metaphorically designated as "many times" (*anekakāla*). It should not be thought that our explanation in the *Svairī-sūtra*—where we interpreted the word *sahi* as "shining forth within himself as the inner self"—contradicts the sūtra; for he is indeed the seer.

By showing the distinction within the *prakṛti* portion— that it consists of both perception and recollection— thereby demonstrating a difference in time due to its orientation toward the object of knowledge, and by showing unity through the *pratyaya* (suffix) portion, [the author] indicates that [the self] possesses multiple times. For it is illogical for one who is not a perceiver to be a rememberer.

"By asserting that memory is not established merely through a succession of cognitions whose nature consists solely of independent cause and effect, the rememberer is likewise imagined to be just like the seer. (1.2.6)— this is the statement of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
He refutes [this] here, that is, in the commentary (*vṛtti*). In the state of being manifest, "knowability" (*vedyatā*) is used figuratively;

having intended as the reason the purpose—which culminates in being the locus of repose, the state of being focused thereon, the state of being free from seeking anything else, and the state of being undeniable—he [proceeds].

For, in the state of being an object of cognition—characterized by dependence on another manifestation—another manifestor would have to be required; yet that does not exist. Thus, there is a sublation of the primary meaning. And with respect to the cognizable, in view of conventional usage...

(42) Since "manifestness" is designated [by the term "existence"], the basis for the metaphorical usage is the inherence of existence and manifestness in a single substrate, by virtue of conventional practice and cognitive presumption. 4.
Even for yogins, these [cognitions] do not appear as objects of sight within another act of seeing;
rather, they shine solely by the authority of self-awareness, even when they appear in the domain of the cognized object.

[Objection: "Is it not so? Just as the penetration of light [into objects] has been accepted on the strength of reasoning (*yukti*), so too must the difference between the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) be accepted on the strength of experience (*anubhava*).
And it is precisely for the sake of supporting that [difference] that the power of *māyā* is postulated. Therefore, just as a jar...
Just as [an object] appears separate from the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*), so too does the consciousness of another appear to the yogin. And that [consciousness of another] is threefold:
"He knows this," "This was my experience in another body characterized by a previous birth," and "This was previously seen by another in such a way, and is now being remembered."
Thus, all of this has been demonstrated in the *Itivṛtti* as perceptions residing in other subjects;

it is also indicated in the *Sūtra* by the plural form "of visions" (*dṛśaḥ*). Furthermore, in the *Ṭīkā*, the first point was investigated in the passage ending with "then there would be the manifestation of innate bliss," and the second...

By the passage ending with "this is indeed memory," and by the passage beginning with "the third, in another cognizer," this threefold cognition is what is to be known (*vedya*). Consequently, in the state of *māyā*, it follows that one cognition is knowable by another cognition. And by that, [it follows] for both experience and memory as well.

If it is argued that the relationship between the object and the subject, and through that, the convergence of objects by virtue of having a single objective domain, leads to the establishment of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), and thus how can a single cognizer be established— then, having accepted this very conclusion (*siddhānta*),
this discussion regarding the lack of restriction results in the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenet (*apasiddhānta*).
This is the intention of the objector. Regarding the phrase "tad atra" (therefore, in this case), the ellipsis is that "there is an answer to this," namely the previously stated one.

He reminds us of that very point with the words "yoginām api" (even for yogis). Alternatively, "tat" refers to the beginning of the sentence; [it means] "according to the principle previously stated."
"Vision is indeed its own manifestation...

(1.3.2), according to the reasoning stated in such passages; "of that"—meaning even of consciousness as it is accepted by others. Having thus briefly explained the sūtra beginning with "In this way, for yogins" and ending with "appear," [the author proceeds].
The *abhyupagama-siddhānta* is the examination of specific features of that [object] following its acceptance without prior investigation. (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.31)

Thus, in order to demonstrate the firmness of the reason that supports the subject matter under discussion as it has been stated, he explains the remainder of the Sūtra— which was spoken by resorting to a *abhyupagama-siddhānta* (a tenet accepted for the sake of argument)—
by way of introduction with the words "the ground of what is to be grasped. It was stated that "difference [arises] from the force of experience."

And that [cognition] may indeed be appropriate in the case of a yogi’s knowledge at the initial moment; for there is room for the statement that "this person knows" or "I know," since the yogi’s perception of another does not involve a fusion with our own objective referent (*asmadartha*). But in the case at hand, even that is absent, as in the thought "I experienced."
Because only that experience which has become our own objective body manifests; by the word "api" (also/even),
he states that what was proposed by the opponent as an illustrative example is not applicable here, saying "dṛśaḥ" (of perceptions)—
that is, the perceptions belonging to others do not [constitute] a specific instance of seeing.

In the consciousness arising from the ultimate limit of the excellence of the cultivation of the true nature of reality, [objects] appear as objects of cognition. For the Buddhists, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone is the very essence of knowledge;
how then could that [essence] be an object of cognition? For the Sāṃkhyas, apprehension is merely the reflection of the *puruṣa*.

And the person (*puruṣa*) has stages that are imperceptible. Even for the followers of Kaṇāda (*Kāṇāda*), how could knowledge—which inheres in another self—be known by the yogic mind, which functions within its own body?
For the followers of Jaimini (*Jaiminīya*) as well, [knowledge] exists through identity with another self; therefore, this much is the case for the yogi.
The perception of another's consciousness is that manifestation which co-exists with the body and so forth of another,

consisting of the appearance of blue, sweetness, pleasure, passion, and so on. In that case, the blue and other such qualities are indeed objects of cognition as distinct entities, whereas the aspect of manifestation shines forth only as "I."

However, due to the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the manifestation of the body and so forth as the subject (*pramātṛ*), one conceives that "this-ness" (*idantā*), which resides in those [objects], as belonging to the aspect of light (*prakāśa*). But when the firm latent impression of the distinction between self and other collapses,
seeing everything as one's own self, one perceives the very distinction between self and other as being one's own creation.

Even with respect to that [yogic cognition], one cognition is not to be known by another cognition. Or rather, let the knowability of another’s cognition in the case of a yogi’s cognition exist solely through the power of an unexamined, sudden, and suspected intuition; however, it is not so in the case of memory—this is the meaning of the sūtra. The word “bhānti” (they appear) is to be construed like the eye of a crow [in both eyes]. Now, as for the yogi...

Since one who possesses the excellence of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) is also [included] here in this system, how is it that only the excellence of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) is described as his characteristic (*vṛtti*)? He says:
"Because it is being employed. Here, the point to be proven (*sādhya*) is indeed that cognition is cognizable by another cognition.

In that regard, since the cognition of another's mind and so forth—which are beyond direct perception—is employed as an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), what is the use of further elaborating on this? And this [point] is stated when the specific vision of yogins is heard.
It is understood that the mind inclines toward the perception of yogins, which is well-known in the world through many treatises.
Thus he says, "of the perception of yogins. In the *Vṛtti*, the term "gone" (*gata*) is employed merely in the sense of "attained" as it is commonly known in the world;
however, in the *Ṭīkā*, it is shown to culminate in identity by way of inherence (*samavāya*).

The plural forms in "dṛśaḥ" (perceptions) and "upalambhāḥ" (apprehensions) are explained by the word "tattat" (this or that). Anticipating the question, "How is it that this is their intrinsic nature (svabhāva)? it is stated: "For this alone is their defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa).
That which distinguishes a thing from others is its very intrinsic nature, just as [the capacity to hold water] is the intrinsic nature of a jar.
The nature [of a jar] consists in having the form of a broad base and belly.

Likewise, the fact that cognition has the nature of pure self-awareness (*svasaṃvinmātra*) is what distinguishes it from other insentient things; therefore, that alone is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
For an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is precisely that which does not deviate [from itself]. For this very reason, [it is not the case] for a jar...

Substantiality (*dravyatva*) is its own nature; however, that which is possible as its form may indeed be characterized by the forms of earth and so forth, owing to its specific uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*). That by which something is not abandoned, and that from which it is not abandoned—that alone is its [defining characteristic], free from under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
The characteristic (*lakṹ�aṇa*) is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If something else were the intrinsic nature, then that which is not it would become it, and that which is it would become not it.

One's own [nature] is indeed joined with both difference and non-difference; by uniting it with a portion of the object, and thereby uniting consciousness itself with the object, the word "and" (*ca*) indicates even a fourth restriction: that it is one's own consciousness alone (*svā saṃvideva*).

[Objection: But surely cognition is the illumination of both self and other; therefore, how can it be said that "it belongs to itself alone"? To this he says: "For [it illuminates] even another," and "and being of such a nature. By the word "existent" (sat), he means this: if that which is the defining characteristic of something does not appear, then that thing would not have appeared at all.

Furthermore, the manifestation of form as constrained by the fourfold restriction would indeed be impossible if cognition were knowable by another cognition; thus, [it is said] "its own consciousness alone" on page 45.

He shows the nature of the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) with the words "even his consciousness is other" (*parāpi asya saṃvit*). However, in the phrase "his own consciousness alone" (*svasya saṃvideva*), the counter-correlative is even non-consciousness (*asaṃvidapi*). The word "that" (*tat*) has "his own" (*svasya*) as its ellipsis. He indicates that this [consciousness] occurs "previously" by the statement "because the insentient (*jaḍa*) has such a characteristic," implying that even the insentient might be his form, but not—

The intended meaning is that it is consciousness itself. However, in the phrase "consciousness of itself," no counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) has been shown, because such a correlate would be irrelevant to the present context, and even if it were the illumination by another (*paraprakāśyatva*), it would not be the cause of insentience (*jāḍya*). But [one might object]: "In this way, the knowledge of a yogi would have the knowledge of another as its object."

Anticipating the objection as to how linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) could be possible, he gradually establishes his own position with the words "But then" (*tadā tu*), the sense being: when this linguistic convention occurs. By the phrase "presented" (*pratyupasthita*), he demonstrates the proximity of both the yogi’s cognition and the cognition of another through the power of their respective causes.

In that regard, the cognition of another first manifests because it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*); and since the cognition of a yogin possesses an excellence of purity such that its range is unimpeded, even in relation to that, the cognition of another remains self-luminous without depending on its own existence, and does not remain concealed.

"He shows it to that yogin. Regarding "of this"—that is, of the cognition belonging to another subject—"in this way"—meaning according to the manner described—there is no "transgression," that is, no overstepping, of its nature as cognition, which consists of a determinate perception; so it is conceived. Now, even this, from our perspective...
The intention is that this [dependence] is tenable in that sense, but not by way of one cognition being known by another cognition.

The term "by another" (*pareṇa*) refers to the awareness of a different object. For it is through a case-ending used as a *karmapravacanīya* that a relation is expressed; indeed, that [ending] takes the place of the genitive. And there is no relationship of object and subject between two cognitions.

The connection is as follows: since the state of being an object (*viṣayitā*) of cognition with respect to its object, such as a jar, is precisely what is called "conformity" (*sārūpya*), namely, the imitation of that [object's] form. For by a cognition that imitates the form of the object, that object is apprehended and taken up; thus, the object possesses the status of being the objective support (*ālambanatā*).

Because of conformity (*sārūpya*). And that [conformity] is pervaded by both difference and non-difference; for it is absent in the case of total difference, as between water and a pillar, and in the case of total non-difference, as a pot is with respect to its own self. Nor is there a difference of cognition from another cognition.

(Page 46) Someone [objects]: because distinctions of place, time, and form have been refuted, and because a distinction based on the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the object of cognition is not ultimately real, [consciousness] is distinct from the objective portion such as blue, or from the subjective basis such as passion and so forth.

Even though it is an object by virtue of being manifest, the cognitive aspect cannot logically possess the status of an object. In the case of two mirrors, however, all their forms—including those of space, time, and essential nature—are distinct;
thus, let there be a similarity resulting from the mutual reflection of images, but this is not the case for two cognitions. Therefore, this [is as follows]:

The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: there is no relationship of object and subject between two cognitions, because an ultimate difference [between them] is not perceived; this is a non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi). For similarity (sārūpya), which is the defining characteristic of being a subject, is pervaded by difference—even when [the cognition] is distinguished [from its object].

With the intention that the pervader-of-the-pervader is simply a pervader, the noble Dharmakīrti did not engage in an analysis of the "pervader-of-the-pervader" and so forth. Furthermore, since the non-perception of a cause can be stated even when there is a non-perception of the cause-of-the-cause, he likewise did not [explicitly treat] the "contradictory-to-the-cause-of-the-cause" and so on.

It was thought: "And since it has a constructed form, its treatment as a subject (*dharmī*) is logical. The expression "of the two cognitions" (*jñānayoḥ*) follows the usage of the term *māyā*. Furthermore, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the nature of consciousness—which possesses power—is not obscured by *māyā*, just as the burning power of fire is not obscured by it. For even an obscuration...

In reality, it is precisely that which produces a nature distinct from its prior state. Now, one might object: "But you yourself, while establishing difference, have stated that the 'having-the-form-of-that' (tadākāratva) constitutes the objectivity (viṣayitā) of a cognition, whereas the 'having-the-form-of-another-cognition' [is the subjectivity];
anticipating this doubt, he says, "Furthermore" (kiṃca). Such being the case...

If [consciousness] were to terminate in unity with the object, it would not be established that one cognition is cognizable by another cognition. And this is logical: for if that which is the intrinsic nature of something is not manifested, while some other form of it is manifested, then that [intrinsic nature] has not been made an object.

Just as in the cognitions of mother-of-pearl as silver or a yellow conch-shell, [the cognition] takes the mother-of-pearl or the conch-shell as its object; and since the very nature of knowledge is that which grasps [the object], if that [nature] were not manifested while the state of being the grasped object was manifested, then it would not have been made an object [of cognition]. For if it were made an object, it would necessarily occur only in some instances.

Since pervasion would otherwise entail the contingency of non-restriction in the counter-example (vipakṣa), it is pervaded by the very manifestation of its own nature; thus, this is the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi). Because of its brevity, the phrase "not in other perceptions" from the commentary is not explained here, as it was already stated previously according to the Sūtra.
(Page 47) By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "only those who have ascended to their own Self," this is indicated. Now, one might object:
if in this way the manifestation occurs through having ascended to one's own Self, then the knowledge of another is revealed, and thus there would be the conventional usage of "another."

How so? He says "by way of being conditioned" (*aupādhikatvena*), referring to the "supreme subject" (*parapramātṛ*). For within a single consciousness of a yogin, the body, breath, and so forth of another are considered the subject (*grāhaka*); blue and other objects are considered the object (*grāhya*);
and the cognition consisting of mental states such as passion is likewise the supreme subject-form in its ultimate sense—all of these are indeed equal.

It manifests. In that regard, although by virtue of its fitness the cognition has attained identity with the subjective aspect (*grāhakabhāga*), it is conceptualized as "other" through the coloring (*ārūṣaṇā*) caused by its association with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body—which are primarily grasped and accepted as "other"—whereas it is actually apprehended only as "self. The body and so forth, however, are [conceptualized] as "other."

It exists as distinct from one's own ego-sense (*svāhaṅkāra*). And because the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) has not yet been exhausted, it is both grasped and conceptualized. He explains "reality" (*tattva*) by means of the phrase "that which makes the Supreme Self known.
The meaning is that reality is the state of making the Supreme Self known. [Objection: But was it not the case that "that which makes the Supreme Self known" was not introduced [at the outset]?

He dispels the doubt as to how that [yogic cognition] can be referred to by a pronoun with the words "of the omniscient one" (*sarvajñasya*). The point is this: because the term "omniscient one" was introduced earlier in the context of the experience of another, it functions here as a synonym for "the knower of another's self. Now, if [it is argued that] the yogin [knows] through the cognition of another...

If [the Self] were to enter into the portion of the subject, then, due to the resulting confusion with the *mātrās* (measures) and other factors residing therein, it would be beset by the intermingling of thousands of pleasures and pains; thus, it would have fallen into a condition more wretched even than that of transmigrating beings.
As it has been said: "This alone is our happiness, namely, that which is pleasant (*sātam*)."

Regarding "consciousness": whatever attains identity with something else partakes of its properties, just as other water becomes tinged with the color of saffron paste through contact with a handful of water colored by that paste.
Thus, the cognition of a yogi [attains identity] with other cognitions; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), for non-identity is the contradictory [opposite].

"The state of possessing that which lacks its property" (*ataddharmavattva*) is pervaded [by the absence of the probandum]; this is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that excludes [the reason] from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).

Here, there arises the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving the pervasion of a contradictory [reason]. He rejects this with the words "and not" (*na ca*). The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a doubt; by the two singular terms, [he refers to] something additional to pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, in the objective aspect (*grāhyabhāga*).
Thus he states the state of rest. And so, we shall explain that pleasure and the other qualities are indeed attributes of *prakṛti*;
their abiding is therefore in the unreal subject of cognition (*buddhi-pramātṛ*), who stands in the place of the body and so forth, and not in the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvedana*).

(48) And thus, just as his consciousness does not undergo identification with the qualities of another's body, such as being fair-complexioned and so forth— due to the constraint of the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) [which dictates] "I am fair"— it nevertheless undergoes such identification with the qualities of its own body.

"I am dark-complexioned"; likewise, its non-distinction from the attributes of another's cognition will be explained later. Thus, in the passage [4.1.3], "Therefore, pleasure and so forth do not exist in the real subject," that which was stated... [is established].
Although the reason will be stated later, it is already applicable; thus, the word *eva* indicates that this is an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (a conclusion established by the context).
For indeed, a reason is also called an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*. Now, [one might ask:
from the state of the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛtā*), which is appropriate for the experience of an object of knowledge that is non-different from the ground of the perceiver...

Those who have crossed over there do not possess the conceit of being subjects (*grāhaka*); how they become such is stated [as follows]: "real" (*vāstava*). Those who have attained the real subject by means of the power of the light of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), culminating in perfect and firm certainty.
Having attained that very state, they possess the conceit of being knowers (*pramātṛ*); though that nature of theirs is eternally manifest,
[they perceive it] as if maintaining a body, like the whirling of a firebrand.
Thus, because of the possibility of the persistence of the residual traces (*śeṣavartana*),
at the time of emergence (*vyutthāna*)— which consists in descending into the state of being a subject (*pramātṛbhāva*) such as the body born of destiny and latent impressions—
it appears as if it has set; this is what is designated by the term "state" (*daśā*).

By the phrase "grasping presented by its respective own causes," he states that the arising of pleasure, pain, and so forth is necessarily contingent. And that pleasure, pain, and so forth, once arisen, are directly experienced (*sākṣātkriyate*) by those [faculties] and are cognized (*saṃvedyate*), just like any other object of grasping.
As it is said in the Abhinavabhārati:
"And she, proud of her own skill, attended upon the sage with offerings of unrestrained enjoyments."
Even that satisfaction belongs to those who are dispassionate;
for there is no happiness for those whose pleasure depends upon the sense organs.

Thus, even in direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*), one does not conceive "I am happy" as being permeated by pleasure within the subject (*pramātṛ*); rather, for that very reason, one conceives of favor and injury caused by pleasure and pain [as belonging to the object]. This was sung by the Blessed One:
"Unperturbed in mind amidst sorrows, and free from longing amidst joys" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.58).
This shows that joy and the like are produced by agitation and longing; therefore, in their absence, those [emotions] are absent.
"...freed from joy, resentment, fear, and anger... (12.15).

Now, if it is argued that if grace and injury are not experienced in this way, then just as an external jar—though its nature consists of pleasure and so forth—is not of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion for one who is indifferent, so too [is the case here].
Even that which takes the form of pleasure and so forth when residing in the intellect would not be pleasure itself;
for the manifestation of the nature of pleasure and so forth is characterized by benefit and injury,
otherwise everyone would be incessantly overwhelmed by pleasure and pain, since the nature that pervades it would be absent.
"Therefore, its non-manifestation is absolute"—this is the conclusion. True;

however, even for one who has attained the state of the ultimate subject (*paramārthapramātṛ*), because of the firmness of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of identifying the body as "I," there occurs a sensation of burning when a limb is touched by glowing coals.
Even though suffering in the intellect possesses a form arising at the moments of its emergence and subsistence,
and even though its form is scrutinized through the direct realization of the non-apprehension of the "I" residing within that intellect,
it [is nonetheless transcended] due to the intensity of resting in the conceit of being the true subject who has brought [the reality] face-to-face.
