Because of its persistence— which consists of conceptualization and the nature of firm conviction— the thought "I am happy" does not rest within the portion of the "I," due to the absence of such repose; for in this way, like a traveler on a road, one does not [cling] to those various causes of pleasure and pain encountered by chance as they arise.
Because it is followed by attachment and aversion as its basis, one conceives of it [as such]; therefore, it is said that there is no happiness and so forth.

However, for those who, having loosened the firmness of their latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding the body and so on, abide by some cause through a mere conceit of ownership toward the locus—as if toward a house—[for them...]

The cause characterized by the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) regarding the body, intellect, and so forth— which brings about favor and injury and manifests pleasure and the like— does not exist; for even when there is contact with sandalwood and such, the auxiliary factor known as that "I-conceit" is absent, due to the deficiency of the causal totality (*sāmagrī*).
Because the cause is incomplete, pleasure, pain, and so forth do not arise at all. As it has been said:
"For those who are like the axe and the sandalwood, there is what is called detachment...
Thus, the Guru explained that this refers to those for whom [the axe] is like sandalwood.

The venerable teacher Lakṣmaṇagupta says: But surely, if there were a total absence of the conceit of "I-ness" (*ahaṃbhāva-abhimāna*), even the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) consisting in the impelling of the instruments and so forth would be lost. For that [sovereignty]...
(page 50)
"Desire does not function as its impeller;
rather, through contact with the power of the Self, the person becomes equal to it.

According to this principle, [the activity] is produced solely by the immersion into the "I-sense" (ahantā); thus, due to the non-perception of any other cause, one must conclude that [desire] is indeed [of that nature].

This is indeed true; however, it is from that [source] that the manifestation of supreme bliss occurs— a consciousness whose nature is free from the impurity of external longing, which has cast aside all desire through the arising of total fullness characterized by resting in one's own innate, uncreated Self, and which shines forth in its unveiled state.

When that occurs, then those tiny droplets of the experience of pleasure and so forth produced by sense objects— submerged in the ocean of bliss— do not manifest themselves as separate from the self for those whose egoism regarding the body and other such things has been loosened. "Then" means at that time.

In the state of immersion into the true subject, or else "then"—that is, at the occasion of the arising of pleasure or pain—whatever [occurs] for the world here and there, those indeed constitute attentiveness toward that connection. (Vi.bhai. 106)

Thus, by the power of this instruction, those who rest in the firmness of the inquiry into one's own true nature (*svarūpa-vimarśa-draḍhima*) are united with supreme bliss (*parānanda*). As it has been said:
"When great bliss is attained, or when a long-lost kinsman is seen... (*Viṣṇubhaktikalpalatā* 71).
And so forth;

"Even in suffering and even in expansion, through the application of fortitude for the sake of stability" (Śivadṛṣṭi 5.9), and so on. The word *vā* should be understood as having the sense of an option established according to the disposition of the respective practitioner.
Thus, having refuted the relationship between the knower and the known (*vedya-vedakatā*) regarding the first type of knowledge of others' minds,

he now refutes it even in the case of knowing one's own past-life experiences, by demonstrating that such knowledge must be considered a form of memory (*smṛti*), characterized by the non-forgetting of an experienced object.

"Even when there is direct perception of another previous birth"— the intention here is that even in the case of a specific previous birth, the "ascent of the self" (ātmāroha) in the form of memory, namely the thought "I experienced [this]," is indeed established. Furthermore, because of the conventional usage of the term "one who remembers past lives" (jātismara), the sense is that memory itself is thus complete.

However, regarding those previous births of others that the yogi has not personally experienced, the cognition that arises through the practice of instructions for directly perceiving latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) is said to have the nature of a novel knowledge, because it lacks contact with prior experience.

(On page 51) There is no contradiction in the passage beginning with "For whichever yogin," and so forth. Having thus introduced the second mode into the context of memory, he treats the third in the same way: "seen by another perceiver" (*pramātrantaradṛṣṭam*), which occurs when [something] has been seen by someone.

A jar was seen by an ordinary perceiver, but it was not previously seen by a yogi; subsequently, at the time of conceptualization, the yogi perceives another [jar] by intensifying the very fact of its having been seen through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Thus, at the moment of conceptualization, [memory] consists precisely in the non-forgetting of an experienced object.
For one conceptualizes that [object] precisely as something previously seen, and not as something new by thinking "I know it. Now,
do not take as a valid means of knowledge here the mere reopening of that very same prior manifestation, thinking "this was known by me," rather than a new manifestation arisen at this moment.
For that yogi’s state of being a rememberer at that time consists precisely in entering into identity with the prior manifestation [of that object].

It is for this very reason that even the revelation of Dharma by Manu and others occurs through their omniscience; otherwise, it would be impossible for the Supreme Lord to manifest as "this beginningless [revelation] is thus."
By making that [divine] light one's authority, what arises is called "memory" (*smṛti*).

For indeed, the scripture (*śruti*) is an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) arising from the grace of that unprecedented, supreme Lord’s light. Now, if a yogi remembers what was experienced by another subject, then that other subject—
And since that [perceiver] is one and the same, how can it be established that "this was seen by him"? He replies:

"In his own internal self. That is to say, because the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the firmness of the sense of "I" toward that which is one's own internal self—the body, vital breath, and so forth—has not ceased, he perceives another's body and such as being "other."

From that [state], one engages in worldly discourse with another cognizer, thinking, "This was seen by me. However, for that yogin whose firm latent impression (*saṃskāra*) has been attenuated— though not entirely destroyed, for if that impression were destroyed,
he would indeed be the Lord (*īśvara*) himself— he acts as a lord only while that impression is still on the verge of destruction.

Even while perceiving the body and so forth as "I" within a firm latent impression (*saṃskāra*) that possesses every [possible] mode, he perceives the entire universe as "I" right in the midst of that. Thus, for him who governs the universe like a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), his own body and so forth are like the capital city that serves as his seat of power. In this way, [the nature of] the object of knowledge (*vedyatā*)—
Having refuted [the opponent's view] with respect to the experience of the yogi, he concludes: "Thus it is established" (tadevam iti sthitam).
This refers to that very point.
(Page 52)
While asserting the firmness of his own position, he states that the alternative view is merely a concession (*abhyupagamavāda*);
yet even so, there is no relationship of the known and the knower between memory and experience. He says this with the words "by mere consciousness" (*bodhamātreṇa*).
With the words "individually" (*prātisvikena*), he rejects what we have stated regarding the coloring by the object (*vedyoparāga*) and so forth.
[He describes that] as having the nature of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of knowledge. He points this out with the word "pure" (*śuddha*). And the intended meaning here is this:

in each respective philosophical system (*darśana*), whatever pure form of consciousness there may be—just as the purity of knowledge consists in its being the form of all objects and being independent of any external support.
Some say that even beyond this, there is a supreme purity that is formless.
This mind is luminous by nature; the defilements are adventitious. The power of consciousness is unchanging, non-transmigrating, manifesting objects, pure, and infinite.
The knowers of reality recognize the supreme form as pure, unconditioned, and undivided, once the limiting adjuncts consisting of the aggregate of qualities have been abandoned.
"Thus, etc."—the sense is that such a state, free from passion (*niruparāga*), does not attain the state of being an object (*vedyatā*) in the knowledge of another's mind;

thus [the author] shows the application of the word "appear" (*bhāseran*) in both cases, stating that it is to be construed like the "crow's eye" maxim (*kākākṣivat*). By the aforementioned method, the state of being known by another and the status of being an object for cognition are refuted.

For this reason: even in accepting such a position, there is only a mere seed [of the argument]. In the Buddhist view, cognitions are distinct particularities (*svalakṣaṇa*); in the Naiyāyika system, cognition is known by another cognition.
Both of these have been refuted. Even in one's own system, there is a seed—namely, the power of *māyā*.

"One should do so"—but this is not tenable. For it is not that the very nature of external consciousness is altered by *māyā*, because that would entail the impossibility of the manifestation of the universe. Indeed, she (*māyā*) is the power of consciousness; being dependent upon it, how could she exist in its absence? As for creation, however, it occurs even within one's own self.
Let it be so; however, it is not capable of subverting pure consciousness, which is the nature of the creator, because—as has been stated—its nature is unobscured... (Svacchanda Tantra 2).
Thus it is said: "In this regard, the causal ground (*nimitta*) is that wherein all this effect resides and from which it has emerged" (Svacchanda Tantra 2.46, p.

Thus [it is said]. For if that [consciousness] were not concealed, where would even a hundred veils appear, and from what could they arise? Indeed, it appears only in consciousness and arises from that very source; therefore, since there is no appearance and no arising, what is the use of a veil? Thus, the power of Māyā cannot divide consciousness, for if it were divisible, it would follow that it is non-consciousness (abodhatva).
Nevertheless, because consciousness never sets, otherwise what would be the illumination even of consciousness?
If it were [otherwise], this would not be possible; as stated in the *Nareśvaraviveka*:
"Nor can that which is impossible be brought about even by the power of *māyā*."

Thus it is said. For at that very time, in that very place, toward that very person, it is not the case that one can believe "it does not exist" and "it exists" in that same way, merely by the statement "this is so because of illusion. And this impossibility regarding the fourth quarter (the *turyapāda*) should be understood as being indicated by the repetition [of the word] accompanied by a change in intonation (*kāku*). The particle *tu* serves to reinforce what has been stated.
He says: "In this case," the meaning is that even though there is a distinction between the agent, the object, and the cognition, the experience resides solely in the agent.

Furthermore, he states "and of the self" because, unlike for the Vaiśeṣika, the self is not merely the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the two cognitions; rather, it exists as a neutral substrate (*audāsīnyāt*) for both. For it stands merely as the substratum of the two.

Just as a jar [is not capable of uniting] form and taste, it is likewise not capable of uniting two [cognitions]. Furthermore, another cognition has precisely the two cognitions as its objects; like form and taste, they possess the status of being qualities (*guṇatva*). The word *yāvat* means "at which time" (*yadā*).

Even when one remembers, "That very perception which was mine is thus," it is still through a distinction; for that memory is precisely the determination (vyākaraṇa) of this [perception], in the form: "This was seen by me."

Now, one might object: when a jar is being remembered while residing in the state of being an object of knowledge (*vedya*), let the experience (*anubhava*) meet with its grasper (*grāhaka*). But when that very same jar is being remembered and has been made the object of knowledge, what more need be said?
It is replied: even in the statement, "I had an experience of the jar," it is the jar alone that is the object of knowledge. As it has been said:
In this regard, the venerable [author] states: "The cognition 'the cognition of a jar' is distinct from the cognition of the jar itself;
whereas the cognition 'jar,' which occurs in relation to the object, is that [latter]. (Vākyapadīya 3.1.105)
(54) Thus it is said: "The noble one also...
for he discerns that which has been abandoned by the mind."

Thus: the word "sā" (that) is the primary reference to memory. Its function is expressed as "it was seen by me," because even when the act of seeing is presented as distinct [from memory], the difference between them has not yet fully developed as a separate quality.
To demonstrate its division, the commentary states: "I had knowledge of that jar."

Because differentiation arises primarily from that very [reality] which has been created, the perception of the root is not sublated by the perception of the explanation; rather, it is reinforced. All of this has already been stated previously. The rest is clear. Indeed, all of this has been determined in detail within the Sūtras, Vṛttis, and Ṭīkās.
By the word "kathana" (narration), it is meant that although this is clear, it does not in fact constitute a fundamental sublation;

rather, memory subsists upon a determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) that occurs immediately after experience, because recollection is impossible regarding that which has not been conceptually determined (*avikalpita*). Therefore, by means of memory, which looks toward that determinative cognition—
That which has not been made an object of that [perception] is touched upon like a sky-flower;

nor is the aspect of experience (anubhavāṃśa) determined as an object of cognition by the subsequent conceptual determination (adhyavasāya) arising immediately after perception, because it comes to rest in a state of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) within the "I" as the subjective pole. Thus he demonstrates.
And that cognition by which I perceive this through the thread, thinking "this is a jar," is also a perception residing in the cognizer. (7)
The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and that which is memory" (*yā ca*) indicates that memory is dependent upon this [perception].

That determination (*avasāya*) which arises in the form "I see" is, first of all, a reflective awareness (*pratyavamṛśantī*) directed toward the aspect of the apprehender (*grāhakāṃśe*) within the determiner; thus, through the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of that experience, it is considered to be exactly so.

One realizes [it]. Even where a vision (*darśana*) is not explicitly indicated by its own word, there too "this" is referred to as being immediate (*pratyakṣatā*). And that [immediacy] is not a form to be cultivated, but rather the vision itself. Furthermore, it is not determined as a property of an entity (*bhāvadharma*) by means of the object "this."
Because there is no differentiation [between them],
therefore experience is not an object of cognition in the act of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).

Because of the perception of a fusion with the "I-sense" (asmadartha), which is opposed to the "this-ness" (idantā) that pervades all objects of cognition; for an experience is not manifested as an object of cognition through memory, since it is not determined as such, or rather,
because it is determined as being fused with the "I-sense"— this being the reason for the manifestation of memory.
The meaning of the sūtra is that there is a non-apprehension of either the cause or its contradictory.

Furthermore, memory is a specific kind of determinate cognition (*adhyavasāya*). Nowhere does a determinate cognition take experience as its object by way of the "this-ness" (*idantā*) [of the present]. Therefore, how could that [memory] be such [as you claim]?
The purport of the aphorism is that [the cognition] would either perform [this function] or, while performing it, would abandon its nature as a determinative resolve (*adhyavasāya*).
He introduces this with the words "in perception," etc., by way of a concise explanation.
The connection is that "the vision" is being referred to by the indication of "this-ness" (*idantā*). Now, [an objection]:

In the determinative cognition "this is a jar," there is no employment of the word *asmad* (the first-person pronoun), nor is there the employment of the word *dṛś* (the demonstrative); so where does [the cognition] rest, and what is being referred to? True, there is no employment of these two; nevertheless, even without them, there is a reference to the objects of both of them in the form "this. This very point he demonstrates with the words beginning with "I" (*aham*).

But surely, by the word "this" (idam), it is only the form of the jar that is being referred to? No, he says: "otherwise," meaning that if there were no reflection upon its perceptibility, it would not be distinct from an independent conceptual construction (svatantra-vikalpa). Here, the word "this" does not find its fulfillment merely in the reflection upon the form of the jar; rather—

Through the reflection upon its being situated in a suitable location, [the cognition] comes to rest in the reflection upon its perceptibility (*pratyakṣatā*). Now, one might object: "But perceptibility is also a property of the jar alone. He says "no": "Perceptibility," he says, "is within the sphere of the *ahaṃkāra* (I-consciousness)," meaning it consists of the subject (*pramātṛmaya*). "For" (*hi*) means because it is so.
Therefore, by the word "asmāt" (from this), there is a connection with the preceding [text], meaning that the reference to perception applies to both cases.

Regarding the phrase "of the nature of direct perception": that which was stated in the Sūtra as "this" (*ayam*)—the determination (*avasāya*)—is the very form of direct perception, having the nature of ascertainment (*adhyavasāna-svabhāva*), and not merely [the cognition] of a jar; such is the explanation in the Vṛtti.
It is explained that this very perception is what is being referred back by the statement "this.

For although the word "this" (ayam) relies upon the nature of the jar through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it nevertheless does not find its final rest in that alone. As it has been said:
(Page 56) "The fulfillment of this 'this-ness' (*idam*), which is a fragmented reflection, [occurs when it is absorbed into the subject]" (*Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi* 15).
And therefore, it brings about the very repose within itself of the state of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*). It is directly perceived.
Even in the cognition "this is a jar," its status as a direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*) rests solely within itself, just as in the case of [the thought] "my jar.

And by the word "even" (*api*) in the Sūtra, he says this: whatever the nature of the vision (*darśana*) may be, that alone is to be defined as capable of appearing in self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). What use is there for an investigation into the conceptualizing portions (*vikalpāṃśa*) therein?
Or let it be so; nevertheless, even this conceptualization does not reveal the "this" as being "that.

Such a conceptualization as "this vision is mine" is merely a construction—just like the analysis of the meanings of roots and suffixes—even for anyone, including a worldly person who considers himself a forceful investigator.

If that [act of seeing] were itself "seeing," it would require another act of seeing—just as one says "that pot"—leading to an infinite regress. Furthermore, it has been stated that the root *dṛś* (to see) is a verb whose action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*), as in the example: "The king causes his servants to see" (*darśayate bhṛtyān rājā*). Even by the followers of Jaimini, the act of seeing, which consists in the manifestation of the fruit of the activity, is said to reside precisely within the self. Therefore, [one does not say] "the pot..."

"I see this pot," "the pot is mine," and "my vision is directed toward the pot"—these are merely variations in expression; in terms of their actual meaning, however, they are entirely non-different. Likewise, in the case of recollection as well—whether one says "that," "I experienced it," "it was experienced by me," or "that was my vision"—this too is merely a variation in verbal expression.
The intended meaning of the two sūtras. || 7 ||

The body of consciousness alone possesses the powers of knowledge and so forth; and since it has been stated that the reality of both memory and direct experience is one and the same—the nature of pure consciousness—this follows by implication: that the subject and object belonging to the realm of *māyā* appear as nothing other than consisting of pure consciousness. Therefore, [the following] which is about to be discussed...
Nothing further need be said regarding the sutra; rather, that very same meaning should be summarized by unifying it.

With this intention—aimed at a mind as sharp as the tip of a blade of kusha grass, skilled in reflecting upon the meaning of the section—he introduces [the topic] and, summarizing this matter, says the following, characterized by this summary:

"Therefore, when one perceives something and even reflects, 'This is that which was seen by me,' both objects appear to the cognizer as non-different from the relationship between the grasped and the grasper. (8)
Because of that which was previously stated, this is the intended meaning here:
that [which exists] within the subject whose nature is pure consciousness (*viśuddhasaṃvidrūpa*) as the form of the grasped and the grasper... (page 57)
Two objects of cognition appear as distinct through mutual dependence,
characterized by the reflective awareness (*amarśana*) of experience and memory— namely, "How was it seen by me? and "It was seen by me"—
by disregarding the objective aspect of the act of seeing, such as "this" and "that."
[The cognition] is characterized by a reflective awareness (*āmarśa*) in which the aspect of the object being experienced and the aspect of the object being remembered are predominant;

the word *api* has the sense of "also. Alternatively, following the commentary, the construction may be: "the word *api* is displaced [in its position], meaning that even though they are distinct, they both appear in one place. As for those of coarse vision who [misunderstand] the meaning of this section...

For those who are unable to discern [the distinction], he introduces [the following] with the phrase "Or rather" (*athavā*), under the impression that this is a statement of a new subject matter preceded by an objection.
The connection is as follows: "Or rather," he says, intending to provide a resolution. Of the whole...

Since the manner of avoidance has not been explicitly stated by [the author] himself, this is not a reference to the present tense, but rather a future application. For it is appropriate that the future state resides within the intended meaning.
What, then, is the indication by which one intends to avoid that? He says: "seeing and so forth."

For even though it has been established by such verses as "Indeed, there is no experience... (1.4.4) that the manifestation of perception and so forth rests within the subject (*mātṛ*), the matter at hand remains...

Thus, the [argument that] there is unity of cognitions occurring at different times is not at all established, because the notions "I am fair," "I am hungry," and "I am happy"— which consist of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the intellect (*buddhi*)— are not of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*) and are absolutely distinct. To this, the following is the refutation:

"Consisting of that" (*tanmaya*): because the cognizer is established as having the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*) characterized by self-awareness (*āmarśana*), even though he becomes an imagined subject (*grāhaka*), he appears within that very [consciousness] just like the object (*grāhya*). "Therefore" (*tat*):
for this reason, the oneness of consciousness has not failed to be established; such is the intended meaning. [In the] Sūtra.

Since recollection is preceded by experience, experience was the primary subject matter; however, with the intention that it is precisely that [experience] which is under discussion, it alone was mentioned first in the *Vṛtti*. In the *Vivṛti* as well, following that same logic, [the author] speaks here of "vision" (*dṛk*) in relation to the intention and the high esteem for the aspect of the seer (*draṣṭṛ-bhāga*).
It is primarily referred to as such;
in both recollection and perceptual determination, it is indeed characterized by attention.

This has been shown by words such as *puraḥsara* (preceding) and *pūrva* (prior), while disregard (*anādaraṇa*) is indicated by words such as *parityāga* (rejection). For instance, when there is no intentional focus and a high regard for the objective aspect (*dṛśyabhāga*), the subjective aspect (*dṛgbhāga*) is not attended to; rather, it is the objective aspect alone that is attended to. Thus, there are four modes in direct experience and sixteen modes in memory.
And when recognition touches both [past and present], it becomes sixty-fourfold;

when doubled again by the predominance of the distinction between the prior and subsequent parts, and further divided within the present by distinctions such as what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted, it exists also in independent conceptualization characterized by poetic imagination (*utprekṣā*) and so forth.
In this way, within every such cognition, the subject and the object have distinct appearances in mutual dependence;
and through mutual dependence, having attained the state of subject and object by means of the union of the dual creation, they manifest as distinct. Where?
In the pure subject, whose nature is consciousness and whose essence is the independent agent of grasping (*parāmarśana*),

the *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) of the *dvandva* compound is indicated by the word "mutually dependent" (*anyonyāpekṣau*) in the aphorism, as this term serves as the base for the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). Furthermore, a simultaneous intention (*sahavivakṣā*) is appropriate here precisely because both [terms] are objects of apprehension.
And because of their state as subjects (*grāhakatva*). As it has been said: "By those two [faculties] through which one object is [perceived], another object is also [perceived].
Now, how can there be a distinct manifestation for those two, separate from one another? He replies:

due to the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of "this-ness" (*idantā*), even while the state of being an object (*vedyatā*) remains present, there occurs a constructed reflective awareness of "I" (*aham*).
Since the subject has been forcibly led to become the locus of the imagined [object]— as in "I am this white man"—

and since the object, such as a jar, although its ultimate reality is pure light, has been brought by sheer force into the range of the reflective awareness that regards it as distinct from light through the notion of "this-ness" (*idantā*), therefore these two...
"Separated yet projected. Now, if they are separated yet projected, how then are they projected within a single cognizer?
Is their projection within the cognizer like that of two jewels upon a thread? No, he says. How then?
"Consisting of that. There is nothing in these two that exceeds the ultimate reality of the pure cognizer.

The body (*vapuḥ*). If it is asked, "How is this to be understood?", he says: "First, of the perceiver... The word "first" (*tāvat*) indicates that this is established without effort. Alternatively, even though the stability of objects is constrained by the vital breaths and the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), [the following applies].
Though it is restrained within the individual soul (jīva), it remains there in that Supreme Self (paramātman) as well.
(Page 59) "How could there be restraint by means of breath for that [Self] which is itself the Self?"—this principle from the *Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi* (verse 20) should be followed here;
such is the intended meaning of the word "tāvat" (for now). Although, at first glance...

This [object] shines forth while being reflected upon as distinct from the Light, with the thought "this is to be grasped"; nevertheless, the fulfillment of this reflective awareness of "this" as something separate consists in that very reflective awareness which rests in its own essential nature: "I am this. (Ajadapramātṛsiddhi 15)

Thus, the repose of light within itself is indeed proclaimed as the state of "I-ness" (ahambhāva). And according to this principle, the ultimate goal is precisely the repose in "I-ness"; such is the intended meaning of the word *sāra* (the essence).
In the *Ṭīkā*: "Immediately after" means that this very point will be elaborated upon in the section beginning with [1.5.1] "of those things appearing as present... and so forth. Now, let it be so.

Manifestness—that, however, does not shine forth in the manifestation of the object's own nature, because it is the jar itself that shines forth. True; for the jar, this very shining forth is precisely its manifestness, otherwise the jar would remain unmanifested.

If it is argued that the word "fundamental" (*maulika*) means "ultimate" (*pāramārthika*), and let it be granted that the object (*grāhya*)—which appears as "this"—is indeed severed from the Light by the Lord’s power, namely *māyā*;
how, then, can the subject (*grāhaka*), which manifests as "I," be severed from the Light? This is the objection of the opponent.
And this [consciousness] shatters the delusion that "this is the grasper.

For entities have as their ultimate reality pure consciousness, characterized by absolute luminosity, since otherwise their manifestation would be impossible; and in relation to that [consciousness], if the power of māyā [operates upon] entities...

If one were to sever [the connection], it would imply that they manifest while being of a nature that is not luminous; and this is not tenable—to say that they both manifest and do not manifest. Therefore, one must accept that they are always non-different from ultimate luminosity itself.
(Page 60) Now, surely the power of the Blessed One, which accomplishes the most difficult of tasks, what could it not do? And so,
even for those who possess consciousness and enjoy agency, when the impurity of karma has been destroyed—

"It is said: 'The Māyā-impurity belongs to those whose objects of experience and mantras are divided, and they are the Vidyeśvaras' (3.2.9). Therefore, with respect to the supreme light which is the nature of consciousness, the manifestation of entities as distinct is not tenable. Anticipating this objection, he clarifies [the point]:

"Or even while it is being performed": for even though consciousness, though its nature is the universe, undergoes a fragmentation— another name for which is *māyīya* (pertaining to *māyā*)— consisting in the non-manifestation of its universal nature, brought about by the power of the Lord called *māyā*.
The impurity called Māyā is said to be the cause of making objects [of consciousness] into objects of knowledge;
it is the root...

Thus, according to this view, because there is no internal contraction within extroversion, that nature of luminosity would exist toward all objects of knowledge; consequently, its manifestation as differentiated would result in omniscience. Yet, not everyone is omniscient.

Furthermore, even in the state of non-omniscience, there is a manifestation characterized by differentiation. This is because the category of objects of knowledge—comprising both gross and subtle forms—is now the object of a creative act characterized by a manifestation that was previously non-existent;
this is denoted by the term "effect" (*kārya*), referring to the creation of the elements (*bhūta-sṛṣṭi*) in the form of the perceiver. Now...

This is the occasion for inquiry. With the intention that the creation of entities is precisely what serves that purpose, the author of the commentary has shown only two of the four types of creation mentioned in the scriptures.
And thus, the manifestation of things as distinct when there is no omniscience is established in this way—provided that...

Even within the aspect of manifestation, there would be some contraction in the form "I am of the nature of consciousness"; for it is logical that the contracted aspect of manifestation as "I" has a restricted manifestation, like the visual light contracted by the hollow of a tube. Thus it has been said:
"But any other sense of 'I-ness' (ahambhāva) even toward objects of knowledge is the individual impurity (āṇava-mala).

Now, [one might object]: "In this way, since it falls entirely within the category of the grasped (grāhya), such as the body and so forth, it would once again be non-different from the relationship between the grasped and the grasper (grāhyagrāhakatā)."
(Page 61) Anticipating the objection that the term "grāhaka" (the grasper) is thus left unestablished in the sūtra, he says:
"And even the nature of the object of cognition (*vedyasvabhāva*). The word "then" (*tadānīm*) refers to the occasion [of the thought] "this body is emaciated," and so forth.

Let it be that the body and so forth possess manifest knowability; however, in cognitions such as "I am thin" or "I perceive the jar," there is only the overflowing manifestation of the very essence of the consecration of consciousness as "I," and not the aspect of being an object of perception. But [one might object]: if this is so, then for the "thinness" and so forth as well...

Since this-ness (*idantā*) necessarily arises from manifestation, if there is first of all a concealment by means of the form "I," then that is simply the nature of the Lord (*īśvara*); so what is the meaning of the word "as if" (*iva*)? And since the Lord is precisely the reality of the ultimate knowing subject (*pramātṛ*), what is the purpose of employing the term "grasper" (*grāhaka*)? Or, if it is not [concealment]...
"In that case, since the covering (ācchādana) is of the nature of an object of cognition (*grāhya-rūpa*) like a jar or other objects, what further purpose is served by it?"— to this,

he primarily addresses the first objection with the passage beginning "merely" (*kevalam*) and ending with "something other than the mass of objects of cognition" (*vedyarāśer anyaiva*). Incidentally, the second objection is also addressed right here.
It will be described as "it exists. That which is "that" appears to the Lord as the collection of entities. How so? He says:
"mutually," and so forth. These three are also specific modes of activity; each one is non-different from the others, and for that very reason, the universe alone is ultimately real.

"His form is such"— even so, there is no contradiction with the body that has arisen from the clarity of manifestation. But here, in this state of *māyā*, that which is distinct from other subjects and objects of knowledge,
consisting of the nature of breath (*prāṇa*), intellect (*dhī*), and the void (*śūnya*), through the immersion into the "I-sense" (*ahantā*)—

Through the consecration of the sovereignty of consciousness, it is called the "inner self" (pratyagātman), which is known by its own self-awareness as distinct from others; the connection is that this [self], having become the subject (grāhaka), [perceives] an object (grāhya) external to itself, such as a jar or the like.

Furthermore, because it participates in the contraction of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, that consciousness is called "atomic" (*aṇu*) due to its limitation, as it cannot tolerate its own universal form. Yet, in this regard, there is no such thing as a "first occurrence" for the Blessed One concerning the power of *māyā*, which produces the dyad of the grasped and the grasper; thus, His eternity remains intact.

It has been said: "But surely, if that [objectivity] has been dissolved into the consciousness of the vital breath and so forth through the penetration of the sense of 'I', then there is once again no distinction between objects from that [consciousness]. True; however, it is not that the distinction consisting in their being perceived as "mine" has been dissolved.
(Page 62) In this regard, because that which is firmly grasped is not set aside, the definition of a bound soul (*paśu*) is thereby accepted. As it is said in the *Śrīkiraṇā*:
The individual soul (paśu) is eternal, formless, ignorant, inactive, devoid of qualities, and powerless;
it is all-pervasive, situated within the belly of Māyā, and is incapable of reflecting upon the attainment or loss of enjoyments.

Thus: due to the connection with the fetters (pāśa) such as atomicity (aṇutva), he is a bound soul (paśu); due to being beginningless, he is eternal; due to the penetration of the sense of "I" (ahantā), he is formless and all-pervasive; because he is by nature an object of cognition, he is devoid of knowledge and action;
he has fallen into the realm of Māyā, and for that very reason, he is not independent, since he is a cognizer.

He has transcended the multitude of qualities such as the *sattva* that are objects of cognition; yet, even while being of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*), because he is incomplete, he is overcome by a longing for enjoyment, since he incessantly desires fullness. He applies this to the present context with the words "it is another indeed. In the manner thus described, such is the state of being an object of cognition (*vedyatā*) regarding the body and so forth.

That which is neither an object knowable by Īśvara nor an object knowable by worldly beings such as a jar, and whose state of being a knower is also distinct from the state of being a knower belonging to Īśvara— for this reason,
therefore, even the two aspects of "this" and "I" [possess] a form that is grounded in Īśvara.

The state of being distinct (*vilakṣaṇatva*) pertains to the subject of *māyā*; therefore, the meaning of the word "as if" (*iva*) in the phrase "as if [the state] of the Lord" is appropriate. He clarifies the absence of dissolution with the words "for thus" (*tathāhi*). For, in whatever measure the state of being an object (*vedyatā*) of the vital breaths and so forth is removed through the power of the instruction on contemplation (*bhāvanā*), that very state of being the knower (*vedakatā*) [remains].

It is manifested; and in that very manner, from the arising of the attribute of the sovereignty of consciousness (*saṃvitsvātantrya*), there arises the attainment of powers such as moving through the air (*khecaratva*). This principle applies even to the body—that even objects like jars appear as its peers—let alone the intellect, the vital breath, and so forth; this is the meaning of the particle *eva* (indeed). Now, [an objection]: [The text continues: "But..."

Regarding what was stated—that there would be a separation caused by *māyā*—it might follow that impurity would belong to the Blessed One himself due to his connection with *māyā*. To this he says "no": "This [is *māyā*]" (*seyam*). In such a supremely wondrous manifestation, that sovereignty characterized by non-obstruction exists within—
It is of the nature of a manifestation of the accumulation of characteristics that expand the mass of established entities; it does not imply impurity, as in the case of a magician.
For impurity is characterized by the obstruction of the consciousness's desired object, whereas this [manifestation] is its opposite: the possession of unimpeded autonomy.

Thus ends the perception of the contradictory nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*). Now, if the body and so forth—which are strictly objects of cognition—are themselves treated as the cognizer, then what is the cognizer of that [body] in its state as an object? He says: "When... and "that very same... which refers to that [cognizer].

Regarding the object to be grasped, such as a jar, it has been made into a grasper. The intention is that this refers to a yogi who desires to grasp [the object] through direct perceptual knowledge (*sākṣātkāra-jñāna*). The consciousness-principle (*cit-tattva*), which was previously contracted by the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of the entire body, vital breath, intellect, and so forth, becomes the perceiver of those very things—the vital breath, the intellect, and the rest.
Even in the direct realization that "this is the absence of breath and so forth," there arises—
relative to that [absence]— another void consisting of the negation of the very form of that which was cognizable,
as if it were expanded; and within that too, by a sequence beginning with "even more expanded," and so on.

In the Āgamas, the ultimate form of the subject (pramātṛ), which is expressed by the term "the emptiness of emptiness" (śūnyātiśūnya), shines forth as the Great Emptiness (mahāśūnya). Nor should it be said that this [Great Emptiness] is merely of the nature of existence because it is the "absence of absence"; for if it were so, then since an absence is of the nature of a void, another absence would likewise be of the nature of a void.

This will be explained: with respect to the object of knowledge (*vedya*), the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*) is insubstantiality; and through the falling away of the wall [of duality], it is the state of being the knower (*vedakatva*). For this very reason, that which is called the "void beyond the void" (*śūnyātiśūnya*) is the nature of pure consciousness, entirely free from the mass of objects of knowledge.
Because it is known through the self-awareness of consciousness (*citsvasaṃvedana*), there is no infinite regress. As it has been said:
"For whatever is perceived, in that [process] there is no 'I' whatsoever;
rather, I am liberated from this, and I am not such as to be an object of sight."
Thus, the negation of objective existence is established in reality as the state of "I-consciousness" (ahaṃbhāva);
for a yogin’s vision, this perceivable world, beginning with the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), appears clearly as that very consciousness.
In that regard, even the negation of existence is not absolutely void;
because it ascends into the consciousness of the "I," it is therefore identical with that very [consciousness].

Thus, for this very reason, the scripture states that through the practice of meditative absorption on space (*ākāśa-samāpatti*), by means of practicing the gradual expansion of one's focus from the interior of a house, to the courtyard, to the forest, and so forth, one attains absorption in the supreme space (*paramākāśa*) that exists outside the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).

In this context, regarding the "Great Bodilessness" (*mahāvidehā*) which is the unconstructed external state of being, this very same ultimate nature of having space as one's body is stated as that which is to be attained.
Through a gradual process, the body becomes an object of cognition; then its vital breath (*prāṇa*), then the intellect (*dhī*) of that [breath], and then the void (*śūnya*) of that [intellect].

(Page 64) This meaning, namely "the knower" (*vedaka*), is well known and thus has not been explicitly stated here; however, according to the sequence [of the argument], if everything is an object of cognition (*vedya*), then emptiness alone is the knower. Now, [one might ask] regarding the yogi:
For one who has ascended to asamprajñāta-samādhi preceded by the practice of the causal sign of cessation (virāma-pratyaya),

it is possible to bring about the non-objectivity of the body, vital breath, and so forth; however, the non-yogi has not even heard of a void that transcends the body and its constituents, even by word— hearing— so how could this [state] be for him in comparison to that?
Anticipating the objection that [the body] must be an object of cognition, he says: "But by another.
This means that there is no direct perception of this body and so forth—which is untouched by the sense of "I"—as being of the same nature as external objects of cognition such as a jar;
rather, the direct perception is simply "I am this," and only that. As for its status as an object of cognition...

By this [means] it is conceptualized, but its supreme state— being entirely free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as existence, substantiality, whiteness, and so forth— is not directly realized, just as [the true nature] of a substance is not realized when it is merely conceptualized.
Furthermore, in the act of conceptualization, one need not await the attainment of that [supreme] form, for the sake of establishing its status as pure objectivity (*vedyatā*).

There would be a search for another means of knowledge (*vedaka*). For one who, while still living in the world of mortals, imagines for himself the state of being a dweller in heaven, does not depend upon the actual attainment of that [state]. Therefore, this is the formal argument: the attainment of that form must be expected through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because it is not of the nature of direct perception (*asākṣātkārātmakatvāt*).
For the conformity of cognition to the intrinsic nature of an object is pervaded by its being of the nature of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*);

otherwise, nothing would constitute a direct perception. And since the state of being a direct perception is contrary to that [conformity], this is an "observation of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). [Objection: But in the case of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, which are objects of knowledge...
Let pure consciousness alone be called the subject; why is the void postulated in the interval?
Nevertheless, such is the realization of the yogi: whatever is conceptualized, none of that possesses that [conceptualized] form.

Thus, regarding this Self which—by the principle of "not this, not this" (neti neti)—is liberated from all that is knowable: as for the notion "I am," such as the worldly person thinks, "I am hungry," "I am thirsty," or "I am happy," what is the purpose of such a conceptualization? It is said [in response]: nevertheless, even though the yogi perceives the body and so forth simultaneously.

What is the use of an internal void in the interval? To this he replies: "Otherwise. If the void were not a perceiver (*vedaka*), then nothing would manifest as distinct from the Great Light, because it would follow that there is no manifestation at all; thus, how could the state of being an object (*vedyatā*), which exists through its very life of differentiation, [be established]?

(page 65) It would follow [that the Lord is not omniscient]. Now, one might object: when the Supreme Lord, for the sake of bestowing grace, teaches himself directly to his disciples, saying "I alone am your Self," then [the objection applies] to the Blessed One who is the knower.

What else could there be that is to be known? It is said: "even when... Here, "that" refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*). By the inclusion of the word "or" in the phrase "as the Lord or as manifestation," he says this: indeed, the undivided nature of pure consciousness does not become an object of knowledge; rather, it appears as such through the exclusion of what is not its own nature.

Knowing [this], the Lord, having created that which was to be produced as a manifestation never before seen—a form through the medium of various attributes—reflects upon that very thing and instructs his disciples: "This Lord, who is my own form, is your Self," but he does not [mean] the form of the Veda itself. In that regard also:

That which exists as self-luminous by virtue of being the teacher is precisely what ought to be taught and instructed to disciples as their own Self; this is the logical position. The body and so forth, however, are not fit to be taught as the Self; this serves as a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). As they have said:
The feet of the Siddhas have traversed this path; that majesty of yours is beyond the reach of speech and mind,
which expresses it with trepidation only by way of negating what it is not— even the Veda does so.

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the phrase *tadeva*, other [authorities] read it as *tadaivam*. That appearance of the Self (*ātmābhāsa*), being a created [manifestation], is not an object of knowledge (*vedya*) common to all subjects like the body and so forth; rather, it shines forth supremely within the consciousness and the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of both the teacher and the disciple, but not externally—this is the meaning.
"Like the body and so forth"—by the method thus stated, the form of the Veda is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). Now, it may be objected:

"In this way, the Blessed One has not taught his own form to his disciples as their very Self (*ātman*), but rather as some kind of created appearance (*nirmita-ābhāsa*. To this he replies: "And because of the identity of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa-ekya*)."

"Even that" refers to the essential nature previously described as consisting of appearances; "that very same" means it is indeed the essential nature of the Supreme Lord and nothing more, as will be stated in the passage:
"He who has not been liberated by his own freedom... (1.5.16).
In this context, the intention is that the manifestation is first denoted as merged with its own essential nature, namely "that" (*tad*).
(Page 66)

The neuter form in the word *tadapi* is appropriate. He concludes with *tadevam* for the sake of stabilizing the disciple’s intellect, summarizing the true nature of the meaning of the Sūtra which has been interspersed with many other subjects of knowledge (*prameya*). It has been stated that the state of being an object of cognition (*vedyatā*)—whether it be that of a jar and so forth, the body and so forth, or the essential nature itself—is manifold, appearing in forms such as direct perception, conceptualization, and the like.

The manifold nature of the subject has been described for the illusory perceiver (māyā-pramātṛ), the yogin, Īśvara, and the Lord Paramaśiva. This very dyad of the grasped and the grasper is differentiated by infinite internal subdivisions.
Since it shines as that very form within the Blessed One, whose nature is supreme light— just as a mirror reflects an image and thus possesses the manifold forms of the objects within it—
this is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason). For if shining as that form were to occur in something that is not identical with it, [it would be a contradiction].

That would be indeterminate; for even a jar might manifest as a cloth, which entails the consequence of indeterminacy that contradicts the rule of pervasion. Therefore, manifesting in that form is excluded from the counter-example (the vipakṣa) because of being non-identical with it, and is thus pervaded by identity with it.
The non-establishment of the pervaded. || 8 ||
Thus ends the fourth reflection on the power of memory in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī*, composed by the illustrious Great Māheśvara, the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. || 4 ||

Now begins the fifth investigation: I praise that abode which, through the desire for the blossoming of bliss arising from unsurpassed enlightenment, is full, sovereign, and beautiful with the surging flood of nectar.

Having thus reflected upon the power of memory and, by extension, the operation of conceptual construction, [the author] now proceeds to an investigation of the power of knowledge upon which both depend, concerning the manifestations of the present...
With these twenty-one verses beginning with "ityādyayā" and ending with "sakramaṃ pratibhāsate," he examines [the subject] in detail. In that regard, such being the case...

With the verse beginning "jñānaśakti," he makes his formal proposition; with the following two verses, he states that light alone is the true nature of objects. Having raised a doubt regarding the existence of objects external to light—using the arguments against the Vijñānavāda to strengthen his position—he proceeds with the next two verses.

By the first [verse], he states that even if those [external objects] do not exist, nothing at all is obstructed. Demonstrating the reality of the object within his own philosophical system, he rejects perception regarding an external object by means of one [verse], and inference by means of two. This is because objects necessarily exist within the conscious self (*cidātman*) by virtue of their being of the nature of mental reflection (*parāmarśa*).
One [teacher] said: "The essence of the light whose nature is the subject is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) alone.
By means of a fourfold [exposition] consisting of the determination of experience, scripture, logic, and the essential nature [of reality], he said:
"The object of knowledge is nothing other than the reflective awareness of cognition, which is pure and does not abandon its state as the subject."
By the triad beginning with "it expands," [the author] shows that even though its nature is solely luminosity,

there is a distinction between knowledge and the knower and so forth by means of one [verse]; and by the dyad [beginning with "just as in the knower"], he shows that in pure knowledge as well— which possesses both non-conceptual and conceptual forms— its very life is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) alone.

The intention is as follows: by way of a conclusion, he supports with a single argument that which was refuted in the prima facie position regarding the difference between the knower and the known— namely,
"the manifestation of existing entities as they appear."
It is only for those who exist within that it is possible [to appear] by means of an external form. || 1 ||

To begin with, in the case of recollection and conceptualization, the object does not appear as something distinct and common to all cognizers. Even in that [other] experience which is of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is nonetheless not separate from that experience itself.

"What need is there to speak of [the same] regarding memory and other such functions that depend upon it?"—thus, both the word *api* ("even") and the word *yāvat* ("as far as") have been read in the commentary (*vṛtti*) as supplementary to the sūtra. As for the meaning of the sūtra: those [cognitions] which manifest with the form "this" (*idam*) due to their vividness and presence are [perceived] as external in nature.
They are differentiated by way of their separation from the subject of Māyā, such as Śūnya and the rest;
therefore, they are severed from that subject of Māyā. That manifestation of theirs, which occurs through such limitation, belongs only to those who remain within [the sphere of Māyā].

It is logically consistent— that is, it is established by valid means of knowledge— for those who do not abandon their identity with the ultimate subject (pramātṛtattva), whose nature is pure consciousness. That which is the manifestation of an object as if separated, from the perspective of an imagined subject, while its non-difference from consciousness remains unrenounced, is [the power] of the Lord.

This refers to the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*). The word "now" clarifies that this is a different mode [of manifestation]. The remainder is clear from the commentary (*vṛtti*) and its exposition (*vivṛti*). || 1 ||
Regarding the statement "it has been indicated," the author of the *Ṭīkā* introduces the following aphorism based upon that indication:
"Prior to [its own] manifestation, the object would be unmanifest, since it lacks the nature of light.
Furthermore, the light of the object cannot be distinct from the self, for the object's very nature is light. (2)

The first half [of the verse] removes the duality between the object and its manifestation from both sides, by stating "without being of the nature of light": it is not logical for an object to be manifest if it is distinct from light, nor is it logical for light to exist if it is distinct from the manifest object.

He explains it in brief: just as when cognition does not arise, blue is neither blue for everyone nor for anyone at all, but rather only within itself; and even within itself, it is nothing at all—so too would it be even when cognition has arisen, and it would not manifest as "this blue is mine"; [it] "would be" (syāt).

"Its identity with light would not exist as before"—this is the second [point], expressed by the words "the very nature of experience" (*anubhavarūpataiva*) and so forth. Since, as in the previous case, there would be a lack of manifestation, therefore that which is called "manifestation" is not distinct from the object. From this, it follows that [the object is] light.

Such is the nature of the object. And thus says the commentary: "That light which constitutes its own essential nature is the very luminosity of the object; it is not something distinct from that object" (page 69).

"Manifestation" (prakāśaḥ) is that which is the state of an object being manifest; this is what is logical. Alternatively, the introduction of the first half-verse is concluded with the words "prasaṅgāt," while the summary of the meaning of the third quarter is stated by the words "arthācca" and so forth. And this is the meaning:

In response to the doubt that "let luminosity be resting solely within the body of the object, and like the object, possess a distinct nature," he says: "And luminosity cannot be distinct. If it were of the same nature as the object, then, like the object, its difference [from other objects] would follow; yet that is not tenable, because it would entail the impossibility of synthetic unification (*anusandhāna*).

He explains this with the words "and from the object" (*arthācca*). If the object itself consists of the nature of being manifest, then for that reason, a difference would result within the light itself; or else, there would be a difference in the essential nature belonging to that light which exists by depending upon it.

[One] attains [it]. And that is not logical. Therefore, what is called the "manifestness" (*prakāśamānatā*) of an object is the self, its ultimate form; it is not some separate entity. Furthermore, the manifestness of an object is its nature as experience (*anubhava-rūpatā*), which is the self; it is not [something other than] manifestness itself.
"the nature of the object itself"—thus it is said. In this view, the function (*vṛtti*) is to be understood as follows:

that which is the manifestness of the object is the light, the experience (*anubhava*); however, this light, whose essence is manifestness, does not constitute the very nature of the object, nor is it submerged within the body of the object. For if that were the case, [the following would occur]:

It might be argued that [the jar] would be distinct due to a difference in its objective nature (*arthabheda*), yet it is not logically so. Now, one might object: "The very nature of the jar is its jar-ness; that existed even prior to the arising of the cognition. So what else is there for it to be 'manifest'? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of the jar... not anything," and so forth. For this is as follows:

The true nature of the Supreme is such because it cannot be established as something other than itself; however, what was stated previously—that [the teaching] is equally useful for all—was said with reference to a hypothetical inquiry based on the possibility [of its being otherwise], since it is equally applicable to everyone. For even utility depends upon the state of being manifest, and not merely upon the existence of a thing. Now, one might object:

From the causal material (upādāna) in the form of the moment of the jar, which is assisted by other factors such as the sense faculties, there arises a specific moment characterized by the appearance of the jar; thus, there is indeed a distinction from its prior state at the time of the arising of consciousness. However, for us, this is not like the [distinction] maintained by those who assert the existence of permanent entities.

In response to the doubt, "Is this indeed that very jar?", he says: "Moreover... [and] "of the cognizer. For it is from that—that is, from the causal complex consisting of the sense organs and so forth—[that the cognition of] the jar arises.

A distinction arises from the state of being manifest, and even from light; for even in the case of light, there is a difference in its primary nature from the jar and so forth. Furthermore, the arising of cognition occurs within the continuum of the subject (pramātṛ) with respect to the jar and the light;
and in that regard, just as that arising of cognition does not exist in relation to the jar, nor does the jar exist in relation to the light.

Even though the causality is equal, or even when there is dependence on the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*), [an entity] attains the status of being an object of linguistic usage (*vyavahāryatā*) because its own nature is self-contained; likewise, that specific quality residing in the jar called "manifestness" would not be an object of linguistic usage for the cognizer. For whatever [belongs] to whom...

Its own nature (*svarūpa*) does not reside in another, as the nature of blue does not reside in yellow; likewise, the manifestation of the jar does not reside in the subject (*pramātṛ*). If it were to reside in another, its status as its own nature would be untenable, because it would entail the superimposition of contradictory attributes. For [to say it] resides in another...

"Identity with another" is not "being one's own nature"; thus, there is the perception of a contradictory nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*). For the very purpose of indicating this formal argument (*prayoga*), he states explicitly—even though it was already implied by the sense—"it would simply not exist. Now, [this means] being established in its own nature alone.
If it is argued that this is designated as such precisely because conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) spread without obstruction, then a restriction would be untenable, according to the principle:
"Where there is autonomy of will... To demonstrate this, he says: "or for all subjects (*pramātṛ*). But [one might object]: "Which one indeed..."

The manifestation of the specific state of being a jar—which is such [as it appears] through the senses and so forth—becomes the cause for its arising; it is designated as such only in relation to that very subject (pramātṛ). Thus, the rule is established.
He refutes this with "no" (na hi). Regarding the phrase "for the sake of utility," it does not mean that the state of being a jar belongs to the potter alone.

[Objection: But surely, a relationship of cause and effect is observed in the case of the seed and the sprout, or the potter and the jar; in the same way, it will be that Caitra’s jar is manifesting. This much is what is to be proven here, and that is already established. So what further utility [is there]?
With the intention of [addressing] this [objection], he raises a doubt with the words "But even if... He does not tolerate this, meaning it is not tenable.
By this much, it has been stated that the manifestation belongs to the jar as produced by that [consciousness].
(page 71)

Just as sprout-ness is produced by the seed and pot-ness is produced by the potter, yet that sprout-ness and pot-ness are not conventionally designated by relying upon the causal complex as their basis while it is being engaged in its own functional activity at that time, but rather only in dependence upon the appearance of those causes.

This is because of the conventional usage regarding the nature of the sprout and so forth. However, the state of being manifest is invariably employed in convention by depending upon a foundational subject (pramātṛ), such that one says "it belongs to me" or "it belongs to Caitra. This conventional usage, which is restricted by its adherence to that [subject], brings about identity (*tādātmya*).

Just as the reflection of a jar appears as if adhering to a mirror, identity (*tādātmya*) consists in having that very form, whereas being established in itself (*svaniṣṭhatva*) consists in not having that form. How, then, could a single entity possess these two distinct forms—one its own and the other belonging to another?
For manifestation is simply the state of the jar being made manifest.
It brings about identity with the subject (*pramātṛtādātmya*) by necessity, because it appears as being invariably attached to that [subject];

and since identity with the jar (*ghaṭatādātmya*) is its very nature, how could it appear by transcending that? Even purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), appearing in this way, becomes such [only through that identity]; thus, in that case too, this same [principle] applies.
The word "object" (*artha*) is used to convey the final sense that, even through causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), externality is not established according to the view of Dharmottara. As Bhaṭṭa said:
"By means of [cognitions] which are inseparable from manifestation and whose nature is restricted to existence..."
An entity distinct from its properties does not attain external establishment.

Thus [it is said]. For nowhere has that state of being manifest ever been seen appearing as the subject while not resting upon the wall [of the object], such that we might establish its reality there and claim that [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to it; with this intention, he says: "and not having its own nature."

Now, one might raise the following objection: "Is it not the case that the external object, whose distinctions are established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is essentially nothing more than a collection of atoms? While being designated through mental projection (*prathā*), it may appear through delusion as if connected to something else, like a gross form. What contradiction is there in this? Anticipating this view of the opponent, he says: "Of the light... (*prakāśasya*).

Error is defined as the state of appearing while not being engaged with a real object, and nothing else. And that [state] exists by virtue of being anchored in the substrate of the subject; yet since that [subject] is nothing at all, even the portion consisting of pure consciousness is not established.
Furthermore, in error, that [consciousness] exists as non-error.
(Page 72) This must necessarily be maintained, because one admits that there is error regarding the objective aspect (*arthāṃśa*).
If even the cognition itself were non-existent, it would be an error, and [the world] would become like a stone. According to this interpretation:

The Teacher reads the word *na* [negation] as "the white conch is not manifesting. If it does not undergo any manifestation at all, then to say that a white conch manifests as yellow is a hollow statement.
However, if it is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that the object of illumination possesses the nature of the illuminator itself—
In that case, the negative particle (*nañ*) is supplied and read [in the text]. And thus the construction is as follows:

regarding what was stated by the opponent—that "difference is established by means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*)—the valid cognition here is indeed manifestation (*prakāśa*). Therefore, if difference is established [by that], yet the conventional usage of it being attached to something else occurs through delusion (*bhrānti*), then this [following] has been said.

It is argued that [the object] is established as distinct from manifestation; therefore, because it appears as distinct from the consciousness of manifestation, yet due to delusion appears as "mine" by being attached to it through identity with that consciousness. But this is not tenable within a single act of engagement.

Because it is impossible for that which appears as having either that form or a non-that form [to be otherwise]; for it does not happen that a white conch, while appearing as such, appears as yellow. Thus, having stated the impossibility of a difference from the light on account of its being manifest, [the author proceeds] by way of purifying his own intention and with a primary focus on the purification of the object.

Manifesting the discursive nature of the treatise’s discourse, he first propounds reasoning by way of raising a doubt, [saying] "this is thus. Because it cannot be established otherwise, that [reasoning] is expressed as "therefore this is so";
thus, "thus" (evam) refers to its appearing as a distinct entity through delusion.

"It occurs according to the method that will be explained"—this is what is being considered. He states that which is to be explained with the words "if it is the jar itself. The particle *eva* (itself/only) implies that there is no other manifestation whatsoever.
Thus, the meaning of the particle *eva* is brought forward by the word "itself" (*eva*), such that the possibility [is raised] that "the jar is nothing other than this."

He indicates the seed with the words "in this way, for one [subject]": as for the contradiction stated—that at that very same time, by the power of cognition, [the object] is both different and non-different from the Light—that does not occur, because there is no difference between the Light and the jar. Furthermore, the manifestation of difference is possible even when there is non-difference.

For even when there is the perception of a single nature in a stone statue, the conceit of difference— such as "this is its body"— occurs through the power of conceptual construction; it is merely a conventional usage based on prior cognition.

The term "unreal" (*ayathāvastu*) indicates everything, including the conventional usage of terms such as "clothing" and so forth, as well as the conventional usage of "error" when there is no prior cognition [of reality]. He states the reason for this with the words "even there" (*tatrāpi*). The word *pratheta* is used in the optative mood (*liṅ*) in the sense of a reason.
For in both positions, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is that consciousness consists of the jar, and the jar consists of consciousness.

The distinction consisting of the relationship between subject and object—expressed as "the consciousness of the jar" or "the jar of consciousness"—cannot manifest itself by subverting its fundamental non-difference; for the manifestation of a distinction, such as "the body of a stone statue," does not subvert the manifestation of non-distinction. Indeed, if it were to subvert it...

The cause is the state of uprooting that [usage]; its opposite is the state of not uprooting it. Pervaded by that [non-uprooting] is the state of being of the nature of that usage, because it is rooted in it. By means of this, the absence of the effect of that which is incompatible with its own pervader is established.

This is the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory of the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). "That" refers to the reason previously stated. "In this way" means that since a difference between consciousness and the jar must necessarily be admitted; however, because it is possible for that [difference] to be two-sided, when there is doubt, there is merely the exclusion of other alternatives.

This must be done in order to cause the subjects of illusion (*māyā-pramātṛ*) to realize it. In reality, however, the jar is consciousness and consciousness is the jar; thus, no distinction whatsoever exists here, as was shown in the *Ādisiddhasūtra*:
"He who sees me... (Bhagavad Gītā 6.31).

By such statements as these, it is shown that the subjects under the influence of *māyā*— those who are to be instructed— do not yet conceive of the jar itself as being completely delimited "as this" due to their grasping at duality; nor do they conceive of it as insentient, precisely because of its insentience, [and thus fail to realize its nature as light].

Since it is initially unestablished, it cannot endure being treated as a mere restatement (anuvāda), and because it lacks expectancy for something else, it is incomplete; and if consciousness were taught as non-different from these [objects],
then that too would be perceived as being similarly limited.

And they would intend [an object] that is devoid of the connection with the consciousness of another cloth and so forth, which is insentient, which serves as the locus for the existence of positive attributes such as the nature of consciousness, and which, by virtue of having no further requirements,
is simply fit to appear as "this. And [they would intend] the opposite of this.

Its reality must be taught in such a way that its ultimate truth enters the heart correctly, without inversion; just as, although the properties of being a tree and being a *śiṃśapā* are in fact coextensive (*samavyāptika*), they differ in their fitness for conventional usage.

(Page 74) The state of being a *śiṃśapā* is taught as the pervaded (*vyāpya*), not as the pervader (*vyāpaka*), because it is excluded from non-trees, or because the universal of "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatva-sāmānya*) also exists in *dhava* trees and others.

Because it is the object of conventional discourse, the Lord, in accordance with those to be instructed, first taught the reality of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*) as having the nature of Śiva: in some Āgamas primarily by way of its transcendence of all things,
in others by way of its acceptance as consisting of all things, and in still others for the sake of manifesting both forms.

It has been taught. Regarding that which is to be taught here for those of the first aeon (*prāthamakalpika*), this was stated with the introductory phrase "firstly" (*tāvat*) with the intention that, at the outset, the non-dual [reality] should be taught by way of consciousness (*saṃvit*).

The imperative mood (*loṭ*) in the word "let it be" (*astu*) is used to express the appropriateness of the time in order to denote that very state of being for those of the first aeon. And then... [it is said].

By the locative case, he indicates that the resolution of the contradiction previously mentioned regarding duality has already been accomplished in the state where consciousness itself— transcending objects such as the jar— accepts and assumes an infinite variety of forms like the jar, by way of the analogy of the mirror. By means of the jar...
He states that even the defect which was suspected regarding the teaching of non-duality does not apply here,
by saying "in other objects of cognition" (*prameyāntare*). For one who maintains non-duality while asserting the primacy of jars and the like,
there would first of all be other subjects (*pramātrantara*) in relation to those other objects of cognition, consisting of conceptual and non-conceptual forms of consciousness.

The synthesis (*anusandhāna*) of those many cognitions— which, according to our view, are metaphorically conceived through their connection with the coloring (*uparāga*) of the objects of a single knower, such that "I who know the jar and so forth am the very same one who knows the cloth and so forth"— as well as the synthesis [of these cognitions] even with other knowers such as Caitra and Maitra; [this is what is meant].
For one who possesses the perfected and unwavering consciousness, as stated by the venerable Parameṣṭhin:
"I have no satisfaction from worship, nor indeed any weariness from non-worship;
worship is always performed through non-differentiation from the worshippers" (Śivadr̥ṣṭi 7.93).
Thus, it has been said by the venerable supreme teacher as well: "The vision of things exactly as they exist... (Uttara-stotra 13.7), and so too by the Blessed One.
"He who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction—
he is wise among men; he is called a performer of all actions" (Bhagavad Gītā 4.18).

Thus [it is said]: the state of being the agent of all actions and the capacity to sever the bonds of all karmas, together with the reflective awareness (*anusandhāna*) of the previously established specific subject (*pramātṛviśeṣa*) along with the specific objects of knowledge (*prameyaviśeṣa*), such as "I know blue"; and the [awareness] of one object of knowledge in relation to another object of knowledge.

The various modes of relation, whether in the form of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or otherwise— such as "the wood-apple is blue," "it is sweet," or "water with a jar"— all of these are logically possible because [consciousness] is non-inert, possesses a single nature, and is established prior [to all objects].

In order to show that all this is inseparable from the nature of luminosity (*prakāśa*), luminosity is presented as the substratum (*dharmin*) by means of the genitive case, serving as the foundation. "Because it is eternally established" means that it is free from expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*) due to its independence from objects of cognition (*vedya*). "Having resolved" (*āgūrya*) means with the heart.
Raising the point for discussion: by qualifying the Light with the term "subject" (*pramātṛ*), one expresses its independent nature as distinct from [mere] cognition; thus, all this is accepted.
In the quarter-verse of the *Gītā*, the two locative cases express the state of being an object characterized as "existence nowhere else."
And he demonstrates that the fullness [of reality] resides precisely in the state of instruction with the words, "even though its nature is light" (*prakāśātmano'pi ca*).

For even from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), what else is there called a "pot"? Therefore, how can the charge of duality be leveled against the non-dual? Since only light exists, what is the meaning of "both"?

For instance, regarding what is said—namely, "as before," "just as at the beginning," or "distinct from its previous form"—is this merely a matter of reflection based on the assumption that some jar appears with a nature that is not luminosity? [One might object: "But isn't luminosity the very essence of the jar?"

What is this [point] regarding the commentary? For the jar is the substratum (*dharmin*), and that [existence] is its property (*dharma*). He refutes this by saying "another property" (*dharmāntara*). And this [is the principle]: "The identity of things occurring at different times... (1.4.3).
