This has been explained here [in the previous section]. Now, one might object: "An insentient entity (*aprakāśātman*) shines forth precisely through its connection with consciousness. To this he replies: "By its very own nature" (*svarūpeṇaiva*). For when it is said that "it shines forth," if the object were not permeated by that [consciousness], then it would be the case that something which is itself not shining forth is being made to shine forth. And this...

To say this would indeed be a cause for shame; for it was precisely for this purpose that the inherence (*samavāya*) with the quality of whiteness was accepted, so that the palace itself might be made white in nature. Otherwise, the quality of whiteness here [would be useless].

(Page 76) If it were said that [the person] is situated neither in a white palace nor in a non-white one, then by the power of inherence (*samavāya*), only the mere relationship of locus and located would be perceived, as in the case of a mat and Caitra. But surely—
The quality of whiteness inheres in the palace; therefore, let it be said that there is a state of non-difference [between them] in that case.

But light, whose nature is cognition, does not inhere in the object, but rather in the self. Alas! In that case, even the subject under discussion is ruined. For in the absence of a connection with light, how could the object [be manifest]?
"It shines forth. But was it not said that its very cognition is the shining? In that case, "that object shines forth" means this: "this is the cognition, and this is within the Self.
As stated previously, by saying this, the identity of the object, the cognition, and the Self would have been demonstrated. But [one might object]: "But..."
If the manifestation of an object were distinct from the light that constitutes our own nature—that is, from the subject—then it would be "the jar manifests to me," and not "I manifest as the jar.
True, this manifestation as a separation does exist; however, it belongs to the imagined subject, such as the body and so forth.

Because it is characterized by qualities such as attenuation (*kṛśa*) and so forth, it is precisely that for which the state of being an object of knowledge has not yet dissolved, and upon which the status of a subject (*pramātṛbhāva*) has been superimposed by the power of *māyā*. Of what nature is it? It is the ultimate ground (*niṣṭhā*) of those various states (*avasthiti*) of objects such as blue and so forth, which exist through both their differentiation and their specific distinctions.

That state of the subject is such: it consists of that very Light which, being free from desire and resting because there is no separate [object] existing apart from it, has attained a state of having a locus—even though it is without a locus—by becoming the foundational wall. It is not, however, [the state of the subject] when it is uncontracted by the body and so forth.

The manifestation of a jar or other objects occurs as distinct from the light of ultimate reality (paramārtha-prakāśa), which is devoid of any fragmented or variegated state due to its lack of non-luminosity; the reason for this is their "non-luminosity" (aprakāśatā). || 2 ||
Thus, first of all, the claim that cognition is distinct from the object and yet constitutes its manifestation is an untenable position. Or, even if it were granted;
[the author] demonstrates by means of a sūtra that if such a distinction is admitted, it would lead to the undesirable consequence of a confusion of the essential natures of the objects.
If the light were both differentiated and non-differentiated, there would be a confusion of objects;
for an object to be manifested must have the nature of light, and that which is not light cannot be established.
That light which, being undivided, consists of pure consciousness alone, is nothing at all with respect to objects.

Because it is impossible for something distinct to reside in another [as its substrate], such being the case, there is the capacity for blue and other objects to be colored by the very nature of that [consciousness] through the power of manifestation; thus we have "blue manifestation" and "yellow manifestation. In this regard, because all objects are included within manifestation, [it is called] manifestation.

Thus, only this much non-dual reality remains. Furthermore, the distinction between blue and yellow must be admitted on the basis of the power of manifestation (*prakāśa*). And that manifestation is non-dual and identical in both cases. If, by virtue of its favoring one, it is blue, why is it not yellow, or rather, why is it not non-blue?

Nor is it yellow; furthermore, even that would not be established. Even the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda) would fail to find a firm footing. There would be no determination of such things as the clarity of an object known by a single cognition, nor of memory and so forth;
thus, there would be a manifold confusion. Therefore, if for manifestation...

[If one argues that] there is a confusion [of categories], the word "ca" (and) is used to indicate this. "That" means: since in this way a confusion would necessarily follow if light were distinct from the object, and yet it is not so; therefore, by implication, light is non-different from the manifesting object. For if there were difference, there would be a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).
Through the connection with objects, such as through proficiency and so forth, and by way of recollection and the like, there arises the contingency of the light being mixed with its objects.
Yet, its non-mixture with objects is perceived, which is contrary to that [contingency].

Thus, by the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), the distinctness of the light from the object is negated. But [it may be objected]: [The objection continues: "But..."

Let the object itself, such as blue and so forth, be thus; what is the use of postulating a cognition called "manifestation" (prakāśa) that has a nature distinct from it yet is non-different from its own essence, which only brings about the defect of the object being conflated with the subject? He says: "And not unmanifest. The word "and" (ca) serves to indicate the prima facie position.

This is what is meant: for that which is non-luminous and insentient (*jaḍa*), there is no establishment whatsoever within itself. For it has been said: "If blue were previously not-blue in itself, or if it were nothing else at all, what would be the harm in that?
And thus, the establishment of the non-insentient subject (*ajaḍapramātṛ*) follows.
"Thus, these insentient things, which are mere mental constructs regarding the self, exist only as manifestations of light;
for light alone exists by its own nature through itself and others.
(13) Therefore, the meaning of the aphorism is that the object is indeed non-different from consciousness, whose nature is light. [In the Vṛtti:]

By the word *mātra*, mere non-difference is explained; thus, the foundation for the suspicion of confusion—arising from [the light's] being common to all objects—is established. "Of that" refers to the pure manifestation (*prakāśamātra*).
(Page 78)
The connection is that the restriction of objects (*viṣayaniyama*) is without foundation and cannot be established by any reason whatsoever.

He demonstrates the form of this restriction of objects with the words "of a jar," and so forth. He explains the meaning of the third quarter of the verse in the commentary by the term "the nature of light" (*prakāśātmatā*), [interpreting it as] "the establishment of the object. That... [is as follows].

This has been explained by the word "tasmāt" (therefore). The author of the Vivṛti introduces [the next section] with the words "prakāśamānataiva" (manifestness itself) in order to briefly define this meaning. By this, the latter half of the verse was introduced first, because this subject matter is desired here; however, as a means to that [end],...
Having first explained the first half [of the verse] in brief and subsequently introduced it,
he explains the first half of the first verse by means of the words "tasya ca arthāt" and so forth.
By the phrase "prakāśasya," meaning "of the light that is devoid of forms such as blue," he explains the word *abhinnam*.

The phrase "in its own self alone" (*svātmamātre*) and so forth has been explained; however, the term "confusion" (*saṃkara*) has been explained by the phrase "with respect to a distinct object" (*viṣayāpekṣayā*) and so forth. The opponent does not accept what was stated regarding the fact that knowledge culminates in its own self alone, for knowledge is indeed of the nature of illuminating both itself and others; otherwise, it would be indistinguishable from the insentient (*jaḍa*).
What is the distinction? It is stated as follows: "Self and non-self" is of such a nature.

That which is the manifestation of the self-nature of that self—which consists of the illumination of both itself and others—is [the distinction]; it is not some other state of consciousness residing in another, by which [the distinction would be made].

One might raise an objection based on the distinction between self and other; he refutes this by saying "that is not so. For if even that which is accepted as "other," such as blue and so forth, were not to present its own nature here in this cognition under the guise of a reflection in a mirror, then the contradiction—given the opposition between self and non-self—would indeed be impossible to remove.
For it would necessarily follow that its being manifest [by itself] entails a difference in essential nature;
and thus the *Viniścaya* states, "It is not that," and so forth.
For this [work] establishes the non-difference between blue and the cognition thereof based on the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*).
Thus, it has been established that blue and so forth are merely the form of consciousness (*vijñānākāra*).

Furthermore, its manifestation as "cognition" (*saṃvedana*) is likewise due to its identity with that [form]; for that which is called "cognition" cannot logically belong to anything else distinct from cognition itself.

(Page 79) Having thus explained the first point— characterized by the impossibility of dependence on another in any way— in order to establish the confusion [of categories], [the author now addresses] the case where dependence on another is without basis.

He explains another point of this nature with the words "Or let it be," etc., [showing] that if one were to accept [the opponent's view], then because there would be no distinction, everything would result in being dependent on another; consequently, the non-confusion [of entities] produced by such fixed dependence on another would once again be untenable.

Consequently, the restriction is established solely by the possession of a form (sākāratā). As it has been said in that regard: "Since cognition is of a nature similar [to its object] through mere experience, it must possess that very nature by which it is differentiated according to each respective object."

Thus, the sense is that the blue form is not separate from cognition. Even without that form, there exists in each respective case—whether regarding a restricted object such as blue or yellow—a specific state of cognition consisting in its abiding in a particular manner; this is the "determination according to each object" (*pratikarma-vyavasthā*), which takes the form of a fixed dependence upon another [the object]. That [state]...

The opponent states "But even so" (*athāpi*) in order to establish [the object's status] through a different relationship. That very thing which, being situated in a suitable location, is the producer of cognition—that alone is the manifestation of that cognition;
that alone is the object (*viṣaya*) of the cognition. As it has been said: "That which is not a cause is not an object. This refers to the cognition (*saṃvedana*).

If it is argued that an object is perceived only through coexistence, then how can it be accepted that blue— which exists at a time prior to consciousness and serves as its cause— is called an "object," since such a claim is contradicted by experience? In that case, let the object be simultaneous with the cognition itself.

And proximity, which acts as the restrictor, consists in dependence upon a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*). For it is from a single such causal complex— characterized by the moment of the object and the cognition— which exists sequentially through their mutual relationship as material cause (*upādāna*) and auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*), that [the result arises].

Facing one another like a pair of bulls eager for the taste of combat, they became capable of union through the relationship of object and subject; they attained an awareness of objects characterized by the nature of the insentient and the sentient, acquired through a succession of material causes. Regarding this as well, he states the fault with the words "tato'pi" (even from that).

Furthermore, there is no distinction between blue and yellow regarding their capacity to tolerate the restriction of proximity, even based on the cause characterized by dependence on a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces them; otherwise, how could that cognition have both as its objects? Moreover, if [cognition] were formless, it would be [mere] consciousness.

That which is intense in the blue is experienced as dull by that which is intended [as the subject], or rather, it is precisely through its intensity that even the yellow— intended as being experienced as dull— is related [to it].

It might be argued that [the distinction] is desired because blue is also [perceived] with dullness due to its being a related object, or else because both are equally indistinct and dull. For in the view that consciousness is formless (*nirākāra*), there is no specific difference in the cognition itself; it is precisely this that was called "confusion" (*saṃkara*) by means of [the attribution of] clarity, dullness, and so forth. He states the confusion also by way of memory (*smṛti*).

Thus it is said: when the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) imparted by the simultaneous experience of both blue and yellow is awakened by the sight of blue alone, then that former experience, being awakened without distinction, belongs to the blue alone and not to the yellow;
for there is no rule [to the contrary], and thus it also consists of the manifestation of yellow.
Even when [the object] is seen while drinking, that memory would occur; and this is so for one who has previously perceived the manifold nature of all things situated on a mountain peak,
and whose latent impressions (saṃskāra) have been awakened by the sight of any one of those things again.

In the world, there is the common experience that memory is the recollection of all previously experienced objects. [The author] refutes the opponent’s conjecture—that "the restriction [of memory to its specific object] will occur by the power of an awakener"—with the words "even though," and so forth. [He does this] because of the phrase "of the previous experience," which refers to that [experience] which re-emerges within memory.
[This refers to] the state of being. "That" refers to the experience.

Now, even when there is the perception of a form, although the awakening perception of blue is restricted, that which is to be awakened—the prior form of experience—by way of its latent impression (*saṃskāra*), would likewise possess the dual forms of both blue and yellow; thus, the same logical consequence applies.
"It cuts away doubt that the form is the object. For even though this [consciousness] is joined with two forms, by the power of awakening it awakens having made that [intended] form prominent;
however, the second form remains merely concealed, as if indifferent or as if cast aside, in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

There is no fault in saying "it performs [the action]. The fault of confusion (*saṃkara*) was stated by way of memory; therefore, its refutation within our own position should be understood as intended to illustrate the pacification of all the aforementioned faults of confusion.

For instance: because it is constrained by the form of that [object], there is a determination for each respective object; due to the sharpness or dullness of the forms of blue and yellow, they do not become confused with one another. And this is according to the principle to be explained later in the system of momentary cognitions accompanied by forms (*sākāra-kṣaṇika-jñāna-santāna*).

To demonstrate that [the theory of] latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is untenable because it fails to account for their maintenance and fulfillment, whereas it is tenable within the vision of a single, independent consciousness that is inward-turned and encompasses all experiences— this is what is being established.
In the phrase "awakened by the consciousness of an experience similar to that," the word *saṃvit* (consciousness) has been employed.

Thus, by this much, the intention—that this fault does not apply to our own position regarding the Sūtra—is indicated by what lies implicit within. And so he will say later, beginning with the word *tat* from the Sūtra, "all indeed."

Since this collection of faults, which is difficult to avoid for the opposing side, does not arise at all from the very root in one's own view, he explains this with the words "therefore" (*tataḥ*). "Of light alone" (*prakāśasyaiva*) means that its very life consists in being of the nature of light; and that [nature] exists in a jar, in a cloth, and even in a cart.

Independent and consisting of the nature of the cognizer, she manifests objects such as jars within her own self— like reflections in a mirror. Just as reflections appear in a mirror as if attached to it,
and not as established in their own selves while disregarding their non-difference from the mirror, so too do these [objects].
"Objects such as jars appear adhered to that very Light and subsisting upon it; they do not exist independently of themselves.
This primary nature of the object of cognition, which has been explained here at length and elsewhere as 'in this [Light], things are like non-existent,' [is established]. (Aja. Pra. Si. 13)

By these and other such statements, that too is established in this sūtra, by which the previously introduced state of having internalized the infinite forms of the universe is brought to its ultimate fulfillment in the Blessed Lord. || 4 ||
If that various accidental manifestation were to imply an external object, it would not be possible for a non-differentiated consciousness to be the cause of such diverse manifestations. (5)

Now, it may be argued that by this much you have established the truth that the entire range of appearances, such as blue and so forth, has a nature non-different from consciousness; however, if the range of appearances of existence (*sattva*) were also the nature of consciousness, then consciousness would always manifest as such. But this is not the case. Therefore, [the appearance of existence] must be sequential.

Regarding those various appearances, the cause for their restriction within that manifestation must be stated. Furthermore, consciousness cannot be the cause therein, because it is non-variegated and thus the emergence of variegated, sequential appearances would be impossible;
for the difference in effects is dependent upon the difference in causes. Therefore, [this must belong] to consciousness alone—its single [nature].
The external category of objects, assuming their respective forms, is capable of presenting successive appearances in the manner of reflections (page 82).

It is to be conceptualized through inference. And although this [self] is established by inference, because there is a determination (*adhyavasāya*) that "this is [the self]"— which is characterized by having its root in an object supported by corroboration through inference—

it is not at all improper to say that it is established by the means of perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇaka*), even though it is a fruit of a means of knowledge [arising from] a connection (*pratibandha*).
Therefore, it is said that [the object] exists as an external form because there is a separation from the manifestation of the nature of consciousness;
furthermore, this is due to the function of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), since the conventional usage of perception depends upon such determination.
The particle *ca* (and) refers both to the meaning of this sūtra and to the meaning of the forthcoming sūtra.

The proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*) states that this is merely a possibility: "That manifestation which was described as being diverse despite the non-diversity of the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and which appears to be adventitious because it cannot have the manifesting cognition itself as its cause, and thus has an unknown cause— that [manifestation]," [is not possible].

It is conceivable that [the world] is external and lacks a means [of cognition]. For a gradual differentiation of appearances is not logical from a non-variegated consciousness; therefore, if another [opponent] should think that the external alone is inferred as the cause, this is the meaning of the sūtra. He introduces that [objection] with the words "Now, if it is thought" (*atha matam*). This refers to the phrase "if this [is the case]" (*etat cet*).

The commentary (*vyākhyāna*) is that which touches upon the ultimate meaning of the sūtras yet to come; it is what is to be explained. By the word "various" (*vicitra*), [the commentary] explains "this and that" (*tattat*); by the word "succession" (*krama*), [it explains] the absence of simultaneity (*ākasmikatva*). It may be argued that even a single cause, through the application of its own power, might indeed manifest a manifold effect simultaneously; however, this is not the case for succession.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates that the second half of the verse is presented as the reason (*hetu*) in the Sūtra;

and with the intention that a reason must be something already established, it was explained first in the Commentary (*vṛtti*), even though the Sūtra begins with the goal (*upeya*) and proceeds in its proper order.

Up to the words "even though there is no distinction for that," the commentator likewise explains with the passage beginning "first of all, distinct from cognition," and so forth. By the term "visible" (*dṛśya*), he indicates that the external object is inferable, while explaining its accidental nature through its having ignorance as its cause. In that regard:

He shows that the proponent of external objects as inferable is a fellow student who accepts the subject matter of the present treatise regarding cognition appearing with forms (*sākāra*). Here, "insentience" (*jaḍatva*) should be understood at the outset from the perspective of what is established for the opponent, as he says: "And [it] is also conscious."

"Because they are objects of cognition. Now, one might object: external objects are indeed established by direct perception, their existence or non-existence being determined by the attainment of correspondence with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
(Page 83)

Anticipating the objection of Dharmottara— that those very cognitions of appearances, which possess a nature determined by the arrangement of their objects and arise in succession, will become the causes [of one another] by entering into a single causal complex— he says "and not" (*na ca*). The phrase "by the stated reasoning" refers to the two preceding sūtras.

For it has been stated there that how could perception itself, which is of the nature of illumination, exist if [the object] were of an unilluminated nature? Therefore, as the teacher Dharmottara said: "The difference of the external [object] is established by experience; as for its non-difference," [it is not].
In that regard, cognition, by its very nature as mere experience,
must possess that character by which it is differentiated according to each respective object.
Thus, that which is established by the force of reasoning as being non-empirical is rendered untenable;

for it is experience itself that says there is no [object] distinct [from consciousness], and even when the Vijñānavādin speaks of "cognition," it appears as such because of its identity with that [consciousness].

"...not of anything else. According to this principle, what is the meaning of this statement that "difference is established by experience"? For that very reason, the difference between pleasure and pain is merely imagined through their mutual exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Indeed, if their distinct forms were not experienced...

It might be so in the case of blue and momentariness, for instance; however, here too, the claim that there is a perception of distinct forms is untenable, because it has already been stated that perception consists precisely in identity with consciousness (*saṃvedana*).
Furthermore, the determination of objects according to their respective functions is also of the very nature of direct realization consisting in self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
"This blue is being experienced," "this yellow is being experienced"—
such statements, made by one who is merely disputing, are indicated through the shadow of a reason,
just as in the case of saying, "This jar exists because it is established by perception. Yet, by that much, its lack of experiential reality has not been asserted.
For it has been stated more than once that conventional practice lacks the capacity to subvert its own root.

Furthermore, the Bhaṭṭa has also stated that perception is not merely that which is perceived by a deluded person, but rather that which is known by an investigator; and why should that which is established by firm inference not also be considered established?

Enough with falling into the side of one's own view regarding what is an improper position for another. Now, having raised the objection: "Just as being manifest is the very nature of a jar, so too will its 'jar-ness' be [its nature], just as blueness, momentariness, being an effect, being a cause, and so forth [are its natures]," he says: "No."

"And" (*ca*) [is used here]. The reason for this is "manifest and non-manifest. For if there were a portion of the jar that was distinct from its manifest nature, it would have to be of a non-manifest nature; however, it does not exist as such, since it is nothing other than blue itself.
Arising from its own cause and performing its own causal function,

let it be apprehended as it pleases— unseparated from properties such as momentariness that are constructed through the exclusion of what it is not (*atadvyāvṛtti*) and are common to other entities; however, it is not [to be so apprehended] otherwise.
It is not logical for a single entity to possess the identity of blue and yellow, which are mutually exclusive;
furthermore, since the nature of a jar is opposed to manifestation, it cannot be of one essence with manifestation.
For if they were of one essence, there would be no contradiction—which is the pervading condition for unity—and yet here a contradiction is perceived.

This is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). The nature of blue is not incompatible with luminosity, because it is not distinct from luminosity. If it is argued that luminosity is exactly that much [in extent], then the manifestation of yellow could never occur, because blue is distinct from yellow. Luminosity must therefore have the very nature of blue, yellow, and so forth.

If this is argued, then it would appear as such all at once. If it is argued that it possesses a manifold nature consisting of blue, yellow, and so forth in succession, then there would be no state of luminosity during sleep and similar conditions; for consciousness, which is the locus of the ego, would be devoid of the nature of all things such as blue and the rest.
Since its intrinsic nature is attained through awakening by means of a pure body consisting solely of the manifestation of perception,
whatever further exists here— whether blue, yellow, white, pleasant, or unpleasant—
all that is in addition to the manifestation and is therefore of a non-manifest nature.
One would incur a contradiction. Furthermore, there is no fixed rule regarding sequence here—

such as that the appearance of blue follows immediately after the nature of pure consciousness, and from that immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) the appearance of yellow arises— because thousands of such diverse variations are observed without any fixed order.
It was rightly stated that [the two] are distinct because of the impossibility of a cause-and-effect relationship, due to the superposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*).

The word "only" (*eva*) is indicated by the particle *vai* in the commentary. For this very reason—namely, because the form (*ākāra*) of the jar and so forth, which has become the body of cognition, does not exceed the nature of its own awareness (*saṃvedana*).

There is not even a mere atom of form; therefore, since there is no such thing as grossness that exists in ultimate reality, upon what basis could an objection be raised? For that which is gross is extended across space and occupies different locations, yet it cannot be both in one location and in another location simultaneously.
It must be so;
for that is not some gross object which could be made the subject of such an inquiry.

For in the cognition of a variegated form, that which is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the cognition— namely, blue and so forth, which appears as identical in nature to the cognition itself— is impossible to perceive as distinct from consciousness; therefore,
being non-different [from it] and yet being distinguished from yellow and so forth, it is impossible to perceive [as such], and thus there is no other form.

Therefore, that which is to be known through conceptual construction as distinct from cognition takes on a separate existence. For, when one discriminates that [object] as being separate by way of its unity or multiplicity and so forth, one falls into the state of an external object imagined through delusion;
this occurs at the time when the self-awareness of those variegated forms has subsided and conceptual construction has arisen, whereby the discriminator [perceives it].

If it is argued that "that very same [object] is blue and that very same is yellow," and so forth—a life-force consisting of such inquiries—[the object] is a variegated unity, then this is even more variegated than that!
Thus, by the unfolding of hundreds of such aspects of the expressible, one perceives the object; that [perception] does not belong to consciousness.

When [the object] has become a manifest form, a certain distinction arises by which a doubt might be raised: "How can there be only a single gross form? For an external [object] cannot logically possess a gross form, yet it is precisely that which is perceived; thus, the notion that "grossness is a property of appearance" serves as the prologue to the denial of external objects.

This is so; that the object perceived is merely of the nature of atoms will also be refuted in the *Bāhyārthānupapatti-sūtra*. Therefore, the form of consciousness does not differ at all from its manifestation. This very point is expressed by the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even in the case of variegated forms. Let this suffice.

To that extent, consciousness— which serves as the locus of the ego— is either established in a state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) or fixed upon a single manifestation, such that there is no suspicion whatsoever of the emergence of any other form superior to that consciousness;
this remains the case even when it possesses a variegated form, insofar as it maintains its nature as pure consciousness.
The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) should also be explained with reference to contradiction (*virodha*), even though it is primarily employed in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).

This is the meaning: just as there is no contradiction between an elephant and a horse by means of a mirror, nor between those two themselves, because they both have the mirror as their single ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); so too, [there is no contradiction] with cognition (*bodha*).

"Because blue and yellow are, in their ultimate sense, nothing other than a single cognition. Now, one might object: the Buddhist has thus resolved to establish the external object through inference; yet he does not maintain that there is only a single cognition.

(Page 86) What, then, is this "bed of the text"? This bed of the text is as follows: when an external object exists, distinct in terms of place and time, the cognitions produced by it possess forms [of that object] due to the difference in their causes.

It is logical that they are distinct; however, since their nature as a single cognition (*bodhaikarūpatā*) must necessarily be accepted by the opponent, the Proponent of Cognition (*vijñānavādī*) is in every respect a subverter of all philosophical systems.
With this underlying intention, the Proponent of External Objects (*bāhyārthavādī*) demonstrates how the former has fallen into a doctrine of non-dual, single cognition.

Now, it might be objected: just as the specific varieties of gem such as sapphire (*indranīla*), ruby (*padmarāga*), and moonstone (*indukānta*) do not exceed the nature of "gem," since there is no possibility of anything among them being a non-gem; and just as the specific varieties of the genus "cow" such as the brindled, the black, and the broken-horned do not exceed that [genus] "cowness" (*gotva*); and therefore, they do not exceed it.

Because there is an absence of the state of not being "cow-ness" [in the case of the cow]; and just as the sapphire (*indranīla*), the great sapphire (*mahānīla*), lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), the *garuḍa* gem, and the *śukra* jewel are merely specific varieties of the blue itself—not exceeding the nature of blueness—since it is impossible for anything among them to be non-blue; so too are the cognition of blue, the cognition of yellow, and the cognition of sweet.

The cognition of hardness, the cognition of fragrance, and so forth, are merely specific modes of cognition itself; they do not possess a nature distinct from cognition, which would entail the undesirable consequence of them being non-luminous in nature. Therefore, these very [cognitions], whose essence consists in specific non-conceptual cognitions of blue and so on, [serve as the means of knowledge] for others as well.

Anticipating the objection that "things which are themselves not of that nature—such as the recollection of blue or conceptual constructions—will become the cause [of the appearance of variety] by way of depositing impressions (*saṃskāra*)," he refutes this with the words "and not" (*na ca*). He states the reason for this with "since" (*yataḥ*). It is not [the case that] "it is a tree."

The connection with the preceding is that "there exists some [consciousness] alone. He states the distinction of the consciousness under discussion from the category used as an illustration by saying, "not so here. The term "of another" refers to the states of sleep, intoxication, fainting, meditative absorption (*samādhi*), liberation (*kaivalya*), and so forth.
Consciousness shines forth as being entirely devoid of the form of the cognition of blue and so on;

even at the time of the cognition of blue and so on, the nature of the awareness distinct from that [object]—namely, "I"—manifests precisely as lacking any penetration by the form of blue and so on. Thus he shows this regarding the locus of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).
And as for the word "ca" (and): this knowledge is also of the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*). (1.2.7) (page 87)

In this regard, we have already deliberated upon the fact that whatever constitutes the innate form (*nijarūpa*) of a thing always shines together with that very thing—just as a tree shines along with its specific nature consisting of branches and so forth. We have shown this by demonstrating the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), namely, that consciousness does not always shine together with its particular attributes (*viśeṣa*). But surely...
In your own system, it will be determined that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) consists in the perception of multiple universals (*sāmānya*);
likewise [it is established] in such passages as: "The existent jar-substance...
(2.3.4), and so forth.

And in such enumerations as "of the lights of separate lamps... (2.3.5), [the same applies]. Consequently, even jewel-ness (*maṇitva*), tree-ness (*vṛkṣatva*), and cow-ness (*gotva*) are of the nature of appearances (*ābhāsa*), even though they are devoid of entry into particularities such as the brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*). Just so...

Because they perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), they possess entry into specific distinctions even in the form of *śāvaleyas* and so forth; likewise, it will be so in the present case as well. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "or rather" (*yathā vā*); the word *vā* indicates a doubt. If such is your doubt, then [we reply] by this following method.

Since there is no distinction in consciousness when other manifestations— such as space, time, and so forth, or [particulars] such as being "lame" or "hornless"— enter into union with the manifestation called "cowness" through the process of identification (*tādātmya-saṃmelana*), which is its universal form, then at that time...

The differentiation among these [cognitions] consists in their capacity to accomplish specific causal functions that exceed the common causal function of being a cognition; however, within a cognition, the cognitive aspect itself is not colored by other appearances,
for another cognition possesses the nature of the subject (pramātṛ).

"...for it is said in [ĪPV 2.2.4]: 'The state of resting within one's own self consists in either uniting appearances through the direction of relations such as grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth, or in differentiating them';
moreover, there exists no other perceiver of consciousness. Now, one might object:
Are clarity, lack of clarity, and so forth not distinctions of consciousness? We say: "Yes. To what, then, do they belong?

He says: "To the object alone. For instance, from a distance, the true nature of an object, being obscured by intervening factors such as dust and the like, imparts a specific quality of dullness to the cognition, just as [the color] blue [does].

There is a distinction in the cognition of blue; conversely, in the case of its opposite, there is the opposite. Now, why is it that you, who are trembling with fear, do not tolerate the entry of other appearances into cognition according to the path of reasoning? To this he says:

"Because of the nature of consciousness," and so forth. "It has been stated" refers to the commentary on the preceding sūtra. "Of the nature of being" (*bhāvātman*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, as is "of the nature of light" (*prakāśātmanaḥ*). If, upon considering what the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of light is, one were to say that it is of the form of an entity (*bhāvarūpa*), then the consequence would be its lack of luminosity; how [could this be]?
The intended meaning here is that there is the possibility of other appearances entering into it. Furthermore,

regarding the phrase "that too," the intended meaning of the previous word "one" (*ekam*)— namely, that the state of being both manifest and unmanifest in a single jar is contradictory— has already been explained in its shadow, with respect to consciousness.
Because it is mixed with other appearances and because it lacks internal differentiation of its own, it possesses a single form;

thus, the word "api" (also) indicates that another aspect of the intended meaning has now been described for this [consciousness]. For consciousness, blue and so forth are not particularities, because they do not sublate its other nature, just as in the case of a mirror.
This is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). The exclusion of one particularity by another particularity is the pervader;
for if it were not an exclusion, there would follow the consequence of a universal nature, which is incompatible with the nature of a particular.
And that [exclusion] is not perceived here, insofar as the cognition of blue itself is the cognition of an omniscient being.

Just as in a clear mirror, [consciousness] is coextensive with its manifold forms (*vaiśvarūpya*); therefore, blue and other objects— which do not exceed consciousness and are incapable of dividing it— appear as if above, within, outside, or nowhere at all,
floating as reflections (*pratibimba*) that do not exceed the mirror itself, such as the likenesses of elephants, horses, and so forth.

They are so called. Now, one might object: "How could even unity, being itself another manifestation (*ābhāsa*), enter into consciousness? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "not many. This is said with the intent of setting aside the supposed difference [of unity] that arises from the influence of other manifestations entering into it.

This refers to the phrase "this is a single word. And by speaking in this way, how could the author establish a difference in cognition even for those who maintain an extensive [ontological] discourse, given that there is no other appearance— such as place, time, or form— which serves as the cause for such difference?
Since there is no such thing as anything capable of being mixed with the nature of consciousness,

it has been demonstrated that this so-called doctrine of distinct, momentary streams of cognition is, in ultimate reality, nothing other than the doctrine of non-dual consciousness itself, merely concealed by such terminology.

But how can there be a cognition of blue or a cognition of yellow if there is no cognition of difference? This is a difference of manifestations (*ābhāsa*), not a difference in consciousness itself. And since manifestations, being like reflections, lack the nature of real entities, how [can they be differentiated]?
Having explained the meaning of the scriptural portion— "How could they split themselves, or how could they split consciousness, since consciousness is undivided?"—
I shall now introduce this subsequent section, which functions as a reason, in order to establish the thesis that it is not possible for that consciousness to be the cause of diverse appearances.

With this intention, he first explains the first half of the aphorism, which defines the object to be proven (*sādhya-artha*), stating "mutually": it implies a cause that consists of appearances distinct from consciousness— which has come to rest in the mirror of cognition— and a form of consciousness distinct from those appearances.
—such is the connection. Regarding the sequence in the narrative, even that sequence is not fixed;

rather, [the author] distinguishes the manifestations through many different modes. Thus, he explains the word *viśiṣyamāṇa* (being distinguished) found in the commentary by its intended meaning with the words *nacāpyete*. [The manifestation is] "distinct from cognition."

The intention is that it is precisely because [the object] is not manifesting. The word "external" (*bāhya*) is conventionally established for a real entity (*vastu*) that performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*);
it does not denote merely that which is outside of manifestation, because there is no such usage as "a rabbit's horn is external. Thus, by the teacher Dharmottara, *apoha*...

Although it has been stated in the words "internally" that there is an externalization of the luminous nature of consciousness, one might object that it was not spoken of as being external, nor did he say "it is outside. With this intention,
the word *artha* (object) used in the commentary is explained by the phrase "being such [an object]."

Those appearances of blue and so forth which have attained the excellence of being reflections of consciousness must necessarily be similar to their projector, just as in the case of the appearances in a mirror. Consequently, by means of inference, it is established that the blue object is indeed similar to the appearance of blue; that alone is the external object.

[This is] the conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). Thus, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the form of blue and so forth existing within consciousness requires a similar object that provides it [to consciousness], because it is a reflection, like a reflection in a mirror.
For, according to you, reflections by their very nature possess a fixed sequence.
It is pervasive; and since that [pervasiveness] would not be possible if it were causeless— given the lack of dependence on a donor—
it follows that its nature as a reflection is pervaded by the state of being a donor, which is the probandum (sādhya) and from which it is not excluded.

(90) The establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Now, it may be objected: "An external form has never before been observed by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); how then can it be inferred when its pervasion has not been grasped? He replies: "And just as..."

For just as a sense organ is never apprehended through direct perception, yet its pervasion is apprehended by means of its being merely a cause; in the same way, it is inferred merely as a cause, and not in any reflected form whatsoever. That [cause], however, once inferred, comes to rest in a specific [object] by virtue of the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).

The intention is as follows: that which is the fixed cause for the perception of form, even though it resides within the self, and is distinct from both darkness and light—that is the eye; and so it is here as well. "Suddenly" means "at some time.
The connection is that [the cognition] postulates a subject (kartṛ) for the cognition of form and so forth. But [one might object]: in that case, it would be just like a sense organ...
That might be merely some cause; but from where do [qualities] such as blue or yellow come? To this it is replied:

"only" (*kevalam*). That which is the perceptual cognition whose object is the form of knowledge, its final determination in the form of the ascertainment "I see"—since that [external object] is not the object of that [determination], it too...

It is conceptualized as that which is to be determined (*avaseya*), and not merely as a cause; for there is a cognitive determination (*adhyavasāya*) therein that "this is the object. To show the distinction from an inference based on mere causality, he says "for not...
regarding cognitions produced by the senses, which consist of direct perceptual experience (*pratyakṣasaṃvedana*).

The sense faculty (*indriya*) is the cause [of its cognition], but it is not the object (*viṣaya*), because the determination "I perceive the sense faculty through that cognition" does not arise. For the sense faculty is indeed the object of inference alone, since it is determined precisely by the determination [of the cognition] of that [faculty]; and that of which inference is the object—

The meaning of "non-existence elsewhere" (*ananyatrabhāva*) is "the object. Now, regarding the phrase "here again," he states a specific distinction in the context at hand. If it is asked, "How can that which is not grasped be determined as being 'seen'? he replies: "Because of similarity" (*sārūpyāt*). This means that whatever variety of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) there may be—coexisting with place and time—that belongs to the object within the range of another cognition, to that extent [it is determined].
"Everything is complete for the one who offers it"— by this logic of the combination of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*),

there arises a determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) whose object is the form of knowledge; due to an error produced by similarity (*sārūpya*), [the cognizer] thinks, "I am determining an objective form distinct from the knowledge as being 'this' (*idantā*)," and thus it is produced, but not [in reality].

And this [cognition], although born of error, is a determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) because it determines the grasped form of cognition as being external, just as there is a determination of silver with respect to a mother-of-pearl shell that has been grasped.
Although its nature is mere error, because it determines— on the basis of a causal connection with the object— an object that is the primary cause capable of imparting its form to cognition,

even this erroneous [cognition] possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) within itself, according to the principle that "even an error is a valid cognition when there is a connection."
He demonstrates this when he says:
"Since there is no [cognition] in the absence of an object, even perception possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
When that which has a dependent nature is the cause [of cognition], both [perception and inference] are equal."

Thus, this operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), occurring through the force of perception and assuming the form of a determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) such as "I see," favors perception—
just as a minister [favors] a king who has been brought under his control.

One operates by way of the apprehending subject; therefore, the external object is indeed grasped by perception, and thus the worldly perspective is followed. [The opponent asks: "In that case, what is the function of inference? [The author] replies:
"It is accompanied by correspondence," meaning that there exists a source which is the fundamental cause and the deliverer of forms.
"The object is similar to its form"— this much is the function of inference. If, however,

inference were to subvert that external object which is being determined, just as the reason for existence [the *sattvahetu*] subverts stability, then this determination of externality would be entirely groundless.

If a determination were to occur regarding an external object that has not been apprehended, such as the determination of water even when there is the apprehension of a mirage, it would not be the fruit of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) because its object is unapprehended. And if,
just as the reason of existence (*sattva*) establishes momentariness— which is not itself determined [by the reason]— so too...

The reason for [the object] being a reflection is that it is an external object; since that [object] is incapable of functioning in worldly discourse by means of an object perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there would be no discourse at all. This is what he states with the words "but not like non-momentariness," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by the employment of the sense-faculties" (*indriyopayogena*), it means that the sense-faculty (*indriya*) is employed (*upayujyate*) in this [process].
In consciousness, by that [consciousness] which has as its object an external thing made the locus of determination; "previously" means prior to the operation of inference. But is it not...
accidental and causeless?
Thus it is well known that they are neither accidental nor eternal, nor are they caused by eternal cognition.
Thus, there would follow the undesirable consequence that effects are produced without a cause.

In such passages, he dispels the doubt that "inferring a cause from what is causeless is not logical" by stating "arising from an unknown cause. In the negative compound *nañ-samāsa*, the specific meaning of the word *kim*— aided by the sense indicated by the particle *cit*— is "some [unknown] thing" (*kaścit*).

And in the case of a *taddhita* derivation, it is restricted to such instances as "curd-rice" (*dadhyodana*) or "drummer" (*mārdaṅgika*). Since a universal that is devoid of repose in a particular cannot function as a limit,
and since a particular is necessarily present, the verbal formulation "come from the universal" implies "from an unknown particular."

It remains established. Therefore, because it is said that "this matter is accidental" (*ākasmika*), its arising from an unknown cause is understood through the intended meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) and the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*);
thus, the statement regarding the sentence-meaning is like the auditory faculty being affected by a disease.

According to this principle, just as the primary meaning [of "causeless"] applies when a cause exists, so too does it apply when a cause is absent; thus, because of this commonality with ignorance (*ajñāna*), the term is employed here and there through *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) based on similarity to denote that which is causeless. However, since it is not the case here [in the present context], what was stated is correct.

The establishment of external objects [is claimed] from the variety of appearances, which are sequential yet lack a fixed order due to being accidental—that is, having unknown causes. Furthermore, this [external object] must necessarily be accepted, because one is acting with the haste of attempting to justify a consciousness that possesses its own independent forms; otherwise, it would be untenable.

"The intended meaning of the Sūtras, Vṛtti, and Vivṛtis is that [the author] will cause the non-dual doctrine of the Lord (Īśvarādvayavāda), which uproots all the tenets of one's own schools, to enter [into common acceptance]. || 4 ||
Then, that very proponent of external objects, having raised the objection of the Vijñānavādin, refutes it:
"Nor can a diverse awakening of latent impressions (vāsanā) serve as the cause here."
What is the cause for the diversity of that awakening as well?

The diverse awakening of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which have been present since beginningless time and possess the power to give rise to fresh appearances such as blue and so forth, is precisely what constitutes the cause for this diversity of sequential appearances at the outset; finally, however, it is the awakening of those [impressions] existing in the form of mental traces (*saṃskāra*) that constitutes conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

(Page 93) "It becomes the cause for the manifestation of non-recollection and so forth"—thus the Vijñānavādin postulates. He refutes this with "No. He states the reason for this with "Of that too," referring to that which is considered to be manifold in nature.

The awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is diverse either because of the diversity within itself, or because of the diverse nature of the latent impressions, or because of the difference in the factors that awaken them. And yet all three of these are unreal;
for that which is called a "latent impression" has no form distinct from consciousness. Furthermore, that [consciousness]...

Awakening alone is one, because everything else is non-existent due to its lack of manifestation; the same may be said regarding awakening itself. Furthermore, no causes for awakening can be established as existing outside of consciousness, since everything that manifests [must do so within it].

Because the ultimate reality consists solely of consciousness whose nature is light. Therefore, if it is argued that the variety of appearances cannot be accounted for by anything else, and thus it is logical that there must be an external object that serves as the provider and bestows this variety of appearances—this is the meaning of the Sūtra, representing the view of the proponents of external objects (bāhyārthavādin). The commentary (*vṛtti*) on this point is as follows:
This is clear. He introduces that [point] in brief with the words "without an external object," and so forth.
"Of its variety" means of the variety in the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
for a latent impression is, like the perfuming of cloth and other items with musk, of a nature that is constantly dependent [on something else].

In order to establish that the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) is the sole ultimate reality, he explains her nature as power; with the words "Awakening" (*bodha*), and so forth, he explains "awakening. Regarding the word "of that" (*tasya*), [he explains] "this" (*etad*) as that which is characterized by the successive appearances of blue, yellow, and so on.

Its own effect; the readiness (*ābhimukhya*) for its production when it is to be performed is "ripening" (*paripāka*), which, by having reached its final stage, is "awakening" (*prabodha*). Let it be so; however, what is well-known as a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is that which generates memory from a latent tendency (*vāsanā*), but not this.
The sense is that we do not yet wish to establish [the existence of] a "prover of a novel experience";

let this matter rest for now as a point of renunciation (*sāṃnyāsika*). For it has been stated that consciousness alone [is the reality], because anything additional lacks the capacity to enter into the very body of consciousness due to its lack of luminosity.

By you yourselves, your own vow is being stated: that the word "consciousness" (bodha) merely becomes predominant when its latent impressions (vāsanā) are awakened, but there is not even a trace of an object (arthaleśa). The phrase "even this" means even that which possesses such other internal distinctions as have been described. Now, as for the diversity of appearances (ābhāsavaicitrya)—

The variety of manifestations (*bhāsavaicitrya*) must be established as an effect; yet even that is not in the slightest degree distinct from consciousness, for if it were, the consequence would be that it is not manifest at all, even though it appears as if it were distinct. Of such a nature as this...

"Whatever the nature of the *yakṣa* (the effect), such will be the *bali* (the cause)"—by this reasoning, the cause, namely the variety of the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), although in the ultimate sense not distinct from consciousness (*bodha*), will appear as if it were distinct; so what is this? For even the variety of the effect [is not real].
There is nothing ultimate whatsoever for which an impossibility would need to be avoided through effort.

[The author] does not tolerate this, saying "if not" (*na cet*). The word "this" (*etat*) refers to what is about to be stated. He demonstrates that with the words "even when there is a difference in appearance" (*ābhāsabhede’pi*), and so forth. Regarding the word "not" (*na*), he states the justification with the word "since" (*yataḥ*): for an effect is [defined by its] novelty.

That which appears is said to be "manifest. And that [manifest] may be either a real entity (*vastu*) because it is capable of causal efficiency (*svārthakriyā*), or a non-entity (*avastu*) due to the opposite [lack of such capacity], like the appearance of real silver or the appearance of silver in a piece of lime.
Furthermore, the cause is indeed capable precisely because it is a cause, since the defining characteristic of a real entity is causal efficiency.

Thus, it must be a real entity (*vastu*) and not a non-entity (*avastu*), precisely because a non-entity is characterized by the absence of all causal capacity. Causality is negated because incapacity—which is the opposite of the capacity that pervades causality—is perceived; this occurs both through the perception of what is opposed to the pervader and through its lack of the nature of consciousness.
The state of being a real entity (*vastutva*). And thus, since there is no diversity [in consciousness itself], how can there be a diversity of effects? To this he says:

"of that which has become a real entity" (*vastubhūtasya*), meaning of that whose nature is consciousness (*bodhatayā*) as a real entity. And by whatever form [the consciousness appears], such as "consciousness possessing the awakening of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of blue," or "consciousness possessing the awakening of the latent impression of yellow," and so forth...

It is manifold; it extends to that form characterized by the distinctions of blue, yellow, and so forth. And since that [manifold appearance] is an error, that form, being non-existent as a reality, how could it bring about a state of actual manifoldness for consciousness? Now, what is the use of an actual manifoldness? For just as the manifoldness of effects is not ultimate, so too is this.

With the intention that there may also be a diversity of causes, he raises an objection with the words "even so" (*athāpi*). This very point was stated previously in the passage beginning with "even though there is a difference in manifestation" (*ābhāsabhede’pi*). However, it was stated there as follows:
"Even in the case of the effect, in the group of manifestations such as blue..."
(Page 95) Only the nature of consciousness (*bodharūpa*) is ultimately real, and since that very same nature exists even in the cause,
their equality was established by way of ultimate reality; now, however, [their] non-ultimate reality [is being considered].

"Regarding the diversity of objects for both [the subject and the object]," by this other formulation, it is not redundant. "This does not tolerate that; it is improper"—to provide the reason for this, he says: "of a non-entity. "In the acceptance of that" means in the admission of its causality. "Here" refers to the sequence of the manifestation of blue and so forth. "For indeed" [refers to] the effect, as follows:

The phrase "seen afterwards" implies that it was not seen previously; this is the point of contrast, as there is no such cause for what was merely seen before. [Objection: Is it not the case that the definition of a cause is simply that it must invariably be seen beforehand? [Response: He says, "even of such a thing," referring to that which was merely seen before.

For this alone is causality: the capacity to manifest a real entity (*vastu*) or an unreal one (*avastu*). And that very capacity is its reality (*vastutva*). [Objection: If the effect is unreal, then how can it possess the status of being an effect?
[Response: What loss is there in this? Let it be so by virtue of its unreality.

The causal status of that which possesses its own inherent capacity would not exist if it were not performing another effect. This is what is stated [in the verse]: "But if the effect lacks capacity... Now, one might object: how could that which is produced by a cause—being generated by the power of a specific cause—not be a real entity? Or, if it were a non-entity (avastu),...
If the capacity [of the cause] were obtained only through the connection with that effect, then the cause would have no capacity of its own;
thus, even the cause would become a non-entity. This too has been stated by him [through the phrase] "of the effect":
because the effect is a non-entity, there could be no causality in the cause, since capacity exists only in relation to an effect.

The meaning is "due to non-existence. However, the fact that the effect is a non-entity (*avastu*) does not constitute an obstacle [to its production]. For if it were like the theory of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*), the effect would not even be a non-entity; rather, it would arise by virtue of the capacity [of the cause]. But this is not the case. Indeed, the effect, being a non-entity, is brought forth by the cause; and at that very moment, it is that.

The effect is said to be that which is indefinable (nirupākhya). And by saying "it is shown by its own capacity," the coming-into-being (bhavana) residing in the effect is indicated. That which is accepted by others as being eternal and not subject to coming-into-being is of no use anywhere.

Thus, that effect is indeed non-existent [prior to its arising]. However, if it has emerged through the power of the cause and is endowed with capacity in its entirety, it is a real entity (*vastu*); if not, it is a non-entity (*avastu*). Furthermore, even errors (*bhrāntayaḥ*) possess the nature of cognition (*bodha-rūpatvena*).
The objects themselves must indeed be real, just as [the appearance] of two moons is [real] for one with cataracts.

Let it be that the "two moons" lack reality because they are devoid of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), but not so for the cognition of them, which is distinct from other cognitions. Thus he says: "For even in the case of errors... due to ophthalmia.

The cognition of a yellow conch [is produced] by jaundice (*kāca*), and the cognition of two conches [is produced] by the visual disorder *timira*— this is indeed observed. Now, if the effect in error consists in the form of the cognition itself, then since cognition is a real entity (*vastu*), how can it be said to be an "effect"?
"Furthermore, even though it is non-existent (*avastu*). Now, if a double moon and the like are non-existent, yet that very thing is the effect;

then how can that which is produced by the power of the operation of causes be non-existent? Or, how could the cause be a real entity (*vastu*) by virtue of its capacity being directed toward that [non-existent effect]? Having raised this doubt, he says "Or rather" (*athavā*). This is what is meant:

In considering the nature of causality, we have stated that one must necessarily maintain that the very essence of consciousness consists solely in its immersion in the ultimate reality; thus, both this nature of consciousness and its ultimacy have been asserted by us. And that—

Even if thousands of other modes of expression were employed, it would remain non-differentiated; for that [object] is not ultimately real, because it follows that nothing could manifest beyond the manifestation itself. This is indeed the supreme, non-rejectable vow, both according to scripture and through reasoning. He demonstrates this intended meaning with the words "only this much."

Because the awakening of a cognition characterized by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of blue is immediately followed by an undesirable consequence, that cognition is exactly equal to a cognition characterized by the awakening of the latent impression of yellow; since the latter is also [equal] to the former, there is only a single, uniform cognition—this is the summary meaning. Having thus stated the reality of things (*vastutattva*), [the author proceeds].

He says "even so" (*athāpi*) by way of a concessive argument (*abhyupagamya-vāda*). Previously, it was stated that even when there is the awakening of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of blue and the awakening of the latent impression of yellow, the nature of consciousness (*bodha-rūpa*) is one. Or, let it be granted that the nature of consciousness is not one; nevertheless, due to the application of those two latent impressions, [there is] the awakening of the latent impression of blue.

The distinction must be stated as arising from the awakening of the yellow latent impression (*vāsanā*) and by the power of that impression. But how is there a distinction even between the two impressions themselves, or between blue and yellow, by way of [the objects] blue and yellow? Blue— (page 97)
If it is argued that this is due to the awakening of two yellow latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then it is simply a circular argument (*cakraka*).

If it is argued that the distinction between them arises from the predominance of distinct karmic latent impressions, then a cause for the distinction between those karmas must also be stated. [Furthermore,] a cognition of a blue appearance immediately following another cognition of a blue appearance is not different [from it].

If it is argued that [the appearance] exists by virtue of being a mental formation (*saṃskāra*), then from where does the blue-appearance of a previous cognition that has already passed arise as something distinct from its nature as cognition? And why is there an initial blue-appearance for an infant? If one assumes that this occurs due to [impressions] carried over from a previous birth, then [one must explain] the attainment of the very first form of blue.

The introduction must be stated: if consciousness (*bodha*) is by its very nature a succession of appearances such as blue, yellow, and so forth, then how can it possess the state of pure selfhood during sleep, fainting, meditative absorption, and the like?
If it is argued that even this [pure state] is its nature, just like the appearances of blue, yellow, and so forth, we say no.

It has already been largely stated that this is because purity and impurity are contradictory. Furthermore, if it is admitted that consciousness possesses a variegated nature at all times, it would follow that liberation is impossible. Therefore, this mind is luminous by nature, and the impurities are adventitious.
Thus, the non-dual knowledge of the perfection of wisdom... [is established].
Thus.
"...consisting of the knowledge of the two watches [of the night]...
and so forth; thus, there would be the total destruction of one's own accepted scriptures and commitments—enough said! Therefore, this very point is established:
if [the world] were produced from a succession of its own respective external causes that are beginningless, [it would be distinct] from the nature of pure consciousness.

"Something must indeed be an external object"—thus the proponent of external objects (bāhyārthavādin) revives his own position. This is what he says: "In every respect, [the object] is distinct from consciousness. In this way, first, the cause consisting of the sovereign power of karma is considered as residing within one's own continuum.

It was suspected that the preceding blue appearance, acting as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), might predominantly be a yellow appearance; however, it was stated that this is not tenable regarding the variety of sequential appearances such as blue, yellow, and so forth. Now, [consider] the variety residing in the mental continuum of another.

To one who might suspect that [the mind] is the cause by way of being the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) in the sequence of the variegated appearances of blue and so forth, the proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*) says:
(page 98)
If those other cognitions, which are of the nature of extrinsic subjects and are intended to be established as the cause for manifesting the variety of appearances,
were distinct from that single stream of consciousness due to the difference in the appearances they are meant to produce; then [the following would occur].
The status of being a cause is thus conceivable. But how is that so?

For instance, the very nature of consciousness is eternally "I," inward-turned; whereas space and time arise as belonging to a different level [of reality] through the power of the manifestation of "this-ness" (idantā).
It has been stated more than once that [the two] do not differ, because they are incapable of approaching the state of being qualifiers of that cognition.
Furthermore, if there were a difference in their essential nature (*svarūpa*), it would follow that one of them is non-cognition, since its nature would be non-luminous;
thus, consciousness (*saṃvit*) possesses no differentiation in terms of space or time. Nor does it possess differentiation from the insentient (*jaḍa*) even in terms of its essential nature.

[This arises] from consciousness, which is the Intellect (*cit*). Therefore, in reality, there is no establishment of another cognizer. However, in the context of a hypothetical admission (*abhyupagamavāda*), other cognizers are indeed always present;
and they exist simultaneously within hundreds and thousands of varieties of manifestations, all within a single moment. And thus...

Since the various manifestations residing in all other subjects— whether they be perfectly enlightened Buddhas or unenlightened beings— other than that single [subject], have entered into the state of being causes within each individual continuum, it is impossible to establish any fixed rule regarding a difference in manifestation for any particular subject whatsoever.
This method of justification is the cause of a ten-millionfold delusion. With this intention, he says:

"Even though it is established. [Objection: But surely all this collection of appearances of entities—which are considered insentient, such as the appearances of fuel, fire, seeds, and water—is [perceived] by sentient beings.

There is no dispute here that things are first brought into proximity with a mutually suitable location by causal conditions (*pratyaya*) capable of effecting their mutual presentation, designation, approach, and accomplishment, so that they may be situated in a place appropriate for the fulfillment of their respective effects.
The conditions for engagement and the conscious subjects possess desire;

and that desire arises only by encompassing a manifold variety of manifestations occurring in a fixed sequence over infinite time, like the desire of one who turns the water-wheel at the mill of the *layavijñāna*.

For the king’s desire for invasion manifests precisely through its essence as the formulation of hundreds of thousands of various appearances, such as crushing, plundering, breaking, and shattering the enemy kingdom.
The term "appearance" (*ābhāsa*) has been employed extensively throughout this treatise.

In the system of consciousness-only (*vijñānavāda*), because external objects do not exist, the very forms of consciousness themselves constitute the approaching conditions (*upasarpaṇapratyaya*) and so forth, by way of being the successive prior states.
It indicates that there is a successive relationship between causes and effects— meaning that because they are considered effects through a succession governed by a fixed rule,
and are determined as such by that conceit, and because they are considered causes due to their prior necessity, [they are established as such].
Diverse appearances are produced by its own specific volition in the form of consciousness;
thus, for this reason, the following types of causes have arisen:
namely, that which is indeed the first appearance of a cause, originated from a particular state of the *ālayavijñāna* known as "volition."

Just as the appearance of the body arises from the desire to go, which is produced by the self-consciousness directed toward the intention of reaching a village, that very appearance projects the appearance of the intervening path and the appearances of grass and blue objects situated along it, until the fruit— the appearance of reaching the village— is attained.
Furthermore, by that very desire— which arises from the intention toward another result consisting of the semblance of satisfaction—

and which brings forth the semblance of cooking regarded as the primary cause, there is projected the entire sequence of actions beginning with placing [the pot] on the fire and ending with the final swallowing of the food; from that, [the sequence proceeds].

One should understand that [the desire for] the various diversions of drinking parties and so forth is included by this term "desire" (icchā). Alternatively, what is the use of postulating such an extensive causal relationship that implies a continuous stream of manifold desires? [The entire series] is condensed into a single impulse at the very moment of the first conception.
Thus, that very manifestation of the spreading creeper of karma, which consists of the consciousness of the single *kalā*,

projects the manifestations of pleasure, pain, and their means, which occur in a fixed sequence until the limit of the manifestation at the moment of death. It is the same in another future birth as well, and not otherwise.
Furthermore, for those appearances situated in between, another cause is employed;

for example, by this very will, "I shall cause him to fall from the mountain peak," there arise the appearances of the various conjunctions and disjunctions with specific locations as he falls, and the suffering, delusion, and so forth produced thereby.
The succession is indeed implied; for that very reason, it cannot be obstructed in the interim. As the Sage said:
"In this world, he will reflect upon the ripening of his very actions."
Consider what good or evil will become of you there in the next world.
Thus, by stating that the appearances of the middle state (*madhyābhāsa*) cannot be obstructed even in part,
it is said that they are invariably concomitant with the projection of the appearances of action (*karmābhāsākṣepa*). For this very reason:
"...one should not purify *prārabdha* alone" (Svacchanda Tantra 4.141).
Thus, its impossibility has been stated in the Āgama:
"For that [which is *prārabdha*] is indeed [exhausted] through experience (*bhoga*)."

And so it is; for instance, from the appearance of a specific moment (kṣaṇābhāsa) in the form of a particular ascendant, they determine everything up until the moment of death at the time of calculating the horoscope,
including the projection of the appearances of other births based on the appearance of the specific ascendant of the moment of death occurring at that birth.

Whether it be considered as having no limit or as having liberation (*apavarga*) as its limit, it is indeed counted [as such]. Nor is it a novel claim that there is a single cause for a continuous series of appearances (*ābhāsa-prabandha*) that follows a fixed sequence; rather, this is evident even in the case of the continuous series of the rising and setting of planets and constellations during childhood and so forth, and in the succession of the seasons.

He shows that this is indeed most evident by saying "just as": for those things which have the nature of persisting for a fixed duration of time, there is a determined succession among them—variegated and distinct from one another—in the form of a continuous stream of appearances occurring in successive order; of that [succession], some single thing alone is the cause.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, when it is stated "thus," it is connected with the preceding action; first of all, this [argument] is merely an illustration, for it does not hold true in every case. It holds true, however, in the case of the movement of planets, lunar mansions, and zodiacal signs as determined by the rising of the Kṛttikās and so forth, and in the beginning of the seasons where [the sequence] is fixed.

Such is the sequence. However, regarding childhood, youth, and so forth, there is no fixed necessity, because we observe that the inevitable sequence occurs in one way at one time and quite another way at another. Therefore, [this applies] to those factors situated in the middle, such as the variety of food and the like.

[This refers to] the process of attaining youth and old age in varying degrees, the journey along the path which brings about old age, and the consumption of elixirs which possess the sole power of preserving youth— each of these,
being subject to its own inherent necessity, cannot withstand the challenge that they are caused by nothing other than prior karma.

How could there be a denial of that which exists as a cause? Furthermore, no other variety of cause is perceived for this intermediate [consciousness].
