Therefore, it follows that the immediately preceding manifestation alone possesses causality therein. Thus, it is not [the case that external objects are the cause].

(101) Thus far, only the first [reason] possesses the status of a logical ground (*hetu*). Now, it might be asked: "What is the use of this childhood and so forth, which pertains to a specific individual? We have cited childhood and so forth with reference to humanity in general.
Regarding the matter that a single initial cause impels a manifold, sequential continuum— this too is not tenable, because even in that case there is an absence of being impelled by an initial cause;
for instance, when one has entered a dark chamber from a bright space, [the perception] does not arise solely through the power of an initial cause.
There is the perfection of the eyes and other causes of perception; for if that were the case, everything existing within the interior of a room would be perceived the very moment one has entered it;
rather, in this matter, there is a mutual dependence among the eyes and the other senses.

A specific transformation (pariṇāmaviśeṣa), characterized by the attainment of a particular excellence, must be taken into account. This is just as, when a sprout is to be produced, there occurs a specific transformation consisting of an excellence generated by the successive proximity of the seed, the earth, and water; and likewise...

When the perfection of the cooked rice (odana) is to be achieved, there must be the pot, the rice, and the water; otherwise, if there were no regard for other transformations, the sprout and the cooked rice would arise instantaneously. For in that case, the causal totality (sāmagrī) is complete. Indeed, nothing further need be introduced there, nor should anything be removed.
Therefore, some distance must be maintained.

Likewise, for the successive occurrences of the rising of the sun, the moon, and so forth, as well as the dispersal of mist and the like, there must necessarily be a transformation consisting of mutual assistance through a sequence. Otherwise, [it would not be possible].

In just a few moments, one passes from childhood to youth, from that to middle age, and from that to old age; thus, death would be imminent at every step. Yet, there is indeed the waiting for another period of time. Therefore, in the interim, by virtue of a succession of bodies of the same kind—

Even by means of the continuum of the body, which is devoid of the departure from a prior state and the arising of a subsequent state, one must remain for some time. Thus it is said: "It remains as it is. And likewise, even in the calculation of horoscopes (*jātaka*), it is not stated at every step that "on this day, one will see this, touch that, or say such-and-such."

It does not arise from the perception of activities such as laughing or scratching at the edges [of the body], but rather consists merely in the perception of specific states that are conducive to the onset of pleasure or pain.
And this is logical; otherwise, if one were to perceive the reality of a single birth, one would know everything by virtue of being attached to that [reality].
Therefore, the notion that [the variety of states] in infancy and so forth is projected by a single primary cause is untenable, given the observation of hundreds of diverse manifestations.
In the case of operating a water-wheel with its buckets, however, the sequence of filling, emptying, and turning those buckets is always uniform;
even there, if any variation were to occur, it would necessarily depend upon some other auxiliary factor. And such [an auxiliary] does not exist in the present case.

Regarding the diversity of appearances such as blue and so forth, there is the entry of some other auxiliary factor— just as in the case of the application of elixirs for youth and the like— since no fixed auxiliary cause is observed. For instance, through the application of an elixir, youth may persist for a long time, or even that which has already passed [may be restored].
In this case, there is certainty that a cooperative factor (sahakārī) returns, as in the case of the application of *punarnavā* [herb];
however, regarding a blue appearance—whether stable or unstable—there is no certainty that this cooperative factor sets or arises again. Nor is it like entering a dark room from a luminous space.
There would indeed be a dependence on mutual transformation where a fixed connection with the expectation of another time appears; however, in this case,
even immediately after a momentary appearance of blue, an appearance of yellow is actually observed.
It is also not logical that [the sequence] is projected by the first cause, because there would be no fixed order.

He recalls the previously mentioned first cause with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*). The phrase "in both cases" means when it is being considered; therein, the first cause consists of volition (*icchātmaka*).

It was previously stated [in the passage] beginning with "the fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is implicitly included by the very first desire" that it is implied; regarding that implication, he states the absence of a fixed sequence by saying "just as at one time" and "at another time," [specifying] "of that same person or of another person," because it arises from a cause of that same kind.

It is logical that the effect must be of the same nature as its cause; yet here, although the desire— expressed in the form "I shall produce fire in this very person or in another person"— is entirely complete in its possession of that same nature, [the fire] nevertheless arises in the interval.

The necessity of the sequence of appearances as blue, yellow, and so forth, establishes their belonging to that same class. Now, regarding the second possible cause mentioned previously— namely, "or by former actions" and so on— the absence of a fixed sequence which the proponent of external objects (bāhyārthavādin) seeks to establish therein [is as follows]:
With respect to a single person, it is not possible, because in a single birth,
[the result] is projected by the causal force of that very first karmic impulse belonging to that one individual alone.

With the intention that there exists a sequence of appearances beginning with blue and ending with the appearance of death, he states "of persons" (*puruṣāṇām*) to indicate the absence of a fixed order of succession from the perspective of other persons.
By means of the plural number, [he refers] to the group of appearances such as the body, which is the first effect in all persons.
The intention is as follows: since the preceding moment of hearing is also established as being of that same class by observing its belonging to that same category,
it is logical that from the first cause of that class, there should arise— by a fixed sequence— a continuous stream of appearances such as blue, which are themselves of that same class.

Furthermore, it is illogical for every appearance to be projected by karma, because it is impossible for every appearance to have pleasure and pain as its result; for merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are established as being employed solely for the purpose of bringing about the means to those [pleasures and pains]. As they say:

"Having joy and suffering as their fruits, because they have merit and demerit as their causes. Even though, according to the view that maintains the existence of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) and a Lord (īśvara), even the sight of grass and such things encountered on the road necessarily functions toward pleasure and pain through some indirect succession, for everything [is so].

Since it is not admitted that [an entity] arises without being permeated by what is undesirable, even so, for one who thinks that karma alone is the sole primary cause, this is the direct refutation: how can that which leads neither to pleasure nor to pain be projected by karma? But for others...
For those who maintain that there are many causes, since karma itself is extremely diverse due to the variety of causal complexes (*sāmagrī*),
it is not faulty to accept that the means for achieving pleasure and pain also possess a great variety of states, such as being mediated or unmediated by other factors.

Now, it may be argued: let it not be that desire alone is the primary cause for the variety of appearances such as blue and so forth, nor even prior karma; rather, in each respective case, the appearance of its own cause will be the primary cause of that particular effect-appearance. And that [cause]—whether insentient or otherwise—is that very condition which brings about the [effect’s] approach.

If one thinks that the numerous first causes thus described will give rise to the variety of appearances existing in the interval, [the author] dispels that delusion in detail with the passage beginning with "nāpi mṛddaṇḍa" and ending with "abhisandhānam asti. Alternatively, [it may be explained as follows:]

This introduction to the present work is made precisely as a supplement to what preceded. Now, one might object: just as in childhood and other stages, even though youth is projected by the initial causal karma, it persists for a very long time through auxiliary factors such as the use of elixirs (*rasāyana*), so too here [in this case].

(Page 104) By virtue of auxiliary causes (*sahakārivaśāt*), those various manifestations (*ābhāsāḥ*) will persist for a long time. For instance, in the persistence of the manifestation of a jar, the manifestation of clay, the staff, and so forth, is the cause; [likewise] of the manifestation of smoke...

There is the appearance of the causal complex consisting of fire, fuel, and so forth; there is the appearance of a weaver, a spindle, a loom, and so forth for the appearance of a cloth. This should be stated similarly in other cases. He refutes this with the words "nor even," providing the reason:
because when one perceives the appearances of a jar, a cloth, and so forth, which exist within a house, in the interval—that is, in the middle—[there is no such appearance].

"Even the name of the appearance of the lump of clay, the staff, and so forth, does not remain. Now, one might object: "In the potter's house, first of all, the appearance of the lump of clay is indeed perceived;
furthermore, for one who brings a jar from that house, there is the appearance of the cognition of approaching [the house], which belongs to the resident of the house..."

It will be an auxiliary factor in the persistence of the manifestation of the jar; let it be so for as long as [the jar] remains. But once it has gone to its own home, what then would be the auxiliary factor for the persistence of that manifestation? This is what he says: "Nor is there approaching," and so on. Now, just as when fire is desired to be inferred, [there is the persistence of] the manifestation of smoke...

Although it is not itself perceived, the light of fire—which exists as a cause residing within subjects such as the one who is blind, the one who is moving toward that location, and the omniscient one—is denoted by the term "dominant condition" (*adhipatipratyaya*) because, despite being unperceived, it functions as a cause through its similarity to the dominant factor and its status as a causal agent; thus it is. In this way...

Even the person who brought the jar will be a cooperative factor (sahakārī) here while remaining in his own home. But when he has become a mere memory (yaśaḥśeṣībhūta), what is to be done? Who can be relied upon as a cooperative factor for the persistence of the appearance of the jar? For that which is destroyed, there is none.

The state of being a cause follows from the absence of any defining characteristic (*anupākhyatvāt*); having a defining characteristic (*sopākhyatva*) is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of causality. And this [absence] is perceived here. Furthermore, a pseudo-omniscient being such as a worm cannot possess causality, because [if he did], it would entail the consequence of an infinite arising of appearances; this and more will be explained further on.

Regarding this, he says: "Nor by mere predominance. Even so, the connection is that the causality which is asserted in this way does not exist. The reason for this is stated as "its approaching" (*tadupasarpaṇa*). To illustrate this very point, he says: "For indeed... [He continues: "What causality can there be for that which has perished, wherein predominance could be a distinguishing feature? For this very reason," since it is not so...
The appearance of smoke [does not arise] from the appearance of fire; for this reason,
from such an appearance of smoke as that which is released from a cowherd's water-vessel (*gopālaghaṭikā*), there is no appearance of fire.

Inference [is not established] because it does not have that as its effect. Regarding what was stated—that even when the cognition of approaching [the object] has perished—he refutes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) raised by the words "even though" (*yadyapi*) and so forth, with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).
This is to be connected with the phrase "this is not tenable" (*naitadyuktam*). In reality, [agents such as] washermen, carpenters, blacksmiths, and others...

[The opponent argues: "They exist even in other places of rebirth, such as heaven or hell. [The author] shows that by this much, the establishment of the appearance as an effect does not occur, stating: "In the doctrine of the reality of appearances (*ābhāsa-vastutva-vāda*). Furthermore, at that time, they do not appear as the causes for approaching those [other realms]. And as for their appearing...

The appearance of another condition for the approach that serves as the cause for that manifestation would itself require yet another [condition], and thus there would be an infinite regress of prior appearances. But such a thing does not exist; this is what he expresses by the words "succession" (*paramparā*) and "interruption" (*viccheda*). Now, one might think: [this applies] to an omniscient being...

To that extent, there exists a manifestation of a succession of appearances; thus, for us and others, the appearances of the notions of approaching [objects] existing therein— just like the appearance of fire inferred from smoke—
are the causes of the differentiation of the appearances of wood, walls, and so forth, by virtue of their status as sovereign conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*).
"Let them be"—thus [it might be argued]. To this he replies: "And because there is no such restriction.

For there is no rule that all appearances—such as houses, chariots, and jars, which are produced by the cognition of approaching all those [causes]—must always be perceived; nor is there any other auxiliary cause [required].

In the Vijñānavāda system, it is logically tenable to accept that [the object] exists as something distinct from the cognition itself— specifically, from the consciousness consisting of the knower’s desire which serves as the causal condition for approaching that object— by means of which this lack of restriction [regarding the object's existence] becomes possible. Furthermore, at that time, those [objects] occupying other places of occurrence do not yet possess any desire [to be perceived], even now.

"Let houses and so forth appear"— even at the time of their prior manifestation, these [objects] have no such intention as "let these appear for this long a duration. Even if there were such an intention, it would apply only to the middle portion of the places of renown, such as monasteries and the like.

Destruction has been observed. Furthermore, they were not omniscient previously, such that they could have conceived of this infinite variety—how this appearance of a house follows immediately after this appearance, or how it is preceded by this and separated from it. Nor indeed [could] these...
Such an intention [cannot exist] regarding other present conditions for approaching [the object], because such [an intention] is not observed there.
106) Thus, since the fact that [the action] is projected by the first cause has been refuted at length, therefore—

It follows that the variety of appearances arises from a succession of immediate antecedent conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*), as there is no other possible alternative. Yet even this is untenable because it lacks necessity. Now, it might be argued:
"A single cognizer, whether he be a potter, a mere worm, or even an omniscient being, remains situated within his own lineage."

It necessarily exists, and it has already arisen in the form of the manifestation of a jar (*ghaṭābhāsa*). In that case, its cause is the manifestation of the clay, the staff, and the potter; therefore, even when those have perished, since it remains as the manifestation of a jar arising from that very manifestation of a jar, there is also another cognizer (*pramātṛ*).
"It possesses the appearance of that place; for that [place] also, there is the connection with its appearance"—in this regard, too, one must discern:

does this manifestation of the jar, which consists solely of the appearance of the previously situated subject, enter into the internal sphere of another subject who arrives at a different time? It is by this method [that one should investigate].
In that case, there is either a unity between the two appearances despite the difference in the appearances of breath, pleasure, pain, and so forth;
or else, from the cause which is the appearance of the previously established subject, another adventitious appearance residing in a [new] subject arises in the form of an effect. In this regard:

In the former case, there is an adherence to the views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). For instance, if one accepts that two cognizers— the pre-existing and the adventitious— are of the nature of a single cognition,
then because there is no distinction [between them] and all are of the nature of a single consciousness, it follows that they constitute a single self (ekātmatā).
To begin with, the doctrine of a single self (ekātmavāda) is undesirable; even there, another difficulty arises:

that single self, by virtue of its autonomy, manifesting various conjunctions and disjunctions, creates a manifold diversity of subjects from within itself, while at the same time establishing non-difference in certain aspects of manifestation.

Thinking that this Vijñānavāda, which holds "this [world] is of the nature of Maheśvara," has been well-supported by the Yogācāra, the proponent of external objects (Bāhyārthavādī) refutes the first position with the words "For this...
He then considers the second position as well, starting with the words "Now, even if there is difference... and so forth.

The flaw from the perspective of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that, because it would be external, there would follow the consequence of its non-manifestation; thus, no means of valid cognition whatsoever could apply here. Furthermore, if it were corporeal (*mūrta*), its lack of grossness (*asthūlatā*) would be untenable, given the distinctions of being in this location or that location, being red or not red, shaking or not shaking, and being obstructed or unobstructed.
Because of the imposition of contradictory properties, there is no unity; nor is there the nature of multiple atoms,
because such an appearance [of a single atom] does not exist even for an atom.

Because it is untenable due to the occurrence of the conjunction of six parts; and since there is no other category of entity for a thing apart from unity and multiplicity—this is the fault from the perspective of the object of cognition (prameya). Thus, regarding the contingency of being faulty, the two words "external" and "embodied" [are used]. He refutes even this, saying: "This also is not," for they are capable [of such a response].

Thus, even in a single state, a collection of appearances belonging to the cognizer is produced by those [causes] whose capacities have been individually observed—just as a multitude of rice sprouts is produced by rice seeds—following their own respective numbers. If it is argued that multiplicity is not perceived due to the blending of similar things, [the answer is: this would not occur in the absence of such blending.
He shows what is to be said with the words "And therefore" (*tataśca*).

Furthermore, apart from being a single manifestation of the adventitious perceiver, there can be no connection with appearances such as clear or unclear. [Objection: But is it not the case that for another person suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*), such a thing does not exist?

The appearance of hair and so forth is real; however, it exists solely through the power of one's own visual impairment (*timira*), and not because of that appearance itself. For if it were otherwise, it would occur even for one who is free from visual impairment. Thus he says: "Even for the deluded person, [it arises] from another. This is an illustration. Previously, when there was the appearance of a single moon for one free from visual impairment, the one with visual impairment [also perceives it].

A newcomer [to the world] would not possess the appearance of two moons; therefore, the self-appearance of another perceiver is not produced by the appearance of that [other], because it is distinct from it. Indeed, non-distinctness from that is the pervading condition for the production of its appearance. Otherwise, from the appearance of a jar, there would follow the appearance of a cloth.
Thus, there is an unrestricted manifoldity [of views]. Its opposite is "being of a different nature" (*tadvilakṣaṇatva*);

this is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalambha*). Now, to the proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*) who is intent on refuting the Yogācāra position: "This position is inherently weak; it is not mine."

"He is to be counted [among our own]; however, with the intention that he will actually refute the Yogācāras, the proponent of the doctrine of the sole identity of God (Īśvaraikātmyavādin)—acting as if he were penetrating his inner thoughts in order to encourage him—says: 'But in the case of the doctrine of the sole identity of God' (*īśvaraikātmyavāde tu*). The word *tu*..."

By highlighting this distinction, he clarifies the specific nature of the encouragement: "It is true that you are the foremost among those who uphold the authoritative tradition— that indeed this fault consists in the transition from clarity to lack of clarity, and so forth, as well as the arising of appearances such as hair-tufts."
And because of the word "ca" (and), there is also the arising of other optional appearances;
this has been demonstrated [on page 108] in the doctrine of the non-duality of Īśvara. Therefore, the position of the outsiders (*tīrthika*) is [refuted] in every respect.

In your system, that evil-souled proponent of Vijñānavāda— who, like a beast of burden, is solely intent on seizing the long-accumulated principles of momentariness, selflessness, and so forth— will inevitably cause [the doctrine] to enter; therefore, strike him down with every possible assault.
"From its own nature" means that there are indeed two kinds [of manifestation]:
that which, by being the object of all the senses, exists as external and stable—that common creation for all subjects is "waking. (3.2.17)
"Thus, this common creation, as well as the other [uncommon] creation of the Lord, possesses a clear manifestation" (4.1.11).
By such statements, the common creation will be described as having the Lord alone as its agent, in which case— so far as that goes— ...
In the aspect of manifestation (*ābhāsāṃśa*), there occurs for the subjects a state of oneness through the dissolution of duality;

this is its unique creation, which subsists upon the creation of the Lord (*īśasṛṣṭi*). By the [verse] "4.1.9," however, [it is indicated that] there is a unique [creation] performed by subjects in the form of bound souls (*paśu*), wherein no merging occurs.

Regarding the cognizers: and in that view, since the category [of objects] consists of both the distinct and indistinct, such as hair and so forth, as well as conceptual constructions and the like, how could there be the fault of the unity of manifestation given their lack of commonality? Furthermore, even in that case, there is the presiding influence of Īśvara, as will be stated.
"Even this [consciousness], though appearing as such through ignorance, is truly the power of the Lord, being of His very nature" (4.1.9).

Now, the proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādī*), having been encouraged, raises an objection using the words "Now" (*atha*) and so forth, and then refutes it with the words "It is not tenable" (*na yuktam*) and so forth. Now, this proponent of external objects...

Urged on by the encouragement and instigation of one who maintains the doctrine of the Lord’s absolute unity (*bhagavad-ekātmyavādin*), he strikes without hesitation and takes up the introductory foundation (*pīṭhabandha*) in order to refute at length the proof of other mental continua (*santānāntara*) within the system of the Vijñānavādins, saying: "In his own [view]... as many as there are forms of other mental continua.
If there were as many cognitions of other subjects as there are appearances of jars, then mutual interaction between them would not be possible;
therefore, you must allow for this loophole by admitting the doctrine of a single appearance.
Consequently, you must accept an external object, wherein [all these appear] as one.

(Page 109) When objects are apprehended by different subjects, the practical transactions of buying, selling, and so forth, become possible. Furthermore, when a single external operation and expression residing in the body are admitted, [the following occurs] of that...
Since it is the effect of volitional effort, the continuum of another's cognition— which serves as the cause— is inferred without contradiction by that very same observed mark of the effect; thus,
there is linguistic convention even regarding the object that is another cognizer.

The concealment of questions and answers, embarrassment, the suppression of intention, closing one's eyes, and so forth, performed toward one another, are possible; however, that which gives rise to the opponent’s position must not be accepted by one who knows the method (*nayavid*). Thus, [the method] is pervaded by the non-suppression of one’s own position—which is the cause for its acceptance—and by the suppression of that [opponent’s position], which is contrary to it.

The phrase "being that which gives rise to the opponent's position" constitutes the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory of the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). As for what is indicated by the word "only" (*eva*)— namely, that there would be no linguistic convention regarding the appearance of another's jar— the reason for this is that the appearances of jars belonging to other subjects are imperceptible (*parokṣatvāt*).

Because the cognition of another’s property is beyond one’s own direct perception, there would be a much greater multiplicity of distinctions within the appearance of a jar— which exists as a form of the objective aspect— due to the difference between cognizing subjects; thus, the conventional usage "this is the appearance of a jar for him," "that is the appearance of a jar for him," and "it is also for another" would not occur, especially since the form of the objective aspect is exceedingly vast.

In the case of an army, a multitude, or the like—which are denoted by the term "other cognizers"—there would be neither even a touch nor a possibility of the linguistic usage "this one also cognizes," "that one also cognizes," let alone its actual accomplishment. Such is the construction of the text; however, this is not with respect to the appearances of jars and so forth.

The word "ca" (and) must be supplied [in the sūtra], so that there would not be an impossibility of the genitive and locative cases here, as in the examples "the owner of cows" (*gavāṃ svāmī*) and "in those [places] where" (*yeṣu*).
Indeed, by the force of the particle "eva" (only/alone), [the cognition occurs] with respect to the appearances of other jars and with respect to other subjects (*pramātṛ*).

The connection is that even the touch of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) would not occur. Regarding an object that is in every way beyond the scope of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there can be no linguistic convention, just as there is none toward one who is merely looking at another while concealing their true appearance through feigned indifference.
And thus are the forms of the grasped and the grasper residing in the cognizer. For linguistic convention—

It consists of the nature of cognition and its designation. In this context, the reason is that [cognition] is within the scope of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is experienced as such in all cases; its opposite is being outside that scope. Thus, this is the "perception of what is incompatible with the cause" (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*).
Now, one might object: even if an external object exists, let the jar be within the scope of the means of valid knowledge, perception.
The appearance as the grasper, however, must be made an object of cognition through inference alone,
because one perceives that [appearance] elsewhere after having observed an action preceded by cognition in one's own body.
If it is conceptualized as cognition...
According to this principle, in this system of philosophy, even the aspect appearing as the apprehended object (grāhyābhāsāṃśa) will become the object of inference;

therefore, its status as being outside the scope of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is unestablished. For instance, that which has attained the state of appearing to the self-consciousness of the inferring person named Caitra—his mother—is [the object].
The manifestation of activity and speech is accompanied by a bodily appearance belonging to Maitra;
the pervasion of that [manifestation] with volition is grasped within oneself as being animated by the relation of cause and effect.
And indeed, by means of such an internal consciousness—which possesses manifestations such as a jar in this manner—[the inference proceeds].

This is a semblance of activity and a semblance of verbal expression of such a kind. Therefore, because the state of being an effect has been apprehended from that semblance of activity and so forth, there is an inference of the nature of the grasper as conjoined with the respective semblances of the graspable. And by means of what is thus inferred...
[This is] the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). As it has been said:
"This same principle applies even to that which is merely a mental construction (*citramātra*).
Having stated this by means of the word "even" (*api*), which implies its possibility, [the author] refutes it, saying: "it is not tenable."

The reason for this is expressed by the word "nahi" (for not). That person Maitra who is the object of inference—by his own volition (*samīhā*), an appearance of speech and so forth is produced that resides precisely within the self-apprehending consciousness of that [Maitra] himself; it does not reside within the consciousness of Caitra as perceived by the inferrer. Thus, that which is not [produced] by Maitra’s volition...
This manifestation—"he speaks"—is established in Caitra’s consciousness as its effect;
how then could it lead to the inference of Maitra’s volition, which is not its cause?
But surely, when Maitra’s volition exists, Maitra appears in Caitra’s consciousness—this is the manifestation. That...

How could it not be its effect? He says: "For this cognizer... Indeed, the appearance that is established in self-awareness—namely, "I speak eloquently according to the will of Maitra"—is considered its cause; for that alone is intended as the instrument (karaṇa), and not anything else.

"Maitra speaks [on behalf of] Caitra’s cognition"—thus, by the desire of Maitra, there would be the performance of an action belonging to the manifestation. The reason for this is "of him" (tasya). For that [action], having entered into Caitra’s consciousness, is not intended to be performed by the desire of Caitra. Now, what is the purpose of such a desire?

(Page 111) How can a sprout be desired from a seed, and yet it be its effect? He says: "Indeed, it is not the case that something is both undesired and an effect of desire. This very [fact] is what distinguishes a cause from the insentient.

This refers to that which is intended by the term "instrument" (*karaṇa*). If one asks what the reason for this is, it is because in the opposite case—where there is no intentional instrument—there would be the fallacy known as *atiprasaṅga* (over-extension). He states this with the words "of the universe.
And from that, there would follow a manifold disorder, such as the confusion of good and evil deeds, and so forth. Moreover, it is not merely this much; rather:
He shows that even the subject at hand would be undermined by the words "and thus" (*evaṃ ca*).

This [position] is contrary to all the world and unestablished; such is the meaning of the phrase "being postulated. Caitra’s desire for silence and so forth is of the nature of an effort (*samīhā*). Therefore, by that very [desire], it resides within his own consciousness.

It may be postulated that the appearance "Maitra speaks" is produced [by Maitra]. If it is argued that this [appearance] is not desired by Caitra’s volition, then the same rule applies: it is likewise not desired by Maitra’s volition either. Furthermore, the inference-maker Caitra’s own volition is established; in this regard, the only additional factor is: "precisely by my own volition."

"This appearance has been produced as being grounded in my own self-awareness"— up to this point, [the author] demonstrates the accumulation [of evidence] by showing that a self-awareness characterized by unseen friendship need not be postulated, thereby demonstrating the impossibility of resolving [the existence of] another mental continuum (*santānāntara*). But surely this was already refuted by the Teacher himself?

In order to clarify for one who might have the delusion, "Having raised this doubt, why is this objection being put forward?", [the author] refutes its meaning by first citing that passage, starting with "As for what was said...
and ending with "...as if not described as such. By the expression "as if not described as such," the proponent of external objects (bāhyārthavādī) [is indicated].

This reveals the following: even the authoritative Ācārya Dharmakīrti speaks in this manner out of partiality for that [position], in accordance with the treatises of Ācārya Dignāga, and not because this is his own personal preference. Of him...

The meaning of the *Santānāntarasiddhi* treatise is as follows: just as in the externalist systems (*bāhyamata*), another's volition is inferred from speech originating in another's body, so too in the system of consciousness-only (*vijñānavāda*), it is inferred from the appearance of speech originating in the appearance of another's body. In that regard, if the opponent should say:

In the externalist theory (*bāhyavāda*), there is indeed only one expression; in that case, it is logical that from this [expression] there is an inference of the intention [to speak]. However, in the system of consciousness-only (*vijñānavāda*), there are two appearances: [the appearance of the object] and [the appearance of] "this person" while Caitra, the inferrer, speaks.

(Page 112) By means of the non-interruption of one's own self; however, in the case of Maitra, who is the object of inference, [the statement] "I am speaking" occurs through the non-interruption of one's own self.
And in that regard, for Caitra, there is the speech whose manifestation is uninterrupted within his own self.

The pervasion has been apprehended as [the fact that] one's own action is the effect of one's own volition, but not that a manifestation appearing as distinct is the effect of another's volition. Therefore, how could that [volition] be inferred? To this it is replied:
that specific action which is distinct from actions such as those of a wall, namely the manifestation of speech and so forth—that alone [is the probans].

It is a universal (*sāmānya*) because it excludes intermediate distinctions such as interruption or non-interruption. That [universal], being perceived, is the indicator (*gamaka*) of that [particular]. Of what? Of that very lack of distinction (*aviśeṣa*) which effects the production of speech here, which, by disregarding other particulars such as "I" or "this," constitutes the universal. But is it not just as follows?
Just as there is a difference between a jar and an anthill despite their commonality of being composed of earth—
namely, that they are produced by specific causes such as a potter or an ant— likewise,
there is a cause for the distinction between interrupted and uninterrupted cognitions, as well as between verbal expression and mental appearance.

It would be distinct [from its cause]; that is, it would exist as such only if a production from specific causes were perceived in the same way as a jar or an anthill. However, this is not the case for arrows that have been shot, nor for stones, nor for mechanical contrivances and the like, even though they appear to be interrupted [in their continuity].

Those appearances of activity, such as moving or wandering, belonging to others; or those appearances of activity, such as moving and so forth, occurring at the time of death in another— whether sentient or insentient— produced by discharged arrows, stones, mechanical devices, and the like.

Uninterrupted [actions] have been observed to be preceded by one's own volitional effort (*samīhāpūrvaka*). Therefore, how can there be a rule that those which are interrupted must necessarily be preceded by the volitional effort of another?
Furthermore, regarding the state of being preceded by the volitional effort of another, as in the case of being struck by an arrow propelled by someone else, [the thought] "I... [does not arise].

"It moves, it falls"—thus is observed the appearance of actions such as trembling, even though one's own self is not actually divided [from those movements]. Therefore, there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) of mere volition (*samīhāmātra*) with respect to the mere appearance of activity.

However, in the case of the appearance of another's body which has been made the subject of the argument (*pakṣīkṛta*), due to the force of its being a property of that [subject], one's own volition is not perceived.

Since there is no third category, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), even though it is merely the desire for that [object] which exists in the cognition of pervasion and the recollection [of it],
it is established as being, in effect, the inference of another's desire. This very point has not been [accepted] by that authoritative person (*prāmāṇika*).
And it is heard that it was described by him as if he were unauthoritative, yet it was described by him as if through established renown; we...

But we conjecture as follows: perhaps even this which has been described by authoritative persons has become equivalent to what is described by non-authoritative persons due to defects such as partiality toward one's own system or negligence. The word *iva* is used either in the sense of a poetic conjecture (*utprekṣā*) or a simile (*upamā*). Why is this so?
Anticipating this, he says, "For instance" (*tathā hi*). With the intention that "let the opponent first state his answer,

so that I may find another opportunity for its refutation," the proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādī*) first demonstrates the lack of utility for the qualification of the probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣaṇa*) in establishing the subject under discussion.
Regarding the word "of action": actions such as burning or fanning are not preceded by volition;

thus, it is appropriate that the property of the means of proof (sādhana) be qualified by a qualifying term. However, once volition has been inferred, the existence of another's mental continuum is established; so what is the purpose of a qualifying term in that case? But surely—

There is no purpose whatsoever served by inferring another mental continuum (*santānāntara*), for it is inferred solely for the sake of establishing conventional practice (*vyavahāra*). And from mere action alone— just as one infers a prior cause in the form of an intention (*samīhā*) from the configuration of a hand or the like that has become manifest— even though that intention itself has passed away, it is established.

Even though that [self] is established as being connected with other present efforts, how could the mere statement "this one lives" be useful in any specific linguistic usage? For by means of an action— which is of the nature of a manifestation of speech—
that speaker, in the form of a speaker, [thinks] "I speak," in this very manner—

That which possesses a form co-inherent with the appearance of that [object’s] verbal expression is established; the meaning of the words "just this" (*yāvat*) is that it is precisely this [form] which is fit to be the object of proof (*sādhya*). And since this is so, the meaning of the phrase "therefore this follows" (*tata etad āyātam*) is as follows:
by means of that specific appearance of action (*kriyāviśeṣābhāsa*) which has an uninterrupted form belonging to the subject characterized as Maitra.

Such is that [self] to be proven, whose manifestation of activity— such as breathing, opening the eyes, and speaking— is uninterrupted; therefore, when one intends to infer another continuum based on the manifestation "I speak," for that inferrer, the referent of the word "we" (asmadartha), which is expressed by the first-person pronoun, exists as a distinct continuum.
Even though he is [merely] authorized, he is as if directly perceived; therefore, from such an appearance of a specific action,

it is logical to infer a specific effort— that is, a sovereignty consisting in the desire to speak, the exertion thereof, and the subsequent arousal of the vital breaths and so forth, which is applicable to worldly transactions such as asking and answering desired questions.
The word "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is used even with respect to the probandum (*sādhya*) in order to make this known.
On this point, the proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*) says: "It is thus. For here, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) must be investigated.

It subverts the entire process. For instance, the appearance "I am speaking" does not manifest for Caitra, because he infers in this way: "He indeed speaks," and not "I am speaking. For if such a conceit were present, the act of speaking would be conflated with the referent of the "I" (asmadartha).

What has been stated here refers only to one's own effort (*samīhā*), not to the effort of another, nor does it entail the identity of self and other. For that person, Maitra, who has the manifestation (*ābhāsa*) "I am speaking," his effort is established by his own self-consciousness (*svasaṃvit*); what need is there for inference? Having taken this into account, he says:

Regarding the phrase "far removed": that form which is already established prior to inference cannot, in reality, be an object of inference. And our subject (the mountain) is already established, like a mountain. The reason for being an object of inference is non-establishment (*asiddhatva*); and here, its opposite is perceived. Thus [it is far removed].

This is the perception of what is opposed to the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*). "That which has the nature of being 'I' exists elsewhere"—this is the perception of what is opposed to the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*). If it is argued that "otherness" (*paratva*) exists here because there is the cognition "this is I" with respect to another body, then the consequence of "otherness" would also apply to oneself, since the cause is no different; for here too, one indeed has the cognition "I."

"Even in a body that one considers as one's own—what distinction, then, is there between self and other? Or rather, the passage ending with "even by way of being past" is the statement of the Vijñānavādin. The proponent of external objects (Bāhyārthavādin), while explaining that very point in a different manner in order to refute it, restates [the opponent's position] with the words beginning with "And thus," and so forth.

By the passage ending with the word "viśeṣa-śabdaḥ," [the author] shows that while you employ the term "viśeṣa" under the guise of accepting a refutation, your intention here actually undermines the very subject at hand; thus he says, "In this way. By this method, the proponent of non-dualism (*advaitavādī*) [is refuted].

Having necessarily obtained an opportunity, he enters; for when both [subject and object] attain mutual identity through their mere appearance, there arises the manifestation of our own objective reality,
and because the power of sovereignty— which is the cause of the manifestation of the distinction between self and other— attains unity with another appearance.

"Because it is possible"—this is the remaining intention [of the author]. Now, one might object: "Is there not a disregard for the meaning of the suffixes in the form of the first and third persons? This is certainly not the case.
For from the mere act of utterance, there arises that very form of the base-meaning, which is a mere volition.
It would be established. Thus he says: "In this case as well.
[Page 115] "In the form of universals" means by abandoning the distinctions of being directed toward itself or others. "Is intended" means...

At the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the probans (*sādhana-dharma*) is [grasped] as the pervader (*vyāpaka*); and at the time of inference (*anumiti*), it is [grasped] as the object of inference (*anumeya*). To this, he says: "The apprehension of its specific qualities is useless. Consequently, since there is no attainment of the intended object to be proven (*sādhya-artha*), it is merely a vain effort, like that of a *piśāca* or a *yakṣa*.

Whether it be an omniscient being or a mere worm, there is no one—anyone at all—who acts as a mover of stones and such things, by whose will this [body] might thus tremble and speak; since such certainty is absent, worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) cannot be established. And for this very reason, just as the desire of another may lead to the trembling of my body, so too may my own desire.

The intention is that [the opponent] has seen [the agent] as capable of causing the trembling of another body. Furthermore, regarding what was stated starting with "like a discharged arrow" and so forth— that even in cases of both interruption and non-interruption, the appearance of activity is caused solely by mere volition (*samīhā*)— this applies to the portion consisting of the distinction between self and other.

Regarding the phrase "because deviation is observed," in that regard, deviation is also observed in the case of volitional effort (*samīhā*). For the appearance of activity—whether continuous or interrupted, such as "I fall," "I move," "it moves," or "it falls"—is seen even without volitional effort, due to the force of the wind and so forth; thus, [the reason] by means of the appearance of activity...

It is not even appropriate to infer volitional effort (*samīhā*) by means of an inference based solely on the cause; for that which occurs even without another thing cannot be the effect of that thing, just as smoke is not the effect of water. And thus, since trembling occurs even without volitional effort, there is here a contradiction with the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) that pervades the state of being an effect.

The fact that it is invariably concomitant with that [the movement] is perceived; thus, there is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). Now, this [movement] is indeed distinct from the mere appearance of trembling produced by the force of wind and so forth, just as [smoke] arising from the appearance of fire is distinct [from other types of smoke].

In the world as well, from the appearance of smoke arises the appearance of fire, which is apprehended by a single diligent person and recognized through practice; and therefore, by abandoning the distinction between interruption and non-interruption, it is of a universal nature,
and because its activity differs from that produced by wind and so forth, it exists by the abandonment of interruption and non-interruption.

If it were argued that "the universal" (sāmānya) is merely volition (samīhāmātra), and that its effect is [perception], and that by means of that effect one may infer its own cause— nevertheless, even when stated in that manner, [it must be understood] by setting aside specific distinctions such as interruption (viccheda) and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding that volition which is accepted as the cause, the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) that is established between it and the action— such as the trembling of another person, and by implication, one's own trembling— is as follows: [it is] that...

[The action] is established as being qualified precisely by the specific characteristic of being intended (*samīhitatva*). For indeed, an action—whether residing in oneself or another—that is not intended by anyone and which arises from other causes such as the speed of the wind, cannot logically be the effect of an intention (*samīhā*). Therefore, let the distinctions of "separation" and "non-separation" be abandoned for now.

But the state of being intended is impossible to abandon. If that which is unintended were to arise from intention, then upon one person’s intention to speak, the entire universe of moving and non-moving things would become a speaker. Now, if it is argued that only an action such as speaking, when intended, is the effect of intention, and not [anything else]—

[Objection: It is unintended. [Question: What follows from this? [Response: Anticipating this, he provides the following argument to demonstrate the fault, beginning with "And not... Here, in the act of speaking, there is the intention "I am this [person]. From that arises the appearance of speech belonging to one's own continuum in the form of the speaker, such that one thinks, "Therefore, I speak. And at that very same time—

In the case of an inferential cognizer (anumātṛ-pramātṛ) who is distinct from the one who intends [the speech]—that is, in the form of another mental continuum (parasantāna)—there is an appearance of speech (*vyāhārābhāsa*) such as "he speaks. Because this appearance lacks agency by the inferential cognizer and instead has Maitra as its agent, it is a second [instance of speech] that inheres in that other continuum consisting of Maitra. Thus, here:
The term "pertaining to another's mental continuum" (*parasantānagata*) is to be explained in two ways:
it appears to the inferrer who is distinct from the person desiring [the object], and it exists for the person desiring [the object] who is distinct from the inferrer.
This [sound], together with the aforementioned [qualities], is to be employed as the logical reason when another mental continuum is to be inferred; the former [quality alone] is not.

The pure is not "other," nor is the other pure, because both exist respectively through one's own effort and even in the absence of effort. Regarding this [pure state], the state of being situated in another is appropriate when expressed by the first-person pronoun (*aham*) in conjunction with the act of communicating through transmission to another, as in the thought, "I shall speak."

If that qualification— namely, that speech is a specific kind of utterance distinct from the utterances of an unintentional mechanical puppet— is abandoned, then one might infer mere volition from mere speaking, but not [volition directed toward a specific object].
"Desiring to go forth"—by excluding such specific [qualifications], one says "he desires to go forth.
And this alone is what is specifically to be inferred, because the state of being another mental continuum has as its very lifeblood this [quality of] form. And therefore, just as...

(Page 117) If, when one intends to infer fire from sandalwood, the fragrance of the smoke is abandoned, then only fire in general is established; not fire from sandalwood. This applies for as long as the probandum [is intended].

That qualification of the probans (*sādhanadharma*) must be accepted as necessary without which it cannot be established— just as the quality of possessing the fragrance of sandalwood is required for the inference of sandalwood fire in the case of smoke—
but the first human goal (*puruṣārtha*), consisting of the supreme human goal characterized by being "situated in another" (*paragata*), is not established.

The reason for not accepting another continuum (*santānāntara*) is precisely its being devoid of the specific qualities that constitute its denotation; it is not because it would fail to serve as the basis for establishing what is to be proven. And since this [other continuum] is the opposite of that [reason], there is an "observation of what is incompatible with the cause" (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*). Just as, for example, the fragrance of sandalwood is not [independent] in relation to its being derived from sandalwood.
A further distinction [is not established] because it does not exist by excluding that [other];

for only that which exists by excluding something else is a further distinction in relation to it, just as the state of being made of *candana* wood is [a distinction] in relation to the state of being made of *tṛṇa* grass.
Otherwise, even the spotted cow (*śābaleya*) would be a further distinction from "cowness" (*gotva*).

Otherwise, the conventional usage of "universal" and "particular" would collapse, because both the cow (*go*) and the brindled one (*śābaleya*) would result in being mere particulars. Furthermore, how could there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between two particulars? Yet such a relation exists—as in the expression "the cow is the brindled one. Therefore, they are mutually...

When one observes that a specific conventional usage—which is seen to be pervaded by a certain rule—entails its opposite, namely non-rule, it is excluded from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) because it cannot remain there while avoiding that [non-rule]. Thus, by virtue of depending on that avoidance, it is pervaded [by the rule]. And that which is contrary to it...

This is the non-abiding in the avoidance of that [absence], which constitutes the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). Thus, in the present case as well, the fact that activity, speech, and so forth—which have Maitra as their agent—reside within Caitra, who is the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*) consisting of another continuum, means they possess the nature of a manifestation (*ābhāsa*); namely, "this Maitra speaks."

In this manner, there is no distinction whatsoever apart from that [act of exclusion], other than the fact that the manifestation of the activity of "friendliness" (*maitrī*) and so forth— which is appropriate for the first person used in the sense of a "resting place" (the *prathamapuruṣa*) because the referent "I" has fallen away— is instead expressed as "I act" (*vyāpriye*),
which is appropriate for the third person (*uttamapuruṣa*). Excluding that [distinction], there is nothing else.

"Because it is not seated [there]. And thus, just as when one desires to infer fire produced from sandalwood fuel from smoke, the fact that the smoke is an effect of a fire originating from sandalwood fuel must necessarily be taken into account, and that [fact] is perceivable precisely through the presence of the fragrance of sandalwood; for instance:
Therefore, olfactory perception is capable of apprehending the possession of that fragrance— thus [it is said].

For one staying within the inner apartments, there is the apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāptigrahaṇa*) through a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from the manifest power of the fragrant smoke of the sandalwood fire; even at the time of inference, there is the determination of smoke as qualified by its fragrance and sweetness. It is exactly thus.

And since it is possible for there to exist a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) whose nature is to effect a synthesis arising from the power of visual and olfactory perception, it is established that from a specific fragrant smoke,
there is the apprehension of fire as having sandalwood for its fuel— that is, the apprehension of [the smoke] as an effect of sandalwood fire.

At the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be required; however, that is not possible. The same applies here in the present case as well, and it does not hold in this context. For specifically here, the effort of another (*parasamīhā*) is what is to be inferred. Otherwise, if mere effort in general were to be inferred, [the argument would fail].

Even for one who is like a *piśāca*, the desired [result] would be accomplished in the semblance of activity regarding Caitra. Now, if it is argued that the desire is accomplished only as residing in the appearance of the form of the speaker of that [object], which is known by the consciousness of the inferring subject (*anumātṛ*) and the knowing subject (*pramātṛ*), then [the same applies] when there are a thousand knowing subjects, each being an inferring subject.
From the thousands of appearances of speech that have entered into the thousands of appearances of compassion transferred to them,
a thousandfold exertion shall be accomplished;
thus, for those many inferential subjects, because they are grounded in a single cognizing subject—

The relationship characterized by the meeting of transactions would not exist; and by this very logic, even when another subject (pramātṛ) perceives a jar-illumination, because that jar-illumination is distinct [from one's own], there could be no transaction of buying and selling regarding a single jar-illumination between the two transacting subjects. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, the world, being swallowed by the great elements, is not born [again]. Therefore, when the activity of another— which is to be inferred and is like fire from sandalwood— is to be inferred, it must be apprehended as residing in another at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), just as one apprehends the fragrant smoke and the sandalwood fire.
The apprehension of another’s intention (*samīhā*) through the appearance of speech is not possible;

rather, it is the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which functions as discourse at the same time [as the speech], that is employed as the object of such discourse. Furthermore, there is no state of being "other" [in this case]. For if it were of the nature of another’s intention, it would depend on the vital principle of the continuity or non-continuity of the activity of association.

Since the mind, preceded by another's ascertainment, exists here within the subject of inference characterized as another continuum, there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*). Thus, even at the time of inference,
[the cognition] "I am speaking" would have to be inherent in the mental continuum of another person, such as Maitra, which consists of consciousness.
First, this [appearance] exists on the foundational level; then, as it transfers into me and becomes established within me,
this semblance of speech speaks— this is what is meant by its "belonging to another's continuum."

The qualification is to be apprehended by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, no other means of valid cognition applies here, because the mental continuum of another person cannot be ascertained in this context. If it were indeed ascertained, inference would become redundant. Furthermore, if one were to infer [the qualification] from that very [other means], there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). And thus:

To begin with, the fact that [a state] resides in another's mental continuum is difficult to know. Even if it were known, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) regarding the point that this—being of the nature of a manifestation of linguistic usage—is an effect of another's intention. This is what he says: "And not in another's mental continuum..."

And so forth. By this much, it has been stated that even if one accepts that the activity of another's desire is the cause, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that [activity]. Now, however, regarding the appearance of the form "I am speaking" within one's own continuum as being "he speaks" by virtue of belonging to another's continuum—this is what is meant by its "belonging to another."

The proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādī*) states, by means of the passage beginning with "the appearance of speech" (*vyāhārābhāsasya*), that the nature [of speech] is severed from the willer; thus, that [appearance] does not constitute the effect of the will itself. For Maitra, first of all, there exists in reality the will: "I shall speak"; thereafter, the appearance arises: "I am speaking."

Let that which belongs to his own continuum arise for him; however, the appearance of speech belonging to another’s continuum—such as when Maitra, who is resting in Caitra, speaks—that is not to be produced by an effort belonging to Maitra, for it is not an object of his effort. Is this not so?
It is true that when a particular [object] is desired, the universal is also desired;

however, it is only as having the body of one of the particulars within that which is desired that it becomes desired. Otherwise, if it were desired independently, then by the will of a potter, the three worlds would become pots.

One might expect it to be perceived as complete; but since that is not the case, this follows: even when there is a desire directed toward a universal, only a specific particular is actually desired, which consequently appears as it arises, setting aside other particulars. Therefore, by this...
Although, in one sense, the universal (*sāmānya*) is intended, nevertheless, there exists within one's own self a semblance of speech (*vyāhārābhāsa*) of the nature "I am speaking" (*vyāharāmi*).
(Page 120)
That [speech] is established as being true by virtue of its being produced from a desire [to speak]. As for the fact that the speaker— identified as Caitra—
is a stream of consciousness distinct from the stream of the desirer,
[the speaker] declares his belonging to that [other stream] through the very act of speech, which is appropriate for such an appearance, as in "This is Maitra."

It is a specific form; of whom could it be the product? It belongs neither to Caitra nor to Maitra, for the volitional effort (*samīhā*) of either is not present therein. For if volitional effort were capable of producing such a thing—namely, the appearance "I am speaking" in Maitra—at that very same time, [the appearance] would have to exist in Caitra as well.
"To speak" means "let the manifestation arise. Thus, when Maitra intends:

"Let that manifestation which is mine—consisting of 'I am speaking'—arise in Caitra as well, uninterrupted," then Caitra too becomes a participant in this uninterrupted manifestation: "This Maitra is speaking."

If it were so, then by his will—desiring to display marvelous feats, or desiring to acquire fame—the entire universe would at that very moment appear as such [an illusion], and yet it would not be seen by anyone as something shameful;
for in that case, there would have to be a desire for non-production. But this is not the case. Therefore, it is not the effect of an effort.

In another continuum, the appearance of speech and so forth is characterized by interruption. That [appearance] is not the effect of his volition, because it does not occur otherwise when there is no other volition, as a jar is not the effect of a weaver's [volition].
And likewise, since the appearance of interrupted speech belongs to Maitra, it is not the effect of [Devadatta’s] volition.

The state of being the effect of a volitional effort is pervaded by the occurrence of that effort in another form, just as the closing of a fist is [the transformation] of the hand. Otherwise, every volitional effect would belong to everyone;
thus, there would be an infinite proliferation of confusion regarding the ownership of one's own good and evil deeds and so forth. And that—
"In this case, no change that is pervasive is perceived"—this is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

This is what was stated by the words "and in another," and so forth. Through the effort of another, Maitra—even though it concerns a universal—it touches upon a particular, resulting in a semblance of speech directed toward another.
Even in the case of Caitra’s cognition, it would be produced in the form "I speak" as something uninterrupted;

however, since this is not the case, there is no evidence that [the intention] is the effect of an effort residing in another. This very point [is established] by including the inclusion of increase and decrease.
(Page 121) He concludes with "thus" (*evam*). Regarding what has been stated, "that" (*tat*) means for that reason this is obtained:
namely, that even by means of that general appearance of speech (*vyāharaṇābhāsasāmānya*) which occurs when specific qualities such as being desired (*samīhita*) and so forth are abandoned.

Furthermore, the appearance of speech occurring in Caitra—which is distinct [from Maitra's]—is desired to arise simultaneously with the appearance "I am speaking" occurring in Maitra’s continuum; for this very reason, it cannot be suspected of being its effect. There is no causality of Maitra’s volition toward that other appearance [in Caitra].
Nor does that other manifestation possess the status of an effect in dependence upon that [act of] willing;

and as for that other manifestation which takes the form "he speaks" occurring simultaneously with the manifestation "I speak," that is not at all the effect of will— for within that much, there is no will.

The reason is that [the other's intention] is not intended for oneself to that extent. But surely, when neither "being intended" nor "not being intended" is taken into account, but rather merely the general appearance of speech itself;
then why would that appearance residing in another not [be a cause] for the intention residing in Maitra, along with the other appearance?

The relation of cause and effect. True; he shows that this [intention] would succeed only if it were independent of particulars by saying "pertaining to itself alone. For, according to the principle of the *Yogasiddhi* section, even a universal, when intended, results in being restricted to a particular; and here too—
Indeed, a specific state is experienced such that the desire "I shall spit" arises;

then, by means of effort, the internal wind— which possesses velocity and is conjoined with a particular internal part— strikes the location covered by phlegm as its instrument, and thereby, through the medium of action, [expels] the phlegm from there.

By separating [the phlegm] through the intervention of another volition, one effects the external expulsion of phlegm with the thought, "I spit. However, this does not occur in the continuum of Caitra. Because it is manifested by the desire of Maitra, the word "spitting" is used for this object. Thus ends the term "spitting."

Because it is employed by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), it is not ungrammatical (*asādhu*). For that very reason, Candrācārya stated: "In the case of *ṣṭhivu* and *ṣivu*, there is also lengthening" (1.3.98). Therefore, even when there is an intention toward the general form, the intention toward the specific form is necessarily concomitant; and here, the specific form intended is precisely that which has the uninterrupted shape *ṣṭhīvāmi*.
Therefore, it is logical that the volition of Maitra [is not connected] with the appearance of Caitra, which is unvolited and disconnected.
(Page 122)

There is no relationship of cause and effect; nor can it be said that this subsequent, discrete manifestation directed toward Caitra is produced by that preceding, uninterrupted manifestation, because if those two were necessarily simultaneous,
the relation of cause and effect would be impossible— this is the additional point [to be understood] here.

[The word] *āvāpaḥ*. The form *iṣṭiḥ* is correct according to the statement of the author of the Bhāṣya: "here [the word] *iṣṭiḥ*. Otherwise, [if it were not so], it would be sublated by the rule *striyām* or by the portion [of the rule] *ktin* in the absence of similarity of form;

[but] the author of the Bhāṣya intends it as a word derived with the suffix denoting the instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*). And if it is argued that this is an augment prescribed by the supplementary rule (*aupasaṃkhyānika*) for the roots *śru*, *yaja*, and *īṣ*, then it applies here as well.

That very thing will come to pass; and there is no contradiction in meaning, for in the theory of *bhāvanā*, it is accepted that the verbal root-meaning possesses both instrumentality with respect to the result and itself the state of being an end to be accomplished.
Thus, the term *iṣṭi*—derived from "that by which the result is brought about (*bhāvyate*) through the object of desire"—is established as nothing other than desire itself.

Even when there is no dependence on karma, that by which one desires is accepted as the nature inherent in the agent; by this [activity], the state of being a desirer (*eṣitṛtva*) is brought about. For by means of that, the agent becomes a desirer. One should attend to this principle in each respective case—enough with these intermediate details. Now, the proponent of the doctrine of consciousness (*vijñānavādī*)...

Demonstrating that the state of being an object of desire for another manifestation necessarily exists together with the manifestation of one's own uninterrupted speech due to a difference in intention (*abhisandhāna*),
[the author] establishes through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) that the state of being a manifested separation is the effect of volitional effort (*samīhā*).

He demonstrates [the point] by means of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "Now, where... The phrase "in quite another way" means "without exception. When the Vijñānavādin has spoken thus, the Bāhyārthavādin remains silent for a moment while reflecting; meanwhile, the Advaitin [speaks].

With a heart hurried by the restless longing to dispel the delusions of others, and being endured by the proponent of external objects (bāhyārthavādin) in the hope that he might be supported by his own hand,
[the author] will demonstrate the ultimate reality of things, beginning with the words "He does not tolerate this" (*tat na sahate tad etat*). Even though...
Likewise, even in the case of Maitra’s own effort— where the appearance "Maitra dances" or "Maitra spits" arises—
how could Caitra know that this dancing, which is not concealed, is an effect of another's effort? For he does not [perceive] the other's effort...
Even now, indeed, it has been understood. By this very same reasoning, one must consider how Maitra—who does not know Caitra—could likewise have such an effort. But surely he...
When Caitra, having worshipped the Blessed One,
dances to please him with *recaka* movements and graceful gestures (*aṅgahāra*) in a confined space and a secluded place; and when he dances, gladdened by a joyful assembly,
together with Prayata and Maitra— without having sent them out from there— at that time:

"Let even one who is dear see [it], let even one who is friendly see it"—such is his intention. By this, he has grasped its pervasion within himself, based on the prior non-exclusion [of others] and the intention to reach the domain of another through the practice thereof. How is this so? It is as follows:
When one dances or causes another to dance without being prompted by anyone else, there is an underlying intention (*abhisandhāna*) in that act—

namely, "May Maitra also see it. This statement would be logically tenable only if [the dancer] were aware of the nature of the subject (*draṣṭṛtā-svabhāva*) within the semblance of Maitra’s body, which consists of volitional effort (*samīhā-rūpa*).

But even at the time when one desires to grasp the relationship of cause and effect existing within one's own continuum, how can there be knowledge of another's continuum? For consider: when two commoners or servants are spitting at each other, or two youths are challenging each other as debaters, or two young men are dancing, then [one perceives] "this is the other" and "this is that."
The intention "let him know" is preceded by the knowledge of another cognizer.
And that knowledge of another is preceded by the knowledge of the appearance of dancing produced by such an intention;
thus, there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). He says "of such a nature" with respect to the other.

"This manifestation is arising"—it is by means of this intended thought that this appearance of speech is produced; once this has been ascertained, one must then form a certainty regarding another subject. And when that other subject is thus known, and that knowledge is known within him...
The internal intention is appropriate toward one's own self, [thinking], "Let this appearance arise in another.
From that, there arises an activity that cannot be diverted; from that, the birth of an appearance of speech;
from that, the ascertainment of the causal relationship; and the knowledge of another cognizer, due to the aforementioned distinction.
"Because of the appearance of speech"— thus [it is said]. Therefore, there is a mutual dependence [between the two],
since the causal relationship between a specific appearance of speech and a specific volition is grasped at the very moment [of their occurrence].
For one who intends to produce appearances belonging to another, there is the cessation of the desired [appearances] of the dances and so forth belonging to that other person.
And let it be stated:

if the causal relationship of smoke were understood from some other means of valid cognition—distinct from inference and consisting for the most part of perception—that grasps a pervasion which is otherwise useless; [then inference would be possible].

And just as in the case of fire: just as one fire is cognized by means of smoke other than that [fire], so too would the determination of another perceiver be possible through the manifestation of another [perceiver's] interrupted dancing and so forth; yet this is not the case—this is what he shows with the words "yāvatā" (to the extent that). "From another" means from perception (*pratyakṣa*). For [in such a case] it would be scripture (*āgama*).

This form of verbal expression was uttered by this one who possesses perfect knowledge in order to awaken us— who are of the nature of other subjects— following a sequence beginning with a "parataḥ-saṃpāta" [an external encounter];
it has been explained or performed as either a ritual action (*kārya*) or a constant duty (*nitya*), mutually between us.

[The cognition] occurs only when there is a determination of another being as a cognizer; therefore, even in the case of perceiving another's mental continuum, there is indeed mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Thus, without having examined the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), although [the external object] does not exist according to the actual state of things, it is [grasped] along with such an intention (*abhisandhāna*).

It has been demonstrated that the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) of what appears as a fragmented discourse cannot be known. Now, however, he clarifies that—due to the impossibility of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*)—this [causal relationship] does not exist in reality, by stating "and not" (*na ca*). The connection is with the words "and not... is logical" (*na ca yuktā*).

He demonstrates the absence of any distinction [between the two cases] with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). A child crying does not intend, "May another hear me"—whether he is alone or in a crowd, when crying due to some pain, he is perceived by means of an indistinct sound; yet there is no basis for the inference of crying in another person [merely from hearing that sound].

It does not arise. [Objection: Surely, if there is the intention "let him not see," there must necessarily be an act of covering or shielding and so forth; and in that case, its non-arising certainly exists—what, then, is the point of the reductio (*prasaṅga*)? The meaning is this: if it were stated in such a manner...

There would be a causal relationship between the removal [of the veil] and the arising of its appearance, but not with the intention; and that [intention] is what is introduced here as the object of inference.
If it is argued that the appearance of the withdrawal of the veil is the effect of the intention, then in that case too, there is the veil.
The notion that "this friendly person is bringing [something]" is merely a mental appearance (*ābhāsa*);
since there is no further investigation into specific qualities such as the absence of intervening obstructions for that appearance, this argument amounts to nothing.
This remains true even if one intends, "May he not see it."
Even when the withdrawal of the veil occurs,
there is still the arising of thousands of appearances residing in other subjects, beginning from the omniscient one down to a mere worm; thus, it is not the case that...

In the absence of such an intention, the non-arising of an appearance as such would be logical, because there is no distinction [between them]. Since this is not tenable for the Vijñānavādin, for that reason—*tat* meaning *tasmāt* (therefore)—this person falls, goes, or runs according to his own will; thus is he designated by the world.
Because it falls [into the sphere of the object], it rests upon our own self, being distinct from the falling of a wall or similar objects;
it does not project the appearance of another cognizer, and thus it must be supported by that which has been made its witness. What is that?
He says: by means of the intellect—that is, by knowledge—and by the arisen effort, which is desire extending up to exertion.
The cognizer who is disciplined and friendly toward all beings possesses within himself an uninterrupted manifestation of the thought "I am speaking," which appears directly to his own self;

it arises precisely through the sequence of the application of causes, such as the striking of the vocal organs and places of articulation, as understood through internal tactile sensation and other means.
