It is determined that [the object] is "arising"; and within that very [moment], the cognizer Caitra is created by the Supreme Lord through unification with another manifestation, having been withdrawn [from his own state], so that he incessantly creates the three worlds again and again with hundreds of mental constructs.
"Even while conceptualizing, the one unborn [Lord] remains free from conceptual construction; He triumphs. (Sta. Ci.
112) Thus, for the sake of the eternal diversion of creation... (U. Sto. 22.9)

And by this principle, he too understands everything as being just like Maitra; however, due to the subsequent strengthening of the sense of "I" regarding the body and so forth, and the disappearance of the calculation that distinguishes between self and other, he conceptualizes it thus:
"Maitra speaks"—in this way, this is the position accepted by the proponents of God (Īśvaravādins).

This should be understood from this concluding passage. However, if one were to apply the phrase "this is for those of dull intellect" and so forth as representing the view of an externalist (bāhyavādin), then the conclusion would not cohere here. For by this [verse], the uniformity of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) has been stated; and since that [uniformity] exists even in the case of external objects, [the opponent] would find encouragement.
The proponent of external objects says: "And thus it is. For that very reason, activity toward Caitra as appearing to Maitra at that specific place and time, exactly as he appears, is logical.
(page 126)

Otherwise, as for the claim that "Maitra trembles," how can one be certain that the appearance of Caitra, which is accompanied by the appearance of that [trembling] location, is not produced by another cognizer named Maitra residing in the world of Brahmā?
For all that could be said at that time is simply this: if it appears here.
And it appears as if external to its own nature, having been transferred from another, like a jar or other object in a mirror.
Against the opposing view—that what is not of such a nature cannot be transferred from another—there exists a subverting argument:
being of that very nature (its own nature) is the opposite of being external to its own nature, just as [the property of] clarity is the opposite of [being external].

Because of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving what is contradictory to its own nature—namely, that [the speech] resides in the mirror—the reason is excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), and is thus pervaded by the very thing to be proven (*sādhya*). Furthermore, in the case of the cognizer Caitra, the utterance appears as something external to his own nature, in the form "Maitra is speaking"; therefore, by this [fact], it is [distinguished] from another.

"It must have undergone transference"—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Furthermore, anything else [such as a reflection] is indeed difficult to ascertain by virtue of its being located in that same place and time and so forth. In the case of a mirror, the original object (*bimba*) is established by another means of direct perception; however, it is not so here. And as for the reflection in the mirror...

The state of being produced immediately after the original object (*bimba*) does not imply simultaneity with it; however, in this case, since there is indeed simultaneity, how could there be a relationship of the "giver" (*samarpaka*) and the "receiver" (*samarpya*)? He indicates this by pointing out the impossibility [of such a relationship].
Furthermore, even in that case, what is seen in the mirror is either simultaneity or rapid succession (*āśubhāva*).
With this intention, however, he indicates by the very words "wherein no thesis arises" that [the thesis] would belong to him alone, and not to another. Thus it was rightly said:
"There is no restriction of place or time, nor is there any restriction of a [specific] continuum."
Furthermore, if representation does not exist as an external object, purposeful activity is not tenable.

Thus. Having thus stated the fault of not ascertaining its location and so forth, he brings forward another fault against the Vijñānavādin with the words "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*). The word "and" (*ca*) is used in a conjunctive sense. He expresses this other fault by means of that which serves as the prototype for the appearance, namely, [the cognition] thinking, "I am expressing," while [the object] appears [as such].

According to the principle that "that which has become a reflection appears as if separate and is presented [as such]," even the appearance of a jar— being distinct from the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) and unable to maintain grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the object "we" (*asmadartha*)— becomes "this" (*idam*).

It follows that [the word] must stand in accordance with the propriety of the first person (*prathamapuruṣa*), having been supplied by something belonging to another; and in that case, on the contrary, there is a fault— namely, that everything...
Thus, it follows that the manifestations residing in other subjects must be the providers [of the object], since there is no distinction [in this regard].

For even in the case of two mirrors, when they reflect one another's images, an infinite number of reflections arises; how much more so, then, when there is the mutual reflection of millions upon millions of subjects! Thus he says:

[Otherwise] there would be an infinite regress. Furthermore, even that manifestation (ābhāsa) which is accepted as being presented [to the subject], though residing in another cognizer, appears as "this" due to its distinction from resting within the "I" (asmadartha);
because it is capable of the conceit of separateness, it is like a reflection—and thus, by the presenter of that [reflection] as well...

It must be so conceived; even there, it would have to be conceived in the same way, leading to an infinite regress. To avoid this, one must ultimately admit that the jar itself—merged with the "I" (the subject), distinct from all other subjects, and whose essence is manifestation—is of the nature: "I, the jar, am manifest."

And even in that case, if "pot-ness" were not something additional, then the pot and the cloth—as they appear in the forms "I am a pot" and "I am a cloth"—would be one and the same. If, however, it is additional, then since it too must be a reflection, there must exist another original (bimba) that is devoid of the nature of appearance; this is the external [object].
Thus the point is established. With this intention it was said:

"This is another variety of the doctrine of external objects (bāhyārthavāda) for those who maintain that [objects] are external to cognition. And in that case, once an external object is accepted, what [is the status] of the appearances of other subjects?
On the contrary, because it would involve the presentation of the manifestation of another cognizer,

it would be beset by the fault of infinite regress; thus, there is a desire to avoid the defect of infinite regress by [asserting] that "that very external object will be the provider of manifestations for everyone."

He raises a doubt regarding another's position with the words "athāpi" (even so). Their function consists merely in awakening latent impressions (*vāsanā*), not in imparting their own reflection; and a latent impression produced by the experience of a previous jar, even when awakened by thousands of jars, brings forth that very same [single] one.

It brings forth the manifestation (*ābhāsa*) of a jar previously experienced; therefore, there is no infinite regress (*atiprasaṅga*) of manifestations whose nature is never-ending. However, this is not the case with other manifestations that are imperceptible (*parokṣa*), for there is no possibility of such a perception regarding them, as [the jar] was manifested in a location previously experienced.
Furthermore, there would have to be a manifestation [of the jar], or else, if there were no manifestation of space and time,
there would be a manifestation of the jar alone. But how could there be a manifestation of two jars or more, which were not previously experienced?
[Objection: But surely even the appearance of two jars occurred; it is simply that its latent impression (*vāsanā*) is now awakened. [Reply:

True, but the status of being a qualified object (*viśeṣyatva*) never belonged to the appearance itself—due to [the presence of] its specific location, time, form, and other concomitant cognitions. Therefore, it is only the latent impression of the appearance of the jar as thus qualified [that is awakened].
In the absence [of that], how could there be an awakening by which the arising of its manifestation would occur? For, when a distinct latent impression (vāsanā) is awakened,
a restriction of the qualifier-qualified relationship necessarily appears as something unprecedented, and so too does its latent impression.
"It could not have existed at all; how then could there be awakening through its sovereignty?"—this means "even while it is not appearing.

He explains "is awakened" with the words beginning "appearing as such" (*tathābhāsa*). When this sequence of expression is established, it would be said that "that object is being denoted. Such would be the form of the statement.

Of what form [is this]? He says: "In another means of valid cognition," and so forth, ending with "iti. By the word "tu" (but), he shows that the previously mentioned *prasaṅga*—namely, that sovereignty culminating in an appearance—is not tenable in the present context. "Seen" refers to [the fire] in the kitchen. But is this not the reason (*hetu*) in the aphorism?
"Why was the *prabodhaka* (the awakener) not refuted after being raised as an objection? [The author] says: "By the proponents of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*) themselves.

For something unprecedented is being stated here; indeed, an effort has already been made in this regard by the teacher Dharmottara and others to establish the existence of external objects and so forth. To explain:

The single ālayavijñāna, which serves as the substratum for those latent impressions (*vāsanā*)— the potencies that produce the cognitions of sound and so forth, as well as pleasure and so forth, along with the mind (*manas*) characterized by ego-grasping (*ahaṃkāra*) as the seventh—
continues as a stream even during sleep, intoxication, and the like, despite the absence of the sevenfold active cognitions (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
Since that [present cognition] lacks a cause residing within its own continuum and because the continua of others are always present, how could it produce successive cognitions? Therefore, he says:
"And it is observed. Here, the word "and" (*ca*) serves as a conjunction; it implies that not only what was stated previously applies here.

The intention is as follows: the principle stated in the previous sūtra—that "even this [object] must be postulated as something additional, like the sense-faculties"—is that which is the external object. As the Noble One [said]:
(page 129)
"...the external [object] would be established through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Now, it may be argued that even by the proponent of the non-duality of God (*īśvarādvayavādin*), the occurrence of faults in his own position has been stated. True;
however, this is so provided that even the doctrine of external objects—which are distinct from consciousness and well-established for all the world—cannot be sustained.
Therefore, for those who accept valid means of knowledge, it is logical that the path of the non-dual doctrine of God (īśvarādvayavāda) is the truth once all states of existence have ceased;
and since this is indeed tenable, what is the use of the effort of ascending other extraordinary and difficult-to-climb doctrines?
Thus he says: "The non-duality of God. (5)
Thus, when the proponent of external objects has been refuted according to the system of consciousness,

and the possibility of external objects has been firmly established by the words "if [it is so]," the proponent of non-dualism (Īśvarādvayavādī) says: "This might be so, provided that one rests content with those very appearances."
In conventional practice, what is the use of any other external [object] that is logically untenable?
But—this is the remainder of the sentence—it might be as you have said;

however, there is another possibility even more firmly established than the one you have suggested. Or rather, let this be your assumption for now; yet even if that were seen, [the following] will be stated.
"What is this 'additional' [quality] of ours that makes it worthy of such high regard? He says: 'In those very [objects]' (*teṣveva*).

Here, in the context of refutation, how can there be the grasping of that very [object]? Being part of the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrīkatva*) is common even to the sense faculties and so forth; moreover, it is not logical for another [cognition] to have its locus in another [object]. [Note: *parasya ca na paraniṣṭhatā yuktā* is the reading.]

Because otherness has as its very life-force the fact of not residing in anything else, it is incorrect to say that the manifestation of what is not the self is the very nature of consciousness. For that which is sublated is not the very nature [of the thing], just as yellowness is not the nature of a conch shell; and the fact that cognition resides in something else is sublated.

The uncontradicted nature (*abādhitatva*), which pervades intrinsic nature (*svabhāvatā*), is perceived as being contradictory [to the absence of external objects]. Therefore, even if an external object exists, it must necessarily be within those very appearances (*ābhāsa*) projected by it—which you yourself have accepted—and which manifest without rival. This is what has been said:

Even an external object that has been inferred must be said to be manifesting; for if there were a difference between manifestation and cognition, it would follow that [the object] is unmanifest, and thus even the state of being inferred would be like a state of unconsciousness for the entity.
(130) For this very reason, if another cognizer (*pramātrantara*)— inferred from the inferential cognition itself— is distinct [from that cognition],
then reasons such as "the necessity of being perceived simultaneously" (*sahopalambhaniyama*) would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Consequently, [one must admit] that there exists at least...

The *Saṃbhava* [Tantra] states: "If that which shines externally to consciousness were [truly] external, then blue and other such objects would also be external; yet this is not tenable, because it would lead to the consequence of their non-appearance. Furthermore, direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) is manifestation (*prakāśa*);

therefore, that which is established by direct perception as distinct from that [manifestation] is non-existent. Thus, those things capable of unfolding within the singular sovereignty [of consciousness],"

These are appearances, and they are not useless, because through them alone there is mutual worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*); even regarding imagined external objects, which manifest only as their own appearances, there is worldly transaction such as the appearances of buying, selling, giving, and receiving— and thus, once that transaction is completed within them...

The meaning of the aphorism is this: what is the use of further investigating an external category of objects—which is distinct from consciousness, which for that very reason lacks luminosity, which is devoid of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and which has been refuted by subverting evidence? The term "by objects" (*arthaiḥ*) refers even to those imagined as being external.
Furthermore, the external object— whether characterized by parts, devoid of parts, or both—
is sublated by valid cognition (pramāṇa), relying on such refutations as the imposition of contradictory properties (viruddhadharmādhyāsa).
Once the whole (avayavin) has been refuted, the atoms (paramāṇu) that are to be inferred through the sequence of its disintegration are likewise [refuted].
Non-existence. When the substance that is perceived is absent, what can be said of the qualities, actions, universals, and so forth residing in it? In its absence, what is inherence?
Furthermore, [the existence of] self, time, space, and so on [is established] by their utility for the specific characteristics found in perceived effects.

"Conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*) means that in the absence of such [external objects], nothing external exists. As the Sūtra of the Sage states: "The non-establishment of everything follows from the non-establishment of the whole" (*Nyāyasūtra* 2.1.34). And an object consisting of partless atoms is sublated by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The construction of the commentary (*vṛtti*) is as follows: "having conceptualized the sixfold conjunction and so forth in many ways through many modes. He introduces all of this in brief with the words "with respect to the empirical agent" (*vyavahartrapekṣayā*), and so on. It is the empirical agent alone who seeks the reality of things.

(131) Indeed, the search for that is not a mere whim. "Without flaw" (*nirapāya*): a flaw (*apāya*) consists of the absence of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the possibility of defects; [the cognition] is free from these. "Exceedingly more" (*adhikatara*): it is superior even to the [cognition of] reflections in a mirror.

The meaning is as follows: reflections are merely additional to consciousness; and that which is even more additional than those is never seen anywhere to exist. Therefore, how could that object act according to its own will?
Thus, it is not supported by the force of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And this is what is observed by authoritative persons: that...

Even when a thing exists, they do not exert themselves regarding a part that is useless for their purpose once it has been examined, such as the investigation of the six elements regarding the sense faculties and so forth, or the followers of the Jaina (Bārhatya) school. For by these [the former], there is only this much: the five elements and consciousness.
The completion of the transaction is accepted right there, because other factors such as the sense organs do not intervene;
this is likewise held by others regarding the four elements,
both in the case of a specific modification called "consciousness" arising from a diverse combination, and in the case where that modification has not arisen.

The cessation of the conventional usage of subject and object has been reached. The word "just as" (yathaiva) is connected with the word "so too" (tathaiva). The phrase "it might be so" (syādetat) introduces the two examples in order to explain the possibility expressed in the Sūtra. By the word "not a factor" (anaṅga), [the Sūtra's] phrase "what else? (kimanyena) is [explained].
This has been explained. One who is skilled in investigation should seek the true nature even of an object that is useless;

however, in this case regarding an external object, even this [investigation] does not exist—thus he says "nor even" (*nāpi*). By this, it is distinguished as being "due to its irrationality" (*anupapattyā*). It consists of a succession of cognitions (*pratītiparamparātmaka*); [this applies] even to buying, selling, and so forth.

The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are nothing other than such manifestation. Whatever manifests for this [subject] in this manner, that very thing serves as the utility for me—who am manifest—within the very manifestation of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Thus, by means of this price consisting of the manifestation of both, [the relationship is established].
"I shall make this [knowledge] manifest for its own utility"— because it is thus, therefore (tat).

"Only external" means that even by the Buddhists, who assert validity on the basis of determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*), it has been stated that inference also has only an external object as its domain.
"The validity of both [types of cognition] has for its object a real entity...
However, in our view, it has been stated that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) must necessarily be grounded in a real entity.

"And if the determination were an error... (1.3.5), and so forth in other passages. For that very reason, what the proponent of the external object says—that conceptual construction has the manifestation of the unreal—is simply impossible within our own system. [ka. *niravataraṇam*]

[The reading: For the proponent of cognition with form (*sākārajñānavādin*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is a manifestation within itself, whereas regarding the object, it is a determination (*avasāya*). If this is said, how can there be the manifestation of what is non-existent? Let that matter rest for now. [Conceptual construction] is a common sense-faculty (*sāmānyendriya*) by virtue of being the instrument for the act of apprehension (*upalabdhi-kriyā*) as the appearance of conceptual construction.

Heaven is so called because it has as its object unsurpassed bliss and the means to that [bliss]; and liberation (apavarga), whose essence is the fullness of the singular core of innate, undrawn-forth bliss,
likewise necessarily proceeds toward the ground of non-existence [of suffering] in no other way.

Because it would be impossible to desire it, to seek its means, to receive instruction on it, to ascertain it, or to practice it, as the author has stated elsewhere: "In the case of desiring a desired object, one either reflects upon the desired object itself or upon that which brings about the desired object."
Nor is the unseen (adṛṣṭa) desired [as the goal], for heaven too is merely a realm for visible enjoyment.

Thus, even causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is to be desired only as something appearing; therefore, it too rests within appearance, and from that as well, there is no establishment of an external object. As the Bhaṭṭa [Kumārila] said:
"But if there is a difference in appearance, what is the object..."?
Having begun thus,
if one asks, "To what result does knowledge lead?", then what is the recourse if the reading is "tatphalāya" (to that result) or "tatphalam vā" (or that result)?

Thus he has stated that it is only the succession of appearances (*ābhāsa-paramparā*) that serves as the instrument for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Consequently, the claim that "the external object is established by means of common consensus" is, on the contrary, the very opposite of the truth.
Having thus asserted that appearances alone constitute reality, and because this is supported by valid authority (*prāmāṇika*), one need not even suspect a flaw in one's own position.
He shows that by demonstrating the purity of intention (*āśaya-śuddhi*), [the word] "only" (*kevalam*) is intended to express non-delusion.
This is subject to inquiry; it is worthy of being questioned. What? He says: "of the state of appearing" (*ābhāsamānatāyāḥ*).
[This applies] both previously and subsequently.

Thus [it is said]. However, neither before nor after does the manifestation of the *ābhāsa* show any contraction of time or space; furthermore, manifestation does not depend on a cause, whether it occurs necessarily or not. If that [cause] does not exist—

That [existence] would be causeless; and consequently, due to the absence of the relation between cause and effect, one seeking a jar would not fetch clay, nor would one go to the potter’s workshop, nor would one seeking smoke take up fire.
For the relationship between the signified and the signifier is rooted in the nature of cause and effect, as established by perception.

In that case, there is the apprehension of either the cause (*janaka*) or that which depends on the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīna*). For the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), its very existence is the life-force [of the inference]. For the essential-reason (*svabhāvahetu*) as well—there is the cognition of something non-existent, such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth, which depends on the same causal complex.
By means of inferring the properties of the cause, just as [one infers] the transformation of fuel by means of smoke.
Thus [it is said]. This very path of reasoning applies everywhere; as it will be stated:

"The effect, the cause, or the essential nature—these alone are born from the root of origination" (2.4.11). And this much of worldly transaction collapses if there were no cause. Now, one might object:
This objection has been raised; but is it truly a refutation? No, he says: "And this...
For the Divine is indeed the very self of consciousness... (1.5.7).
Thus [it is said].
Since this [objection] is also not a fault regarding the introductory statements (*uddeśa*) such as "And for the Lord who is established in the self" (1.5.10), and since there is no other defect,
he shows that this follows [from the previous reasoning] with the words "and thus," up to the point where it says "the supreme ground in the scriptures."

The intended meaning is this: even though it is the supreme secret, it does not fail to manifest; rather, it is indeed manifest. This has been explained by the great teachers in the *Ādisiddha-sūtra* within the *Śivadṛṣṭi*, as being the nature of the proposition and the reason for the entire meaning of the scriptures.
The demonstration of the means of proof for establishing conventional discourse has been set forth even regarding the Lord who is self-luminous;

he explains this with its intended meaning. In that regard, as was previously stated—"All this is indeed the Person"—that non-duality which was introduced without distinction, that [is not what is meant here].
It ascends correctly to the heart: that there is a single form for the flashing objects such as jars, which are otherwise mutually distinct.
(Page 134)

For who would believe a groundless statement based on mere words all of a sudden? Therefore, it is appropriate that the designation "non-dual" (advaya) occurs through the mediation of the stages of living consciousness; this is indicated by the locative case.
And that [non-duality] exists because, due to its nature as a manifestation, it lacks self-containedness.

Having grasped in one’s heart that this has been explained by the statement, "Because insentient things, when attached to another, result in identity with that other, since they consist of the nature of consciousness" (the variant reading being "because they consist of that"), the genitive case in the phrase "of jars and so forth" (*ghaṭādīnām*) is justified.

It is employed [in this way] because its nature is that of an appearance (*ābhāsa*), with reference to its primary dependence [on the subject]. Precisely because of its sovereignty—since it consists of the self-reflective awareness of the Self independent of anything else—there is no obstruction to the expansion of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*). For that very reason, because the expansion of the will is unimpeded, it consists of vision and action (*dṛk-kriyā*).
The expansion (*prasara*) consists of the nature of the eternally active present. As that same illustrious [author] has said:

"When he remains absorbed in the experience of the mere delight of consciousness (*cidāhlāda*), then his will is of such extent, his knowledge is of such extent, and likewise his action is of such extent" (ŚDVṛ 1.3).
Having begun thus:
"In this way, there is never a separation of the mind— which has attained its true nature through power— from these three aspects, nor from their presence or absence" (Śivadṛṣṭi 1.6).

Thus, by this [verse], the status of Will and the other powers is established as belonging to the Lord— who exists everywhere as the very nature of consciousness and bliss, uniform and imperishable, abiding as the substratum (dharmin) in the form of the possessor of power (śaktimat)— and to Will and the rest, which are being manifested through the force of the intensification of His sovereignty.
It was revealed to the three goddesses, which is why he is renowned as Tryambaka. Thus it is said in the Śatarudriya:
"When the three goddesses constantly worship him..."

And so forth. Precisely because its manifestation is uninterrupted, there is an absence of connection with new appearances; therefore, no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is applicable or useful therein. For this very reason, that which has no beginning (*anādi*) and is the primordial source of all things—this has been explained under the section on "Established from the Beginning" (*ādisiddha*).
This has been explained in detail here [on page 135]. By this much, the meaning of "vibrating" (*sphurat*) has been explained. Here, the present participle suffix *śatṛ* is employed.
When it is said that he "becomes pervasive" (*vyāpnuvan*), he is called "the Pervasive One" (*vibhu*).

Because no specific limitation regarding what may be affected by aversion is mentioned, its sovereignty (*vibhutva*)—which consists in the manifestation of universal form (*vaiśvarūpya*) like a mirror through the inclusion of all other things without exception—is thus described. Likewise, since [the Self] is independent (*svatantra*) as the "I" within all entities, the expansion of its will (*icchā*) is unobstructed; and for that reason as well...
Through the union of expanding vision and action, by virtue of the identity with light and reflective awareness,
he is independent of means of knowledge and the like, and is untouched by time; thus,
having attained the state of universal form (*vaiśvarūpya*), he remains non-different from that very [universal form].

Because the diversity of appearances is manifested like the various reflections in a mirror, and once this much is established, the attainment of fullness follows by necessity; thus, due to the absence of any desire for anything external,
the repose of the Light within itself is proclaimed as the state of "I-ness" (ahambhāva).
And that very state of rest has been described as arising from the cessation of all dependence.

According to the principle stated in *Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi* (23): "Autonomy, agency, and supreme lordship are also primary," [the Self] has the nature of the manifestation of supreme bliss; thus, one should rely on the sequence as required for the specific application.
An explanation of the words of the Sūtra has been provided. By forming the compound *nirvṛtacit* as a possessive (*matvarthīya*) ending in *-in*— meaning "one for whom *nirvṛti* exists eternally"—
the author demonstrates the absolute non-separation and the state of unified identity (*ekārthībhūtatā*) between light and bliss.

He defines the Lord, whose nature is consciousness-bliss (*vijñānānanda*), as the substratum (*dharmin*). "His own form alone" means that which is the ultimate, absolute form of jars and other objects is indeed His own form;
and because He manifests His very self as jars and other objects, He is "one whose form is His own" (*svākāra*). And that...
He is Śiva because he is the embodiment of the highest good; he is the Supreme Self (paramātman) because his essential nature is the ultimate reality beyond all conceptualized subjects;

he is the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) because he encompasses the manifestation of the well-known states of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara; and he is the Accomplished One (siddha) because he shines forth independently of the operations of the means of valid cognition. Thus...

In this very manner, and as stated elsewhere in the *Śrīśivasūtras*: "Of those," meaning of objects such as jars, "by virtue of their nature as light," according to the sequence of the ladder of living consciousness (page 136).
The ascent to the form of the Supreme Self and the universal form (*vaiśvarūpya*) of the Supreme Self; and the universe,
which exists through the division of the gross earth and so forth and the subtle forms and so forth in ten ways,
and through the division of the organs of action, the intellect, and the internal organ in thirteen ways.

It is twofold through its connection with the *prakṛti-tattva*, which consists of total equilibrium (*sāmyātmaka*) and is agitated by the causal principles (*tatkāraṇa*)—namely the *guṇa-tattvas*—which are themselves agitated by taking as their material cause (*upādāna*) those entities considered to be insentient (*jaḍa*). [In the Kha manuscript, the reading is "agitated by the instruments" (*karaṇākṣubhita*). Furthermore, it is twofold through its connection with the *puruṣa-tattva*, which is the vital principle for grasping these aforementioned distinctions, and with the *āvaraṇa-tattva*, which serves as its instrument.

The Supreme Lord, the Blessed One, possesses a thirty-sixfold form within the Paramātman, consisting of a group of seven— namely *rāga*, *niyati*, *kalā*, *vidyā*, *kāla*, *māyā*, and *ātman*— and a group of five principles (*tattva*) characterized as *vidyeśvara*, *sadāśiva*, *śakti*, and *śiva*, which are distinguished by the progressive gradations of the removal of obscurations.

Having attained a state of non-difference from the venerable Lord Paramaśiva, even every single atom, by means of the perceiver, has entered that ground of the Supreme Self non-dually; thus, it is indeed of the very nature of that universal form. For this very reason, in the venerable *Viṣamadṛśi*...

The fifteenfold and other divisions, produced by the distinctions of cognizers and their relations, differentiate the earth-principle (*dharātattva*) within the elements such as earth through the distinction between the possessor of power and the power itself.
Together with its own essential nature, that [principle] is to be known as fifteenfold. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.2)

These have been established by such passages; let this suffice for now. This has also been explained in the *Siddhasūtra* beginning with the words "even a location" (*pradeśo'pi*). And this is not merely a verbal assertion, nor is it based on mere dry logic; rather, it is experienced exactly in that way.

"Because of the observation of the connection with causal efficiency"—thus he says "for this very reason. Let the reality of self-awareness stand aside; for what could be said there? Even that which is insentient is established as being "thus," as far as the body extends, within the state of being the Supreme Lord—this is the meaning of the particle *eva* (only/just). It is established.

Through the meditation on identity with individualized principles (*tattva*), one may become water-like by means of water and attain the state of dry land by means of land; through such methods, other supernatural powers (*siddhi*) are obtained. By means of the meditation on universal identity (*samasta-tādātmya-bhāvanā*)—[Ka.].

In the context of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there is the reading [as follows]: through the immersion into the singular nature of the Supreme Lord within the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatā*), there is the attainment of supreme perfection. That which was praised by me [is as follows].
(Page 137)
I do not even perceive myself; indeed, by the forceful onset of the sprouts of hair-pores bristling all over, I violently obstruct even the most minute directions.
For as I cry out "Bhairava! Bhairava! the knot in my heart is being rent asunder.
Even the body, with the burden of the cage of fetters of its faculties shattered, acts as liberation itself.

And so forth. Furthermore, even in the case of a jar and the like, hundreds of ritual actions—such as the pacification of poison—are observed to depend precisely upon that [divine presence], being contingent on the proximity of the jar, the sacrificial ground, the altar-shape, and so on, which have been consecrated through the meditation on identity with the mantra. And since this is a secret matter, it is not elaborated upon further here at this juncture.

"Having become attached" means by way of an obsession (*abhiniveśa*) that is intense— comparable to the stubborn grasping of a foolish Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), as indicated by the reading *śrotriyagraha* in manuscript *ka*—
and which is unable to endure being set aside. "Beyond that" refers to both visible purposes and the unseen, as well as the conceptualizations of Garuḍa, which arise from mere appearances (*ābhāsa*).
For in the neutralization of poison, there is no distinction between [the two cases] regarding the mere cognition of causal efficacy (*arthakriyājñāna*) based on appearance. What more need be said?
Even the attainment of the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*) depends upon the differentiation of such appearances;
what other object could be desired that would not be accomplished by appearances, yet would be accomplished by things external to appearances?
As the venerable [author] has said:
"Intellect and words function with respect to things as they truly are;
no conventional usage exists for them by means of any other reality" (Vākyapadīya 3.7.108).

Thus, by this [statement], it is shown that only that which has ascended to the state of being well-known through narrative (prakhyopākhyā) is useful for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), by relying on specific stages of manifestation (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*);
whereas the appearances of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), dreams, and so forth, do not clearly serve as causes of joy and the like.

[The world exists] as mere cognition. Furthermore, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is not necessarily restricted [to a specific effect]; for instance, ocean water, even while performing the function of quenching thirst, is not thereby [automatically] a "substance" [in that sense].

On the other hand, the distinction between various appearances (*ābhāsa*) is uniform everywhere. The determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) of the cognizer is not capable of altering the nature of entities. Even [objects] such as clay, though desired [for a particular purpose],...

Since one who seeks the functional efficacy (*arthakriyā*) of gold has already been observed [to act], what is the use of that? He first explains the word "and" (*ca*) found in the commentary as being immediately followed by the phrase "sublated by valid cognition" (*pramāṇabādhitaḥ*), saying "not merely.
First, there is no valid cognition that establishes the existence of an external object.
(Page 138) Perception alone has been described by the opponent as the foremost among the means of valid cognition;
however, that very [perception], being of the nature of light, instead establishes its non-difference from light. That very word "ca" (and/also)—
He explains [the meaning] with the word "tathā" (likewise), indicating that the phrase "due to the attribution of contradictory properties, etc. should also be connected immediately after this.
By the word "tathā," the sense of "not only" is drawn in through conjunction.
And it is not only this sublation which proceeds by way of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that constitutes an obstacle; rather, [it includes others as well].

"Even from its own side" (*svato 'pi*) means that even by way of the cognition engaged in determining the nature of the object of knowledge through its own mouth, it uproots—indeed, as the reading in manuscript *kha* suggests, "as if it uproots"—the very nature of the object of knowledge by revealing its non-existence; that is to say, the external [object]. For the previous [sublation] was the sublater.

Regardless of the actual nature of the object of cognition—whether it possesses parts or is partless, whether it is contradictory or non-contradictory—let it be as it may; however, the principle that "what is distinct from manifestation does not manifest" has been applied with universal force. This, however, is the intermediate [position].

If it were so, how would it manifest in this way? Or, if it is indeed so, then how is it that "it is thus"? This will depend upon both the object of cognition (*meyam*) and its manifestation (*bhāsanam*). However, a third case will occur by relying on a mere, dry object (*vastu*) itself, independent of any manifestation.

Regarding the phrase "and in the case of independence from perception": this being the case, he states the middle refutation as "by way of having the nature of being one or many. Perception, for its part, consists in such [cognitions] as "this cloth is variegated" or "it is spread out," which reside upon the object itself. [Note: The reading *vartiniḥsandhibandhatvāt* is preferred.]

Because it possesses parts (*sandhimattvāt*), one conceives that a single object of cognition (*prameya*)—though divided by space and form due to its extension and variety—is grasped as such; yet it is not so, because unity and plurality are mutually exclusive and thus contradictory. [Objection: But surely, that which is one is precisely...

"This [composite] would appear as manifold; there would be a contradiction, but it is not thus"—this is the objection raised at the outset with the word "atha" (now/if). He refutes this with "tadapi na" (that also is not so). If the whole were to enter into the parts by means of the property of the parts, then the whole would never move, nor would it be covered, nor would it be colored.

[Such] an understanding would arise; for no one, having set aside the contact with the parts, could directly attribute trembling, covering, redness, and so forth to the whole. If, on the other hand, [the action] were to enter [the whole], then while one part possesses trembling and so forth, [the whole would also possess them].

Just as that whole possesses trembling and so forth due to the presence of those properties [in its parts], so too it possesses non-trembling and so forth due to the presence of the properties of other parts that are not possessed of trembling and so forth.
Thus, by the destruction or non-destruction of the parts, there follows the calamity of the destruction or non-destruction of the whole;

this is like a hero whose heart is enslaved by the addiction of complying with the hearts of a pair of beloved women— one plunged into excessive joy and the other into grief— caused by the death of a kinsman who arrived as a great festival during the occasion of their shared latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
"This poor whole (avayavī) has fallen into a miserable state"—
if it is claimed that because it exists there in its entirety, it also exists elsewhere, and thus its existence is "pervasive" (vyāsajya-vṛtti),
that is a mere arbitrary assertion made while disregarding the operation of valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). For [otherwise] there would be no contradiction between those two [locations].
If [the entity] is one, what is the meaning of "pervading" (*vyāsajya*)? Furthermore, its being "extended" (*vitatatva*) would not even appear.

Or, if there is a contradiction, how could both "subsisting therein" and "not subsisting therein" belong to a single thing—what, then, is the meaning of "pervading"? In that case, "subsisting therein" itself constitutes "subsisting elsewhere. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*):

There is no contradiction because the objects are distinct, just as in the case of color. The claim that there is a distinction between the material cause and the auxiliary cause for color and taste is also incorrect; for color has no other status as a material cause or an auxiliary cause apart from its very nature as color. Rather, that very same color is momentary and is the effect, just as [in the previous example].
It would be merely a vessel for conventional usage dependent on other factors;

likewise, it would be capable of accommodating the designations "material cause" (*upādāna*) and "cooperative cause" (*sahakārin*) in dependence upon other entities that are respectively similar or dissimilar in their fixed posterior existence. There is no contradiction with conventional usage.

It differentiates objects because it does not depend upon them. If that which does not depend upon them were to differentiate objects, then a pot and a cloth—being distinct—would cause consciousness itself to be differentiated; thus, there would be no fixed rule regarding differentiation.
Yet, a fixed rule is observed. Therefore, dependence upon those [objects] is the cause of differentiation, and its opposite is not.

And since it does not have that as its basis, this is the "perception of what is incompatible with the cause" (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*). For that very reason, when there is a difference in entities, the cause is unimpaired; the contradiction resides in the entity itself, and that [contradiction] exists in the difference of place and in the difference in the conventional usage of stability. For if, while a certain Maitra is sitting comfortably in his own house...

Those engaged in worldly transaction deal with form as something differentiated, thinking, "This is my friend," "This is my enemy," "This is neutral to me," or "This is nothing to me"; yet, by this much, he does not conceive that his own essential nature has suffered any injury within himself.
(Page 140) If the master, overcome by anger, should say: "If you do not stand outside right now, without abandoning your seat here," then this—

One might imagine that the difference in location is utterly contradictory to one's own state of not having fallen into death; however, even what was said regarding "there" is merely a word. For if it were so, then a single object would be both "that jar" and "a cloth"—it would be a cloth in that very place, yet not a cloth in another place.

What else, distinct from the forms of the jar and the cloth, is denoted by those two other words? If you say it is "space" (*deśa*), then because that [space] is diverse, the contradiction remains. Even here, setting aside those two parts which are divided by spatial divisions (*digbhāga*), what else exists there that is being questioned as being "other"? That would only be the case if one were to admit a distinction between different spaces.
Furthermore, there is indeed a contradiction: if it [the whole] exists when each part is absent, then upon the disappearance of all parts, it would perish.

To the question "What is the fault here?", he says: "Each one," because it depends upon the parts. For the meaning of "together" (saha) is only possible with something distinct, just as a father [is said to be together] with a son; such is the sense. Thus, the external [object] as accepted by the followers of Kaṇāda—

Having refuted [the opponent's position], he now refutes even what has been stated by the Vaibhāṣikas—namely, that "atoms are partless. The implication is that for this very reason, the objection regarding the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) was not even raised. As for the term "aggregated" (*saṃcitāḥ*), it refers to light that brings about the perception of humans, the influence of karma, and so forth, as well as the perception of cats and other such beings.
This means that they exist in a state of non-interval due to the lack of separation by the atoms of darkness (*timira*).

And it is not the case that this [extension] occurs when [the object] consists of atoms. "Extension" (*vaitatya*) is the possession of distinct spatial divisions (*digbhāgabhedavatva*). And that [extension] would [occur] if many atoms were in different locations; however, because [atoms] are formless (*amūrta*), [this is not possible].

Having raised the objection—"Since there is no capacity for them to occupy one another's space, why does [the formation of a pot] not occur once [the atoms] have been obtained?"—he says "For it is thus" (*tathā hi*). The intention is as follows: if atoms were separated by intervals, then [a pot] would be invisible, and there would be no fixed limit to the accumulation [of atoms].

There are hundreds of defects: the incapacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), the impossibility of holding or drawing [the object], the perception of both a mass of light and a jar in the very same location [the reading "perception of location" (*deśadarśana*) is found in manuscript *kha*], and the unwanted consequence of perceiving other objects such as earthy or fiery entities; however, if there is contiguity (*nairantarya*)...
It is mutual contact. In that regard, if one atom were to contact another atom,
there would be no part left uncontacted.

There is no other part of this [atom] distinct from it, and likewise for the other; thus, even when the two are joined together, they could not produce a form greater [than themselves]. The same should be said regarding the joining of others as well. He says "infinite" (ananta) to this effect. Such is the defect in the case of sequential conjunction; however, he will speak of the case of non-sequential conjunction later.

By the phrase "of that which is joined with a single atom," and so forth: when two atoms are joined simultaneously to a central atom, then the central atom is joined by its entire form as it is closely attached to one atom; thus, even those considered to be the preceding and succeeding [atoms] [are likewise joined].

If the atoms were to have their bodies submerged within the atom situated in their midst, it would follow that there is the appearance of only a single atom. Furthermore, conjunction cannot here be established as non-pervasive, because there is no possibility of another part that could be unpervaded. By two [atoms]...

If a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and a composite form (*avayavirūpa*) were to be produced by two conjoined [atoms], then, by relinquishing its status as the "ultimate" (*parama*) relative to its producers, it would be both atomic in form and yet something gross. Furthermore, the composite entity to be produced has already been refuted. "In perception" (*ādarśane*) refers to indeterminate sensory observation (*ālocana*).

This is the meaning. "Inability to be characterized" means, in other words, "indeterminacy. Now, one might object: "When many atoms are perceived, they appear in this manner; so what is the point of these objections? Anticipating this, he says: "The first," referring to that configuration which consists of the differentiation of the appearance of directions.
If, when a collection of atoms is being perceived, its essence consists merely of a mental conceit, then—

since there is no distinction in the fact that it is a collection of atoms— how could there be this rule, agreed upon by all cognizers, that "this is straight in one place, this is curved elsewhere, this is square in another, and this is triangular in yet another"?
If there were no difference in appearance due to their performing distinct causal functions,

then even the statement "those atoms are such-and-such" would necessitate the acceptance of some other reality distinct from mere atomhood— something grounded in an external object concealed by the word "such-and-such"— this is the certain conclusion.

If such a thing as this is not accepted as existing externally, then why should even the blue be accepted as having external existence? And if the blue is not admitted, of what could atomhood be established?
For only when the blue is established can its [status as] a real entity—which is characterized by properties contradictory to those that pervade reality—be proven.
(142) When the nature of a composite whole— which is invariably concomitant with the superimposition of contradictory properties— is negated,
the nature of partless atoms is established; and because there is no temporal distinction, momentariness is proven.

Because that which performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is the real entity (*vastu*), whereas if there were a difference in space and time, it would necessarily result in non-reality due to the occurrence of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmayoga*). Thus, it is established that blue is indeed contracted in terms of place, time, and form; it is not extended, nor is it stable, nor is it variegated. That...

If blue is that which performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*), then straightness, curvature, and so forth must also be accepted as being substantially real (*vastusat*), because causal efficacy is established through those very forms. Furthermore, since blue is not perceived as consisting of atoms (*paramāṇu*),
this [argument] also finds no room for application elsewhere than to pure blue.

Because that which performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*) is made an object by conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), and only to that extent does it possess existence due to its causal efficacy, any other configuration is non-existent, like a stationary [object].
This is what he says with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). In this way, many atoms appear within a single cognition.

"Capable of appearing" means that they are simply this much, namely "this. Now he states the third sublation: "by their very nature. When the atoms are brought together in a hexagon, such as in a die and so forth, then they are resorted to as having the status of a limit (*avadhi*) within the fixed [structure]. (Note: *dhruve* is the reading in manuscript *ka*.)

Six atoms are joined simultaneously at a single point in the center. If this were not postulated, how could there be the formation of a composite object consisting of six hexagons? Consequently, that central atom must necessarily have six parts. If it is argued that a part is itself an atom, then the same difficulty applies there as well. And thus—
Thus, this very same consequence regarding parts and the whole follows all the way down to the ultimate dissolution (*apralaya*).
Furthermore, the claim that "conjunction resides in a single part" implies nothing other than conjunction with a single part.
This delusion of six parts is produced by the six limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of non-pervasive conjunction.

This too is without substance; for if the atom is partless, its non-pervasion due to its atomicity is a mere matter of words. For even in a partless entity, such as the great [ether], there is the possibility of connection with spatial directions—whether imagined, as in the case of ether, or unimagined, as in the case of mountains and the like. Thus it is.
By virtue of being hexagonal; furthermore, by the two particles *tad api vā*, this is stated: no configuration whatsoever is possible, for every configuration depends upon the existence of sides.

Nor is it tenable to claim that this conceit of spatial arrangement (*saṃniveśābhimāna*) is produced by the power of appearance (*pratibhāsa*). For, in the absence of a determining cause for the appearance, the assertion that there is a conceit of spatial arrangement in a specific place and in a specific way as a matter of necessity is devoid of reason. Furthermore, [there is] the connection with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
Whatever is the preeminent authority in establishing the existence of external objects, all of that depends upon their arrangement, and not merely upon clay-atoms,
because we observe that a jar and a lump of clay perform the same function. Such is the case with those atoms.

Thus, even this mere statement is not tenable if it rejects the distinction of an excess of structural arrangement (*saṃniveśādhikya*). As for what is said— that by the very fact that a single cognition grasps one thing while grasping another, there is an appearance of expansion (*vaitatyābhāsa*) similar to the appearance of duality (*dvitvāvabhāsa*)— in that case as well, just as...

Likewise, when those two are perceived, there is an appearance of duality, but there is no such appearance of a spatial configuration (*saṃniveśa*). And since this [configuration], being a conceptual existence (*prajñaptisat*), performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*) within the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti*), why resort to the further trouble of supporting the theory of an accumulation of atoms? Furthermore, [regarding] the whole (*avayavin*)...

To refute [the opponent], the proponent who maintains that substance consists merely of an aggregation of atoms has stated: "In one part of a jar there is shade, in another part there is sunlight; the middle portion is covered by both sides, while the two sides are uncovered; and therefore—"

How could a whole (avayavin), whose body rests upon such constituent parts (avayava), simultaneously tolerate contradictory states—namely, being in contact with sunlight and not, being obscured and not? By the mention of "obscured," qualities such as redness and so forth are also implied. For instance, in a multicolored thread, one part is red.
One part is not red, another part is black, and yet another is yellow, and so forth. Therefore,
since "freedom from connection with contradictory properties" is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of "being a real entity" (*vastutva*),
by the perception of its opposite— the conjunction with contradictory properties— [the absence of that reality is established].
The negation of the reality of the whole (avayavin) applies equally even to that atom;

for if there were two atoms on either side of a central atom, then the atom facing the sun would have contact with sunlight due to its forward position, whereas the one situated behind it would lack such contact.
And it is logical that there is an obscuration by two [atoms] for that which is situated in the middle;
however, since it is impossible for that which is situated in the middle and partless to have two sides,
[the formation of an aggregate] must begin from three atoms.

(Page 144) Regarding an object ending with such things as a large jar, the distinctions that are perceived— such as the division between shadow and light, being covered or uncovered, and being colored or colorless— are [unaccountable] under the theory of an accumulation of atoms (*aṇu-saṃcaya-vāda*).
As for what was stated—that [the object] is established without dispute—that is merely a matter of verbal assertion and not a matter of logical reasoning;

for this rule is untenable without the possession of parts (*sāṃśatva*). Alternatively, if a partless entity were to possess two sides and so forth, there would arise the absurdity of it simultaneously occupying that space and not occupying that space. [This is because] in that which consists of two parts...

If this [atom] were a unity, it would follow that one must accept the very doctrine of a composite whole (*avayavin*). Furthermore, by subjecting each part to the inquiry of whether it possesses further parts and whether it is atomic, there would result the consequence of infinite regress (*pralaya*).
Moreover, in every case, within an aggregate of atoms such as those of shadow, light, blue, yellow, and so forth—
There is no possibility of a limit that delimits an entity through a heterogeneous nature; for if there were such a delimitation, how could there be a cognition of unity in a variegated [object]?
Furthermore, since in reality there is an absence of middle, front, back, and so forth, there would be a lack of restriction;
thus, how could there be a cognition of distinct spatial arrangements? These and other such defects arise. He summarizes this as follows:

"By the Vijñānavādins": this point has been explained at length in various places, such as in the *Ālambanaparīkṣā* and other works by Diṅnāga, in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and its commentary (*Bhāṣya*), in the *Prajñālaṃkāra* and other treatises of the Bhāṭṭa school, and elsewhere. This...

The meaning is this: by this collection of refutations, which demonstrates the non-existence of the object, that means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding external objects—namely, perception—which was assumed by the opponent, must be rendered a fallacious means of cognition due to its incapacity; consequently, it remains devoid of any means of valid cognition.
"How can an external object be established?"— one should rest with this much [inquiry], for otherwise,

once a thing has been established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), a refutation would be utterly ineffective. Furthermore, the absence of a means of valid cognition regarding an external object has already been explained at length.
By the passage beginning with "of those appearing as present...
(1.5.1), and as will be explained at length later, what is the use here of these sapless investigations that merely report [the facts]? || 6 ||
Now, one might object: "Has not the existence of the external world been established by the reason of the variety in the sequence of appearances?
So how can it be said that such [an external world] is untenable? Anticipating this doubt, the Sūtra states:
"For the Lord, whose nature is consciousness alone, projects outward—by the power of His will—that which was situated within."
Like a yogi, it may manifest the multitude of objects without any material substratum. || 7 ||
First of all, that consciousness is the locus for the determination of objects is accepted by all proponents of philosophical systems.
(page 145)

Furthermore, by virtue of investigation and other means, that [reality] is one. And its sovereignty—consisting of the freedom to conjoin and disjoin appearances, which constitutes its divinity—has been established.
Moreover, the identity of objects with Light has been explained at length, and will be explained further.
Therefore, that which contains within it a manifold variety must arise from its very sovereignty;

and for that [sovereignty] to be admitted, there must exist a specific volition characterized by unimpeded autonomy. Furthermore, the creation [of objects] through volition is indeed observed in cases such as dreams and mental constructs.
By setting aside the well-known causal series of clay and so forth for [objects such as] a jar;

if it is argued that in this case the jar and so forth are unreal, let it be so for now. Nevertheless, it is established that a yogi creates a city, an army, and so on, solely by the power of his will. For in that case, by his will—
If it is asserted that the atoms conjoined instantaneously constitute the material cause (*upādāna*),

then [the potter] who is well-known as the producer of the jar must be accompanied by all auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), such as the training in all crafts, merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and the rod.

If one were to accept that the collection of causes, such as potsherds, appropriate for its own material cause [the clay], is required, then it would follow that this yogin is simply a particular kind of potter. However, even by the slightest deviation from established norms—
such as the creation of the appearance of objects perceived during dreams, volitions, desires, grief, and so forth— [this distinction is lost].
The capacity belongs to consciousness alone. Having manifested the desire, why do you exert yourself in vain to seek another cause? As Bhaṭṭa Divākaravatsa said:
"But [the cause] of your power of manifestation is not seen."
In dreams, the cause for the variety of objects is something else;
yet, by virtue of its observed efficacy, this [consciousness] is always the sole cause for the manifestation of the entire cosmic expansion.

Thus, even though the consciousness of a yogi is colored by the body, vital breaths, and so forth, it is the creator within that sphere due to its purity; for, in relation to other subjects who possess their own bodies, vital breaths, and so on, that object appears as external.
The principle of Consciousness alone (*cittattva*) is the creator everywhere. To demonstrate this very point, [the author] says in the *Vṛtti*:

Furthermore, in the *Ṭīkāvataraṇikā*, the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) is not explained separately, because it has already been explained by the very statement of the form of the illustrated subject (*dārṣṭāntika*); for in that context, due to the application of repetition (*āvṛtti*), the text is expressive of both [the illustration and the illustrated]. Since "God" (*deva*) is the conscious self (*cidātman*).

(Page 146) Therefore, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the word "prakāśayati" (he manifests) expresses the motive; for by the word "hi" (because), since the conscious Self (*cidātman*), by virtue of being the deity,
manifests the variety of appearances, for that reason, what need is there for any other external [cause] which is logically untenable?

Thus, the connection is with what precedes; this is the application of the sūtra. The word *eva* (indeed) illuminates that this matter is established without effort and accomplishes a vast multitude of desired ends.
This very point has been made explicit by the passage beginning with "by way of being the nature of one's own self" (*svātmarūpatayā*) and so forth, [referring to] both the agent and the object.

By means of this qualification, the meaning is as follows: since the essence of consciousness (*cittattva*) is "I," which is the self-nature consisting of a manifestation and reflective awareness (*prakāśavimarśa*) that does not depend on anything else, therefore its manifestation is inherently established and not something to be accomplished through effort; and so too is the manifestation of the multitude of objects, which are non-different from it.
"Because its nature is luminosity, manifestation is logical. This is the commentary on the phrase "situated within.
[The reason] is "because of possessing infinite powers. Indeed, this entire universe exists as a variety of powers within the Blessed Lord alone. As the scripture says:
Power and the possessor of power are said to be the two fundamental categories of reality;
indeed, the entire universe consists of powers, while Maheśvara is the possessor of power.

Thus [it is said]. Desiring to explain the meaning of the sūtra in brief, he introduces the object to be established—which resides in the preceding sūtra—in order to indicate that the word *hi* (for/since) functions as a reason, by means of the words beginning with "and not" (*na ca*).
He explains the word *hi* with the word "since" (*yataḥ*). The meaning is that this matter which is about to be stated serves as the reason for this present point.
"Thus" (*tathā*) means by way of appearing as external. He explains the meaning of the word "only" (*eva*) with the words beginning with "previously" (*pūrvam*).

"In every respect" (*sarvathā*) means not by the existence of an external object, nor by the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), nor by the appearance of a single mass of prior karma, nor by a distinction of will.

This variety of manifestations is established through the distinction of the semblance of causes, and not through the semblances of approach, verbal expression, or other subjects; therein, it performs what is exceedingly difficult to accomplish.

The Supreme Lord alone, whose power is observed to be unimpeded, is the refuge. Now, one might object: "In relation to what is there 'externality'? It cannot be in relation to the Light (prakāśa), for that would entail the consequence that anything external to it could never be manifest. Anticipating this objection, [the author replies] that it is in relation to the imagined subject (kalpitapramātṛ).

This is to show that [the object] possesses externality, and never arises from the illumination of another; thus, [he speaks of] the creation of objects of knowledge (*prameya-sṛṣṭi*), which consists of the levels of reality (*tattva*) and worlds (*bhuvana*), and exists in both gross and subtle forms.
(Page 147)

Having determined his own essential nature through the very association with the creation of the subject— which consists of the elements and is made manifold by the creation of existence characterized as a continuous stream of mental states differentiated by fifty distinct conditions—
he first establishes the structural foundation (*pīṭhabandha*) with the words "of that" and so forth. By the word "us," he does not mean his own self.

Nor is it that He displays [the world] as distinct from existing things; rather, He displays it as distinct for the sake of imagined subjects (*kalpitapramātṛ*). It is only with reference to them, and not with reference to His own Self, nor with reference to existing things, that there is the state of being a creator—this is to be applied in both cases. In this regard, this is the creation:

It is described in the Āgama as being fourfold due to its connection with the supreme, the subtle, the arrayed, and the pervasive. He analyzes that [fourfold nature] with the words "and he," referring to the Lord (Īśvara).
As long as there is a state of resting within consciousness, like a reflection in a mirror, that is the state of the Lord.

Immediately after the stage of Sadāśiva, which is the glory of the portion of [pure] consciousness, there arises within the state of manifest objectivity (*idambhāva*) the sense of "I am this" regarding the class of created things. To that extent, through fullness, the preservation of one's own nature, and the application of excellence, there is transcendence (*paratva*), characterized by having no other material cause.
By this, he explains the ultimate state of being without material cause (*nirupādānatā*).

Furthermore, these two qualifiers should also be applied to the creation of the *vyūha* and *vibhava* [forms]. For "supremacy" (*paratva*) resides in the three higher [forms], "subtlety" (*sūkṣmatva*) in two, and [it] exists in one—the *vyūha*. Each is sustained by its respective predecessor.

For indeed, as we shall elaborate in the section on scripture (*āgama*), each subsequent stage is superior. Furthermore, in reality, both the emanations of the *vyūha* and *vibhava* forms are without any material cause (*nirupādāna*). However, through the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*), the appearance of a material cause exists even in the case of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and so forth. From the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*) arise the subtle elements and the sense organs.
That [Mahat] arises from the Great Principle (mahat), that from the qualities (guṇas), they from equilibrium (sāmya), that from the primordial matter (kalā), and that from Māyā;
and Māyā, though it is the manifestation of the Lord’s power, is essentially a reality whose nature is insentience, appearing as the material cause of the universe. And this—
"The principle of the system (*tantrayukti*) is defined as looking ahead to what follows.

For instance, that which he will state regarding the emission of manifestation—that it occurs "by the power of necessity (*niyatiśakti*) through its own cause"—must be understood as applying to the extremely subtle and the structured emissions as well. This is because one must not bypass the primary emission.

In this context, the creation consisting of those [five] tanmātras alone is mentioned; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), which has the sense of "type" and includes other subsequent principles, it is meant that therein—

The intended meaning is this: sound and the other sense objects, having become objects of cognition (*prameya*) by virtue of their grossness, serve as the motivating factors for establishing the intellectual organs (*buddhīndriya*), the organs of action (*karmendriya*), and the volitions associated with them, which in turn produce the means for perceiving those very objects. And it is precisely through the power of perceiving those objects that one attains a subject (*pramātṛ*) appropriate to them.
The establishment of the six coverings (kañcukas) and so forth belongs to that subject who possesses them as instruments; thus, those alone are the vital breaths (prāṇas) everywhere.

Accordingly, even in the *Pañcabrahmayoga*, it is only space and the other elements that are employed in the form of subtle sound and the rest—therefore, whatever is an object of knowledge (prameya), that [is derived from them].

All this is indeed composed of that alone from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). For that very reason, the ultimate reality of the universe as consisting of the five principles (*pañcatattva*) is also described in the *Āgama*. We shall elaborate upon this in the section concerning the *Āgamas*. Regarding the term "yogins," he explains it as follows: "those for whom that" refers to those for whom the ultimate reality consists of the manifestations of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and so forth.

"From the non-specific" means from the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). For smell, when it is divested of its subordinate specificities such as fragrance and the like, appears simply as "smell"; that alone is what manifests there, and nothing further shines forth—thus it is called both "subtle element" (*tanmātra*) and "non-specific" (*aviśeṣa*). [This is] the arrangement (*vyūha*).
The agitation of sound and the other [tanmātras], as well as their mutual association, possess one, two, three, four, and five qualities respectively, starting from space (vyoman),
according to this principle. Thus, "the attainment of visibility" refers to the state of form and the others among all subjects.
The capacity to accomplish specific purposeful actions characterized by perception—that is the limit [of manifestation].

Therefore, if the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*) has attained such perceptibility, what other distinct appearance could there be that would constitute its true nature? That which is perceptible to a few becomes perceptible to all people.

And when that universal which has the form of an appearance is extended through a certain manifestation (*vibhava*), then that [manifestation] is called its true nature (*tattva*). A jar or the like is not extended by any other form;
for it is a manifold becoming (*bhavana*) consisting of earth and other elements in a state of mixture, mutual pervasion, and diverse division.

—Thus, "vibhava" (manifestation) is said. This is what he expresses by the words "due to infinity" (*ānantyāt*): because limitation (*pariccheda*), which consists of an end or a finite measure (*iyattā*), is impossible. And "from those" (*tataśca*) means from the *tattvas*. "In the form of the worlds" (*bhuvanākāreṇa*) means by way of having the nature of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and so forth, which serve as the substratum for experience (*bhoga*).

(149) "As 'pot' and 'cloth,' in the form of objects of enjoyment. Others, however, say that the creation of pots and so forth is itself the creation of entities (*bhāva*). For the *tattvas* are indeed of the nature of general manifestations.

Through their manifold relationship as qualities and the possessor of qualities, and by being combined in their totality, they manifest in the form of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the substratum of both, consisting of the elements, states of existence, and worlds. As for the creation of cognition (pratyayasarga), however—

The property of the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*) has entered into those very [entities] by the power of necessity (*niyati*); therefore, as long as that necessity is not subverted—as is ascertained from another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—the inference of cause and effect certainly exists. But in the ultimate sense, it is the Blessed Lord alone.
Just as in dreams, mirrors, and so forth,

even when the appearance of a jar preceded by causes such as a potter occurs, it should be understood that in those cases too, the power belongs solely to the nature of purity and the nature of autonomy. (Ka.)
The reading *mantavyam* [should be understood as] "by way of its own cause"; this he clarifies with the words "for the jar... and so forth.

The subject (*pramātṛ*) residing therein—whether it be a worm, an omniscient being, or anything else—is indeed the potter. His manifestation (*ābhāsa*), which is the light (*prakāśa*) resting in the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) "this is a jar," is precisely that which constitutes the primary essence under discussion.

The Lord is he who produces that jar whose form it has; thus, by the power of *niyati* (destiny), it consists of the manifestation of the subject residing therein. "From another" means from the causal complex consisting of the manifestations of the weaver, the threads, and so forth. Thus, in the case of the primordial manifestation of the jar.

The persistence of that very appearance within the emanation created by the Blessed One is established as "stability" (sthiti). And "tataḥ" means after the creation; "tat" refers to that emanated object, even when the appearance of the potter, the staff, and so forth has ceased.

Through the repose of the subject who has moved to another location, [the Lord] generates the manifold appearance of a jar and so forth together with that appearance; He creates its association with that [appearance], maintains the persistence of the appearance of the jar, and withdraws from previous subjects their possession of that appearance.
As stated by the author himself:
"Salutations to You, who always delight in creation, who always abide in the bliss of persistence, and who are ever-satisfied by devouring the three worlds. (Śivastotrāvalī 20.9)
Thus, even by the venerable Parameṣṭhin,
for the sake of his own activity, [it was taught] because of his Śiva-nature which consists of the fivefold function.
"For one who has entered [into activity], where is there a search for other causes?
(Śivadr̥ṣṭi 1.13), and... these [powers] are eternally established.
It flows indeed by its own nature; that flowing nature is Śiva.
Thus, Bhaṭṭa Śrī Nārāyaṇa also [says]:
"Though incessantly conceptualizing the three worlds with hundreds of mental constructs at every moment, the certain, one, unborn, and free from conceptualization is victorious. (Sta. Ci. 120)
Thus [it is said]. Now, for what purpose is the carrying of the jar to another place and so forth manifested in the middle? He says:

"By the power of necessity (niyati-śakti). When there is the carrying of the jar from the potter’s house elsewhere, then this is the event; but when there is the arrival of other subjects (pramātṛ), then what is the event?
He says, "In the eastern region," and so forth. "In that portion" means in the portion consisting of the manifestation of the jar.
"By internal entry" means by becoming one with the Light. By this sequence, He makes the manifestations of jars and so forth the objects of apprehension for those subjects who have arrived.

"And those subjects who grasp that [object]. Now, since subjects are distinct, how could the appearance of a jar—which exists as an object of cognition for one subject—pass over to another subject? To this, he replies: "Because, in reality, they are of a single nature."
This is not unprecedented; on the contrary, the point is that this differentiation is adventitious. Why?
Because this manifestation belongs to that which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), and all those [entities] have consciousness as their essential nature (*citsvabhāva*). [Objection:
But if this is so, why do the manifestations of bodies (*śarīrābhāsa*) not likewise [differentiate] from one another? [Reply: Who says they do not? Thus he says:

"Whatever there may be" means: whatever is perceivable by the external senses belonging to cognizers—that is, the body and so forth—is common; however, other things such as pleasure, volition, and the like are not so, for they are uncommon. And regarding objects of cognition (*prameya*), whatever is perceivable by the external senses—
To that extent, visible form (*rūpa*) and so forth are common [to all], whereas taste (*rasa*) and so forth are uncommon.
