Thus he says, "but exclusively" (*kevalam tu*). Internal tangibles (*spraṣṭavya*) are internal suffering such as pain (*śūla*) and the like.
Or else, it is the pleasure felt upon touching the bulb (kanda), the heart, or the channels (nāḍī), to be experienced at the time of meditative absorption;

or it consists of sound in the form of the *bindu*, *nāda*, and so forth; or it is described as "active engagement with objects. Fragrance and the other [objects of the senses] are likewise [experienced] one by one through the power of Niyati.

It is established as a rule within the subject belonging to *māyā*, whereas with respect to subjects such as the Mantreśvaras, it is indeed common; thus he speaks by means of the term "belonging to *māyā*. [The word] "done" [indicates] that it is by way of necessity (*niyati*). If that is so, then how can there be verbal communication for another person through the faces and so forth of another? To this he says: "But surely..."

Let it be that the appearance of a jar is one and the same in Devadatta and Viṣṇumitra; however, the appearance of speech (*vyāhārābhāsa*)—as in the speaker thinking "I speak" and likewise in the listener thinking "he speaks"—how can there be non-difference between these two? And if there is difference, there is inference.

This is not tenable—this has been explained at length in the *Vāsanāsūtra*. It is true; however, let it be considered how this [position] is consistent: here, whatever is to be made the object of the external senses, all that is indeed common [to all]. And thus, that which comes within the range of the ear...

Regarding the word "bring the jar," that sound which is denoted by the act of utterance appears as one and the same for both [the speaker and the listener]. Therefore, just like the appearance of one's own utterance, it shines forth in reality through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) even as non-conceptual; however, in the case of conceptualization (*vikalpa*),...

Even though "otherness" (paratā) is determined through the mental construction (*saṃskāra*) of the distinction between self and other, it is ineffective—just as the stability of a blue object [is not real]—because it exists otherwise than in the mere appearance of verbal expression (*vyāharaṇābhāsa*). Furthermore, at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the pervasion is established by that very [appearance]; thus, [the cognition] arises from that specific appearance.

Desiring to utter [the word] that coexists with that body, he infers that it rests upon our own meaning; for his realization is this: the appearance "I am speaking in this body" arises solely from the firmness of the conceit of being the subject (pramātṛ) of the body.

One who conceives that body as being "other" designates it as such through its permeation [by consciousness], saying, "this one speaks. In reality, however, even another cognizer is not an object of inference.
This has already been established in the introduction itself in the sūtra: "In that case, knowledge is self-evident...
(1.1.5). It is also stated in the *Vāsanāprabodha-sūtra* as follows: "Thus it is."

"Separated from the cognizer who is joined with the effort of the intellect," and so forth. Therefore, this inference—which is a means of establishing mere linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*)—is based on primary self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) once that is established; and this [inference], which consists of the synthesis of appearances, is what I am expressing.

He speaks—thus, both [aspects] are involved. Since one [aspect] is mixed with the manifestation of the "I" (ahantā), while the other is mixed with the manifestation of the body along with an excess of the manifestation of speech, therefore, setting aside that excessive manifestation, that which shines as a unity in the form of the manifestation of speech must be made the cause. And that...

It is indeed of a single form, and not of a diverse nature as in the system of the Vijñānavādins; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. Furthermore, within the power of necessity (niyati-śakti), there occurs the awakening of latent impressions (vāsanā-prabodha) regarding external objects, the predominance of karma, the manifestation of the cause of the primary will, and the manifestation of approach (upasarpaṇa).
Even the manifestation as the cognizer (*pramātrābhāsa*) functions as a cause in relation to each respective [object]; thus, he raises an objection here with the words "But surely...

(*nanu ca*). The underlying thought is this: since the manifestation of the jar already exists within the cognizer here, what is the use of another cognizer merging with it? [This happens] immediately...
"Let the appearance of a jar be produced by this [consciousness] as it has been transferred into the cognition of another cognizer;
by that much, the fact that the other cognizer simultaneously possesses the intended appearance of a jar is established.
What is the point of the reckless assumption of the non-difference of an extraordinary (alaukika) cognizer? To this, he replies: "This is not so."

He recalls the proof by stating "it has been said. This is the intended meaning: that manifestation, which resides in the previous subject, would either be a cause for the arising of the manifestation of a jar existing within another subject while being cognizable to him, or it would be entirely non-cognizable. It cannot be the former.

If it were cognizable, it could not be so because of the absence of a means for its cognition. For the cognition of that [other mind] occurs through the inference of another mental continuum (*santānāntara*), and that [inference] is not possible, as has been demonstrated by the proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*) himself. Alternatively, if it were non-cognizable...
If that alone were the cause, then because there is no distinction between other mental continua, all of them would become producers of that appearance;
thus, the aforementioned faults would ensue. He states this with the words "because of over-extension" (*atiprasaṅgāt*). Thus...
Having ascended from this ladder— the view that "blue and so forth are mere cognition"—
to another ladder consisting of the nature of a single, unitary cognition,
one attains sovereignty over the vertical expanse [of reality].
The reading is "ūrdhvadhārām. He poses the question: "Is it not thus? [He answers: "By way of sovereignty (*ādhipatyena*).

One should not understand this as a causal relationship (*kāraṇatā*) here; rather, it is merely its existence (*tatsattāmātra*). For if there were a doctrine of a single nature (*ekarūpa*), what would constitute the relation of cause and effect? Or alternatively:

With the intention that a manifestation of a cognizer (pramātṛ-ābhāsa) formed by mutual conjunction arises from manifestations of cognizers that were previously not so conjoined, the term "dominant cause" (adhipati) is stated as a specific type of cause. He shows that the fault of over-extension (atiprasaṅga) is avoided by mere unity with the words "and not thus. Furthermore, the fault mentioned in the previous sūtra does not apply.

He shows this by saying "avatarati" (it descends) and "na cāpi" (nor even). To this he replies: "This too does not exist. The meaning is that this state of being non-divine in nature is simply impossible for consciousness (*saṃvit*). For this alone is the distinction of consciousness from the insentient (*jaḍa*): its quality of being an undivided light (*aparicchinna-prakāśatva*). Even in its aspect as blue...

"It shines," "it also shines as yellow," and so forth—by such statements, the causal relationship between distinct entities, whether through their arising or their manifestation, is established; this will be elaborated upon in the section on Action (*kriyādhikāra*).
Therefore, that [causal relationship] too is manifested by the Supreme Lord alone, just as in a dream, between the jar and the potter.

And by the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*), [the world] appears as a jar and so forth in the world through the medium of the appearance of clay and so on; or, in the case of a magician’s performance, through the medium of the appearance of mantras, herbs, and gems; or else, preceded by the appearance of the disturbance of the bodily humors (*dhātu-prakopa*) and friends and so forth.

In cases such as cataracts or dreams, or in the creative emanations of a yogi, that very [object] shines forth preceded by the mere manifestation of the will; thus far has sovereignty been demonstrated here,
as well as previously the autonomy regarding memory and so forth through the conjunction of manifestations and other means, and furthermore, [sovereignty] which is yet to come.
It will be demonstrated [later]. Therefore, if consciousness (*saṃvit*) is established as one, then its sovereignty must also be admitted;
otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of it being insentient (*jaḍatva*), which is contrary to its very nature.
Consciousness is of the nature of the Lord (*īśvara*) precisely because it is consciousness.

(154) Thus is the reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Consciousness alone is the cause of the universe, because [the world] does not arise from anything else, and it arises when that [consciousness] is present. For this very reason, the sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) of the principle of consciousness (*cittattva*) which was mentioned—therefore...
An example perceived by yogis has been adduced for the sake of the reason (*hetu*). For what purpose? It says: "in order to demonstrate this. What is that? It says:
"of those wandering in *saṃsāra*, etc. With the words "otherwise," etc., he provides further elaboration.
"Adduction" (*upādāna*) means, in short, without the well-known collection of causes (*kāraṇasāmagrī*). Nor is there a state of non-reality (*avastutva*).
He shows that the creation of a yogi does not differ in kind from things produced by well-known causes by stating, "it performs a causal function. For the yogi intends:
"Let a jar arise that is indeed capable of performing the well-known causal functions."

He demonstrates that this is non-worldly (*alaukika*) with the words "hair" (*keśa*). Nor is there a lack of reality (*avastutva*) there, because the cognition (*vimarśa*) of hair, horses, and so forth does indeed exist. Furthermore, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) such as pleasure or agitation certainly exists there;
however, the kind of causal efficiency accomplished by other hairs does not exist here. And that [efficiency] is what is intended by the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).
"Alas, by virtue of being the cause for the conventional usage of the term 'existent,' the water of the ocean would be non-existent;
[but] because it enters into another causal complex (*sāmagrī*), it is not so—this is the same [in both cases]. For fire that has been suppressed does not burn nor does it cook.
Nor can existence be established from causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), because that [efficiency] is a distinct appearance (*ābhāsāntara*)," and so forth.
This has already been largely stated. Furthermore, it will be explained that even in the absence of that [external object], the appearance is not unreal:

"The causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of objects is innate; it is not determined by the will of God. For that [efficiency] is fixed by Him; therefore, its non-activity would not be anything other than its activity. (2.3.12)

Thus [it is said]. He explains this with the words "tadevam" (thus, in this way). Now, one might object: by the word "jāta" in the expression "arthajātam" (the collection of objects), totality is implied; yet the Lord does not manifest everything simultaneously. For he would have to manifest the object being created at the time of the Great Creation (*mahāsarga*), or perhaps at the stage of its initial production in the interim.
However, at the time of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), whatever collection of objects appears remains indeed established. To this it is replied:

"And as long as... At the time of origination means during the great creation (*mahāsarga*), in the absence of any appearance of a cause; yet, together with that [appearance], at the time of the first origination.
"At the time of empirical transaction" (*vyavahārakāle*) means that he separates [the object] from other subjects and joins it with others;
this is explained as being "for the sake of the constant delight of creation. Thus it is clarified.

The meaning is that in the commentary (*vṛtti*), the word *jāta* is explained as being synonymous with the word *artharāśi* (heap of objects) in such a manner. It is not correct to explain [the commentary] by saying: "The text in the commentary which reads *artharāśiḥ* has been elucidated by the entire body of the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) beginning with 'as much as anything' and ending with 'all objects.'"
Because it is inappropriate for the author of the commentary (*vivṛtikāra*) to lack authoritative evidence in his own explanation of what he has stated. || 7 ||
Now, when something appears as necessarily residing in another, it is observed to be of two kinds:

some is transferred by way of similarity, like an elephant and so forth in a mirror; some is manifested through the power of its own potentiality, just like the experience in a dream. This [present case] is not yet certain—is it...?

Having raised the doubt as to whether the group of appearances arises from the sovereign freedom of consciousness according to the analogy of dreaming, or rather through the power of transferring itself into other external objects similar to itself— like reflections in a mirror— the inference of external objects that present them is established by means of their effects.

In order to refute [the opponent's view] by means of another scriptural passage, he first states the nature of inference as it exists in reality: "Inference is certainly not accepted regarding that which has never appeared before;
rather, it concerns only that which has appeared, such as seeds and so forth, through the manifestation of the causal object. (8)

Whatever constitutes inference is entirely of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). And conceptual construction does not arise with respect to that which has not been previously experienced. This is accepted by all proponents of philosophical systems. Now, as for that which is inferred—such as the unseen force of the sense organs—is there not a prior experience in that case?

It is true that [the cause] has not previously been observed through any specific form by anyone, starting from the senses; rather, it is inferred only in a general way as some cause in addition to the visible form and light. In that regard, when clay and water are present, the sprout does not arise; for that [sprout], while arising when the seed exists, [does not arise when the seed is absent].
When the staff and the wheel are present, the jar does not arise; when the lump of clay is present, it does arise.

Thus, through the sequence of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), the certainty arises that [the jar] has as its cause a seed exceeding that [staff and wheel], and as its cause a lump of clay exceeding that [lump of clay]. And therein, what is called "causality" is—
The universal, which is excluded from non-causes and excluded from what is not additional,
is indeed apprehended through the operation of perception, since the exclusion of each [non-cause] culminates in the exclusion of the additional.

For in that context, the seed is understood as the entity whose nature is that of a cause; otherwise, if the term "cause" were not conventionally designated for a single seed, it would not be conventionally designated for a lump of clay and so forth. Therefore, there exists a commonality consisting in the appearance of causality (the reading *kāraṇabhāsa* is found in manuscript *kha*).

That which was previously apprehended through direct perception—upon that basis, conceptualization is appropriate there. And inference is indeed a specific kind of conceptualization. Inference does not occur with respect to an object that has not appeared [to consciousness], because it is of the nature of conceptualization.
For if it were to occur with respect to an object that has not appeared, it would be a novel cognition and thus non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).
And since this [present state] is contrary to that, there is the "perception of what is incompatible with the essential nature" (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*); such is the meaning of the aphorism.
The author of the commentary clarifies the first part of the aphorism by defining its implicit meaning through the passage beginning with "previously appeared" and ending with "inference."

The compound "pūrvāvabhātāntaḥsthitaḥ" is a *pūrvakāla* (prior-time) compound. For even when the word "prior" (*pūrva*) is employed, the occurrence of the state of being situated within at a later time is suggested (*vyaṅgya*). Moreover, inferential cognition (*anumāna*) is not merely reflective awareness (*vimarśana*), but rather—
It consists of the ascertainment of an object capable of attaining activity; thus he says "nāntarīyaka" and so forth.

With the intention that the purport of this sūtra lies in the conclusion of the forthcoming sūtra beginning with "ābhāsaḥ punaḥ," he introduces this sūtra precisely as an introduction to the meaning of the future sūtra.

Regarding the phrase "of the external": the intention is that [the external object] lacks establishment by means of valid cognition—not only because it is sublated by logical arguments such as the consequence of having parts (*sāṃśatva*), but also because it is not accepted even as perception by investigators, and furthermore, it is not established by valid cognition even in the sense of being knowable by a plowman. And this will be addressed in the forthcoming sūtra concerning inference (*anumāna*).

With the intention that even perception (*pratyakṣa*) is indeed refuted when [the object] is being refuted, the author of the *Ṭīkā* says: "First, by means of perception... For the appearance of blue is indeed one;
and it resides within cognition, otherwise how could it appear? Even the state of having the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrīkatva*) does not belong to the other.

One should establish its perfection [of cognition] just as one does for color, taste, and so forth. If it is argued that "form itself is such-and-such for this cognition," oh, what a grasp at supporting one's own position!
(page 157)

According to the opponent: that which, starting from the universal (sāmānya) and so forth, is itself treated as the supreme object (paramāstra), he considers to be the superimposition of contradictory properties (viruddhadharmādhyāsa). Therefore, this form (ākāra) is non-different from cognition;
in that case, no other [entity] appears as its depositor (samarpaka). [The reading "vā" is not found in manuscript kha.]

Just as in the case of [reflections] appearing in a mirror; and as for what was said—that [the objects] do not appear separately due to their being merged together (*samānābhihāra*)—that is not so. For even when there is a merging together, there is indeed a separate appearance, otherwise the very nature of a confused roar (*kalakalatā*) would be impossible. However, they do not appear as distinct entities; but here, in the case of that which presents [the object],...

If they were to appear separately, or if they were not to appear as distinct entities, then the blue form, being a massed form like a confused clamor, would appear as a doubling of blue. If it is argued that space, time, and so forth are likewise identical [in both cases], then here too there is the consequence of doubling; thus, the fault remains in the theory of having forms (sākāratva), even when an external object exists.

It has been stated that what is formless cannot be a grasper. Furthermore, regarding the claim that [the object] is established even by perception and thus corroborated by inference—and not established as something previously unknown like momentariness—that too is addressed here: although perception indeed depends upon conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*),...
Although it is proclaimed that "this is valid cognition," nevertheless, this is the ultimate truth therein:

perception, manifesting in self-awareness as the form of the appearance of blue, has its status as a means of valid cognition already established; it is merely by means of conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) that it is so designated in conventional usage. For this very reason...

Even though conceptual construction determines stability and so forth as being ungrasped by that [perception], it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to them; for conceptual construction,

while imitating the operation of perception by thinking "I am manifesting even what has already been manifested," does not rely upon validity through its own independence as a conceptualization of what is already established.

Therefore, this [cognition], by producing a determination (*adhyavasāya*) that takes what has not been grasped as being grasped, must indeed be excluded from being the fruit of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As for what was stated—that the validity of perception here [in this case] is due to the force of its connection with an external object—even there, is there a grasping of that connection or not? If there is a grasping, [then...]

In that case, since it arises from the apprehension of an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*), the cognition produced would be inferential and of a determinative nature; it would not be perception in that regard. And inference remains to be examined. If it is argued that "in reality, the invariable concomitance exists," then that [reality] must be established.
This discussion would apply if there were an external object;
however, since that [object] is not yet established even today, what is the purpose of this objection? Nor is it [established] in reality.

The restriction [that perception is valid] regarding an object exists, not because it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the object, but rather because of its quality of being a direct manifestation (*sākṣātkāritva*);
otherwise, that [cognition] would also have to be perception with respect to the eye.
This is because [perception] is absent when the object is absent.
Thus, the statement regarding positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is for the sake of establishing that [cognition] is produced from an object (*arthaja*).

And because it is produced from an object, it possesses direct perception of the object (*artha-sākṣātkāritva*). In this way, the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of both [the eye and light] has been stated as being rooted in their inseparable connection with the object. However, in this case, the object itself remains unestablished. Now, as for light here...

It is said: "The external object is directly perceived"—this is the conceit [of the opponent], and it is the conventional means of valid cognition (*sāṃvyavahārika-pramāṇa*) that is being examined. Why then is everything established for the entire world, such as stability, generality (*sāmānya*), substance (*dravya*), and so forth, not accepted? Even regarding those, others are deluded.

And the fact that they are deceptive is the same [in both cases]. As for what was said regarding the observation of something similar being presented— as in the case of a reflection in a mirror and so forth—
therein both [the original object and the reflection] consist of the nature of the prototype (bimba) and the reflection (pratibimba).

From the perspective of ultimate reality, it consists merely of the form of consciousness, like a dream or like a reflection appearing in a mirror. In that case, there is no certain conceptual determination as to what is presented by what. Furthermore, if it is argued that an appearance residing in cognition cannot be established without an external object that presents it, then what [is the status] of dreams, the double moon, and so forth?
This must be addressed: moreover, the analogy of the mirror is not appropriate here.

For in this case, a cognition bearing the form of blue arises from the perception of the object, which serves as its material cause (*upādāna*). In that instance, it would be logical to say that the form of the elephant arises from the mirror and the elephant; however, even when the elephant has departed, [the reflection remains].

Like a lump of clay, it exists in a body characterized by consciousness— a continuum that follows a succession similar to itself, yet unlike the mirror which possesses a continuum following a nature that is momentarily similar to lightning.
The form of an arrow, brought about by the favor of an assemblage of auxiliary factors such as the staff and the wheel,
persists in the shape of an elephant;
likewise, the production of an undivided continuum continues until the proximity of another cause possessing an undesirable power.
The relationship between the object presented and that which presents it is established at the very same time as the mirror and the elephant;
for this very reason, this is not an ultimately real relation of cause and effect, but rather—

The conventional usage of "original object" (*bimba*) and "reflection" (*pratibimba*) arises from that very [analogy]; thus, there is even a popular maxim that this is an error and not the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), which has not yet been refuted by anyone regarding the form of cognition (*jñānākāra*). In the present case, however, there is indeed a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between cognition and the object; for it is precisely because of this that the object of apprehension (*grāhya*)— [Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated. The translation above reflects the full logical flow of the argument as presented.]
The state of existing at a prior time. As it has been said:

"If it is asked how that which exists at a different time can be the object of apprehension, those who know the reasoning understand that its very status as a cause—capable of imparting its form to the cognition—is what constitutes its being an object."

Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, the object of apprehension does not appear as being at a different time, for there is a cognitive determination (*adhyavasāya*) precisely as being simultaneous in the form "I am apprehending this. If it is argued that this simultaneity is determined only with respect to the aspect of cognition appearing as a reflection, then you fool, how could you have said [such a thing]?

"The external form is determined, and by the force of that determination, the externality [of the object] is established through perception"—but how can it be said that the preceding momentary object, which is intended to be the projector (*arpaka*), is similar [to the cognition]?

For in the case of a reflection in a mirror, it is certain that the original object (*bimba*) is also perceived; thus, similarity alone [is established]. But here [in the case of cognition], [this is not so].

But since even the name of the object (*bimba*) is not understood, how could there be such equality? Therefore, if perception were to operate prior to inference, then that subsequent inference would [be the means] regarding the state of being cognized (*saṃvedanatā*).
[The reading: "It might indeed be so applied; however, it is not thus. To this he says:

"Because of the absence of two appearances. Now, one might object: "Granted that there are not two appearances, nevertheless, the external object will still be accessible through perception even if it does not appear."

[The opponent says: "It is simply that which is accessible through inference. [The author] replies: "No; he says 'that which appears' because it is precisely this appearingness (*ābhāsamānatā*)—the thought 'I see this'—that constitutes being an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣaprameyatā*). [The opponent objects: "But surely this [appearingness] belongs to a single blue thing; therefore, blue is established by direct perception. And that very [blue] will be the external object. Why [posit consciousness as the object]?"

By means of seeking a second appearance as blue. Regarding this, it is also said: "of that which is distinct. And thus, [the object] is established as being neither [inherently] manifest nor unmanifest. (1.5.3)

This has been explained in detail below. By this, the objection—"Since blue is uncontradicted because it performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), why should its externality be abandoned?"—is also refuted, because no instance of external causal efficiency whatsoever is established.
[This is so] because of the non-appearance of the object that results from the appearance of activity and the appearance of attainment.

For such is the nature of conventional reality, and there is nothing further; since the external object is not touched by perception, even inference is impossible by the logic of "the stick and the cake" (daṇḍāpūpikayā)—thus he says, "nor even...
[The non-perception of smoke and fire [leads to] the perception of fire when there is the perception of smoke].

The causal relationship is established all at once by two types of perception and three types of non-perception— namely, that the non-perception of smoke follows from the very aforementioned perception of fire.
In this regard, even non-perception is simply the perception of something else.
It is precisely from the operation of perception that the non-causality [of the external object] is established through the proof of the [existence of] the cognition.

And since the external object is not perceived, the causal relationship between it and anything else is not established; therefore, when that [object] is the object of inference, cognition is not a "reason based on an effect" (*kāryahetu*). Now, if...

"One might argue that 'externality'—which is a different property (*svabhāvāntara*) of the blue—is to be proven by the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), such as its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). To this, he replies: "In the case of what is imperceptible. That is to say: how can even a reason of essential nature be a prover for a probandum whose locus (*dharmin*) is imperceptible? The mention of "perceptible" [is intended to exclude such cases].

This is an illustration by means of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). For when a subject (*dharmin*) is established by a valid means of cognition, a nature (*svabhāva*) that is pervaded by another nature—which is itself established and necessarily concomitant with that [subject]—establishes the property (*dharma*) that is concomitant with that [subject] alone. And here, it is not merely blue...

There is nothing whatsoever established by means of valid cognition as independent, such that for a given subject (*dharmin*), its nature characterized by externality— which is necessarily concomitant with that [subject]— could be proven by valid cognition through the property known as causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), since [the subject] is unmanifest.

Because manifestation is impossible [otherwise]. And if it were of the nature of manifestation, then every subject (*dharmin*)—in the form of the means of proof (*sādhana*) and the object to be proven (*sādhya*)—would be established as non-different from consciousness itself.

By this very logic, it is indicated that in the system of Vijñānavāda, the establishment of another mental continuum (*santānāntara*) is untenable. For instance, in that case, whatever belongs to Caitra...
If the appearance of a body endowed with friendliness were directly perceived there, and on that basis another continuum in the form of a cognizer were to be inferred, then...
There would be no determination of the limited extent (iyattā) of the cognizer who is the object of inference;
for by the number of inferential subjects, there would be as many cognizers to be inferred.
In this regard, that very appearance of Maitra’s body which resides within the self of Maitra—therein alone...

The continuum of cognition is inferred by all inferential subjects. This [inference] would be possible only if that subject (*dharmin*) were established; however, how can that very [continuum] be established, given that it is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and because inference is dependent upon the mind? [Objection: But is it not the case that "blue" is not [perceived] here? [Response: No, it is not blue here.
It is not established that the subject (*dharmin*) possesses a property (*dharma*) consisting in being distinct from its own cognition;

rather, it is established that the consciousness appearing as blue—which is itself established through self-cognition—is possessed of a cause by means of an unperceived external cause. And although the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not grasped by that [consciousness], nevertheless...

Regarding the phrase "by way of the exclusion of the effect": since this effect—namely, the cognition appearing as blue—is occasional, it would not be possible for it to exist in such a state without an additional cause; thus, from this exclusion which possesses such a rule, there is also a positive concomitance (anvaya) by way of a general principle.

It is indeed established. To this, he says: "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). If, first of all, merely an additional cause is being proven, then that very independence (*svātantrya*), which is of the nature of will and consists of the sovereignty of consciousness—exceeding the nature of mere consciousness as accepted by the followers of Kapila—is already admitted as the cause.

The name would thus be established and proven. However, if it is argued that something additional—namely, its being external to consciousness—is being proven, that is untenable. Since that which is external to consciousness does not appear even in a dream, it cannot be an object of conceptualization; therefore, its status as an inferable object is untenable. To this extent...

The passage beginning with "inference" (*anumānam*) has been explained in brief. He now explains the passage beginning with "the sense organ" (*indriyam*) by saying "of the eye and so forth. To establish first that inference occurs precisely when [the object] has already appeared previously, he says "for inference... Since this is so, the meaning of the sūtra is correct. But [one might object]:
Is inference merely conceptual construction? No, he says: "non-deviant" (*avyabhicārī*).

By means of the essential nature as a logical reason (*svabhāvahetu*), the object to be proven—which is already established as having the form of valid cognition due to identity (*tādātmya*)—is simply brought into common usage by people who, out of delusion, had not previously applied such usage. As for the effect as a logical reason (*kāryahetu*), however...
"An unprecedented [result] is established"—
thus, in that very case, inference possesses independent validity. Furthermore:

It will be stated that the essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) is rooted solely in the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) ... [as in the verse]: "Or rather, an essential nature is born from that very root of origination" (2.4.11). With this intention, he suggests that the entire proliferation of logical reasons (*hetuprapañca*) is merely a sprout of the reason of effect (*kāryahetu*).

This is the word for the effect (*kāryapada*). To establish its validity even when it takes the form of inferential conceptualization (*anumānavikalpa*), he says "And that" (*tac ca*). The syntactical connection is: "Inference, as the agent, makes [the object] manifest.
And "not merely by that much" refers to the remainder of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) residing within.
Even though a mere separation, characterized by the manifestation of an external form, has been manifested, it would not—
without specific place and time—
bring about the engagement in activities culminating in physical action through inference. Thus it is said.

That conceptualization which pertains to an object qualified by specific place and time and is fit for purposeful action is of the nature of valid cognition; because it is non-contradictory, it is called inference (*anumāna*). Any other [conceptualization], however, pertains to a solitary object-entity alone.

Whether it be a collection of unrelated objects, or even one appearing as related; whether it be non-different from what was previously experienced, or even if it is different; whether it be externally non-present, or even if it is present; because of its connection with fixed place and time, it is unfit for physical activity.

Furthermore, regarding the necessity of activity characterized by the mental and verbal operations that establish the intrinsic nature of objects, when perception itself reveals the power of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
there arises conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) such as "this is a jar," "ten pomegranates," "this is its taste," or "on the bank of the river. Wherever [such occurs]...

"Smoke"—this [cognition] is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it lacks the capacity to prompt action. However, he shows that inference (*anumāna*) is distinct from this by saying "but this," [meaning] "from the reflection upon pervasion" (*vyāptivimarśāt*), that is, from the cognition: "wherever there is smoke, there is fire. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the fire which is possible in the locus (*dharmin*) is already present here?"

Because of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), that [fire] is accepted through the reflection on pervasion (*vyāpti*), since pervasion is grasped in a general sense; and because "there" refers to the locus (*dharmin*) as a particular, fire qualified by that [locus] is what is being proved—
thus, the particular would be the object of inference, not the universal.

Fearing that [the definition] "inference has a universal as its object" would be undermined, he says: "when the property (*dharma*) is perceived," [meaning] when it possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
The property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is indeed the third member of inference. And since that is apprehended by present direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
the conceptualization of pervasion (*vyāpti*)— being supported by the conceptualization of direct perception— is not [itself] inference.

It brings about the status of having a specific object, because the specific aspect is established by perception, and because the relation of locus and located is manifested in a general way within the pervasion [expressed as] "wherever... there.
He explains the passage beginning with "the sense organ" and so forth by means of the passage beginning with "only that which was previously experienced," and so on. Now, [an objection]:
"How can the sense organ be experienced, for it is eternally beyond perception? To this he replies, "Not so. Now, one might raise the objection:
"In the cognition of the causality of a seed or of soil, how could the causality belonging to something else be known?
He dispels this doubt with the words "not there," meaning in the cognition of the seed's causality. [The phrase] "later on" refers to what follows.

[Objection: But surely, when clay is known to be the efficient cause (*nimittatā*) with respect to a jar, the seed is also accepted as being an efficient cause; so why [is it not included]? To this it is replied: "Because it is applicable" (*prasakta*). The meaning is that this applicability arises from the appearance of a general causal nature. [Objection: But surely...

At the time of the cognition of a particular (viśeṣa), how could the universal (sāmānya) be cognized? And why should it not be so? On the contrary, it has been stated on this occasion—namely, that even for an omniscient one, the universal shines forth—that the very life of a genus (jāti) consists in its being colored by a particular. This is also the view of the Buddhists (Saugatas).
The determination (*adhyavasāya*) consists in the exclusion of each [other object]—

this is the very resting point of the exclusion of each [object] for perception, whose status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is thus conventionally designated. Here too, the operation of the means of valid cognition extends to every individual manifestation (*pratyābhāsa*).
It will be stated [in the following verse]:
"Cognition whose object is a single designation, which does not differentiate between place, time, and so forth... (2.3.2).

Thus [it is said]. For it is perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-perception (*anupalambha*) that establish the relation of cause and effect. In this context, perception is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to each individual appearance (*pratyābhāsa*); and non-perception is likewise so because its nature consists in the perception of something else. Furthermore, we shall explain that the universal (*sāmānya*) is nothing but an appearance.
Furthermore, from the cognition "the jar is made of clay," it follows that whatever conforms to the necessary rule of one thing [with respect to another] is the effect of that [thing].
The universal (sāmānya) indeed appears [in perception]. Consequently, that which the apprehension of form follows as its necessary rule is the eye;

thus, that [eye] has already been grasped by means of a prior instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, it is entirely appropriate to designate it as "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) by way of a general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*). Thus he says: "it will be established. (8)
"But this is not an event belonging to the external world; how, then, could it be inferred? To this he replies:

"Furthermore, the manifestation [of the object] somehow arose from the manifestation itself, and never from the external thing. Therefore, the existence of this [external thing] is established neither by perception nor by inference. (9)

The word "again" (punah) highlights the distinction [of the internal object] from the sense organs and so forth, which are also seen as causes in a general sense. That form of the object which is external to the appearance— that is, which exists outside the manifestation and is not manifesting— is [the internal object].

In no way whatsoever—even by setting aside other distinctions—it has not appeared as something external, because it does not appear as such. How, then, can "appearing" and "not appearing" be brought together at once in a single place, since they are essentially characterized by mutual exclusion? Indeed, it is not possible.

"By way of its non-blue nature, this is blue. Therefore, the external object is not established merely by perception, but also by inference. The phrase "in any way whatsoever" is repeated [here]. Thus, the meaning is as follows:
first of all, there is no inference regarding the external; or even if it were to exist, it would still be of the nature of consciousness.
To that extent, it is self-cognizable; and it has been stated previously that the cognition of something distinct is untenable:
"The object to be manifested is of the nature of manifestation...
(1.3.5). Therefore, whatever means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) you may invoke, tell the truth regarding difference.

The meaning of the aphorism is this: the command "be a witness" impels non-duality itself—which perceives the unreality of duality and, being impartial, is unable to deviate from the path of justice—to shatter that very duality;
thus, in no way whatsoever can anything exist outside of Light.

(Page 165) Now, to dispel the doubt that "the jar is indeed seen as existing outside of the light, as its object is distinct from that of the cloth," the term "jar and so forth" (*ghaṭādi*) serves as a qualification of the manifestation (*ābhāsa*) in the commentary (*vṛtti*). For that [manifestation]...
"It does not even have illumination"—this is the meaning. He explains "by that" (*tena*) as "therefore" (*tataḥ*).

Having joined the word "even" (*api*) immediately after "therefore," the meaning of the commentary should be explained as follows: first of all, inference simply does not exist; "even from that" means even from an inference that might possibly exist, [it does not follow].

He explains the phrase "of the external" (*bāhyasya*) in the aphorism by the words "occasional," etc., clarifying that the intended meaning is "the establishment [of the reality] of the external object. The word "of that" (*tasya*) should be construed with "the sovereignty of the principle of consciousness" (*cittattvasya yadaiśvaryam*). The term "directly" (*āhatya*) refers to another qualification consisting of externality, which is superimposed upon the general nature of causality.

The meaning is that it must be "stamped" (ṭaṅkayitavya). And "that" refers to the object qualified by externality. From the village, from the mirror, from the house, from the body, or from consciousness—externality is a single generality (*sāmānya*);
and this is established in the cognition "external to the house. Consequently, it is the signifier (*samarpaka*).

With the intention that external existence might be established even from the fact of being perceived—due to the cause of the variety of successive appearances—he raises the prima facie objection with the words, "But [is it not the case that] the eye and so forth... This externality of the jar is not one and the same as its being external to the village or to consciousness; for it is external to consciousness.

It is of the nature of non-perception, but not something external to the house that lacks the nature of being a house. For if this were so, a part of the house such as a wall, though inside the house, or a jar and so forth, though situated within the house, would have to be considered outside the house.
But it is not so. And that which is close to the house is what is external.

It is not from the house, nor likewise from the cognition itself, because that [object], being formless, lacks the capacity for spatial designation such as proximity and so forth. Therefore, with the intention that this [object] appears as a single entity by means of the mere generality of sound, he replies here: "To this, it is said."

Regarding the phrase "it did not exist at all," which negates the manifestation belonging to a prior time: for one who might be confused by this, the author provides clarification with the words "for here" (*atra hi*). For in the world, even that which is absolutely impossible is designated in such a way:
"this has never been seen, nor has it been heard of even until today. This is said through repetition (*āvṛttyā*).
Desiring to explain the portion of the Sūtra, he first [addresses] the portion concerning the subject matter of the Sūtra.

With the intention of showing another perspective, he summarizes by way of conclusion with the words "And this... The connection is with the word "has been stated. He asks, "How has its having non-manifesting objects been stated by others?
and answers with "For conceptual construction (vikalpa)... He explains that portion of the Sūtra by repeating it, saying "Even determination (adhyavasāya)..."
By the word "again" (*punaḥ*), he indicates that his own position possesses a distinction from the position of others. [This is] as stated:
"And because the determination [of an object] is an error...
"And it should illuminate its own object at its own time" (1.4.2), and so forth in these introductory statements; and it will be stated later: "only that which is perceived as distinct... (1.5.21).

In such passages as these, the suffix *ṇyat* is used in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*) to form the word *bādhyam*. The meaning of the particle *api* in the phrase "tato 'pi" is "even from," implying "even from a possible inference or even from another means of valid cognition. || 9 ||
Since there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever that can produce the appearance of an external object in the form of an internal reflection of consciousness,
therefore it has been rightly said:
"For the Lord, who is the very self of consciousness, [perceives] that which resides within... (1.5.7).

In this regard, however, the following must be examined: if the mass of objects indeed resides within the conscious self, then why does it not manifest? Who indeed would venture to say that it does not manifest? To this, he says:
By means of the Sūtra,
there is indeed the manifestation of the multitude of entities residing within the Self of the Lord;
without that [manifestation], the reflective awareness of will does not proceed.

The word "also" (*api*) has a displaced position [in the sentence]. It is not only the manifestation of the multitude of external objects—which appear in this very form—that is established for all the world;
rather, there is indeed also the manifestation of the Lord, whose sole nature is light, by virtue of His abiding within.
There is only a manifestation [of the object] through the fitness of *ahantā* (I-consciousness), due to the non-emergence of "this-ness" (*idantā*) characterized by external existence.
(Page 167)

It is not that [the object] does not exist; for if, in the absence of that [object], there were no regulating factor denoted by the word "desire" in the initial consideration—"I shall make a cloth"—then, just as in the case of a jar, the production of a cloth would occur even without a cloth being desired. Therefore, there must necessarily be a cloth that is to be desired; that very [cloth] is the [regulating factor] of that cloth.

If it is argued that this is an emanation (*nirmāṇa*), let it be so—whether on the level of the intellect (*buddhi*) or even on the level of impure knowledge (*aśuddhavidyā*). However, it is logical that emanation belongs only to one who is already established in consciousness and desires to remain therein. Furthermore, if one were to postulate another desire because the conscious being has not yet specified its intent, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). As for that which...
In the *Nareśvaraviveka*,
it is stated that when there is a desire to create (*nirmitsā*), the object to be created must be sought as non-different [from the subject];
otherwise, because it would appear as "this-ness" (*idantā*), it would be nothing other than a mere creation (*nirmiti*).
Furthermore, there must first be a desire to create that [desire to create], and likewise for that [desire];
this account results in an infinite regress, and consequently, there is a failure regarding the subject at hand.
And so forth. Therefore, from the necessarily occurring reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), its manifestation (*prakāśa*) is inferred. And this has been shown previously:
"And [the Lord] should manifest [objects] at their own time... (1.4.2).

This was stated in the commentary on this sūtra, during the explanation of the phrase "that whose reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) has the nature of light. By the gloss "as in the case of the Self" (*ātmanīva*), the state of being established in the Self (*ātmasaṃsthatva*) is made clear as the underlying reason here. For when the Self is manifesting, how could that which abides in non-difference from it not [be manifest]?

It would manifest. And so he will explain later with the words, "And the non-difference from the Self. He says that by the word "one" (*eka*), there must necessarily be a desire constrained [by its object]:
"The conscious self alone... (1.5.7).
He establishes the connection of this [verse] with the preceding sūtra by means of the words "of the knower" (*pramātuḥ*) and so forth.

By the phrase "in the appropriate manner," he means "as the self" (*aham-ātmanā*). He provides a concise explanation of the statement "there is indeed manifestation" by saying "it certainly shines" (*bhāsate eva*). The remaining portion is explained concisely because it is seen to be implied by the act of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).

[“By means of discernment” (ka.)]. Thus, “the cognizer,” and so forth—this refers to that which was previously called “the God” (page 168). Now, one might ask: what is the point of this [statement], “for one who is established in the Self”?
He shows that there is no fallacy [in his argument] because of the qualification "of the appearing entity" by means of the word "of everything.

By the word "thence" (*tataḥ*), which is stated again, it is understood as follows: although the entire universe is always situated within the Self of the Lord, nevertheless, it exists only through His power.

In relation to forms such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, which have assumed the state of a subject through superimposition, even this [world] appears as "this" with a sense of difference;

however, at that time, within the vibration whose nature is the desire to emit (*sisṛkṣā*), that entire universe abides perfectly within the Self, not having resorted to any state of difference whatsoever. And that [Self] is itself [present] even in objects.
When the Lord intends to create a stable and universal manifestation,

or at the initial commencement of a dream or an illusion, and likewise when He intends to create the unstable and non-universal bondage-creation (*pāśava-sarga*), one who is as if permeated by the form of the Lord [perceives] that much.

According to this principle, the reflective awareness of the light [of consciousness]— which is innate and arises solely from the manifestation of its own nature— is directed toward those various entities to be created by the knower, such as the *tattvas* and *bhuvanas*, as well as toward other objects of being. However, in the case of conceptualization, imaginative construction, and so forth, [it functions differently].

If there is the existence of a prior experience, this light is "unnatural" because it is merely the re-emergence of the reflective awareness of a previous manifestation; or rather, the light is "natural" because the "this-ness" (idantā) does not arise in any way whatsoever, as it abides solely in the form of "I" (aham). And that—

When the first creation was intended to be performed, that state of "I-ness" which belongs to the created world— once it has reached its limit as "this-ness"— is, as if motionless in the midst of creation, due to its non-manifestation as "this-ness";
since this depends upon the prior manifestation, it possesses a quality of being innate by virtue of both the aspect of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) and the aspect of light (*prakāśa*).

This should be applied to the manifestation of the "I" (ahaṃprakāśa). Now, one might object: "Granted that there may be a manifestation (*prakāśa*) with respect to objects, but from where does this 'I' come? He replies: "And that [manifestation]"—for the manifestation certainly exists. Nor can it be the case that its nature is merely that of a constructed form (*nirmāṇarūpa*), such as "this" (*idam*); for it has already been stated that in that case there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it is argued that it is indeed "this":

There is no interruption; therefore, it follows that there is non-interruption. Furthermore, it has been shown that this very non-interruption, characterized by the repose in the Self, is the form of the Light as the "I-consciousness" (*ahamiti*). And the connection with the manifestation as externality is what constitutes the "this" (*idamiti*).
It shines forth. And without that [consciousness], how could blue not be merely another form of appearance?
This same process applies even to the appearance of externality—this is the sequence [according to the *vārtā*].

All this remains established as manifesting as "I" within the self, both on the plane of the desire to create and on the plane of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). However, those seized by the obsession with absolute difference mistakenly imagine the non-existence of blue and other objects when they are in a state of external impossibility. And yet—

This is logical; thus he says, "of that" (tasya). If there were no internal luminosity (*prakāśa*) of blue and other objects, how could there be a desire for them? For that creation which is preceded by desire—being appropriate to a conscious being—is thereby undermined. [An objection: Let there be a desire directed toward the objects to be created, such as blue; what is the use of their luminosity? He replies:

Regarding the phrase "of manifestation and reflective awareness" (*prakāśaparāmarśayoḥ*): desire is indeed a specific form of reflective awareness, and reflective awareness is the very nature of manifestation. It is not logical for there to be a "nature" in the absence of that which possesses the nature. This has been demonstrated at length.
"And it should illuminate its own objects at its own time" (Sūtra 1.4.2). And this "this" refers to that light characterized by acceptance, which consists of the state of being a creator;
that very [light] is will (*icchā*). And since it is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), what conscious person would deny it?

He shows this by saying "I eat. That which is to be grasped in its general form—such as the nature of an object of enjoyment or a destination—and that which is the grasper when there is no mention of specific distinctions such as the body, senses, vital breaths, or intellect; [this is what is meant].

Then, within that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) which consists of internal discourse (*antaḥsaṃjalpa*) and the differentiation of various appearances within the intermediate self, there occurs a first expansion characterized by will (*icchā*), denoted by the term *paśyantī*, which has not yet attained the form [of the differentiated objects] wherein subject and object exist.
Since there is no emergence of discernment even through the form of generality, this reality shines forth by itself.

He states the reason for this with the words "since" (*yataḥ*): if, in reality, there were no manifestation of that which is non-different—consisting of both subject and object, and whose division has not yet dawned—then [that reality] would immediately...
In the reading of scripts, in rapid recitation, and in swift articulation,
[there occurs] the transition from one line to another line, from one region to another region, and from one point of articulation (*sthāna*) and organ of production (*karaṇa*) to another. (Page 170)

Furthermore, as one moves from one place of articulation (*sthāna*) and one mode of formation (*karaṇa*) to another, one does not reflect upon those various portions that are to be abandoned and those to be grasped; nor does one reflect upon the agent of that abandoning and grasping, even while perceiving those diverse [articulations].

How could these acts of relinquishment and acquisition come to be, given that they are observed to be preceded by a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)? Therefore, these [acts] lead one to infer their own cause, which is reflective awareness.
And this reflective awareness of theirs is not merely distinct [from them]; for if it were distinct from them, [the relationship would not hold].
In the presence of a continuous stream of verbal and mental activity consisting of the recollection of linguistic conventions, rapidity itself would not be possible. And it has been said:
"In some cases, regarding exclusion (*apoha*), there is no movement of speech or mind," and so forth. Therefore, this is the formal argument:

If the manifestation of the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) exists [in the act] of rejecting or accepting, it is an action of consciousness because it is an activity—this is a *kāryahetu* (reason based on an effect). Whatever exists and is not separate must necessarily be non-separate, because there is no third category—this is a *svabhāvahetu* (reason based on essential nature). This is how the passage beginning with "speaking, running, and so forth" [should be understood].

The existence of the knower and the known even through their non-difference— this much alone is to be explained as the reason [for the aforementioned state], but it does not touch upon such matters as "I eat" or "I go.
Thus say the venerable Parameṣṭhipāda:
But when, through the unfolding of the delight in the manifestation of his own conscious nature,
he proceeds to create a manifold world of effects with various arrangements;
"Let the mind be turned upward; this is the first *tuṭi* of the Will. Having begun thus [in Śiva-dṛṣṭi 1.8], it continues:
"And that [Will] is to be perceived in the region of the heart, from the time of recollecting the task to be done."
At the moment of the manifestation of intense joy, at the instant of the first glimpse.
Due to a lack of discernment regarding what has been seen, in the occasion of emission and its expansion,
as well as in the context of speaking of emission, in recitation, and likewise in running.
"In these very circumstances, there is the agitation of all powers.
Here, the intended meaning is this: consciousness consists of the state of being completely full of all powers.
(Page 171)
When he, by his own autonomy, contemplates that form which is essentially consciousness,
he abides in the bud of will (*icchākalikā*), characterized as the first unfolding of its expansion, wherein the nature of consciousness has become oriented toward that object.
Contemplating the future state of the entire class consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge— which exists as a unified form even before its manifestation—
one perceives the various future divisions as powers that have been condensed through a process of non-differentiation, like a cluster of fruits on a single stalk.

It arouses [the memory], and from that very [arousal] the effect, whose sequence is determined by its existence, arises. For example, with the desire "May I remember this verse," by the mere wish— without the need for a search to activate a continuous series of individual memories regarding the intervening letters, words, and so forth— a single [act of attention] brings about the result.

"Arising from a succession of recollections with a fixed order. Nor should it be argued: "Everything exists within consciousness in an undifferentiated state; so how can there be the emergence of a restricted set of effects? For, [the subject] thinks, "I shall produce this particular effect in this manner," and thus [directs his attention] toward the collection of things required for that specific effect.
The initial desire, arising first, conceptualizes everything as being useful.

However, from the nature of the subject—which is refined by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of that [initial state] and assisted by the cultivation of practice—there arises a sequence of effects touched by successive cognitions through repeated practice. Thus...
This should also be understood to apply to reciting, rinsing the mouth, and so forth. As the author of the treatise himself has said:
"For this very reason, for those who possess [mental] cultivation, even without exclusion (apoha), pain and the like arise from mere awakening alone."

Thus, that which has been made the object of the first volition produces an effect characterized by diversity, provided that no other intervening volition arises to obstruct that desired outcome. Furthermore, by the power of *niyati* (destiny), various auxiliary factors must be awaited in each respective case, just as strength and so forth are required for running. Therefore, this remains established:

For one who intends to produce a particular jar or a particular cloth, the "to-be-done-ness" (kartavyatā) and so forth of the potter, the weaver, and others certainly manifest within the first vibration of desire. Thus, in this determination,
during the discussion on the refutation of the Vijñānavāda school, that which was suspected as the cause of the variety of appearances—
That too is indeed logical; for, in its primary sense, it is the will of the Lord alone that remains, having embraced thousands of continuous successions of infinite creation and dissolution.
(Page 172)

The cause of that [manifestation], which possesses a fixed sequence, is the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) itself; specifically, it is the will of the venerable Sadāśiva and others, of the Mantreśvaras and others, and indeed of Brahmā and others. Even in that case, it occurs precisely at the moment of the appearance of birth.

The perception takes the form of a continuous stream of karma joined in a single impulse; within that stream, there is the appearance of the primary cause, the appearance of the contributory condition (*upasarpaṇa-pratyaya*), or at the end, the appearance of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). For that too—

The yellow appearance is indeed distinct from the blue appearance, which arises from a variegated state produced by the merging of the various subjects with the portion of the manifestation. For this very reason, it must be said: "Why does the yellow appearance not always arise from that same blue appearance?"—for that blue appearance is never absent at any time.
"...it occurs again and again without rest... (Sta. Ci.
112). According to this principle, one might ask: "In that case, what would one who seeks an appearance of smoke take up? To this it has been said:

Precisely where the causal relationship has been apprehended within a portion of the manifestation by the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*), there alone is the material cause for one who seeks that [result]. And this will be explained in the context of the absence of the creation of a yogi: (2.4.11).

In this regard, even the first section on action possesses causality only when viewed through the mouth of Niyati; this will be explained in the context of the expansion of the karmic impurity (kārmamala). For instance, at the very moment of the appearance of birth, that which consists of the vibration of specific zodiacal signs contained therein—
Then, due to its immediate succession,

that semblance of the *pramāṇa* (the means of knowledge) is rendered variegated in its entirety through the conjunction with other determinate appearances necessarily co-present with it, and through the conjunction with the appearance of another subject (*pramātṛ*).
For the wise person, there will necessarily occur the direct realization of all infinite and remaining appearances in the midst of birth; for, in the ultimate sense,
he has assumed the universal form (*vaiśvarūpya*) consisting of various appearances situated in their respective fixed places and times.

The Supreme Lord alone, whose body is light, is the cause everywhere. For even if Mount Meru were to exist in the potter’s house, or if the day of the end of a great aeon (mahākalpa) were to coincide with the moment of making a pot, such a thing would certainly not arise there at that time.

The "Kumbha" is the manifestation of a single moment situated within the continuous manifestation of the Kāli of the three worlds; even as it exists encompassing the entire universe, it is the very nature of the Supreme Lord. It is that very [nature]. (kha.)

Creating this or that by its own will, it manifests through its own infinite variety; thus, even the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*) in this system is not at all inferior to the doctrine of stability (*sthiratvavāda*). As the Avadhūta Ācārya has said:
O Blessed One, when you manifest within yourself the power of irresistible will (*prākāmya*), assuming various forms at every moment,
even that [power] attains its true purpose only in you.
For the most part, the doctrine of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda) has been composed by those who are clever.

Thus [it is said]. Let this matter rest for now. This is established: the universe shines within the conscious self (cidātman) in its proper form as "I" alone, on the ground of the primary reflective awareness of will (icchā-parāmarśa).
Others, however, interpret the subsequent text according to [the expressions] "I eat" and "I go."

Those who explain [the rule] read it as *pācana-dhāvana* (cooking and running), [interpreting it thus]: "Immediately after the desire to eat, one employs cooking; from the desire to go, one runs. And because of the word *yataḥ*, the ablative case (*apādāna-pañcamī*) is used in relation to the action of arising (*udeti*). || 10 ||

Now, one might object: "How can it be said that reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) in the Blessed One has the nature of desire (*icchā*)? For reflective awareness is indeed conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). And in the Blessed One, whose nature is pure consciousness, there is no room for the association with words—which is invariably concomitant with being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*) and being subject to conceptualization (*vikalpyatva*), both of which depend on the force of linguistic convention (*samaya*). To this, [the author] replies: "That very [consciousness]..."
The basis for conceptualization (*vikalpatā*) lies in the fact that when the Light is colored by an object of cognition, conceptualization—
resting upon the objective aspect through its association with verbal expression— may occasionally occur in relation to that object;
yet, even though it is itself non-conceptual, pure Consciousness does not take the form of conceptualization.
Because the state of being an object of cognition is not perceived. The cause of the nature of conceptualization is desirability;
the pervader of that [desirability] is cognizability. Thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader of the cause (kāraṇavyāpakānupalabdhi).
For even the cause is indeed a pervader of the effect of the effect.

And since pervasiveness is indeed appropriate for both the pervader and the pervader-of-the-pervader, it is with this intention that the non-perception of the pervader alone is logical; what is the point of increasing the mere proliferation of words?
(page 174)

However, this is merely the intention of Āryadharmakīrti, who does not enumerate these individual applications separately—as was stated previously. Therefore, in this case, non-acceptance itself is the resolution (*samādhi*). For it is not the case that here a verbal construction dependent on a conventional system (*samaya*) has been stated, such that...
[Otherwise] the state of being a mere mental construct (*vikalpatā*) would ensue; rather, the nature of awareness (*bodha*) is inherently that of reflective awareness (*vimarśarūpatā*).
With the intention that "this is precisely what we desire," the Sūtra says:
"They know the nature of manifestation to be reflective awareness; otherwise [it would be nothing]."
Even though light is colored by objects, it remains like an insentient substance such as a crystal. || 11 ||
Being manifest, it is indeed manifestation itself;

and while existing, its own nature is self-luminosity. It is called "manifestation" (*avabhāsa*) because it illuminates objects—that is, light—and its innate, non-conventional reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is "I."

Those who know the reality—those who consider the essence of mantra to be the principle of consciousness (*bodhatattva*), such as the principles of the venerable *Mātṛkā* and *Mālinī*—know that essential nature (*svabhāva*) which consists of sovereignty and is characterized by resting in the Self. And this is logical; for if indeed...
If its nature were not sovereignty characterized by reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*),

then light would be light only in itself, and a jar would be a jar only in itself; consequently, there would be no distinction between the conscious and the unconscious— characterized by being non-inert and inert respectively— even between light and non-light within the self, just as there is a distinction between a jar and a cloth.
[Objection: It is a distinction [of the object], namely that the manifestation belongs to another. [Reply: Then the jar, too, belongs to the clay. [Objection: It is produced by another. [Reply:
Then the subsequent moment of the jar is likewise [produced by another]. [Objection:
Consciousness has the property of being produced by the same causal complex as the other. [Reply: Then color also has that [property] in relation to taste.

If it is argued that being oriented toward another is the cause of its being a consciousness, then even a magnet would be a consciousness because it is oriented toward iron. Or, if it is said that consciousness, by its very nature, illuminates the non-self just as it illuminates itself, then how can the illumination of the self be the same as the illumination of the non-self?
"Form would exist"—this alone must be considered, because it is impossible for one thing to reside in another. [Objection:
But surely this very form has arisen as residing in something else throughout the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
(Page 175)
No other form of cognition has ever been perceived; thus, whose reproach is this?
It is not that of anyone else, but rather [yours], due to the delusion of partiality toward your own philosophical position.
For in this way, even universals, wholes, and so forth, have existed since beginningless saṃsāra as having precisely this same nature—that they are of a single form.
By stating "even those who have rested in many [traditions]," and so forth, one might ask: why should they not stretch out their feet?
Thus, all discursive inquiry has come to an end. Enough of this. Now, due to the exhaustion of other modes of movement, the consciousness would attain a state of similarity with the other;
the nature of consciousness would belong even to the crystal. The word "api" (even/also) [indicates this].

It illuminates the exhaustion of other possible destinies. Since this is so, therefore, this alone is the nature of consciousness as consciousness—that it does not manifest by means of another manifestation like a jar or similar objects;
that is, it manifests without dependence on anything else. And this very independence is what constitutes its nature.

There is a firm establishment of the "I" in the uninterrupted wonder of the experiencing self, which consists of the state of being an enjoyer and is characterized by the reflective awareness of one's own nature. For blue is [established] through such manifestation; that [manifestation] too is established through the arising of cognition;
and that [cognition] too is established in the ultimate sense as "I am thus manifesting," because it requires nothing else.
[Kha. reading: "Because of deliberation (*vimarśa*), and thereafter because of the absence of further desire"—this has been stated more than once.
In the *Vṛtti*, he explains the word *svabhāva* from the *sūtra* as "the primary self," meaning one's own (*sva*) unerring state (*bhāva*). He explains "otherwise" as "without that."
He explains that "the object is not colored [by cognition]" with the words "the object.
Fearing that by the mention of "distinctness" (bhedita) only the determination of each respective object might be established, but not its non-inertness (ajāḍya),
the commentator first explains the second half of the verse, beginning with "otherwise" (anyathā).
Because that object serves as the reason (*hetu*) for the subject matter at hand—the probandum (*sādhya*) stated in the first half [of the verse]. Now, one might ask:

"In what way does the mirror not differ from the jar? He replies: "And it is not [different] by way of insentience (*jāḍya*). It is true that it differs by way of its own distinct nature, like a cloth differs from a jar; however, insentience is exactly the same in both cases.

For what reason? Because, although a mirror may bear the reflection (*chāyā*) of a jar, it does nothing for the jar, since it lacks the nature of performing its [the jar's] function; likewise, even though light bears the reflection of an object, it does not [benefit] the object.

(Page 176) It would take the form of individualized transactional activity (*vyavahāra*). Now, it might be argued that mere similarity (*sārūpya*) is not the sole determinant for consciousness, but rather the nature of luminosity (*prakāśarūpatva*). And that [luminosity] both shines forth and [is] the supreme light.

"It acts"—such is the nature [of the statement]. If that is so, then even a mirror is a mirror and makes a jar appear as a mirror; what difference is there between this assertion and the statement that "light is light and makes a jar manifest"? To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "of the jar and the mirror": the state of being a jar and the state of being self-luminous are equal; for both the mirror and consciousness manifest themselves by means of another. What is the difference? Thus, luminosity is not established by this much alone, but rather—
"By means of the very entry of will, which consists of absolute freedom. The word *eva* (only/very) is displaced in its position.

The word *iti* has the sense of "because"; the word *tat* has the sense of "therefore. Because it is thus, therefore, from that which is perceived from the nominal stem *prakāśa*—namely, "illumination"—[the instrumental form *prakāśena* is derived]. By this much... [the reading *prakāśenetyetā* is noted as a variant in manuscript *kha*]. From that...
That which is perceived as a unique characteristic— the nature of the agent’s causal agency (*kartṛ-pratyayatā*),
consisting of an intense impetus (*saṃrambha*) and immersion (*āveśa*) in freedom, characterized by independence (*nairapekṣya*),
which is found neither in a jar nor in a mirror— that very thing constitutes the non-inertness of Light.

The connection [is as follows]: Alternatively, the construction is this—when it is said "the jar itself" or "the supreme form itself," even there, by the word "itself," that which is jar-ness and supreme-form-ness is accepted as being independent and resting within its own self by means of this very body (*vapuṣā*); therein...

By asserting independence (*nairapekṣya*), it is precisely this desire that is expressed. And through its connection with that [desire], the nature of manifestation itself belongs to the jar and the eye, because they rest solely within the self of the cognizer.
Thus, their state as insentient matter never occurs. As he will say:
"Thus, for one who desires to abide in this manner as the world-soul appearing as jars, cloths, and so forth, his very will is the cause, the agency, and the action. (2.4.21).
He states this very point in the words: "It is simply the nature of light. Since this is so, therefore, by himself...

"It shines" means it manifests as the nature of consciousness; "it illuminates the supreme" means it shines in the form of objects such as jars, through the manifestation of other-natures projected by its own sovereignty.
(page 177)

In this context, that which is the meaning of the suffix— namely, the nature of autonomy characterized by agency, which is distinct from the aspect of the primordial nature (prakṛti) because it consists of luminosity and purity—
is precisely the essential core of this light of consciousness, which is unlike the insentient light of the sun and other such sources.
By establishing its distinction from insentient light such as that of the sun, and thereby removing the suspicion of insentience,
it is said to "destroy insentience" (jāḍyamapadhvaṃsayati).
