This "destruction of suspicion" is metaphorically attributed to the object of suspicion itself, due to the relationship between the object and the subject.

On account of the sign (*nimitta*). Furthermore, the purpose here—in this metaphorical usage—is the demonstration that the essence of reality consists in its manifestation; thus, it is demonstrated that even an object that conforms to the intellect exists in that same way. Now, what other nature could there be for the Light (*prakāśa*)? [The reading *aprakāśasya* is not found in manuscript *kha*.]

With the single effort of the phrase "of the pure" (*viśuddhasya*), he dispels two doubts: first, in relation to what is this called the "primary nature" (*mukhya-svabhāva*); and second, how is its primacy established? He does so by stating that for light which is unmixed and, for that very reason, distinct from the light of the sun and other sources, there is a conformity with the Supreme (*parasārūpyam*).

There exists another intrinsic nature, namely the capacity for identity with that which appears as a reflection, by virtue of which the cognition of a jar or other objects is distinguished; nevertheless, that [capacity] is not primary, because it is possible even in insentient things such as jewels and mirrors, whereas reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is not possible in the insentient.

It is logical that He is the primary Self because He has no other object; this is what is meant by the word "also" (*api*). In both the Sūtra and the Vṛtti, this word "also" serves the purpose of including another essential nature. Now, one might ask:
when it ought to have been said that "He would be insentient due to the absence of reflection," why was it stated instead that "He would be devoid of wonder" (*camatkṛti*)?

Commentary: Anticipating the objection that "wonder" (*camatkṛti*) is indeed the activity of one who enjoys, consisting of the bliss of the consummation of experience, he says: "And that very [bliss]..."—referring to that which has been described as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of the Light.
This is what is meant: of one's own self, which is one's true nature...

The manifestation of one's own nature in its fullness, bearing the character of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), is called bliss (*ānanda*); whereas, by contrast, [the state] characterized by abiding in a limited sense of self (*ahaṃbhāva*)— which is turbid due to the contraction of the body and so forth, and incomplete as it pertains to the inner self— is [not bliss].
Because the body is empty, and since the mind of one afflicted by hunger is rendered helpless by the longing for food external [to the self],
this self-reflection cannot occur through a single, undivided state of being.

Therefore, this [individual] remains as if devoid of bliss (*anānanda*). "In a whisper" (*upāṃśu*) refers to that which is unvoiced (*aghoṣa*), which is heard by oneself alone and not by another; they have approached (*upagatāḥ*).

The phrase "whose rays (or expansions) have entered right into its own vicinity" serves as an illustration for the hands and other limbs as well, insofar as their respective effects— whether gross or subtle— are involved. Furthermore, in all these instances, there is a permeation by the sound of the activity of speech, which consists of both articulated and inarticulated forms.

It is perceived primarily [as such]. Therefore, it has been stated: "I shall grasp this," "I am grasping it," and "it has been grasped. Furthermore, the apprehension of phonemes (*varṇa*) and words (*pada*) occurs there because of the conceit that they are being heard.
For the cognition that a phoneme is being heard is indeed very clear; however, in the case of a word consisting of few phonemes, [the cognition is less so].

This might indeed be so; however, it was stated that in the case of a sentence—which is apprehended by cognitions consisting of the synthesis [of words], recollection, and subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*)—the state of being heard is not manifest. And thus, even by the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), regarding the sentence-sphoṭa...

For the most part, it has been shown that the word-sound is apprehended solely by the intellect. As the venerable [Bhartṛhari] said: "When the intellect has reached its full development through repetition, the word-sound is determined by the final phoneme together with the seeds deposited by the preceding sounds" (Vākyapadīya 1.85).

Thus, this is first of all the *parā* (supreme) speech. The second, however, is the *madhyamā* (intermediate) speech: that power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) which impels the internal organ—characterized by mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṃkāra*)—resting within the middle ground upon the support of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the form of the *puryaṣṭaka*. This is the *madhyamā* speech.

And that internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), impelled by that [consciousness], proceeds toward its own function characterized by conceptualization— namely, volition (*saṃkalpana*), determination (*niścaya*), and self-identification (*abhimanana*). At that time, that Speech consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśamayī vāk*) [manifests] the object of apprehension (*grāhya*), such as the volitional content and so forth, and the subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*), which consists of the one who wills and so forth, by means of itself.
Because she intensely contemplates— that is, thoroughly reflects upon— the expressive word (abhidhāna) such as "I, Caitra, intend this jar," through its distinct and clear sequential order,
she is called *madhyamā* (the intermediate), since she exists in the middle between [the unmanifest] thought and the [external] word.
[The power of meditation (*dhyānaśakti*) is of the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).
On the third [level], however, [there is the cessation] of the two designations pertaining to the grasped and the grasper, as well as of the two things designated.
The sequence belonging to the grasped and the grasper, which occurs according to its own nature through space and time,

does not exist in a manifest form; for this reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), being non-conceptual by nature, is itself without succession and undivided, like a seam that has drawn that [sequence] within itself.

The characteristic of succession remains concealed by its own division; therefore, that succession which has been withdrawn—meaning gathered together and internally contracted—from all objects of perception (*grāhya*) and subjects of perception (*grāhaka*), on account of this very withdrawal of succession, is subtle here. It is this [consciousness] that speaks of "that which is real," "something indescribable," and so forth.

Since, through a clear process, within words such as *saras* and *rasa*, and within sentences such as *devadatta-turaga* and so forth— when they have been brought together as if by a "massing" (*piṇḍīkaraṇa*) consisting of the contraction of their sequence— that internal discourse (*abhijalpa*), which consists of words and sentences, exists in a form that serves as the basis for the aphorism (*sūtra*).
It means "subtle. As the venerable [author] has said:

"But *paśyantī*, although possessing differentiation, has its power of sequential order withdrawn," and so forth. And he shows that this very [power] is of the nature of the power of will (*icchāśakti*) by stating, "the desire to act" (*kāryacikīrṣā*).
This [desire to know] also has the nature of the desire to know (*bubhutsā*);

and for this very reason, it is said that the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) is the sustainer of the powers of knowledge and action (*jñāna-kriyā-śakti*). However, even the desire to know has the nature of consciousness itself, because it manifests that object there through the fullness of its appearance.

However, a clear distinction is observed between the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and the actual performance of the action. For even when an object flashes forth in the desire to act, it is said that "it has not been done.
This state continues until the object reaches a state of complete clarity, characterized by being perceivable through both types of sense organs and being the intended object.

For we shall state that capacity is the instrument (*karaṇa*). The term "seeing" (*paśyantī*) is used to express that the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) has the nature of unimpeded manifestation, by virtue of its being of the nature of uninterrupted seeing;
it is so called because it is described as having the form of the expansion of light (*prakāśa*). And she—

This power of will (*icchā-śakti*), favoring the group of sensory organs which is the manifestation of the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*), brings forth indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpa-ālocana*). By the word "again" (*punaḥ*), he states that this [power] is distinct from even those three; by the word "one" (*ekā*), all three—beginning with *paśyantī*—are to be understood as being addressed.
The meaning is that it is not broken in that manner.
(Page 190) That which has attained the state of being non-sequential is the entirety of all designations without exception.

When the denotation of words is investigated, it consists of both aspects— the form [of the object] and that which is of the nature of the grasped and the grasper; thus, the pregnant [consciousness] remains having embraced all of that,
but not like the state of Supreme Śiva, who is the possessor of power.

It is that in which the manifold variety of the grasped, the grasper, and so forth has not yet dawned; for this very reason, it consists of that savor or aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) directed toward the Lord’s own expansion (*svābhoga*), which is essentially the reflective awareness of His own expansion (*nijābhogaparāmarśātmā*).
As it has been said:
"...you touch the entire universe while entering into its form" (Uttara-stotra 13.15). And the Supreme Lord is never at any time devoid of that form, as the venerable Parameṣṭhin has said:

Where it is described that there is the state of Śiva in both the tranquil and the gross, tell me: what is that tranquility? And in that which is tranquil, do you not maintain the existence of a real entity?

"If there is a union of the three powers of such a nature in reality" (*Śivadr̥ṣṭi* 3.56), and so forth. Having thus explained "the Supreme" (*parā*), he explains "arisen from its own essence" (*svarasoditā*) by [saying] "like its own nature" (*svarūpavat*). He corroborates this with the terminology of the scriptures, saying "ever-arisen" (*nityoditā*), in the sense of being perpetually non-setting.

That which is denoted by the term *anāhata* (the Unstruck) is the Great One (*mahān*), all-pervasive, characterized by the functions of thinking (*manana*) and protection (*trāṇa*), whose activity of manifesting all sounds has been concealed; [the speech] consists of that. "From its own nature" means from the expressive [word] characterized as *paśyantī*, whose essence is subtle internal discourse (*sūkṣmasaṃjalpa*). "Of that too" means...

"Of her who perceives [the object] as one whose denoted meaning and the word expressing it are non-different"—in this phrase, the compound *abhinnavācya* is used as a stem (*prātipadika*) in its technical sense (*vṛtti*) within the expression;
that is to say, she is one who speaks in the *vṛtti* by means of a word whose denoted meaning is non-different. "The denoted meaning also" [is likewise non-different].
In Paśyantī, however, the signifier has an indistinct sequence, whereas in the signified, the sequence exists but is merely concealed.

Alternatively, this observation regarding the result of the statement on the function [of speech] is as follows: as long as the signified is perceived in Paśyantī as non-different from its own essential nature, so long that signified has attained non-difference from the signifier.
For its own nature (*svarūpa*) is indeed non-expressive; thus [it is expressed] by means of a compound with either the genitive or the ablative case.

Having explained it as a *karmadhāraya* compound, he explains it again with the words "or rather" (*athavā*). [The term] "subtle" (*sūkṣmā*) means that it is not "supreme" (*parā*). Now, the ancient grammarians maintain that among all the stages of the process pertaining to the signified and the signifier, it is indeed *paśyantī* that is the supreme reality; raising the objection there as to how it could possess succession, [the author] says:

He says: "even in the state of vision" (*paśyantī-avasthāyām*). "Of that which is being contemplated" (*cintyamānasya*) means that which, while being contemplated, is about to reach the state of being a clear object of thought in the *madhyamā* stage. "Of the two intentions" (*abhisandhyoḥ*): "intention" (*abhisandhi*) is the non-differentiated synthesis, which is non-conceptual sensory cognition.

The first activity of the knower consists of the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) free from both vitarka and vicāra, and is characterized by direct manifestation. In that state, when one perceives through non-conceptual perception both a sound and the taste inherent within it, if those two acts of observation do not have distinct objects, [they are unified].

One should accept that the sequence residing in the object is present at the moment of self-reflection; otherwise, how could two distinct conceptualizations follow immediately one after the other? Therefore, even at the time of initial perception (*ālocana*), that [sequence] exists, though concealed by its initial form, in the shape of expressive words such as "sara" or "rasa."
The sequential and the expressible, which follow that [process], indeed manifest as mutually distinct forms.

Likewise, when the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is intensely conceptualized in the lake, even during the state of immersion (*samāpatti*) where its form momentarily flashes forth in succession, a mutual distinction must be asserted; otherwise—

First, at the time of entering the concentration without discursive thought (*avitarka-samāpatti*), conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) would not be applicable there as a distinction; nor would the yogi, in the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*), remember those two concentrations as distinct.
Thus, one who intends to speak of the lake [remembers] the water.

The principle is this: if the first perception of one who intends to speak, or who desires to go, or who wishes to see, is not distinct, then even the resulting prayer and so forth would likewise lack distinction. Although this is indeed the case in instances such as "a jar" and "a bowl," nevertheless, in those cases, the difference is perfectly clear.

Even in the case of being fused together: for instance, when copper and silver are fused, or when iron and lead are fused, who could have the conceit of their unity? [One would say: "This is the form of a lump of copper-gold," and "this too is likewise"; so what is the difference?

(Page 192) Such a delusion might indeed arise; it must necessarily be dispelled. By demonstrating the nature of the sequence, with the intention of showing that "this is a mass of copper and gold, whereas this is a mass of gold and copper," [it is said] "the essence of the lake."

It has been said: "But if [the state] in Paśyantī consists of thought (cintāmaya), then what is Madhyamā? He replies: "Madhyamā is the gross word. For it is precisely Madhyamā that is called the ground of conceptualization (vikalpa);
and the very life of conceptualization is contact with verbal expression (abhilāṣa). Indeed, this [Madhyamā] resides therein.

It is of the nature of the signifier (*vācaka*), because it alone functions as the signifier of the form of the "I" (*ahantā*). For it is there that the establishment of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) and so forth is possible.
As for the specific individual characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is perceptible by the ear, that is not the form of the signifying word;
for the relationship between signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) has its life-force in the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the form "this is that."
For it will be stated [later]: "And a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) cannot be superimposed upon another particular characteristic.
Therefore, that sequential nature of sound which consists in its being the form of speech finds its rest clearly only in the intermediate state. Consequently, that which was said by the Blessed One—

Being for the most part a mere sprout of that conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it does not deserve to be designated as something distinct. Indeed, it is not logical to say that an external jar has a form other than the jar that is being conceptualized;
for that very appearance of a jar, through its conjunction with other appearances such as space and so forth, [becomes the object].

It attains the state of a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Sound, too, is exactly like that. Although it is a full manifestation by virtue of its gross form, it is designated as a "specific characteristic" by means of a body capable of being perceived by the pair of ears, due to the intermingling with other manifestations. Therefore—

Thus, because the state of gross sound-form exists in the *madhyamā*, the meaning is that it has "clearly" arrived by way of the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). "In this" refers to that which is indicated by this very sūtra. "Precisely for this reason" means:
since the state of being produced by reflection (*cintāmayatva*) is established by the means of valid cognition in the *paśyantī*, therefore [the result] belongs to the *paśyantī*.
The state of otherness (*paratva*) has been refuted in the *Śivadṛṣṭi* treatise. How? Having stated this, [the author] restates it with the following passage. For there, the text (p.
193) says:

"Now, our power of knowledge, which is the very nature of Sadāśiva... (*Śivadṛṣṭi* 2.1), and so forth. [Objection: But surely that which is the supreme form is precisely what is denoted by the term *paśyantī*.
Anticipating the objection that [consciousness] will exist [as an object], he says "no.
For the verb *dṛś* (to see) is a transitive root; let it be explained what it is that they see—whether those appearances are external and real, or even unreal.
"Vision established in the form of present action is called Paśyantī" (Śivadr̥ṣṭi 2.20);
and "Now, by its very name, Paśyantī is clearly insentient" (Śivadr̥ṣṭi 2.80)—
by such passages [the author] shows that [vision] is contracted by the coloring of space and time through its nature being directed toward objects.

It has been stated: "How might vision (*dṛśi*) be supreme and perfectly full (*paripūrṇā*)? For fullness is indeed appropriate by virtue of transcending space and time. But why is the contraction of space, time, and form admitted in the *paśyantī* [level of speech]? Alas! Then, seeing that which is uncontracted, one sees only the uncontracted.
One should conceptualize in the *madhyamā* [speech] and speak in the *vaikharī* in order to transmit it to another.

For when blue is seen, yellow cannot be conceptualized or spoken of. Therefore, even though it is non-conceptual, the *paśyantī* must be admitted as being contracted. This is what he expresses by the words "for the sake of each word-meaning" (*pratiśabdārtham hi*).
"Wherever it is spoken"— this is the meaning. The preceding speech, namely *paśyantī*,

having set aside both a different word and a different meaning, and correctly holding— that is, grasping— the other word and the other meaning directly from that [previous] word and meaning, how indeed could it be *parā* (the supreme)?

It would become full, because that [universal] has become restricted by those two—word and object—in terms of place, time, and form. Here, he provides an example for clarification, beginning with "broad-based" (*pṛthubudhna*). By this, there is the intention toward another object through the exclusion of other objects.

This has been demonstrated. By the phrase "the cloth and so forth," there is an intention toward a subsequent word while excluding other words. Now, one might object: "Since *paśyantī* consists of an intention toward a form that is uncontracted, it is complete; therefore, it must be *parā* itself. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The universe (*viśva*)."
By means of excluding each individual form (*ekaikatārūpavyavacchedena*),
[the word "all"] expresses totality (*sākalya*); and by excluding words such as "jar" (*ghaṭādiśabdavyavacchidā*), it intends the word "universe" (*viśva*).
She too is indeed contracted—this is the sense. Now, the Paśyantī [speech] is of the nature of the state of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*).
In that state, whatever form consists of "this-ness" (*idantā*), it shines forth as permeated by the sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*)—that is, as "I am this.
In that regard, whether it be a jar or even the entire universe, within the "this-ness" aspect, it flashes forth within the full sense of "I."

Having raised the doubt— "How could [the Lord] cause her to contract when she perceives [him] as 'immersed' (nimagna), that is, because her contraction has dissolved?"— he says this in order to establish that it is not the non-contracted state of the *māyīya* ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) itself,
but rather its contraction [that is being negated]: "of the non-contracted..."
He shows the division of the objects [of knowledge] with the words "And that" (*sā ca*). The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include other objects of knowledge.

For the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is devoid of the limitations of the body, vital breath, intellect, and so forth, there is a power called the capacity to produce variegated appearances; by means of that, [the relationship between] the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*) belonging to the universe [is established].

When differentiation is projected as a creative manifestation (*ullāsa*), then that desire for such manifestation on the part of the Lord in His form as Īśvara is called the "desire to manifest the universe. In that state, there is no other subject apart from Īśvara in relation to whom those entities might appear in a different state.

"Partaking of non-constriction" means resting in the sense of "I-ness" (*ahaṃbhāva*). "Attaining fullness" does not refer to the greatness of *paśyantī*, for that consists in the formative threading of duality; rather, this greatness belongs to the sense of "I-ness. Consequently, how could there be [constriction] even there, given that it is free from the contraction produced by the state of "this-ness" (*idantā*)?

The underlying intention is that there would be a state of "otherness" (paratva). For this very reason, it has been demonstrated in the *Śivadṛṣṭi* that while such an extent of progression as exists here may not be perceived by the grammarians, something even further than this is possible within our own philosophical system.
"...our nature is that of Sadāśiva" (Śivadr̥ṣṭi 2.1).

However, for those under the influence of *māyā*, even their sense of "I-ness" (*ahantā*) is contracted by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the body and so forth, and even their "this-ness" (*idantā*) is restricted to the exclusion of other objects of knowledge (*prameya*); and these other objects of knowledge exist in relation to other subjects (*pramātṛ*).

Furthermore, there is another state of that very object of cognition which is not perceived by that cognizer but is perceived by another, such as the state of being an object of detachment for a woman of passion.
Thus, it exists contracted on both sides as "I" and "this" for the subjects under the influence of Māyā.

(195) It is of a non-conceptual nature. Now, one might ask: how was it previously stated in the commentary on the *Ādisiddha-sūtra* that "in that state, even the bound soul (*paśu*) possesses the divine nature (*aiśvara-bhāva*)"? To this, he replies with the words "tāvatī" (to that extent).
In other words, that very state in which the object of knowledge is submerged within the knowing subject is what has been called its sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
Thus, "I am going to the village" is the *mahāpaśyantī*; relative to "I am departing from the house," which is the *paśyantī*, everything up to the stage of Sadāśiva and Īśvara is *mahāpaśyantī*.
It should be understood that this is said with reference to the entire range of the *paśyantī* level residing within the subject of *māyā*. Now, one might ask:
"What then is the status of the subjects of *māyā* in the supreme state (*paradaśā*)? He replies: "The Supreme (*parā*).
This refers to the reflective awareness "I" (*aham*), which exists even in the pure state for the sake of strengthening meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and so forth.

If the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the sense of "I" regarding the body and so forth were to dissolve, then at that very moment, due to the falling away of the body and so on, there would be no emergence from that state. Therefore, as long as that impression persists, it will certainly continue to contract even that state. However, in comparison to one's own *paśyantī* [level of speech], that state possesses a higher degree of transcendence (*paratva*).

"Because of the deficiency of the manifestation of the object of knowledge. If this is so, one might ask: "What is that uncontracted state in every respect wherein 'supremacy' (paratva) is appropriate?

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And therefore" (*tataśca*). This means: for the reason that this aforementioned division of objects has been stated. That which is "I" (*aham*), the eternal nature of consciousness—

It is empty of the beginning and end produced by space, time, and form; it is eternally manifest, and that very thing is explained as "the supreme" (*parā*) because it arises by its own inherent force (*svarasodita*). Therefore—meaning, because its supremacy is thus established—it is called "speech" (*vāṅnāma*).

If the Grammarians do not accept that she— who is of the nature of sound, consisting of the great mantra "I" (ahaṃ), whose life-breath is pure agency, and who speaks with this very body— is present, then she, being of the nature of an instrument, would be even lower than the group of the sense organs of cognition.

Speech is a certain modification of the ego (ahaṃkāra-vṛtti) whose nature is that of an organ of action; it is common to animals, living beings, and those such as beasts, and it produces sound, just like the hands and other organs.
In that case, how could there be "supremacy" (paratva)? Therefore, by relying on this very reasoning—"from this also"—the word "that" (tat) refers to supremacy.
In this regard, it is stated in the *Śrīśivadṛṣṭi*: "Of that"—meaning of the speech known as Paśyantī. This is the intended meaning:
here, first of all, the Supreme Lord is the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*); His power is manifold, consisting of both differentiated and non-differentiated forms.
The eight groups of Mātṛkā goddesses are the eight powers of Rudra; the fifty letters are the fifty powers of Rudra.
The Blessed One is the great embodiment of the five mantras.

By the Blessed One speaking thus and so forth, it is first established in the scriptures that the Lord, whose body is light (*prakāśa*), possesses the nature of speech as his sole essence through his reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). Furthermore, those phonemes belonging to the realm of *māyā* which consist of sound are like jars and other such objects; and that which brings them forth is...

Knowledge consisting of both the non-conceptual and the conceptual, which takes the form of *paśyantī* and *madhyamā*, stands in the place of [the primary] knowledge; and the organ of speech (*vāgindriya*), which brings that [knowledge] into effect, stands in the place of the hands and other organs, and is cast into the side of *māyā*, which consists of duality. How, then, is this so?
It would be the supreme reality (*paratattva*). For that [individual soul] consists of the objects of sense and the organs of cognition;

yet, as for the fact that even there one observes the accomplishment of its own specific functions, that is caused by contact with the power of the supreme reality, but rather through contact with its own [individual] power... (Spandakārikā 8).
According to this principle, it has been thus described by the Blessed One:

"O Goddess worshipped by heroes, when embraced by those [mantras], they become bestowers of the fruits of all desires for the foremost of practitioners; it is not otherwise. (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra 3.28)
And so forth. That which is not limited by time, space, form, or function is not "other," like a jar.

Likewise, the cognition of sound, its sense organ, and so on, belong to the bound soul (pāśava). "Supremacy" (paratva) is said to be fullness (pūrṇatva), and limitation (saṃkoca) is its opposite; thus, this is the perception of a contradiction with one's own nature. As it has been said:
In the *Śrīśivadṛṣṭi*, a Śaiva work, [it is stated]: "Speech possesses the nature of a sense organ... (3.10), and so forth.
"Like the sense organs of the hands and so forth, this Brahman cannot be the organ of speech.
(2.17) And in that very same [work], it is said: "Through the experience of reflective awareness, this Speech first took its resort [in him]. (2.19)
Having raised this doubt, [the author] says:
"If you say this, then let the *paśyantī* be practiced first, according to what is appropriate. (2.20)
By the passage beginning with "He who sees thus [sees] the Paśyantī is considered the supreme God" (2.64),
the Lord's nature as the Word is established; for that very reason...

The Supreme Lord, whose greatness is the manifestation of bliss, is victorious— he who is praised with beautiful, heart-captivating speech by the investigator of the essence of consciousness, the venerable Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa, as he is perceived through the visionary state of *paśyantī*. (Stavacintāmaṇi 1)
Thus it is said. And here, by the word *paśyantī*, the level of Śrī Sadāśiva, whose nature is the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), is expressed;
that which is the supreme *mahāpaśyantī*, consisting of non-differentiation, belonging to those *mahāpaśyantīs* whose form is the inner self (*pratyagātman*). And by that...

It has been shown that this glory of bliss (*ānanda*), which consists of supreme autonomy (*svātantrya*) and is to be made to blossom, is the Supreme Speech (*parā vāk*) of the Blessed Lord. Through the worldly illustration that the mutual manifestation of love causes the blossoming of passion (*rati*), which is essentially blissful, bliss itself is made manifest.
Having taken all this into account, he explains the second half of the verse with the words "and that very [power].
He demonstrates what is excluded by the word "primary" (*mukhya*) with the passage beginning "for instance" (*tathā hi*). That which is distinct [from the primary], its sovereignty is not complete.

Because the possibility of obstruction is perceived. Unobstructedness is the pervader of perfect sovereignty, as it is said: "From sovereignty comes non-obstruction. And the possibility of obstruction is the opposite of that; thus, this is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

That which is not of the nature of the self does not follow the will of the perceiver to the ultimate degree, because it lacks the concomitance of following its own causes and so forth. And that which does not follow the will of something else has no sovereignty over it, just as Kalinga has no sovereignty over Vaṅga. As Vīranāga said:
"Arising from its cause, and its persistence through the power of its own conditions, and aging over time," and so forth.
For sovereignty consists in the capacity to act according to one's will, and this [state of being subject to causes] is its opposite.
(Page 198)
Sovereignty itself is bliss and fullness—thus it has been established. For this very reason, the Sage said:
"Everything dependent on another is suffering; everything under one's own control is happiness.
By the word "etcetera," Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are included. For instance, regarding that which is to be created...

Regarding that which is to be established and that which is to be withdrawn, the presiding deities are Brahmā and others who hold office within Māyāgarbha; and all the world-protectors (lokapālas), who follow his will, are to be understood as being indicated by the mention of Indra. Here, however, by the word "tu" (but/however):

He states the distinction regarding the state of the glorious Sadāśiveśvara: "become one's own self" (ātmabhūtam) means that, by being delimited through the sense of "I," it has attained the nature of the Self as if it were the body; "dependent on another" (paratantram) means by virtue of having a duality imagined through its own will.

The word *svātantryam* (sovereignty) is to be separated [from the preceding compound] here; it refers to that which has been introduced in this aphorism as "this" (*idam*), which requires the unfolding of the power of *māyā*, the aspect of "this-ness" (*idantā*), whose life-force is non-recognition (*akhyāti*). [The phrase] "in the infinite" (*anantāyām*) [is used] because, in the absence of a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), the possibility of excluding it exists, and thus [the infinite] takes the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

"In that which is not suspected [of being other]," "in that which is indefinable" means in that which is non-conventional (*asāmayikī*). "In that which flows by its own nature" means in that which is eternally manifest. That is to say, it is not something imagined, as is the case with the body and so forth.
This, however, is pure sovereignty, wherein the entire objective portion (*idambhāga*) is absorbed into the "I-ness" (*ahantā*).

The syntactical connection of the statement is: "Because [the Self] is pure, it possesses supreme sovereignty following immersion. The reason for its purity is expressed by the phrase "as in the state of sovereignty," which serves as a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
The underlying sense is that impurity consists precisely in the intrusion of another form belonging to a different class. Wherein there is no subordination (*aparatā*), [therein lies purity].
That is supreme. And he shows that this [supremacy] occurs by virtue of exclusion (*vyatireka*) with the words, "the other, such as Indra, Brahmā, and so forth.

As for the distinction between being "other" as being either complete or partial, the author of the *Vṛtti* did not touch upon it, but the author of the *Vivṛti* has demonstrated it. Since this very autonomy (*svātantrya*) is sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), therefore...
We have rightly said: "Therefore, O friend, [the Self] is distinct from the insentient" (1.5.12). || 13 ||

This is also shown in another very concise aphorism within the *Rahasyāgamas*: "That radiance is the Great Being (*mahāsattā*), undifferentiated by space or time. He introduces that [aphorism] as follows: (p. 199) "That radiance is the Great Being, undifferentiated by space or time."
This very [mantra], being the essence, is declared to be the heart of the Supreme Lord.

"Her other [aspect] also"—the meaning is that it is of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), distinguished from the activities of the hands, feet, and so forth. "In the *Āgamas*, the teachings of the Supreme Lord"—by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," this refers to the Vedānta and other systems; "in the treatises proclaimed by the Sages, composed by the Siddhas, and expounded by the Gurus."
The author of the Sūtra states that which constitutes its nature, as derived from the variety of its names and etymologies:
"In that [power], vibration is established" (Spandakārikā 22).
"The outflows of the vibration of the qualities and so forth...
(Spanda Kārikā 19), thus...
"for the sake of discerning the reality of Spanda" (Spanda Kārikā 21).
In such passages as these, by the word *spanda*,
this "wave" (*ūrmi*) of the waveless ocean of consciousness is celebrated;
thus, by the word *ūrmi*.
"...the throbbing, liberated consciousness... (*Śivadṛṣṭi* 1.2).
By the word "throbbing" (*sphurattā*), that power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) is expressed. What more need be said?
[It is attained] through the power of the penance consisting in the practice of the reflective awareness of consciousness, which is set in motion by the ripening of previous merit.
It has been established by Bhaṭṭa Śaṅkaranandana, who attained the opening [of realization],
that direct perception is self-established, for "this [perception] is indeed its state of radiance.
For it is well known that "radiance," "vibration," and so forth constitute a certain kind of movement.

And what is this "slightness" [of movement]? It is precisely this appearance of movement even in that which is immovable. Even in the world, one who is established in immobility, though filled with the sovereignty of abundant resolve, is said to be "possessing vibration.
Thus, following this very worldly convention regarding "throbbing," he explains it as follows:

By the words "the jar and so forth," etc., [the reading in manuscript *kha* is *yadā ca*, whereas *yathā ca*; here it means] "since" (*yataḥ*). "That" (*tam*) refers to consciousness (*bodha*). For in the thought "the jar flashes forth for me," the flashing-forth (*sphurattā*) is indeed attached to the "I"-portion (*ahamaṃśa*).
It is transferred into the state of being. For what is the meaning of "the jar flashes forth"? It means:
"I, whose nature is light, flash forth in the form of the jar—neither slightly exceeding nor not exceeding the nature of consciousness—and thus I shine by my own sovereignty."

"Even when mounted upon that single [perceptual] state, the jar is thus [cognized]. For this very reason, it was stated by Bhaṭṭa Candrānanda: "For one who perceives a form through its delineation, that which appears accompanied by the manifestation [of the object]—the manifestation of the thing's own nature—is the *pratibhā* (intuition) of entities..."
Having spoken thus, [she],
who was dependent upon herself...

Thus [it is said]. "Otherwise, however" means if their manifestation were its own. "Of another as well" refers to that which belongs to a different place and time. Others read "of another as well? For if their very nature were their manifestation, then by the power of the essential nature belonging to another...
Even when there is an intervention by that [medium], everything would become an object of such conceit;

and this should be understood as being said by way of concession (*abhyupagamena*). For in reality, one thing cannot truly reside in another—as has been stated more than once. Thus, it is consciousness alone that flashes forth like water, and through its immersion (*āveśa*), even jars and other objects do so.

The phrase "like grass and so forth" is an absolute rule: when something lacks a certain form upon separation from another, it possesses that [form] through its immersion in that [other], just as grass possesses flickeringness when in contact with wind, water, and so forth. Thus, the nature of jars and other objects is such that their manifestation is never separated from consciousness.

For the non-manifestation of that [object] when it is separated from its opposite ceases because of the exclusion of its penetration; this is established through pervasion (*vyāpti*) by observing that "being its own nature" contradicts "not being its own nature," which is the pervader of itself. For this very reason, it was stated by the venerable Parameṣṭhin:
"The Self alone vibrates within all entities... (Śivadṛṣṭi 1.2).

Thus, the agency of an entity—consisting in its being manifest, its existing, and its appearing—must be established as being produced solely by the penetration of consciousness (*bodhāveśa*). Now, one might object: "By this much, only manifestation has been described, but not—"

Anticipating the objection that this might be merely the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśaśakti*), he says "only" (*kevalam*). Even for light (*prakāśa*), its own essential nature is precisely characterized by reflective awareness; for without that, it would be distinct from non-light due to this [reflective awareness].

It has been established that [the self] is difficult to find. Now, in order to explain the term "Great Being" (*mahāsattā*), he first explains "being" (*sattā*) with the words "by way of form" (*rūpeṇa*).
The word "and" (*ca*) collects another point to be explained. "By way of form" means by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). As for the phrase "of another":

Since there can be no resting point of establishment for existence (*sattā*), causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*), and so forth—each of which is undermined by an infinite regress resulting from the search for another nature beyond them—therefore, that function (*vṛtti*) which was stated for the purpose of explaining the word "Great" (*mahat*), namely "that which has non-existence as its counter-correlative," [is not tenable]. (Note: *vapra* is a variant reading for *vapuḥ*).

He explains this with the words: "And [that which is] distinct from the object of cognition. By the word "api" (also/even), he indicates that while prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the others might somehow possess the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpatā*), this same logic applies even to absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). [Objection:
But surely non-existence is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of existence. [Response: True.

[This refers] to the existence of something external, and not to its being manifest; for [the author] shows by means of the passage beginning with "of that which has cognition as its counter-correlate" (*bodhapratiyoginaḥ*) that without such manifestation, what could even have the status of a counter-correlate? Otherwise—if even manifestation itself were suspected of being a counter-correlate on account of non-manifestation—then...

Consequently, the reflective awareness "I am" whose essence is the negation of that [object] would be nothing but a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); yet it will be stated that this reflective awareness "I," which is of the nature of light... (1.6.1).
The intended meaning here is that this has been explained "in detail. Now, one might object:
is not "existence" (*sattā*) a universal (*sāmānya*) consisting of a mere appearance, similar to "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), "pot-ness" (*ghatatva*), and so forth?

And how can that [existence], having entered the domain of the cognizable (*prameya*), be of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is the attribute of the pure subject (*śuddhapramātṛdharma*)?

He dispels the doubt that [existence] might be defined by stating, "And existence is not [so]. For that word "existence" (*sattā*) is employed through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). This [word], however, is derived from the root *as* meaning "to be" with the suffix *-śatṛ* and then with an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), signifying its literal etymological sense; that is to say, it is a qualifier of a further qualifier.

Regarding the phrase "not the counter-positive of non-existence": having begun the explanation of the commentary on the Sūtra passage beginning with "eternal" (*nityā*), which states that [the *prakṛti*] never departs from its state in any respect whatsoever across space and time, the following is commenced.
(Page 202)

The connection is with the phrase "of the reality of consciousness" (cittattvasya) and "eternality" (nityatā). It should also be understood that "always" (sarvadā) implies "everywhere" (sarvatra) as well. By this, the following is stated: that which is fragmented and separate may, at some place and at some time, be entered by space and time acting as causes.

These two are qualifiers of that which is produced alone, not of that which is unproduced; they belong only to cognition when it has fallen into the category of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) and is capable of being joined with the properties of being designated by another appearance associated with the subject (*pramātṛ*).

This is a qualification [of consciousness], not of a cognition that transcends the object of knowledge and consists solely of the subject. But surely, permanence was indicated as the topic to be stated in the Sūtra, since it alone was clarified in the Vṛtti; and in that regard, the very reason is the non-contact with time. In that case, what is the purpose of introducing space?

Anticipating the objection that this applies to both the Sūtra and the Vṛtti, he says "in connection with time," which means "in connection with the absence of limitation. [The opponent asks: "But surely even an atom, though occupying a limited space, possesses eternity. [And yet] consciousness is not limited in any way whatsoever."

The power of discernment (*vimarśa-śakti*) is to be defined; how could it be that the absence of time was indicated in the Sūtra? On the contrary, this is a lack of skill on the part of the commentator—that he did not follow the non-restriction of space—and suspecting this, he explains otherwise with the words "Or rather" (*athavā*); for that which necessarily exists is eternal (*nitya*).

Determination (*naiyatya*) is the absence of non-existence. And although there is no abiding in its own nature for that which possesses spatial limitation, nevertheless, in this case, the relative [absence]—in the sense that "this is not that"—is indeed possible; thus, even its absence exists by way of permanence.

[This] is observed in the commentary. Now, why [should it be said that] those two are indeed properties of the object of knowledge? He says: "For space and time... And this has been explained [in the passage]:
"And cognition is of the nature of consciousness... (1.2.7).

In this sūtra, having explained at length, the sense is as follows: "Inward-turned alone" means that this consciousness—which is created by absolute freedom (svātantrya)—now ascends into conceptual constructions such as "this" or "that," as if it were made outward-turned.
Now, [one might ask]: if the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is thus joined with space and time, what is this "that"?
The great universal (*mahāsāmānya*), which consists of pure existence (*sattā*), shines forth, as does the other [universals] such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and so on;
its pervasiveness and eternality [are established].
He dispels the objection that [the two] would not exist by means of the passage beginning with "this" (*idam*).

Here, the contraction of forms characterized by mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is not a restricting factor; for consciousness and its reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) occur in every form. This point also should be understood as being indicated here.
Thus has this Great Being been explained as the power of Śambhu, whose nature consists of pure existence due to her autonomy.
So it is said.
"That which was in the beginning was indeed Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1)—
thus it has been described in the Śrīrahasya and in the Śrutyanta; and in the Kakṣyāstotra as well,
it is stated that the existence of the universe is "great."

Thus [it is said]. Now he explains the passage beginning with "by way of its essence" (*sāratayā*) and so forth. The word "here" (*iha*) means everywhere in the world. And this has been explained at length in the aphorism: "For thus, of insentient things... (1.4). The phrase "even the manifestation of objects" (*arthanirbhāso 'pi*) means even that which is similar to a mirror and the like.
And so it has been stated by me in the *Śrītantrasāra* and other works:
"Just as a world of diverse arrangements shines within a mirror, so does the entire universe shine here within the Self."
"Consciousness, by means of the principle whose essence is its own self-reflection, reflects the universe; a mirror does not do so. (3 Āhnika).
And of that agency, it is because it brings about the manifestation of its own nature.
"...and non-manifestation is established.
Thus, without that [will], the reflective awareness of will does not proceed. (1.10)

Thus, by this logic, since the multitude of entities is distinct from light, neither the status of being a cognizer nor the state of pure consciousness is tenable. He states this very point with the words "by what has been said," referring to what was previously mentioned and what will be stated on page 204.

Thus, in the section on action (*kriyādhikāra*): the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) consists merely in a fixed sequence of prior and posterior; this will be refuted at length later, for [it does not apply] to those things that reside solely within their own self... (2.4.15).

By the words "and so forth," the meaning is as follows: "of that too" refers to that [consciousness] which is appropriate to the state of Śrī Sadāśiva-Īśvara, having the nature of both the supreme (*parā*) and the intermediate (*parāparā*), expressed as "I am this. "The supreme" means simply "I am.
He demonstrates that even the form which is "I am" is not like a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) restricted by contact with an object of knowledge, such as "this is blue."
"Of her" refers to that which has the nature of Paraśiva. "Of this" refers to that which is manifesting everywhere.

"That very same" refers to that which, by way of the expansion of its sovereignty, takes the form of reflective awareness extending to the external. "This" refers to that which favors the light of all things. "The former" refers to the stage of the internal levels of the powers such as Will (icchā) and the rest.

"Until then she does not grasp"—meaning that she possesses not even a trace of lack of independence (*asvātantrya*), for she is "of the nature of pure consciousness" (*citimātrarūpā*), since this alone constitutes her state of being conscious. He explains her form as supreme autonomy (*parasvātantrya*) by saying "purified" (*śodhitā*); [previously], in the lower state, it was differentiated.

Since it is undivided within the state of both the supreme and the non-supreme, whatever object exists in the form of an effect to be known is, within this power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), simultaneously dissolved and capable of being revived;
and having been revived, it remains entirely without succession. This is that thirty-seventh digit of reality (*tattva-kalā*).

The connection is that "the pure [reality] is the principle beyond the thirty-sixth. By this much, its essential nature (*sāratva*) has been determined—that which was explained at length in the *Śrīviṣamadarśanasāraśāstra* by means of the definition of power (*śakti*). To this extent, the term "essence" (*sāra*) from the Sūtra is both a restatement (*anuvāda*) and a prescription (*vidhi*).

This has been explained. He explains the term *parameṣṭhinaḥ* as "in the supreme station," which consists of thirty-seven forms, as it is said: "To the one established upon the Yoga-pīṭha... [and so forth].
Thus, in order to explain the true nature of mantra, the Blessed One [taught] its yoga and its powers... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 4.5) (p.
Thus, she is also [described] elsewhere as that supreme, highest goddess in the *Yoga* and the *Bhairavayāmala*,
and so forth. Now, one might object:

"That which is devoid of thought is the Supreme... having thus been stated, one might wonder what else remains therein; anticipating this doubt, he cites the scripture with the words "from the Supreme" (*parāt*).
Having explained [the term] as "of the Supreme Lord" (*parameṣṭhinaḥ*), there is the restatement [of that] in the aphorism regarding its being the essence (*sāratayā*).
When it is to be proven that [the Heart-mantra] is the heart by virtue of being the cause, he explains it with the words "just as" (*yathā*).

The connection is: "consciousness is the foundation" (*cetanaṃ pratiṣṭhā*); and the connection is: "even for those who possess consciousness, just as... (*cetanāvatām api yathā*). As it has been said:
Although this witness (sākṣin) abides pervading this entire body,
its supreme seat is nevertheless the casket of the heart-lotus.

And so forth. He applies this to the present context with the words "in the very same way. "Of the conscious universe" means of the Blessed Lord Paramaśiva. That supreme power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) is designated by the term "the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*)" of the Supreme Lord, and also by the term "the heart" of the Supreme Lord.

It must be said: [Objection] But what is the use of that power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), since it is impossible for that which is non-existent to be an effect? Let it simply be stated that the Supreme Lord is the soul of the universe and the form of the universe, filled with effects such as the principles (*tattva*) and the worlds (*bhuvana*). [Response] This is not tenable; thus he says "otherwise," meaning without the power of reflective awareness.

Just as the capacity of the fluid within a peacock’s egg to manifest as blue, yellow, and so forth constitutes its causality (*kāraṇatā*) and not its agency (*kartṛtā*), so too should the Blessed One’s capacity to manifest the entire universe be understood; it is not merely causality that is appropriate. This is because [the Lord] consists of the nature of wonder (*camatkṛti*).
For pure sovereignty is indeed that repose which culminates in the supreme enjoyment consisting of bliss,
wherein not even the slightest trace of obstruction— which constitutes a lack of sovereignty—
is conceivable.
"For this very reason, the self... (1.5.15).
The passage beginning with "svātantryāmuktam" (1.5.16) and so forth reveals the manifold manifestation (*nirmāṇa*) that is about to be described. Therefore,
because it is the essence as the cause of supreme excellence, it is the foundation, the locus, the ultimate heart.

That belongs to the Blessed One. The word *iti* refers back to the meaning of the commentary stated in this entire sūtra; it should be connected to each [term] in the commentary as well: "the state of being manifest," "existence," and "the form of the foundation" (*pratiṣṭhārūpā*), which is the "heart. The term "the form of the foundation" is [to be understood] through the nominative case as the essential core (*sāratayā*).

It has been explained that by this word, injunction (*vidhi*) is also indicated. Others, however, maintain that with reference solely to the Siddhānta scriptures, the mantra is the heart of the Lord; and since the mantra consists of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), the term "heart" is used in the Āgamas to denote *vimarśa* (reflective awareness).

They explain the first half [of the verse], considering it as having the sense of a restatement (*anuvāda*), as being the essence (*sāra*), and as providing the reason (*hetu*). The point is that the term "heart" (*hṛdaya*) here does not have a figurative application (*upacarita*), but rather its primary, literal sense (*mukhya*) alone. As it has been said:
"For I am the foundation of Brahman, of the immortal and the imperishable,
of the eternal dharma, and of absolute bliss" (Gītā 14.27). By this [verse], [the nature] of Brahman as Being and Supreme Bliss [is established].
It has been shown that [the Self] consists of the reflective awareness "I am the place of rest. Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere:
"That which is the essence of this world is the Supreme Power (Parā Śakti) in the Mālinī [Tantra]."
"Without them, there would be no word, no meaning, nor even the movement of consciousness.
Thus, they have indeed attained the state of being the Mother therein... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 3.9).
And so forth:
"There is no such cognition...
[if] it were of the nature of speech" (Vākyapadīya 1.125).

And so forth. Since even the Buddhists, Sāṃkhyas, and others have accepted that the repose of manifestation (*prakāśa*) lies precisely in determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*), it is logical that manifestation has as its very essence *vimarśa* (reflective awareness). || 14 ||

Now, one might raise the doubt: "How can the power of reflective awareness (vimarśa-śakti) be thus consecrated within the Blessed One who possesses infinite powers? To address this, two aphorisms [are presented]:
"Therefore, he [the Self] may make himself an object of knowledge as if existing separately."
It is the object of knowledge, yet its sovereignty is not fragmented by the directedness toward that [object]. || 15 ||

The Lord, having projected through his volitions the self— which is by nature free and non-dual— into states such as those of Īśvara and others, causes it to engage in worldly activity by means of that very freedom.

In this context, the power of sovereignty (*svātantrya-śakti*), characterized by agency, exists by encompassing the entire series of cosmic powers; thus, the essential point is that this very power, whose nature is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), is the primary reality. He introduces the first verse regarding this with the words "And therefore" (*ataśca*), which are in grammatical apposition.

The meanings of the ablative case (*pañcamyarthāḥ*) have been explained by this [verse] through the words "from this" (*ataḥ*). Having read the word "this" (*ayam*), he explains it as "the Supreme Lord" (*parameśvaraḥ*). He explains the emphatic particle (*evakāraḥ*), which follows immediately after the word "Self" (*ātman*), with the words beginning "the universe" (*viśvam*), in order to clarify that there is no other form for the universe.

"Because its nature is that of a knower, it makes the unknowable known"—this is what is rendered probable by a firm inference, since it has been stated that no other cause is possible. He explains this firm probability, characterized as a *niyoga* (an imperative injunction), by means of the word "necessarily" (*niyamāt*). And by this very [inference]...

The entire passage beginning with "the state of separate existence is to be known by the word... has been explained in brief. For its literal sense is one of contingency (*prasaṅga*), whereas its intended meaning (*tātparya*) lies in the reversal of that contingency:
if the state of separate existence were to be known, then, in being oriented toward that, this [subject] would be dependent (*paratantra*), meaning it would be non-autonomous (*asvatantra*).

That which is insentient (jaḍa) is not independent; and how could there be independence regarding the object of knowledge for that which is insentient? Such is the logical consequence. Furthermore, this [independence] is established by its own self-awareness (svasaṃvit). Therefore, because it is independent and not directed toward another, it makes the universe itself its own object of knowledge.

(Page 208) Thus, the meaning of the sūtra is that the desired conclusion is established through the reversal of the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*). "From a cause" means as a sprout [arises] from a seed and so forth. "It would arise" means that if this were logically possible; however, it is not possible.

This is the remaining intention. Now, one might object: "A potter acts by intending a jar already manifested in his mind, but he does not intend himself"; in order to dispel this possibility, [the author] says, "even in the future.
The phrase "separate entities" means they rest only in the form of the jar, and not in the nature of consciousness.

The meaning is "established. This is what is being said: it has been explained in detail that, in reality, the potter is not the agent; for his agency is not pure. "Of a contradictory nature" means having the nature of another. [Objection: But how is it pure? [The author] replies: "For it is unconditioned," and so forth.
For restriction (*niyantraṇa*) is indeed obstruction, lack of autonomy, or impure autonomy. [Objection:
In that case, "contradiction" would be a mere word. [Reply: He says, "with respect to the world. [Objection:
But who is this "world" other than the Supreme Lord? [Reply: True; it is indeed He.

He shows that the world consists of thousands of dyads of the object and the subject, preceded by the concealment of the power of *māyā* through its being grasped; thus he says, "with respect to the world. Now, one might object:
since agency is not tenable when [the self] is divided, how could it belong to all beings from Brahmā down to the animals?
Who says that their agency exists anywhere? To whom, then, does it belong? He says:

to the Supreme Lord alone. It is merely figurative; its essence consists solely in the conceit (abhimāna) fashioned by His will, lasting only as long as that conceit persists, and not according to the actual state of things.
"Therefore, upon the abandonment of the grasp of ego-inflation, there is no bondage of karma whatsoever.
This and other such points have been determined in various sections of the *Gītā* and other scriptures. However, because [the Self] is all-pervading (*vibhu*), its [agency] is not merely figurative.

Agency: And if there were a turning toward an object of knowledge distinct [from consciousness], this [agency] would be merely metaphorical; it would not be ultimate. Thus, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that if the *cittattva* (the essence of consciousness) lacked agency, the universe would be nothing at all. Yet, it does exist. Therefore, that [agency] is non-metaphorical. Or rather, its non-metaphorical nature is as follows: if...
The object of knowledge and its effect are not distinct from it;
rather, the Self itself is made the object of knowledge. And in this regard, it is the power of absolute freedom alone that unfolds; therefore, it is that very [power].

The summary meaning of both the commentary (*vṛtti*) and the sub-commentary (*vivṛti*) is "the primary matter" (*pradhāna*). Introducing the second verse, [the author] relies upon the meaning of the preceding sūtra with the passage beginning "not only... and ending with "...makes it an object of knowledge," specifically by means of the phrase "for this very reason. To qualify this, [he uses the term] "at that time," meaning [the object] shining forth as one with that very [consciousness] at that moment.

As he will say: "When [the speaker] speaks of himself," and so forth. For that which is characterized by the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of "Śiva, the Supreme Lord" and so on, does not possess a purely objective state of being known (*vedyatā*), as he will say:
"Of the words 'Śiva' and so forth," and so on. Even that which is difficult to accomplish—of the self...
The production of the state of being known as a jar or the like, and the instrumentality [of that act], are indeed possible at some time;
however, this is impossible: namely, that while being the knower, it is also the known, and while being the known, it is also the knower.
Even that [impossible state] is accomplished through absolute freedom (svātantrya), because in reality there is an identity between the knower and the known. That...

Although the reality of being the knower (*vedakatā*) exists even at the time when an object such as a jar is made known, it must— as if severed from the portion of the knower by the power of *māyā*— be concealed; however, in the reflective awareness of Śiva and so forth, that state of being known belongs precisely to that which remains unsevered from the portion of the knower.
"Otherwise" means that if one were unable to act even in this manner, then one would have to know and perform an object that is not contradictory [to it]; for otherwise,
since it would be impossible to produce a cognition whose form is excluded by the restriction, one who knows and performs everything [would be required].
The meaning of the word "all" would be lost for him. [Objection: But surely he may know and do everything.
However, as for that which is produced and designated by words such as "Śiva," how can it be said to be inseparable from his sovereignty?
To this, he says: "Śiva, etc. From that—that is, from the uttered words "Śiva" and so forth—[it follows] "of that very [sovereignty]."
Of the Veda-maker, who possesses the nature of the Omniscient One and so forth and occupies the position of a teacher—
it has been established by the force of this reasoning that the speaker at that time was created as one whose very form is that of the Veda-maker.
He says "even when" (*yadāpi*) to show that this is likewise [established] by the force of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).
"I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, seated in the heart of all beings" (Bhagavad Gītā 10.20).
In passages such as, "And I am seated within the heart of all...

(Bhagavad Gītā 15.15), it is not taught that his form consists of the body and so forth—that he is the self of all seated within the hearts of all—because that would contradict perception and other means of valid knowledge. Thus he says: "by virtue of being the nature of consciousness."
In this regard, he states his own illustration with the words "Just as... up to "...the Supreme Lord.

And because it is so, "that too" follows from that. What? He says: "I who speak"—by virtue of this designation, the speaker's own self is Śiva; by the force of this designation, [it is established] for that which exists as the object to be demonstrated.

By the force of the indication "I am that very one who is the expounder and who speaks this," whatever its characteristic may be—namely, the state of being an agent (kartṛtva)—that exists in the undivided [consciousness]. "As long as he" means: even he indeed. "By that very same" means...
It is presented by way of being an agent characterized as a non-defective communicator.

The word *yāvat* has the sense of the word *api*, thus indicating the difficulty [of the task]. [Objection: "Granted that it may be communicated in such a way, but how is it known that it was created in that manner? [The author] replies: "And precisely because it is being communicated. [Objection: But...
"What is the purpose of such an emanation? It is said: "And of that very [Lord]," meaning of Him whose sovereignty is unimpaired.

For otherwise, there would be no distinction between the contemplative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of one who is "Lord" and one who is "not Lord. Thus, in cases such as "the Lord is worshipped, meditated upon, or taught by me," this emanated form is indeed distinct.
[The world appears] from the manifestation of the subject, and not as something absolutely separate, because it manifests thus within its own self;

"thus" means by way of not abandoning its sovereignty; "by that very [one]" means by Īśvara. Others, however, maintain that by these two verses, beginning with "precisely because of this sovereignty," the creation starting from Śiva is primarily the subject to be expressed.

[The object to be established is omitted in manuscript *kha*. Because this point is already well-known, the creation of blue and so forth mentioned in the preceding verse serves as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), specifically for the purpose of applying it as an illustration (page 211).

The introductory passage beginning with "kevalam" (only) connects as follows: they interpret "vyavahārayet" (he should practice) as the potential mood (*liṅ*) used in the sense of capability (*śaki*). Thus the construction is:
having thus fashioned himself [as the deity], the self is capable of performing within itself the practices of teaching, worship, meditative cultivation, and so forth.

Therefore, one should likewise make the Self an object of knowledge; in this regard, we have rightly stated that the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) alone is the cause of the manifestation’s very nature:
"The nature of manifestation... (1.5.11).

Thus, in order to explain that the primary thing to be enjoined is precisely the act of making [the object] an object of knowledge (*jñeyīkaraṇa*), the commentary uses the expression "it causes to appear" (*ābhāsayati*); otherwise, the expression "having caused to appear, it possesses worldly transaction" (*ābhāsya vyavahāravatī*) would have been more appropriate. (15–16)

But surely, how can that very same Self be both the object to be established (*pratipādya*) and the establisher (*pratipādaka*)? For illumination (*prakāśa*) is differentiated: the establisher is without appearance (*nirābhāsa*), while the object to be established possesses appearance (*sābhāsa*). There is non-difference due to the non-difference of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), even though there is a difference in appearance, just as in the case of the clear and the unclear.
"Indeed, from the moment the milk flows from the cow’s udder, it undergoes transformation;
yet at that very instant, the designation 'it is not milk' does not exist.

(Śivadr̥ṣṭi 1.18)—according to this principle. This [principle] also does not apply here, because the subject who explains is characterized by the reflective awareness "I," whereas [the object] is characterized by "this."
However, for the sake of the one being instructed, here follows the sūtra which anticipates the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) in order to provide an answer:
"Because of the difference in the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) as 'I' and so forth, this Self is not other [than the individual self]. (*kha* reads *pakṣaḥ* instead of *asya*).*
Because this creation is perceived as "I," it is like an object denoted by a verbal suffix. (17)
He introduces this by way of summarizing the commencement of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "the difference in appearance" (*ābhāsabheda*).

The section ending with "even in this difference of reflective awareness" (*etad-parāmarśabhede 'pi*) is the explanation of the prima facie argument. He will state [later] that "the objects [are distinguished] by their distance and proximity" (2.3.10).

On this point [page 212], the phrase "the reflective awareness of the root" (*mūlaparāmarśa*) and so forth constitutes the subsequent explanation. The reflective awareness of the root is "I" (*aham*); its non-abandonment is the very basis for the notion that "this is the Lord" (*īśvara*).

Because conceptualization (*parāmarśa*) is unstable, it persists even at that time as a continuous penetration (*anuvedhaka*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the indication in the Sūtra is intended to characterize the suffixes of tense and action, as well as the power (*śakti*) which has become non-existent.

He explains: although the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the appearance and [the appearance] itself are distinct due to the difference in action, they both become established within a single reflective awareness—as in the cases: "The honey being drunk intoxicates," and "This potter is being made. He says this with the words "by way of fitness" (*yogyatayā*). With the words "at some time" (*kadācit*), he refers to time (*kālena*).

Action (*kriyā*) is also perceived [in the previous case], but here there is a difference from that; thus he says, "But here... By this, it is established that the two reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśau*) are indeed distinct. To show that the two manifestations (*ābhāsau*) are also distinct, there is the commentary beginning with "And when there is a difference of manifestation" (*ābhāsabhede ca*); he explains that as follows: "It is indeed separate" (*vyatirikta eva*).
Of the one who brings [them] into being; "of the non-manifest" means by way of being the knower. "At that very time" means at that same moment.
That which, at one and the same time, possesses distinct manifestations and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), is distinct, like a jar and a cloth;
this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). If even such a thing were non-distinct, then distinction would not exist anywhere.

The word "syāt" (might be) indicates that if its pervader—namely, the possibility [of such a state] in some cases—were to be lost, then by the non-perception of that pervader, the reason would be excluded from the counter-example; thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established.

In this way, through the distinction between the reflective awareness of "I-ness" (*ahantā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*), and the manifestation (*ābhāsa*) characterized by them, [the difference] of the Self...

And the phrase "the difference of the form of the Veda is suspected" is an explanation of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) previously raised in the Sūtra. Furthermore, by the word "tathāpi" (even so),
there is another meaning of the particle "api" (also/even) present in addition to the single "ca" (and) used for conjunction.

Explaining it, [the author] elucidates the portion of the established doctrine (siddhānta) touched upon by the particle "eva" in the commentary on the sūtra "na iti," stating: "The Self" means that at the time of manifestation, there is no other;
"the Lord" (īśvara) means He rules; "the Independent One" (svatantra) means He is the life-force; and "Śiva" means supreme bliss.
Rest (*viśrānti*) is the reality (*tattva*); the subject (*pramātā*) is that which measures, knows, and acts—this is the given fact.

(Page 213) Therefore, if in all these cases the firm establishment (*nirūḍhi*) as "I" has not arisen, then even the reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśa*) such as "self" (*ātman*) and so forth do not exist.
For reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) itself [is such] because it does not find rest; and reflective awareness is precisely the locus of rest.

Now, if this is so, how can it be said that even the reflective awareness "I am the Self" (*ātmā*) has the same essence as the reflective awareness "I" (*ahaṃ*), while it is also said that "the Self is created therein"? He replies: "Only," meaning that at the very outset, [it is] "I."
In such cases as "the Self" (*ātman*) and so forth, although there is initially an unfolding of dependence characterized by "this-ness" (*idantā*) as an object of knowledge,
creation is said to occur with the intention of that very "I-reflection" (*ahaṃparāmarśa*), which remains internally present as a pervasive undercurrent even while that [objectivity] exists.
"Having internalized," that is, by way of inclusion, "having contained within," and having made it an intervening factor;
for indeed, if the sense of "I-ness" (ahantā) were not to flash forth immediately after the reflective awareness of "the Self" (ātman), there would be no resting-place for the subject.

Between the reflective awareness resting in the self (*ātmaparāmarśa-viśrānti*) and the reflective awareness [of the object], there is an intervening reflective awareness "I" (*aham*), just as between the reflective awareness of the process of cooking and the reflective awareness of its completion, there is the reflective awareness "he cooks. Now, one might object that even in the reflective awareness "I," the "this-ness" (*idantā*) flashes forth at the outset.

In cases such as "I am emaciated," it is true; however, that reflective awareness of "I" which is permeated by the notion of "this-ness" (idantā) ultimately rests within the pure reflective awareness of "I"—as has been stated more than once:
"Even though the state of objects... (Āgamaprāmāṇya, verse 20).

According to this principle, there is only autonomy (*svātantrya*) in both forms of "I-ness" (*ahantā*); however, the former is contracted by the body and so forth. Thus he says: "without being interrupted by another reflective awareness" (*parāmarśāntarāvyavadhānena*). But here, at the beginning, it is said: "this Self" (*ātmāyam*).
It has been stated that the "I-consciousness" acts as an intermediary because dependence produced by the status of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*) appears [therein].

This is corroborated by the phrase "for this very reason": since direct awareness (*sākṣātparāmarśa*) is more internal than mediated awareness (*vyavahitaparāmarśa*), therefore even those [afflictions] mentioned in the *Kleśakarmasūtra* [are sublated].

Disregarding that denotability of the Supreme Lord which was described by the word *īśvara* as being untouched by dependence, there is another aphorism: for the collection of secret seed-mantras (*bījamantra*) indicated by the *praṇava* has consciousness-reflection (*saṃvid-vimarśa*) as its ultimate reality, and it is of the nature of the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
It does not manifest any dependent (*paratantra*) object at all; for this very reason, such a word is called an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
For that which is projected externally would indeed possess other powers, such as gender and number, but [this is not the case here].
Because it is internal, consisting of the nature of consciousness or its attribute, for this very reason, conjunction, optionality, and so forth— which do not reside in external objects—
also illuminate the attribute characterized by the manifestation of the sovereignty of consciousness. Thus, even particles such as *ca* (and) [function in this way].

They are said to be "resting upon meanings that are non-existent and unreal. However, in cases such as *samuccaya* (conjunction), that very form appears as something created; from that [creation] follows the connection with gender, number, and so forth. And even there—in the cognition of the meaning—there is indeed an intervention.
And by means of the *praṇava*...

That Lord, whose nature is autonomy consisting of the reflective awareness of the four states beginning with waking, and who reflects upon the non-obstruction of the powers of will and the rest— which take the form of all accepted conventions such as contradictory injunctions and prohibitions— is truly realized as the autonomous self-nature.
Thus it has been stated:
"The repetition of that [mantra] and the contemplation of its meaning" (Yoga Sūtra 1.28).
However, words that touch upon the nature of the object of knowledge [do so] through such an intermediary form.
They perform the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of that, as it is stated in the *Āgama*:

"Because of the continuous utterance of the word 'Bhairava'—which means 'He who swallows all,' 'He who makes everything resound,' 'The Giver of All,' and 'The Pervader of the Whole'—one becomes Śiva" (Vi.bhai. 130).

For this very reason, the Blessed One himself has explained the exposition of the mantras for the words beginning with *Śiva* within the "Glorious Great King of Mantras" (*Śrīmad-vyomavyāpi-mahāmantrarāja*).
Following that very [explanation], the sage Vyāsa and others have also [proceeded].
"When the three goddesses [approached] him...

and so forth they described; by relying upon which, others provide explanations for the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), the etymologies (*nirvacana*), and so on, up to the *Sahasranāma*. From that very source, the followers of the *Pāñcarātra*...
They pay heed to the etymological derivation (*nirukta*). He explains [the rule] "like an object expressed by a verbal suffix" (*tiṅvācyakarmavat*) with the words "as follows.

At the beginning, it is established as independent (*svatantra*); at the conclusion, it is that which is being accomplished (*sādhyamāna*), having reached the limit of the dependent meaning (*paratantrārtha*). This occurs in the sequence [of the word] *pacati*.
The reflections [of cognition] upon action, genus, and quality; by the inclusion of "etcetera," time and so forth are meant. As the venerable author has said (p.
