"Direction, means of accomplishment, action, and time—these denote entities that are absolutely unstable in their nature as the power (*śakti*) of things. (Vākyapadīya 3.6.1).
For this very reason, there is no connection with number, time, and so forth, for these [directions and the like] which act as if they were substances (*dravyāyamāṇa*).
It is contradictory [to say] that this present time possesses the two qualities of duality and unity, while [saying] "Karkī was previously future at the birth of Viṣṇu" or "he will be past.
However, in the case of number, time, and so forth, as apprehended through reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) such as "he threw down the jars," it [is not contradictory].

"It does not exist at all. For that very reason, those [cognitions] are reflections upon reality (*tattva*), and not others. He explains another example given in the commentary (*vṛtti*) in order to establish his own view, starting with "And just as...
Since the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) has already been stated previously, there is no further conclusion with the word "so" (*tathā*). [The term used is] "memory" (*smṛti*).

It consists of the conceptualization of the present. With the intention that there is no similarity between this example and the subject at hand—since in both cases, whether in memory or in direct experience, the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is the same, namely "this is a jar"—he says, "In this case too. Although the other reflective awareness "that" occurs at the beginning, [it is followed by] "this jar."

It manifests as resting upon a prior reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Now, one might object: "The word 'that' (*saḥ*) is not a form that differentiates the reflective awareness of the object; this is merely a difference in appearance (*ābhāsa-bheda*) caused by a difference in time.
With the intention of showing that a difference in appearance is not what constitutes differentiation, he states an alternative view with the words "directly" (*sākṣāt*), and so forth.
The point is that even though there is no complete identity [between the two], the example applies to the present case in terms of the factor of intervention (*vyavadhāna*).
He demonstrates that this alone is logical with the passage beginning with "parāmarśa" and ending with "uktaprāyam.
Therefore, because the Self consists of a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of distinct appearances, when it functions as subject and object simultaneously—

Regarding the term "difference" (*bheda*) here, the intended meaning is that the distinction between fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*)—which serves as the differentiator—is dependent upon a distinction in reflective awareness (*vimarśa*);

yet, such a distinction in reflective awareness does not exist at all, and thus that [reason] is also like a non-entity, rendering the reason absolutely unestablished (*asiddha*). Now, one might object: even the reflective awareness "this is a jar" (*ghaṭa iti*) ultimately rests within the "I-ness" (*ahantā*) alone.
As it has been said:

"Of this [cognition] which consists of the interrupted reflection 'this'... (*Āgamaprāmāṇya* 15), and so forth. Therefore, how can even the creation of jars and other objects be devoid of the state of being an object of cognition, such that...
Anticipating the objection that liberation is said to consist merely in the sovereignty over the creation of the self and so forth, he says: "And in the realm of Māyā...
(page 216).

This is true; however, the cognizer, desiring the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) of an object such as a jar, conceives that very action as being produced solely by a distinct reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*),
and thus does not attend to his own ultimate reflective awareness of "I-ness" (*ahantā*).
However, an object such as the self does not achieve its purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) without resting upon a final reflective awareness;

just as an action such as cooking requires a reflective awareness of its completion, [the author] therefore establishes that final rest as the very criterion of validity (*pramāṇa*) here. For this is indeed the sphere of *māyā*.

It is reflected upon that therein lies the contradiction between "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*), as well as the mutual contradiction among objects such as pots and cloths within the sphere of "this-ness"— as he said, "and of the objects of perception. Furthermore,
this distinction between the "I-ness" of Caitra, Maitra, and so forth, is dependent upon the difference in the perceived forms of their bodies and other attributes.

With this intention, he did not say "and of the perceivers. "Abiding therein" means abiding in pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). "Purity" refers to the state of the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) in comparison to the illusory ego-sense (*māyīyāhaṃbhāva*) which is colored by the body and so forth. And that...
The pure one endures everything, for he is the ultimate reality of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*). And this has been stated [in the verse]: "And of the Lord... (1.5.10). || 17 ||

Now, an objection may be raised: "Is it not your own accepted view that the Self alone is the Supreme Lord? And the Self, being of the nature of the subject, carries out worldly activity solely through cognition, determination, recollection, volition, and so forth, and not by means of the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); therefore, to whom else could that [power] belong? In response to this doubt, the Sūtra [is stated]:

That very power of Māyā belonging to the All-pervasive Lord, when its sphere consists of differentiated objects of cognition, is designated by such names as knowledge, volition, and determination. (18)

It is true that the Self, the pervasive Supreme Lord, is indeed the perceiver (*grāhaka*) due to the contraction caused by the power of *māyā*; likewise, the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*),
being contracted by the coloring of the objects of knowledge through the contraction of the power of *māyā*, takes the form of cognition, memory, and so forth.

It is said: the intended meaning is that, by way of mere designation, there is no other distinct principle such as "knowledge" (*jñāna*) that exists apart from the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśaśakti*). And by this, the following doubt is also pacified:
"But surely, the reflective awarenesses of the universe..."

(Page 217) Since the reality consists of nothing more than the "I" (*daham*), how can it be said that knowledge, memory, and so forth are powers (*śakti*) of the Lord? Furthermore, how can there be distinctions such as doubt and the like among knowledge and the other faculties?

And how is there the variety of blue and so forth? The intended meaning is that this [variety] arises from the coloring (uparāga) of the object of knowledge (vedya) belonging to Māyā. He introduces this with the words "saiva ca" (and that very same). Māyā is the manifestation of the impossible;

power (śakti) is the capacity therein. By virtue of that, within the divided subject of knowledge (vedaka), there is a divided object of knowledge (vedya), and [the subject is] distinct from the object of knowledge.

The passage from "vedakācca" up to "tatra tatra" should be explained as being in grammatical apposition with the subject (*pramātṛ*), and in a different grammatical relation (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) with the object (*prameya*); otherwise, even in the aphorism, the phrase "bhinne bhinnena ca" would be inconsistent. The term "tatra tatra" means "in various [cases]," because it is precisely due to this variety that there is a distinction among the names such as "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and so forth. "Evam" (thus) refers to the collection of arguments (*yuktijāta*) that has been stated.

Therefore, this meaning must not be denied. What is it? He says: "the meaning. It is "of a single form," and not many manifestations, because of the absence of causes for such differentiation—namely, space, time, form, and so forth. It is "the soul of the universe" (*viśvātmā*) by virtue of being the subject of all.

[He is] omniscient because it is impossible for another [to know all]; [he is] the creator of the universe (viśvakṛt), for otherwise this manifold variety would be entirely causeless—this has been established at length, and will be established further.
Now, when it should be said that [the world] is manifested by the Lord through his power of illusion (māyā-śakti), what is the purpose of this expression used in the commentary?

Having considered this, he says "because of its utility" (*upayogāt*). The sense is that this is to be understood as a figurative usage (*upacāra*), intended with the purpose of illuminating a superior utility. Furthermore, this genitive case should also be construed in relation to the phrase "it is manifested" (*bhāsyate*). The same applies in the commentary (*vṛtti*). For [otherwise], it would not belong to anything else.

It is said by someone that the powers such as knowledge belong to the All-pervasive Lord (vibhu), but not to individual selves (ātman); he demonstrates this with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) and "even in the state of Māyā" (*māyāpade’pi*). Therein, he explains "knowledge" (*jñāna*) as "ever-new" (*abhinava*), meaning unprecedented. "Of the knower" (*pramātuḥ*) refers to the one who is under the influence of Māyā. But if this is so—
To the question "How is it manifested by the All-pervasive One?", he says "And that," and so forth. "That" means for that reason.

"Belonging to Him" (tadīyā) means belonging to the Lord (aiśvarī). "That very [thing]"—namely, knowledge—is connected with what precedes. He explains "direct perception" (adhyakṣam) as "the sense organ" (indriya), and so on.

The meaning is that [the sense-organ] is presided over by the senses (*akṣa*) as its instrument (*karaṇa*). Now, one might object: "Direct perception must necessarily have an object; why then was it not mentioned in the commentary (*vṛtti*)? To this he says: "Who says such a thing?"

Regarding the term "the subject at hand": it has indeed been stated that the universe is manifested through differentiation. He explains the commentary on the phrase "of that very [universe] when differentiated" by refuting the previously raised prima facie objection;

the meaning of "of that very [universe]" is "of that which has been experienced. Now, one might object: let this be so in the case of memory and determinative cognition, but what about in the case of volition (*saṃkalpa*)?

A new [cognition] arises having a single object, as does the conceptual construction (vikalpa) consisting of doubt, poetic fancy (utprekṣā), and so forth, which is included by the mention of "and the rest" (*ādi*).
Therefore, how is it that in the commentary (*vṛtti*) it is stated that it [conceptualization] is common to memory, volition, and determination?
To this, he replies: "[It arises] from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of experience. Thus...

In the commentary, it was stated "of that very [object]" with reference to the external intention; or rather, "of that very" is not explained as "of what has been experienced," but rather as "of that which is under the sway of the power of Māyā. He shows another interpretation, stating that even at that time, this form belongs to the object of conceptualization as well.
...and so forth. Now, an objection may be raised: volition is a modification of the mind (*manas*) of the inner self (*pratyagātman*);
determination is a modification of the intellect (*buddhi*); and likewise, knowledge is either a modification of the sense organs or a modification of the intellect.
Since the mind, the intellect, and the senses are insentient (*jaḍa*), how can knowledge and the other [mental states] belong to them?
The word "also" (*api*) used in the commentary contains within it the objection that [the elements] have consciousness as their intrinsic nature (*cit-svabhāva*);
to explain this, he says, "even though" (*yadyapi*). Here he clarifies the response with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).
Although the state of affairs is such that... (*a. pra. si. 20*).

According to this principle, the inner self (pratyagātman) has as its ultimate reality pure consciousness alone; thus, the very nature of the functions of the mind, intellect, and senses is that of consciousness characterized by reflective awareness (vimarśa). And it is precisely in this way that the author of the commentary introduced the subject, as he demonstrates in the commentary with the words "the power of consciousness" (citiśaktiḥ); the word "and" (ca) here indicates a reason, because:

The inner self (*pratyagātman*) is said to be the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) with respect to its manifestation (*vṛtti*); therefore, the supreme agency (*kartṛtā*) here should be understood as the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), or else the relationship of cause and effect may be applied in the reverse order. For the result is indeed the same. [Objection:
But surely determination (*adhyavasāya*) has already been accepted as being accomplished by cognition alone. [Reply: True; however, there exists this other [agency] for whose sake [it occurs].

Furthermore, he shows that it is a term for "determination" (*adhyavasāya*) by stating: "And determination... [and] "by way of identity with direct perception" (*sākṣātkāraikyena*). This much [is the point].

Because it has the nature of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). The function of perception is determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*); and by means of that function, one does not remain distinct from its possessor, or there is identity through the power of determinative cognition. As it has been said:
"For conceptual constructions appear as if they were perceptions. At the outset, there is the form of doubt: "Is there a well? or "Is there not?"
The meaning is that it is not clearly manifest as suchness. || 18 ||
Now, one might object: let there be reflective deliberation (*vimarśa*), consisting of the association with verbal expression, in the category of conceptual cognitions such as memory;

however, in an experience whose nature is direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*)—which is of the form of immediate seeing—such reflective deliberation is impossible, because it cannot involve the recollection of conventions caused by that [perception], since memory only functions to awaken latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Since the non-perception of a cause makes the absence of reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa) alone logical, the following aphorism is provided to shatter the delusion of others: "How could there be no reflective awareness even at the moment of direct perception?"
Running and other such actions would be possible even without the act of reconnection [to a new body]. || 19 ||

He introduces this by subsequently pointing out, as the thesis to be proven, the meaning of the portion of the aphorism beginning with "How otherwise... which takes the form of a logical argument and constitutes the subject matter of the first part of the aphorism. [The opponent asks: "But [how can there be inference] without a reflective awareness (parāmarśa)? [The author replies: "True."
For that [object] does exist, but it is subsequent to the initial perception (*ālocana*). This is what is not accepted by the passage beginning with "at a later time" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in itself," there are two alternatives: either in a prior cognition consisting of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), or in a direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*).
Addressing the first alternative, he says "in itself. Here, "therein" refers to the direct intuition. It is not [the case that the object exists]...

Regarding the phrase "it is appropriate," he states the reason with the word "since" (*yataḥ*). By the words beginning with "as long as" (*yāvad*), the meaning is that whatever object is of such a nature, its status as a reason (*hetutvam*) applies to this point. When the probandum (*sādhya*) has been previously indicated, the ablative case is used for the word beginning with *yat* in order to convey its status as a reason. For it is not the case here that...

The word "that" (*tat*), from which the causal case-ending arises, would convey the causality of that object; this [objection] he refutes with the word "that" (*tat*). He says "of the object" (*arthasya*) because conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) pertains to an object, not to itself, since in its own nature it consists of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*). He refutes this as follows: "Even so..."
(220) Thus:

for where that [cognition] does not consist of direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*), there it is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); and where it does not consist of direct intuition, that object remains unmanifest—thus, regarding that which is unmanifest...
When performing a reflective discernment (*vimarśana*) regarding a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), why would one not perform it with respect to everything that appeared in a prior cognition?

For there is no distinction [between them] insofar as they are equally non-manifesting. With the intention that conceptualization is appropriate only for what has been manifested, and not for anything else, the terms "prior" (*pūrva*) and "cognition" (*jñāna*) are employed. In this regard:

He anticipates an objection from another regarding the presentation of a specific qualification for the sake of refutation with the words "even if" (*athāpi*). He refutes this with the words "even there" (*tatrāpi*), meaning: even when it is stated in this way. [The phrase] "it has been established" (*pratipāditam*) means:
[this is] true... (1.3.1)

Having begun with these words, in this section [of the text] ending with "the vision is indeed its own manifestation" (1.3.2), the word "tataḥ" means "from the aforementioned reasoning. That which is accompanied by the object of conceptualization (*vikalpya*)... [variant *kalpyeta* in manuscript *kha*].

Unity is the nature of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*); its absence of conceptualization (*nirvikalpatva*) is the reason for this. Now, as for that form of conceptualization which consists in the synthesis of what has been seen—[the reading *saṃkalpakātmakam* is found in manuscript kha]—and which was shown to be impossible within the cognition of direct perception, that...

He shows that even the conceptualization of that [object] is impossible because no prior or subsequent apprehension of a pervader is perceived; for in the absence of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), there can be no cognition of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*). Thus he says: "Nor also... [The means for the recollection of linguistic convention... (PV 3.174).

Thus it has been established. In that regard, the recollection of a convention depends upon the depositing of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) and the awakening of that latent impression; and these two cannot be performed by a non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*). For it has been said: "A vivid experience deposits the seed of memory."

"From such a perception, his awakening occurs. And we recognize no other greater intensity of experience than that which rests in reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). As for what was set forth by Bhaṭṭa:
"The sprouting of this [consciousness] is its proficiency...
Even there, regarding that sprouting, the resting within the subject as "I" shines forth in this very manner.
Do we perceive that [perception] as having such a nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), or rather as having some other form?

Even for perception, such a state is nothing but its full-fledged manifestation; for if it lacked the nature of reflective awareness, how could there be the implantation or the awakening of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*)? Furthermore, that which...
For the sake of examining validity, Bhaṭṭa stated: "Manifestation is for the purpose of its own object;
it is the awakener of the latent impression."
It could not be otherwise; let it be accepted that its activity occurs even in conceptual construction.

Thus it is said. In that regard, if the manifestation of light is not accepted as having a form such as being more intense (*paṭīyas*) than its unmanifested state, then there is nothing [to be gained]. Furthermore, even that which is not more intense would result in the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). Thus, the qualification "more intense" is rendered meaningless in Kīrti’s treatise. And as for the determination (*viniścaya*) in that context:
"It is confirmed by that very perception, arising through the power of consciousness regarding those things already perceived," and so forth;
in that regard, the capacity of consciousness certainly exists as something distinct from incapacity— enough [of this].

He demonstrates this very point in sequence with the words "for not," and so forth. Since the nature of fire itself is the causality of smoke, when fire is perceived, that [causality] is necessarily perceived; thus, even for an inhabitant of the Coconut Island (*nālikera-dvīpa*), there would arise a memory due to the establishment of such a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), namely: "This is the cause of smoke."

Furthermore, since the effect characterized by recollection is absent, how could it be that a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) has been deposited as something inferable solely from its effect? Thus, having demonstrated that a cognition devoid of reflection (*vimarśa*) does not effect the deposition of a latent impression, he demonstrates that it likewise does not effect its awakening, stating: "nor is there smoke."
Is it not the case that the causality of an object is merely for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) due to its being a secondary attribute (*paropādhika*),
and not for the sake of direct perception, which is by nature the mere manifestation of the unconditioned particular (*anupādhika-svalakṣaṇa*)?

Fearing that it might be objected that such causality is not even observed, he shows another illustration with the words "in walking on a path. The phrase "and also not" connects with what precedes. "In itself" is an example for the absence of implantation (*ādhāna*), while "the companion," and so forth, is an example for the absence of awakening (*prabodhana*).

He concludes thus with the words "and therefore": because of the absence of a cause consisting of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), there is an absence of the causes for the deposition, awakening, and designation of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of that effect; [consequently], of the effect...

Since recollection is absent, and its cause is not perceived, that which is called "synthesis" (*saṃkalana*) would not even be a conceptual construction (*vikalpana*). He shows that synthesis of what has been seen is not tenable not only due to the absence of its cause, but also by its very nature, with the words "nor... (*na ca*). For what has been seen—

There are two types of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). How could these two be synthesized? For conceptual synthesis (*saṃkalana-vikalpa*) does not have them as its object; moreover, if that which is not an object were to be synthesized, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, [conceptualization] has the recollection of convention (*saṃketa-smaraṇa*) as its means... (Pramāṇavārttika 3.174).

Each of these points has been refuted word by word. Furthermore, in the *Viniścaya*, it was concluded that "sensory cognition does not enter into conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) which consists of the association with objects.
That alone would be logical if conceptual construction were essentially nothing other than the association with universals (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), and substances (*dravya*).

"It would have its own nature [as memory], but it is not so"—with this in mind, he begins with "Nor again... Now, let it be granted that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has another form consisting of recollection (*smaraṇa*); however, that need not be rejected, because such a thing is not even to be suspected in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*), given its possession of the characteristics of direct apprehension, such as the grasping of "this-ness" (*idantā*) and clarity (*spaṣṭatva*).

In the conceptual construction "this is a cow, white, moving, horned," which arises for those whose delusions have been refined by verbal expression (*bhāṣā-bhāvita-vibhrama*), the nature of direct perception (*adhyakṣa-rūpatā*) is possible; therefore, that very conceptualization must be excluded from the nature of direct perception. But what fault is there if memory itself is considered conceptual in that respect?
Anticipating this objection, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) states his own position with the words "And that... and so forth.

Regarding the two alternatives—whether the manifestation and conceptualization of the remembered object occur sequentially or non-sequentially—he first refutes the former with the word "therein" (*tatra*). [He says] "and not thus," meaning that there is no perception of blue [in that manner].

Therefore, regarding the statement "then there is determinative cognition" (*adhyavasāya*): just as a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises immediately after a perception, it is not the case that in the recollection of a deceased father, there is a perception of the deceased father; rather, its nature as a conceptualization is what is experienced. For if it were [a perception] in that manner, it would clearly be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself, and not recollection (*smaraṇa*).

The intention is that there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a "this-is-so" (*ayam-iti*) reflective awareness, which is contradictory to the "that-is-so" (*sa-iti*) reflective awareness that pervades the nature of recollection. Having refuted the first alternative, he applies the second by showing how it falls within his own system, beginning with the word "atha. Why? Because there is indeed the possibility that [the object] exists simultaneously with its manifestation.

"It is not contradictory for conceptualization [to exist] simultaneously. Why then is it not accepted that even direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) has the nature of conceptualizing at the very same time as the object appears? This is what the opponent does not accept.
"Or even if it is tolerated. If there were conceptualization (*vikalpana*) of that which appears in memory or in determination (*adhyavasāya*), then that objection would indeed be raised;
for appearance and conceptualization can only occur either sequentially or simultaneously, as there is no third possibility.
To the extent that there is no conceptualization of that which is appearing here—
whether it be the form of its own nature appearing in the vision of consciousness, or whether it is non-existent according to the intellect,
or "not external" according to the logic of the Vaibhāṣika view— that [object] cannot be conceptualized, for it is...

That which is manifested is the ultimate; however, it is that very thing which is conceptualized and determined. And that which is appearing is not what is determined. To this, he says "that": whatever you have asserted, it is precisely for the purpose of investigating that very point that this subject matter expressed by this sūtra has been introduced.

We maintain that reflective awareness (vimarśa) exists precisely when there is manifestation; in that case, how can the opponent—who asserts the mere proposition that "there is no reflective awareness in what is manifesting"—not be defeated? Furthermore, he demonstrates that this proposition contradicts both one's own direct experience and one's own accepted tenets.

"Having its own appearance" means "having its own manifestation" (*svapratibhāsa*). For the statement "its own manifestation is determined as an object" expresses that the manifestation itself is the object of determination (*adhyavaseyatā*); and since that very [determination] is what is to be conceptualized (*vikalpanīya*), it follows that it is the manifestation itself that is conceptualized. This refers to that which is appearing.

The intended meaning is that the investigation into succession and simultaneity is appropriate only when [the object] is being conceptualized. As for the phrase "contradiction by reasoning," it refers to the means of recollecting the linguistic convention... (Pramāṇavārttika 3.174).
"...because [the meaning] arises through the force of the context," and so forth.

That [objection], however, is a sublation by reasoning (*yuktibādha*), which is refuted right here in this very sūtra according to the method already stated and to be stated later, and will also be refuted in other sūtras. And when that [objection] has been removed...

If the very appearance of one's own reflection is conceptualized as "cognition," then there is no temporal difference whatsoever between the appearance and the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*). Now, [one might object that] reflective awareness involves the association with words; [The response: ...[continues from previous context].

And that [recognition] arises from the recollection of a convention; that [recollection] too arises from the awakening of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*); and that [impression] too arises from a prior perception of a similar kind.
Therefore, how could there be any deliberation (*vimarśana*) regarding that [perception], which is like a great-great-grandfather?

To dispel such a doubt, he says "And not... as if posing a question to the opponent, in order to remove the obstacle to the recollection of the convention—which is established through the power of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) when the application of the expression is accomplished—even though [the cognition] is born from that mental impression. Thus: "Even though it is produced by a mental impression... and so forth.

All this is established by virtue of being produced through mental formations (*saṃskāra*); however, the word "also" (*api*) indicates that one need not further postulate a second [mental factor], namely the recollection of linguistic convention (*śabda-saṃketa-smaraṇa*), on top of that. "In between" (*antarā*) means between the appearance and the conceptualization. Now, it might be argued: "Let there be nothing in between; [the cognition arises] from the recollection of that [convention]."

But it will indeed exist previously. This too he negates with the words "and not. Here, the very fact of arising simultaneously is the reason. Regarding the phrase "the impression of experience": by means of this, the manifestation of blue itself seems to revive once again. Regarding the word "specific": for immediately after a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the seed of memory [is awakened].

It has been stated that [the object] is "established" (*ādhāna*). This means that it arises from its own cause, which consists of two types of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) awakened by such a perception that culminates in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
"From another" (*parataḥ*) means from a second [cause]. And this alone is logical; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

He shows that there is also the recollection of convention (*saṃketasmaraṇa*). By this, he demonstrates that if the recollection of convention alone were the cause for the application of verbal expression in all cases, then no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) whatsoever would arise;
thus, he states that even though [conceptual construction] arises from other causes, there is indeed an application of words precisely because of the arising of conceptual construction.

In this way, even in the case of memory—which lacks the connection with verbal expression—the obstacle posed by the need for a subsequent recollection of the convention has been removed by another [factor].

He says "therefore" (*tataḥ*) in order to apply that very same principle to direct experience (*anubhava*), which consists in the connection with verbal expression; the meaning is: "from that very specificality of causes as stated by you. That...
He demonstrates this with the words "its own word" (*svaśabda*) and so forth. "That too" refers to the experience (*anubhava*). "Of that" refers to the object (*artha*).
"Or otherwise" means by way of being a producer, having the same causal complex, and so on; for [the cognition] arises through the efficacy (*sāmarthya*) of the object.
Thus, the reason is not probative; for we do not maintain that experience possesses the property of being expressible by virtue of the nature residing in the object,
because the aspect consisting of expression does not manifest within the domain of the object.

"The determination that 'this is a jar'... [is explained] according to the principle to be stated later; however, the underlying intention (*ākūta*) is that it occurs rather through the power of mental attention (*manaskāra*). Now, as for the definition: "That consciousness which has immediately passed away from the six [consciousnesses] is the mind (*manas*)."

Thus, the mental attention (*manaskāra*) is the immediate cognition itself, just as the cognition of yellow follows the cognition of blue; and he dispels the doubt that the cognition of yellow is not associated with the verbal expression of the word "blue" by saying "for this very [reason]. It is like the excellence of the sense faculty or of light.

One must take into account what has been stated by the word "kāra" as being excessive: namely, the clarity [of the sense organ], the suitability of the object's location, and even the attentiveness of the mind. And this very attentiveness is defined as the capacity to awaken the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the words denoting the object one desires to see.

Nevertheless, it has been stated by the Abhidharmikas themselves that "attention (manaskāra) is the directing of the mind," and this "directing" is said to be nothing other than being oriented toward investigation. By them— that is,
by the Buddhists— [the nature of] consciousness is defined as the state of being awareness.
By those who say "from the immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*),

it is meant that the specific quality (*viśeṣa*) arising from the strength of one causal factor within an effect produced by a totality of causes is not contradicted by another specific quality arising from a different causal factor, just as in the case of a jar.

The configuration [of consciousness] occurs by way of having the nature of earth (mṛd-rūpatā). Thus, the fact that the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in consciousness is brought about by the strength of the causal factor consisting of mental attention is not contradicted by the state of possessing an object (*viṣayavattā*), which is produced by another cause consisting of the external object itself. For as for contradiction...

The cause of that which has the nature of non-coexistence is the impossibility of another cause, namely, the absence of a specific configuration in the lump of clay. And its opposite is the possibility of another cause;

thus, this is the "perception of what is incompatible with the cause" (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*). Regarding this, he says: "Therefore, just as... [and] "it produces" refers to mental attention (*manaskāra*).

This is the connection [of the words]. However, because the expansion of attentiveness (*avadhāna*) occurs progressively according to its varying degrees of intensity, it first proceeds toward the innermost nature— the form of the "I" (*aham*)— by means of the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

First, there is the act of appropriation (*svīkāra*); from that comes the presiding over the level of Sadāśiva through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "this" and "I"; from that, again, as merely "this," characterized by duality alone;
and from that, as specific [objects] such as "a jar" and so forth. And yet, there is no finality whatsoever regarding these particularities here.
Since the subject ceases [his activity] precisely from that point, that alone is the subsequent particularity;
thus, the subject comes to rest through the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of that very thing—therefore, recollection extends only up to that limit.
For this reason, he says "subtle" (*sūkṣma*), with reference to each successive expansion.
Because subtlety reaches its ultimate limit in each preceding stage, the venerable Bhartṛhari said:

"Paśyantī has withdrawn the end of sequential order; although there is no difference [between her and the other levels], she possesses the power of sequential order inherent within her. She is both immobile and mobile, and she is both one who has attained composure and one who has not."
It is that which has its form resting upon consciousness, whose form is not dissolved [into objects], and which is formless;
it is the manifestation of delimited objects, the manifestation of mixed objects, the manifestation of all objects, and the manifestation of the quiescent. By this indeed—
The manifoldness of "I-ness" (*ahantā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*) has been described by way of their immeasurable divisions.

Thus, it is precisely through the reflective awareness of "this-ness" encountered on the path that the cognizer comes to rest; and it is only up to that point that there is recollection, with each preceding stage being relative to each succeeding one.
Because its nature consists of the cultivated state of the withdrawn sound (*saṃvartita-śabda-bhāvanā-rūpa*), it is said to be non-conceptual (*avikalpa*),

even though it possesses the nature of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) consisting of a specific reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). As for the first [form], which has two aspects— namely, "I" (*aham*) and "I am this" (*ahamidam*)— in that case, there is only the pure nature of reflective awareness, and not...
That [the mind] has conceptualization as its nature will be established in the very next chapter. Now, one might object:

"How can this mind, which consists of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), possess this connection with verbal expression and latent impressions (*abhilāpa-saṃskāra*) that you have postulated under the term 'attention' (*avadhāna*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Just as... (yathā).

"Immediately following" refers to that moment which follows in relation to the preceding generative moment. "Mutually" means that here no waiting for another time is perceived, as is the case when entering a room. "Together" means not separately. Previously, those [factors] such as the sense faculties were of such a nature.
They are devoid of the capacity of mental attention (*manaskāra*) that generates reflection; however, subsequently,
by the power of their own causes, they possess such latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

However, he shows that for things existing in such a state, there are no material causes (*upādāna*), auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*), or even final conditions of proximity (*upasarpaṇa-pratyaya*) that function as causes for their continued existence—this is indicated by the words "even upon impact" (*athābhipāte 'pi*).
Now, one might object: "Such causes are not perceived. To this it is replied: "of those existing in the universe" (*viśvavartinām*).
Even Mount Meru is not without cause in its persistence or in the production of a jar;
for, when that [cause] remains according to its specific place and time, the persistence, production, and so forth of those things occur without obstruction. And thus says the Abhidharma:
"Other than itself, [all things are] the efficient cause" (*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* 2.50);

thus he stated that a cause has the nature of being a cause for that which is distinct from its effect. With this very intention, the noble Prajñākaragupta [asserted that] even a future thing, by virtue of its abiding in its own time...
[He] stated the causality. Having thus restated the opponent’s position, he applies this very same reasoning for the sake of establishing his own view with the words, "Even so, for that very reason.
He confirms this very point with the word "necessarily" (*avaśyam*). To begin with, perception is by its very nature devoid of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) in the case of an infant.

For this is your position: that which was previously seen through convention, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by that [seeing] must be awakened, and subsequently, following memory, there must occur the act of reflective discernment (*parāmarśakriyā*);
however, for an infant, because of the absence of prior seeing, the latent impression itself does not exist.
"All this perception of his is devoid of conceptual determination (*parāmarśa*);

and since the application of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) is not possible regarding that which is not conceptually determined, he demonstrates this at length with the words 'For instance' (*tathā hi*): 'mere hearing,' 'mere seeing.'"

The meaning is that there are two cognitions, each residing in its own particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of word and object, which are incapable of mutual contact. By saying "and not thus," he shows the opposite of that [consequence] immediately following the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*):
"the first cognition of a child is not non-reflective (*aparāmarśaka*)."
Because it arises from the grasping of a convention, the production of a convention is pervaded by that which is the opposite of non-reflexive awareness— namely, reflexive awareness;
for its other pervading factor is the concomitance characterized by the mutual superimposition of word and object.

There is apprehension, and its opposite is non-sequential apprehension. The state of being a reflective awareness (*parāmarśakatva*)— which is excluded from that which produces a convention because it is absent in what is opposed to its pervader—
is withdrawn from that which is a reflective awareness arising from a convention.
"It is pervaded by being a referent" is the perception of a pervasion by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhiḥ*). Furthermore, even in the case of the first [instance],
it is observed that the apprehension of the convention for a novel word occurs only when it is referred to by another word.

Just as the word "pika" is understood when the cuckoo (*kokila*) is perceived, so too, without a verbalization (*śabdana*) that arises from the power of consciousness— occurring at the limit of that [perception] and independent of convention—
the mere application of conventional words would not be possible. For everything is indeed expressible by all words.

Regarding the phrase "of the object": ultimately, even through a mere phoneme, such as a portion of the sound *huṃ*, there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that is indeed non-conventional (*asāmayika*). However, for the sake of regulating linguistic usage, a specific word is conventionally assigned; and since that too exists within the being of the subject (*pramātṛsāttve*), it is indeed "other"—for such is the ultimate reality of convention (*saṃketaparamārtha*). Of that... [text ends].

Why not accept that this conceptual determination (*parāmarśa*) is the very nature of the perception of the object? For if it were accepted as such, then the objection regarding the recollection of linguistic convention (*saṃketasmaraṇa*), as stated in the passage concerning "the means for the recollection of convention" (*pra.vā. 3.174*), would be refuted.
And so forth;

even when the object is being utilized, there is again the application of words for the sake of recollection, and so on. For instance, [the phrase] "as the convention" is used even when a separate existence has been attained.
The identity between perception and conceptualization, which is established by the force of their being experienced together, must be supported;
as it has been said:
"For conceptualizations appear as if they were direct perceptions."
Thus [is the case] for one whose impressions of the philosophical view have not fallen away.
And so forth. Thereafter, their absolute distinction must be stated through reasoning. And in that [distinction]:

It is merely the recollection of the linguistic convention that unfolds. And once the obstacles to that have been dispelled, that which is established by uncontradicted experience must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, for the sake of establishing worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), nothing at all could be accepted.

This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). [The author] refutes the opponent's position— that it is unestablished (*asiddha*) because an infant lacks the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from previous perceptions— by stating "of the infant" (*bālasya*) on page 229.
By such statements as these: "Indeed, what is remembered in childhood—that which lacks such proficiency of the internal organ—is not remembered in youth;
who would believe this? And if it were remembered in youth, it would be remembered [then];
otherwise, one would not even remember one's nurse. Thus, due to the absence of the effect, that [childhood experience] does not exist. But was it not already said?
The absence of conceptual construction (kalpanā) is indeed the means for establishing the direct perception (pratyakṣa) of sensory cognition;
for even one who stands with his inner self motionless, having withdrawn all thought from every side,
perceives form with the eye— this is cognition born of direct experience.

Furthermore, while conceptualizing something, one thinks, "I had such a conceptualization," but one does not perceive this during the previously mentioned state when there is no movement of the senses.
Thus it has been said. That is true, but it is not sufficient to prove the absence of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).
For instance, when all thought has been withdrawn, no determination (*adhyavasāya*) should arise immediately thereafter;

for if such a determination were to arise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of no distinction between one who is still and one who is otherwise. And if no determination arises, then that [state]...

[The opponent argues: "The state [of the object] exists; how then can it be said that it is not amenable to linguistic usage? If it is argued that "it will be dealt with through memory," [the author] first states the untenability of that position within his own system, beginning with the words "for perception and memory... as was previously discussed in the *Smaraṇāhnika*.

For this has been established by the passage beginning with "He is indeed the perceiver of objects previously experienced" (1.4.1)— namely, that if the essence of consciousness (*cittattva*), which consists of inward-turned reflective awareness (*parāmarśamaya*), is one and the same for both perception and memory, then [the recognition of identity occurs].

The state of having an unbroken object-field is not otherwise. For the Seer, whose nature is consciousness, this alone constitutes the state of being a seer: that within the reflective awareness of "this-ness," there exists the state of being composed of the reflective awareness of "I" as the foundational locus and the ground of support.
Thus, even stillness is indeed composed of reflective awareness, according to the supreme [teacher].

He states that this must necessarily be accepted with the words "real" (*vāstava*). He refers to the "cognizer" (*pramātā*) as one whose life consists of conceptual constructions such as "I am manifesting thus at this time," and whose nature is a continuum (*saṃtāna*);
he says this with the phrase "and its unity. Precisely for this reason, because it has the nature of a flowing stream...
From their simultaneous arising, both conceptual constructions persist through the continuum of the body and the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Therefore, it is said that there is "oneness" between them.

Here he provides the logical justification with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*). The latent impression (*saṃskāra*) born of experience comes to rest within the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) who consists of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). For it has been said: "That which is not reflected upon does not plant the seed of memory.
It is not desired [that the impression rests elsewhere], for even the establishment of a relationship [between the object and the cognition] depends on this.

Even there, that which is the object of the worldly person's conceptualization belongs to the knower whose essence is difference— the non-manifestation of non-difference from consciousness. By this [means], that activity is blocked so that it does not proceed toward another conceptual construction.
"Because if there were contact with another conceptualization, it would follow that there is a plurality of subjects.

(9, 10) And thus, if conceptualization does not arise, there would be no state of being an agent of linguistic convention (*vyavahāryatā*) for the state of stillness (*staimitya*). Nor is it logical for conceptualization to arise immediately [after stillness], because it would follow that there is no distinction between the states of stillness and its opposite.

It has been said: "But surely, even if no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises immediately after that [perception], it will nevertheless arise at the moment when a memory is about to arise at a later time. No, he says: "And not... "Of them" refers to those who maintain that the cognizer is unreal. Why is there no arising of the cognizer whose nature is conceptual construction?

This is logical. He says "in between": that which occurs between the state of stillness (*stimitatā*) and memory (*smṛti*) is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). By means of that [construction], there is this interruption of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the perception of stillness; therefore, even though it occurs at a different time from the present moment, it is [non-existent] precisely because of the interruption of the latent impressions.

For this reason, just as there would be no recollection in the case of a non-conceptual experience (*nirvikalpa-anubhava*) whose latent impression (*saṃskāra*) has been interrupted by an internal experience of blue and its subsequent conceptualization, so too there would be no recollection in the case of an experience of stillness (*stimitatā*). Alternatively, these two statements may be taken separately:
by the phrase "interrupted" (*antara*) and so forth, it is meant that because of the intermingling with conceptualization occurring at another time, the state of stillness itself would not exist.

It has been stated: "For this very reason," and so forth; therein, it was indicated by the statement "and that [object], while conceptualizing it again," that no recollection would occur. Therefore, in that state of stillness (*staimitya*), the subject must necessarily exist in the form of conceptualization, and not as something separate from it.
The persistence of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is established precisely through its identity with a state of steady vision (*stimitadarśana*).
Consequently, rather than being a means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is instead characterized by its very identity with conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

"It is established"—thus, this reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*). Now, one might object: a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) occurring at a different time is not capable of dividing a steady experience; so how could its latent impression (*saṃskāra*) be severed?
For a conceptual construction occurring immediately after [the experience], being indistinguishable due to its lack of interval, may indeed—

One should sever the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of non-conceptualization. Anticipating the objection that "at a later time, when a subject characterized by conceptualization arises, there is no sublation whatsoever of the state of inertia (*staimitya*), nor of the memory thereof," he says: "And even conceptualization... The word "and" (*ca*) indicates the aforementioned doubt. It is [a conceptualization] consisting of memory (*smārta*).

Thus, because it consists in the grasping of what has already been grasped, every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is by its very nature nothing but memory (*smṛti*). It is only that, at times, due to being colored by the shadow of a previous experience, it arises as "this" (*ayam*); however, it does not appear in the form of "that" (*saḥ*). Furthermore, what is called "recollection" (*smaraṇa*) is [the cognition] together with the original perception (*darśana*).
It occurs when there is identity of object. Identity of object depends upon the resting [of consciousness] in the subject; that [resting] also exists only when the subject exists;

and that subject, too, consists of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). And yet, it is precisely conceptual construction that arises now—thus, there is a circularity (*cakraka*). The term *smārta* means "that which belongs to memory" (*smṛti*); here the suffix is used in its own primary sense (*svārthika*). Even though it is used in its own primary sense...

The deviation from gender [of the suffix] is established by its very nature, as in the case of expressions such as *śamīra aupayikaḥ*. Alternatively, the word *smṛti* may refer to the genus (*jāti*), or it may end in the plural to denote a class (*varga*). In that case, by applying a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) in the sense of "belonging to," it is stated that [the conceptual construction] belongs to the genus of memory or belongs to the class of memory. Or else, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is dependent upon the memory of linguistic convention (*śabda-saṃketa-smṛti*).

How could that [conceptual thought] be "based on memory" (smārta) in the absence of memory? And since memory is not possible without the emergence of a subject (pramātṛ), conceptual thought would simply not exist if one does not accept an experience consisting of the subject whose nature is reflective awareness (vimarśa).

Whether [the conceptualization] occurs immediately after the experience or at a later time, if there is no reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), it is not a conceptualization because of the absence of memory;

this is a non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*). If there is no reflective awareness, there is no memory because of the impossibility of identity between the objects; this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Thus much by this section of the text.

The very absence of stagnation (*staimitya*) has thus been demonstrated. Now, one might raise the objection: "But surely the memory of stagnation is experienced without contradiction; how could that exist if it were non-existent? Anticipating this doubt (page 232):
Even though there is deliberation (*vimarśa*), the justification for its stillness (*staimitya*) is stated by the phrase "refined" (*saṃskṛta*).

There is no contradiction whatsoever between the occurrence of deliberation and stillness; for instance, even while occurring through the power of attentive mental application, [the cognition] has as its object the thing being perceived.

The reflective aspect (*vimarśabhāga*), which is non-different from the aspect of luminosity (*prakāśāṃśa*) and exists for only a single moment, is not led into a state of dullness by the habitual practice of conceptualizing subsequent moments; therefore, it is not remembered at a later time.
[Objection: But surely the same applies to the aspect of luminosity as well; thus, that reflection residing within the portion of luminosity would also [not be remembered].

It is recorded [in tradition]: "Not so; for the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the luminous aspect—which, though characterized by resting within its own self-awareness—is composed of the conviction of internalization because it is internal; and even if it lasts for only a moment, because it is internal, it possesses a state of firm establishment."

"Only in that which is more distinct"—by this it is meant that the impression (*saṃskāra*) must necessarily be deposited; therefore, it is remembered as residing solely in the aspect of light (*prakāśāṃśa*). However, since the objective portion (*arthabhāga*) is external to the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) residing in that [objective portion] only takes root when it has been repeatedly practiced through a succession of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*); not otherwise. Thus, everything [is explained].
"Correct. He says "thus," which means he states that [the nature of] being composed of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) is established in all cases.

By this, he indicates that the word ending in the locative case (*tvarite*) is connected with the preceding [word]. The term expressing the reason (*hetupada*) is for the purpose of explaining the words in the Sūtra such as "running" (*dhāvana*), which were included under the heading of "action" (*kriyāgrahaṇa*).

He states the counter-argument with the words "for knowledge... The phrase "dependent upon its own causes" should be construed as qualifying both the preceding and the following terms, like the eye of a crow (which moves between two sockets). As they say:
"The eye, though directed toward a jar, does not fail to see a cloth."
Thus, [it is said]: "By means of recollection and verbal expression...
Thus. Now, that which [is intended] for the explanation of the meaning of the prefix *pra-* in the word *dhāvana* as having the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*).

Regarding the term "swift step," he states what is to be excluded from it: "even action," such as lying down or sitting, or the unplanned cutting of grass and so forth. "By the force of latent impressions" means by those generated by the initial desire. For this very reason, repeated observations in various instances are not required.

"By the deliberation of desire"—this refers again to what has arisen within another intermediate state. "It may be"—the meaning is that this is not impossible. "Another," namely, the form of space (page 233).

"Whatever substance (*dravya*)—by the word 'etcetera' (*ādi*), qualities (*guṇa*) characterized as white, yellow, and so forth; or whatever else, such as a substance, that has a different location or a different nature—that is the object [of this cognition]. Thus he says:
the meaning is that he expresses this very thing by the word 'being seen' (*dṛśyamāna*). He explains the word "synthesis" (*anusandhāna*).

The instrumental case in "by the application of such a desire" (*tādṛgicchāyojanena*) is used in the sense of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). That which is characterized by the coordination of the desires for rejection,

acquisition, and seeking— namely, the state of being sought (*eṣaṇīyatva*) defined by [the thought] "this is desired," "this is sought after," and "this is to be sought"— without that [state], whatever rejection or acquisition occurs at every moment...

The connection is that "that is not tenable. He explains that "recitation" here is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for rapid recitation, memorization, and so forth, by saying "even in rapid recitation. Since the production of a phoneme occurs when there is mutual contact between the place (*sthāna*), such as the head or palate, and the organ (*karaṇa*), such as the tip of the tongue;

The phrase "the arising of touch and so forth" refers to the category of the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*). Now, one might ask: where in the Sūtra is this found that has been shown in the Commentary? He replies: "for that purpose. One might further object: by this extensive discussion, it has been established that desire—which exists as a state of fusion through the characteristic of perception—is the very self (*ātman*); yet this [point] is irrelevant to the present topic.

For it must be established that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is its very self. True; however, he shows that this is precisely what has been stated in the words "and of desire" (*icchāyāśca*). For desire is indeed a particular form of reflective awareness;
therein, there must necessarily be a reflective awareness of the form "this is that," which touches upon the object of desire even in its general aspect.
And in that state, one indeed abides through the powers of will, knowledge, and action,
which function as the identity with the light consisting of consciousness and bliss. As it was said by the venerable Parameṣṭhipāda:
"At the time of experiencing intense joy...
(1.9), beginning with these words, and continuing until: "...in reciting and likewise in running."
"In these very contexts, there is the state of vibrating with all powers" (1.11).
The analysis of the compound is "the self of vision. Now, [one might ask: is it not the case that [she] is the self of vision?
(page 234)

It is not yet established that desire (*icchā*) consists specifically of the form of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), for desire indeed follows after perception. He refutes this with the words "And not... For if that were the case, what would be the distinction between slow action and rapidity? Now, [one might object]:

"...the means for the recollection of the convention" (Pramāṇavārttika 3.174). By means of this established sequence of reasoning, he sets aside the doubt that the nature of perception as being of the essence of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is sublated, and thus reminds [the reader] by saying "and it has been said. Now, one might object:

"Let there be identity with desire alone, on account of the impossibility of rapidity otherwise; what is the use of this admission of identity with the reflective awareness 'this is that' regarding perception? To this, he says: "And not...
This is the formal argument: in cases such as rapid running or reading, desire is not distinct from perception.
Because rapidity is perceived; for if there were separation, there would be only non-rapidity,
brought about by a temporal distinction resulting from the multiplicity of successive forms—
thus, rapidity is pervaded by its opposite, non-separation.

This is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). Consequently, in that very state, vision does not lack the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), because it consists of will (*icchā*). If there were will in the absence of reflective awareness, then even while walking on a path, it would concern objects such as grass; thus, it would not be determinate. Therefore...
Since [the occurrence of] deliberation (*vimarśa*) is otherwise impossible, it is pervaded by desire;

this is the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). Now, one might object: direct perceptual knowledge (*sākṣātkārijñāna*) arises from the power of the object, and the word is not the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the object, nor...

Knowledge arising through the power of one thing cannot be the illuminator of another; nor is it logical for the appearance of one thing to occur within knowledge produced by the power of another. As it has been said:
"Arising through the efficacy of an object, that [knowledge] must conform to the very form of that [object]."
and so forth. Furthermore, consciousness arises from the power of the sense faculties;

however, it is not logical for there to be an appearance of sound through visual cognition, nor is the capacity of sound to produce visual cognition ever observed. As it has been said: "Or even if it exists..."
"Because the self lacks the capacity for the arising of cognitions through other sense-faculties," and so forth. He refutes this [on page 235]:
"And not" (*na ca*)— the connection is "and it should not be said. For if we were to assert that,

when a jar is appearing through the power of its object and the power of the sense organ, sound appears [along with it] just as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth appear when a cloth is appearing, then...
We may indeed object that [the word] is real; however, we have not accepted either of these two positions.

For this word is a designator (*vācaka*), and it cannot be a designator of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which exists as an object perceivable by the restricted senses; let it be so. But if this [word] does not appear as something perceptible by the senses, then how...?
It shines forth. He says: "It has for its object self-cognition. By this, that which was stated by the Noble One is also refuted:
"And this property of cognition does not fail to touch the objects, because it applies them [to those objects]."

Thus, at the time of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), no application of words whatsoever is perceived in relation to the object. Furthermore, even this grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—such as "this is a cow"—is merely another conceptualization characterized by the joining of two distinct acts of awareness (*vimarśa*); it is not [the object itself].

In this context, some kind of mutual blending of the word and its object—both of which consist of external particularities (*svalakṣaṇa*)—appears. As for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the word upon the object that will be discussed later, it will be explained that this occurs only on the level of cognition (*bodha*), because the two are in reality non-different from cognition. Now, if that word were of the nature of a particularity (*svalakṣaṇa*)...

It does not exist [as a self]; what then is it? It is said to be the "universal" (sāmānya). If one asks, "From where indeed does this arise?", he says: "from mental attention" (manaskāra). But surely, the function of mental attention is merely to bring about the state of awareness, as it is said to be the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).

Regarding the phrase "the nature of consciousness" (*bodharūpatā*): this refers to the capacity of form and so forth to bring about for consciousness the state of having an object. Consequently, anticipating the doubt as to who could perform the function of bestowing upon that [consciousness] the power of verbal expression in excess of its own cognition, he says "and not... (*na ca*). And here, this...
The point is as follows: when blue is being perceived, the perception of blue—which consists of pleasure and so forth—is experienced.

In that case, the possession of an object is produced by the blue, and the state of being conscious is produced by mental attention (*manaskāra*); however, it must be considered by what the nature of pleasure is produced. It is certainly not by the object.

(Page 236) Because it is accepted that pleasure and the like have the form of objects, [pleasure] is not [cognized] by mental attention (*manaskāra*), since the latter has the capacity only for the mere act of awareness. And yet, that [pleasure] appears; therefore, in this case, there is a particular latent impression (*saṃskāra*) residing in the mental attention.
The nature of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) must be designated as the cause; as it has been stated by you yourselves:
"Because of the difference in pleasure and pain, [it arises] through the specific distinction of cultivation."

Thus, even though it appears as having the nature of a word, it is understood that the mental operation (*manaskāra*)—which is a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) characterized by attentiveness (*avahitatva*) and possesses a specific nature—is the activity [of cognition]. What, then, remains here to be established regarding its manifestation? Regarding the phrase "of the mere object" (*arthamātrasya*), this is the intention of the word "mere" (*mātra*): [The intention is that] the object alone, devoid of conceptual construction, is what is directly perceived. This is because the object, being of the nature of a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), is not capable of being expressed by words; therefore, it is not associated with verbal expression. Consequently, the object is apprehended solely through its own form, without being mixed with anything else. Thus, the meaning of the word "mere" is that the object is grasped independently of all other factors. Furthermore, the word "mere" serves to exclude the conceptualization of the object's universal aspect (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). For the universal aspect is not the object of direct perception, since it is not a real entity (*vastu*). Therefore, the term "mere" indicates that the object is perceived in its own specific form, free from the conceptualization of universals. Finally, the word "mere" excludes the association of the object with the forms of other objects. Since the object is distinct from other things, it is not apprehended as being identical to them. Thus, the word "mere" signifies that the object is perceived in its own unique form, unmixed with the forms of other entities. Therefore, the meaning of the word "mere" is that the object is perceived solely in its own form, without being mixed with anything else. This is the intended meaning of the word "mere. Even though, in our view, pleasure and the like possess the nature of the object (*artharūpatva*), nevertheless, a specific mental impression (*bhāvanā*) functions as a necessary auxiliary in their manifestation; it is not the pure object alone. This same principle applies to the present case as well. For instance, because the object consists of light (*prakāśamayatva*) and light itself—

Because its life consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), even though the object is essentially reflective awareness, that object— when awakened by a particular reflective awareness composed of words formed by the combination of non-specific sounds—
is accompanied by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) consisting of a mental effort (*manaskāra*) rendered proficient through the grasping of linguistic conventions (*saṃketa*).
It is the pure [consciousness] that acts, not the impure. However, when the reflective awareness of Māyā is undetermined—
resembling the pointing out of a finger-tip or a head, and not yet attaining a specific fusion with the letters *i*, *da*, and so forth— it is the activity of the power of Māyā alone.
But if it is non-deceptive, then since the "I"-nature is perpetually arisen, there is no need for any consideration of a cause. Now, one might object:

because a unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not an object of conventional usage, it cannot be the referent of a linguistic convention; and a universal (*sāmānya*), being unreal, is not graspable by the senses. Therefore, how can [the universal] be [known] when the unique particular is perceived?

Anticipating the objection that this would result in the impossibility of specific linguistic designation, [the author] maintains that the particular (svalakṣaṇa) consists of a mass of appearances, while the universal (sāmānya)— which is merely appearance and is uncontracted by the appearances of space and time—
is the ultimate reality; and it is precisely this [universal] that is made an object by the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Having grasped in his heart that [the cognition] occurs for every manifestation due to the operation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) which will be described hereafter,
he defines it as "delightfulness. In that regard, while the blue is being perceived,
[the cognition] indeed rests upon the manifestation of delightfulness.

Just as [the nature of] pleasure consists in being of the form of pleasure, or in being of the form of that which produces pleasure, so too the nature of the word "blue" consists in its resting within the manifestation of blue, or in its being that which produces the word "blue."

"There will be"—thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. To support this state of resting solely in appearance, he says "even at other times. He applies this to the present context with the words "in the same way. This very point addresses the doubt: "If the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not recur, what kind of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) could there be in that regard? [The text continues: ...this very [point].
It has been stated that [pleasure consists of] "delightfulness" and so forth. Now, one might object:
surely there exists a specific pleasure produced by particular characteristics such as the fragrance of unprecedented camphor;
or, when a song or the like previously heard is heard again, there is a pleasure occurring at that very moment.

Whatever is pleasure must be constituted by its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) at that very moment; therefore, it is said "this. That very song is "delightful"—that which constitutes its delightfulness on the side of the object exists by virtue of its location within the specific characteristic.

Now, as for that superimposition (*adhyāsa*), which is the projection onto the universal (*sāmānya*) whose essence consists in being conceptualizable as having the form of an object—what [is its nature]?

The limit is characterized by rest therein; that which has been brought to the heart of the listener by means of that [limit] is that distinguished state of blissful nature. In that case, how could there be any utility for meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*)? For meditative cultivation is by nature the repeated turning of conceptual thought (*vikalpa*); how could it apply to a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that transcends conceptual thought? This too—
"He brings about a distinguished [result]" means that even in such a case, meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is certainly indispensable.
For a jackal does not take delight in the sound of singing, nor a deer in the fragrance of jasmine, as a bee does;
even there, it is due to the persistence of latencies (*vāsanā*) cultivated over many lifetimes.
Because one who is free from passion is not seen to be born [again].
(Nyāya Sūtra 3.1.25) Because of the connection with memories practiced in a previous life, there is the manifestation of joy, fear, and sorrow in one who has been born. (Nyāya Sūtra 3.1.19)

Thus, there is the manifestation only of those latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that are conducive to their specific maturation; and these are beginningless because the fundamental desire (*āśis*) is eternal. Furthermore, even when separated by birth, space, and time, there is an immediate succession [between impressions], because memory and the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) are of a single nature.

And by this principle, one must necessarily admit that [the awakening] culminates in mental attention (*manaskāra*), for that awakening which has been brought about by the power of a continuous causal process occurs through mental attention.

In a cognition that has transcended its own nature and has been imparted a similarity to the object by that object, there is the capacity to bestow the state of being happiness itself. Furthermore, regarding your position that pleasure and the like do not possess the form of the object:
[And in that case...]
"Through the excellence of cultivation...

Since this reason must necessarily be established, you too must diligently adopt this entire point. Even from our perspective, regarding the side of the object, as for the placement that "this is beautiful," [it is as follows].

The limit of that [object] which comes to rest within the intellect— which bears the reflection of cognition and in which pleasure is awakened by its connection with the pleasure residing in an object of the same class—
is that which is conventionally expressed as "I am happy" by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) attained through it, in whatever cognition [that occurs].

The state of being of the nature of bliss indeed requires that [mental] cultivation as a cooperative cause, according to the reasoning already set forth. He concludes this briefly with the words "by reasoning alone," and so on. The construction there is as follows:
because the internal expressive form consists of *abhijalpa* (discursive verbalization), and not by way of being an objective form.

The application of verbal expression is indeed appropriate even in a cognition characterized by the first moment of perception; however, there is no application of verbal expression [in that initial state]. Therefore, he says: "That which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)—produced by its own material cause (*svopādāna*), which is the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) known as mental attention (*manaskāra*)."

Because it is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), it is not subject to denial; that activity of the cognizer—the perceiver—which is well known as "verbalizing," "determining," or "indicating" and which is distinct from the act of seeing—has that [activity] as its basis. By virtue of that [activity], which necessarily occurs, she is [established] by force itself.
[The object] has been brought forward. Now, it has indeed been stated here by others:

"Because an object that cannot be designated—just as in the case of seeing an object—is not manifested in the cognition of one whose senses are not engaged by a word, [the word] is the sole knower [of that object]."

Thus [it is said]. He refutes this with the words "accompanied by the auxiliary condition of the object" (*arthasahakārisahita*). This refers to the application of verbal expression (*abhilāpayojanā*) arising from a cultivated mental attention (*manaskāra*) which depends upon the object as its auxiliary condition.

Regarding cognition (*bodha*), how could it be of a single uniform nature when it is independent of that [object]? For when the object is present as a cooperative cause, cognition—being conformed to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object—is accompanied by reflective awareness (*savimarśa*);
whereas in the absence of that [object], for one whose eyes are not engaged, it is without an external object, having itself as its object or having a non-existent thing as its object.
Or, if it has a universal as its object, why is it not accompanied by deliberation (*savitarka*)? What is improper in this regard?
"That [cognition]... refers to what was previously mentioned; there is no such cognition... (*Vākyapadīya* 1.124).

And by such statements, [this] has been established hundreds of times even in other philosophical systems (*darśana*). Now, if there is verbalization (*śabdana*) in every cognition of blue and so forth as "this is now," then nothing at all would be non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). Let it be so from the perspective of others; what is undermined for us? But how can you yourselves maintain non-conceptuality, since—
This must necessarily be established. For you have said that even for a bound soul (paśu), the divine state exists during that state of non-conceptualization (nirvikalpaka).
To this, he says: "But for us... The word "but" (tu) serves to distinguish our view from that of others.

"Right now, at this very moment, being impassioned, I know; I act with a contracted nature"— thus [the soul], enveloped by the sixfold sheaths consisting of necessity (niyati), time (kāla), attachment (rāga), impure knowledge (aśuddhavidyā), limited agency (kalā), and māyā.

The one called Puruṣa, whose nature is light and who is the subject of Māyā— of him, that which is the pervasive form of the activity "I know" (vedmi) throughout the entire group of specific functions of the cognitive organs, beginning with "I see" (paśyāmi), therein lies the instrument (karaṇa).
