The principle of impure knowledge (*aśuddhavidyātattva*) is of a general nature; and that is not something independent, but rather the very power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Lord. Therefore, those specific forms of His—such as the eyes and so forth—which possess particular functions such as "I perceive form" and "I perceive touch," [the Self] is manifested by them.

Even when the light [of consciousness], though slightly withdrawn by the contraction of the power of *māyā*, is once again restored within such an object of cognition (*vedya*) as blue and so forth that is suddenly perceived— because that light is by its very nature composed of reflective awareness (*parāmarśamayatva*), there arises the reflective discernment "I am."

When that [object] has become an object of experience, because it is characterized by the exclusion (*apohana*) of the state of being a separate subject and object through the mode of "this-ness" (*idantā*), there is no state of being expressible or of being conceptualized.

In that state, since the mental operation of conceptualization— which consists of subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) and which gives rise to the distinction between the knower and the known— has not yet arisen, this is not impossible according to our view. And in that case, there is an absence of being referable as "this-ness" (*idantā*).
Cognition whose objects consist solely of blue and so forth has the nature of merely manifesting difference, because the latent impression of *māyā* persists even there;

it is not, however, the fullness of *Īśvaratā* (Lordship) in every respect. And its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) will be explained in the definition of the means of valid cognition.

In such passages as "this is such-and-such" (2.3.1), at that time the state of the subject of māyā remains merely concealed; however, when the activity of conceptualization arises, that [state] exists as uncovered, and from the duality initiated by that [activity], [the world proceeds].

The designation "this," which differentiates the knower from the known and rests upon the object of knowledge, manifests as an expansion of form relative to what preceded it; being itself of the nature of conceptualization, it establishes non-conceptuality in what precedes it relative to itself. For the latent impression of words (*śabdabhāvanā*) is indeed concealed.

In dependence upon the expanded verbalization (*śabdabhāvanā*) consisting of various conceptual constructions, it is called "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*) because of the absence of such manifold conceptual constructions regarding things as they truly are. If this is so,
then in your view, the state of being indefinable as "this-ness" (*idantā-nirdeśyatā*) is nothing but conceptual construction, and that does not touch the actual reality (*vastu*).
Regarding an object grasped by the eyes and other senses, there would be no reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of "this-ness" (*idantā*).

However, let there be the reflective awareness of "I" (*aham*) in that regard; yet, no practical transaction (*vyavahāra*) occurs through that alone, because the actual transaction takes the form: "I am perceiving this blue object being seen. He rejects this [objection] with the words "And that," referring to the designation of "this-ness."

For it has already been established previously— such as in [verse] 1.3.5, "And because the determination [of an object] is an error," and so forth— that even conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not have a non-existent thing as its ultimate object;
and this will be stated further on.
"Having that pair as its object... and so forth, [as stated] in verse 2.2.3. || 19 ||

(Page 241) But has it not been stated in general that reflection (*vimarśa*) is the very life of manifestation? How is that so? Let it be subtle in some cases; however, in that which is gross, where there is clear conceptualization (*vikalpatā*), [it must be present].

This is the articulation of gross sound, such as "this is blue" or "that"; how can that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is appropriate for the state of *māyā*, be the life-force of the light of the *māyā*-subject?
For one who harbors such a doubt, we do not [assert] that gross sound is merely like an object (*artha*) in order to quell that delusion.

It shines forth separately; that which is the intrinsic nature of the object is considered to be the life of manifestation, or else it is remembered (the variant *ka* reads *vimarśa*) as *vimarśa*. This is what expresses the intended meaning. Likewise, *vimarśa* is *adhyavasāya* (determination), and he who thinks that this is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*) and not of consciousness (*cit*), which is of the nature of pure manifestation—[the variant *kha* reads *no citaḥ*].
For the Sāṃkhya, this [sūtra] is primarily intended to pacify that misconception; likewise,

for one who does not perceive anything other than the distinction between word and meaning, and whose ignorance consists in thinking, "What else could be the body of reflective awareness (vimarśa)?", this sūtra provides awakening.
The determination "this is a jar" is the power of the Supreme Lord, which appears like the Self itself as something transcending name and form, and not as a mere "this-ness."

The name is "jar," while the form is its broad-based, bulbous shape; likewise, the name is "this," while the form is "hard"—thus it should be applied by distinguishing between the particular and the universal.
For this very reason, there are two occurrences of the word *iti* in the commentary, which are fixed upon the determination of the object to be determined.

Both of these are objects of determination (*adhyavaseya*); however, the reflective deliberation (*vimarśa*) regarding them is itself the act of determination (*adhyavasāya*). That which is distinct from both and is never an object of "this-ness" (*idantā*), but rather manifests as "I" just like the Self—that is the determination.

Our position is that the life of the light of the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*) is [this consciousness], and not that the verbal expression itself is the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*). By this, the first objection is refuted. In ultimate reality, that power belongs to the Supreme Lord alone, whose very nature is light; for he alone is...

[Thus it is said in Kha. One determines, remembers, and knows by virtue of having the nature of the subject as the Lord of Beings (paśupramātṛ); however, this is not at all the individual essence of the insentient principle of intellect (buddhitattva). And this has been stated (on page 242):
... "possessing the power of knowledge, memory, and the removal [of ignorance]" (1.3.7).

By this, the second delusion is also dispelled. Furthermore, the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*), which transcends name and form, shines forth just like the Self (*ātman*) as "I. And therefore—

Even though there is an absence of the inability to point it out as "this," that [object] is nonetheless undeniable; thus, an answer has been given to the third [objection] as well. This should be connected with the words "determination" (*adhyavasāya*) and "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) in the phrase "this is a jar. The meaning of the Sūtra is likewise [to be understood] in the commentary (*vṛtti*). He introduces this [point] with the words "this-ness" (*idantā*).

The first objection is resolved as follows: that form of the jar which exists through the superimposition of a name such as "jar" and is distinct [from consciousness], being perceivable as "this," is the object of the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) insofar as it is its determined content (*adhyavaseyatva*); however, it is not the case that the jar itself is perceived as "this" by its own nature. But this is not... [the second objection].

The second [point] begins with "pure" (*śuddha*) and so forth. Now, one might object: "It will be stated in the section on the Āgamas that here, determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) is of the nature of *prakṛti*. He replies: "True; however, unlike in Sāṃkhya, its ultimate rest does not lie therein. Alternatively, this should be construed with the words "but not" (*natu*), as in: "but not [so]."

"It does not exist at all. By this, the intention of refuting the third doubt is shown. Now, he explains the name "name" through its divisions, starting with "at times": even in a single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that appears indistinctly, there is the name "universal" (*sāmānya-nāman*). In that very same [particular], [the name "other" (*anya-nāman*); *kha* manuscript].

"In the case of a clear manifestation, it is a qualifying name"—thus, the distinction in reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) has been explained based on the distinction in manifestation. Now, he explains that this [distinction] also arises from the distinction in the object of cognition (*prameya*), saying "or else":
in the case of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is the object of perception, there is a reflective awareness of its specific qualities.

For even when there is the perception of the mere form of the self, by means of the reflective awareness that "this is one or another particular," a specific particular is indeed accepted. However, as for the conceptual construction (*vikalpana*) that occurs in the absence of being an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it does not depend on a specific temporal moment such as "that time" or "this time" following the act of seeing. In that case—
Whenever there is non-conceptualization, there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) in a general sense.

For even a particular (*viśeṣa*), when being reflected upon therein, ultimately becomes identical with the universal (*sāmānya*). Now, does the particular "jar" manifest only through conceptualization? Or, even while it manifests, is it [grasped] as "this"?
(Page 243) If [the world] were of the nature of ultimate reality, there would be no contingency of diversity in conceptual constructions such as "pot" or "cloth. To this it is replied:
[in the case of the thought] "pot," there is a specific form (*viśeṣarūpatā*).

The phrase "this is [such-and-such]," which is complete in its sentence-meaning and free from desire for anything else, indicates a general form (*sāmānyarūpatā*) that is appropriate to the conceptualization of the word-meaning (*padārthavikalpa*). Now, one might object:
does not even the ascertainment (*niścaya*) that arises immediately after perception possess the nature of a determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*)?

Fearing that it might be suspected that the manner in which the manifestation of reflective awareness— such as memory, conceptualization, and so forth— is explained in the sūtra cited here, "māyāśaktyā... (1.5.18), has not been investigated in this context, he says:

Regarding the phrase "by the word *adhyavasāya* here": its application is to a specific [meaning], like the expression "ox and bull" (*govālīvarda*) in the preceding sūtra. By this explanation of *adhyavasāya* as having a general form here, he shows that the doubt regarding the subsequent sūtra is also resolved; thus it is said, "and so it is," by that very [means].
The connection is that it will be explained later in the manner of a rebuttal; otherwise,
if it were stated that there is an appearance as a self within a determinative ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*) in the form of certainty,
then because time-power (*kāla-śakti*) is absent in the self, an appearance as having succession would not be logical— this is addressed right there.

The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: that [order] ought to be established; however, in the case of the *Smṛti* and so forth, since that [order] is not established by the context (*prakaraṇa*), even the suspicion of a lack of order (*akramatva*) is inappropriate. Alternatively, this is precisely the meaning intended by the author of the Sūtras, and it does not mean that this is merely an interpretation following the introduction of the Commentator (*Ṭīkākāra*).

The commentator explains that the portion "this jar" (ghaṭo 'yam) is connected with the word for name (*nāmaśabda*), the word for designation (*parāmarśaśabda*), the word for form (*rūpaśabda*), as well as the word for determination (*adhyavasāśabda*); [the reading *avasāyaśabda* is not found in manuscript kha]. [The jar] is the object, the designator, and the cognition.
Thus, both "this" and "that" appear as identical. As the Supreme Teacher [Vyāsa] has said:
"Due to the mutual superimposition of word, object, and cognition, there is a confusion of them" (Yogasūtra 3.17).
So too says the most eminent of the Mīmāṃsakas:
"For the proponents of the denotable object and its cognition, the designation is simply 'cow' (*gaur*). (Ślokavārttika 4.182).
This very point is clarified by the word "therein" (*tatra*), because [the form] is manifest and thus cannot be denied. It is the denoter (*vācaka*).

The word, by relinquishing its nature as a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) perceivable by the auditory organ, reveals the word as either a *sphoṭa* or a universal (*sāmānya*) form apprehended by the intellect. By the term "the denotable," it indicates that this [word] possesses a specific characteristic suitable for direct perception and exists as something distinct from the word that is the denoter.

Setting aside that which is graspable by the intellect, he determines the nature of the *sphoṭa*—which is partless, characterized as a universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), or consisting merely of that [universal]—or else [he determines] the form [of the word].
And "reflective awareness" (*parāmarśa*) consists in the operation of conceptualization (*vikalpana*). But surely, it is only the signified and the signifier [that are determined]?

Two [things] are being reflected upon (*parāmṛśyete*), but there is no third reflection whatsoever. Oh, this illustrious one does not even perceive his own statement! That which is said to be "reflected upon" is precisely this very third reflection that has already been mentioned. He says this very thing in the words: "only within name and form. In the absence of reflection...
For indeed, if they were not grasped by reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), they would be like flowers in the sky. But surely, let there be this reflective awareness;

why has it not been stated that "that [awareness] shines," or rather, that "the triad shines"? For it is precisely what you yourself do not accept—that [the object] appears as "this" (*idantayā*). He says: "And it appears. This refers to the reflective awareness.
It has been stated, and will be stated further, that even when something is grasped within what is not manifest, it is as if it were ungrasped.

Now, it does indeed appear, yet not as "this" (idantā); since there is no third possibility, it follows that it appears as "I" (ahantā). And this "I" is nothing other than the Self (ātman). Therefore, what other act of determination (adhyavasāya) could there be?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "And this [is]...

In the immediately following sūtra, it will be stated that the coloring (*uparāga*) of the object of knowledge by another object of knowledge belongs solely to that which has a distinct object of cognition; it is by virtue of that [coloring] [that the distinction is established].

Since it manifests as something departing from [the Self], it appears as if distinct from the Self upon its departure, yet in reality it is not distinct; for this very reason, it is fit to be designated as "the power (śakti) which is an attribute (dharma) of the Self.
This state of being both distinct and non-distinct is indicated by the word "as if" (iva) in the Sūtra, signifying a lack of identity with that [Self].

This is shown by the term expressing the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of identity, and in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by the word *maya*. For the suffix *mayaṭ* denotes that which is the subject under discussion; since it expresses here that which is the subject in the form of the meaning of the suffix as distinct from the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), it [indicates] the base-meaning within the context of the suffix-meaning.
Bringing about a state of differentiation, it reveals both excess and non-excess. And therefore, that sense of "I" which is contracted by the body and so forth is distinct from [the other].

The subject (*pramātā*) is said to be the one who determines (*adhyavasātā*), not accepting any contraction [of consciousness]. However, immediately following that, there is another contraction by means of what is to be conceptualized externally; that which is endowed with this is the form "I" (*ahamiti*).
This is the intended meaning of "determination" (*adhyavasāya*). Furthermore, as for what was stated—that even a name appears as "this-ness" (*idantā*)—that...

He begins the explanation by raising an objection with the words, "Now, even of the name... The meaning of the word "even" (*api*) is this: let there be the appearance of the separation of form; however, that which is admitted even for the name—that it is unreal—is because [the name] "this jar is red" arises from the reflective awareness of "this-ness" (*idantā*). Furthermore, if even of the name...
If that were the case, then even that denoter would appear as "this" (idantayā) at the time of linguistic usage;

yet it does not so exist. For this grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—as in "This jar is bright"—appears as being permeated by the word "this. And [it does not appear so] for the denoter.

Since redness arises [in the cognition], in the manifestation of "this-ness" (idantā), the connection with another property co-referential with it is the pervader; and its opposite is the non-connection with it.
Thus, by the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi), that which is referred to as "this-ness" is not denotative. And what word [could there be]?
kha. |] Sound, moreover, does not appear as something separate because it lacks such [independent] existence.

For the "apprehension of 'this-ness'" (*idantāmarśa*) is the pervader of that which appears as separate; thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader—this is the meaning of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). He refutes this with the words "In this regard, it is said. The underlying intention is as follows: here...

Is this manifestation as "this is that" intended by you to be the pervader of the appearance of the subject's separation, occurring through its distinctness? And one should not be deluded in this way;
for if that were so, then in the case of "this white cloth is moving," [the movement] would belong to the cloth alone here.

The reflective awareness [of them] as separate entities does not occur, because— as you yourself have stated— there is no co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the quality of whiteness and the action of moving. Consequently, the quality "white" and the action "moving" would appear to the cognizer as non-distinct from the "I," at which time [the cognition would be] "I."

[The two] would have appeared [as separate]. And thus, there would be no connection between these two with the cloth, which falls within the category of "this-ness" (idantā), because they belong to different levels of reality (*bhinnakakṣyatvāt*). Now, it might be argued: "The very nature of whiteness and motion is that their life-force consists in their dependence upon the cloth and so forth."

(Page 246) That very "thisness" (*idantā*) residing in the cloth belongs to those two as well by their own nature; is it not like a movement that has gone onto a boat, which is subject to the boat's dependence? There is no separate reflection upon "thisness."
The manifestation of the separation from the cognizer is not its pervader; rather, it is merely the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of "this-ness" (*idantā*).

And that [reflective awareness] exists even in the denoter (*vācaka*). For instance, in the case of "this is a jar," by the power of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), the nature of the object—which has been unified with the word "jar" as its denoter and which partakes in its penetration—is [perceived].

The non-apprehension of "this-ness" (idantāparāmarśa) indeed occurs even for that which has the form of a denoter; otherwise, by the reasoning already stated, there would follow the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the word "jar" would manifest as "I," which contradicts actual experience. Therefore, the manifestation of "this-ness" certainly exists—this is the reason for the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Both [of these views] are incorrect; for if they were apprehended separately, then the nature of being a signifier (*vācaka*) and the nature of being a quality or an action would, on the contrary, not be apprehended. This is because the signifier is superimposed [upon the object], while qualities and actions are [only] extremely [loosely] connected [to it].

For it is precisely dependence on the object (*vastu-pāratantryam*) that constitutes its vitality. If this were merely the word "jar," then its specific nature would be apprehended solely as the form of the signified (*vācya-rūpa*), and not as the signifier (*vācaka*).
And even in that case, there is its universal form, which is denoted by the word "own-form" (*svarūpa-śabda*) and which functions as the signifier.
It is well known that even for that [quality], there occurs a reflective awareness of "this-ness" (idantā) through its non-separation from that [substance] due to their interpenetration;

just as in the case of "this white quality," the quality is reflected upon as being essentially the substance itself, and not as having the nature of a quality. Even in that case, however, it is perceived by virtue of its dependence upon that [substance].

The universal of a quality (*guṇasāmānya*) itself, whose life-breath is dependence, becomes apprehended as "this" through non-separation. Thus, in such cases as "this is whiteness" or "this is the universal of whiteness," even though the universal has attained substantiality (*dravyībhāva*), its state of being "this" occurs only as a qualifier of the quality, not as a primary entity.

However, by virtue of its predominance (*pradhānatā*), because it brings about the capacity to tolerate other attributes within the state of "this-ness" (*idambhāva*), it is precisely the state of being a substance (*dravyībhāva*). For instance, [it is so] by way of its predominance, its utility for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), its being the object of differentiation (*bhedya*), its being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of other attributes, or— as indicated by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*)— by such properties as possessing action (*kriyāvattva*), and so forth.
This is the state of being a substance.
And all of this, in the form of various appearances, shines forth as the primary object of reference in the thought "this," as in expressions such as "the king's man."

(Page 247) Because kings and the like are not the primary objects of reference (*parāmṛśya*), there is no reflection upon the aforementioned fallacies that would give rise to [their] substantiality (*dravyatva*). This also applies to the present case.

In the reflective awareness "this is a jar," because the word "jar" assumes a subordinate status (guṇabhāva) toward its referent, this awareness of "this" occurs precisely through non-difference from that [referent]; otherwise, that word would be reflected upon as independent and not superimposed upon the referent, according to the rule "from *agni* comes *-ḍhak*," rather than being a designator of the referent.
Even there, whether one observes multiple words or observes both the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*),
that which manifests as the denoter appears precisely as being inclined toward the denoted object whose essence is its own form. Now,
if the denoter thus possesses the state of being an object of reflective awareness (*parāmṛśyatā*), this very point is what has fallen into doubt by means of the word "this" (*idam*).

Because there is no direct re-cognition [of the object]. Furthermore, in the case of the expression "white cloth," when the quality of whiteness has already been manifested and re-cognized prior to the time it functions as a qualifier, neither a renewed manifestation nor a renewed re-cognition is possible under the view that multiple cognitions have a single objective basis (*ālambana*). Moreover, the word "cloth" does not have its conventional denotation established [at that moment].

It becomes fit for cognition alone, either by its very nature as possessing white qualities, or because it manifests that which has been superimposed upon it from the time of the convention onwards; for this very reason, there is no relation of qualifier and qualified here, but rather the conventional usage of "superimposition" (adhyāsa). And therefore—

Anticipating the objection that "the reflective awareness of a name as distinct from the reality of the subject is indeed doubtful, since there is no separate reflective awareness of 'this-ness' apart from it," he says: "But by its own name.
Here, it is shown that if there were no reflective awareness of what has been manifested, its very state of being manifested would be impossible.

Consequently, just as there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the external blue object as it appears, expressed as "blue," so too there must necessarily be a reflective awareness of the appearing signifier itself. And apart from its own essential nature, that [signifier] does not exist as some other, heterogeneous word.

Whether it be in a general form or a particular form, by means of which that particular form denoting "blue" might be reflected upon; for such reflection by another word similar to it, based on its having multiple words as its substratum,
would lead to an infinite regress, resulting in the undesirable consequence of the very absence of the reflective awareness of "blue."
Because it is impossible for blue to be a manifestation [in itself], the nature of an object consists precisely in the reflective awareness of its own form.
Since the word "blue" is reflective, its self-luminosity consists precisely in its capacity for the reflective awareness of both itself and others.

(Page 248) It has been explained that reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is indeed the true nature of luminosity. However, the luminosity of a lamp consists in its being an essence that cannot tolerate properties such as "shadow," which acts as an obstruction to vision.

It exists within itself as it does in objects such as a jar; and by that very luminous nature which serves for the illumination of an object—that is, for the form of the cognition of the object—it likewise serves for the illumination of its own self, which is the form of self-cognition.
To this extent lies the field of the fruit and the field of the seed of light.

It is said that "illumination" (*prakāśa*) consists of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) and manifestation (*dīpana*). Knowledge, however, manifesting by its own self, makes the object manifest through that very manifestation; thus, it clearly illuminates both itself and the other. Therefore, a lamp illuminates both itself and others, as does sound.

It consists of the words "self" and "other. Knowledge has the nature of manifesting both self and other, whereas reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), being of the nature of the awareness of both self and other, is not counted separately; for it is indeed of the very same nature as knowledge.
The denoter [the word] is reflected upon during the reflective awareness of its object, because it is itself being manifested.

Its very nature is such that in the absence of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), there would be no manifestation at all, because that would entail the consequence of insentience (*jaḍatva*), which is contrary to its own nature. Thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by the very nature of the denoter (*vācaka*); for, like the cognition of a lamp, it lacks both the object of that action and anything other than it.
This is what he states with the words "for not by that," and so forth. "Without denoting" means without referring to [the object]. Now, one might object:
"Objecthood is simply being within the range of the senses; let that apply to sound just as it does to smoke.
For what is so extraordinary about this for a signifier? To this, he replies: "It is precisely the state of being the expressed."
The meaning is that it is to be grasped. If one asks, "From what does this distinction arise? he says, "In the context" (*prakṛte*).
This means that this distinction arises from the context of the determination that [the word] denotes its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). For it was thus introduced:
"Just as the form of the self and the form of the object of knowledge appear in cognition,
so too the form of the object and its own form shine forth in speech" (Vākyapadīya 1.50).
Just as light possesses two powers—the state of being grasped and the state of grasping—so too do all words... (Vākya-padīya 1.55) (p.

And so it is said. This very point is clarified by the passage beginning with "the word *jñāna*," and so forth. Now, just as the light of a lamp does not require another light within the visual cognition (*akṣijñāna*), so too sound does not require another sound within the auditory cognition (*śrotrajñāna*); this is precisely its independence (*anapekṣā*).

Having raised the objection that [the word] denotes its own form (*svarūpa*) and not the jar in this way, it was stated: "or even light. For denoting its own form is not well-known in the case of light. Now, one might argue: let it be granted that by this much the own form is the expressed object (*vācya-abhidheya*); however, its being an object of reflective awareness (*parāmṛśyatā*) must still be established here.

With the words "and denotation" (*abhidhā ca*), he dispels the doubt that [denotation] exists as something distinct from the reality of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*). Denotation is the act of making known (*śabdana*) by way of being directed toward [the object], culminating in the sovereignty of acting according to one's will;
it consists of maintaining, implanting, and resting within the subject characterized as both the speaker and the perceiver.
"Apprehension" (*parāmarśana*) is one and the same meaning; for it will be stated later: "Indeed, by means of the non-discrimination of its own nature alone.
Thus, he concludes what was previously stated under its own name—that "it indeed exists"—with the words "therefore, it indeed exists.
It is precisely preceded by that [non-discrimination] that another expression, denoting the object, refers to (*parāmṛśati*) the essential nature (*svarūpa*).
[ka. Because its nature consists in the reflective awareness of an object, like the cognition of certainty and so forth; this is the *svabhāva* (essential nature) [of the argument].

For cognitions such as certainty and doubt are indeed of the very form of certainty with respect to themselves. If they were not of the nature of certainty, there could be no determinate linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding the specific character of consciousness; for even if that were the case, [such usage would not occur].

In that regard, because it has the nature of ascertainment and so forth, if [it is argued that] even when there is manifestation despite not being self-manifesting, the perception of the object is established merely from the manifestation of the object, then for one whose apprehension is not perceived...

If this were not stated, then, due to the dependence of one certainty upon another certainty for practical discourse (*vyavahāra*), there would be an infinite regress—just as there is when consciousness depends on another consciousness because it lacks self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*). [Objection:
But that certainty pertains to the object, not to itself; so how can you say that practical discourse occurs? [Response: This must be explained.
For these conceptual constructions are not unperceived;
thus,
the fluctuations of the mind are always known to their master, the Puruṣa, because of his lack of transformation.
Thus (p.
if one object-cognition were visible to another object-cognition, there would be an infinite regress of cognitions perceiving cognitions.

And how can such things as this be proclaimed by the Śākyas, Sāṃkhyas, and others? For "perception" (*pratisaṃvedana*) is said to be the act of manifesting through reaching the culmination of correct conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), by way of proceeding toward a state that faces the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*). This is because it does not differ from the light of the Person (*puruṣa*).
Since its nature is luminosity and its nature is ascertainment, just as it is with respect to the object itself, so too is it with respect to its own self;
thus, there is no need for another ascertainment. [Objection:
But in this way, the self is indeed impossible to designate by convention...
According to this principle, how could that which is called "non-conceptuality" even regarding concepts exist within one's own self?
In our established doctrine, however, the nature of manifestation is as follows... (1.5.11).
By this principle, all cognitions consist of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), even though they are free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*);

and it is precisely through such reflective awareness that worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) reaches its completion. For in that state, there is no suspicion of superimposing what is not that nature, as there is in the case of an external object, whereby conceptualization would be required for itself.

This is because there is no cognition of a cognizer of that [object] distinct from the cognition of it, who would perform such operations as the attribution of [error] or its removal. However, the Bhaṭṭa does not accept this dependence on *adhyavasāya* (determinative judgment) for the sake of validity itself. Thus he says:
"The established form is not to be determined as being established in that manner [by another].

For it is precisely through self-luminous awareness (*prakāśa-svasaṃvedana*) that the object is manifested, and since that awareness itself is manifested, what further need is there for anything else? This is so even for those who maintain that validity depends upon conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).

This is the only possible conclusion here: just as in the case of the conceptual construction (vikalpa) "there is water in the well," which occurs immediately after the appearance of an object not superimposed [upon it], or in the case of the conceptual construction "this is silver," even though there is no experience of touching upon two alternatives, there is likewise an absence of any proving or subverting means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
It is said that the nature of doubt is established as a result; likewise, in self-awareness,
if there were no suspicion of error, it would not be joined with the cause of delusion.
By this reasoning, since there is no basis for the occurrence of superimposition, it results in being essentially of the nature of certainty. As the teacher Dharmottara said:
For there is no doubt even regarding mere non-cognition, just as there is none regarding existence,

and so forth. In that regard, even in that view, if the identity with such a determinative cognition did not belong to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), then [the object] would exist merely as a manifestation undetermined by that [cognition].

Once empirical usage (*vyavahāra*) is established, for what purpose is even direct experience (*anubhava*) relegated to the state of being tormented by the wretchedness of looking toward the face of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*)? Or, if it is argued that manifestation (*prakāśa*) cannot be an object of empirical usage without conceptual determination, then the same must apply to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

It is thus; this very same path applies even to the illumination of the night. If the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) were distinct [from consciousness], there would be an infinite regress; if it were non-distinct, it necessarily falls into identity with reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
And precisely because of this identity with reflective awareness, [the same applies] to pleasure and so forth, as well as to passion and so forth.

If it were of the nature of doubt and so forth, its separate determination within the category of mental factors (caitta) would be purposeful, because superimposition and the like would be impossible; however, since those are possible in the case of an object, this separate determination of it serves indeed the purpose of removing superimposition. Thus...

[kha. Even though the manifestation of an object consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), as it has been said even by others: "In the case of hair and the like, consciousness is erroneous and directed outwardly.
Enough of this prolixity. Therefore, the essential nature [of the object] indeed exists through the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*).

It is established that reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) has as its essential nature the reflective awareness of an object, just like the perception of a certainty (*niścaya*) and so forth. Now, if the intrinsic form (*svarūpa*) of the word "jar" is grasped by the auditory faculty, it might indeed be subject to reflective awareness; for reflective awareness is the very nature of light (*prakāśa*). That...
In the absence of illumination, how could it [the word] exist? Furthermore, there is no activity of hearing here [in the word itself].

To resolve this, he says: "And that... Now, one might object: let it be granted that a single form is postulated through the force of a uniform cognition among the individual instances of the word "jar," which are differentiated by various speakers such as parrots, starlings, and others.

Setting aside the inquiry into the sequence of the parts of the individual [phonemes]— which share the same status as [the universal] "throwing upwards" (utkṣepaṇatva) and so on— he dispels the doubt that the universal "pot-word-ness" (ghaṭaśabdatvasāmānya) is not well-known in the world as being denotative.

"In that very [place]" means that the convention (*saṃketa*) is formed with respect to a universal (*sāmānya*) that persists through the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahārakālānuvartin*). And since no such particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) exists, the convention pertains only to the universal. But if this is so—

It is indeed logical that the denoter is referred to by its own name; however, as for what was stated—that the nature of the denoted and the denoter appear as distinct entities through the "this-ness" (*idantā*)—how can that be justified? For "this-ness" is precisely distinction. And yet, the essential nature of the denoting word...
Anticipating the objection that "that [object] appears as something divided from the ground of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which has the subject (*pramātṛ*) as its essence;

therefore, because it has non-separation as its essence, it is indeed appropriate for the sense of 'I'," he says: "And by that. This is because [the object] is in grammatical apposition with that which is being reflected upon in the form of the expressive word (*vācaka-śabda*).
The appearance of an object, being reflected upon through the projection of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) by means of its own manifestation, has its object thus determined;

therefore, that [appearance] too is indeed perceived as "this" (*idantayā*). Now, one might ask: why does it not appear directly as "this," just like the object itself, without any mediation? To this, he says: "of the signifier."
The meaning is: "precisely because it is expressive" (*vācakatvāt*). For expressiveness (*vācakatva*) consists in being a reflective awareness (*parāmarśakatā*);
and since that is the very innate form of the subject (*pramātṛ*), this unfortunate state never occurs to one who is expressive.
Now, if he is thus the subject himself, how can it be said: "there is [a distinction] by way of a difference from the name"?

Regarding the term "parāmarśa" (reflective awareness): therein it is said that it is the "specification of the denotable object. This refers to the imposition (*upādāna*), or coloring (*uparāga*), by means of a specific denotable object characterized by such features as a broad base and a bulbous belly. Nor is this [imposition] like that of lac upon crystal, because in reality there is no difference between them here; rather—

On the ground of differentiation constructed by *māyā*, [the distinction] is superimposed through the power of convention; by that reason of superimposition, just as there is a distinct object of cognition... (1.5.21)

Thus, according to the method of the forthcoming sūtra, the reality of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*), which is naturally disposed to manifest as "I," is designated by its aspect of pure consciousness (*saṃvedana*) as the instrument (*karaṇa*), on the grounds that it is colored by the object of knowledge (*vedya*)—that is, as "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). Likewise, it is designated by its aspect of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) on the grounds that it is colored by the denotable object (*vācya*). [End of fragment]

The term "denotation" (*abhidhāna*) is designated as an instrument (*karaṇa*), and not as an object (*karman*) in its pure state of dependence. For it is precisely because the instrument finds its rest in the agent that it serves as the locus of the ultimate vibration, which is the very nature of autonomy.

Its status as the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*) is independent of anything else; however, its dependence is spoken of because it touches upon the objective aspect (*karmāṃśa*), for the sword, as it were, attains identity with the hero’s hand.

That very practice, through its repetition, is the root cause of this instrumentality. For one who has just taken up a weapon is defeated rather than victorious. Thus it was said by me alone, who am characterized by the union of both agent and object: "By that [instrument] through which one performs an action..."
The agent performs the instrument; that [is the nature of the instrument]...

Thus [it is said]. Now, an objection: even for consciousness (*bodha*), there is a state of being an object of cognition (*vedyatā*) without mediation, such that "this is the experience. But does this same possibility exist for the signifier (*vācaka*)? He says: "Yes, it does," meaning for that which has been displaced from the status of being a signifier by the term "not directly" (*asākṣāt*). Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the signifier itself being the signified (*vācyatva*) when it is not direct.

The disciple is instructed as follows: regarding the phrase "He who is the cause of the world conquers" (*jayati bhuvanakāraṇam*), the connection is that for the purpose of instructing that "conquers" (*jayati*) is a word denoting an action, there is a relationship between the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*). The phrase "of the denoter as well" (*vācakasyāpi*) refers to the fact that in expressions such as "this is a jar," it is the very same person who speaks who [is the subject].
The meaning is that, according to the principle "the Self is [defined by] sovereignty," it does not abandon its ultimate resting place in denotative capacity; however, when...

When expressiveness (*vācakatva*) is not touched upon at all, then it shows that there is indeed real denotability (*vācyatva*); this is indicated by the phrase "but sometimes. When, in teaching and so forth, the speaker’s intention is directed solely toward the essential nature of the word itself, with the desire to convey it to the student acting as the cause;
When cognition comes to rest, it does not touch denotative capacity at all within the pure essential nature itself. Thus, there arises the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) "this is fire.
In this case, the essential nature alone is presented as the predicate (*vidheya*); however, in the expression "from this fire, the suffix *ḍhak* [is applied],"...

For here, since it is being restated (*anūdyamānatayā*), the suffix *ḍhak* is to be prescribed; thus, by the distinction between the primary and the subordinate, there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) as "this-ness" (*idantayā*). This has been stated by means of two examples. Now, one might object:
in the case of "Recite this fire-hymn" (*agnim etaṃ paṭha*), the recitation belongs only to the denoter (*vācaka*), and therefore [the result] must come from the denoter alone.

Anticipating the objection that "the suffix *ḍhak* [is applied] after *agni*" (Pāṇini 4.2.33), he says: "And at that time. In the sentence "Fire burns," the word which is the designator (*vācaka*) must be reproduced by this word "fire" (*agni*). That [word], in the context of a conventional statement regarding the object...

In each case, it is said that [the word] has indeed become a subordinate factor (guṇabhāvāpanna); thus, this word "fire" is referred to by way of its denotable object. However, in this state, that very same [word] is merely displaced from the level of being a subordinate factor; in ultimate reality, it is the signifier itself.
That object is indeed composed of that [consciousness]. However, when one wishes to communicate the external object by uttering the clear words "this jar," the aspect of manifestation (*prakāśāṃśa*)—
due to the power of *māyā-śakti*— is projected onto the side of the jar as if it were distinct, such that one says, "this jar manifests."

The state of "thisness" (idantā) has indeed descended [into consciousness], yet not as something separate or primary; likewise, the aspect of reflective awareness (vimarśa) is also thus. Therefore, the reality of both consciousness and reflective awareness is simply "I" (aham).
Furthermore, even "thisness" is dissolved within the very sense of "I"; thus, although it may appear to have fallen away from that [state of "I"], it remains so.

The intended meaning is that while they exist as subordinate factors (*guṇabhāva*), even when they exist as predominant in another [context], they merely touch upon the level of subordination and then leave that level behind.
In this regard, only the third stage is useful for practical application; therefore, he examines that very stage in detail.

[The author] says "external object" and so forth. Now, having raised the objection that "sound is not a property of the object in the same way that whiteness [is]," he provides a remote example, saying "lion.
For just as the nature of a lion is superimposed upon a young brahmin, in exactly the same way, the nature of the signifier is [superimposed] upon the signified.

The nature of the signifier (vācaka) is never superimposed upon the signified (vācya), nor is the nature of the signified ever devoid of superimposition from the signifier; for they do not function as a "foot" (*pādāna*)—as in the case of a "lion-cub" (*vaṭu-siṃha*).
Thus, this superimposition is described as distinct [from metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*)]. For that very reason, there is no metaphorical transfer here. [The word *iva* is used.]

kha. | The state of being the object of distinct conceptual cognitions belongs to that which is superimposed and to the locus of superimposition. The connection is: "only when [the lion] has been conceptually grasped as 'even in the lion'. Since there is no limit to the completion of the cognition, for that very reason the cognition is not completed; only so long as it is not completed by that cognition [does the process continue].
Rather, it is that very cognition which seeks another [cognition] for the sake of establishing its own status as an agent; therefore,
the substantiality (*dravyatva*) of an object— such as the quality of whiteness or a lion— is established.

"It would not be so"—this is the connection with what precedes. Or, the phrase "of the object" (arthasya) should be connected with what follows: "the reflective awareness that 'this is the object' also pertains to its designator.
He states the reason for this: "because, while denoting its own nature, [the word] refers [to the object], and thus there is the manifestation of non-difference."
He reflects that [the word] "denotes" because it effects the interpenetration (*otaprotīkaraṇa*) of the object with its own form. Now, one might object:

"It is only when smoke is itself being reflected upon that it is useful for the reflection upon fire, and in that case, there is no appearance of identity. True; for that very reason, however, it is said that smoke is not a denoter.
A word, however, is expressive precisely because it manifests non-differentiation. This is what is meant by the phrase "its own form" (*svarūpa*).

That reflective awareness (*parāmarśana*) which is characterized by the very non-distinction of the object from the nature of the reflective awareness of the expressive [word] is called the act of denotation (*abhidhāna-kriyā*); it is not [denotation] through distinction.

It is like the smoke produced by fire. Although this has been stated previously, it is introduced here again to quell another doubt. Someone might say: "The linguistic usage of words and their meanings depends upon the observation of the origin [of language], and that [observation] occurs only through the discernment of their intrinsic forms; thus, the word is the signifier..."

"But the meaning is what is to be expressed"—from where has this lack of discrimination (aviveka) come? To this he replies: "And thus indeed. The word *ca* indicates a doubt. "Thus indeed" means precisely through such a lack of discrimination. The locative case in *vṛddhavyavahāre* is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*). That is to say, the linguistic usage of elders proceeds precisely through a lack of discrimination.
Non-discrimination based on that [identity] is likewise caused by linguistic convention; it is twofold, occurring either through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or otherwise.

The former is grounded solely in non-difference, while the latter is merely a means for the cognition of non-distinction, as in the expression "the head of Rāhu. This he demonstrates as follows: "For this..."

...and so forth. In that case, the practice of the learned alone should be accepted as authoritative. He says: "The worldly object should be understood by the investigators just as it is by the world.
For such is the rule (*nyāya*). But [one might object]: when [an object] is distinct from two [others], separate, and indeed unconnected—
When a convention is established by two sentences that denote either a word or a meaning,
then there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

It is not a matter of grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), but rather a lack of coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). For in that case, one might suspect that those two things are entirely unrelated and indifferent; anticipating this, he says "even when" (*yadāpi*). This means: even when such a convention (*saṃketa*) is established, [it remains so]. He explains how the convention is established by saying "when":

And so forth. Here, by the sentence ending with "is said," only the word (*śabda*) is touched upon; even the name of the object (*artha*) is not mentioned. By the phrase ending with "should be understood," which does not touch the word, the object itself is touched upon as something standing apart (*taṭastha*). To the question, "What is meant by that? he says: "This," and so forth.

An object— whether determined by perception and conceptualization, belonging to the same class as the visible, or demonstrated through a unique recognition— must be treated as the basis for linguistic convention consisting of communication to others by means of the non-difference between the word "pot" and its mental reference; otherwise, it would not exist [in a functional sense].
Another cannot be made to understand through brevity;

and in the absence of reflection, how could understanding itself arise in another? This matter is stated even by means of two sentences. And in this matter, the very non-discrimination of the essential nature is the reality.

This is what is meant: even regarding the meaning of the two sentences, whatever has been unified into a single sentence-meaning by the words "when" (*yadā*) and "then" (*tadā*), that very thing is this "reflection upon" (*parāmarśana*); thus the intended sense remains that you must perform this very reflection upon the meaning. Now, [an objection]:

The objection—that even when there is a single sentence stating "when smoke is seen, then fire is to be inferred," there is no identity between smoke and fire, and the same applies here—is refuted by the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). For if such an intention were absent, for what purpose would the convention be established? Indeed, it serves no other purpose.

There is a purpose [for this], namely the establishment of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra-siddhi*), and it has been stated that this occurs precisely through non-difference (*abheda*). Now, one might object: "Setting aside the worldly cognition of non-difference, the convention (*saṃketa*) will serve some other purpose. This is not accepted; for it is not so. Now, it may be argued: "The cognition, being of the nature of experience (*anubhava-rūpa*), is already established; what need is there for a convention therein?"
Even if [the cognition] consists of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), if it consists of another word, then what is the use of a further convention?

To this he says: "But... Even though the innate operation of reflective awareness (*parāmarśavyāpāra*) is accomplished as consisting of words such as "pot," even when it begins with the word "pot" in its established form.
(In page 257) It is like a natural fluidity which, even when initiated by fragments of hard salt, consists essentially of the fluidity of the salty taste.
Now, one might object: let there be a relationship of signifier and signified between smoke and fire; what is the use of this [distinction]?

To one who might be deluded by the non-discrimination of the essential nature (*svarūpa*), [the author] causes understanding by demonstrating the variety of the means of apprehension as established by experience, from the words "for something indeed" up to "it appears. "By its own capacity alone" means by its very fitness (*yogyatā*). "The sense organ"—for that indeed...

Just as a seed and so forth are the cause for the cognition of a sprout and so forth even while they themselves are not perceived therein, so too [the word] enters into the cognition of "there" (*tatra*), whether that cognition is one other than it or that very same one— this is another point of debate. For instance, in the case of the cognition of the meaning of the sentence "fire from smoke":

In the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), smoke—because it possesses the characteristics such as the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*) known to function as a logical reason (*hetu*)—enters [the cognition] as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) by virtue of its inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the probandum (*sādhya*). This is like the staff in the cognition of a "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*), whether through the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or, according to the theory of the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*) as objects of a single cognition. For indeed...

The conceptual construction of the sentence-meaning occurs with respect to fire alone, even in the absence of smoke; however, with regard to the external fire which is the object of determination (*adhyavaseya*), there is no activity toward that alone [i.e., the mere concept]. It is with this intention that smoke, although not having entered into that cognition, [is said to be the means of proof].

It is said that [the object] has entered into another cognition, just as in the cognition "the man with a staff lies down," [the staff] is [perceived] precisely because it exists as a qualifier for a distinct objective support of knowledge. The word "again" (punaḥ) indicates the distinction from these two [other] positions and marks. By the inclusion of the term "object" (artha), auditory cognition is [excluded].

It is refuted [as being a separate means of knowledge], for it exists merely as a producer [of cognition] like the sense organs, nor does it truly become included [within inference], like smoke. Or rather, through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatayā*), the object of the word arises from smoke itself,
because the cognition occurs in a manner distinct from perception and inference.

The nature of that which is called "denotation" (abhidhā) is such that the very object being denoted becomes composed of sound, having assumed the form of the word; it is not that the word does not appear to the eye, nor does it appear in another cognition like smoke [which appears as distinct from the fire]. Nor is it the case that, within that very cognition, [the word is absent] due to the object.
It does not appear as something separate, like a jar from the ground; rather, it appears precisely conjoined with that object, interwoven as warp and woof.
(page 258)
One might object: "What is this relationship between word and meaning, which are perceived by different sense organs?

Anticipating this doubt, he shows—by means of the passage beginning with "for not" and ending with "the pervasion of the word"—that the word here is the signifier (*vācaka*) and its nature is to be grasped by the auditory organ, and that there is no other state [of it].
For it is not only within the range of the auditory organ...

The connection is that [the object] is not sound, but rather it is of the nature of a reflective judgment (*pratyavamarśa*). With the intermediate passage beginning "even though it is clearly heard," he states the reason for the negation of the restriction: "it would not be sound in that way," yet even then, there is the linguistic usage of "sound."

He mutters the mantra in a whisper... the sense is that this is because of the conventional usage [of speech] as being distinct and manifest with respect to sound. "Speech is measured in four parts... (Ṛgveda 1.164.45).

In order to demonstrate the fourfold pervasion (*vyāpti*) by this method, he says: "I am," and so forth. By this, the supreme state (*parāvasthā*) is expressed; that which begins with "first" and so on is the state of *paśyantī*, the intermediate state (*parāparāvasthā*) belonging to Sadāśiva. By just this much, for the time being, this [is established].
In the act of demonstration, [the author] is independent because the object to be demonstrated has just then been introduced;
however, by the words "from another," etc., the *Madhyamābhūmi* is shown to touch both *vidyā* and *māyā*.
By the phrase "by way of being composed of mind" (*manomayatvena*), there is the manifestation of the subject of *māyā* whose nature is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The function called *prāṇana* (vitalization) is, by its very nature, sequential and flickering; by means of this vitalizing function, through the arising of the breath, the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*) are mutually differentiated and rendered fragile in their essential form. That manifestation which occurs between these two on the level of *madhyamā*—that is [the object of this discussion].

It slightly constructs the proliferation (*prapañca*) of the separate apprehended and apprehender; for that proliferation, existing in the interval, is distinct from the Great Consciousness (*mahāsaṃvid*) and has not yet attained clarity externally. Therefore, it has only the Self as its object, and not—
It is common to all cognizers; it is extremely flickering and not stable. For volition does not abide in one place. Indeed, consciousness seized by the flickering wind does not appear as stable.
"Just as even the solar orb, though fixed, [appears] with internal waves," and for that very reason—

"In a Rākṣasa, the state of a Rākṣasa... and so forth has been described. That which is called "saṃsaraṇa" (transmigration), characterized by the state of constant coming and going, is like a tree because of its many branches and so on, through the sequence of the fourteen kinds of creation and so forth. Of that—
This conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is the root; for it is upon this very [proliferation], while it remains in the intermediate state,
that there occurs an irrigation by means of the moisture consisting of attachment, aversion, and so forth— which are characterized by dogmatic adherence—
and thereby the drying up of the state of distinctness (*pṛthagbhāva*) is brought about on the external ground.
"Things are united and do not become divided...
according to this principle. In the absence of the relationship expressed as "this is mine," how can there be attachment or aversion?

Furthermore, since even the sense of "this-ness" (idantā) has its roots in the growth of the sense of "I" (ahambhāva), and since differentiation does not take root [in that state], how could there be a basis for differentiation?

Regarding the statement "therein also there are no [defilements such as] passion," it has been shown that in the Middle Stage (*madhyamābhūmi*) itself, both the manifestation of the illusory subject and object (*grāhyagrāhaka*) and their connection (*saṃbandha*) occur;
therein alone do passion and the other defilements exist, and the root is to be nourished by the *sekha* initiation. Thus it is demonstrated.
It has been stated that because the root is unstable, the growth of saṃsāra is manifold.
By the phrase "situated in the interval," this is also expressed: he who touches the internal form of that very ground is one who is intent upon *vidyā* alone. As it has been said:
"This very power of Śiva consists of action... (Spanda Kārikā 48), beginning thus, [it continues]:
"...when known as abiding on the wrong path, she brings about success."
Thus it is said: "But he who runs outward after that very [power] nourishes only saṃsāra. As it has been stated: 'Abiding in the state of a bound soul (paśu), she is the binder...'"
Thus, he establishes that it is precisely on this middle ground (*madhyamābhūmi*) that the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the signified and the signifier occurs.
(Page 260)
And there, in that middle state (*madhyamā*) characterized by the construction of the manifold of the known (*vedya*) and the knower (*vedaka*);

"only on the plane of the subject" means identity with the limited subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*) characterized by intellect and vital breath (*buddhi-prāṇa*). "As this-ness" (*idantayā*) means, in short, as a full differentiation even from that subject belonging to *māyā*. But not—

[Is it not so? For by such an appearance, what purpose would there be for superimposition (*adhyāsa*), as in the case of a jar on the ground? By that denotative word "tena" (by that), the level of the subject (*pramātṛ*) consisting of *māyā* is not abandoned during the intermediate state (*madhyamā-daśā*). For at that time, the object itself appears separately by virtue of its being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*).

The word, however, merely colors the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) and does not, in the slightest degree, become separate from it; such is the nature of the one who forms this conceptualization. For at that time, "I" is the manifestation of the subject of Māyā. Thus it has been said regarding the ineffability of the essential nature (*svarūpāvācyatva*).

Thus, this denotative word (*vācaka*), which serves as the cause for producing the variegation of non-egoity (*ahantā*), becomes a pointer to the object (*artha*) precisely when it is itself being pointed to. Since the pointing toward the object occurs together with the very nature of the denotative word, the "thisness" (*idantā*) pertaining to the object is also present in the denotative word, which is superimposed upon the object.

It seems to spread forth, yet its state of being "this" (idam-bhāva) is not direct. Precisely because of the superimposition of the object, when a word is employed for purposes such as pacification or malevolent magic, the object appears in that manner; otherwise, in the case of its recitation in the absence of a listener to be addressed, [there would be no effect], just as in the case of a finger-gesture [which lacks efficacy] in the absence of another agreed-upon gesture.

Just as there is no tranquility and so forth in the case of that which is uninterrupted, so it is here as well; thus, this [state] is even more purely phenomenal (*prātītika*) through superimposition (*adhyāsa*), and it is not merely a cause here—it is precisely that reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*).
By such statements, he describes the state of *vaikharī* as being an expansion of the very next state.
By the word *eva* ("only"), it is shown that this very initial state extends up to this limit. By the passage beginning with "the subject" (*pramātṛ*) and ending with "only" (*eva*),

[the author], while demonstrating the non-separation from the level of the Intermediate State (*madhyamā-bhūmi*)— which consists of the subject of Māyā— even here, illustrates how each preceding state is inseparable from each succeeding state.

Having attained the nature of that other activity of the knower which consists of placement (*sthāna*), articulation (*karaṇa*), and emission (*abhiharaṇa*), and having assumed the form of sound produced by that activity,
it manifests in a distinct form perceptible by the sense of hearing, while the objects of cognition remain distinct.
Touching upon the nature of the superimposition of its own essence and that which is to be known by it,
it becomes an extremely clear form; for *vaikharī* is indeed of the nature of activity and of the nature of an effect.

And [the word] "ca" is absent in manuscript Kha. Furthermore, it [the power of speech] has the form of an effect (*kāryarūpā*). Even in that state, while presiding over the bodily plane (*dehabhūmikā*) of the subject of illusion (*māyāpramātṛ*), it manifests as being absolutely distinct, like an object of cognition such as blue; therefore, it is said that the pervasion of speech extends only up to that limit, and not beyond.

The limit [of manifestation] is blue and so forth; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is a single pervasion by sound even for blue and the rest. As the venerable Parameṣṭhin has said:
"This [reality], though excluded from being a jar and so forth, is perceived by the eye and other senses" (ŚDVṛ 2.8).

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: "Sound is apprehended solely by the sense of hearing; as for its presence in the *madhyamā* and other [channels], the claim that it possesses the nature of sound (*śabdatva*) is merely a product of one's own imagination. To dispel this delusion of the follower of Kaṇāda, [the author] demonstrates the usage found in the scriptures of the Supreme Lord with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). Since...

The pervasion of sound extends this far; beyond that, repetition (*japa*) is said to consist of the supreme form and so forth. O Goddess, for one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), it is the supreme; for one already liberated, it is that which marks the distinction [of the state].
The intermediate [form], called enjoyment and liberation, is the whispered repetition (*upāṃśu*), which bestows supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
The verbal [mantra] is the conqueror of spirits and poisons, while that accompanied by sound is for malevolent rites;
thus, for one who knows how to recite, these six types of mantras accomplish all aims.

Thus [it is said]. Otherwise, how could there be recitation (*japa*) in the form of the *parā* and other levels? For recitation is defined as having the very nature of the repetition of sound; the conventional usage of the term "recitation" does not apply to the repetition of meditation, reflection, and so forth. Indeed, the traditional grammarians remember: "The root *jap* [is used] in the sense of manifest speech. But [one might object]: "By another scripture..."

By the phrase "kevalam" [only], he dispels the doubt that the definition of sound (*śabda*) as that which is audible is shown by the verse from the *Śrīkālapādīya* cited in the sūtra: "Consciousness (*citi*) has the nature of reflective awareness... (1.5.13). This [definition] is dependent upon worldly convention.

Therefore, the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) and the aforementioned grasping (*grahaṇa*) occur therein. For, as introduced in the *Svacchanda Tantra* with the words, "In reality, that which is called Sādākhya is the supreme seed (*bīja*) residing within all beings," it is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of that very [seed] which is stated by this [text]. Precisely for this reason—
The employment of the suffix *mayaṭ* is appropriate there. Now, if *japa* is the repetition of words, then [it would apply] when that is uninterrupted.

How can there be the practice of *japa* (repetition) regarding the nature of the supreme speech (*paravāgrūpa*), which does not touch upon temporal distinctions? For the very nature of repetition (*āvartana*) is utterance occurring through successive interruptions; thus, in the state of the supreme (*parāvasthā*), because it is manifested all at once (*sakṛdvibhātatva*), *japa* therein consists precisely in this simultaneous, single manifestation. This is the sense.

And in that context, the conventional usage of "āvartana" (repetition) applies only to the mere act of rising [of the breath]. However, by the word *sakṛt* (once), which denotes a single occurrence or is a synonym for "always," any suspicion of interruption is excluded, as was stated previously: "arising spontaneously. As for that which...
"That meditation which is cultivated again and again in the supreme state (*pare bhāve*)—that is *japa* here;
it is the *nāda* itself, whose essence is mantra; such is the nature of what is to be recited" (Vi.bhai.
145). Thus, even in the state of the Supreme (*parā*), there is the conventional usage of "repetition" (*āvartana*); this applies when one has touched upon this [state].
In the state where the *paśyantī* has fallen into the mirror of the *madhyamā*, it is thus established that at the time of convention (*saṃketa*),

the act of convention is grounded solely in the word; having explained that the "denotation" (*abhidhāna*) is the reflective awareness of the object through the non-differentiation from its own form, this same path remains valid even at the time of linguistic usage.
The phrase "and at the time of linguistic usage" indicates that this convention (*saṃketa*) is dependent upon the observation of another's face; the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "also.

This method applies not only to proficiency rooted in convention, but also to that rooted in linguistic usage; thus, by means of this [statement], that very point is explained in detail through its division.

As for what was stated, namely, "and in this very way, the linguistic usage of the elders [proceeds]," the word "the listener too" means that not only the speaker is composed of such words; "in that very same way" means just like the speaker, there being neither less nor more therein. By saying "that very [act] is the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*)," [it refers to the act] from the command "bring the jar," and so forth.

He shows here the distinction from the verbalization that will be described later. And he shows that this linguistic usage does not depend upon convention by saying "by verbalization itself. [An objection: But surely one's own and another's verbalization must be unified by means of convention, and that [unification] cannot be so if it is not cognized.

To show that this is easy, he says: "That too. [The cognition of] sound is internal because it is self-cognized (*svasaṃvedana*), whereas it is external [to another] because it is known through inference (*anumāna*). And when that inference is to be performed, sound itself is coarse from the perspective of coarse vision.
(Page 263)

In the actual state of things, it is an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), and not merely a nature-reason (*svabhāvahetu*). For its ultimate limit is indeed the state of being a word. Its status as inferential has been accepted even by others; however, in the ultimate sense, because there is no obstacle to the cognition of the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, it exists precisely in the form of verbal authority (*śabdapramāṇa*).

The word, while reflecting even the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) residing in the speaker— which is non-verbal in nature— precisely as its own identity and as [objects] such as blue, does so by means of the non-difference between its own reflective awareness and that [external] one;
thus it makes the other appear as if consisting of the reflective awareness of its own nature, and as if consisting of the reflective awareness of those objects such as blue.

It also effects a state consisting of the reflective awareness of that agent and the reflective awareness of that [awareness]. Now, it might be argued: "In this way, worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is expressed by the word *mayaṭ*;
and what else is that [transaction], other than the arrangement of the nature of consciousness as described therein? [The author] shows that there is no other such thing at all.

"And of the very act of verbalizing" (śabdanasyaiva ca). This refers to my own reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) as "this," and his as "I"—this alone is the linguistic transaction (*vyavahāra*) characterized by mutual pervasion (*parasparavyāpti*).
The prefix *vi-* denotes the exchange of actions (*karmavyatihāra*), for it was stated previously that the root *hṛ* signifies "attainment. But surely—

"The speaker's perception of 'bring the jar' is not the same as that of the person being addressed. Who says this? For it is indeed the same; for instance, the command (*praiṣa*) is intended by him [the speaker].
Indeed, when there is the reflection "I am commanding this person," the command is intended by both the speaker and the listener.
"It vibrates: 'I have been sent. Here, the relationship of agent and object manifests solely by virtue of the status of the communicator and the communicated;
for he [the former] is the agent precisely because he communicates the command, while the other is the object precisely because he is the one to be communicated.

Because the word is employed precisely with such an intention (*abhisandhāna*), he who is a bystander is not the one to be addressed; therefore, he does not have the cognition of being urged toward himself. Rather, because he knows the convention (*samaya*), he too understands that the urging is directed toward that [object], thinking: "This person is being urged by this [other]."
Because [the object] is sent forth as an apprehension; this alone is the distinction between the qualified and the unqualified regarding apprehension.

Even in the case of "the jar stands," there is indeed a variety of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) in such a transition, namely: "he makes me apprehend this," and "I am making him apprehend this. For [the object] is that which is to be relied upon (*upajīvya*).
The agent appears as independent through the act of grasping (*parāmarśa*), whereas that which subsists upon him attains the status of an object precisely because of its dependence on him.
(Page 264)
The reversal is like that of an object and its reflection; regarding the transition [of meaning],

the diversity of agency and objecthood in the simple statement "the jar remains" has not been touched by any word in its form as a *pada*, but is rather to be understood from the sentence through the assistance of context and other factors.

But by what could that [cognition] have been removed from its proximity, for it is indeed perceived in that vicinity? If it is argued that it is "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddhatva*), then there would be no sentence-meaning whatsoever that is accessible through the sentence.
Therefore, whatever is invariably perceived without interruption in the proximity of the sentence, to that extent—

The status of being the meaning of the sentence is indeed faultless (anavadya). With this very intention, some hold that every sentence rests upon what is to be done (*kartavyatā*), by virtue of the necessity of performance (*pratipatti-kartavyatā*). Or rather, what is the use of this? Let it be so.

It is not grasped by the word, but is understood through inference alone; however, the distinction is that the injunction (*praiṣa*) is in no way touched by the word in its form as a linguistic item (*pada*). Yet, he expresses it again by means of a word. And by means of this repeated word, the initial reference is indeed of the same class as the speaker, whereas the final one—

Even while one is reflecting upon the state of being an object of communication within oneself, there arises another reflection that is contrary to that of the speaker. For such is the very nature of an injunction (*praiṣa*):

that the speaker possesses the status of an instigator (*preṣakatā*), whereas the person to be communicated with possesses the status of one who is instigated (*preṣyatā*). This remains true even when the linguistic transaction is carried out through the mediation of another.
The primary [word] alone is independent; any other, however, merely imitates it and is not, in reality, a speaker at all.

That [other word] is merely a speaker of its own form, just like a written record; yet, when an injunction (*praiṣa*) is understood from a form that has been apprehended, there arises the cognition of the relationship between the communicator and the one to be communicated. Now, if the injunction is what is being understood—

Thus, the *lākāra* (the verbal suffix) consists merely in the expression of a number residing in either the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*). How then can it be said that the *praiṣa* (the command) is also denoted by the term *lākāra*? It is replied: here [in this context]...

Since, based on what is established through a beginningless succession of linguistic usage, as long as a verbal expression arises from a word, so long does that [word] denote it—this is the ultimate truth. Furthermore, since there is such a reflective awareness even in the case of an injunction (*praiṣa*), why should that too not be denotable? Is it fitness (*yogyatā*) or convention (*samaya*)? What [is it]?
Because it is constrained by the diversity of the primary and subordinate status [of meanings], even with respect to a single object, [the function] is obstructed,
whereby some burden would fall upon the word. And therefore—
Just as for one whose eyes are open, visual consciousness appears simultaneously with all objects—whatever suitable object is located in a suitable place—and yet it incurs no burden whatsoever;
so too it is with sound. Thus, even a command is, in the ultimate sense, designated by that [sound] alone.

It is just like number (*saṃkhyā*) and the rest. However, the grammatical procedures (*prakriyā*) are of indefinite form.
