For in some cases, it is accepted that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denotes the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth—whether as the means (*sādhana*), direction, person (*puruṣa*), or consciousness (*citi*)—and thus the agent and other factors are held to be expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*). Let these matters, which reside in the words used for exposition, be discussed according to one's preference.

As for the grammatical processes (*prakriyā*), what indeed is the distinction regarding the word when the object to be expressed is grounded in conventional usage? Enough with this further digression. Regarding "transference" (*saṃkramaṇa*): the point is that this reversal is observed between the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*). [The term is used] "in accordance with" (*anurūpeṇa*).
The meaning is that [the word] has arrived through the force of its injunctive application (*praiṣa*). Thus,
having examined the ultimate reality of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra-paramārtha*) in order to state the true nature of the acquisition of meaning (*vyutpatti*) which is rooted in such usage,
it is logical that even an acquisition of meaning based on convention (*saṃketa*) must likewise be rooted in linguistic usage itself.

He states [the conclusion] by way of a summary and return, saying: "Thus, it is so" (*tadevam*); the connection is that this is the cognition (*pratīti*). It should be understood that "it is useful for conventional practice" (*vyavahāropayoginī*) refers to its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*).
For instance, through the power of convention, such as the contraction of fingers and so forth, [cognition] takes on the status of being an object of giving and the like.

It is useful for linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*), but the nature of the word itself is not so; for when that [nature] is cognized, it enters into the state of being a "word" by way of being something to be established (*sādhyamāna*), since its established essence (*siddhasvabhāva*) has been relinquished in the aspect of reflective awareness (*parāmarśana*). This is true even in the case of the convention regarding a finger.

At the times of linguistic acquisition and practical usage, it is the very nature of verbalization that unfolds. For this very reason, verbalization is not merely a matter of convention. Even if it were so, its utility would not extend to other conventional things; for when a finger is pointed, another thing of the same kind is not necessarily [indicated].

It is useful, for conventional designation is not restricted to a single occasion because it enters into other conventions; thus, the exclusion of being merely conventional is pervaded by that [non-entry]. Since the purpose has been accomplished by one alone, there is no further utility for another.

And this is the perception of that which is contrary to it. For that very reason, it has been stated that the function of verbalization (*śabdana*) consists in cognition. Therefore, at the moment of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), the word, having attained the nature of verbalization, [cognizes] the object as well.
Making itself one with the jar as it appears externally, the Self renders itself as if consisting of the object,
and the object as if consisting of its own Self; nevertheless, on the plane of external manifestation,

the practice of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) occurs precisely because of the difference between the two, for otherwise, how could there be any practice [of distinction] if there were absolute identity?

That is its conventional usage. For this very reason, he shows that [the argument] subverts the theory of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) by means of such reasons as "being perceptible by different sense organs," in the words "but not... This [objection], namely "words do not exist in the object" and so forth, is thus without scope. But surely, there is also a single verbal designation for both the qualifier and the qualified?

Just as in the case of word and meaning, one might suspect that there too the usage of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) in the form described would occur; however, [the author] dispels this doubt with the words "in the case of *daṇḍī*. Thus, by means of this methodological sequence, he has established that those two do not reside in a single word.

He also states that even from the ultimate perspective (*pāramārthika*), form is "only one. At that time, there is an absence of the state of difference. If it is expressed by each individual word as being one, then what could be superimposed upon what? But surely, in reality, the staff and the person are indeed distinct.

The actual state of things (*vastuvṛtta*) is not relevant here; rather, it is manifestation (*avabhāsana*) that prevails. And that [manifestation] does not exist as a distinction within the unitary conceptual cognition of "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*), which stands in the place of the apprehension of the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*). Nor does [the actual state of things] subsist in accordance with the actual state of things.

The usage based on superimposition (*adhyāsavyavahāra*). This is shown by the phrase "in this very way" (*evameva ca*), meaning that they appear as distinct [as in the variant reading *śya ga.*]. "This" refers to the reality consisting of the sense of the sentence: that which is called the mutual superimposition of the two. Now, does such an appearance not reveal a distinction?

Grammatical difference (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) indicates a distinction between word and meaning, whereas reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), by contrast, implies grammatical identity (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Anticipating the question of which of these is more appropriate for linguistic usage, he says: "grammatical identity" in the expansion of *vaikharī* speech; and "non-difference" on the level of *madhyamā*.

However, when a distinction is brought about by the power of manifestation (*prakāśa*), one does not take account of a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). He states the reason for this with the word "by means of verbal expression" (*śabdena*). It has been said:
For it has been said: "The manifestation of the intrinsic nature... (1.5.10), and it will be stated further.
"Because of the distance or proximity of objects... (Pāṇini 2.3.34), and so forth.

Thus, this "denotability" is simply the superimposition of the nature of the denoter upon [the object]; and that superimposition brings about the status of being a "denoter"—this is the entity that functions in linguistic usage.
The characteristic of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) never exists in a manner other than this [interpenetration]; such is the absolute certainty.

Consequently, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: in conventional usage, where the signifier and the signified are mutually superimposed, there is the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), such as pleasure or pain, due to their mutual differentiation; this is the essential nature (*svabhāva*).

For indeed, there is a difference in functional efficacy (*arthakriyā*) between two white cloths due to their mutual coloring (*uparāga*). Similarly, the word "young woman" (*taruṇī*), even when merely heard, is pleasing because of its coloring by the object; likewise, a woman, even when being seen, is pleasing because of the coloring [by the thought] "this is that lovely one. But surely—

What kind of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) exists on the level of the *paśyantī*? He explains that there is none at all therein; this is the meaning of the phrase "for this very reason," because the linguistic usage of superimposition appears through differentiation.
As for the expression "let it be for now," this will be elaborated upon later.
"In order to obstruct its own repose...
(4.1.10), and so forth, in these introductory statements. He concludes the current topic with the words "But it remains as it is":
at the time of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), the word shines forth as distinct, that is, as separate from the cognizer; and of that...

The very nature [of the object] itself is the appropriate and fitting "this-ness" (idantā) that constitutes reflective awareness; nor is linguistic proficiency (vyutpatti) required for that, for such proficiency serves to quell the suspicion of deviation. And that [suspicion] cannot possibly arise with respect to the essential nature [of a thing], since it exists for the sake of establishing specific conventional usage.

Because it results from the exclusion of restrictions by means of making known the restriction of power (*śakti*), and because that [exclusion] is not possible for the essential nature (*svarūpa*) itself; for if that were internal (*antaraṅga*), linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) would be useless. But [one might ask]: where [is there usage] with the essential nature as the denotable?

(Page 268) Discourse on usage (*vyavahāra*). He says, "This fire. And that very thing is the reflective awareness of "this-ness" (*idantā*) by way of its own form (*svarūpa*). But [it may be objected]: in this way, [in the command] "bring the fire," there would be the bringing of the form itself.

Anticipating the objection, "Why does it not [function] like the object? he says, "Merely. For, by the force of the context and other factors, the desire for a specific purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)—namely, "we shall remove the cold"—is known; and that [desire] can be accomplished only by the object itself, not by the form of the word. As for that which is [accomplished] by that very [word]...

In that context, the object of proof (*sādhya*) itself is clearly perceived as the denotable meaning—as in "the suffix *ḍhak* [is applied] after *agni*" or "recite *agni*. And although in the case of "bring the fire" (*agnim āhara*), the bringing of that which has the form of the object of proof (*tatsvarūpādhyasya*) is indeed the bringing of that very form; and it is precisely in this way that its bringing occurs.
This is logical, according to the principle that the denoter should not be brought forward independently;

nevertheless, with the intention that people consider only the objective portion (*vastubhāga*) to be primary because it is from that alone that purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is obtained, it was stated [in the verse] "because it is not perceived" (*anupalakṣaṇāt*). Likewise, [the suffix] *ḍhak* is applied after the word *agni*.

In this case as well, although the manifestation of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is indeed that which is superimposed upon the denotable object, and thus the cognition arises from the expressive word "fire" itself by virtue of its meaning, nevertheless,
the sequence of priority and posteriority is maintained precisely through its subsistence in the verbal component.

It is precisely the denotation of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) that is being stated. For, in reality, word and object appear in the path of cognition as being absolutely inseparable; hence, this is a case of superimposition (*adhyāsa*). And the fact that [the word] denotes the essential nature is established by experience itself; it is only because people are deluded that they do not employ it in their linguistic practice. Therefore, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is presented here for that purpose.
The intention of the word *vyāmoha* is that it has been defined; [the term] *adhyavasā* ends in the suffix *aṅ* and is feminine.

But surely, the sensations depend upon such reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), and that awareness— whose true essence consists in resting in the "I"— does not occupy the plane of the object; therefore, it is distinct from space and time, which are appropriate for contact with the object.
Since nothing is obstructed, it follows that the entirety of consciousness is indeed without succession and is one;

yet, within consciousness, succession appears—[this succession, according to Kha and Ka, is with respect to its own parts and with respect to other cognitions]. With respect to its own parts, succession appears.
Furthermore, because no linguistic usage of "cognition" is observed in the absence of succession when there is dependence on another cognition, therefore...

[Then, from Kha: In this mass of consciousness (*saṃvedana*), there is perceived—contrary to that non-sequential unity which, by manifesting the sense of "I," pervades the manifestation of one's own nature—the state of being sequential and manifold. [The reading *upayujyate* is found in manuscript Ka.]

And since even the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin), by stating "possessing the power of knowledge, memory, and the removal [of ignorance]" (1.3.7), accepts this, for one who might think that the manifestation of the nature of the self is not possible for determinative cognition (adhyavasāya), [the author replies: him...
Just as in the case of a Sūtra, it is the very same meaning taught in one Sūtra that is manifested by another Sūtra merely in accordance with different perceived places and times;
[otherwise] cognition, memory, determination, and so forth would appear as possessing a temporal sequence. (21)
This serves as a qualification of the meaning of the sentence: it reveals that the ultimate repose in "I" remains entirely unbroken, yet immediately following that, a sense of succession appears.
For instance, this state of succession occurs both spatially and temporally.
That which appears as extensive or non-extensive, and as slow or rapid, in the cognitions of a mountain and a jujube fruit,

is due to the coloring by space and time residing in distinct objects of cognition; and that plurality which is touched upon by the designation of difference in essential nature belongs to the distinct objects of reflective awareness.

This is due to the conformity with the object of cognition (*saṃvedya*). Here, "conformity" refers to the predominance of the objective aspect (*vedyāṃśa*), as well as the distinctness of the object of cognition; and since place and time are closely connected to that [object], they are included therein—hence the use of the copulative compound (*dvandva*).

This meaning has been touched upon by the author of the *Vṛtti* through the word "etc. (*ādi*). By this, it is precisely the nature of being both distinct and non-distinct [from the self] that is indicated.
The reality (*tattva*) consists of knowledge and the rest. For an object has as its essence its manifestation.

Thus, that which appears is itself *śakti* (power) by virtue of being the nature of intense activity (*saṃrambha*); it is *dharma* (attribute) by virtue of being a distinction in the form of an established state; it is *guṇa* (quality) by virtue of being dependent upon that [subject]; and it is *vyāpāra* (function).
Thus, it is designated by way of its nature as extended across the preceding and succeeding [moments].

As for that differentiation which produces subordinate genera such as cognition, memory, and volition, that was stated previously [in 1.5.18] as being due to the power of *māyā*. By this [present verse], however, [it is shown that] even though cognition and the rest belong to a single genus, [the distinction of the knower...]

The distinction—namely, the cognition of blue, the cognition of yellow, the recollection of blue, the recollection of yellow, and so forth—which is [produced by] a single birth... [kha]. And that which... (page 270)

The distinctions pertaining to cognition—such as spatial and temporal sequence, obscuration, extension and non-extension, slowness and speed—are now being examined. Alternatively, the entire diversity of essential natures belongs to the All-pervasive Lord through the power of Māyā... (1.5.18).

It is stated by this very sūtra that "here, the space and time of the object of cognition" is a compound. In this interpretation, the word "etcetera" (ādi) in the commentary refers to qualities residing in the object, such as its attractiveness, because the cognition itself is characterized precisely by forms such as pleasure and pain; and that very [quality] is what is expressed by the word "form" (rūpa).

It is stated in the *Ṭīkā*: "In this context, it is explained that the term 'place and time' (*deśakāla*) serves as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the 'side' (*pakṣa*). Therefore, the internal distinction of cognition—consisting of perception, conceptualization, memory, and so forth—arises according to whether the object of consciousness is manifest, unmanifest, or otherwise. Within each of these [states], too..."

The cognition of blue and the cognition of yellow are more internal (*antaraṅgatara*); even within the cognition of blue, pleasure, pain, and the act of perception are most internal (*antaraṅgatama*). "This cognition is slow" and "this is fast" are external (*bahiraṅga*); "this is prior" and "this is subsequent" are more external (*bahiraṅgatara*); [and] the subtle...

The meaning of the sūtra is that the distinction of consciousness (*saṃvedana*) is produced by the coloring (*uparāga*) of the primary object of cognition (*saṃvedya*), such that "knowledge of a gnat" and "gross knowledge of an elephant" are the most external [levels].
He introduces this with the words "tadevam" (thus, therefore). The meaning of the word "kevalam" (pure/alone) is expressed by the phrase "sa punaḥ" (but that, moreover).

With the words ending in "parāmarśa," he demonstrates— by way of establishing the introductory foundation— that the real ground of non-duality indeed exists here, as indicated by that which reveals the possibility of further distinctions.
By means of the sentence ending with the word "api" (even), he addresses the doubt that although non-duality exists, it does not manifest.

He refutes [this objection]. He explains that the word "object of cognition" (*saṃvedya*)—which rests upon the state of being referred to—is intended to express that the essence of cognition consists in reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Now, one might object:
"Since even the object of cognition is non-different from the Lord himself, how can there be any difference in the object of cognition? Anticipating this doubt:
He says, "even of the Universal Self" (*viśvātmanaḥ*). The word *api* (even) indicates the aforementioned doubt.
"The collection of objects" (*padārthajātam*) means that which is perceivable is manifested by the power of *māyā*. "For this very reason" (*ata eva*) means because of *māyā*.

The manifestation of the jar and so forth as distinct [from consciousness] arises from that very cause; for that same reason, they are joined with the properties of being an object of cognition, as well as space and time.
However, if the reality consists of pure consciousness (*saṃvedanamayatva*), then even for the jar and so forth, this miserable state does not exist—this is precisely why [it is said].

This has been stated by the word "iti. It will be demonstrated that space and time are the forms of the differentiated object of cognition, and that sequence is dependent upon differentiation... (2.1.4).

Regarding this point: the phrase "even from that which is of the same class" means that even one jar [is perceived] from another jar. Now, one might raise the objection: "Since that jar is of the nature of an object of cognition (*vedya*), how could it impart the status of consciousness (*saṃvedana*)—which belongs to a different category? He removes this objection with the words "And this... [stating that] even in its state as an object of cognition, it cannot touch upon consciousness.

The phrase "to overstep" implies that its state is not more remote than [the state of] sensation; thus, it is entirely appropriate to apply the objection regarding the factor of sensation. By the word "yadi," the non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*) is indicated for the purpose of stating the relationship between cause and effect. As for what the object of that [non-occurrence] is, it will be explained as follows:

The word *tat* (that) indicates that the meaning of the sentence rests upon a causal relationship (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) based on the non-occurrence of that action; this is because [the two] are non-different (*abheda*). "It would not be" refers to the nature of consciousness at that time. On the contrary, it would "overpower the object"—this is its own inherent state.

That [consciousness] indeed transcends the sequence. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that manifestation itself is not possible for this [object] when the object of cognition (*bodhya*) has emerged? He replies: "By the power of *māyā*.

This means that this state of emergence appears through the force of ego-inflation (*abhimāna*), but not in reality. The term "support of the object of cognition" (*bodhyāvaṣṭambhaḥ*) is used in the objective sense (*karmaṇi*).

The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in "of awakening" (*bodhya*) denotes the agent; that is to say, it seizes the object of awakening and causes its own form to be absorbed into that [awakening]. Alternatively, in this commentary, the genitive in "of awakening" (*bodhasya*) is used in the sense of the agent, whereas [the genitive] in "of knowledge, memory, etc. (*jñānasmṛtyādīnām*) is used in the sense of the object.
Thus, [it refers to] whatever specific difference in essential nature exists for each of those [states] such as knowledge and memory.

In the commentary, however, [it is said] "by a distinction of essential nature characterized by knowledge, memory, and so forth. For if it were otherwise, there would be redundancy with the meaning of this sūtra: "Thus, by the power of Māyā... (1.5.18), provided that such [redundancy] is possible.
A coarse perspective should not be adopted regarding a subtle state; therefore,
the intent of this [sūtra] is to summarize the meaning of the preceding sūtra (page 272).
"It has not been explained by our venerable teacher," [refers to] the word "meaning" (*artha*) in the sentence of the commentary (*vṛtti*).

And thus, the construction here is as follows: even though cognition is of a single nature by virtue of being of the form of knowledge and so forth, a cognition colored by different places, times, and so on, becomes a memory from another cognition.
And [the phrase] "na ca smaraṇād anyad ābhāsate" (and nothing other than memory appears) is the intended meaning of the entire sūtra and its commentary;
summarizing this, he says "even that which is produced by *māyā*. This is what is meant:
that which is the support of consciousness by means of the nature of consciousness as its primary factor, [is not...]
This is impossible, precisely because that which is to be known has consciousness as its very nature.

Therefore, what is so wonderful about consciousness appearing— embraced by the aspect of the object of knowledge as something manifesting— that it should be differentiated by the distinctions of its own form, place, or time?
It manifests within itself the state of conforming to that form—this is the intention behind the word "part" (bhāga):

although Māyā is the power that creates the pair consisting of the grasped and the grasper, nevertheless, the operation of Māyā does not pertain to the conscious part (cidbhāga) of the grasper, but rather only to its non-conscious portion (acid-aṃśa). That...

It is established that the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) of the Lord, although appearing as if distinct due to the differentiation of the objects of cognition, is in reality not separate from Him. Thus, by this sequence of arguments, knowledge is of the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*). (1.2.7)

Thus, that delusion of others has been dispelled; for it has been established that the power of an object is indeed nothing other than its imagined differentiation. May there be auspiciousness! || 21 ||

Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Examination of the Power of Knowledge (*jñānaśaktivimarśa*), in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī* composed by the illustrious Great Māheśvara, the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. || 5 ||

Now begins the sixth reflection: I salute the ocean of consciousness, which is surging with waves of nectar, wherein all the waves manifest from the state of the Lord fashioned by the will of the mass of bliss that is "I."

Having reflected upon the powers of memory (*smṛti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), he elaborates upon the power of exclusion (*apohana*), which sustains both of them, by means of ten verses beginning with: "The reflective awareness of 'I'... (*ahaṃpratyavamarśa...*)

By [the passage] beginning with "ityādinā" and ending with "sarvasya jīvataḥ," one [author] has stated that the distinction (*viśeṣa*) lies in the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*).

In the first verse, the operation of exclusion (*apohana*) is refuted within the pure awareness of "I" (*aham-vimarśa*). Then, by means of the [subsequent] verse, it is stated that this very operation of exclusion belongs only to our own philosophical system; furthermore, by means of two verses, it is shown that the impure awareness of "I" is conceptual (*vikalpa*), and that even the act of synthesis (*anusandhāna*) is likewise nothing but conceptualization.
By one [verse], it is shown that the Lord’s nature as creator consists precisely of such a continuity;
by another, a single verse is given for the purpose of withdrawing the existence of the manifestation of objects within the primordial conscious Self (cidātman);
and by two [verses], it is stated that in experience, memory, and so forth, it is the manifestation of objects itself that is manifold.
And this designation is utilized for the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the Lord, whose nature is the subject under discussion;
such is the intended meaning of the word "by one" (*ekena*). It was stated previously:
"The essential nature of manifestation is reflective awareness... (1.5.11).
Thus: reflection (*vimarśa*) occurs through the conjunction with verbal expression (*abhilāpa*), and that necessarily brings about the state of conceptualization (*vikalpatva*).
How could that—which is appropriate for the worldly states of *māyā*—exist in the Lord?
To pacify this doubt, the aphorism [is stated]:

That reflective awareness which, though its nature is light and consists of speech, is not a conceptual construction (vikalpa); for that [conceptual construction] is defined as a certainty that implies a pair of opposites. (1)

The supreme Self of that light which is devoid of the contraction of the body and so forth— whose essence is its own nature— is one consisting of rest in the freedom of not looking at a face [or, as in manuscript *ga*, "not looking at a face"].

The reflective awareness "I am," whose nature is the foundational self (*pratiṣṭhātman*), is not a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Why, then, does this suspicion of its being a conceptual construction arise? He replies: even though it has the form of speech, it consists of a consciousness that manifests internally as something distinct from the form perceivable by the ear.

The meaning is: "Even though his body is composed of words whose true essence consists in the superimposition of Śiva upon the senses. Why is this not a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)? He says: "For that..."—namely, the joining together (*yojanā*) of even diverse things, such as molasses, curd, and black pepper, or the conceptualization of a single thing in its various aspects.

The conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and ascertainment (*niścaya*) consist of the imagination of various doubted forms, their severance, their differentiation, their removal from one place, and finally their preservation by causing them to enter the vessel of the cognizer’s intellect and thereby establishing their firmness. And in this regard:

In every case, there must necessarily be a duality of that form and non-that form; otherwise, what would be joined, what would be differentiated, and what would be suspected? This is the meaning of the aphorism. As for the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) within the Self, it belongs to the Light (*prakāśa*), and not like that of an object such as blue, which is "this" (*idam*). Nor...
Just as [the notion] of the body and so forth [is projected], the state of being a conceptualized subject [is projected] onto another subject as "I";

this is what is meant. One should apply [the analysis] thus: "I" with respect to the self (as the subject) and "I" with respect to the object (the object of experience). In this way, by means of the term "in the self" used in a non-co-referential sense (*vaiyadhikaraṇyena*) in the *Vṛtti*, the true nature of this "I" is demonstrated.

The ultimate sense of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the Sūtra has been explained. The phrase "because it has the nature of the supreme speech" (*paravāgrūpatvāt*) serves as the reason for the absence of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in its aspect as the "for-the-other" (*parārtha*);
whereas in its aspect as the "subsequent object-entity" (*uttarapadārtha*), it possesses verbalization (*sābhilāpatā*). For that indeed is conceptual construction.
He explains that by the word "negation" (niṣedha), there is a removal [of doubt; the reading "niranumānam" is found in manuscript G].
It should be construed thus: it is precisely because it is preceded by the negation of the counter-positive (pratiyogin) that it is denotable by the word "certainty" (niścaya).
Regarding the conceptual construction (vikalpa), the commentary provides an explanation of one mode [of its operation], while other modes...

Because it is permeated by that. Here, "in this" refers to pure luminosity. By this much of an exposition, the meaning of the Sūtra has been explained. He introduces this [next section] with the words "if. This is because he establishes that "of it"—that is, of reflective awareness—is the nature of speech.
(Page 275) By the words "thus [is] the speech of another," it is understood that [this] has been attained. And the intention is that this is not tenable.
By this much, even that which consists of speech (*vāgvapuh*) has been explained. As for the phrase "for the sake of determination," it refers to what [will be established] by the subsequent sūtras.

It will be defined; the meaning is that this introductory framework (pīṭhabandha) is being established for it. The word "first" (tāvat) implies that the investigation of the impure [nature] will be undertaken later. Regarding the term "of the Light" (prakāśasya), he states the thing from which it is distinguished: "of the body and so forth. Now, one might object: "Is the body and so forth not something distinct [from the Light]?"
Anticipating the objection, "How could that [non-duality] be excluded from light? he says, "And that.

The word "in the Self" (*ātmani*), which is intended to exclude the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that occurs when light is turned into an object of knowledge (*vedyībhūta*) in such things as the body, has also been explained by this very passage. And "that" (*tacca*) means "that too."

The connection is with the phrase "withdrawn into the Self. Now, one might object: how can there be the possibility of speech, which is by nature an instrument (*karaṇa*), within pure luminosity (*prakāśa*), such that it was stated that [the Self] has speech as its form?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "because it consists of sounding" (*śabdanātmatvāt*). For speaking is indeed sounding.

The meaning is that sound is not produced by the vocal organ (*vāgindriya*). Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of employing the word "other" (*para*) in this commentary? To this he replies with the word "merely" (*kevalam*). It refers to that action which brings [the object] within the range of hearing—the action that originates sound—such as "he speaks," "he prattles," or "he tells"; [sound] is [defined] by being produced by such an action.

The connection is as follows: since that power of speech has not attained the state of being an object—that is, since it has not accepted the level of gross sound—therefore this reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa) does not consist of the subtle nature of sound, which is characterized by being the instrument for its production. For reflective awareness itself...

The essence of sound is the organ of speech (*vāgindriya*) for the subject on the level of the supreme principle (*parabhūmi*) or the subtle plane; in its gross state, it is sound in the form of the object of cognition (*prameya*). This will be explained in detail in the section on the scriptures (*āgamādhikāra*). Now, one might object: "Conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is a cognition associated with verbal expression."
In that case, what suspicion could there be of its being conceptual (*vikalpa*) if its nature were that of "denotation" (*śabdana*)? He says: "And [it is] of words themselves.

Although one might raise the objection—"Indeed, here the suffix *ghañ* does not denote the action (*bhāva*), but rather the instrument (*karaṇa*), and denotation is of the nature of an action"—he pacifies this by means of the passage beginning with "even if," and so forth.

Nevertheless, as indicated by the words "tathāpi" and so forth: how could a word, which by virtue of its established nature is an object of cognition (*prameya*) and possesses a single nature consisting solely in being expressed like a [real] object, undergo the state of being an instrument (*karaṇa*)?

And therefore, by the principle that "that very form of the agent which consists of action is itself the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is perceived as being accompanied by activity, while being in fact the fruit (*phala*) itself," it is designated as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
It is by means of this movement (*parispanda*) that the cognizer attains the desired object.
It is established in this way: "He utters"— that vibration which constitutes the act of uttering is the instrument (karaṇa),
because by its power that [act] is established.

Thus, by this principle, it amounts to saying that the verbal expression (*abhilāpa*) is being pointed out. In the act of expressing, the very activity of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*), because it possesses the nature of being the agent-instrument (*pramātṛkaraṇatva*), just like the activity of valid cognition (*pramākriyā*).

Indeed, the state of being an instrument is pervaded by (or attained through) being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*), and that [status] exists through independence from anything else. Therefore, if...

If the instrument (*karaṇa*) were distinct from the activity of the cognizer (*pramātṛkriyā*), then a dependence on something else—which is contradictory to independence from that—would necessarily follow. Thus, by the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), [the reason], being excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), also excludes the pervaded (*vyāpya*). Therefore, of the pervader...

Through non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is excluded; likewise, even in the case of what is opposed to the cause (*kāraṇaviruddha*), the effect is excluded due to the absence of the cause—thus is the pervasion established. The word "tathā" refers to the term "expression" (*abhilāpa*). The phrase "by them as well" refers to the Buddhists (*bauddha*).
Now, it may be argued that by this much, the nature of reality (*tattva*) is simply the fitness for association with words, which is to say, being an object of verbalization.
This has been explained; however, it was not accepted by earlier [authorities]. As the teacher Dharmottara said:
"When it could have been stated as 'appearing as conjoined,' for what purpose is the term 'capable' (*yogya*) included?"
Having begun thus and having established that "even for one who has not mastered the linguistic convention, there arises a conceptual cognition," it concludes:
However, because it arises independently of the operation upon an object, its appearance is indeterminate; and consequently, it possesses an appearance capable of being associated with words.

Thus [it is said]. He shows that this very point is untenable for the opponent, but tenable for us alone, by saying "nanu" (is it not so?). For that very thing—namely, the state of having indeterminate appearances—is not logical for the opponent. The reason for this is "nahi" (for not). For the innate nature of cognition consists precisely in the determination of its object. Therefore, for this [cognition]...

How could there be a nature of non-determination? Or, if there were a nature of non-determination, it would simply be of the form of doubt. And this is stated merely as a possibility; for in reality, even doubt is necessarily a specific manifestation, such as "it must be a post" or "it must be a person."

In this case, the object appears as being embraced by the meaning of the word; however, since that [meaning] exists only behind (or perceived only through) the object, conceptualization regarding the object itself is not possible. For there is no such apprehension here as "the object is being conceptualized," but rather it is that [object] alone. As for the partial [aspect], however, there is error, and that too—

Since it is strictly one-pointed, it is not logical that what is called "awareness" should be of an indeterminate nature with respect to its object. Furthermore, for one who maintains that validity depends upon conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), both that determination and the indeterminate manifestation—[the reading *avyavasāya* is found in Ka and Ga]—would be... what?
[The opponent] says: "If it is argued that conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) appear as perceptions," this position is all the more shattered.
However, regarding his own position, he states the following justification: "But for the perceiver... This is what is meant:
for one [who holds the view] in whom perception is established by the power of the object due to the primacy of the object...

And the view is that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) conforms to that [perceived] form; when its object is determined, all of this is indeed of a determined form. For us, however, it is the cognizer (*pramātā*) who emerges as the primary reality, and not some wretched "object" (*artha*) that exists. Therefore, that cognizer, by his own autonomy (*svātantrya*), [projects] whatever manifestation...
To the extent that one reflects, to that extent there is conceptual construction (vikalpa); however, it does not exist in other appearances.
Thus, because it does not touch upon the nature of the entire mass of appearances, let it indeed be called an indeterminate manifestation;
even the conceptualization of the differentiation of the exclusion of what is not that [object] is likewise [indeterminate].

If [it is asked], "How could there be [the manifestation] when it is constrained by the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of forms that are entirely devoid of expectation?"— that too depends solely upon the cognizer; this is the nature of latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
Since the superimposition of what is not that [the object] and the exclusion of what is not that depend upon the cognizer alone,

when the cognizer does not attend to those appearances— such as place, time, and so forth— which are useful for the manifestation and clarity of the object, but instead attends to resting in the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the mere appearance of the jar;
In that case, it is logical that there is an indefinite manifestation. But surely, let the word flash forth as an object;
what, however, is this so-called "verbalization" (śabdanam)? To this he says: "And verbalization...
White color, the universal property of existence (sattā), and words fall upon the plane of the subject and are [perceived] by the subject.

When being reflected upon in the act of reflection, they become fused and are augmented by the form of reflection as a preceding and succeeding sequence; thus they partake of the nature of actions such as "it becomes white," "he exists," or "he speaks.
For even an entity that is essentially established (siddha) falls into a state of preceding and succeeding sequence through the power of reflection.

Immersed in the form of action, it shines like a son who is cherished as "one who desires a son" (*putrīyatā*). Even those [verbs] whose objects are expressed (*vācyakarmāṇaḥ*)—meaning those for which the object is either the verbal definition (*śabdalakṣaṇa*), such as that which is to be produced (*nirvartya*), or the objective definition (*arthalakṣaṇa*), such as that which is to be reached (*prāpya*)—are likewise described as having both word and meaning as their actions (*śabdārtha-śabdakriyāḥ*). For if...

If the word did not resort to the nature of action (*kriyārūpatā*), how could that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*) be the meaning expressed by the verbal root? For a jar is not the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to make), nor is a village the meaning of *gam* (to go). Now, as for what was stated in the *Vṛtti*—that the qualifier "inherent" (*svabhāvabhūtaḥ*) is a specific qualification of the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*)—what is it that this excludes?

Indeed, there is no reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that does not constitute the very nature of light. To this he says: "Precisely for this reason. That light which resides in the jar—expressed as "the jar shines"—is, by the power of *māyā*, made to reside in the jar, even though its true nature is light.
*Vimarśa* can also be described as "otherness" (*paratva*) or even as "non-self-nature" (*anātmabhāva*). Why? He says: "For this very reason.

For this very reason—that is, because of this analysis of the word we have performed, which distinguishes it from words that take the form of objects (*viṣaya-rūpa-śabda*). Since this is the operation of the subject (*pramātṛ*), it belongs to him alone.

When resting in the state of the subject (*pramātṛ*), the object of cognition (*prameya*) becomes non-self-natured. Although, according to the principle stated, there is no mutual deviation between light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*),
nevertheless, due to the power of *māyā*, because light appears as separate, the reflective awareness "this is a jar" does not [arise].
Being one's own self,
[consciousness] does not touch the state of being fixed upon an object within itself, because illumination is immediately characterized by the subject.

The qualification [in the verse] is intended to demonstrate that the reflective awareness "I" regarding the body cannot be suspected of being non-self (anātman). Now, one might raise the objection: "How can this Light of Consciousness come into contact with the nature of an object of knowledge? To dispel this doubt, he says: "But by the power of Māyā."

Having thus explained the meaning of the phrase "the body of speech" (*vāgvapuḥ*) by this much, he elucidates [the passage] beginning with "not that" (*nāsau*) and so forth with the words "because of its not having the nature of a word" (*śabdanarūpatvāt*). Although the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is universal in form, nevertheless,
that particular manifestation of reflective awareness which is devoid of any other form that serves as the basis for conceptualization (*vikalpa*)— that is [what is meant].

With the intention that [the object] is indeed distinct from the manifestation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), he says "the object" (*artha*) to indicate that the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) consists of the word which follows both [the object and the concept]. However,
a mere nothingness— a void form untouched even by a trace of luminosity— cannot serve as a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
Up to the point: "of that" means of that which does not possess that nature. "In its own self" means in that which is the opposite of not possessing that nature, the ultimate reality;

it cannot be suspected of being the universal self. Therefore, that [doubt] must be removed, otherwise it would not be certain. Now, one might object: by removing this, on the contrary, it becomes incomplete (or rather, unprecedented).

[ga. It is certain. He shows that this is indeed true and that it is functional within the sphere of *māyā* by saying "consisting of differentiation" (*bhedamaya*). The phrase "the very nature of the subject" (*pramātṛsvabhāva*) means that this activity, denoted by the word "cognition" (*pramiti*), belongs to the subject alone and is distinct from the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); by means of this, the subject is designated as autonomous (*svatantra*). This is the meaning.

Here, he explains the term *atra* as it occurs in the commentary; the qualification *viśuddhe* (in the pure) is for the purpose of excluding the subject (*pramātṛ*) under the influence of *māyā*. By the phrase *prakāśātmani* (in that whose nature is light), the impossibility of a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is indicated; for that which is not manifest cannot be a counter-correlative.

This has been shown. To say that "that which is manifest exists in a state of identity with manifestation, yet is the counter-correlative (pratiyogin) of manifestation" is nothing but a source of shame. || 1 ||
But surely, an opposite (pratiyogin) is possible in the case of a jar, yet not in the case of light; why is this so? [Because it is] not characterized by the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*).
(Page 280)
For indeed, just as with a non-pot, even when a pot is manifest, there would necessarily be a lack of manifestation [of its nature]; having raised this doubt, the Sūtra states:
"For there would be a manifestation of two distinct things, the pot and the non-pot;
however, there is no manifestation of another distinct entity apart from Light itself. (2)

For in the realm of illusion (*māyāpada*), a pot and a non-pot appear as distinct; consequently, the possibility of a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) exists here. Indeed, it is suspected that in a location suitable for a pot, there may be a cloth or other object—a non-pot—which, possessing the nature of occupying that same space, is produced by its own causes and generates a cognition [of itself].

But as for that "non-manifestation" which is suspected in the light of reality—which is devoid of the limited power (*kalā*) of contraction such as the body—it is logical that it should be manifested by that very light; for through manifestation, its state of non-manifestation is lost. The word "hi" (for) indicates the reason. Since this is so, it follows that this is not a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); such is the meaning of the aphorism. [The word] "hi" [is used].

The author of the *Vṛtti* explains the meaning with the word "tathāhi" (*thus indeed*) in order to connect this *vṛtti* with another *vṛtti*. For this very reason, the meaning of the word "hi" (*indeed*) is not explained again in the *vṛtti*.
In this way, the explanation of the word "hi" found in the future sūtra—"tathā ca"—should be recalled. By that—

One should not be deluded by the thought that this is not a connection with the Sūtra. [The author] says "na hi" (for not) in order to demonstrate through reasoning—the determination of the logical reason (*hetu*)—as indicated by the word "hi," the impossibility of such an opposing view (*pratipakṣa*), thereby introducing the meaning of the Sūtra. He asks: "Why, then, is the reasoning stated here? and answers:

Regarding the phrase "being suspected": for the impossibility of an opponent is not free from doubt, because an unmanifest opponent deserves to be spoken of. By what kind of reasoning? He says: "For thus," beginning with this sentence of the commentary (*vṛtti*), the remainder is that [the reasoning] has been indicated right at the outset.
The term *tathāhi* forms either a *karmadhāraya* compound with *upakramaṇīyayā yuktyā* (by means of the reasoning to be introduced),
or it indicates that the meaning of this sūtra serves as the reason (*hetu*) for the meaning of the preceding sūtra; thus,
the definitive conclusion (*viniścaya*) depends upon both [of these].

Thus he explains the meaning of this passage, beginning with "of conceptual construction" (*vikalpasya*). Here, the relationship of cause and effect proceeds in sequence: first, there is the apprehension, then the removal (*apohana*), which is a negation;
however, that is merely a negation and not a definitive certainty (*niścaya*), because [the mind] rests in affirmation by virtue of its nature as luminosity (*prakāśarūpatā*).
Regarding certainty—[the author] says:
"It is blue indeed. For [the word] "indeed" (*eva*) indicates a restriction that is obtained by excluding everything else.

[The restriction is as follows: There is a resting solely in the blue as a positive form (*vidhirūpa*), because there is an implication of its opposite—such as yellow—which, in relation to the blue under discussion, lacks that characteristic and is inseparable from the exclusion of the blue. Thus, it pertains to both objects.
For the object of the negative aspect is that which does not possess that form, whereas the object of the affirmative aspect possesses that form;

indeed, conceptualization (*vikalpana*) is a manifold construction consisting of both the being affirmed and the being negated. Now, one might object: "In this case, since the two forms—'that' and 'not-that'—do not constitute the object as they do in a conjunction (*samuccaya*), how can there be a dual object?"

He addresses the objection with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*). Precisely because there is a dual objective due to the distinctness of the referents of the two members of the compound, for that very reason there is a distinction from simple conjunction (*samuccaya*) regarding certainty, conceptualization, and recitations [*recited* (ka.)]. He says this in the passage beginning with "and even where... (*yatrāpi ca*).

"Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)" refers to that which is distinct from certainty, consisting either of verbal expression or of the nature of the self. Now, while a distinction may indeed exist among these [categories] through their combination according to the stated method, how can there be a convergence into one when they depend on both, given that there is no difference [between them]? He says: "Only..."
Thus, in a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) whose nature is certainty, such as the perception "this is a jar," the culmination is indeed in unity;

for in that case, only one thing is perceived through direct experience, while the other—attained merely through superimposition—is set aside. However, in doubt and conceptual construction, both are perceived.
Because of its oscillating nature. If that is so, how can it be said that there is a single culmination (*ekaparyavasāna*) when [the cognition] has already been perceived?

And what is the distinction between these two? It is said: "Elsewhere" refers to verbal cognition distinct from certainty; therein lies the culmination in oneness according to the subject's inclination. By that [inclination]—[in one case, the culmination is thus, as in manuscript *ga*].
For whatever—be it rice, barley, or anything else—is intended by the cognizer, upon that very object he brings his cognition to rest as the cause for its practical application (*anuṣṭhāna*).
Alternatively, [the form] *svanaha* may also be derived with the suffix *ghañ* according to Pāṇini 3.3.62, *svana-haso rvā*.
Now, one might ask: since the root *rec* is not restricted [to a specific meaning], how could it ever bring [the cognition] to rest in both cases? To this [it is replied]:...
He says: "In the case of a conjunction (*samuccaya*), since the subject's inclination is restricted by the power of the meaning established through contradiction, how could it be unrestricted?
(page 282)
The connection is: "And in the case of doubt, [it] culminates in unity.
The word "and" (ca) conjoins the previously mentioned distinction from certainty, which is indicated by the word "but" (tu).
Precisely for that reason, because there is a general certainty regarding both the object being analyzed and the doubt itself.

He concludes the distinction [of doubt] with the passage beginning "But not" and ending with "particularity. Alternatively, the word "but" (tu), functioning in the sense of an option (*vikalpa*), highlights the distinction of doubt.
This is intended to state that, within this context, there is only one kind of certainty (*niścaya*).
It should be understood that the mere distinction between those two has been summarized without differentiation.
Regarding the phrase "due to the power of cognition": for here, in both cases, cognition actually has both as its object.
As for the fact that the acceptance of both results in a single conclusion—namely, "these two alone"—this is equal in all three cases as well.

The particle *eva* is used to indicate that this distinction of modes belongs to the object itself; thus, because it follows the nature of the object, the application of the term "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*) is not tenable as a definitive [designation]. Having thus demonstrated the nature of conceptual construction by means of a summary—beginning with the words "tad evam" and so forth—while relying upon the preceding sūtra:

Having established that this meaning must necessarily be accepted by means of the locative case *saptamī*, and applying it to the present context, the author begins to explain the passage beginning with "just as in the case of light" (*prakāśasyeva*), which was stated in order to demonstrate the distinctness of the reflective awareness of the "I" (*ahaṃpratyavamarśa*) from the conscious self (*cidātman*).

And so forth. "Residing in reflective awareness" (*vimarśagata*) means that because of the repose in reflective awareness, the state of being a conceptual construction (*vikalpatā*) is possible only in the very place of reflective awareness, and not in the place of manifestation (*avabhāsa*); therefore, it is precisely there that [conceptuality] must be rejected—this is the intended meaning. "By way of identity" (*tādātmyena*) means by taking its place. "Manifestation" (*avabhāsa*)...

The word "being conceived" (*saṃbhāvyamāna*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Regarding the phrase "of the second," when this is stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*), one might ask what the meaning of the separate word is; therefore, he says "the light of consciousness" (*citprakāśa*). The fulfillment of the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is not effected by a second [entity] imagined through one's own conceptual construction (*svakalpanākalpita*). For [this is not the case] with blue...
The states of being cause, being effect, momentariness, and so forth, reside within the category of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); for that is not anything separate [from consciousness].
Furthermore, because objects such as pots are produced by the conceptual constructions of one's own mind, they are not the counter-correlate of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*).
Indeed, being a counter-correlate consists in occupying its place; and that [occupying its place] occurs only through separateness (*pṛthaktva*).
Reality is pervaded by [the capacity for] causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), because that which is non-real lacks the possibility of performing such functions or occupying a location.

And since "being imagined" is contradictory to that [reality], this is a case of the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*). Now, one might think: "The contradiction of blue is with its own displacement (*svapracyāvana*), which is a non-entity (*avastu*) and a mere void; thus, that [displacement] is its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), while yellow and so forth possess it through their necessary concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with it. This is not so.
For that which consists in remaining while mutually excluding one another is precisely what will be established as contradiction.

And there can be no mutual purpose, nor any purpose of exclusion, with that which is void (*tuccha*). Nor is any persistence of the void appropriate; therefore, the very fact of being yellow and so forth constitutes the actual voidness of blue.

However, it is said that there is a contradiction "by way of the void" (*tucchamukhena*) by making the nature of the void—which is the object of worldly transaction (*vyavahārya*)—the primary focus. But in the present case, the voidness being transacted is indeed permeated by manifestation and reflective awareness (*prakāśavimarśa*), because worldly transaction consists of description and narrative; thus, how [can there be a contradiction]?
It might be permissible to cast that [objection] into the category of being an adversary to the *cittattva* which consists of that [consciousness];

thus, the word "distinct" (*bhinnasya*) was rightly stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*). Nevertheless, even so, in the realm of *māyā*, it is not possible to effect the exclusion (*apohana*) of a second [entity], such as a jar, from the pure reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
The connection is that it is "possible" and "appropriate. The reason for this is the absence of contradiction.

Here too, the reason is given by way of a qualification: "by entering within consciousness. Since the term "object" (grāhya) implies the subject (grāhaka) as well, the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*) is also present here. Thus, the meaning is as follows: [then this... (variant reading *tato'yaṃ ka*).

If it enters within the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), or if it is made to enter within by the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), then its state of being an object (*grāhyabhāva*)—which is established even in relation to the illusory cognizer (*māyāpramātṛ*)—becomes logically justified; otherwise, how could that which is manifest possess the status of an object? Thus, [the object] exists together with the light of consciousness.

How could there be a contradiction for a jar or the like while it is manifest? How could it endure the removal of the superimposition of the doubt regarding its non-manifestation, which has fallen under the power of direct experience (*saṃvedana*)? "For this very reason" means because the exclusion (*apohana*) of the jar and so forth is not logical. "In reality" means...
As long as the reflective awareness "I" (aham-vimarśa) is grounded in non-conceptual luminosity, the entire universe is contained within it;
however, through the power of Māyā, when that awareness occurs in the mental sphere as a conceptual construction, the reflective awareness "I" is contracted to the level of the body and so forth.
It culminates precisely in the state of conceptualization; thus, imagining his repose to be in that very state,
he [fails to realize] that universal oneness which consists of both light and reflective awareness.

The intended meaning is that one considers [the object] to be unmanifested and unreflected upon. Now, this objection is raised by one who thinks that the mere state of being "second" (i.e., dual) is the sole cause for exclusion (*apohana*).
To this, the reply is "nevertheless. And it is not the case that "so," for the connection is not contradictory.

This is the meaning. For the very nature of an entity consists in its mutual exclusion from others. Now, one might ask: what is the use of considering opposition (*virodha*), since it is simply the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) that must be excluded? True; however, he says "and it is opposed" (*viruddhaśca*) to indicate that a counter-correlate becomes such precisely by being an opponent—that is, it is only that which is opposed (*viruddha*) which constitutes the counter-correlate. That...

The word "ca" (and) means that whose removal (*apohana*) is suspected by others. The term "designation" (*vyapadeśa*) explains the word "name" (*saṃjñā*), for it is by means of the insubstantial that the substantial is designated.
And this is to show that such indeed is the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpana*); thus [ends] the commentary on the aphorism.
The first half [of the verse], since its meaning is well-known and clear, was not explained by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*).
However, the commentator explains it as "this is a jar" (*ghaṭo 'yam iti*). And here, the phrase "iti" [is used] because this form of exclusion (*apohana*) is well-established;
it is necessarily required in the present context regarding the object of cognition (*prameya*) in order to dispel doubts concerning that very form.

The particle *ca* serves to include the objects of cognition (*prameya*). The certainty regarding the exclusion (*apohana*) of a jar that might be suspected in that [place] is what is being considered. "In its place" means that in the location suitable for it—wherever a cloth or the like might be suspected in place of a particular jar—that [jar] arises by the power of its own causes.
And that [other object] does not exist in that place, because that space has been pervaded and occupied on all sides by the jar;
thus, the cloth and so forth become the locus for such designations as the "counter-correlate" (*pratiyogin*) of that jar.

Now, as for what was said regarding the possibility of occupying that space and the refutation thereof— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical flow of the argument.]

In the case of the contradiction of non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna-virodha*), as in the case of cold and heat and so forth, the understanding of contradiction occurs through the principle that "when one exists, the other is absent," since its cause is not limited; however,
this principle does not apply clearly to the contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthiti-lakṣaṇa*).
[It is] consistent [or "is included," according to Ka]. How then has only this much been shown as the definition of the contradictory (*viruddha*), and how [does it apply] to the present case?

Regarding the application of the principle of mutual exclusion and non-coexistence: anticipating this objection, [the author] shows that this very contradiction consisting of mutual exclusion encompasses both non-coexistence and the relationship of the slayer and the slain, and that these two are not additional to it, by stating: "for it occupies its place," etc. Indeed (*hi*).

Since this is so, the meaning is that all of this is logically established. "Sometimes" refers to cases where the worldly convention of non-coexistence is well-known; "sometimes" refers to cases where the worldly convention of mutual exclusion is well-known. "Of an entity" (bhāvasya) refers to a jar, [the term] being used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).

The genitive case is used when a relationship is intended to be expressed. Thus, it is the "assault" (*ākrānti*)—that is, the occupation—of that which is the object (*karman*), namely the state of being a non-pot (*aghaṭarūpatā*) which is conceived as the locus of the contrary, by the agent (*kartṛ*) which is the entity consisting of the pot, having a constructed nature. Such is the reality of the matter.
The grammatical refinement (*śabda-saṃskāra*) occurs merely through a connection; this should be understood similarly in other cases as well.

For the nature of error (*viparyaya-rūpatā*) would otherwise be untenable. Indeed, it is not possible for an existing jar to possess the nature of a non-jar; therefore, because of that reason, [the object] which is imagined is being suspected.
The cessation of the superimposed nature of error occurs by its own natural flow—that is, by the power of its own nature brought about through a succession of its own causes;

nevertheless, cognizing subjects (pramātṛ) imagine that it has been produced by that very [cause], just as one might say a jar was made [by a potter]. For a cognizing subject who has entered the sphere of such inquiry imagines in this manner.
This is the greatness of the pot's own nature (svabhāva): that its locus is never invaded by what is not a pot. For if it were so invaded, it would no longer be a pot at all.
And yet, here the pot does exist, because of its own causes and its own means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

"Success is unshakeable" (*siddhir avikampanīyā*). Therefore, the connection is as follows: the "assumption" (*ākramaṇa*) of the locus of error, which has the agent of existence as its subject and consists of an imagined form. He clarifies this by means of an illustration with the words "just as. "Of that" (*tat*) means belonging to that jar, having it as its agent.

The "occupation" (*ākramaṇa*) refers to the occupation of the locus of the absence of the jar by that which has a conceptualized form; or alternatively, that locus of the absence of the jar is conceptualized—that is, it is made so by conceptual construction—and its occupation by the jar is the explanation.
In the former case as well, it is the occupation of that locus of error which has been conceptualized.

He concludes this with the words "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*): the contradiction that arises from the suspected identity of essence (*ekātmatā*)— namely, the obstruction of one particularity by its own particularity, which is the non-acceptance [of it] within itself— that alone is the one [contradiction].

The intention is that it is well known that "contradiction" everywhere consists in mutual exclusion. That [contradiction]—namely, contradiction—is preceded by the cognition of the cessation of the conceptualized (kalpita), as in the case of a cloth in the absence of a jar, or the cognition of the cessation of the non-conceptualized (akalpita), as in the case of cold in a place of heat; or rather, it is preceded by the cognition of the cessation of both the conceptualized and the non-conceptualized.
"Of whom there is renown"—such is he. "Merely" means by way of distinction.

"Is designated"—this is the remainder of the intended meaning (*ākūta*). Through the two words "cognition" (*pratīti*) and "renown" (*prathā*), the state of being imagined or unimagined is not applicable in reality anywhere; for indeed, the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), which are essentially [particulars], do not [intermingle] with one another.
"They either mix, oppose, or coalesce, yet they do not divide"—
according to this principle, the cognizer, resting upon the plane of inquiry, follows after manifestation (*prathā*).
It functions in this way: it has been shown that if contradiction were equal [in both cases], then the investigation into what is real and what is unreal would be entirely irrelevant.
Furthermore, he demonstrates that if there were no mutual exclusion or non-penetration, there would be no contradiction even between things such as cold and heat.

He confirms the very logic already stated with the words "and so it is" (*tathā ca*). For instance, coexistence (*sahāvasthāna*) in the sense of simultaneous existence certainly does not occur; thus, the non-coexistence of cold and heat and the like is not absolute. Furthermore, the location is nothing other than the essential nature (*svarūpa*) itself, and [the relationship] depends upon that.

This principle, which has already been stated regarding the relationship of victim and slayer (*badhyaghātakabhāva*), applies even to space, the ground, and so forth—as in the case of the snake and the mongoose; the word "also" (*api*) indicates that this is not limited merely to cold and heat and the like.
[The phrase] "by that [mongoose]" refers to the mongoose, while "of that place" refers to the location occupied by the nature of the mongoose.
The state of being identical with a particular location consists in its being occupied by the body of a serpent,
while the state of not being identical with it consists in its being occupied by the body of a mongoose, or conversely, in its not being occupied by the coils of a serpent.
The contradiction between these two characteristics— which results in the determination of that specific location— is one of essential nature (*svarūpa-virodha*).
The connection is that even for the snake and the mongoose, there is opposition based on their having that single ultimate reality as their object;
therefore, when there is opposition between two locations, the state of being in that location [applies] to one and not to the other.
(Page 287)
As for the one who attempts to resolve the contradiction by means of a difference in objects—claiming that [the cognition] has a different location—that does nothing for the Buddhist;

rather, he has merely exhausted himself in vain. For the opponent asserts the contradiction precisely through the two locations; thus, the resolution of that contradiction must be achieved by that very same means.

This reply, which destroys all contradictions, would also suppress the contradiction between blue and non-blue: that in what is blue there is non-blue, and in what is non-blue there is blue; and that it is the very same thing because of the difference in its objects—namely, that in one case it occupies that location and in another it occupies a different location, and that it is the very same thing because of the difference in its objects. For these two [cases]...

What distinction is there between the sentence and its meaning, since the contradiction regarding either the location or the essential nature cannot be resolved by that very same [distinction]? This much, however, must be stated: when the difference in essential nature is established through a difference in cognition, and when the relationship of container and contained is likewise established by cognition, then [the two] exist in the location of one and the same thing.

There are many causes; for instance, there may be many [causes] for one [effect], yet they are not multiple causes in such a way that a contradiction would arise based on whether something is caused by that or another. This will be addressed later, so enough with this digression. Now, even when one location is not occupied by the other, it is still said:

There is a natural enmity between the snake and the mongoose; therefore, it is said [in the verse]: "That which is expressed in worldly usage and that among whom there is eternal enmity" (2.4.9). Anticipating the objection as to how this mode of enmity applies everywhere, he says:
"But at other times. Having thus also explained the appearance of two distinct things, [he continues].
By means of the opposite of this very subject, he follows up with what is established without effort, saying "and thus" (*evaṃ ca*).
He applies an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*), stating that "the notion 'I am a jar' is not possible.
Therefore, the oneness of form of the Light (*prakāśa*) is indeed impossible.

He says "nor even" (nāpi) to show that the capacity to endure [the presence of] those [other objects] (*tanmātrasahatva*) is not to be excluded when there is the nature of luminosity (*prakāśarūpatva*).
"Therein" (*tatra*) means in the luminosity; "this" (*asau*) refers to the jar (*ghaṭa*). "Therefore" (*ataḥ*) means because it is not possible for it [to exist] therein;
the meaning is: because it is not fit to be rejected either by its own exclusive form (*svena kevalena vapuṣā*) or by its non-exclusive form (*akevalena*). "That" (*sa*) refers to the jar.
"Then" (*tataḥ*) means from manifestation (*prakāśāt*). What, then, is the manifestation that is incompatible with contradiction? He says: "What then?
And he says "equal" (*tulya*) because such [a manifestation] does not exist; this refers to the word "other" (*itara*) in the commentary (*vṛtti*). But surely... (page 288)

Just as in the case of the object of cognition (*prameya*), where non-blue is conceivable within the locus of blue and that [non-blue] exists as something other than it, so too in the case of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), there might be the delusion that another entity could be conceivable within the locus of the conscious nature (*cidrūpa*).
He dispels this delusion by means of the word "only" (*mātra*) in the phrase "only that much" (*tāvanmātra*).

For it is not unprecedented that an object of cognition (*prameya*), being an illusory creation (*māyā-nirmita*) consisting of a mass of appearances, can tolerate manifold variety; however, pure luminosity (*śuddha-prakāśa*), in its nature as the subject (*pramātṛ*), cannot tolerate even the slightest internal differentiation. For this reason, [it] does not shine as something other than luminosity itself.

The phrase "it might be" refers to the statement regarding the function [of the cognition]. He also says "nevertheless" (*tathāpi ca*) by way of concession: even if there were distinctions of place and time, let the illuminations be distinct solely through a difference in their own nature;
nevertheless, in the ascertainment "this is blue," other blues are not excluded, on the contrary...

...consisting of the conceptualization of what has been seen [the reading *kalanātmakam* is found in manuscript *ga*]. According to this principle, those [perceptions] are to be joined together; otherwise, because linguistic usage cannot be established through verbal expression based on memory alone, they would instead be merely "yellow" and so forth, animated by the absence of "blue."

[The objects] are to be excluded; likewise, in the case of manifestation (*prakāśa*), other manifestations that belong to the level of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) are not to be negated (*apohana*) when [the manifestation] is to be ascertained—thus, once again, the status of conceptualization (*vikalpatā*) is not established. But surely...

"If there is no manifestation [of the effect] in that [cause], why is the operation of the cause desired?"—according to this principle, since that [object] would manifest by its very nature, it would therefore not appear; and precisely for that reason, its exclusion (*apoha*) will be absolute. This is what he sets aside with the words "or when the counter-correlate does not appear," because of the cause.

Exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is determined by the actual nature of things (*vastugatyā*), and since it does not fail when a counter-example is impossible, this is to be accepted; however, in this case, there is no consideration of real entities. What then?
It is a discussion of cognition. For exclusion (*apohana*) is the operation of the cognizer (*pramātṛvyāpāra*), and therein—

The occurrence of superimposition (*āropaṇa*) and so forth is inevitable. And how could that [superimposition] occur with respect to something never before perceived, even if it is produced by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), since conceptual construction—being dependent upon the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of experience—is impossible in the case of that which is absolutely unperceived? This point the opponent does not tolerate.

(Page 289) [The objection begins with] "nanu" (but surely). For here, if one were to conceptualize— that is, superimpose— the appearance of a non-existent jar and then negate it, there would consequently be many distinct cognitions occurring at different times.

Because of the faults of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), circularity (*cakraka*), and infinite regress (*anavasthā*), it was stated thus: "that which does not appear has no exclusion (*apohana*). The underlying intention (*ākūta-śeṣa*) is that, on the contrary, for one who desires exclusion, the very non-appearance of that [object] must be sought as its exclusion. He refutes this with the words: "It has been said in this regard."

Thinking that all of this has been resolved through the method of objection (*ākṣepa-vācoyukti*), he explains for the sake of the objection itself with the words "For here... and so forth: "The swan of consciousness (*saṃvitti-haṃsī*) simultaneously abandons what is to be discarded and takes up what is to be accepted by its own power—this much [is the case]."

Therefore, its independence remains indeed [in this unreal state]. Those who know it consider it to be that which partakes in the definition of abandonment and acquisition. "Pratipatti" means "pratiyatī," which is to say, that which is personally realized by oneself. "Otherwise" means if...
According to the stated method, a single operation consisting of rejection and acceptance—which has the nature of being characterized by [the object]—would not arise for the cognizer.
But surely one desires a jar, and consequently acts? True, the desire to obtain is what impels action;
however, that desire alone is not sufficient unless it is constrained by the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The word "mere" (*mātra*) is used so that one might initiate an activity directed toward a specific object. Furthermore,

if desire (*arthitā*) were accepted as the cause of activity while being independent of the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then at that very moment, even the desire for the cessation of suffering would [be such a cause].

Therefore, since the cause of cessation is the very same as that toward which there was activity, it would follow that at the very moment one acts toward something, one simultaneously ceases from it—this is a great calamity.

Thus he says, "by the suspicion of the undesirable. For it was previously established that when there is a desire for an object, activity occurs based on mere suspicion alone, without requiring certainty; and this applies to cessation as well.
It is the same. Having established this, he concludes with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

For just as words such as "hidden" (*rahita*) and so forth refer primarily to an entity characterized by an absence qualified by an implied counter-positive, so too do all words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) and the like; this is what he demonstrates with the word "thus" (*evam*). This is also the view of the opponent.

"This is agreed upon," he says, "by the word 'one'. To the extent that cognition is described as having the nature of a reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of a single blue object, to that same extent it exists in that one [place].
The resting cognizer, by his own majesty as a cognizer,

possessing the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of both the duality of that which is to be done and that which effects it, distinguishes the group of things that effect it as something to be accepted from the group of things that do not effect it as something to be rejected; this occurs precisely through the operation of the cognizer.
Reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is called "subsequent reflective awareness" (*pratyavamarśa*) because, by being oriented toward what is to be accepted, it turns away from what is to be abandoned.
To explain the purport of the sentence in order to apply the meaning of the passage studied to the present context, he says: "By this...
Thus, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: regarding all objects of knowledge...

The practice [of cognition] terminates in the operation of negating the superimposition of an appearance that is to be excluded, because its nature is that of a determinate cognition, just like the cognition "it is merely distinct" and so forth; this is the essential property (*svabhāva*).
For the reason (*hetu*) is excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) out of fear of perceiving what is incompatible with its essential property. For if it were not...
If one were to conclude with this much, it would result in nothing other than a state of uncertainty; and this has just now been demonstrated.
