Applying this to the subject at hand—the object of knowledge—he concludes the present topic with the words "tadevam" (thus, therefore).
The reflective awareness of pure consciousness as "I" is not a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
"Because there is no perception of the counter-correlate, its manifestation, and so forth"— this is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*),

and the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader has indeed been determined in detail [elsewhere]. And since this alone is the subject matter under discussion here as the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the Commentator has directly expounded the latter half of the Sūtra.
[It was] set in motion by Ka; however, previously, it was because the meaning was already understood. || 2 ||

He introduces the Sūtra preceded by a doubt: "Because it excludes what is not that [object] solely through the mere appearance of that or its opposite, this conceptual construction 'this is a jar' is said to be the ascertainment of that. (3)

Regarding the word "nanu": in perception, that which appears is the object (*viṣaya*), and the activity is established upon that; both of these constitute the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) insofar as they are subject to linguistic usage (*vyavaharaṇīyatva*). And in perception, both appear—the jar and the cognition of the jar—but not the non-jar and its negation therein.
In this context, the meaning of "object" (*viṣaya*) is its non-existence elsewhere when [the cognition] is manifest.
That very state of having a determined form— which was indicated by the word *hi* in the Sūtra as the reason for the demonstration of the logical proof—
is expressed here by the commentary term *tathā ca*.
(Page 291) *Upakrāntā*: That very subject (*pramātṛ*) who partakes of— that is, internalizes— the manifestation (*pratibhā*) of that jar, of the non-jar, and of the non-non-jar.

This conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is said to be that determination of what performs a certain function—such as "this is a jar"—by one who is independent, having abandoned dependence on objects, their perception, and so forth, and who excludes the class of things that do not perform that function. For this is why the conceptual construction is such; therefore, the self-reflective awareness (*ahaṃ-pratyavamarśa*) is not [the conceptual construction].

The term "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*) is to be connected with what precedes. Alternatively, since the subject (*pramātṛ*) alone effects such a determination of that [object], therefore—because the aforementioned objection does not apply—the conceptual construction "this is a jar," which consists of that determination, is logically established by internally subsuming the negation of its opposite; such is the connection.

This is the meaning of the aphorism (*sūtra*). Regarding the word "only" (*eva*), it is explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*); and in the explanation of that commentary, with the intention of showing that the "explication" (*vivṛti*)—which consists of the unfolding of its sequence—is primary, it is stated in the aphorism as well:
"also. Now, one might ask: does every cognizer possess such a nature? No; thus he says: "the Lord" (*īśvara*).

Since pure *ahantā* (I-ness), which is all-enduring, exists in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "I," it is therefore not distinct from consciousness nor from other objects of knowledge; yet it is a constituent part, like a limb, because of its manifestation as "this" through a state of separation. Such is that which [is described].

Even a single portion of the category of objects of knowledge [is present] within the Lord as the subject; however, He does not employ the operation of *apohana* (exclusion), because, like a flash of lightning, there is no further growth even as this [operation] unfolds. Where, then, does its growth occur? He says: "In the state of Māyā. Again, [this is said] in contrast to the state of Īśvara.

The *viśeṣaka* (concluding verse): "In that case" means while things stand thus. Now, one might object: even there, when the eye is active, there is non-conceptuality despite the presence of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), for at that time the divine state belongs even to the bound soul (*paśu*); thus, its universal nature has been stated. This very point is raised by the phrase "even though it consists of all things. When?
In that case, rest lies in exclusion (*apohana*). He says: "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*). "Finality" means a firm establishment due to its intensity.

By this, it is shown that even in the state of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpadaśā*), there exists a state of being characterized by *māyā* through the connection with latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), yet it is not entirely absent; for how could the very sovereignty (*īśvaratā*) exist as an object when it is in its state of purity?
It has been shown that there would be a rule regarding the immediate arising of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). "At that time" refers to the moment of conceptual construction;
[this is] by means of reflective awareness (*vimarśana*).

The meaning is: "by one who has entered into such conceptualization. And he clarifies this very point with the words "for he" (*sahi*). "In that way" (*tathā*) means as something illusory (*māyīya*). "Of him" (*tasya*) means even of that which is illusory. Because of the majesty—that is, the greatness or the state of being the universal self—of that essential nature (*svabhāva*) characterized by consciousness which consists of subjectivity (*pramātṛtāmayo*); for that reason [the following occurs].

The phrase "being excluded" (apohyamāna) means that for which an exclusion (apoha) will be performed; this refers to the greatness of both intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and its illusory character (māyīyatva) as differentiators, existing respectively within the Supreme Self (paramātman),
within other illusory subjects (māyā-pramātṛ), and within other objects of knowledge (prameya).

The sixfold [set of teeth], by means of a single function, possesses a variegated form bitten by the fangs of the clever one; its act of cutting— which is identical to the act of chewing upon the leaf of betel— is being excluded due to its own greatness.

Being distinguished from both the knower and other objects of knowledge, it remains as such. By [defining it] as "other," there would be no room for fallacies such as mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). For this very reason, he says "occurring prior.
For if the cause were to arise at that same time [as the effect], the search for another cause would necessarily follow, and thus [the fault] would indeed occur.

The refutation beginning with the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*): Now, [it may be argued that] this entire mass of objects distinct from the jar—which is the object of exclusion (*apohya*) in the term "non-jar"—appears separately according to its own specific characteristics (*svālakṣaṇya*). Nor is there a universal (*sāmānya*) called "jar-ness" (*aghaṭatva*) therein; or even if it existed, there would be no cognition of it. Thus, whoever...
One might be deluded; therefore, he awakens him by saying "the reversal of the jar. The word "ca" (and) indicates a doubt.

The "reversal of the jar" is of the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*). Although that [universal] is not perceived—due to the lack of observation caused by the manifestation of only a single jar—for one who seeks a specific jar, on account of the conceit [that it is not perceived]; [nevertheless...]

Nevertheless, although it is thus conceptualized, it is indeed perceived as a reality. He states the reason for its being a universal form with the words "restricted" (*niyata*). Now, one might object: "Granted that this [object] may lack a specific, restricted form, how can cloth and other such things be that universal? It is replied: the form of cloth and so forth...

For it has been embraced—that is, embraced by that following which is grasped—and not merely like a bamboo circle [held] by a pillar; rather, because of its imposition as having that very same form, there is a determination through non-difference.
He states the reason for this being established: "as stated. For otherwise, activity and so forth would not occur in a determinate manner.

Since this has been established, he states an example well-known in both cases: when the conceptual form, which is of the nature of a universal, [appears] regarding the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is the object of perception...

It exists by means of such arguments as "because of the absence of the form of a restricted jar," and just as it is indeed determined in reality even though not perceived separately, so too is this [self]. For there is no distinction here in that the universal must exist only when there is the cognition of the particular; rather, [it is the opposite].

Regarding the phrase "in the cognition of negation": this is indeed the doctrine of the reality of appearances (*ābhāsa-vastutāvāda*); therefore, the system of Kaṇāda need not necessarily be taken as authoritative here, such as the argument that if a universal were to inhere (*samaveyāt*) in a non-entity (*abhāva*), it would follow that this [non-entity] would possess a positive form (*bāvarūpatā*), and so forth. As it has been said:
"In this regard,
the venerable one [has said]: 'Since all things are established as having activity as their defining characteristic' (Vākyapadīya 3.1.11)."

Thus [it is said]. To resolve the objection—namely, "If there is an appearance of both natures, how then can certainty differ from doubt?"—the commentary states, "by the exclusion of what is not that" (*atadapohanena*). He explains this in its essential meaning through a clear example, beginning with the words "both," etc. For here, the second [nature] is indeed being negated.

It shines, not by way of oscillating with equal status such that its nature as doubt might be suspected; this is what is intended. Even for doubt, because it possesses the exclusion (*vyapohana*) of two things that serve as the basis of that oscillation, it is of the nature of certainty and is thus nothing but a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

"By means of the word 'name'"—this conceptualization is what is meant by "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*). This means that the action denoted by the verbal root is established here precisely as an action. It has been stated [in the previous verse] by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*) through the power of the etymological explanation of the meaning of the prefix *vi-*. (3)

Now, it was stated that the reflective awareness "I am" is not a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); therefore, what of that reflective awareness which occurs regarding the body as "I am fair," regarding the intellect as "I am happy," regarding the vital breath as "I am hungry" or "I am thirsty," and regarding the void (*śūnya*) as "I am devoid of all external and internal forms"? In those cases as well—
In the absence of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), nothing else can be excluded; thus, for them,
a manifold confusion arises through mutual relations with other subjects and objects of cognition, resulting in the collapse of the distinction between self and other.
(Page 294) [An objection] arises here. To this, he provides an answer in two verses:
"The true nature of consciousness (*cittattva*), having abandoned [its form] through illusion (*māyā*), appears as if it were distinct."
Whether in the body, the intellect, or the vital breath, it is imagined as if in space.
The reflective awareness "I" as the subject arises from the exclusion of others;
it is indeed a conceptual construction (vikalpa) produced by the manifestation of its opposite. (5)

Although the reflective awareness of "I" rests upon the very principle of consciousness (cittattva), and although the stability of objects is restricted to the individual soul (jīva) which is constrained by the vital breath and the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), even there it is established in the Supreme Self. (Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi 20)

According to this principle, nevertheless, setting aside— that is, disregarding and transcending— that [consciousness], there occurs the descent of the reflective awareness "I am," which arises through the consecration as the subject of objects such as blue, constructed by the conceit [of subjectivity] regarding the body and so forth; but not by the power of mere convention.
Having set aside and shaken off that pure nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which exists on the level of non-conceptualization,

it assumes the state of conceptualization itself during the stage of thought-constructs; for, following the appearance of another real entity as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), it relies upon the exclusion (*vyapohana*) of that [other].
Regarding the descent [of the power] through the breach of transgression and the concealments mentioned, the cause is indeed the Lord’s own power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*), and not— as others claim—
the conceit of self in what is non-self, as expressed by the phrase "in the impermanent, the impure, the painful, and the non-self."

The state of having ignorance alone as the cause—this should be connected to the word "by means of illusion" (*māyayā*) in all instances in the Sūtra. It is the same in the commentary (*vṛtti*): the connection is that "reflection" (*vimarśa*) is indeed conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). In the phrase "ignorance and so forth" (*avidyādi*), by the inclusion of "and so forth," specific unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*) is intended.

And is the dependence on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatā*) not another non-material cause for consciousness? That which is called the sovereign power (*aiśvarya-śakti*), the will of the independent Lord in His supreme state, is itself,
having extended into the intermediate realm of the stages of Sadāśiva and Īśvara, [manifests as] knowledge through differentiation.
And action (*kriyā*) unfolds in a form established upon both difference and non-difference; however, on the lower level (*aparabhūmi*), it is those very same [two].
He demonstrates with the words "knowledge," etc., that these two are defined as the power of *māyā* when they culminate in differentiation.

This is not merely a conventional identification of "I" with the body; rather, it is the application of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) consisting of the autonomy whose nature is the subjectivity of the knower and the agency of the doer, directed toward the object of knowledge and the action to be performed. Otherwise—

"How could the awareness of autonomy—expressed as 'I go,' 'I move,' or 'I stand,' and whose very life is uninterrupted—be transferred to the body? For the autonomy of one [subject] cannot constitute the action of another.
This [distinction] would indeed occur in the case of a reflective awareness involving interruption, such as 'let this person move'; but in the case of non-interruption,"

The reflection "I go," and so forth—this he demonstrates by stating another reason, namely, "the sense organ" (*indriya*). Having explained [the term] as "in the body," he explains it as "in the intellect" (*buddhi*), because it consists of the three *guṇas*, as indicated by the phrase "having the nature of pleasure and so forth. This is due to the penetration (*āveśa*) of the subject (*grāhaka*).
The meaning is: "because of attaining identity with consciousness. As it has been said:

"This alone is our happiness, namely, the experience of that which is pleasant (*sāta*). Now, one might object: pleasure and so forth are indeed objects of cognition (*vedya*), just like blue and other such things; and therefore, since they are objects of knowledge, they must be insentient (*jaḍa*).
Regarding the statement "Dharma," if someone were to say that it is accepted by the proponent of the reality of the intellect (*buddhi-tattva-vādin*), he replies to him:

"Otherwise [it would not be so]," provided there is an absence of the reflective awareness of "I" (*aham-iti-vimarśa*). For that very reason, when the intellect possesses the reflection of consciousness and takes on the form of pleasure and so forth, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) arises through non-discrimination with respect to the nature of consciousness, pleasure, and the rest.
Being the agent who engages in worldly transaction (*vyavahartā*), one accepts [the object] as that which gives rise to pleasure and pain.
For pleasure and pain are not the form of the external object itself; rather, it is merely determined as such.

This is because, through the logical consistency of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), even the external object is [determined as such] by virtue of its being the producer of pleasure and so forth, which consist of pleasure and pain.

Its nature as such is established. To explain the phrase "in the vital breath" (*prāṇe*), he explains that function which [is described] as "or in an internal touch" (*sparśe*) by saying "of the vital breath" (*prāṇasya*).
The intention is that "touch" (*sparśa*) means that which is perceivable by the sense of touch (*sparśanendriya*); otherwise, it would be perceivable by the eyes and so forth in the body.

Granted that there may be the conceit of "I-ness" (ahantābhimāna) regarding the modification of the intellect (buddhivṛtti), which is accessible to the internal organ; however, it is questioned: by what means is such a conceit apprehended in the case of the internal wind?
Regarding the body—
And since that which has not become an object lacks the status of being a substratum for experience,

the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*)— expressed as "I"— is superimposed upon it; whereas for the intellect (*buddhi*), such a state exists because it possesses the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatā*) for experience.

In the same way, he explains that the status of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) is merely superimposed upon the internal tactile sensation (*sparśa*) when it functions as an instrument, stating "and not here" (*na cātra*). For in the case of a bone-thorn (*asthiśūla*), there is an extremely intense tactile sensation produced by the impact of the bone through the wind (*vāyu*), which brings about the painful experience of suffering.

By which there is the experience of the state of being an instrument (*karaṇatā*) therein. "Internal-ness" (*āntaratvam*) means non-externality (*abāhyatvam*). The phrase "as far as" (*yāvat*) implies that it is internal even because of its being an internal organ (*antaraṅgatvāt*). It pervades all the seats of the sense organs;
therefore, they consider the skin alone to be the single sense organ, due to its non-differentiation (*avyatirekāt*). From that, this...

Prāṇa is superior to the body and all else because it is the locus for the pathways of all the senses. For this very reason—because it is consecrated by the essence of the subject as "I"—it is not merely the internal wind characterized by entering and exiting through the nostrils and mouth; rather, it is that very [consciousness].
It is called *prāṇa*, but there is also a further aspect to it—this is indicated by the word "also" (*api*).

That which is denoted by the term "living" (*jīvana*), consisting of the activity of the knowing subject who exists as a cognizer, is the act of breathing characterized as such; that [activity] resides in the subject known as *prāṇa*. Of what nature is this?
Action. He says: it belongs to that "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*) which is permeated by all the powers of the senses. And here, the qualifier is to be understood by way of the qualified;
for it is that which penetrates [or, according to the Kaśmīrian and Gauḍapāda recensions, that which makes known] it.

The common internal function belonging to the powers of the present sense organs is the "common function of the instruments" (*sāmānyakaraṇavṛtti*), which consists of the five vital airs (*vāyu*) beginning with *prāṇa*. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 29)

Thus it has been defined; that [activity] in which it is introduced as the primary subject and presented as the fruit. For this very reason—indeed, because such is the nature of this operation—its internal character is intended to be all-pervasive. This is because those [powers] which are the forms of the knower’s power...
The sense organs (*indriya*) are the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); through their conjunction one becomes a cognizer (*pramātṛ*).
Their "ground" (*bhūmi*) is the inward-turned form; it is in that state that this activity resides. By means of that—

The intended meaning is that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) possesses internality because it is not external in form, because it is internal, and because it permeates everything. Having deliberated upon the term "in the vital breath" (*prāṇe*), he explains it as being like the sky (*nabhas*) imagined [as the locus], using the words "or rather" (*athavā*). All that...

Thus, that object which is well known as being accessible through the internal and external organs— characterized by the intellect (*buddhi*), the body, and the vital breath (*prāṇa*)— is negated; for indeed, whatever is perceived, among those I am none at all.
But rather, I am secluded from this... [and so forth].

According to this principle, that mere absence is not an object of the internal organ like the entity of pleasure and so forth, nor is it an object of the external organs like the object blue and so forth; and because it is indeed not an object, it is imagined, having conceptualization alone as its ultimate reality, and thus exists as a real entity in that state— the yogin’s reflective awareness of "I" [is directed toward it].
When one void is made the object of cognition, for the yogin, another void alone becomes the subject;

and as long as there is this grasping of duality—thinking that even there yet another [subject] exists—conceptual construction does not cease. Nor is there an infinite regress, for in reality, the state of being the subject belongs solely to pure light (for it is indeed the very nature of light to shine).

However, regarding the body and so forth, there is merely an identification [of the Self] with them; and ultimately, the nature of consciousness is nothing but contraction, which is void. The phrase "voidness" (śūnyatvam) should be connected right here as "that form which is insubstantial," for the purpose of clarifying that absence of sensory perception.

For in the view of those who propound it, space is not entirely void; and that very [space] is emptiness (*śūnyatva*). And for this very reason—that is, because it is not void in its entirety, since it appears as such, and because appearance alone constitutes reality—it follows from that. "Of this" refers to the void.

By the term "reality" (*vastutā*), not only is its substantiality (*vastutva*) stated through its similarity to space, but its pervasiveness (*vyāpitva*) is also stated. Now, one might ask: what pervasiveness can there be for that which is void? For the vastness of space consists precisely in its being the substratum of the conjunctions of all things that possess conjunction; and that does not exist for the void.

(298) Because it is not a substance (*adravyatvāt*). To this, he says: "It has a vast scope" (*mahāviṣayatā*). And how is that? It is said: since every object (*sarvo 'rthaḥ*) is of the nature of being cognizable (*vedyarūpa*), it is therefore the object of negation; thus, the scope of the negation is vast, and not—

There exists such a thing that is not touched by that great negation; as it has been said: "Whatever is perceived in any way, its nature is not admitted. By this repetition (*vīpsā*), it is shown that everything here is to be negated.
And its very state of having a great domain is its empirical pervasiveness; for even in the case of space (*ākāśa*), that alone is its all-pervasiveness (*vaibhava*).
However, it is described as being the substratum of the conjunctions of all conjoined things in order to facilitate its inclusion within its own system. Nor is this [the case] for Him...

He shows that pervasiveness is unprecedented by stating, "only this much" (or "this very thing," as in the *Ga.* manuscript); for they have not observed anything further than that. Because the self of restraint consists of "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) through repetition, and because its nature is the negation of everything, they consider non-existence itself to be Brahman due to its vastness.
Some [say]:
"One should gradually come to rest by means of the intellect held with firmness;
having made the mind abide in the Self, one should not think of anything at all" (Gītā 6.26).

Thus, for here it has been established that the very state of being devoid of all objects of thought is the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*); this is intended with the hope that they should first respect the abandonment of the lower stages, but not that this alone is the supreme reality. To demonstrate this very point:
In the *Śrīspandaśāstra*, it is stated: "Non-existence does not become an object of contemplation...
and so forth. (12)
"One should meditate upon non-existence until one attains identity with it.

Thus, the doctrine of the proponents of Brahman as non-existence (*abhāvabrahmavādin*) is refuted. For that which is remembered is characterized by time, is an object of cognition, and is indeed empty; thus [the thought], "I existed in such a state, being of the nature of nothingness," [is contradicted].

In the descent into the state of being a subject (pramātṛtā) such as the body and so forth, that which is "thus" is indeed an object of knowledge (vedya) that has been made into a knower (vedaka), just like the body and so on. However, the light of the "I" (ahaṃprakāśa), because it is perpetually non-setting and inherently uninterrupted, is not subject to recollection; this has been established in the *Ādisiddhasūtra*.
The author of the treatise, demonstrating that the emptiness of the subject (*pramātṛśūnyatā*) is never appropriate, concludes this as follows: "Thus... (page 299).

Thus: the meaning of the term *vṛtti*—namely, that as long as a thing such as the body appears in its respective fixed form (*nijaniyatarūpa*), to that very extent its exclusion (*apoha*) from its counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) must necessarily be performed—is elucidated by the word *niyamita*. This is indicated by the phrase "just as [one says] 'this is a jar'."

The pervasion has been stated in the *Vṛtti*: the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) as "I" with respect to the body and so forth is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because it has the exclusion of its opposite (*pratiyogivyavaccheda*) as its very life-force. For it has been established at length that having that alone as its defining characteristic is the pervading property (*vyāpaka*) of a conceptual construction; thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
He examines that function which consists in the exclusion of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogyapohana*) in its true nature, beginning with the words "And of these...

and so forth. For instance, just as a jar or the like is the counter-correlate of the body, so too are the intellect (*buddhi*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the void (*śūnya*). And this is not [the case] at the time of the conceit of being the subject (*pramātṛtā*) consisting in the body.
The exclusion (*apohana*) of the intellect, the vital breath, and so forth is experienced; indeed, it is experienced as belonging to the void (*śūnya*).

However, in the case of the intellect and the vital breath, rather, their absorption into oneness is perceived, because of the cognition: "I who am gross, I alone am happy, I am hungry. Therefore, this is the exclusion of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogyapoha*).

This treatise [is written] in response to the doubt as to whether [the body] is to be examined. In the phrase "of these" (*eṣāṃ ca*), the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
The idea is that because the body does not persist at all [in the ultimate state], subjectivity (*pramātṛtā*) is even more degraded therein;
with this intention, it is treated as the final [limit]. Now, if the subsequent [state] is inseparable from the preceding one, then...
How could that [prior state] be established as distinct from the subsequent cognizer? To this, he replies:

"Again, each preceding one... Even when there is deviation in a single direction, the state of being distinct is indeed established, just as in the case of space and wind; such is the meaning. [This refers to] non-deviation.
He analyzes, in sequence, the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) shown by the two sentences of the *grahaṇaka*, beginning with "tathā hi" (for it is thus).
Now, one might ask: even if distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) were real, why would it be so? To this he says: "ayameva" (this very [fact]).
For (*hi*), because when there is an object of knowledge that is not the Self (*anātman*), there occurs an adherence to it as the Self (*ātmābhiniveśa*).

The descent— the downward movement consisting in the abandonment of the level of pure consciousness in its upward form— is the entry of that deep-seated conceit of being a cognizer (*pramātṛtva-abhimāna*), which flows spontaneously and cannot be removed by mere discrimination (*viveka*).

(Page 300) Falling onto the foundational ground, which consists of the nature of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), there occurs this very appropriation of the levels designated as emptiness, vital breath, intellect, and body.

"By means of each preceding yoga"—such is the sequence. For instance, even in the ether (*nabhas*), which is of the nature of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), there exists the capacity to accommodate all space and pervasiveness; thus, it does not possess absolute insentience (*jaḍatā*). From that [ether] comes the wind (*vāyu*), which is devoid of [gross] magnitude, yet consists of the power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*), is inseparable from the ether, and is formless (*nīrūpa*). From that [wind] comes that which possesses form (*rūpavat*).

The conceit of being a subject (pramātṛtābhimāna) gradually descends into a state of degradation through the following sequence: first, in light consisting of radiance; then, in water which is devoid of radiance yet capable of receiving others;
then, in dense earth which is incapable of receiving others; and finally, in gross, extremely inert earth. In that regard:

Because absolute emptiness (*kevala-śūnya*) cannot be engaged with by non-yogins, it is said— relative to the world— that the very breath (*prāṇa*), which consists of touch (*sparśamaya*) and is permeated by the appropriated emptiness,
possesses primacy due to its superior connection with fire, which brings about the burning of the moving and the unmoving. By that [statement]:

The transformation of consciousness (*saṃvit*) is its transition, like an elephant onto a bank, through intense attachment (*abhiniveśa*) into the non-self in the form of the object of knowledge (*vedya*). With respect to the body and so forth, this is previously called "vital breath" (*prāṇa*);
it is the essence of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which consists of the functions of volition (*saṃkalpa*), self-conceit (*abhimana*), and determination (*niścaya*).

That from whose very grace such a state of existence is obtained is the *cittattva* (the principle of consciousness); its vital air (*prāṇa*) has become its substratum and that which is presided over. By that vital air, which is thus constituted and presided over by the principle of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*), and which possesses the accompaniment of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) in the form of the intellect (*buddhi*), the body is presided over.
Consequently, this [body] possesses a connection with the sovereignty appropriate to consciousness; however, it is not presided over by direct perception.
Thus it has been said:
"The Lord, whose nature is light, is said to have the vital breath as his locus."
Prāṇa, Khaga, and Dharma-Haṃsa—these are his three vehicles.
Thus it is said: "Therefore,
whatever body the Lord attains and from whatever he departs,
he goes taking these [senses] with him, just as the wind carries fragrances from their source" (15.8).
Thus, in the *Bhagavadgītā*, the Blessed One [has taught] that the Lord, whose nature is consciousness, acts by means of presiding over the vital breath and the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*).
(Page 301)
The state of being the substratum of the body has been stated; for it is said by the Guru in the Spanda-śāstra as well:
"Since this group of instruments, though deluded, acts like one who is undeluded, [performing] the processes of manifestation, maintenance, and withdrawal along with the internal wheel."
"...he obtains... (*Kārikā* 7).

Here, [it means] "together with the wheel within. Therefore, even when the body has been reduced to ashes, as in a dream, even while joined with a state of delusion consisting of being completely immersed in sleep— (Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary on a verse from the *Trika* or *Pratyabhijñā* tradition, likely the *Parātriṃśikā*. The phrase "sahāntareṇa cakreṇa" refers to the internal wheel of consciousness.)

Since the *puryaṣṭaka* (the subtle body), which encompasses the vital breaths governed by volition, remains in that same state, experience in another world through the medium of presiding over another body is not difficult to establish. Furthermore, many yoginīs are observed to remain within their own bodies while staying in their own homes.

By means of the yoga of the coming and going of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) rendered independent, [the powers] are joined to knowledge and action even regarding an object situated in another body; and the methods for rendering [the breath] independent have indeed been taught. As it is said in the *Śivasūtra*:

"In the state of Brahman, the lotus-bodied one wanders everywhere and at all times in the form of the living beings arising from it," and so forth. Enough of this; in any case, there is indeed a complete separation between the body and the vital breath.
As the Sage said:
"There is no connection between the vital breath and the body that have grown together"—meaning that a true connection is one of absolute non-separation. And so it is stated in the *Kakṣyāstotra*:
This delusion has been shattered by you, who have shown the wondrous transition to Videha and other realms in a dream;
for when the body has passed away into ashes, it exists elsewhere.
Of what nature...?

Thus [it is said]. And just as this sequence occurs in the descent by virtue of the power of the Lord’s sovereign destiny (*niyati*), so too he shows that this very same sequence applies to the ascent—characterized by the relinquishing of each successive lower level and the climbing toward a higher form—by saying "in the same way. This refers to one who remains on the plane of the body.
This corporeality residing within the body— whether it be grossness, subtlety, or even the supremely vast body extending as far as the cosmic egg— is [all contained therein].
Thus, by the principle stated in *Yoga Sūtra* 1.40,

"The mastery of this [mind] extends from the atom to the supreme magnitude," for one who meditates, there arise *vitarka* and *vicāra*, and from those, *ānanda* and *asmitā*; even within the three *guṇas*.
Demonstrating that the predominance of *sattva* belongs to the intellect (*buddhi*) and to the state of *sattva*, and declaring that bliss—

which is of the nature of a *sattva*-modification— is to be relished as an object of knowledge (*prameya*) in that state, he establishes that this is not the stage of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). The word "that" (*tat*) refers to both the body and the *sattva* of the intellect.
—Thus, they disregard both; even though these exist, they do not value them.

Precisely because of this disregard for the senses residing in the field of the body, there is no enjoyment of sound and the other objects, nor is there any experience of pleasure, due to the disregard even for the *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhi*).

Furthermore, due to the absence of all objects of enjoyment (*bhoga*), only the state of pure self-sense (*asmitāmātra*) flashes forth there; it does not, however, take on the form of "nothingness," because that would entail the attainment of a void-like state. Nor is it the nature of pure consciousness (*śuddhacidrūpa*), for it must consist of one or another of the objects of cognition, such as sound and so forth. Its form there is that of touch (*sparśarūpa*).
The object of knowledge exists on the level of the vital breath.
Now, on the plane of vital breath (*prāṇana*),

there is the state of being a "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*), consisting of the pentad beginning with *prāṇa*, the group of five organs of action, the five sense organs, and the triad of internal organs; it is precisely from that [plane] that [this arises].

It has been stated: "The common function of the organs consists of the five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 29). Regarding this, having raised the objection as to why color and other objects are not perceived despite the existence of other sense organs, it was said: "because of the predominance of the organ of touch. But [one might ask]: how so?

In that state, there must necessarily be a resting in mere certainty, or mere ascertainment, or mere conceit; and there is no grasping of touch by means of the intellect or the ego-sense. In this regard:

He says: "And then. In that state, which consists of nothing remaining but the *puryaṣṭaka*, the existence of the sense of touch (*sparśanendriya*) in its subtle form is not contradictory. He shows that there is also an object of touch (*spṛśya*), just as there is the sense of touch, by virtue of its subtle nature as the great element of air (*mahābhūta-vāyu*).
"Origination.
Now, one might ask: "Is there such an origination of the great elements to this extent? He says: "There is."
"Even in the state [of Sadyojāta]," etc. The word "even" (api) illuminates the fact that this impossibility exists not only in the higher and lower states, but also in the lower state itself.
Sadyojāta is earth; Vāmadeva may be water.
Fire is Aghora, man is Vāma, air is Īśāna, and space is proclaimed [as Sadyojāta].

Thus it is recited: "The pentad of powers, characterized by consciousness (*cit*), bliss (*ānanda*), will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*), attains its gradual expansion and displays seven pentads, yet remains undivided; thus it exists as the essence of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*). So it has been said.
In the Śrīkālapāda and other systems,
earth, water, fire, air, and space—
these five principles are those by which the entire world is pervaded.

Thus [it is said]. This will be elaborated upon in the section concerning scripture (*āgama*). Now, one might object: when there is the notion of a self (*ātmabuddhi*) with respect to the sense organs, which are not the self, how can they be considered any one of the [categories] beginning with sound? Indeed, the sense organs are not cognizable by anyone through their own intrinsic nature, such that a conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) could arise toward them. It is with this very intention [that the following is stated].
He says: "Of the distinguished ones. Those [powers] are not to be experienced as having their own individual forms;

for in the Āgamas, they are established as being of the nature of the power of *ahaṅkāra*. But surely, for transmigrating beings, there is the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) regarding the intellect (*buddhi*) and the *ahaṅkāra*; how then [is this so]?

The nature of sound and so forth. It is said: "the intellect" (*buddhi*). That which is the triad of powers—knowledge, action, and *māyā*—within the supreme reality (*paratattva*), that very same triad, when it assumes the predominance of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), will be described as the three qualities (*guṇas*) consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion.
"...of the Lord with respect to the entities that are the forms of His own limbs" (4.1.4).

Now, one might object: the senses of the yogins are indeed perceived as having their own individual bodies; how then can they possess the nature of sound and so forth? Furthermore, in relation to that which is even more subtle than the subtle...

(Page 304) With the phrase "even for yogins," he refutes two objections— that sound and the other [objects] possess a subtle form— with a single effort. Even though the sense organs are derived from *ahaṃkāra*, they are restricted [to specific objects].

For the sake of establishing their status as objects, the outward extension of the respective sense organs occurs from the ego (ahaṅkāra) as qualified by its being the source of those respective sounds and so forth;
thus, their elemental nature is not contradictory. Now, how [is this] in the experience of pleasure and so on?

The existence of sound and so forth. He says: "It is indeed attached to objects. For it is precisely such a thing as a song or the touch of a thorn that is tasted [by consciousness]. Then how is it in deep sleep? He says: "In deep sleep. "Ultimately" means: consisting, for instance, of the touch of the jar-like breasts of a beautiful woman.

There is happiness in sleep; even in its absence, there is happiness consisting of the touch of the vital air (prāṇavāyu) which possesses a healthy nature within one's own body. For this very reason, the touch of the vital air when it is not healthy is of the nature of suffering during sleep.
When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is condensed by *tamas*, it is of the nature of delusion (*moha*). Thus the Guru said:

"I slept happily; my mind was serene," and so forth. In the commentary (*ṭīkā*), the mention of "happiness" (*sukha*) also indicates suffering (*duḥkha*) and delusion (*moha*). Now, [one might object]:
Is there a consciousness that has transcended the clearly manifest objects of cognition, such as sound and so forth? Truly there is;
however, at that time, there is no immersion of the self into what is not the self. This is what he says with the words "but in the state of transcendence" (*uttīrṇatve tu*).
When [consciousness] occurs as having transcended the objects of cognition, such as sound and so forth—[as in the case of *yathā ka*].
Because the contraction caused by the *māyīya* category of *vidyā-kalā* has subsided,

and due to the unfolding of innate cognitive power (*jñāna-śakti*) when there is an absence of the operations of the organs of sense, the organs of action, and the internal organ, one then abandons the realm of the knowable; for at that time, [there is the emergence] of pure consciousness.

Consisting of the reflective awareness of its own bliss and being self-luminous, that state which has transcended deep sleep is called the "Fourth" (turyā) because it cannot be designated by any other term; it is not, however, the state of deep sleep itself. Now, if the state of the Fourth is not the state of deep sleep when one has transcended the objects of knowledge, then what [is the difference] regarding deep sleep?

Fearing that this would contradict what will be stated [in Yoga Sūtra 3.2.15]: "It is both to be experienced and not to be experienced," he says: "In the gross. This refers to when the *asmitā* (ego-sense) regarding the gross body has been abandoned.
The state of emptiness characterized by the cessation of all mental fluctuations— defined by valid cognition, error, conceptualization, sleep, and memory— is merely that much,
being simply the emptiness of gross form; it is not, however, the emptiness of that which transcends the body, such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth.

This is because that which is called the emptiness of the gross body is simply the nature of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, just as the ground has the nature of the absence of a jar; therefore, in that emptiness there is no state of the Fourth (*turyatā*), since in the void there is only the object of knowledge (*vedya*), due to the persistent attachment to the non-self as being the self. But in the case of the non-object of knowledge (*apavedya*)—[in the reading *apavedyatve tu*].

Because this [world] of sound and so forth, which is well-known as being an object of cognition, is not perceived as possessing a gross form, whereas it is stated that sound and the rest are indeed possible even in their supreme state (*parāvasthā*) by virtue of their subtlety; he reveals this very intention by means of the word "form" (*rūpa*). Intending to corroborate this with scripture (*āgama*), [he says...]

He explains by way of negation with the words "otherwise": if that [subject] were even void, then it would not remain as an object of cognition; in that case, the object of cognition would become entirely insubstantial due to the absence of both appearance and designation, and thus the state of being the cognizer alone would be without rival—so how could this be the state of deep sleep? It would be nothing other than the fourth state (turya).

For that [state] would have the sense of equilibrium (*sāmya*). However, when the object of knowledge (*vedya*) exists only as the nature of emptiness (*śūnya*), then suchness (*tathātva*)—that is, the state of deep sleep—is logically established. "Therefore" means:
because what is called cessation (*nivṛtti*) is the object of knowledge in the form of emptiness, and not the absolute non-existence (*tucchatā*) of the entire class of objects of knowledge.
It has the nature of being solely the experiencer devoid of any rival; for that reason, it is stated in the *Śrīrauravasūtrasaṃgraha* after defining [the goal] as follows:
"Now, for the sake of the cessation of the three bonds known as the impurity of the self (*ātma-mala*) and *māyā*..."
"But knowledge proceeds from Śiva for the sake of the manifestation of Śiva-nature.

Thus, the manifestation of Śiva-nature is stated as a distinct purpose; the word "but" (*tu*) indicates the reason that the manifestation of Śiva-nature is not merely the cessation of impurity (*mala*). For instance, in the case of the *kārmamala* (karmic impurity):
"In the case of the agent who lacks awakening, however, the karmic [impurity]...
(3.2.5); thus, there is the cessation of what is about to be described. In ultimate reality, therefore, there are only the two impurities of Māyā and Āṇava.
(page 306)
It is said: even the karmic impurity (kārmamala) shines there as a counter-correlative (pratiyogin) from the perspective of conventional discourse (vyavahāra).
For instance, the very ground is the absence of a jar; yet, in reality and from the perspective of conventional discourse, it is the jar being negated that appears.
In every respect, the jar is neither manifest nor describable.

This which is form is nothing at all; nor is that which is the absence of a jar anything either, for it is simply the light of the pure knower, entirely free from all objects of knowledge. In this very way, the manifestation of divided objects of knowledge belonging to Māyā is here called "Māyā" (3.2.5).

Thus, for that which is about to be defined [as the Self], the *āṇavamala* alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) upon its cessation, while the *māyīyamala* is the conventional reality, being that which is to be negated. Now, it has been said:
"The loss of sovereignty belongs to consciousness, and the lack of consciousness belongs even to sovereignty" (3.2.4).

Thus, that which is innate (*sahaja*), possessing two impurities while being independent of other impurities, and which causes the manifestation of those two impurities— namely, the *māyīya* impurity, which consists in the appearance of beginningless duality due to the absence of the "this-ness" (*idampūrva*) of the Lord’s power, and the *kārmamala*, characterized by merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*).

Considering that [the state of bondage] is dependent upon that [impurity], it is not to be disregarded by means of the *āṇava* [means]; therefore, with respect to both of those, that [state] is innate (*naisargika*). Even though no other impurity remains once that has ceased, nevertheless, its tendency toward decay—that is, its gradual wasting away—is pervasive even when it has been diminished.
"Exhausted" refers to its remaining as a residual latent impression (*vāsanā*) in relation to the cognition [of exhaustion] as its counter-correlative;
then, due to the connection with that latent impression, there arises the turbidity of the contraction-impulse within consciousness,
by which it becomes manifold.

"Arising, vast, tranquil, and perfectly serene... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.45). Because the variety of the stages of deep sleep (*suṣuptabhūmikā*) arises within the interval through such distinctions as these, for that reason, that which is characterized by pure consciousness (*śuddhasaṃvillakṣaṇa*) does not immediately manifest in its true form.

"In every way" regarding "all impurities" means that when even the state of having residual latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) is impossible in any manner whatsoever, it is said to be of a purely void nature in its entire essence.

This is also the case upon the cessation of the *āṇava* impurity. In that stage which is the level of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), however, there is not yet the nature of the Fourth State (*turya*). In that [state]:

With reference to that, he shows that the state of the Fourth (*turyatva*) is indeed manifest in the first stage, the state of deep sleep, by saying "the first. This refers to the non-manifestation of one's own power— the power whose nature is the awareness of freedom (*svātantrya-bodha-svabhāva*), characterized by the qualities of knowing and acting (*jñatva-kartṛtva*).
(Page 307) The connection is as follows:
by means of a nature that is complete and mutually inseparable, there is non-manifestation characterized by non-appearance;
its own impurity exists quite clearly. Now, if this is so—

The cessation of not manifesting one’s own power is the manifestation of one’s own power; and in that state, how could there be deep sleep (*suṣuptatā*), such that it was said [in the previous verse] "even upon the cessation of the innate (*sahaja*) and the atomic (*āṇava*")? He resolves this with the words "but gradually" (*krameṇa tu*). For action, characterized by the manifestation of Śiva-nature, exists as a sequence of prior and subsequent stages.
It depends upon the gradual emergence of the activity characterized by the cessation of impurity (*mala*).
Just as the impurity wanes, so too does the manifestation of light increase, until— due to the infinity of knowledge free from all veiling impurities— the knowable becomes insignificant.

Since the persistence of impurity occurs merely as a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), deep sleep is indeed appropriate due to its state of purity. What, then, is the state of the Fourth (*turyatā*)? It is said: when there is no manifestation or even mention of any of the three impurities in any way whatsoever, then that insubstantiality of theirs which is their insignificance—that is it.

May the nature of consciousness (saṃvidrūpa) of the Lord remain as pure indeed, being entirely liberated from the state of being an object of knowledge, from the bondage of karma, from contraction, and from the portion of impurity. For this will be considered in detail in the section on the scriptures (āgama-adhikāra). Thus, that which was stated—that the sequence of ascending is also fixed—has been determined.

For it has been stated that the nature of the fourfold *samprajñāta-yoga* consists of the state of *vicāra* (or *vitarka*) in the body, the state of *ānanda* in the intellect (*buddhi*), and the state of *asmitā* in the vital breath (*prāṇa*); even beyond that,
there is the yoga of the appearance of the cessation of mental fluctuations (*virāma-pratyaya*) on the ground of emptiness (*śūnyabhūmi*), which is of various kinds.

The nature of asamprajñāta-yoga [is defined] by degrees: up to this point is the state with seed (sabīja-avasthā), but in the fourth stage (turya-bhūmi), it is seedless concentration (nirbīja-samādhi). He concludes the subject matter of the kārikā with the words "this much, for now, is established. "In all states" refers to those characterized as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
"From this also" refers to the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). "In the state of the pure subject" means in the fourth stage (*turya*).
"For this very reason" means because the body and so forth are invariably concomitant with each preceding [state]; that is the meaning.
For if the body were the subject, it would have to be devoid of contact with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and the rest.
If that were the case, then once the body has been reduced to ashes, for whom could there be a state of existence in the next world?
Thus, because there is no one who goes to the next world, there is no next world.

"It dispels the delusion that [the body] will exist, even though there is equality in the state of being embodied. "They are perceived"—this refers to the present time.

Indeed, it is observed that pigeons possess passion and serpents possess anger even without cultivation (*bhāvanā*). "Of these" refers to passion and the rest. "Precisely causelessness" means that cultivation is indeed their cause; if that [cultivation] were not seen to be the cause in this very life, then causelessness would result.

And thus, there would be an impossibility of restricting [the nature of things] by place, time, or inherent character. Since there are many treatises whose primary aim is to establish the existence of the next world through reasoning,
the word "hundreds" is used as a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) to indicate that this has been established in many ways by numerous arguments in each individual treatise.

"By a hundred" is an indication of "many," meaning by many arguments; he shows that "this" refers to the subject under discussion (*prameya*) with the words "but of pure consciousness alone. It culminates precisely in the vital breath and the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka). || 5 ||

In this context, this notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) is both pure and impure, each being twofold according to the distinction between direct experience (anubhava) and reflective synthesis (anusandhi). Among these, the pure [notion] consists of the nature of direct experience as "I" within the self that is Śiva; on the level of Sadāśiva, it takes the form of reflective synthesis as "I am this."

Thus, it has been demonstrated that both of these, being devoid of any resting point in the delimitation of their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*), are free from conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and possess the very nature of pure self-reflective awareness (*śuddha-vimarśa*).
However, the impure [awareness], though its nature is the experience of "I" with respect to the body and so forth, is not so.

It has been established that this [notion] is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), whose very body rests upon the delimitation of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and is not pure reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). However, as for the impure cognition consisting of synthesis— the notion "I"—
because of the differences in the states of the body, this is not a reflective awareness (*parāmarśana*) directed toward that [pure subject], but rather...
Pure consciousness alone is its object, for that is eternal and one;

or else, the body itself is directly realized by this [consciousness]. In either case, there is no conceptualization whatsoever—thus, another aphorism is provided to dispel such delusion. Furthermore:
Although this notion of "I" has as its object the various states of the body, nevertheless,
because it manifests by unifying those distinct bodily states, one person might suspect that it touches upon non-difference as its essence,
while another might suspect it to be mere reflective awareness (*vimarśamātra*). And for the sake of the latter, the Sūtra [states]:
The conceptual construction (kalpanā) is said to be the association of a previous appearance and so forth with an occasional appearance; that too occurs when [the object] appears as distinct.

The phrase "in the body, in the intellect," and so forth, is carried over from the preceding sūtra. Alternatively, since no specific qualificand or particular instance has been mentioned, the body and other such things suitable for this qualification are indeed obtained as indefinite;
with this intention, the plural number is used in the commentary (*vṛtti*). And therein, this is the meaning [this is the primary meaning]: [the cloth...]
Now, it is established that even the synthesis (*anusandhi*) of a jar and so forth possesses the nature of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

The phrase "that which has an occasional manifestation" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa), implying also "that which has a manifestation occurring at a certain place, in a certain manner, and at a certain time. [This applies] to that which consists of a specific particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), whose time, location, and form are not fixed.
In a body of youthful form, by means of a prior appearance— that is,
the appearance of the body as a child— and by means of a former name, one thinks "I am Caitra" alone; and likewise, even by means of a future [appearance].

In the case of an elder, there is the appearance of being an elder; in the case of a living being, there is the appearance of being hungry, the appearance of being thirsty, and the appearance of being weak or very weak; in the case of a Buddha, there is the appearance of happiness, suffering, and so forth;
and even in the case of emptiness, there is the distinction between the appearance of being limited and the appearance of being unlimited.
There is indeed a synthesis [of the object] with other appearances such as fainting, meditative absorption, and so forth;

and the power of memory—which arises from the awakening of latent impressions (vāsanā) deposited by prior experiences—is the cause of that synthesis. However, that synthesis is nothing but mental construction (kalpanā), for it is merely a conceptualization (vikalpa) based upon that [synthesis].

Because there exists only a complete manifestation of differentiated appearance; for the conjunction of two manifestations being conjoined occurs only when their difference has been delineated by the exclusion (*apohana*) of their respective counter-correlates. Moreover, even this body and so forth, though unified with its prior state during the act of conjunction, manifests only as the exclusion of what is not that [prior] form.
Furthermore, since mental application (*yojanā*) is an activity of the cognizer alone that does not depend upon the object, how could it not be a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)?

Thus, in this Sūtra, every term should be explained as being a cause for the nature of conceptualization (*kalpanātva*), as appropriate. In the same way, the synthesis (*anusandhi*) regarding jars and other objects should also be stated.

It is not by way of conceptualization; rather, with the intention that on such a level there is the sublation of some particular difference, the Guru has declared that this kind of contemplation serves as a staircase for ascending to the palace of perfect non-duality. This is the unification with identity through the previous manifestation.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the text refers to] the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and names such as "Caitra" which share the same grammatical substrate (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with it;

the connection in the commentary is that this is indeed conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Furthermore, in this context, there exists a mutual synthesis (*anusandhāna*) even among the body, intellect, vital breath, and the void (*śūnya*); however, that...
In every respect, due to the delusion produced by the assistance of an extremely close proximity— which consists in the abandonment of the true nature of the object—
there is no single, persisting form as a whole (*avayavin*) there, nor does anything exist in the form of a body, as will be explained later; therefore, it is not [the case that...].
In this context, the contemplation of the subject (*pramātṛtā*) as having a form distinct from [the categories] beginning with the void (*śūnya*) has been examined.
He introduces the meaning of the aphorism (*sūtra*) in brief with the words "even he who...

[The implication is: not only is the reflective awareness "I" consisting of the experience of the body and so forth a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), but even that which consists of contemplation (*anusandhi*) is likewise so.
The meaning of the word "api" [is as follows].
He shows that which is the sūtra for the purpose of dispelling the doubt, beginning with "nanu. Of the first...

The term *saṃbandha* (connection). This means the firm establishment (*rūḍhi*) of the cognition of continuous recollection (*anusandhāna-pratyaya*). For example:
"I was a child and fair-skinned, but today I am otherwise"—thus speaks a youth whose body has become dark like a blade of durva grass, hardened by physical exercise. This is [the meaning].

This has been demonstrated by the connection between the various states of the body. And here, the word "or" (*vā*) is not used to indicate another state, because at that time [of pleasure], another state is impossible;
however, since states such as suffering can indeed be possible within states such as happiness, the word "or" is employed later on.
The states of consciousness, such as "I was happy or miserable, but today it is otherwise";

the states of vital breath, such as "I was hungry and thirsty" (or "afflicted by thirst"), but today it is otherwise; and the state of fainting, which is a limited and empty condition of utter delusion.
Through the power of concentration,
the external state of non-conceptualization is the "Great Bodiless" (mahāvidehā); from that follows the destruction of the veil over the light [of consciousness] (Yoga Sūtra 3.43).

[the practice] with trees, mountains, walls, and so forth... (Viśuddha-bhagavatī-mahāyoginī-tantra 68).

According to this principle, when the void of the body and so forth is gradually unfolding, whether one exists together with that unfolding (*unmeṣa*)—

If dissimilarity did not exist even earlier, it would not exist at the end either, because the state of remaining as it was (tādavasthya) would have been unaltered. As it has been stated by the venerable Anantapāda: "Having observed antiquity at the end, the loss of novelty at every moment is inferred."

Thus: "The entry by means of the prior form—that is, the appearance—is a state of intermingling which manifests as unreal on the level of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); therefore, it is not untrue. This refers to the commentary [on the verse] with the word "unity" (*aikya*).

By this sentence ending with "the conjunction of unity" (*aikyayojanā*), [it is shown]. Now, [one might object]: "In that case, since [the object] exists by the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*,"...

The dry Sāṃkhyas think: "Let it be accepted that the prior form remains exactly as it was; what, then, is the purpose of [the process of] conjunction? To awaken them, he says: "of the one. Now, they might argue: "There is no actual separation at all; rather, because it is merely unmanifest, that form is not perceived. To this, he replies: "In this case also..."

He says: "But not so. For if its nature were visibility, and its manifestation were likewise [its nature], then why is it not seen even now? Thus, by concealing it under different names such as "power" (śakti) or "manifestation" (vyakti), one would merely be admitting that the very state of being interrupted—arising from the persistence of that same state—is still present.

Therefore, only within the non-dual monism of consciousness (cidadvayavāda), when the entire aggregate of objective phenomena is accepted as being like reflections in the mirror of pure awareness, does the distinction between power (śakti) and its manifestation (vyakti) become logically tenable;
for this distinction is ultimately nothing other than the closing and opening of the eyes of consciousness itself, variegated by its own inherent powers. It cannot be otherwise.

This has been demonstrated by the venerable Vasuguptapāda, who, while defining the emergence of the manifold expansion of the fivefold cosmic acts— characterized by dissolution and arising through the reversal of the body and its constituent aggregates— showed that it originates solely from the unfolding and closing of the vibration (spanda) whose essence is consciousness.
He clarifies this very point with the words "and impermanence. "Of them" refers to the forms (*ākāra*).
"Will be established" [is the reading in manuscript *ka*].

"Whatever is non-existent is non-existent... (2.4.3); in this context, "otherwise" refers to the pure systems such as Buddhism and Sāṃkhya. And "therefore" means that since the forms [of the body] are impermanent due to their disintegration, the body must therefore be eternal and unitary. Since this...

Therefore, this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not the object, nor is this the synthesis (*yojanā*). Nor should it be suspected that there is no purpose whatsoever for a synthesis in a single [object]. The phrase "of the synthesis" (*anusandhānasya*) means "of that which is intended as a synthesis. By the word "also" (*api*), he states this: that there is an absence of synthesis because the object is exclusively consciousness (*cideka-viṣayatva*).
That which is suspected is not only illogical, but even as regards its being restricted solely to the eternal body;

he clarifies this very point with the words "as in the case of the conscious self" (*cidātmani*). Just as in the conscious nature—which is the ground of direct realization characterized by luminosity—there is a pure reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in the form of "I," which is devoid of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), [so too is it here].

It is not so in the case of the body and other such things. The meaning of the word "api" (even/also) is that because [the state] consists solely of the reflective awareness of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra-vimarśa-mātra-rūpatva*), conceptualization (*vikalpa-rūpatā*) could not possibly arise from what is being conceived (*saṃbhāvyamāna*); yet that is not the case. He states the reason for this impossibility: "because..."

Thus: if only the present, pure form consisting of the body and so forth were to manifest here, this would be a direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*); however, it is not so, as he says: "even of that which has perished. For this very reason—since there is a cognition of what has perished—it is born from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*); therefore, it consists of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). By the use of the particle *eva* (only),...

He shows that even in the case of a present object, there may indeed be the nature of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*). Now, having raised the objection that "direct perception might occur even regarding what has perished," he says: "not when it is non-existent. For direct perception is not produced by non-proximate objects for those who are not yogis; nor is it appropriate for that which is non-existent to possess the capacity to produce [cognition].

"By one who has become thus" means by one who is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). For a previous experience of the knower previously existed as differentiated by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the intensified object; that very [experience], when its differentiation has subsided, is called a "trace" (*saṃskāra*), but not in every respect.

(314) "With destroyed differentiation"; the intended meaning is that he, being awakened, becomes accompanied by the cognition of the present body and so forth, and thus constitutes memory. "In that manner" means that which is connected [to the object] by way of producing a cognition.

Regarding the term "priority" (*pūrvatvam*): even when the *lakāra* suffix denotes the object (*karman*), the word *yat* refers to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) and not to the object itself. However, the prior mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*) of this [object] is nothing but a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), since it is the independent activity of the knowing subject (*pramātṛ*). As for the object situated before one, however, it may indeed [be real].
It has been directly realized;

he describes it with the locative case as being "the groundless foundation" (*abhittibhūta*) for the painting of prior recollection (*pūrvānusandhāna*), which is being sketched by the waves of his own freedom (*nijasvātantrya*).
He clarifies what has already been stated with the words "for not... (*na hi...*). At that time... (*tadā*).
Everything previously mentioned as the object of cognition (*prameya*) is here made the reason for the present context; it functions in the sense of "therefore" (*tataḥ*), meaning "since.

[Objection: But if this is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then what has been accomplished there by that proximate object? [The author] replies: "Merely" (*kevalam*). It is distinct from its momentary state, yet non-distinct from its prior state.

Since its object is the body and so forth unified as one, this is neither pure conceptualization nor pure direct perception; rather, it is called a recognition consisting of a shadow (*chāyāmayī pratyabhijñā*).
It is a cognition through the turning back toward the prior [state] and the facing toward the present.

The intended meaning of the use of the word *pratyabhijñā* (recognition) in its technical application has been explained by this much. Now, as for the phrase "of the body" (*dehasya*), this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). It may well be that [the continuity] is interrupted—due to the body's states such as childhood, due to the intellect's states such as pleasure, and due to the void's varying degrees of contraction and expansion—because they are indeed distinct.

However, no distinction whatsoever is perceived in the tactile sensation characterized by the vital breath (*prāṇa*). For that tactile sensation, occurring within the vital breath which is interwoven with the body like warp and woof, is of the very nature of the body for both non-yogins and yogins alike.

For those whose independent functions of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) have been rendered distinct through the practice of the five-fold *prāṇāyāma*, it is simply the very nature of the vital breath. In either case, there is no distinction whatsoever in this [subject] by which there could be a perception of interruption; and such a subject has been explained as the grasper (*grāhaka*). As for the word "yat" (which):
Since it is thus, for that reason, how is it stated in the *Vṛtti* that through repetition (*vīpsā*) there is a universal separation?

"That too" means that even touch (*sparśa*) possesses the quality of being a grasper; the nature of touch is non-different from the universal form (*sāmānyarūpa*). By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the internal resonance (*antarnāda*) pertaining to the vital breath (*prāṇīya*) is understood, from which [it arises].

That [pleasure] also does not persist at all times; rather, it sometimes produces happiness and sometimes produces suffering, bringing about many different states such as health and ill-health. Thus, there are distinctions even therein.

They certainly do exist. Precisely because this is so, for that very reason, the explanation of the words "sautrāntika" and so forth was stated earlier in the commentary, beginning with the word "śūnya. || 6 ||

Since there would be an infinite regress if the body and so forth were sequentially known by each preceding knower, and since the object of knowledge could never manifest if the knower itself were not manifest,
therefore the Supreme Lord alone is, in the ultimate sense, self-luminous and the universal knower.

The conceit of being a subject (*pramātṛtābhimāna*) regarding the body and so forth is caused solely by the will of the Supreme Lord, who is designated as Māyā; demonstrating this through another aphorism, [the author] shows that the Supreme Lord never abandons his skill in unfolding the fivefold cosmic acts, such as emission (*sṛṣṭi*), and so on.
"...demonstrating [the power] of the Lord who resides within oneself" (1.5.10)—
thus, with reference to that very object of knowledge (*prameya*) which has been introduced, [this occurs] by virtue of being attached to the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
And since the investigation into the power of exclusion (*apohana*) follows as a consequence of that, he concludes that point as well:
"Thus, even in empirical transaction, the Lord, entering the body and so forth, may by His will manifest externally the very mass of objects already shining within. (7)

What was stated [in the previous verse], beginning with "In the body, in the intellect," and so forth, is thus appropriate by virtue of the meaning of this sūtra. For instance, even in the sphere of *māyā* within empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), the body and other objects of cognition are indeed the Lord alone, whose ultimate reality is Light; and precisely because of His lordship, He manifests them through His own will under the designation of *māyā*.

He enters by way of being the subject (*pramātṛtā*) and appropriates that state, manifesting the predominance of that body, vital breath, and so forth; thus he manifests the state of being that subject. And while manifesting it, [he does so] "within," meaning that because its ultimate reality is manifestation, it is an uninterrupted shining that remains on the ground of I-consciousness (*ahantā*) by means of will alone.

The word "outside" (bahiḥ) refers to the sphere of what is cognizable by the external organs as distinct from the internal organs; it manifests this [object] sequentially, both clearly and indistinctly, as "this. Therefore, for this reason, this is indeed appropriate, because there is no infinite regress (anavasthā).
[The suffix -tasi is used here] in the sense of a cause (hetau). Furthermore, for the reason that this aforementioned nature of exclusion (apohana) exists, it is thus.
The collection of entities whose nature will be described hereafter.
What is that? He says: not only among those things already well-known.
During the times of creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace,

as well as throughout the infinite period of worldly transactions— including mutual buying and selling, disputes, instruction, and spectacles— he enters the body, vital breath, and so forth, which are distinct from Caitra, Maitra, and others.
First, by means of unification, he fashions that portion [of the object] and manifests its persistence therein;

then, withdrawing the identity with the previous subject, he demonstrates dissolution through the closing of his own unified and compact nature; finally, by means of the aspect of absorption into unity, he manifests the power of grace (*anugraha-kalā*).

The Lord, who is independent and ever intent on accomplishing the fivefold act, manifests by his will that mass of objects—which is already shining, that is, already in a state of absolute luminosity—externally as a single appearance; thus, this is not impossible, and it has come to pass. In this regard, there is room for such possibility.

Thus, *evam*, that which was previously stated by the Master [in the passage beginning with] "...[svāmina]... (1.5.10) has become fully established.

By such sūtras as these, their intended meaning is as follows: at the time of creation and during the course of worldly transaction, the Lord, making the body and other factors the subjects of cognition (*pramātṛ*), manifests externally the mass of objects that exist within [Himself]. This is the rule, this is the injunction; and it is in this sense of an injunction in the form of a mandate (*vidhi*) that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) occurs.

In order to explain the word "also" (*api*) in the commentary, [the author] says "at the initial creation. To determine that "by will" is the cause for the penetration of space and so forth, as well as for external manifestation, he says "by the power of *māyā*" and "by the power of the agent.
"Successively" means that first there is a separation from the class of subjects (*pramātṛvarga*), and by the latter [power], [there is a further differentiation].
"Union" indicates the penetration of the fivefold set of actions (*kṛtyapañcaka*).
"Maheśvara illumines" is the avoidance of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Thus, it is threefold.
He introduces the meaning of the sūtra with the words "ittham" (thus) and so forth. The word "eva" (indeed) serves to dispel the suspicion of infinite regress.

With the words "na kevalam" (not only), he introduces the conclusion of the preceding matter, namely that the capacity for the uninterrupted continuity of creation and so forth has been previously set forth. [The word] "svam" (one's own).

In the pure ground of Śiva, his form consists of the constituent parts during the state of Śrī Sadāśiva and so forth; this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing a *dvandva*. In the ground of Īśvara, that which appears as "I am this" without division shines clearly as a specific form within the perceptions of the senses.

On the level of the mind (*manobhūmi*), that which is indeed indistinct due to its generic form exists in the state of the venerable Sadāśiva—at the beginning of emission and re-emission—in both the pure form of Sadāśiva and so forth, and in the form of Brahmā and so forth belonging to Māyā.

This is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound characterized by a defining attribute (*lakṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*), though it may also be understood as a *bahuvrīhi*. It is well known in the context of creation, maintenance, and so on.

The meaning is: "just as [previously], so too at all times. By the word "makes manifest" (*ābhāsayati*), it is understood—since no specific qualification is provided—that this occurs through the capacity for creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace. With the words beginning with "pure" (*śuddha*), he explains the term "Lord" (*prabhu*).
And [the author],
reminding the Master of this meaning and intending to describe his impure creation in due order,
first states the pure creation with the words "tasya" and so forth, and thus reminds [the reader].
"...without that, therefore [there is] desire and reflective awareness...
Thus, by showing through the word *icchu* (desirous) that "desire" is indeed its very own nature, [the author asks]: for what purpose does it have such a desire? To explain:
If the creation of the world were for the sake of sport, its perfection as a goal would be impaired;
moreover, motivated by compassion, He would create only that which is auspicious.
This [verse] leaves no room for such confused objections as those mentioned above. As it has been said:
"Since Śiva-nature consists of the performance of the fivefold act, what need is there to search for other causes in one who is engaged in his own activity? (Śivadr̥ṣṭi 1.12).
Thus, when the self-luminous nature is established as independent, what is this delusion? [What activity is there?
