It is primarily characterized by reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
(Page 318)

Cognition is that state of mind which, although existing within the level of Sadāśiva where there is illumination, will occur during the phase of Māyā; for here, the aspect of illumination— which consists of manifestation— is eclipsed due to its subordination, while entities themselves are what are manifested.

The conventional term "nimeṣa" (closing of the eyes) shall be applied to this state of closing, which is like a mass of forms depicted on a variegated cloth darkened by the presence of smoke and honey. And this [is explained] in the section on Revelation: "The Lord is the external unfolding... (3.1.3).

This will be explained hereafter. Precisely because of the predominance of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), this state is called the ground of the resonance that is the essence of the differentiation of all names;
however, when the aspect of reflective awareness is closed, [it becomes otherwise].

The state of Īśvara is designated as the *bindu* stage, characterized by an indivisible nature consisting of the unfolding radiance of consciousness, due to the predominance of the form of light appropriate for the direct realization whose essence is illumination.
This very state will become the object of the senses within the sphere of Māyā.

In this way, regarding the state of being an object toward the two types of cognition, the distinction produced by that [state] results in a division between clarity and its opposite; it is logical that the reality which constitutes its own limbs—and which is therefore undivided from them—being capable and consisting of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*), shall be of the nature of both consciousness (*cit*) and non-consciousness (*acit*). It is not [otherwise].

Thinking that there is nothing whatsoever beyond this, its manifestation is itself the creation of the universe. And this [manifestation] belongs to the Lord as His very own nature; it is not something additional, nor does it belong to anyone else who might be additional.
It is not like [the distinction between] "blue is indistinct" and "yellow is distinct"; such is not the case here.

He states that there is a difference in their respective domains by means of the suffix *cvī* (or *dvi*, according to manuscript *ka*). And yet, even in this creative union (*sṛṣṭiyoga*), there is no deficiency or superiority whatsoever on the part of the Lord; thus he says, "In that state" (*tadā ca*).
"In this" refers to the stage of Pure Śiva (*śuddhaśivadaśā*), in which the levels of Sadāśiva and Īśvara are concealed.

Now, is this twofold state in the Blessed Lord successive, or simultaneous? It is neither—thus he says, "nor even... For succession is a function of time, and that very succession, in relation to another [point], constitutes simultaneity; yet when there is no emergence of time, neither of those two exists at all. But if this is so...
Regarding what was stated— that "then" means "in that state" and "subsequent to that"— this is appropriate here because the conventional usage of "state" presupposes a temporal sequence.
Anticipating the objection that "in the absence of that [the world] would become as if blind," he says "merely" (*kevalam*). This is because,
due to the firm persistence of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of *māyā*, it is impossible to speak of the state beyond *māyā* (*amāyāpada*), which is not limited by time.

Being unable to perceive it directly, and because of the weakness of his own cognition— which, though primarily concerned with the distinction between two forms that are not contradictory, conceives of them as if they were contradictory—
the person to be instructed and the instructor [regard] that which is established in their own realization...

He superimposes even this sequence here. To explain what the reality is like when it is not so superimposed, he says: "In all cases here," namely in the states of Śiva, Sadāśiva, and Īśvara. Spatial differentiation arises from the differentiation of form, and temporal differentiation arises from the differentiation of activity; and these two do not exist here.
"The distinction of manifestations (*ābhāsa*) everywhere...

as will be stated in the section [of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā*], and it was also stated in the *Ādisiddhasūtra*. Having thus examined pure emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), he distinguishes the impure [emanation] with the words "tadevam" (thus, in this way). The word "anantara" (immediately following) refers to what follows.

The ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in connection with words denoting direction (*dik*). Here too, [the expressions] "when" (*yadā*) and "then" (*tadā*) arise solely from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of *māyā*, because there is no division of time within the will of the Lord. By saying "in the mirror," he asserts that even though there is an appearance of excess, there is actually no excess. "In which" (*yāsu*) means "in which [reflections] are being manifested."
The locative case of cause (*nimittasaptamī*) expresses that appearance is caused by something; thus, the meaning is as follows:

when the body and so forth are made into the subject (*grāhaka*) by means of appearance, then sound and so forth—distinct from the sound and other objects employed by the body and so forth—attain the state of being the object (*grāhya*). For it is not the case that...
Otherwise, the appearance of the two continua— the grasped and the grasper— would not be possible.
Since this arrangement of the pure, mixed, and impure exists in this way, for that reason, with reference to this very state of impurity...
"In the section beginning with 'Vision is indeed self-manifesting' (1.3.2),

the mutual absence between that which consists of the consciousness of self and that which consists of the consciousness of others was established through the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory of the pervader, in both the pure and mixed states."

Because there is no cessation [of manifestation]. Now, if the distinction between the subject and so forth does indeed appear, then, in accordance with that appearance, it is precisely that [distinction] which...
(page 320)

One might object: "Let it be real, as for those who maintain the fourfold division; so what is the use of postulating *māyā*? Anticipating this, he says: "And here too (*atrāpi ca*). The particle *ca* indicates a doubt regarding the conventional usage of difference. It is not only in the state of purity (*śuddhadaśā*) that non-duality alone is the essence.

The word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even here" (*yāvad ihāpi*) [is used for emphasis]. There is no reality whatsoever separate from the object of knowledge; rather, what is called "knowability" (*jñeyatā*) is simply consciousness itself. Even that is not something else, but is precisely of the nature of light, consisting of the reality of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*) which, by virtue of its autonomy, is of the essence of the self-manifesting "I-consciousness. Now, with respect to that—
He says "māyīya" (pertaining to māyā) to explain how even māyā could manifest differentiation:

because that which is superimposed upon the subject (pramātṛ), such as the body and so forth, is of the nature of the light of that [Self] as "I," it therefore possesses a manifestation constricted by its connection with the body and so on; consequently, in relation to that [constriction], [māyā manifests differentiation].

The conceit of difference is established. Now, one might object: "In the case of the illusory subject (*māyīya-pramātṛ*), this very state of being illusory consists in the superimposition of the status of a subject; what need is there for a further superimposition of the nature of Light? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Its attribute" (*taddharma*). [The reading *āropeṇa* is found in manuscript G.]

The superimposition of the nature of luminosity is precisely the superimposition of subjectivity; this is the meaning. Therefore, just as the nature of luminosity—though it is merely superimposed by means of the non-ultimate external term—is of a contracted nature, and thus it is not appropriate to regard it as distinct from that [luminosity], so it is here as well.

The sense is this: when the logical inconsistency of this matter remains unaccounted for, one must admit that there exists a power called *māyā*, which causes things to appear as inconsistent, residing within the Lord Paramaśiva—who is self-luminous and whose very nature is light—and who is brought forth by the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of His own scriptures. Now, [an objection may be raised]: "But..."

To the question, "How is it appropriate for that which has been thus superimposed—being [merely] light and reflection—to possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*)?", he says: "In reality. For a jar does not have the nature of a cloth, whether in the realm of *māyā* or even in the pure realm; even then, it is consciousness alone.

It is the manifold form (*viśvarūpā*); however, no jar whatsoever exists independently. Now, one might object: "In this impure realm of *māyā*, the division of time has indeed manifested; therefore, in relation to that, even the Blessed Lady would be subject to it. For as long as the impure realm of *māyā* was not previously projected, [time could not exist].

The conventional usage [of the term] "manifested" (*ullasita*) is as stated immediately thereafter: "When, following the pure creation... and so forth; this [usage] occurs for that long (*tāvat*). (Page 321)
To dispel the delusion that there is a division of time through logical reasoning, he says "and here" (*atra ca*), meaning in the state of *māyā*;

by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the mixed state is included. This fault would indeed arise if, with respect to the Supreme Lord, there were such things as "when" (*yadā*) or "immediately thereafter" (*anantaram*); however, since...
This is stated with reference to the perspective of those like us, who are permeated by the appearance of experiencing the divisions of māyā; but as for the Blessed One,
in what form indeed would he not manifest?

Thus, in the illumination of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), even such notions as "it shines now," "it shone previously," or "it will shine" are ultimately nothing but pure manifestation itself— the unfolding of its own power,
like [reflections] of vast or non-vast spatial dimensions in a mirror; that is merely the unfolding of its own transparency.

In relation to Paramaśiva, there is no conventional distinction whatsoever based on purity, mixture, or impurity, because everything has as its sole ultimate reality that [universal] Light; this is just as, in relation to variegated cognition (*citrabodha*), there is a distinction based on blue, yellow, and so forth. For if there were a conventional distinction in relation to that [Paramaśiva], then—

For them, there would be no manifestation [of other objects], just as a jar is not the manifestation of a cloth and so forth; and because that very [object] is necessarily their manifestation due to the impossibility of any other, the reason— fearing the consequence (prasaṅga) characterized by non-perception (anupalabdhi) which is the pervader (vyāpaka) of that necessity— is excluded from its opposite (vipakṣa).

The reason—characterized by the fact that [the object] has fallen away from having manifestation as its sole ultimate reality—is pervaded by the practice of non-difference, which is the opposite of the practice of difference;
thus, there is the perception of a pervasion by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). Now, how was it stated previously in this manner?

"In the state of the previous subject, the subsequent one does not exist"—this [objection] he refutes with the words "only at that time. At that moment, which is characterized by the station of the universal subject (*viśvapramātṛtā*), how can there be subjectivity (*mātṛtā*) belonging to the body, vital breath, and so forth? For that [subjectivity] is contracted; when its intensity reaches its peak, it becomes non-contracted.

For otherwise, the very status of being the universal subject (*viśvapramātṛtā*) would be untenable. What is meant is this: the subjectivity that belongs to the body—which, while being an object of knowledge (*vedya*), appears as both the distinct object and the knower—is attributed to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the intellect (*buddhi*), the void (*śūnya*), and the light of Supreme Śiva (*paramaśivaprakāśa*) as their respective subjects.
It flashes forth instantaneously while still being perceived, as it has been said:
"But by the touch of his own power, the individual soul becomes equal to Him" (Spanda Kārikā 8).
Furthermore, for the Blessed One, whose sole nature is that of the knower, subjectivity (*pramātṛtā*) is indeed his very essence.

(322) Regarding the term "non-different from the object of knowledge" (*abhinnavedya*): likewise, even though the body and so forth appear, they possess no quality of being a knower (*vedakatā*) because they are non-different from the light of Paraśiva. Now, [one might ask] regarding the body and its like...

The subjectivity (*pramātṛtā*) of limited beings manifests the differentiation of entities on all sides; however, the subjectivity of Supreme Śiva—which is His nature as Light—manifests everything as non-different on all sides.
Thus, He shatters the delusion of the opponent who thinks that it is not possible for both difference and non-difference to belong to a jar or similar object at the same time.

Regarding the word *māyā*: having thus described the impure creation (*aśuddhasarga*), he now elucidates the meaning of the subsequent sūtra— which constitutes the remainder of that very [topic]— concerning the empirical creation (*vyāvahārikasarga*) by means of the passage beginning with "of the pure conscious self" (*śuddhacidātmanaḥ*) and continuing with "of him who has the desire to create the universe" (*tasya viśvanirmāṇecchoḥ*).

Having first described the pure and mixed forms, that which was stated in the passage beginning with "when there is the desire to create the world" regarding the nature of the illusory creation (māyīyasarga)— in order to explain that very point, the author begins with "tathā hi" and continues with "viśvavartinaḥ," describing [the state] as pure, non-differentiated, and consisting of knowledge (vidyāmaya).
It reminds us of the nature that is both different and non-different. "Of the Lord" means of the Blessed Śiva.

"In mutual dependence" means that, in relation to the Lord, they are not different even from one another, for they have consciousness as their single essential reality (*saṃvidekarūpaparamārtha*); in relation to that [consciousness], they would appear as "I am that."

But it is not "everything" in the sense of being designated by the word *sarva* (all) as animated by the principle of objectivity (*idantā*). Regarding "of the Lord," this refers to the Blessed Śiva; such a nature of light exists precisely in the states of Sadāśiva and Īśvara.
And this very nature of Śiva, Sadāśiva, and Īśvara serves as the internal vitalizing force.

Even in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), which consists of the communication of cognitions through descriptions and narratives, [the primordial form] manifests as that which is antecedent. By the phrase "as in the creation of the universe," he indicates this by way of a further reminder.
And then, with the words beginning "tataśca" (and therefore), [he explains] the nature of the original creation (*ādisarga*) at the time of worldly transaction.

This has also been extended to the definition of worldly conduct (*lokyātrā*); he clarifies that: "of those very [objects]" refers to the objects existing in the universe which have been shown to possess three states. "Wind and so forth" means:
by means of the predominant void (*śūnya*), [in which the conventional usage experienced in the void occurs].

Due to the absence of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), it is said that there is only the state of being a subject (*pramātṛ*) consisting of vital breath, intellect, and body. Those who were previously on the plane of Sadāśiva are now the objects of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
(Page 323)

The *santa* [entities] are of a generic nature (*sāmānyātmānaḥ*) and possess faint illumination; however, those which exist in the sphere of the Lord (*īśvarabhuvi*) are now within the range of the external organs, possessing clear illumination and a specific nature (*viśeṣātmānaḥ*). Thus he says, referring to the word *krama* occurring in the commentary, by means of this much explanation of the pure, mixed, and impure states.

He shows that it has been explained: by the word *vṛtti* (functioning) in the phrase "by the power of the agent," the sūtra’s term *icchā* (will) is interpreted in its manifold aspects. When there is an immersion (*āveśa*) of the body and so forth into the nature of the Self, that very will is called the power of *māyā*; however, in the manifestation of external objects, it consists in the appearance of the creation of duality.

"Having the nature of the impure powers of *kalā* and *vidyā*. Now, one might object: "As long as the state of being the Self has been bestowed upon the non-Self by the power of *māyā*, then agency and knowledge have already been bestowed there in their impure form. So, what further function remains for *kalā* and *vidyā*? To this, he replies: "For by the power of *māyā*... [the soul] is contracted.

Although the state of being a knower (*pramātṛtā*) has been granted by the power of *māyā* at the very moment when the capacity for knowing reality is removed from the body and so forth, and the form of the object of knowledge is bestowed—
this is as stated in the *Nareśvaraviveka*:
Therefore, the power called Māyā simultaneously produces a twofold [manifestation]:
all objects of knowledge, both existent and non-existent, as well as certain knowers of those objects.

Thus, even so, by virtue of the union of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) within his own self, he would manifest as "I," distinguished from insentient things such as walls; however, by this much alone, he does not become the subject (*pramātṛ*) of distinct objects such as blue or pleasure. If [subjectivity] were dependent merely on the state of being a subject...
There would be the manifestation of blue and so forth; thus, the states such as deep sleep (*suṣupta*) and the Fourth (*turya*) could not be conceived,
because even there the mere subjectivity exists— distinguished from the insentient—
and because the experience of blue and so forth, which is implied by that subjectivity, is not lacking.

Because it would follow that it would incur the status of being either waking or dreaming. Consequently, when something does not occur despite the presence of another thing, it is not dependent on that alone—just as a sprout is not produced merely by the presence of a seed;
and likewise, even when the mere state of being a subject (pramātṛtā) is present, there is the perception of distinct objects of knowledge.

This is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). For dependence on that alone is pervaded by the necessity of its occurrence when it is possible; if there were no such necessity, then dependence—which is the opposite of independence, which is the undisputed pervader—would absurdly follow.
Therefore, there must necessarily be something to be depended upon that is distinct from Māyā. He demonstrates this by means of the term "kalā," which is established by scripture (āgama).
One also acquires knowledge through speech; for it is recited in the *Āgama*:
"Consciousness, empowered by *kalā*, has its range revealed by *vidyā*" (*Svacchanda Tantra* 11.98).
Here, "empowered" (*udbalitam*) means brought to a state of heightened power (*udbalanam*), that is, led to an excellence of strength (*balotkarṣam*).

That consciousness which has attained the state of having external objects as its domain takes the form of the power of agency (*kartṛśakti*), and that for which blue and other objects have been revealed by *vidyā* [is the subject]. Thus, regarding the instrument (*karaṇa*) that operates when [the self] is differentiated,
the function of *kalā* occurs in a general sense, because even a lame person is seen to make an effort to walk.

But specifically, for the fulfillment of that [perception], the organs of action [are responsible]; whereas as for the perception when [an organ] is divided, there [it is] by way of generality through knowledge, since even a blind person perceives form by means of the distinctness of taste; but specifically, for the fulfillment of that, the organs of cognition [are responsible]. As for the determinations of passion and time:

These have been examined here as an incidental discussion [prasaṅga] insofar as they exist as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) for the states of being a knower and an agent, and not as their instigators; for at the beginning of creation, manifestation takes the form of creation (*nirmāṇa*), whereas during the time of empirical discourse (*vyavahāra*), it takes the form of cognition (*saṃvedana*), since [the object] has already been previously created. That...

Anticipating the objection as to how [the Lord] manifests [objects] without distinction— whether at the time of the initial creation or during the period of worldly transaction— he explains that very manifestation is itself the act of production by the words "And whatever... He clarifies this very point.

[This is] by means of an objection and its resolution, starting with "nanu" and so forth. The phrase "appearing as distinct" implies that [this] is a conventional usage (*pratirūḍha*). "Because of being limited" means because it is constricted from another [source] by virtue of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*).
"Because of the perception of duality" [is said] even though [the subject] is unlimited in its own nature (*svarūpa*).

The intention is that their atomicity (*aṇutva*) results from the limitation of their activity (*vyāpāra-pārimityāt*). Regarding the phrase "of these [among] those," the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), referring to those who are established through scripture (*āgama*) and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as appropriate.
The expression "always indeed" is used because they—those cognizers of the past and even further past—are omniscient; therefore, it is not...
For them, there is never the manifestation of a state not previously experienced. Now, one might object:

"How can even the Lords of Mantras (mantreśvara) and others possess subjectivity (*pramātṛtva*) in the state of liberation when their respective offices have expired? Consequently, it is inconsistent to say that [subjectivity] is eternal. To dispel this doubt:
And he has stated that even in the state of liberation, the liberated souls [remain] distinct from Paramaśiva, who consists of beginningless Śiva-nature.

"There is a distinction between those whose Śiva-nature is manifested through the removal of impurity. By this point, according to the dualistic position, liberated souls (aṇus) are indeed distinct; and their manifestation as Śiva-nature is entirely uninterrupted, including omniscience and the manifestation of the three times.

[The manifestation of those belongs to the illusory level (māyīya). With respect to their manifestation as established in the illusory subject, even that does not fail to shine forth for them, because of their omniscience. By means of the word "and" (ca), he says this: that in the case of the Mantreśvaras, upon the exhaustion of their office, even in liberation, there is another [subject] in that very place.

First, regarding the atom (aṇu): through the power of performing the observance of initiation (*dīkṣā*), vows (*vrata*), recitation (*japa*), austerity (*tapas*), meditative absorption (*samādhāna*), and conduct (*caryā*) as the cause for attaining the state [of Śiva], even that [atom]—upon its transition [to that state]—possesses omniscience; thus, in the case of the *traiyambika* [initiation], the state of being a limited subject (*pramātṛbhāva*) is indeed not at all diminished with respect to the mass of objects, even when compared to a Mantreśvara.

"It is always thus" is the correct [conclusion]. "Of the atoms of the bound souls" (paśvaṇūn) means with reference to the mere minuteness of the atoms of the bound souls in a general sense. By the word "and so forth" (ādi) in the phrase "principles, worlds, and so forth," there is the inclusion of the categories (bhāva), the elements (bhūta), and so on, as well as the limited powers (kalā), mantras, words (pada), and phonemes (varṇa). "Even jars and so forth" [is included].

In view of their belonging to that same class, there are none that are absolutely unprecedented. The word *iti* indicates that the aforementioned fact serves as the reason for the forthcoming point—that they were created and withdrawn at that very time. He states that same reason in brief with the words beginning "by virtue of having been created previously," and so forth.

To this extent, regarding what was stated in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)— namely, "How could there be emanation (*nirmāṇa*) at the time of worldly transaction?"— the prima facie proponent has merely demonstrated that he speaks with reason. To the doubt, "In that case, how is there emanation?", [the author] begins by illuminating the specific possibility of further [explanations]:
"But he sets it aside" (*parākaroti*). "Then" (*tadā*) means at that time. "By which" (*yena*) means by the attainment of unity.
"That being so" (*tathā sati*) means if, for every subject (*pratipramātṛ*), there were distinct and separate appearances of jars and the like, as well as the appearance of the body.
"It has been said" refers to the *Vāsanāprabodhasūtra* (1.5.5).
And in the sūtra: "For the conscious self alone... (1.5.7). Now, one might object: "In this way, the distinction between subjects would surely collapse. To this, he says: "But not... (page 326).

Thus [it is said]. The sense is that the arrangement of distinctions such as thirst and the branches of the tree remains exactly as it was within the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and so forth.

Furthermore, in order to show that there is no disagreement on this point by anyone, and to connect what he will say—namely, "and knowledge"—with the present subject, he states: "That very manifestation is called knowledge."

Thus he explains. [An objection: But surely, the manifestation in the form of a jar or the like is the object of cognition; how then could that be knowledge? He replies: "And it consists of the activity of the cognizer. If it is asked, "How can that very thing belong to him? he replies:
"By virtue of being grounded in the cognizer," and so forth. [An objection: But if this is so, then by the will of the cognizer...

"By means of the logic of connecting with other subjects (*pramātṛ*), there is at every moment the manifestation and withdrawal of both objects of knowledge (*prameya*) and subjects; how then does the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) burn them away?"—this objection, as stated in the *Vṛtti*, is dispelled by the words "and that" (*sā ca*). This is for this purpose as well.
Thus, it is not merely the sequence of the pure and other forms that is the subject matter of the term *krama* as it occurs in the commentary;
rather, there is also the continuous flow of the succession of conjunctions with other subjects (*pramātṛ*). This [flow] has become dispersed.

He summarizes by saying "thus, therefore. The fivefold activity is perceived through both creation and maintenance. That commentary which exists in order to reveal the meaning understood from the Sūtra—apart from the two qualifications "entering the body and so forth" and "outwardly"—is as follows:

Regarding the phrase "the body and so forth," he explains it with the words "but when... The term "all at once" (sakṛdeva) means without succession, that is, as something uninterrupted; by this, the word "simultaneously" (yugapat) in the commentary is explained with the intent of showing the absence of temporal sequence. Now, with what intention did the author of the commentary [speak] while not yet touching the state of Supreme Śiva?

This state of Sadāśiva and Īśvara has been described. It is said here that the primary subject under discussion is that within the conscious Self (*cidātman*), the entire aggregate of objective phenomena appears solely as "I" by virtue of its internal nature.
Regarding this, someone raises a doubt: "How can it be that the category of objective phenomena appears within the manifestation of 'I'?"
It may indeed be so on the plane of Sadāśiva-Īśvara, because it is understood [there] through the unfolding of "this-ness" (*idantā*);

but how does the category of objective entities (*bhāvavarga*) shine even on the planes of Sadāśiva and the others? For that [category] is sequential and possesses a fully developed state of "this-ness" (*prarūḍhedambhāva*). To this, it is replied: first of all, the form of objective entities is indeed "this."
And this [state] exists here as well; however, regarding the gradual process of its unfolding,
it is the manifestation of other powers beginning from the time of Māyā.
In that case, the very manifestation of entities is their ultimate nature, whereas the emergence of internal distinctions is the unfolding of the power of *vidyā*. Therefore,
just as in the state of Sadāśiva and others, things exist precisely as they are through a differentiation that rests in non-duality due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

In *māyā*, things appear as distinct; likewise, in the state of Śiva, they exist here as absolute non-differentiation. Thus, in the realms of Sadāśiva and so forth, they appear through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—this very matter is established by this commentary passage denoting the stage of sovereignty (*aiśvaryadaśā*).

By stating the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), he shows that the subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*) is understood through the context, using the words "established" (*avasthita*) and so forth. And thus, by this aforementioned mode of the object of knowledge (*prameya-prakāra*), the meaning of the sūtra to be stated is established without effort. || 7 ||

"Since the manifestation of the internal object remains present, what is the use of considering other causes?"— with these words, he concludes the subject at hand in order to instill it in the disciple's mind, having temporarily interrupted it with an incidental discussion on the investigation of reflective conceptualization (*pratyavamarśa-vikalpa*) and so forth.
Thus, whether in memory, or in conceptualization, or even in cognition intent upon exclusion (apohana), it is certain that an internal appearance is indeed present. (8)

Thus, by means of the sūtra "In this way, in memory" (*evaṃ smṛtau*), [the author], unifying the three sections concerning the removal of memory, cognition, and exclusion, stated: "The Lord alone illumines this;
therefore, although objects are distinct and external from the perspective of the bound subject (*paśu-pramātṛ*) regarding cognition and so forth..."

Nevertheless, since it is the ultimate subject alone who knows, remembers, and determines, it follows as a matter of course that the appearances of jars and other objects exist only within [the subject]; this is established without effort. However, if the body and so forth were the ultimate subject, then the appearance of jars and other objects would reside therein.

"What could be conjoined with what?"—this is the meaning of the Sūtra. The commentary here is almost entirely self-evident. The word "prāk" refers to the Sūtra on knowledge, memory, and so forth (1.3.7). The word "na hi"—where one *hi* indicates that this very reason was already stated in the Sūtra regarding the manifestation of the Self's own abiding state—thus he shows.
Since this has been stated as the reason for establishing the subject matter at hand, therefore it follows that they manifest precisely as they are internally situated.
This is indeed logical. For if it were so, then in the reflective awareness "this is a jar," the state of being an object of cognition (*vedyatva*) alone would become manifest;
thus, some form of selfhood (*ātmatā*) would exist. By this much, the term "conformity" (*ānurūpya*) has been explained. Now, one might object:
the manifestation of entities consists in the reflective awareness "this," and not in the reflective awareness "I."
Restating this objection, he refutes it with the words "And not...
[as previously stated] up to (1.5.2).

In the two sūtras beginning with "ahaṃpratyavamarśa... (1.6.1), he brings this into agreement with the words "saiva ca" ("and that very same"). The particle *ca* indicates both the means of agreement and the inclusion of another view. This has been stated in the *Kakṣyāstotra*:
If all experienced objects were not well-guarded by being assimilated into your own self,
they would take on the nature of a non-deceptive realization of reality.
then that which is called memory would not exist at all.
And so forth. || 8 ||

Now, if there is indeed no distinction between the internal manifestation in recollective and conceptual cognitions— occurring in ultimate reality— and the external manifestation occurring through the power of *māyā*, then by what is that distinction produced which appears as clarity, lack of clarity, and so forth?
In response to this doubt, the Sūtra states:
"But [the nature] in knowledge, which consists in appearing as an external object, is innate; however, in recollection and so forth, it exists in the form of a prior experience. (9)
Although this lack of distinction exists, nevertheless, a distinction also exists because of the presence of a cause for distinction;

this is what is indicated by the word "but" (kintu). For instance, previously, when the appearance of a jar was emitted within a cognition whose nature is external manifestation, [the reading *avabhāsana* is supported by manuscript *ka*].
Having arrived out of his own autonomy and with no other refuge, [he appears] either at the first sight during the time of conventional practice or at the time of the initial manifestation.

Therefore, it is "clear" because of its connection with the manifestation of the unprecedented (*apūrva-unmeṣa*). For in the act of manifestation, the manifestation being extended is both unprecedented and clear; thus, like a jar (or cloth) produced by the act of creation, it is both unprecedented and clear. Otherwise, how could even a jar [be so]?
Sometimes it may be unprecedented, and sometimes it may not; however, it is only in the form of that [original] action that it is followed by its effects.

But in memory and the like, this [action] does not arrive with independence. Since it arises by taking refuge in the impressions (*vāsanā*) of prior experience, it is therefore—as if soiled by enjoyment—like a discarded flower offering (*nirmālya*), faded and withered.
Such is the manifestation. For what is called "continuity" is indeed the state of experience as a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), and experience consists of the manifestation of blue and so forth;
thus, by the force of attaining identity with that experience, that manifestation of the object appears in recollection and the like.

[What is the appearance of the object? It is not something to be manifested by way of being unobstructed—thus, it is indeed indistinct. By the words "summarizing the meaning of the aphorism" up to "it unfolds," he introduces the first half [of the verse]. The phrase "in both creations" refers to that which is characterized by unity.

In this essence of the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "this" and "I," which is both the pure Lordly state and elsewhere the impure state— even during the time of empirical transaction— there exists a sequence of cognitions (*saṃvid*) consisting of direct perceptions (*sākṣātkāra*), which is a succession of experiences; knowledge (*jñāna*) is thus characterized by the manifestation of external objects.
It has been described in three ways. "Sahaja" (innate) means that which has emerged solely through the sovereign freedom (*svātantrya*) of the Blessed Lord.

He introduces the second half [of the verse] with the word "smṛti" (memory). Now, [one might object]: for the Supreme Lord, whose ultimate reality is unbroken light and awareness (*prakāśavimarśa*) and sovereignty, [is there not...]
Anticipating the objection that "recollection and so forth would be impossible," he refutes it by demonstrating that it is precisely for that very Self,

which has assumed the state of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), that it is logical— according to the principle already stated— that it is that same Self which recollects, resolves, conceives, and excludes with respect to this or that body and so on. Thus, he uproots the objection.

Regarding the phrase "of the knowers of the field" (*kṣetrajñānām*): [an objection is raised]—"But since the commentary states 'in the knowledge that consists of external manifestation,' the divine creation (*aiśvarasarga*) has not been touched upon at all; what, then, is the intention there?"—to this he explains with the words "the state of the Lord" (*īśvaradaśā*). This [state] is not something [separate].

The third stage is such that it can withstand being counted separately; for that consciousness, like the consciousness of Paramaśiva, accompanies everything. Therefore, how could there be any separate consideration of manifestation (*ābhāsa*) therein?

The intended meaning is as follows: "of that" refers to the unification with other subjects. "It has been stated" refers to the statement in the commentary that this occurs "within the *cittattva* (the principle of consciousness).
He confirms this very point with the words "for this very reason. Regarding what was said—that the unification with other subjects is created by the Lord in a gradual sequence—from that...

This is appropriate. As for what is said—that the activity of living beings everywhere is governed by Īśvara—the author clarifies this very point with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*). [He does so] by means of the power of *kalā*.
By virtue of its capacity to support the limited agency of the individual,

the Lord manifests as such by making manifest bodily movements such as walking toward an object like a village that has been made the object of desire; "that [power]" refers to the divine power (*aiśvarī*), which, although consisting merely of a single worldly transaction, is nonetheless sovereign.

The phrase "even from another" (parato'pi) means that even in the midst of such activities as going and so forth, which have been described, it is manifest within me alone. However, he shows that this divine activity is indeed clear even at the time of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) by the words "the double moon, etc. This is a *dvandva* compound containing a *bahuvrīhi*. In that regard:

By the first word, sensory delusion is subsumed, and by the other, mental delusion; thus, having established a fourfold "new creation" within the cognitive sphere of worldly activity— through the integration of another subject, through bodily engagement, and through the two types of delusion— one proceeds to the sphere of action.

Regarding the established rule in common practice, he says "the jar. The phrase "as in the case of the principles" (*tattveṣv iva*) serves as an example of similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) in view of the fact that there is no further production after that.
However, the reason (*hetu*) for establishing this similarity is "because it was created at the beginning of creation."

By the phrase "even without seeing smoke," he dispels the suspicion that this is an inference (*anumāna*). He establishes its distinction from well-known recollection (*smṛti*) with the words "is it not the case that... The word "ascertains" (*avasāyati*) is to be connected with what precedes. [An objection: Why is the word "ādi" (etc./and so on) extended so far?

Why is it not explained that [the cognition] which grasps the conceptualization arising immediately after direct perception [is the object]? To this, he says: "that which is being seen" (*dṛśyamāna*). But surely...

Thus, even though a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises from a recent perception, it is logically correct to regard it as being produced solely by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), just like a conceptual construction of something currently being perceived, because its prior temporal existence does not manifest; with this intention, it is held that such a construction is not to be included under the term "beginning" (*ādi*).

He states another alternative with the words "or else" (*athavā*). He will explain that the subject's (*paśoḥ*) autonomy pertains to the aspect of *joining* the objects to be conceptualized within the independent options of the two sūtras to be stated—namely, that [the object] is indeed innate (*naisargika*)—but not to the aspect of the objects being joined; for one cannot experience water and fire [simultaneously] if they have never been experienced before.

The phrase "someone might connect" means that by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)—which have as their objects those portions being connected by way of having as their object the things being conceptually constructed—are indicated; this is the connection.
This is stated metaphorically (*upacāreṇa*) in order to demonstrate that there is no real distinction here between the object and the subject.

"Those objects" should be understood as conceptual constructions (vikalpa) whose objects are those very things; for it is precisely from such an appearance of an object— known by the name "saṃskāra" because it is a manifestation concealed by the internal veil of darkness— that [the cycle of existence arises].

It has arisen from the awakening of the majesty of the removal of veils; although at that time there is no ultimate identity between that appearance of the object and consciousness because it exists in a state of potentiality due to deep sleep, nevertheless, through the covering of darkness, it does not appear as something separate.
Could it be that [the object] was previously perceived? Since it was already established, now, upon the cessation of the veil (*varaṇa*), that very same thing appears as distinct;
thus, he says that memory consists in the form of differentiating that [object]. He will clarify this very point with the words beginning "the appearance of what was experienced" (*anubhūtābhāsa*).
"Because no specific [agent] is mentioned.

The remaining intention is this: since there is an absence of action without an agent, when no specific [agent] is designated, the comprehension of the general [agent] as the agent necessarily follows. || 9 ||

Now, it has been stated that in a cognition whose nature is the manifestation of the external, the manifestation of the internal occurs without mediation due to its innate character; this is what constitutes "clarity" (sphuṭatva) residing in the manifestation.
This is not the case in other instances such as memory and the like, because there is an intervention by something else.

It is indeed already established that the manifestation lacks clarity because it appears externally and because it is not simultaneous; so for what purpose is the second half [of the verse]? True, but it is as follows:

Apart from direct experience, there would be only a single account for all cognitions; yet this is not the case, as he shows with the aphorism: "That [account] exists only as innate in a conceptual construction that moves according to its own will."
Because it appears in the sphere of the intellect with whatever shape is intended.

"Freely" (*svairam*) means independently, without dependence on the instigation of another; he who acts, arises, and passes away with such a nature—due to the internalization of mental distraction (*cetaso vyākṣepa*)—the external appearance of blue and so forth, which consists of an internal manifestation, is not something that does not exist as natural (*naisargika*). It is indeed natural.

Moreover, it exists. To the objection— “Is it not the case that this [conceptualization] is not innate, for even there, that cow or horse is conceptualized precisely as having been made an object of prior experience?”—
he explains with the words “Just as,” [describing] an elephant within whose mouth three tusks are joined, bristling with ten white teeth.

When situated on the plane of the knower (*pramātṛbhūmi*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)— characterized by a clear intellect— manifests an external object momentarily according to its own will; thus, by virtue of its connection with spatial form (*saṃsthāna*), it possesses conformity to experience (*anubhavānusāritva*), and this [conformity] is innate (*naisargika*).

Even when the portion [of the object] is applied as "it does not exist," it does not depend upon experience because it lacks a reference to the prior time; however, through reflection on the reality of the object, it was previously stated that "those objects are thus. But according to experience, [one proceeds] with the "closing of the eyes" of an elephant (*gajanimīlikā*).
The meaning of the aphorism is that in the theory of the manifestation of objects (*ābhāsavastuvāda*), the established order is according to the manifestation; thus, novelty alone is logical.
Now, one might wonder: "Is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) here independent, as in the Buddhist view, such that it was stated so in the commentary?
He dispels this misconception with the words beginning "the knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*). He states the purpose of the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*):
Regarding the phrase "place and so forth" (deśādi):

this statement is intended to refute the dependence [of the object] upon factors such as the place and time it was apprehended by a previous experience, as well as the assistance of other perceivers. Therefore...

The very appearance of an object is its ultimate reality; and this [appearance], while being experienced, cannot be subjected to the forceful imposition [of a different nature] by squeezing one's fingers.

The meaning is: "it exists," thus [it is] an entity (*bhāva*). "Distinction" (*vibhāga*) means that this distinction of objects, established by experience as consisting in the presence and absence of being produced by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), is accepted. By this distinction of objects, for as long as...
The connection with what was previously perceived is useful, insofar as it is brought within the range of verbal expression; yet that manifestation is not ultimately real, as will be clarified later:
"of the lights of separate lamps... (2.3.7).

Thus it is stated in the Sūtra. Now, one might object: "If [the object] attains its own specific characteristic (*svālakṣaṇya*), then its nature as a universal (*sāmānyarūpatā*), which is contradictory to that, would be lost;
and consequently, even that expressibility by words which was established by means of that [universal nature] would be undermined.

To this we reply: "It is not so," and here we state the reason with the word "tathā" (thus). For when there is the state of being a cluster (*nikurumbarūpatva*), that very state [of being a cluster] exists.

The contradictory nature of being a warrior is like that of being a soldier within an army. It is eternal and all-pervasive because of its connection with all times and places [all places, according to manuscript *ga*]. Consequently, that which was seen previously and that which is seen now are one and the same; it is not, however, through the power of synthesis (*anusandhāna*) or by effort.

The connection is as follows: this "oneness" (*ekatā*) is a conceptual cognition (*vikalpapratyaya*) that serves as the basis for the application of linguistic expression and conventional designation;

that universal (*sāmānya*) belongs to such sensory consciousness (*aindriyikaṃ vijñānaṃ*), which is a manifestation arising from the awakening of its latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Now, if in this respect...
What else, then, is this "arising from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of prior experience" other than something innate? He says: "the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
The phrase "just as before" means that this has been established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) just as in the preceding sūtra.
For within the category of objects whose essence is manifestation, it is the very act of manifesting that unfolds preeminently; for that very reason...
Those who have reached a firm conclusion [regarding the nature of reality] maintain that the world is merely the expansion of the Lord’s power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).

And as long as this act of manifestation remains unprecedented, innate, free from mediation, and characterized by a vividness embraced by its very momentariness, so long too does the manifestation remain vivid and ever-new.

Thus, it has been shown that even for a jar, its newness here is exactly in this manner and not otherwise. For this very reason, by way of the appearance of what was previously perceived, there is no occasion anywhere for talk of "creation" in the ultimate sense; for everything is always itself, by virtue of its nature as light.
Since there is no possibility for the manifestation of anything within ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*), novelty arises rather through the process of the act of appearing.
"Even from Kulagiri and other [scriptures], it occurs through the reasoning stated thus:
'uninterrupted at every moment... (Stavacintāmaṇi 112). Consequently, even the possession of the power of eternal emission (*sṛṣṭi*) and so forth is indeed brought about.

The intended meaning is that it is not the case that this is not possible for the Blessed One. Whatever manifests in whatever manner, that is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*) in that very manner, just like light; and thus, the manifestation of entities as both unprecedented and as having a prior existence is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). For the conventional usage of "ultimate reality" [is defined by this].
It is pervaded by mere manifestation in that manner, because no other cause is possible.

If one thinks that for an inhabitant of the Coconut Island (*nālikeradvīpa*), the appearance of earth and so forth is not known as "this-ness" (*idantā*), yet the appearance of its existence as a real entity (*sattvavastutva*) is indeed known at the time of perceiving his own body—[we reply: But surely...

When, within the embryonic body, his primordial consciousness first awakens as the "I"— having for its object the body and the vital breath— it also takes the body and so forth as its objective domain; at that time,
because that specific characteristic of the body and so forth is absolutely unprecedented [to him],...

"How could there be a conceptual cognition (pratyaya) associated with verbal expression in that case, since it lacks the status of being made an object of linguistic convention, such that it would be born of mental impressions (saṃskāra)?"— it is this doubt that [the author] cuts away with the words "nevertheless" (tathāpi).

"The nature of manifestation... (1.5.11)—this has indeed been established previously here. In the reflective awareness of "this-ness" (*idantā*), even without the intermingling of the phonemes *i*, *u*, and so forth, there occurs a natural indication resembling the movement of a finger, brought about by the Lord’s power of *māyā*.
"In the convention of all other words, [the object] is indeed possible as something artificial, like a painting on a wall.

Having thus stated the division of objects, he concludes the subject at hand and connects it with the words "And so" (*evaṃ ca*). [This refers to] "in the state of having the nature of a universal" (*sāmānyarūpatāyām*).
The meaning is: "in that state where distinctness has not been grasped through a disregard for mutual conjunction.
By the phrase "each preceding [moment] was indeed seen," he primarily highlights the very fact of being previously perceived;
it is not the manifestation of an object as it reaches the state of being an object of independent conceptualization (*svatantra-vikalpa*).

That [object] was previously experienced; however, the universal aspect (*sāmānyāṃśa*) which takes on a form being conjoined within that very conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not something new, for conceptual construction is not independent with respect to that aspect, since it depends upon the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of prior experience. In this context, "in that" (*tatra*) refers to the independent conceptual construction within the commentary (*vṛtti*).
It has been taught that, because it must serve as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and because here a locus characterized by mere proximity (*aupśleṣika*) or the like—

which would require two independent entities— is impossible, and because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of the subject and object being identical in nature, the locus is defined as that which is pervaded by the process of internal inclusion (*antarbhāvana*).
He shows that it is understood [in this way] by the word "independent" (*svatantra*).

Having thus explained the attainment of the internal meaning through the force of the sense (*arthasāmarthya*), he explains it also through the force of the context (*prakaraṇasāmarthya*) by means of adopting an alternative position, starting with "or else" (*athavā*).

Thus, that which was summarized in the *Smṛti*—namely, that "the internal manifestation remains present"—is precisely what has been made manifest by these two sūtras through this division. Accordingly, the locative case in the word *vikalpe* in the sūtra functions by presupposing the previously introduced meaning of *antara*; and in accordance with that:

The word *tatra* also occurs in the commentary (*vṛtti*). And by means of explaining the commentary, the reality (*tattva*) of the Sūtra has been explained here, for it was stated that "the exposition (*vivṛti*) consists in the expansion of the commentary. Thus, one should pay attention to this principle in various places hereafter as well. || 10 ||
In the course of investigating the variety of appearances— which arose as a consequence of establishing the occurrence of internal appearances—
that too has become established without effort, according to the principle: "When one thing is established, another topic is also established" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.30).

Thus, by virtue of attaining this established conclusion (*adhikaraṇasiddhānta*), he demonstrates through the aphorism that the primary purpose of this treatise is the revelation of the means for the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of one's own self as being of the nature of the Lord (*īśvara*).
Therefore, because of the manifestation of the intended representation exactly as it is desired, both cognition and action are clearly established for every living being. (11)
Because it is absolutely non-existent externally, the manifestation of that which has not been experienced as a correct delineation preceded by mental construction (nirmāṇa).
(Page 336)

This has been shown by way of a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*): for this very reason, from Brahmā down to the smallest insect, all living beings who possess vital breath— that is, those who maintain life through the conceit of identifying with a body and so forth that are objects of cognition— possess both knowledge, which consists of manifestation, and action.
Because it consists of the form of the manifestation of *ullekha* (mental delineation), the pair of powers is established as being independent;

this is what we have now stated most excellently and firmly: "The Great Lord is the Self of all by virtue of the union of knowledge and action"—this is the meaning of the aphorism. [This applies to] "all."

The phrase "beginning with the many" (*bahuvānopakramam*) refers to sovereignty (*aiśvaryam*). The use of the singular number indicates that, from the ultimate standpoint, there is indeed only non-duality, even though a dual appearance exists within the realm of *māyā*. The connection is as follows: because it is made to appear externally, it is therefore "externalized," and so forth. And right here in the middle [of this discussion], for the sake of this very reason:

"Clarification by way of exclusion (vyatireka), indeed... [Not "nanu ka"]. And this application of the commentary (*vṛtti*) occurs precisely in this middle section; thus he says "ityādi" and so forth. "Yathā" means:
by which manner of the present context, this has arrived—that the *kṣetrajña* is not only [present] on the plane of the intellect (*buddhi*) by means of memory alone...
It manifests the object as something to be known and as something external,
even through the operation of independent conceptualization; thus, by this method of demonstration, that very purpose for which this effort to begin the treatise exists is also [established].
The sequence for determining the means of recognizing the nature of the Lord has been concluded and attained.

How so? He says: "by this," meaning by the manner of activity consisting of autonomous conceptualization as described. "The conjunction of accomplishments" means that other things previously under discussion are also accomplished.

If that which is "merely not far from the mode" is not illuminated in the commentary (*vṛtti*), then in the aphorism (*sūtra*) this collection of proofs is established by the word *eva* (only/merely) together with the word *ataḥ* (hence). For it is indicated by the word *ataḥ* that the status of being a reason for the preceding aphorism is not abandoned; however, by the word *eva*, the status of being a reason here [is affirmed].

This very point, as it proceeds, establishes another thesis; however, no further reason (*hetvantara*) needs to be stated therein. Thus, by excluding the occasion for stating a further reason, the "accumulation of proofs" (*siddhisamuccaya*) is effected. This is the sense of the phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) in every instance.
The explanation should be understood as follows: "by specific modes of activity.
For even animals, for no apparent reason, appear as if possessed by fear or joy.
By the maxim: "Having observed that an action is preceded by cognition...

[and so forth], the venerable Bhaṭṭapradyumnapāda, having established that the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) are merely the expansion of the power of consciousness (*saṃvit-śakti*), [stated] that...

Having extensively explained the sovereignty of the manifestation of conceptual construction, one should consider that the very meaning of this sūtra is the essential point therein. Thus, by this much, the power of exclusion (*apohana*), which favors the powers of knowledge and memory, has been established in detail. May there be auspiciousness! 11.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Examination of the Power of Exclusion (*apohana*), in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, the great devotee of Maheśvara.
(Page 338) Now begins the seventh investigation:
The flood of the essence of consciousness, agitated by the shimmering waves tossed about by its own expansion.
I salute the great ocean of Bhairava-consciousness, the essence of the flowing nectar of immortality.

Thus, by means of these three reflections, the powers of cognition (*jñāna*), recollection (*smaraṇa*), and exclusion (*apohana*) have been primarily determined; as for the nature of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) which has been merely touched upon here, that was intended solely to establish its status as a power (*śaktitva*) by removing [any notion of] autonomy (*svātantrya*) from those very powers. Now, however—

There exists the substratum of that power, and it is of the nature of Maheśvara because its essence consists in the sovereign freedom (svācchandya) regarding the conjunction and disjunction, the resting, the concealment, and the manifestation of that power; however, it is not...

If that which is the locus of the powers of burning, cooking, sweating, and so forth— being insentient like a mass of fire— and that which is both [the power and its locus] were not internalized... (1.3.7)

This has been indicated in the Sūtra and must now be determined. In that regard, first of all, the mere substratum exists; for the sake of determining this, there is this intuition (pratibhā) which... [is to be examined].
This fourteen-verse section, beginning with "ityādi" and ending with "vyavahāro'nubhūyate," [describes] therein, by means of one [verse], the essential nature of the substratum alone.

This is the designation. Furthermore, by means of these two [positive and negative concomitances], it is established that linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is possible when there is a single substratum (*āśraya*), but not when it is absent; thus, the demonstration of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is presented in sequence. And although linguistic usage resides in the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), its ultimate repose lies in the nature of being (*bhāvarūpatā*).

The nature of the relationship between cause and effect has been stated in one verse; however, that which is characterized by memory, whose ultimate reality is the repose within the subject, is also [stated] in one [verse]; while worldly transaction, which follows all practical activities and is characterized by the distinction between the real and the unreal, is [stated] in eight verses; and [the remainder] in one.
This is the conclusion regarding the summary meaning (*piṇḍārtha*). Now, the meaning of each sūtra is examined. As it was said:
"Of everything" (page 339).

"It is established that knowledge and action belong to the living being; how so? For in the Vaiśeṣika system, the substratum of knowledge and action has already been refuted, since [the self] is distinct from those various attributes... (1.2.6)
Having raised this very objection here, and wishing to establish that single substratum in accordance with his own philosophical system, he first introduces it by way of its essential nature:
"And this intuition (pratibhā), which is colored by the sequence of various objects..."
That Great Lord is the subject, whose nature is non-sequential and infinite consciousness. || 1 ||

Although this activity, appearing as "the jar manifests," is observed as being connected to an object, nevertheless, that is not its own light; rather, it is consciousness itself that shines in such a way, because it flashes forth as residing solely within the subject, in the form "it manifests to me. As the Śruti says:
"Everything shines only after Him who shines" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.15), and so forth.
For this very reason, Bhaṭṭa Candrānanda stated:
"That which appears from the mere delineation of the form of the Seer is connected with His shining."
Pratibhā is the manifestation of entities in a manner contrary [to their ordinary appearance].

Thus, although it was described as having the nature of an objective entity (*bhāvadharma*), by the phrase "residing in the self" (*ātmasaṃśrayā*), it was stated that it is nothing other than the repose within consciousness; however, due to its association with the delineation of objects, that manifestation— which is essentially of the nature of awareness— appears as the substratum for properties such as succession and so forth, which belong to the external world.
It maintains [this]. And therefore, that very thing— namely, the sequence of objects and entities, which consists of a variegated form characterized by succession and non-succession and so forth,
and which is produced by the power of space and time arising from the Lord’s sovereign freedom— is "colored" or endowed with that sequence, that is, the temporal and spatial progression.
According to the principle stated in [the verse] "only that which is distinct from objects of cognition... (1.5.21), this intuition (*pratibhā*) is always self-luminous for everyone;
and in reality, because it lacks the calculation of space and time due to its inward-turned nature, it is [eternal].

(Page 340) That very Blessed One is non-sequential, whose nature is infinite consciousness, whose essence is awareness devoid of delimitations such as space and time, [and who is the ground] of the entire aggregate of means of knowledge and their results.

Maheśvara is one who possesses the sovereignty to perform acts such as the imposition of fetters (saṃyojana) according to his own will, who consists of the pure self-reflection (*ahaṃpratyavamarśa*), and whose lordship is fashioned through the consecration of his own portions within the imagined lords such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others.

The knower (*pramātā*). And since that intuitive flash (*pratibhā*) is undeniable, its locus is established by its very nature as being turned inward; one need not resort to any further effort in this regard—this is what [the author] indicates. He introduces the meaning of the aphorism with the words "as far as" (*yāvacca*); the sense of the word "and" (*ca*) has already been explained. That which...
Whatever appears has an inward-facing manifestation;

that is the Self, the subject, and it is precisely that which is one's essential nature (*svabhāva*), and it is precisely that which is sovereignty (*aiśvarya*)—this is the connection [of the words]. Furthermore, the particle *ca* (and) signifies that once the preceding entity is established, this [nature] is established without effort; thus, it is characterized by a conjunction (*samuccaya*).

He restates what was previously said in order to define it, by way of a concise conclusion, with the words "Thus, therefore" (*tadevam*). In that context—that is, when it has been established in this manner—the state of being external is implied by the very term "sequence.
And that [externality] consists in its being perceivable by both types of sense organs, due to the power of some [particular] thing. (2.4.4)
In this context, it will be stated that [the object] is precisely the ground for the conceit of being within the range of the instruments of the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*).

He demonstrates this with the words "the sense-organ of intellect" (*buddhyakṣa*). By the term *buddhyakṣa*, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) should also be understood, for even that which is the object of the mind (*manas*) is indeed external. Therefore, by the word "precisely" (*eva*), this very externality is indicated.

Having intended [the object] as that which is to be communicated, it was expressed by the word "appearance" (*ābhāsa*). How is it understood if that [intention] is not stated? He says: Because of its very external form, it possesses the status of being primarily an object; therefore, it is logical that it is understood when its nature as an appearance is accepted. This refers to what was introduced at the beginning as "insight" (*pratibhā*).

When it should have been said "she" (sā), what is the intention behind the masculine designation? It is this: that which is the internal sequential manifestation of the reality of consciousness (cittattva) is not established for the world due to the power of delusion caused by the illusory energy (māyā-śakti); therefore, it is established as being sequential.
By the phrase "having restated the external manifestation" (*bāhyāvabhāsamanūdya*),
it is not merely that [manifestation] itself which is being enjoined— which would result in the use of the pronoun *sā*— but rather the subject (*pramātṛ*).

Maheśvara is that *pratibhā* (intuitive flash), which is augmented by the subjecthood (*pramātṛtva*) and the sovereignty (*maheśvarya*) [of the Lord], and has thus attained full development; for that very reason, due to the power of this augmentation, the masculine designation is appropriate. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), however, this is a definition of the fruit.

In the commentary, because it is stated "it has been done," the word *yat* is employed as a restatement (*anuvādaka*) and does not indicate that [the object] is the substratum for the property about to be enjoined; nor is it intended to refer to a previously established form that has been made the recipient of the intention to establish a property.

The word *tat* (that), by virtue of its prescriptive function, indicates that [the Self] is the substratum of other attributes. Nor are the prescription and the restatement in the Sūtra entirely explicit; thus he says, "not indeed explicit" (*na spaṣṭau eva*), using the particle *eva*.
For as long as it is stated, "That alone is the Self," the suspicion that there might be some other Self does not subside.

"The ritual procedure (*vidhāna*) results in the fruit alone"—with these words, he reconciles the commentary's statement that "the Self is a mere appearance," while pacifying a potential doubt by means of the passage beginning with "although" (*yadyapi*). Now, one might object: "How can that which, due to its inward-turned nature, has no connection with time, be said to pervade the time of all consciousness? To this, he says:

"And so," it is said; this has been stated both in the commentary (*vṛtti*) and in the aphorism (*sūtra*). Now, if that very [Self] manifests in this way and the universe is the unfolding of its power, then there is no need to teach its recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). To this, he says:
"merely" (*kevalam*). That which is of such a nature regarding objects in their sequence—
However, [it is] "natural... (1.6.9);
according to these two sūtras, there is the manifestation [of the Self]. The word *tasya* ("of that") is a compound. || 1 ||
Having thus stated the thesis, he first sets forth the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by means of a sūtra in order to establish the nature of that which possesses power through logical reasoning:
"In a single cognizer, through the various gateways of distinct cognitions..."
When entities are established, this kinship is possible. || 2 ||
As for what is proclaimed— that "the determinations of objects are grounded in consciousness"— that is not merely a resting place within various cognitions whose nature is consciousness.
It must be considered that conventional practice is not established by that alone;

rather, those various cognitions regarding objects such as blue or pleasure, which culminate in ascertainment, are themselves the "faces" or means. Being led by these, which are like the currents of a river, [the subject is carried forward].

When, by means of sheer force (*haṭhavāha*), they attain direct repose within the single great ocean of consciousness known as "I," then their mutual relationship— consisting of the states of knower and known, master and servant, cause and effect, and so forth— which is of the nature of worldly transaction, is established through logical reasoning.
It is appropriate. "Jñāteya" is the state of being kinsmen (*jñāti*), and their activity is such that they may recognize one another;

thus, their coordination is characterized by the mutual maintenance of each other's welfare (*yogakṣema*). In the ultimate sense, however, this is rightly understood as having consciousness (*cit*) alone as its vital essence.
He introduces the sūtra with the words "as far as" (*yāvat*) in order to define [the limit] by way of excluding that which is currently being traversed.

These two particles—*yad* (or *yadi*, according to the Ga. manuscript) and *tad*—have the sense of "since" (*yadā... tadā*). Alternatively, they are terms of measure intended to define a specific temporal boundary.

The meaning is that it is not possible to establish a systematic arrangement [of categories] for such a limited duration of accepted time; thus, "in a single group" (*aikadhyam*) refers to a few specific individuals, chosen by the subject's own preference, at a particular time. By the phrase "because of being of the same genus" (*samānajātīyatvāt*), [the author] [refers to] the Sāṃkhya and others.

It has been explained that for those who maintain that the Puruṣa is a single, all-pervading pure consciousness, how could there be any distinction among Puruṣas in the state of liberation, given that any variety of essential nature, location, or time is impossible? Furthermore, there is a mutual merging of subjects and objects.

"Having many branches": the locative compound (*saptamīsamāsa*) is used with the intention of specifying that one legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) is followed by another legal proceeding; however, based on its general nature and with the intent of non-difference, it is explained as a descriptive determinative compound (*karmadhāraya*). And this is so within the doctrine that the manifestation (*ābhāsa*) is the very life of existence.
He shows that conventional reality lacks substantiality precisely because it is merely an appearance, by means of the word "tataḥ" (therefore). || 2 ||

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that every instance of concomitance (samanvaya) ultimately rests upon a causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva), and that this [causal relation] exists only between distinct entities such as seed and sprout, or fire and smoke? Anticipating this doubt, the Sūtra addresses it by means of stating the previously mentioned positive and negative concomitances (anvayavyatireka).
(Page 343) [The author] provides corroboration with the thought that "by way of a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga), the reversal of that reductio (prasaṅgaviparyaya) will be obtained":
"[This applies] to objects possessing a sequence of space and time which are self-contained."
This [reality] is to be accomplished through a single manifestation; otherwise, what kind of coherence could there be? (3)

Otherwise— that is, if rest in a single cognizer is not admitted— then what connection could there be between objects such as blue or pleasure, their cognitions, and the determinations thereof, which are distinct in terms of space and time, sequential, and established solely in their own individual forms?

Not at all. For that possession (*samanvaya*) can be established, accomplished, and made known through a single manifestation—that is, through a manifestation that unifies the appearances of place, time, and essential nature; it cannot be done otherwise. The word "single" (*sakṛt*) has the intended meaning of negating differentiation.
[The author] has applied [this]. He introduces the meaning of the sūtra in brief by means of the sequence of prior and posterior [elements], and so forth.
How could there be a systematic consistency? Not at all. Herein is the reason:
because of the path of prior and posterior, which is characterized by having a sequential order.

Due to the difference of place and time, and because of the difference in essential nature implied by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), this [difference] is not unestablished for these [entities]. To explain this, he explains again according to the sequence of the *sūtra* through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words beginning with "place. Commenting in this manner, [he shows that] even the words of the *sūtra*...

He instructs that the application should be made in both ways. Alternatively, "priority" refers to the relationship of cause and effect; the word "and so forth" (ādi) expresses predominance. Thus, the meaning is this:
regarding that which is called a "relationship characterized by the predominance of the relation between cause and effect," therein—

The meaning that "bondage is association, which is mutual non-abandonment" does not hold. By the words "if," etc., he explains the Sūtra [passage] "not otherwise"; "then" refers to the time of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).
For it has been stated more than once that the nature of entities corresponds to their respective manifestations (*ābhāsa*) as far as those manifestations extend.

Regarding what was stated as "with respect to conventional usage," that very point is clarified by the phrase "as the activity of the subject" (*pramātṛvyāpāratvena*). The term "denoting an entity" (*bhāvavācinī*) means "denoting an action" (*kriyāvācinī*).
(Page 344)
By the word *bhāva* (existence/activity), he also expresses the nature of the operation of the means and the end as something in a state of vibration (*parispanda*).
Now, for what purpose has this been stated separately in the commentary? He replies: "In its own form" (*svarūpe*);
that is, regarding the manifestation in its own form—which consists of both illumination (*prakāśana*) and ascertainment (*niścayana*)—there is this presentation of differentiation.
This is for the purpose of dispelling that doubt. Now, one might object: "Even so, since there is a difference in place and time, a unification (*samanvaya*) will occur;
what is the need for resting within a single cognizer (*ekapramātṛ*"? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "manifestation" (*avabhāsa*).
But has not the author of the *Vṛtti* explained by this much [the phrase] "of those which are self-contained," and not "manifestation" (*prakhya*)?
He says, "The foot does not fail to turn," because "it is precisely due to the difference in manifestation" (*avabhāsabheda*). He will explain this in the passage:

"The sequence depends on difference, and difference [arises] from the presence or absence of manifestation" (2.1.4). "Consisting of non-difference" refers to its essential nature (*svarūpa*); "the manifestation of non-difference" refers to the state of consciousness (*saṃvedana*).
"The non-difference of location has its life-force in the non-difference of essential nature (*svarūpa*). He clarifies this very point with the words "for it is the essential nature itself.
However, due to the connection of being supported by that [essential nature], even the substratum is conventionally designated as "location.
[The opponent suggests: "In that case, one should accept that the object consists of both difference and non-difference. To this he replies, "And not so," with the word "tat" (that).

The inconsistency [of the opponent's position] consists in its being illogical due to contradiction with the meaning of the preceding statement. The word "agent" (*kartṛ*) refers to the state of being composed of a single cognizer. The word "ahead" (*agre*) refers to the occasion for establishing the relationship between cause and effect, recollection, sublation, and so forth. He now determines which portion of the Sūtra the commentary (*vṛtti*) beginning with "that [agent] is non-different" (*so 'bhinnaḥ*) explains.

And regarding this "iti": as for that which is stated in the Sūtra, "In what other way is there a systematic connection (samanvaya)?", the meaning is that the "other" mode of procedure implied by the word "other" has been set forth by this commentary (vṛtti) passage. || 3 ||

It was asked, "What is concomitance? In that regard, first the causal relation itself— which is the most pervasive— is examined by means of the aphorism regarding perceptions and non-perceptions that fall upon various distinct parts [of the objects].
The establishment of the relation between cause and effect arises from a single cognizing subject.
