In this case, when fire is not perceived, smoke is not perceived; therefore, [the existence of] fire is established through direct perception.

Even in the case of perception, since smoke that was previously unperceived becomes perceptible in the immediately succeeding moment at that very time, there is perception; thus, having established five instances of perception and non-perception—namely, two perceptions and three non-perceptions— [The text continues: ...it is said: "In this way, the causal relation between fire and smoke is established through five [instances of] perception and non-perception. This is the meaning. Here, the first non-perception is the non-perception of the cause (fire) prior to the effect (smoke). The second non-perception is the non-perception of the effect when the cause is absent. The third non-perception is the non-perception of the cause after the effect has ceased. The first perception is the perception of the effect when the cause is present. The second perception is the perception of the cause when the effect is present. Thus, by means of these five, the causal relation between fire and smoke is proven. It is not the case that the causal relation is established merely by observing the coexistence of fire and smoke once, for even in the absence of a causal relation, such as in the case of a lamp and its light, their coexistence is observed. Therefore, it is necessary to establish the causal relation through the aforementioned fivefold method of perception and non-perception. Furthermore, one must understand that the word "five" refers to the number of instances of perception and non-perception, and does not refer to the number of individual moments. This is because it is impossible to perceive or non-perceive a single moment. Consequently, the first non-perception consists of the non-perception of fire over a duration beginning from before the smoke appears until the moment immediately preceding its appearance. Similarly, the second non-perception consists of the non-perception of smoke over a duration beginning from before the fire appears until the moment immediately preceding its appearance. Likewise, the third non-perception consists of the non-perception of fire over a duration beginning from the moment immediately after the smoke has ceased until the point where the smoke is no longer perceived. Similarly, the first perception consists of the perception of smoke over a duration beginning from the moment immediately after the fire has appeared until the point where the smoke is no longer perceived. Likewise, the second perception consists of the perception of fire over a duration beginning from the moment immediately after the smoke has appeared until the point where the fire is no longer perceived. In this manner, the causal relation between fire and smoke is established through five instances of perception and non-perception. However, this is not a universal rule; for example, in the case of the causal relation between the seed and the sprout, it is impossible to observe the aforementioned five instances of perception and non-perception. This is because the seed perishes immediately upon contact with water, and thus it is impossible to perceive the seed at the same time as the sprout. Nevertheless, the causal relation between the seed and the sprout is indeed established. Therefore, it should be understood that while the establishment of the causal relation through five instances of perception and non-perception applies primarily to cases such as fire and smoke, the causal relation between the seed and the sprout is established through a different method. Specifically, the causal relation between the seed and the sprout is established by means of the following four instances of perception and non-perception: first, the non-perception of the sprout when the seed is absent; second, the non-perception of the sprout when the seed has perished; third, the perception of the sprout when the seed is present; and fourth, the perception of the sprout when the seed has arisen. In this way, the causal relation between the seed and the sprout is established through four instances of perception and non-perception. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the causal relation is established," it should be understood that this refers to the establishment of the causal relation between the seed and the sprout, rather than the establishment of the causal relation between fire and smoke. This is because the context concerns the refutation of the Sāṃkhya school's doctrine of the transformation of primordial matter (*prakṛti-pariṇāma*). That is to say, the Sāṃkhyas assert that all phenomena arise solely from the transformation of primordial matter, and they do not admit a causal relation between distinct entities. To refute this, it is stated that "the causal relation between the seed and the sprout is established," thereby demonstrating that the causal relation between distinct entities is indeed possible. Alternatively, it may be interpreted that the phrase "the causal relation is established" refers to the establishment of the causal relation between fire and smoke, and the subsequent statement "the causal relation between the seed and the sprout is established" serves to demonstrate that the aforementioned method of establishing the causal relation through five instances of perception and non-perception is not limited to cases like fire and smoke, but applies generally to all causal relations. In this sense, it would mean that the causal relation between the seed and the sprout is also established through five instances of perception and non-perception. However, as explained above, since it is impossible to observe the aforementioned five instances of perception and non-perception in the case of the seed and the sprout, this interpretation is difficult to accept. Therefore, it is more appropriate to interpret it as explained in the first instance. They imagine that the establishment of the relation between cause and effect consists in the ultimate realization of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). But this is merely their own wishful thinking. For instance, let fire be ascertained by the perception of fire, and likewise, let smoke be ascertained by the perception of smoke.

Even by means of non-perceptions (*anupalambha*), the absence of duality and the absence of smoke are thus conventionally designated. Therefore, these perceptions and non-perceptions culminate in the ascertainment of the mere referents of the nominal stems—namely, "fire," "smoke," "absence of fire," and "absence of smoke"—just as in the case of "pot" or "cloth. Thus, these...

In each and every distinct part or portion, they have the nature of falling [into dependence]; that is to say, the nature of the locative case-meaning characterized by dependence, such as: "when there is fire, there is smoke; in the absence of fire, there is an absence of smoke."

How could they determine the nature of the causal relationship, which consists in positive and negative concomitance? In our system, however, those various objects of cognition are unified because they are moments that kindle the single ocean of consciousness, following the stream of the aforementioned perception and non-perception.

The various distinct natures characterized by mutual dependence, which are brought forth by the sovereignty of the subject (*pramātṛ-svātantrya*), are manifested by the subject; they are not like the objects of a dualistic pair (*dvandva*). Being thus manifested is itself causality, and being manifested in that way is causation. Regarding the state of being an effect (*kāryatā*), [it was discussed] previously in the *Vṛtti*.

He explains; the purport of the commentary (*vṛtti*) is that, however, he will point out—in the phrase "but from the other [view]" (*paratastu*) and so forth—the untenability of that [position] in the rival system (*paradarśana*). As for the meaning of the words (*padārtha*), the author of the *Vivṛti* himself will provide the application according to the method of *yojanā*, in order to indicate its wider scope; even in the introductory [verse], the word "also" (*api*)...

By the use of the term "diverse" (bhinnagrahaṇa), he says this: if a single means of valid cognition, such as perception and so forth, which is sought to establish one [object], is itself diverse and occurs sequentially, how could it bring about the establishment of a single object of knowledge? For that would be contradictory; therefore, one must strive to effect its unity.

Furthermore, the very reality of the subject (*pramātṛ-tattva*), being inward-turned and consisting of self-awareness, is capable of subverting the multiplicity of perception and the other means of knowledge; for origination is nothing but being an effect (*kāryatā*).
(Page 346)

Production is causality; both of these, moreover, do not involve anything additional to the positive nature of the entity itself, nor do they pertain to existence [as a separate category], as will be stated:
"That which is non-existent is non-existent... (2.4.3).
In this context,

by the passage ending with "And it is not logical for that which is insentient to be thus... (2.4.19), [the author] establishes that the agency belongs to perception and the other means of knowledge themselves, as indicated by the words "having brought about" (*āpādya*) and "having attained" (*prāpya*).

Regarding the opponent's position, however, he states "But when... because that meaning is untenable. "Appearing as its own object" means that it brings about its own linguistic usage; the sense is that it gives rise to a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that performs that usage.
The word "only" (*eva*) indicates how utterly remote [this view] is from what will be stated next with the words "How much more so... (*kiṃ punaḥ*).

He causes [the word] to manifest in the Buddha; for the intention is that even in the absence of fire, there is still the verbal designation "fire. The word "then" (*tadā*) indicates the time of the conventional usage of the absence of fire, but it does not refer back to that [absence]; for if it did so, the connection with the suffix *dā* would be untenable.
Here, he raises the Buddhist position with the words beginning "Now" (*atha*) and ending with "some harm" (*kācit kṣatiḥ*).

The intended meaning is that there is no single causal relation whatsoever which must be established with such effort by unifying perception and non-perception into a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore... [as follows].

The meaning is: "from that [which is determined] as it was perceived. The compound *yathādṛṣṭaḥ* is formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.4 (*sup-supā*). Because even a manifold object is thus determined by this [perception], for that reason, the relationship of cause and effect becomes indeed determined; such is the connection [of the sentence]. [Objection: But surely, from such a determination alone...

"How might that [relation] be established?"—to quell this doubt, he investigates the cause with the words "for that of which" (*yasya hi*), referring to fire (*agneḥ*). "Its existence" (*yadīyasattām*) refers to the existence of smoke. [Objection: But both fire and smoke have been perceived; where, then, does the relation of the employed (*prayojya*) and the employer (*prayojaka*) find its final rest? He replies: "In this way" (*evam*).
"Therefore" (*tasmāt*) means: because that which is subsequent is not the motivator, nor is that which is simultaneous; therefore.
"As observed" (*yathādṛṣṭam*) is here an *avyayībhāva* compound.
(Page 347)

He says, "without overstepping the [fixed] observation. Now, one might object: in cases such as the rise of Kṛttikā being necessarily followed by the rise of Rohiṇī, there would be a relationship of cause and effect. To this, the resolution is: "it is not an origination. For, according to scripture, the wheel of the constellations and zodiac signs remains fixed, bound to the nave of the Pole Star (dhruva).

This has been understood; for it is indeed observed that the moon, the sun, the stars, and so forth, undergo concealment and non-concealment depending on the presence or absence of high mountains. Now, one might object: "Even if something is not perceived, it can be established through reasoning, such as the sense organs or the unseen force (adṛṣṭa). To this, he says: "Or it is logically possible."

Even that which is logically untenable is accepted as true for some time because its logical consistency has not yet been attained and its causal efficacy has not been recognized; however, in this case it is not so. Thus he says:
"it is employed" (*upayujyate*), [referring to something] whose logical consistency has not been considered and whose causal efficacy has not been observed.
It is not that the establishment of experience through non-sublation—such as that of a southerner [perceiving] a *karabha* (a young elephant)—is not to be trusted;

however, it has been shown that this rule does not apply here. The phrase "it appears" (*avabhāti*) indicates either the logical possibility (*upapatti*) characterized by the presence of a sublater (*bādhaka*) regarding that which is appearing, or the proof of the stability of its existence.

The intention is to state that "the application (*upayoga*) is what must be expressed. To prevent the possibility of [the verb] *avabhāti* having the same agent as the subsequent [verb], the mention of *vā* was not made;
otherwise, it would have been more appropriate to have either three instances of *vā* or just one. Now, [an objection]: [Text continues: ...nanu... (Note: The provided fragment ends here).

Smoke and fire are indeed perceived as distinct; even in their conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), let it be granted that they are designated as having distinct forms. But how could a conceptual construction designate a single causal relationship? As for the conceptual construction again...

He clarifies with the word "again" (*punaḥ*), which indicates a specific distinction, that one should certainly not perform a perception produced by the force of [external] objects. This refers to the joining together, through synthesis, of distinct elements such as the staff and the person, in the form of a future sentence-meaning.

The conceptual construction "this" refers to the joining through differentiation of those things—such as quality and possessor of quality—which are inherently undivided, for the purpose of establishing their possession of intrinsic nature; and since there is a single verbal expression [for both], there is a causal relationship between these two. Thus it is said.
(348) Since those very two objects are apprehended by means of a single expression constructed through convention,
it is precisely from that such apprehension— a delusion arising from the cause of error— that they [perceive] a single relation.

They imagine that which is substantially real through the power of conceit. In this case, a single meaning in the form of the locative case-suffix appears as something distinct from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*); so how can it be said that "many [meanings] have not been seen before"? He refutes this with the words beginning with "And yet...
(*yāpica*). By the word *iva* immediately following the word *lakṣyate*, he indicates its lack of ultimate reality (*aparamārthasattva*).
For that characteristic is merely constructed by the power of conceit (*abhimāna*). As it has been said: ".................. how can that which is non-existent depend [on anything]?
and so forth. The word "that too" (*sāpi*) should be construed as "the form being characterized. The word "these" (*ete*) refers to conceptual constructions (*vikalpāḥ*).

The essence of this intellect consists merely in cognition, being empty of any external objective support (*pratyaya*); therefore, its objective support arises at the very moment of manifestation. Consequently, it shines forth only as the object while that manifestation itself exists.
Thus, according to the principle that "this phenomenon of appearance arises from something," expressive terms are joined together for the purpose of cognizing the distinction between entities;
it is by this logic that, in order to establish the well-known nature of being merely a head, one says "the head of Rāhu."

And [the expression] "cow, cow" is used to demonstrate the performance of a single purposeful action. Now, if some practical purpose is accomplished from such a conceptualized [object], then that object is indeed real.
To this, the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "In that which is so constituted. Even a red lamp seen by one with cataracts [is perceived] by its own...

An object performs a causal function by means of its own form, and not by means of that which is produced by error; it is the same here as well. [Objection: But surely all operations of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) rest upon a determinate ascertainment (avasāya), and such ascertainment is by nature conceptual construction (vikalpa), arising independently of the object.

(Page 349) By this very [argument], one should anticipate the opponent's suspicion that, because it does not touch upon the reality of things (*vastutattva*), the quality of non-contradiction— which was so laboriously established— will be rendered like "an elephant’s bath" (i.e., a futile effort).

"It pacifies [the afflictions] when it has become such" means that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed that which leads to attainment; furthermore, it is said to have the nature of a cognition that is conducive to the successful engagement with an object suitable for attainment.
Consequently, even if the ascertainment (*avasāya*) is obscured by error, nevertheless, regarding the aspect of the object suitable for attainment, it has been ascertained.

Since there is a recollection of the relationship between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) as that of subject and object, when an activity aimed at attaining a desired thing— culminating in the actual acquisition of that thing— is to be undertaken, there is no sublation whatsoever regarding anything occurring in the interval.

Even though the determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*), which precedes the process of activity and is primary because it constitutes the practical application of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), may have a corrupted nature, [the following] is stated here: this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
And the intended meaning (*tātparya*) here is this: in this context, manifestation (*prakāśa*) is indeed inseparable from reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: by the force of deliberation (*vimarśa*), every means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) determines its object of cognition (*prameya*) as necessarily connected with something else, not as something pure (*śuddha*). To say that it does not appear [as such] is an inconsistent statement. For instance, in some cases the object of cognition is [connected] with something of its own kind, in other cases...

It appears as being indeed conjoined with a heterogeneous object of cognition (*prameya*). And in every case, the conjoining with the nature of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is certainly manifested. Nor is that [conjoining] non-difference; for if there were non-difference, what would be the meaning of "conjoining"?
Nor is it difference alone, because there is a recollection of non-difference on the ground of consciousness (*saṃvid-bhūmi*).

For even if there were absolute difference, what would be the purpose of their coalescence? Therefore, from the external form up to its repose in the subject, whatever constitutes the body of an entity, within that its distinctness appears; and by virtue of that, its non-distinctness exists only through its parts.

And that very nature of relation does indeed manifest; it is thus revealed by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is sought after by cognizers (*pramātṛ*). It is precisely in this way that the reality of existence (*bhāvatattva*) is:
for it has been explained at length, and will be further explained, that "in whatever manner something appears, in that very manner it is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)."
The word "yāvat" suggests elsewhere that the probandum is established without effort; this very point is demonstrated by the phrase "where, however," on page 350.

Thus, by means of this collection of particles, he will clarify this very point: that when this object of knowledge (*prameya*) has been stated, this [conclusion] follows by necessity. And the particle *ca* (and) serves to aggregate the objects of knowledge.
Together with all that is capable of being denoted by the word "this" (*idaṃśabda*), which possesses a determinate form in terms of place, time, and shape—[with that, it is connected].

That which is non-difference is precisely what is determined as being characterized by that [non-difference], whether in the determination "this" or in the determination "jar," through the non-difference from all [its features] such as the broad base and so forth. As it has been said:
"Even when [an object] is restricted, this reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) occurs with respect to what stands before one."
It arises solely through the generality of the "this-ness" (idantā) inherent in all existing things.

Thus, in the investigation of the reality of exclusion (*apoha*): at that time, difference (*bheda*) itself does not appear. For difference would appear in this way if those other particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), which are distinct from the particular characteristic intended as the object of perception, were to appear then in their own specific form; or else—

If they were to be excluded, then because only the visible object would appear during that exclusion, those [other objects] would neither appear nor be excluded; thus, they are indeed identical with that visible object. He states the proof for this very point: "Otherwise," meaning that what did not appear at the time of establishing the linguistic convention cannot be determined from that word.

[It is inferred by someone: Just as from the word "pot" [one infers] a cow, so too from the word "this" all the specific individuals situated in front are determined, and from the word "pot," the specific individuals characterized by a broad base and a bulbous belly are determined;
thus, they do not fail to appear at the very moment of the formation of their convention. For, if they were not manifest...
That which is the manifestation of what is contradictory, its effect is the determination of that object through the word by way of a causal chain; this being perceived here,
it negates that which is contradictory to its own cause— this is thus the "perception of an effect of something contradictory to the essential nature" (*svabhāvaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*).

Thus, even when there is a singular reflective awareness (*ekāki-parāmarśa*), it exists in three ways: generally as "this," in its intermediate form as "a jar," and in its most specific form as "this jar is such-and-such.
Having established the manifestation of the relation in these cases, he now demonstrates that in the present context, it is established effortlessly.

Furthermore, by means of the introductory phrase "where," and by the word "therein," it refers to that investigation of reality (*tattvacintā*) which, when being performed, brings about even this which was previously considered impossible; while that [investigation] exists—
(page 351)
The construction is as follows: that which is universally established remains indeed established.
The word "again" (*punaḥ*) here indicates a distinction characterized by the absence of doubt.
By the phrase "a single reflective awareness," the fusion of the various manifestations is intended.

And [the phrase] "of other particular characteristics" clarifies that this very relation appears in many branches. For this very reason, he says: "In the establishment of the relation, all objects are established together with the relation whose nature consists of both difference and non-difference."
"His manner of conducting worldly affairs...
(verse 1). Thus, "discourse" (vāda) is merely a way of speaking; [it is said that] "all phenomena are by their own nature... [and so forth].

The phrase "and so forth" (ityādi) extends up to this point. Having thus introduced the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) at the outset, he restates the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*), etc., and then refutes it with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*), etc.
By the mention of the expansion of intuition (*pratibhā*), this internal manifestation of non-duality is of the nature of *māyā*.
By the phrase "the appearance of difference," he states that difference and non-difference, having distinct objects, are not contradictory.

By the word "both," he means both smoke and fire. "Not otherwise" means that without the manifestation of a relation, there would be "that and that," but not the sense of a genitive case; nor indeed is it the sense of the particle *ca* (and).

Even when there is immersion in a single cognition, there is a certainty through the unfolding of the manifold mutual exclusion (*anyonyāpohana*) as something distinct— namely, "it appears," "as a jar," "of entities," and "it is logically established. It is justified that [the object] is merged in the subject, because its non-differentiated form is attached to the subject.
In the absence of manifestation, difference itself could not be established; therefore, this non-difference is not contradicted by difference—this is the sense.

He provides the reason for why this very [non-difference] is primarily employed when there is a distinction between entities, with the words "for as long as... The fullness of being belongs to manifestation, that is, to the being that is manifesting.

The form extending up to the subject (pramātṛ) is the nature of manifestation, while the full form exists as identical with existence itself, consisting of the nature of consciousness and augmented by the freedom of reflective awareness (vimarśa).

Otherwise, if linguistic and practical activity (*vyavahāra*) were possible through mere manifestation alone, there would be no need for conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*); thus, even momentariness would be subject to such activity. However, since practical activity occurs through conceptual determination...

Since it lacks the nature of luminosity, even that which is insentient (*jaḍa*) could become a cause for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*); thus, there is no need for consciousness (*saṃvedana*). If it is argued that the transaction occurs by means of both [the object and consciousness], we say no, because the two do not exist simultaneously.
Nor is it correct to say that the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*), colored by the shadow of luminosity, functions in such a way; for that...
If it were to perform the function of illumination, then it would be illumination itself; what, then, would be "shadow"?

And since its nature is that of illumination, if it consists of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that very form of illumination, then it follows that illumination itself is essentially reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). Thus, illumination [is established] through determination.

If it is argued that "the conventional usage" (*vyavahṛta*) is the cause of conventional usage (*vyavahāra-hetu*), then conventional usage consists of cognition (*jñāna*) and verbal expression (*abhidhāna*). Now, the first manifestation of a determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) is not itself an object of cognition; for it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), since it has already been stated that if it were luminous by another, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and other such faults. Verbal expression, moreover, is conceptual construction (*vikalpana*); and that too—

If it is of the nature of manifestation, then that very same [objection] must be repeated; and if it is of the nature of non-manifestation, then insentience (*jāḍya*) results—this has already been stated. Self-conceit (*abhimāna*) is likewise to be analyzed in the same way. Therefore, enough of this [discussion], which is like mixing the seasoning of momentariness with one's own imagined relish.

By means of the dregs of the "dry" Sāṃkhya: for whatever possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*) to whatever extent, it possesses that very form, just as blue possesses its blueness. Everything that possesses causal efficiency does so through a body that culminates in the repose of the subject—a body whose nature consists in the conceit of being an effect or a cause.

If it were not understood in this way, no form whatsoever would belong to anyone. Although this has been examined at every step, it is stated here again in brief so that it may not be forgotten. Now, it was argued that if that [form] were not determined, nothing at all would manifest; that is true, yet it is not that [the form] is undetermined, but rather—
"Disregarded" means cast aside with indifference, by those very [beings] fashioned through the Māyā of the Lord;
as he will say:
"Thus, by those who deny their own self-awareness..."

Thus: that which is "this" or "that," the universe unconnected with one another [or connected, according to manuscript *ga*], as well as one's own verbal composition, and whatever else has manifested through the nature of distraction, and whatever exists without inquiry— [all this is the Self].

(Page 353) "Fallen upon the tongue" refers to that very thing, such as delusion, agitation, and so forth. In the context of its function (*vṛtti*), the word *dhīra* emphasizes the state of being (*bhāva*). Because of steadiness, it is characterized by an unshakable state of being a grasper (*grāhakatva*) due to its one-pointedness.
[ka. That which is shaken off (*avadhūta*), or that whose firmness has been shaken off—this is called "neglected" (*avadhīrita*).
[The author] says "no" (*na ca*) to eliminate any room for the opponent's delusion that "surely there is a contradiction here.
"In what follows" (*agre*)... [text continues].

In the section beginning with "the connection between actions... (Pāṇini 2.3.1), it has been established that there is thus a state of identity with the subject (*pramātṛ*) everywhere; furthermore, it has been demonstrated that this identity exists even between two objects of knowledge (*prameya*), such as smoke and fire. Having thus established this, he now demonstrates it elsewhere as well, starting with the words "mutually" (*paraspara*).

The word is undivided and consists of a copulative compound (*dvandva*). The suffix (*pratyaya*) is the cognition (*pratīti*) produced by that [word], or that which produces it. Being composed of unity—meaning those in which unity is the primary subject (*prakṛta*), the topic at hand (*prastuta*), and the locus of rest—they are indeed such, yet they appear as "thus" and as "divided."

They manifest through a distinction that is to be supplied by another word. [Objection: But surely this is the power of the *dvandva* compound... [Reply: Without a distinction being intended to be expressed, what possibility could there be for non-distinction?
To this also he says: "Even when... (*yadāpi*). By the ablative case (*pañcamī*), the relationship has already been indicated.

Even in the absence of that [external relation], unity remains inherent by virtue of being merged within the nature of the action characterized by differentiation; for if all objects being dealt with did not ascend the bridge of such a connection, they could not sustain any course of worldly transaction whatsoever. Now, one might ask: "In this way, what [is the status] of entities?"

They are never disconnected; thus he says "only" (*kevalam*). The incoherent words that are the raving of the insane, as well as their cognitions (*cetāṃsi*), become valid for practical transaction (*vyavahāra*) precisely because they possess denotable objects (*abhidheya*).

And since those objects appear sequentially as objects of knowledge (*jñeyatva*), they are therefore not connected to one another; however, they are indeed connected by means of cognition in its form as the subject (*pramātṛ*).
Furthermore, when [the objects] are in cognition simultaneously, they are also mutually connected through their connection to that single subject.
This is the intended meaning. Now, by whom should their state of being thus connected be designated? If it were by that very madman himself, then—
If they were to adhere to a single self that lacks such adherence, then even that [self] would become insane. And he would not be insane;
here [the author] explains "those too," for the sense is that one who is insane does not engage in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
It has been stated that "not another" means that mutual attainment itself constitutes worldly transaction. In that regard, as for the relationship...

Regarding the definition of "formal conjunction" (*rūpaśleṣa*) and so forth which was refuted by the opponent, [the author] shows that it is in fact supported by the statement: "For formal conjunction is a relation, and how could that exist when there is duality?"—this is what is indicated by the words "And therefore" (*tataśca*). Since:

Mutual attainment alone is the basis for worldly transaction; therefore, even though there are many objects, they become unified within the cognizer in a fused form. For every cognizer, seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), whether acting or desisting himself, impels another to act.

Or rather, the agent of worldly activity (*vyavahartā*) is merely one who turns back [from activity], for no one ever remains as if presided over by a past entity. For such a person whose sole nature is worldly activity, this desire to act— which consists in spontaneously engaging in coming and going accomplished through the application of various means— is what is called "the desire to act."

Whether it be to turn back oneself, or to incite another to act or to desist, the desire arises through the wish to attain happiness or the wish to avoid suffering; once happiness has been attained, there is simply the wish for its preservation, and likewise in the case of the absence of suffering. And this [desire] which...

Desire, which exists at the outset as the cause for engagement in activity or withdrawal from it— whether directed toward oneself or others— in relation to the attainment of pleasure and so forth; in that [desire], the entire category of objects remains undifferentiated during the process of going and coming.

Or, being employed toward cessation, it will attain a manifold division. And that desire for the attainment of pleasure and so forth remains permeating the transmigrating subject throughout his entire life.
Therefore, even when an object to be accomplished through going and so forth has been reached, and even when the attainment of pleasure and so forth has been achieved, [the desire does not cease].

It indeed ceases. Therefore, this person consists of desire alone; he is described in the Śruti as both the giver and the receiver. And it says: "This person consists of faith... (Bhagavad Gītā 17.3).
Thus it is said.

However, this is the distinction: although it is generally full in the first category, it remains as something yet to be filled by some other mode; "this and this of mine... [Note: *pūrakāntareṇa* is a variant reading for *prakārāntareṇa*].
"May it be so through this sequence of means and the means to those means. But finally, by that much—even with such limited fullness—this desire of mine is fulfilled through this sequence.
Yet, that very [desire] is directed toward the intention of accomplishing the pleasure and other states produced from other entities.
Because she is about to be filled, she may also be considered "not yet full. As the scripture says: "The Goddess is always licking [the world] and is always full for the All-pervasive Lord;
she is the wave whose nature is will, and she is the surging river of the Self."

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might ask: how is it that the multitude of various objects exists within her without division? It is replied: "For she... Because it is so, therefore it is logical that she is the ground of non-division for everything;
this is the connection with what precedes. That desire, first of all, is manifested by the subject (pramātṛ), while she herself truly exists.
It is manifested by one whose self is craving for sense-objects; consequently, it does not follow each successive stage according to the maxim of the blind leading the blind,

but rather, even while being raised up, it proceeds according to the maxim of the tethering of a man's feet to the steps of a far-sighted person— [bound, as in the Gaṅgā edition]— aiming toward that goal.

Once aroused, licking it even more profusely and eagerly taking possession of it through her focused intent, she arises and becomes manifest in the initial stage; and in the final stage, being exactly as she was before, she becomes full and rests in her essential form. As it has been said:
And that very state of rest has been described as "due to the cessation of all dependence" (*Aja-darpana-prakāśikā* 23).

He illustrates, in sequence, the object being intended—which may be acceptable, dependent upon, or to be abandoned—beginning with the words "of fire," and so forth. From fire made of sandalwood comes fragrant smoke.

The activity intended as "let it arise," the activity desired as "let it be determined by me who is the king's man," that [activity] where there is indifference through the mere occurrence of a determination, and that [activity] such as "may my region not be filled with thorns, serpents, and the like"— from these...
Cessation is intended; by that, the desire is aroused. Or else, by means of the employment of speech, [the desire] of another, distinct from one's own self, [is aroused].

[ga. It is that intention (abhisandhi) which brings about the engagement of the person to be trained (vineya) with what is to be accepted, or indifference toward what is merely to be disregarded, or the cessation [of activity] regarding what is to be abandoned; by that [intention], it (the universal) is being brought forth. And thus, at the time of that intention, whatever has manifested in a general sense—

And specifically, each respective [object] flashes forth within that desire precisely as an undivided manifestation appropriate to the state of the venerable Sadāśiveśvara. However, when not intentionally aimed at, it flashes forth simply as "I," untouched by the power of separate manifestation, in accordance with the fitness of Śiva-nature; and it is not...
It has already been stated that there is some degree of sequence within the ground of Śrī Sadāśiveśvara;
for that very reason, this [ground], which is always of a full form, appears even to the unawakened as being both the first and the final limit (*koṭi*) in its true nature.
"...at the beginning and end of that [mantra], however, it belongs to the other.

This was stated with reference to one who is not fully awakened (*aprabuddha*). But for the well-awakened (*suprabuddha*), within the three words—the first, middle, and last—there shines forth nothing but uninterrupted light alone. Thus it is said.

The venerable teachers of the Purāṇas maintain that the mention of "being raised up" (*utthāpyamāna*) specifically in the middle [of the rule] is for the sake of depending upon the three preceding forms in the context of *para* (the subsequent element); otherwise,
if the word *vā* were used as being of equal status [to the others], the connection with the preceding forms would not be perceived here.
Because another entity is independent. By means of the words "avalepa" (ointment) and "pūrṇa" (full), he follows the traditional authority (*āgama*).

He applies this to the subject at hand: whether it be "king's man" and so forth, or "smoke and fire," or "snake and thorn"—whatever is diverse through mutual dependence, it is merely the determination of the nature of being a means (*sādhanabhāva-svabhāva*).

Or [it may be] pleasure or pain; and all that, in its entirety, disregarding individual distinctions, consists of various individuals such as royal officials and the like. That which is to be accomplished by it—that is, the specific form of activity directed toward the purpose of its fulfillment—is what is intended.

Activity directed toward both [attainment and avoidance] is diverse, according to the propriety of the object to be attained; whereas the act of cessation has as its sole object that which is to be abandoned. Whether this specific activity is considered to be accomplished by oneself or brought about by another, it is by means of the desire for that particular action that [the agent proceeds] as long as...
As long as an action— variegated by the acceptance of diverse means and results—
is specifically taken as its object, to that extent it is made variegated by the particularities of that action.
The connection with the manifold variety of causal factors and purposes becomes directly touched;

and although that [connection] is joined in form to that very will (*icchā*), it is— relative to the light of the limited subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*) who is contracted on the plane of the mind or the plane of the external senses— [as follows].

The division that exists within external form is indeed not abandoned; for that very reason, because its nature consists of both difference and non-difference, it is called a "relation" (*saṃbandha*). Now, if such a manifestation of division has occurred, then how could duality ever exist? To this [the author replies]: In this regard:
He says: "Even by way of distinction. The particle *ca* indicates a doubt or objection. Thus, there is a formal conjunction (*rūpaśleṣa*) with respect to their mere essential nature (*svarūpamātra*);
however, since they are not intended to be like iron rods [inseparably fused] with one another, but rather as factors of action (*kāraka*) with respect to an activity (*kriyā*).
When they, by way of being qualifiers or as related entities, bring forth a form that is distinct from their individual natures, then,
having entered into the non-inert Will, they too become non-inert and depend upon one another.
Relativity (*apekṣā*) is not untenable either; therefore, [the argument] that "it is non-existent" is refuted by its own admission.

"Indeed, all expectations are entirely abandoned..."—this may apply to the state of pure external form (where "pure" refers to *śuddhe* in the Gaṅgādhara manuscript), but not with respect to the entry into internal consciousness; thus, even a relationship characterized by expectation exists. Likewise...

In this very context of mutual expectation, according to the maxim "when both the past and the future are uttered," because it enters into the relationship of subordinate and principal, the auxiliary (*upakāraka*)—
being dependent on that which is to be assisted (*upakārya*)— is connected with the principal (*pradhāna*). It is subordinate to that.
"it exists"—thus, even a relationship characterized by dependence (*pāratantrya*) is indeed logical. Consequently, [regarding the objection]:

"Once [the object] is established, what dependence could there be?"—this which is said with the confidence of those who maintain the doctrine of an independent external reality that does not depend on cognition, [is refuted].
That is set aside; for there is no establishment or non-establishment whatsoever belonging to the poor entity itself.

By not accepting the practice of the vow (*vratacaryā*) as illuminated by the teacher Prakāśācārya—thus, the relationship is that of the benefactor and the beneficiary (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*). And this [relationship] must necessarily be admitted; otherwise, how could there be the simultaneous manifestation of what is desired and the state of being a seeker (*arthitā*)? And that...

It has already been stated that [the soul] depends upon the power ordained by the Lord. Now, an objection is raised: since a relation consists only of pairs among many, the establishment of a relation belongs only to two things, not to many;
for instance, if each individual were the object of a single unifying cognition along with multiple numbers, [then...]

In the case of "the king's man" and "the chariot and the horse," even then, the cause of the connection with the elephant— which is either unexpressed or merely implied— is brought back once more to the path of explicit reference; thus, as many as are the references regarding the elephant and so forth, just so many are there for the king as well.

"One [element] has a connection with one. How then was it said that "all of them have a connection through the blending of forms (*rūpaśleṣa*)"? This is true; however, this is precisely what is intended here: that the mutual connection, though occurring in pairs, becomes manifold-branched according to the principle of "blending and subsequent blending" (*melitānumelana-nyāya*).

It brings forth a single relationship called "union with the one" (sahamelanā), namely, the ground of the great relationship: "I am Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Bhūhart, and this is [the world]. On that ground, when the manifestation of the particularized aspect has been cast aside, [there remains only] "this."

For at that time, there would indeed be the full manifestation of plenitude, consisting merely of the state of "I-consciousness" (ahambhāva) which has entered into grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the universal nature whose essence is solely the single act of reflective awareness (*ekaparāmarśa*).
Thus, at that moment, that state of Sadāśiva and so forth belonging to the subject within *māyā* would come to be. Precisely for that reason...

In relation to the Blessed Lord, the relationship itself shines forth as the ultimate reality. For, according to the principle that "He knows" and "He remembers," even while touching the state of being a limited subject (*paśu-pramātṛtā*),
the Blessed Lord remains established in the state of Sadāśiva and so on, [realizing] "I am He."

The universe shines forth as consisting of universal manifestation. However, when extracted from that [universal state] through its connection with it, the multitude of objects appears as consisting of limited relations by the very power of its own necessity (*niyati-śakti*).
The mention of "means" (*sādhana*) and "end" (*sādhya*) is precisely for the sake of establishing the attainment of the state of duality described here.
And there is mutual grasping;
even those that are distinct attain oneness...
(page 359)
Thus, the use of the plural number is out of respect for the result. Therefore, this is the meaning established by the authority [of the scripture]:
the relation between entities is not unreal, because it is never unmanifested without it. If its form were unreal, it would be manifested even without that [relation].
"Just as a conch shell [is not yellow] without yellowness"—thus, appearing while lacking [the quality] is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of unreality; otherwise, it would necessarily not be unreal.
And here, the opposite of that is perceived—this is the "perception of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). And the reason (*hetu*) is...

This has indeed been established with effort; for it has been stated that the manifestation of anything is impossible without the appearance of both difference and non-difference. Furthermore, that this very [manifestation] is the relationship has also been explained at length.
This is intended to support the hearts of the disciples, which have been carried away by the continuous flow of various objects of knowledge.
He shows the summary of the meaning of the present sūtra for the sake of establishing the "additional insertion" (adhikāvāpa) with the words "tadevam" (thus, in this way).

By the word *pramāṇa* (means of valid cognition), he indicates their status as instruments (*karaṇatā*). The plural number is used to provide room for the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) that will be discussed later, beginning with the words "for [the instrument] does not... and so forth.
It suggests: "How could the establishment of a single object of cognition (*prameya*) occur through many diverse objects?

This means that they are subservient to, and governed by, the activity of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), namely the operation known as "establishing order. For it is not so; for indeed, [in the case where... (as noted in the Kaśmīra manuscript).

Due to its autonomy, it could not even be an instrument (*karaṇa*), because there is a contradiction between autonomy and dependence, and because the entire collection of factors such as the instrument has dependence as its very life-force. For it is the sword that cuts, when it is possessed by the action of the agent's exertion manifested through the firm gripping of the handle. But surely...
Anticipating the objection that "only the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) exists, and there is no such thing as a separate agent," he says "na ca" (and not). [The meaning is:

Without a cognizer (pramātṛ), the means of valid cognition itself is neither an instigator nor a bringer-about; thus, it is shown immediately by way of demonstrating how it becomes an auxiliary factor for activity up until the attainment of the goal.
[What is to be proven? The very nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), characterized by its validity (*prāmāṇya*), would simply vanish.

The reason for this is stated as "for, in regard to that which is shown by them" (*tadupadarśite hi*). For, regarding an object not shown by means of valid cognition, there can be no state of being worthy of acceptance or rejection.

By the principle that "from recollection arises desire," [cognition] arising [in this manner] is the cause of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*), by virtue of which it possesses what is called "the quality of leading to the attainment [of the object]."
The accomplishment characterized by the abandonment of what is to be discarded and the acquisition of what is to be adopted regarding appropriate objects is brought about;

and since that [accomplishment] is not possible in sensory consciousness precisely because it is non-conceptual, how can it be called a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that leads to attainment? If it is argued that the conceptualization occurring immediately after it would perform this function, that too—

[This is] non-existent. For conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) might merely conceptualize another object, thinking "I see the object seen," but it could not effect a distinction between the desirable and the undesirable based on memory arising from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of a prior experience.
If it is argued that conceptual construction, being of the nature of desire and characterized by longing, acts in such a way, then [the same would apply] to the prior experience as well.

If only the impression (*vāsanā*) of the form of the object is imparted, then how can desire arise in the absence of the recollection of pleasure, pain, or their manifestation? If it is argued that the impression of pleasure and so forth is also imparted there,
and that desire arises from the recollection of that [impression], then indeed, when blue is seen, how [could that be the case]?
Awakening [occurs]; blue and so forth are the causes of pleasure and the like; therefore, from the perception of that [cause], there is recollection regarding its effect. As it has been said:
"Because of the recollection of those very things seen when that [cause] is seen..."

Thus, it has just been stated that even the relationship of cause and effect rests within the single principle of the cognizing subject (*ekapramātṛtattva*), and is to be discerned through perception and non-perception. Furthermore, that very same object sometimes produces pleasure and sometimes pain; therefore, this is entirely beyond doubt.

Regarding the question, "By the mere perception of that object, what latent impression (*vāsanā*) could possibly be awakened?"— even here, it is the sovereignty belonging to the independent subject himself, who consists of the identity with his own self-awareness through infinite prior experiences, conceptualizations, and so forth.

That very [consciousness] unfolds as that which brings about the application of the volition toward a fixed form. This is what he expresses by saying, "it is dependent solely on the subject" (*pramātṛ-adhīna eva*). And this is indeed agreed upon by everyone who is skilled in the investigation of consciousness;
thus he says, "even by the Buddhists," even by those who deny the existence of a subject (*pramātṛ*).

The sense is that this must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, in the absence of external objects, it would be logical that self-cognition alone is the fruit of the means of valid cognition. (Page 361)

However, when an external object exists, it is logical to say that the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) is the manifestation (*prakāśa*) which is grounded in that external object. But when the determination of "desirability" and so forth does not occur from a manifestation grounded in the external alone— which has not ascended to the independent level of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)— then [that determination] cannot exist without it.

According to the principle that "there is no activity in the absence of that [cognition], and thus there is no attainment," the status of being a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) consists in its capacity to lead to attainment, which is dependent upon self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). In that case, they have declared that self-awareness itself is the fruit of the means of valid cognition.
Now, let this be so; nevertheless, how is the cognizer (*pramātā*) accepted by them through such [an explanation]? He says:

"And self-awareness alone" (*svasaṃvedanam eva ca*). By the word "alone" (*eva*), it is shown that no differentiation by way of own-nature, place, or time is possible here. For indeed, space and time, which belong to the external sphere, cannot be joined with inward-turned awareness.

This was stated previously. Even by the Buddhists, in order to exclude the nature of conceptualization regarding self-cognized [states] such as knowledge and pleasure, it has been said: "The essence of pleasure and so forth, which does not partake of anything else, cannot indeed be associated with a linguistic convention."
Therefore, their self-awareness is not accompanied by verbal expression.

In this regard, it has already been demonstrated that a connection with a word— which belongs to a different level and partakes of the nature of an object of apprehension— is impossible for that which is inward-turned and consists of the bliss of self-awareness and so forth; therefore,
whatever is of a different level from something else cannot be joined with it, just as awareness cannot be joined with a word, and likewise:

"Perception occurs through space and time. For conjunction consists in making something one's own by means of it as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); and that [conjunction], occurring only in certain instances, is pervaded by the property of being restricted.

If, however, it were to occur even between things of different orders of existence (*bhinnakakṣya*), then the consequence of non-restriction would follow, which is contrary to the pervader. Therefore...

A connection that is excluded from one level is pervaded by its opposite; and being on a different level is the opposite of that—thus, there is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). Furthermore, it has been stated more than once that even if there were a difference in essential nature (*svarūpa*), the consequence would be a lack of luminosity. Therefore:

By those who accept self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), the reality of the cognizer (*pramātṛtattva*) is necessarily accepted, since it is established through the implication that [self-awareness] is itself eternal, all-pervasive, and of a single nature; enough of this prolixity. The collection of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consists of perception, non-perception, and so forth; the collection of objects of knowledge (*prameya*) consists of cause and effect, and so forth; [regarding] the effect—
Regarding the positive aspects of the relationship between the cause, such as smoke, and its correlate, such as fire: when fire exists, smoke exists.

To show that such [cognitions] as "it does not exist" and so forth— which are negative in nature— rest upon the subject (pramātṛ) by means of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) regarding their object (prameya), and not by their own direct power, he states another interpretation beginning with "Or else. Furthermore, it is not the case that this [non-existence] is entirely non-existent, such that it would be unfit for verbal expression.

Saying "it is for the sake of indication," he proclaims that [the relationship] "should be so. He then explains the commentary beginning with "which is endowed with" (*samanvitā*) and so forth, intended to comment upon the first half-verse of the *śloka*, starting with "if, however" (*yadi punaḥ*).
Anticipating the objection that "the very nature of those two is the relation of cause and effect," he says:

And not so. For it has been stated more than once that an essential nature (*svarūpa*) cannot possibly reside in another. Now, one who seeks smoke does not act toward fire by conceiving the form of smoke as residing in fire, such that the otherness [of the object] would result in the otherness [of the cognition]; rather, [he acts] because [smoke] occurs immediately after fire.

Since smoke has been observed by him as being invariably present [with fire], therefore the seeker of smoke proceeds toward the fire—what contradiction is there in this? Having restated this, he refutes it with the words "in the fire," etc. That which is asserted by the opponent would be so only if fire were antecedent to smoke [and thus] known through the cognition of smoke.

The connection is with the word "by the visible" (*dṛśyena*). For, when smoke is perceived in fire, if the prior existence [of the smoke] has not been ascertained, no state of "immediacy following fire" could be apprehended as belonging to the smoke that is distinct from its nature as smoke itself. In the same way, it must be stated that fire also possesses the property of preceding the smoke; therefore—
To claim that causality and effectuality are grasped by a cognition that apprehends only the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) is false.

For if the intrinsic nature itself were such [i.e., possessed of causality and effectuality], then it would follow that even one who has not touched a second object would have the same cognition of it in a single act of perception; thus, this is an utterly improbable justification.
He strikes a blow with his heel at the very attempt to establish a cause-and-effect relationship based on external perception.

Even so, even in a cognition endowed with the two appearances of a white jar and a yellow cloth, let there be a distinct difference from two cognitions that grasp those respective forms in isolation by their own nature; however—
Just as some dependence is established between the two objects manifested by that cognition, so too [is there dependence] between fire, characterized by prior existence, and smoke,
characterized by immediate subsequent existence, even though they are simultaneous.

The cognition apprehending [an object] is indeed entirely distinct from two other cognitions that each grasp a single form; however, there is nothing in the nature of those two objects as they appear [to the cognition] that consists of mutual dependence.

From that, form is established. Furthermore, he demonstrates through the shadow of his own philosophical view—presented as a logical argument—that even this is impossible, stating: "Or rather, knowledge [too... Consequently, since the two appearances would both rest within the subject (*pramātṛ*), it would be merely two cognitions, not a single cognition.

Thus, having been refuted by the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) on the grounds that he has entered his own cloak [of self-contradiction], the Buddhist, in order to demonstrate the excellence of his own wisdom, anticipates the objection, thinking, "This which you have said is indeed reasonable," and thus raises a doubt with the word "atha" (now/if). If the opponent says: "For you..."
Thus, in the accepted doctrine, there is no such thing as an "appearance" (ābhāsa) that is independent;
rather, it is dependent upon the act of appearing. And that act consists in the operation of the cognizer (pramātṛ).
Therefore, when the act of appearing has two objects that are mutually distinct, then there are two things.

And since the act of manifestation is one, how is it that you cannot tolerate a single cognition as being endowed with two manifestations by means of its entry into its own sheaths? Even from what is thus stated, this might follow:
why are you seeking that particular cognition which is joined with two manifestations?
One should strive in such a way that, having abandoned the two cognitions as if each were a distinct appearance,

one should attain that very [reality]. Since it is only the difference in the nature of the cognition itself that is primary, and not any [difference] between the two objects, therefore, one who desires to reach smoke as another object—

Why, then, would one suddenly bring together the collection of causes such as fire and wood? For it is never observed that one who desires a jar ever maintains a collection of causes such as seeds, cloth, and weavers—even if they were once seen in association with the jar. Thus, by this much, it is established:
In this way, it would follow that cognition itself must be established as possessing two appearances,
because each object terminates in its own appearance. Yet even that cognition does not possess both appearances here, since smoke is not immediately contiguous with the cognition of fire.
And because fire is not understood as being prior by means of smoke as its probans,
the very same refutation previously stated applies; this would be the case if fire...

Because it was previously produced, it would be ascertained at the time of seeing the smoke. Therefore, by means of its very attachment to the object of cognition (*prameya*), the author anticipates another objection regarding that object: "Now, as for its mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
This refers to the single conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that has arisen from the two cognitions of fire and smoke; therein, those two [cognitions] exist simultaneously.

In consciousness, the two objects, manifesting simultaneously, establish their relationship as cause and effect through the mediation of a single appearance; for when two cognitions have arisen together at the same time, the fire— by virtue of its prior existence— is indeed determined at the moment the smoke is perceived.

"It exists"—this [position] he refutes with "that too. For at that time, those two [objects] do not exist in any cognition characterized by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because they have already perished; so how could those two be established? [Objection:
But surely they are established in such a way by a conceptual construction born from their residual impression (*saṃskāra*) and subservient to them.
Anticipating the objection that "that which is established by those two is said to be established by them," he says:
"For conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)... If conceptual construction, while relying upon its own form, seeks to be treated as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it is not [so] by this...

The relationship of priority and posteriority, as touched upon by those two cognitions, is established; yet, if it is so established, then that which has been established by this invalid means becomes situated even further removed from the state of ultimate reality. For indeed, we [hold] that even conceptual construction—

"We desire that they should touch the object"—this is another matter. If it is argued that "those two very appearances, having become conceptualized (*vikalpībhūta*), will act in this way," then he shows that this results in entering our own philosophical system by saying "atha" (now/if). If it is stated up to the point "they will establish [the object]" in this manner, then [it follows that] "tat" (that).

Therefore, from the reason being stated, this—referring to everything up to "siddham" (established) which is immediately about to be spoken—is established. How so? It is by means of the manner of reasoning that will be explained starting with "tatrāpi hi" and so forth, using the word "evam" (thus);
such is the syntactical connection (*vākyasamanvaya*). [Objection: But surely there are only appearances (*ābhāsa*)...

When it is said that "those who have fallen into conceptualization act in this way," one might raise the objection: "How can it be established that there is a single Self which, having reflected upon itself (*ahaṃpratyavamṛśya*), is the one who thus determines [the state of things]?
(Page 365)
"Calming [the objection] in this way," he states the reasoning previously indicated with the words "for even there.

For if, during the state of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), those two were indeed of such a nature, then who could perceive that "they perform now what was not performed before"? This is because [the distinction between] prior existence and so forth depends upon mutual relation.

Furthermore, the establishment of a posterior existence is not tenable; therefore, both of those [means of knowledge] touch only their own respective objects. However, this is established in the following way, as he says: "But in one...
For by means of a pentad of a stream of perception and non-perception, those five objects of cognition are established.

Cast into the single ocean of consciousness, by the power of its own waves of freedom, they are manifested and reflected upon as distinct from one another— like "pot" and "cloth"— through the differentiation of their respective appearances and reflective awarenesses, which consist of mutual dependence.

And therein, that single manifestation of the five which is produced by the operation of manifestation is the manifestation of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*); and the reflective awareness (*avimarśa*) of it is the operation of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).
And this very thing is the application of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), consisting in the conjunction [of the means and the result].

Reasoning (yukti) is said to be that which is useful for all worldly transactions; in its absence, even the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) are entirely ineffective. And thus it was stated by the Supreme Lord himself in the venerable Mukuṭasaṃhitā:
The sole means of proof in all matters is the activity of consciousness itself;
whether regarding worldly enjoyment or liberation, one should therefore place one's trust in it.
And so forth. Since he is indeed the unifier, everything desired is established. || 4 ||
Now, one might object: "If that which was accomplished through perception and non-perception is to be unified, then this much alone suffices for the admission of a cognizer;
what is the use of this [sūtra], since memory itself is already engaged in unifying that?
Anticipating this doubt, the sūtra [is stated].

In the case of memory, that very self-awareness which serves as the means of valid cognition regarding its own existence is itself the proof for the existence of the prior experience, and nothing else.

Whatever manifestation occurs in the recollection of those cognitions— which consist of perception and non-perception— that did not grasp their respective objects of cognition at the time [of the original experience], that manifestation is not something new produced at the time of recollection.

Because its nature is to grasp what has already been grasped, it is in fact nothing other than the prior experience itself. Furthermore, that [prior experience] does not manifest at present as something to be cognized separately, because it no longer exists; even if it were to exist, it would not manifest as an object of cognition.

In the case of manifestation, there would have to be a cognition of what is already known; that is not memory, nor has it been shown many times over that one cognition can be known by another cognition. Therefore, even though this [cognition] exists, if it were self-luminous independently, there would merely be two separate cognitions that are not mutually connected, and not—

Recollection [is as follows]: this must be admitted—that even at the time of recollection, the prior experience, while existing as an internal self-awareness, manifests as non-different from the self-awareness that makes known the very existence of the nature of the recollection. For it is not...

In this context, perception, inference, and so forth proceed as means of knowledge distinct from that self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). However, that uninterrupted awareness which pervades the duration of time is itself the reality of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*); thus, by the power of memory, there is a unification of the two perceptions.
The mention of "perception and the other [means of knowledge]" (*pratyakṣādīnām*) reinforces the unification we have accepted,
which is established by the power of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). And internal linguistic usage is characterized by recollection.

"By the principle that 'through recollection [arises] desire...,' that which pervades all worldly transactions is also dependent upon resting within the reality of the single cognizer; such is the meaning of the aphorism. Thus he has spoken in brief."

"Previously," and so forth. "The means of proof" (*sādhana*) refers to cognition in its established form. He shows its form with the words "previously," and so on. He says "previously" in order to avoid the charge of redundancy with the subject matter already stated in the section on memory (*smṛti*). For, in the section on the investigation of memory (*smṛtivimarśa*),...
Thus it has been said: "If the experiencer were one [and] the rememberer another, how could that other remember?

Since remembrance is not possible without a subject (pramātṛ), the identity of the subject is established through presumptive reasoning (arthāpatti) by means of an inference that begins with a negative concomitance (vyatireka); this is the meaning in this verse.

Experience and recollection are grasped as one by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*); that this very [unity] is the apprehension of a single cognizer is established directly— by nothing other than the direct perception of self-awareness, which is uncontradicted in every respect and undeniable in all its forms.

Since the identity of the cognizer has already been stated, what is the point of repetition? This is the commentary intended to quell the doubt that "the very self-awareness of the prior experience will serve as its own means of valid cognition."
The phrase "due to non-existence" (*abhāvāt*) is the end [of the statement]; he speaks [the following] in order to explain it: "First, cognition...

This means that there is an absence of that which is non-different from it—that is, non-different from the nature of an outward-looking perception—and by the word "also," it is meant that even the aspect of perception considered to be the object of knowledge (*prameya*), though it is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is absent.

It indicates this: having explained non-existence (*abhāva*), he explains the fifth [reason] with the word "tat" (therefore), meaning from that cause which is non-existence. As for the word "yena" (by which), although the discourse begins with a feminine gender, the reference "yena" is made to the entity in the form of the sentence-meaning, characterized by the establishment of the perception of the jar at a time past the moment of recollection.

In order to bring about the status of a sentence-meaning (*vākyārthatā*)— or rather, for its possibility— otherwise, there would be a mere reference to the word-meanings alone. Having thus stated that the self-cognition of experience is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding a prior experience, [the author] states that even memory is not a means of valid cognition in that regard.

He determines that it is consistent with other systems by stating, "and memory itself [is the proof]. It is not the case that memory alone is the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) there, such that its existence is beyond dispute. For would it be a valid means of knowledge there either by way of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), or is this not tenable? To this he says, "of that" (*tasyāḥ*).

Or [it might be argued that it is so] by virtue of having a distinct object; to this he says "nor even" (*nacāpi*). The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the state of being an object. Now, one might object: even that which has perished can be an object for the cognition of a yogi; the same would apply here as well. To this he says "nor even" (*nacāpi*). The particle *ca* expresses a doubt, while the word *api* serves to aggregate the logical reasons for refuting the status of being an object.

[The author] illuminates this point: "Surely, let everyone be one whose vision does not extend beyond this much; for there is no inconsistency in what is perceived. To this, he replies: "Or, if it exists... Indeed, let only that which is perceived be so; however, the attribution of anything further is without proof. If that is the case, then [the objection] applies to the previous position alone.
He shows that [the opponent] might object: "Let there be the attribution of a fault. And this [memory] occurs as "this" (idantayā).

Thus, when it has been made known that even memory is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding a prior experience, the opponent—having no other recourse—might resort to the position previously refuted.
"Since that position is established by experience, one disregards the refutations out of mere hope"— thus [it is said].
Taking this to heart, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) raises that very objection: "In the case of prior self-awareness" (*pūrvasvasaṃvedane*).

Let it be for now that [self-awareness] is established as residing in what was previously self-cognized; however, at the time of recollection, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that [prior state] apprehended? For even here [in the present], it is [apprehended] by virtue of its own luminosity (*svaprakāśatvena*).
Since the awareness of memory persists, it is not possible to assert that "at that time,
it was self-luminous. Furthermore, since this [self-luminosity] is not the object of sensory cognition and the like,
it follows by necessity that this self-awareness is known only through another instance of self-awareness.
"It is revealed as being a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) of a prior experience.

And that [prior experience] is not self-luminous at that time, because it is distinct from the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) [of the memory]; since the self-cognition of the memory is self-luminous at that time, there must likewise be another self-cognition that makes even that [memory] known. Thus...
This series of successive interrogations, which has come down by way of logical necessity, applies precisely to that partless prior experience;

for if one were to postulate parts through the dissection of even a single prior experience in order to conceive of portions of self-awareness, there would be an infinite regress, and that [regress] would strike at the very root.
It destroys the manifestation of prior experience.

Now, if another person—having had all opportunity for immersion in evil paths exhausted—desires by force alone to enter the true path, then he should be enlightened in this manner; thus [the author] says:

"Even now" (*adyāpi*) refers to the time of recollection. "From this" (*ataḥ*) means from that which is currently manifesting and thus cannot be denied. [The opponent asks: "But even if this much is established, what does it have to do with the subject at hand? He replies: "And that very same... Here, the explanation of the word "here" (*atra*) is "in the prior experience. And the syntactic break (*cheda*) occurs right here. But surely...

Memory is the effect of a prior experience; and it is not a marvelous phenomenon that it should cause one to infer its cause—thus, a prior experience is established. Anticipating the objection, "What then is this misplaced agitation?
he addresses it with the word *ca* (and), stating: "And when the prior experience is established... Thus it stands here.

The interpretation of the text is as follows: memory does not arise at the very same moment as the prior experience, in the immediately succeeding instant; however, at the time of memory, if the prior experience were manifest in the preceding moment—just as fire and smoke are—it might indeed be apprehended.

The relationship is one of cause and effect; however, at the moment preceding the recollection, there is no manifestation whatsoever of the experience, and it should not be thought that [the manifestation occurs] only at the time of the recollection itself, since the manifestation occurs through coexistence.

Because the relationship of cause and effect is not established. For this very reason, the word "prior" (*pūrva*) is included in the commentary (*vṛtti*). Memory does not have the status of being an inferential mark (*liṅga*) for an effect, because there is no appearance of the prior experience as something "prior" due to the memory of a past [experience]; if such an appearance existed, that experience could serve as the cause for the memory.

The phrase "it would be established" connects with the [preceding] commentary. Now, one might object: "Granted that the determination of a causal relationship cannot occur here through perception and non-perception, it will nevertheless occur through the very absence of the effect, just as in the case of the unseen faculty (*adṛṣṭa*) and the sense organs. With this intention, the opponent raises the doubt with the word "atha. [The response is: "knowledge..."

It has the form of memory. The phrase "it is conformable" means that since this specific aspect—namely, "the jar was experienced"—emerges from it, its source is logically postulated to be the very form of the prior experience;
for even though it does not manifest [directly] through inferential conceptualization, such is the intended meaning. As Bhaṭṭa said:

"Because of the suitability of the effect, [it occurs] prior to one's own consciousness, the non-consciousness, and the interval of recollection"—this [position] he does not tolerate, saying "that is not so. For the determination of being an effect is not based solely on the exclusion of the effect in cases such as smoke; rather, perception itself is indeed operative here.
