If it is asked, "What is this over-extension (atiprasaṅga)? [the author] shows that this is indeed the fault by saying, "The sense organ also," meaning it would have to be of the nature of cognition. Anticipating the question, "Wherein would its causality reside?", he says, "Blue, etc.," which means an unperceived blue object. Consequently, there would be a different sense organ at every moment.
Furthermore, in that case, there would follow the undesirable consequence of numerous further assumptions, such as that the instrument must be of the same nature [as its effect], and so forth;

moreover, experience is the condition for memory through the mediation of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). Now, if similarity to the material cause (*upādāna*) constitutes causality, it is more logical that the material cause itself—which is even more similar—should be the cause, and this is not the case here.

And by means of memory, which has become the effect, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) alone is postulated as its material cause (*upādāna*). As for the experience (*anubhava*) which was postulated as the causal condition (*saṃskārapratyayatā*) on the grounds that it imparts a specific excellence (*atiśaya*), its very status as a cause is difficult to ascertain; with this intention, he says:
"And memory [arises] from cognition. Now, one might object:
how can the awareness of the experience—such as "I have experienced this jar"—be denied? To this, [the author replies: here...
He says: "Just this much" means that we have indeed consecrated this very [cognition] as non-deceptive.

As for what was said [previously], namely "therefore," what kind of authority (*pramāṇa*) could that possibly rely upon—is it a form of perception (*pratyakṣa*) distinct [from memory], or is it not distinct from memory and self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)?

Or it may take the form of inference (*anumāna*). Since the first and last positions have been refuted, the middle position alone is established by this method. He concludes this with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*), demonstrating that even the status of inference can be applied following upon self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
Regarding "by self-awareness" (*svasaṃvedanena*): "in that" refers to the prior experience. Regarding "also from memory" (*smṛter api*), which occurs elsewhere:

the particle *api*, indicating astonishment, should be connected with the subsequent word *ca* (and) to indicate a conjunction, as it serves as the reason for the phrase "they are self-cognized" (*svasaṃviditāḥ*). For indeed, in one case...
In the subject whose nature is self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), the awareness of experience remains entirely uninterrupted;

therefore, when memory arises within an experience that possesses full attention (*ābhoga*), it draws forth the very experience itself as it depends upon that prior state— this is not merely a matter of formal arrangement.

But inference has no utility here; nor is the accomplishment of worldly transaction possible here, because of the absence of delusion, or because, even if delusion were present, the state of being an effect would be difficult to ascertain. [Objection:
But in this way, in the case of memory, the previous experience itself shines forth—thus, it is just like the former [case].

"It would possess validity. To this he says, "Memory," and so forth. Just as its nature was previously that of direct experience (*anubhava*), so too was its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*);
but now, however, it assumes the form of memory by virtue of being a portion of an experience colored by the past time belonging to the object of knowledge.

Likewise, it lacks validity because it grasps what has already been grasped. For in memory, there is the experience [of the object] as "the jar was manifested," and not "it is being manifested. But if this were so, would not self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) also be invalid? It might well be, if it were to grasp a self that has already been grasped.
The state of being an object of apprehension (*grāhyatva*) would manifest within its own part; however, this is not the case, for if it were so,
there would be a distinction between the past and the present, yet such a distinction does not exist in that which is inward-turned (*antarmukha*).
"Because of the absence of temporal limitation"—this has indeed been determined many times.

He states this very point with the words "But in self-awareness. Since there is an absence of temporal distinction—which necessarily exists when there is objectivity—the absence of objectivity itself is also stated. || 5 ||

Now, one might object: even if the determination of empirical forms such as the relation of cause and effect is not established through mere experience alone, let conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) themselves be the means of valid cognition, as the Naiyāyikas and others maintain. For in the absence of sublation (*bādha*), what could render them invalid?

However, in the case of sublation (*bādhayoga*), even the experience of two moons, a whirling firebrand, and so forth, is invalid; therefore, one must attend only to the existence or non-existence of sublation itself, and not to a single cognizing subject (*pramātṛ*) as established by reasoning, since the purpose served by that [subject] is accomplished solely through the power of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Let it be so for now; however—[the reading *nanu* is found in manuscript Ga].
In this regard, we maintain that the reality of conceptual construction consists of the subject whose nature is the unity of experience; nevertheless,

even though this practice of sublation— which serves as the basis for determining the distinction between the real and the unreal that pervades all internal and external worldly transactions— cannot in any way be reconciled with the systems of other philosophical schools.
In our system, however, this is indeed logically consistent. To demonstrate its consistency within our own position, the Sūtra states:
"The relationship of the sublated and the sublator also [exists] among those things that are opposed to their own inherent nature."
Because all cognitions arise as being ultimately grounded in a single subject. || 6 ||

That [means of knowledge] which is accepted by everyone for the sake of establishing all conventional transactions is also not tenable. For it does not belong to objects, since it is even more impossible for that which is not present;
therefore, it must be said to belong only to cognitions. And those [cognitions], with respect to their own objects and themselves, exist in self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

Like the minds of sages, which remain fixed and possess absolute contentment, these [cognitions] do not conflict with one another; or, if they were to undergo destruction through a cause while mutually excluding each other,
then cognition would be the adversary of a subsequent cognition.

Thus, whether by way of the relationship between the destroyed and the destroyer within one's own system, or by way of the contradiction with the opportunity for another [system] within one's own system, or by way of the contradiction with the existence of another's means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within one's own system— in such cases of contradiction, there is no knowledge whatsoever that is non-contradictory.
Thus, even such a contradiction is indeed no contradiction at all, like that between two friends. However,
when there is a lack of basis for asserting mutual contradiction, sublation (*bādha*) possesses a restricted scope.
"It would not be so"—thus must the cause for raising this contradiction be considered regarding these two.

And that is the single locus of rest known as the principle of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*). For in that [locus], the resting of cognitions does not consist of a single flavor (*ekarasa*) everywhere; for instance, [the cognitions] "this is a jar" and "this is a cloth."

In cognition, [the two] rest precisely without the mutual contact of their manifestations—as in "this is blue" and "this is a lotus," through an inclination toward the coloring of each other's manifestations; and as in "this is smoke from fire," preceded by the manifestation of the existence of the relationship between the effect and the cause. In this same way, other cases are also to be inferred.

Precisely for that reason, by making this [object] consist of a form that arises independently— since it cannot exist as a portion of an object of knowledge (prameya) conceived as external— the subject is called "autonomous" (svatantra) in its act of cognition.
In that regard, within a single cognizer, there occurs both the thought "this is mother-of-pearl" and "this is not silver."

Knowledge, while coming to rest, destroys the persistence of the fruit of the means of valid cognition— which consists of the reflective awareness: "This silver, which was previously subsumed within the entirety of the knowledge of silver, is real and capable of causal efficiency, and it has appeared to me"— by desiring to manifest that very silver [as unreal].

And it comes to rest by destroying [the other]. Thus, when there is a fixed persistence of another cognition within the cognizer through the exclusion of others, for that reason, the status of being sublated is established for that which is to be excluded, and the status of being a sublater is established for the excluder. For that which effects the disruption of the continuity of the result of another.
That [subsequent cognition] is its sublater, just as a universal monarch is the sublater of other kings;
likewise, the cognition "this is not silver" or "this is mother-of-pearl" is the sublater of the cognition of silver.
For sublation, being restricted to a specific object, is pervaded by having a restricted cause; therefore, in the case of the contrary [the absence of such a cause], [there would be no sublation].
Because there is an absence of anything that would pervade [the contradictory], the pervasion of the reason by the probandum is established; thus, this is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason).

Furthermore, the fact that two cognitions fall within a single locus in a relationship of sublated and sublator is also nothing but an essential property (*svabhāva*), because they possess a mutual dependence in their respective forms.
The meaning of the sūtra is that there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) such that in the absence of falling prostrate with one part [of the body], there is an absence of the rule.

In both the *Vṛtti* and the *Vivṛti*, the phrase "one's own and its appearance" (*sva-ābhāsa*) should be construed as "one's own and the object" (*sva-viṣaya*). Alternatively, since sublation is impossible in the aspect of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), it is merely an appearance (*ābhāsamātra*).

(373) That which is indicated here may be subject to contradiction; therefore, even in the Sūtra, the mention of "one's own self" (*svātman*) should be understood as having the intention of referring to a mere appearance. That which is the single configuration (*saṃniveśa*).
The phrase "this" refers to the object of desire to grasp, being the locus indicated by the pointing finger;

although the actual state of the object arises through its support, nevertheless, he refutes even the Bhāṭṭa view by stating that such exclusive dependence on it is difficult to ascertain without the unity of the cognizer.
The opponent says: "Since the cognition of silver occurs precisely by depending upon the mother-of-pearl, it must be understood as the cognition of the mother-of-pearl.

By the words ending with "bādhaḥ kriyeta," he demonstrates that the sublation (*bādha*)—whether it be the removal of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), of the validity (*prāmāṇya*), or of its persistence—is not logically tenable.

"At its own time, [a cognition] does not tolerate another cognition belonging to the same continuum; thus there is sublation (bādhā) while the cognizer exists"—this is what he means by saying "that too" (*so 'pi*). As for the contradiction of non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna-virodha*) which is stated as: "because that which has an insufficient cause does not exist when another [cognition] is present."
In its proximity, by way of producing a moment that lacks capacity, it is the powerful heat— occurring at the same time as the cold and pervading its location— that [prevents it],
and not because there is such a proximity between two cognitions at the same time.

Or [there would be] movement to another place. Now, surely the cognition of mother-of-pearl, having previously engaged with the mother-of-pearl alone, could not tolerate the cognition of silver; for if that [cognition of silver] were not [present], it would have continued to engage there in a continuous stream—this much alone is difficult to establish. For (hi) because all knowledge...

Knowledge itself manifests the object of knowledge; therefore, by the persistence of that object, it assumes a continuous flow, and by its cessation, or by the cessation of other causes, it abandons that flow.
However, there is no other distinct knowledge that possesses a different manifestation—this is the point.
Having performed [its function], it ceases from its continuous flow; how then could that be contradictory to it?
Since this is so, therefore "that too does not exist"—this is the connection with what precedes. This is what is meant:
when the causal complex for generating a preceding appearance is present, it is simply another cognition [that arises].

How could one who holds that a cognition of silver— which has the nature of proceeding as a continuous stream— arises in the form of something else, just as in the case of mother-of-pearl, exert themselves [to refute it], when it has already been dispelled by the cognition of the mother-of-pearl, just as cold is dispelled by heat?
Because neither of these two types of cognition is capable of apprehending [the object] in such a manner,
as each is restricted solely to its own respective domain; thus, this contradiction consists precisely in the impossibility of coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*).

And that which is being suspected and that which is being refuted must be considered. Now, he raises a doubt in order to refute the second position with the word "atha" (now). He points out the nature of validity (*prāmāṇya*) as "the illumination of the object" (*arthaprakāśatva*). "Contradiction" (*virodha*) means sublation (*bādha*). [The term] "illumination of the object" (*arthaprakāśatva*)...

In this context, he explains the word *artha* by means of the term *ābhāsamāna*. "Otherwise" (*anyathā*) means if that [object] were to possess luminosity (*prakāśatva*) without its being a manifestation (*tad-ābhāsatā*). To the question, "What follows if the luminosity of what is manifesting is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?", he says: "And not... (*na ca*). "That too" (*tad api*)...

The word "api" (also) indicates that the same reasoning should be applied by way of repetition to another point as well. He refutes the third position with the words "nor," continuing from the previously mentioned reason for impossibility up to the end of the passage ending in "vyatirekī. Now, regarding the fourth position in our own system:
Intending to demonstrate how [the objection] arises, he refines [the argument] step by step with the words "But even so" (*athāpi*). Regarding the phrase "it is turned back" (*nivartyate*):
here, "turning back" is intended merely in the sense that no room is allowed for it there;
and thus the refutation is consistent, as in the case of "the ignorance of a jar regarding the jar."

"Even the objection that 'there is no room for what has previously occurred there'—the author raises this specific point with the words "and yet" (*atha ca*) in order to refute it. With the intention of showing that this [objection] is applicable only to the view of the proponent (*siddhāntin*), he says "this too. [The phrase] "otherwise" (*anyathā*) means if..."

Knowledge of prior occurrence is not required; furthermore, this [argument] revives the previously mentioned objection regarding the jar as well. He states the reason for its revival with the words "by whom is this [known]?"—the sense being that its occurrence must necessarily be conceived. Now, [one might object]: "But [is it not the case that] residing in a single cognizer..."
That which exists by way of the actual nature of things (*vastuvṛtta*) will indeed be the maker of distinction.
He says "not so" with the word "where," meaning that whatever does not manifest in any way cannot exist by way of the actual nature of things;
this is a matter for which even the drinking of the ordeal-vessel (*kośapāna*) would not be the proof—this is the intended sense. But surely, let it manifest; how so?
He shows that it is neither by means of two cognitions nor by conceptual construction— thus he says, "And not this. And not this...

"It is seen as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)," so he says; "and not without [it]"—by this very [statement], he shows that even if one were to accept that it is cognizable by another cognition, this matter remains difficult to establish. The word *eva* indicates acceptance [the *ga.* manuscript reads *ca*]. This applies to both cases.

"The reason is because it depends on something else. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "All... Even if the independence of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is accepted, he states "even by conceptual construction" to show that this [independence] does not hold up when it is self-made. By means of conceptual construction as well, there is the establishment of priority and posteriority due to its independence.

[It is said: "In those two cognitions (jñāna-dvaye) which are intended to be distinct from the nature of that conceptual construction (vikalpa), it is not logical; for since those two cognitions are not manifested by anything else, it is the object itself that is determined. By this, the meaning is as follows: when a conceptual construction is accepted as being independent (*svatantra*), in whatever [case]...

If it is accepted that [the subject] has the nature of light (*prakāśa*), then it is logical that he alone is independent (*svatantra*). Indeed, there is no other independence for him. Therefore, let him be independent regarding the object; however, not regarding knowledge.
For there is no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) consisting of illumination that is distinct from knowledge, which is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*).

Therefore, where there is no nature of manifestation (*prakāśana-svabhāva*), there this [cognition] consists in a form of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya-rūpa*), because it is connected with an unreal operation of manifestation whose essence is mere conceit;
and consequently, even though a sequence has been determined, it is not at all manifested. Thus.
If the two cognitions were real entities, how could they be known? Is it not the case that those two cognitions are indeed non-different from the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)?
Therefore, by virtue of being self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), that conceptualized pair of cognitions establishes its own temporal sequence of priority and posteriority. Thus...

When both [cognitions] reside in a single cognizer, it is not logical that sublation (*bādhana*)—defined as the rendering impossible of the persistence of a previously arisen cognition—should occur. To this, it is replied: "Or, in the case of non-distinction" (*avyatireke vā*). "As before" (*pūrvavat*) refers to perception...

This follows the same logic as stated in the two preceding sūtras. Regarding "of the two cognitions" (*jñānayoḥ*), it means that their identity is not only with conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), but also mutual between themselves. In the absence of that [identity]...
(page 376)

Therefore, that object which is to be accomplished through the unification [of the two], characterized by priority and posteriority and animated by a relationship consisting of mutual dependence, cannot be brought about. Consequently, "because of the cessation with regard to the object" means because of the uprooting of the persistence of the result.
It must be reflected upon: "And thus, in the definition of the means of valid cognition, that [cognition] is internal and consists of such reflective awareness...
[the cognition] is an uncontradicted awareness regarding the object" (2.3.2).

This will be explained [later]. By the phrase "it is so called in common usage" (vyavahriyate), he demonstrates that the very act of *manana*—which occurs on all sides (*abhitaḥ*), everywhere (*samantāt*), and in a state of direct orientation (*ābhimukhyena*) toward the subject, while disregarding external forms—is itself *vimarśana*, or *abhimanana*, whose essence is repose within the subject (*pramātṛ-viśrānti-sāra*). || 6 ||
"Not thus... (1.7.8), having begun [the discussion] with these words;
"In this way, the knower of form... (1.7.12).

Thus, in order to provide the occasion for the refutation to be stated later in another concluding sūtra, he states in the sūtra— presenting as a point of doubt the account of sublation (bādhavṛttānta) shown by Dharmottaropādhyāya and others:
"Just as the cognition of a bare ground is the cognition of the absence of a jar."
And likewise, the cognition of mother-of-pearl [is the cause] for the knowledge that the cognition of silver is invalid. (7)
The bare ground is the absence of the jar,

because the conventional usage of "absence of the jar" is based upon it; therefore, just as the cognition of the bare ground itself is the cognition of the absence of the jar, so too [is the case here].
The very awareness of validity— characterized by the manifestation of the object as it truly is within the cognition of mother-of-pearl—

is nothing other than the self-awareness of that cognition of mother-of-pearl; and that which manifests is precisely what is called the invalidity, whose nature consists in the unreality (non-correspondence) residing in the cognition of silver that is contrary to the mother-of-pearl.

The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: if an opponent were to say, "Cognition is itself the sublation; so what is the use of the identity of the cognizer in this regard? he introduces that [objection] with a brief explanation:
the word "of things" (*vastūnām*) is the reason [for the objection]. [The phrase] "let it not be" refers to the Buddhist and other systems. Now, [as for the case] of a jar...
Whatever is an entity, how can that be a cloth? For it cannot be accepted that what is the redness of a jar is the cloth.
(Page 377)

To this he replies: "No. For it is not something like the redness of a jar, by means of which one might experience the form of another; rather, it is simply the jar itself no longer existing, and this is merely the total absence of all description and designation for the jar, and not some "not" that exists as a thing.
An object fit for renown and narrative. Now, if this is so, there is no such thing as non-existence;
what, then, is the basis for this reflection? He replies: "But of that...
Its nature consists solely of the essence of conventional usage, which is of the form of conceptual cognition and verbal designation.

Furthermore, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) necessarily functions by depending upon direct experience (*anubhava*). Therefore, that conceptual construction which arises by necessarily conceptualizing non-existence while depending upon a certain experience establishes the status of being an object of conceptualization for that very thing which was the object of the experience—
just as the conceptualization of blue establishes the status of being an object of conceptualization for blue— and this applies to the conceptualization of non-existence as well.

Since it necessarily depends upon the experience of another pure entity, there is an obstruction to its establishment due to the non-perception of the pervader— namely, necessity— in the case of the counter-example; thus, by means of a certain essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*),
that very thing is conceptualized as the absence of another pure entity, and therefore, that itself is non-existence (*abhāva*).

It is established [as such], and because it does not conform to that which is conceptualized, it is called "non-existence" (*abhāva*). For the visible ground is of a positive nature (*vidhirūpa*); therefore, for it to be designated by the form "the non-existence of a jar" is indeed inappropriate.
Having explained the example, he explains the subject of the analogy with the words beginning "in the same way" (*tadvat*).
How does the cognition of mother-of-pearl become a cognition of the invalidity of the cognition of silver?

It certainly does. The reason for this is stated as "because [the person] has acted," and so forth. Here too, the reason is that the cognition of silver had attained the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to its own object, silver; [it becomes a cognition of invalidity] because of the negation of that [status].

"The cognition of silver is a valid means of knowledge"—this is the form of the cognition of mother-of-pearl, because it consists in the absence of that [valid] cognition of silver; such is the syntactical connection of the sentence.
[The author] establishes that the essence of non-existence lies solely in practical activity (*vyavahāra*) by means of the phrase "of the absence of a jar."

Regarding the phrase "that which is dependent": it is neither produced by the absence of a jar nor does it possess a form imparted by that [absence], because for that which lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), birth, death, and so forth are impossible.
Nor is this [absence] comparable to a collection of jars raised up by a potter; thus, it is described by the term "mere conceptual construction" (*kalpanāmātra*).
He asks: "For what purpose does he raise this objection? [The answer is: It is because conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) consists merely in the absence of activity directed toward that object.

The purpose of this arousal [of cognition] is either that which brings about avoidance or acquisition, fixed upon a pure object contrary to that [superimposition], or it is the activity [itself]. For as long as one does not conceptualize— upon seeing the ground— that "there is no demon here," so long will fear, terror, and the like, produced by the presence of a demon, certainly take hold.
Conventional transactions based on that [object] do not occur through the non-apprehension of the imperceptible;

therefore, there is an absence here of the conventional transaction of non-existence. For as long as one does not engage in the convention "there is no jar here," one would not place one's feet upon that ground without hesitation; thus, it is by means of the non-apprehension of the perceptible [that this is established].
The conventional practice regarding existence is established. For conventional practices depend upon the face of determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*);

they occur according to that determination, and not according to the actual state of things (*yathāvastu*). But was it not stated that the cognition produced by the ground has the form of the ground? However, the cognition of the absence of a jar is not...
It has the form of the ground; therefore, it is not produced by the ground. To this, he says: "True, it is thus not produced by the ground;

for it is mental, consisting of conventional usage, and of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). How then is it said that 'this is the cognition of the ground'? He replies: "But of this... Even though this...

Although it exists as being essentially a mental activity preceded by the two types of verbal and physical activity, it nevertheless possesses a distinction from other conceptual constructions (vikalpa) that have objects such as blue and follow the experience of blue and so forth. For instance, conceptual construction is as follows:
That [cognition] is determinate and depends solely upon experience as its regulator.

Since there is no experience of absence that could give rise to this conceptual construction of absence, it arises from the very perception of the ground; therefore, the ground itself is thus treated by it.

Furthermore, when the object of a cognition consisting of the determination of the absence of a jar is sought and attained— since [activities] such as walking about without hesitation have the bare ground as their sole object—
then that [cognition] is simply the cognition of the ground, because it is rooted in the experience of that [ground] and has the attainment of that [ground] as its fruit.

The cognition of the absence of a jar is likewise of such a nature that it is serviceable for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Now, what is the use of purposeful action here? It is said: it is precisely with reference to that [action] that one says, "There is no jar here.
(page 379)

The cognizer engages in practical activity (*vyavaharati*), but not merely through the manifestation [of the object] itself, as one who has already accomplished his purpose; likewise, it is not by that mere engagement in activity. "That" (*tat*) means for that reason. Only that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) regarding the ground is the object of the practical activity of non-existence. Whatever practical activity is for the sake of attaining something, that [activity] does not [proceed] from that [mere manifestation].

An object of another [nature] is like yellow being the object of [the cognition of] blue; for example, there is the conventional usage "there is no jar here" in order to reach the ground. For the purpose of reaching another thing is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of having another thing as its object in conventional usage; this [present case] is contrary to that, and thus it is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). And this...
The principle of the absence of a jar on the bare ground, which will be explained in another sūtra,

should be applied to the conventional usage of the absence of a jar consisting merely of light and touch covering the ground— a usage that establishes what is contrary to the conventional treatment of absence as something distinct [from the locus].

Having thus explained the illustration, he applies this very same principle to the subject at hand with the words "this very [principle]. By the direct perception of the mother-of-pearl shell, the conventional usage of its non-existence is also implied; therefore, among the conventional usages regarding intrinsic nature, that very direct perception of the shell is the fundamental basis.

That [silver] is the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because, through all its worldly transactions, it is precisely the mother-of-pearl—which is the object of that cognition—that is obtained. Thus has been explained the indicative function of the word "if" (*cet*) from the Sūtra as expressing a doubt.
Having thus expounded the meaning of the Sūtra, the commentator...

In this way, in accordance with the meaning of the sūtra that will appear as "evaṃ rūpyavidābhāva... (1.7.12), he refutes the opponent's view which has been raised, for the purpose of settling the student's understanding; otherwise—

Because the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*)— which is interrupted by the appearance of other objects of knowledge introduced in the commentary on the four intervening sūtras that state other objects of knowledge such as the refutation of the example and its justification— would not re-emerge in the student's mind due to being difficult to reconnect.

And this meaning of the word *cet* becomes well-explained by the unfolding of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*); otherwise, since it might be suspected that "this is merely the thing itself," there would be room for the objection: "Why was this said?
He states the manner of that rebuttal with the words "teṣāṃ ca" (and of those), [proceeding] by means of analogy (*upamāna*).

It is "thrown" (asita) forward— that is, cast before the person to be instructed— for the sake of determining through similarity (*sādharmya*) by means of establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*); likewise, when the ascertainment of pervasion has been reached in its proximity (*upa*),
it is not thrown or cast [any further].

(On page 380) "It is taken into account by way of encompassing everything for the purpose of establishing internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*),"—this is the introduction of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). That [example] is dissimilar, not similar. The reason for this is expressed as "for it is not... (*na hi*).

If the cognition of the absence of silver— designated by the term "cognition of the absence of silver" because it is rooted in that [subsequent sublating cognition]— were to be a cognition of the absence of validity in the cognition of silver, then there would be parity between it and the cognition of the absence of a jar, which is similar to the cognition of the surface of the earth, and with the cognition of the absence of silver itself.
But it is not so; therefore, there is a disparity. Regarding the phrase "but it is not so," the reason is stated as "for thus.
For the invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) of the cognition of silver must be understood as a distinct property (*dharmāntara*), namely, its being a false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) occurring at that very time.

Alternatively, invalidity consists in the absence of the property whose nature is validity; it is not the mere non-existence of that [validity] which constitutes the invalidity of the cognition of silver.

For if this were the case, then while in its own moment all cognition would be valid, yet in the moment of another cognition all would be invalid—thus the established rule would once again be undermined.
Now, it might be argued that the invalidity residing in the cognition of silver is nothing other than the cognition of the mother-of-pearl itself.

To this, the reply is "no. The reason for this is as follows: since this validity has been obtained by means of a different object—the nature of the substrate (*dharmī*) consisting of the cognition of silver—that [invalidity] must have that [silver-cognition] as its object.
For that [subsequent cognition] is its invalidity. Or rather, whatever is the definition of the cognition of silver— namely,

its adventitious character (*upādhi*) consisting in invalidity or the absence of validity— that [definition] is, by this cognition "this is invalid," applied to another object, which is another thing to be dealt with.

The cognition of silver and so forth has been obtained. Therefore, just as it cannot be said that the cognition of the white quality of a cloth or the cognition of the absence of the yellow quality is the very same as the cognition of the pot,
so too in the present case, if the cognition of one thing were the cognition of the qualities of another—
Alternatively, it would be a cognition of the non-existence of that property; however, because there is no restrictive cause for that, it leads to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Thus, this state of cognizing something else is pervaded by the nature of not cognizing that property—which is contradictory to the state of cognizing that property; therefore, this is the "perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory" (viruddhavyāptopalabdhi).

He further confirms this very disparity by stating that the example is dissimilar to the subject (*prakṛta*) because of the absence of a jar; for it has already been stated that the absence of a jar is nothing at all. The phrase "as has been stated" implies that [the argument] is logically sound. Thus.

(Page 381) First of all, it is not tenable to claim that the very perception of the mother-of-pearl, while functioning as a valid means of cognition (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*), is the cause for the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding the absence of validity in the cognition of silver.

This much might be the case if the cognition of silver were valid (*pramāṇa*). In that case, what was presented by it would indeed be silver and not mother-of-pearl; thus, due to the non-perception of the [actual] cause, the cognition of mother-of-pearl would not be corroborative (*saṃvādaka*). Yet such a cognition does exist; therefore, the cognition of silver is invalid.
This is because of the perception of a consistent cognition of mother-of-pearl. Consequently,

in the negation of validity through the perception of an effect that is opposed to the cause, the cognition of mother-of-pearl— which has attained the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)— serves as the logical reason (*hetu*), not as a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
He says "here" (*iha*) with reference to the subject at hand. The word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates the aforementioned possibility.

"Indirectly" (*pāramparyeṇa*) means not directly contradictory to that which is to be negated—the validity [of the scripture]—but rather [contradictory] through the intervention of a cause; this is the meaning. [Objection: Even so, is it not established even without what is to be proven?
"By a single cognizer. To this, he says "And that," for they maintain that perception alone is the sublater (*bādhaka*).

[Objection: From this point onward, you will proceed in this manner. [Response: True; nevertheless, this is merely the abandonment of their vow (*vratatyāgamātra*), and not the fulfillment of their desires. Therefore, he says that this will be refuted later.
Thus [he says]. By this, he also indicates another refutation, which will be stated in the sūtra: "Because the locus [of the reason] is unestablished... (1.2.13). || 7 ||
He refutes this [view]:
"In this way, its nature as a non-pot would not be established merely from the cognition of a clean spot;
for even here, there is no absence of the pot-nature, though it be capable of being perceived. (8)
The surface of reality is eternally solitary because all entities are established within their own self-nature;
how then could knowledge of that [solitude] ever establish a separate non-existence? (9)

When the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) is to be established through identity (*tādātmya*), this logical principle applies: "The ground is not a jar," "not a *piśāca*," or "not sound. For in those cases, [the absence is established] by means of perceptibility (*dṛśyatva*), the absence of specific intrinsic natures (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*), the absence of causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), and so forth.
Even when [the object] is impossible, the establishment of its non-existence is indeed possible; for, by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*),
all causes that possess the capacity for perception— that is, which confer the characteristic of being perceptible— are present.

When the non-existence of a perceptible object is intended to be established—such as "there is no jar on this ground"—then the establishment of that non-existence does not occur by the aforementioned method. For if it were so, the non-existence of even a *piśāca* (demon) would be established through its exclusion, since the ground would be established as being "not-a-*piśāca*. But this is not the case; rather, it is that very thing [the jar] which is [negated] "therein" [on the ground].

"It is appropriate to employ such conventional usage, or let it be employed always in that manner, because there is no distinction"—thus, this example is not consistent; this is the meaning of the sūtra. Regarding the refutation of the disparity in the example stated by the commentator himself:

Not seeing the consistency with the text of the Sūtra, he establishes that consistency through a provisional argument (*abhyupagamya-vāda*) by means of the phrase ending in "having accepted" (*abhyupagamya*). Furthermore, as an incidental point, he demonstrates that the author of the Sūtra employs bold assertion (*prauḍha-vāditā*) for the purpose of establishing the reality of the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāva-vyavahāra-tattva*). This, first of all—
He does not state what ought to be stated immediately; rather, as one who has renounced all worldly ties (*saṃnyāsika*), he merely accepts this much:
"How is it that you have employed this very example? "That" refers to the ground.
"It would not exist" means that its non-existence through identity (*tādātmya*) is indeed being considered. But this is the meaning of the sentence:

"It would not be so; it is not even conceivable—that the jar should not exist in that locus. For how could one and the same thing be both the locus and the located? If this were merely conceptual, it would [logically] always be so. This is the construction of the argument: he states this by way of an illustration in order to refute the sublation [of the jar] established through direct perception. Now, [one might object]:

Anticipating the objection that "you have merely intended to express 'groundedness' (bhūtalatā) by the term 'purity' (śuddhatā), so what is the purpose of employing such a qualification?", he says: "In this Sūtra... Subsequently, the opponent speaks as follows in due order: "We also accept a form that is exactly of that kind."
The qualification is appropriate. "To be described" refers to the state of being "separated" (*vivikta*) in the sūtra;
"of such a kind" means having the nature of being established in itself (*svātmaniṣṭhatā*). "This" refers to the absence of the jar and so forth.
"Of this"—namely, of that state of being separated—is used in order to inform others that it exists "always."

(Page 383) This is the explanation of the term "eternal" (*śāśvata*). In the ultimate sense, abiding in one's own self is itself isolation (*viviktatva*); and in order to make that known to others, there is the conventional usage of terms such as "isolation," "purity," and so forth.

The Sūtra, which was introduced as a reason (*hetu*) regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), has been explained, however, as if it were already established (*siddhavat*) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Here, "in this" refers to the case where the probandum is the linguistic usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) by way of negation (*vyatireka*). He refutes [the opponent's position] by resorting to the true nature of things (*vastutattva*) with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). "That too" refers to the so-called "secondness" in a jar.

By this, the meaning of the sūtra is shown: how could that cognition—the cognition of the bare ground—ever establish the absence of a distinct entity? Rather, it would always establish the absence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*).
He raises an objection to clarify the opponent’s intended definition of "notoriety" (*prasiddhi*): "Now... (*atha*)...

"Distinct" (*bhinna*). By establishing this distinction, he connects it to the subject at hand. When [the author says] "But when," the proponent reveals the true state of affairs and repeats the opponent's position—using the words "not so"—in order to provide an opening for the refutation.
"In this way" means by way of the coexistence with the jar. That which is called "coexistence" with the jar is not...
He shows that something may be greater than the ground [of existence] by way of both the object of knowledge (*prameya*) and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), stating:

"greater than its own form" (*svākārādhikaḥ*) in the case of "its own cognition" (*svajñāna*). Now, one might raise the doubt: "In both states, is there such a degree of greatness for the object, or for the cognition? Anticipating this, he says: "Or even that which... (*yo'pi vā*). Now, is it not the case that the jar...?

It is not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the ground, but rather its being accompanied by [something else]. And that [concomitance], although not appearing separately in the appearance "the ground," exists just like substantiality (*vastutā*). He refutes this with the words "nor even... [meaning] "always," even when the jar is absent. [Objection: But surely that concomitance of it [the ground] is produced by the jar, just as the lump of clay [is shaped] by the potter's wheel?

"...as if it were being produced. To this, he says: "Nor even... This means that since the cause must exist prior [to the effect], it would not exist at the time of the jar's production. Or, let us grant that the jar has causality therein;
nevertheless, that form, which rests upon the ground, does not depend upon the jar.

"Conjoined with a jar. Now, even when a particular light produced by the eye exists—[the particularity of the light being its momentary succession]—once the eye has ceased, there is no continuum of cognition, nor is there... [in the sequence beginning with the initiation of successive moments].

"Just as it was in the case of perception (*dṛk*) and so forth, so it will be here. He does not tolerate even this [objection], namely: "even when a jar is not perceived," or rather, he considers that "there is no non-perception of the eye and so forth. Furthermore, nothing whatsoever is unmanifested to anyone.

"It becomes its own nature"—thus he says "of the state of being a real entity" (*vastutvasya*). "It will be stated" refers to the sūtra: "In that very way it exists... (2.3.5). Furthermore, this is not the opinion of the opponent, who does not employ the conventional usage of the non-perception of an effect.

For this is the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*). "In which" means while that investigation into reality (*tattvacintā*) is being performed. By this, both aspects—by way of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object of valid cognition (*prameya*)—are shown as relevant through the application of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). "That" refers to the cognition of the location (*pradeśajñāna*), which is always present.
The intended meaning is that there is no distinction [between the two cases]. If it were argued that just as something is "conjoined" even in the absence of conjunction,
so too an object produced by a jar is perceived as such only when in proximity to it, and likewise for the state of being accompanied—
such that one says "the ground is accompanied by a jar" even in the absence of that [actual conjunction]— that too is incorrect.

As for the phrase "the jar indeed," what is the point of grasping this? If it is argued that this is an inference like [the inference of] smoke, then from where does that [inference] arise without a necessary connection (*pratibandha*)? Nor is the cognition of that [connection] itself the perception of the object, because they are distinct. [The opponent asks: "In that case, what is the appearance of their coexistence? [The author] replies: "This is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpana*)," as indicated by the word "only" (*kevalam*).

The meaning is that this alone is the additional [point] here; or rather, it means that this alone is logical. He begins to corroborate this with the opening words of the *Vārttika*, "Therefore," as follows: because consciousness, though unitary and partless, terminates in each respective object, [the occurrence of one manifestation within another manifestation...]

He does not apply [the term]; for that reason, he has spoken thus with the thought that the cognition of a jar and a cloth establishes its determination as a "jar" by way of independence from the cloth, and likewise establishes it as a "cloth" by way of independence from the jar. He recites his own text, beginning with "therefore" (*ataḥ*); for this reason also, that [is so].
The sensory cognition is established as being free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*). That too—
meaning that which is to be proven by other Buddhists as having such a nature.

Because even while conceptualizing one object on the mental plane (*manobhūmi*), one perceives another at that very same time, and one reflects upon those two as being entirely distinct from one another—thinking, "This I am imagining, but this I am seeing. For if [the knowledge were not so], by way of incorporating the occurrence of each other... [ga. omits *jñāna*].

One would have to establish both the object and the cognition [as distinct]; in that case, here, the states of being an object of vision (*dṛśyatva*) and being an object of conceptualization (*vikalpyatva*) would become conflated. And since experience is not like this, he shows [the opposite] by saying "it would be established" (*sidhyet*), for it deserves to be established in that very way. He applies this to the present context with the words "and thus" (*evaṃ ca*): even though cognition has a dual appearance...

That which depends on mutual relationship is not a determiner, because it lacks the nature of a determiner. For determination is the production of a non-confused ascertainment. If one were to determine through mutual dependence, there would be the production of a confused ascertainment. Therefore, this... [of these (ga.)].

This is the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). He reminds [the opponent] that validity (*prāmāṇya*) was accepted by the other (the Buddhist) precisely according to this very establishment; thus, it is the Buddhist alone who has accepted it in such a way as this, he who established the proof for non-existence in this manner.
"The subject at hand would be undermined;

however, our own wickedness in proclaiming the refutations of others' positions should not be imputed to us"—this is what is indicated by the word "eva" (only) in the phrase "by those who say that. [Objection: But in this way, regarding the cognition of a jar and the ground...
Is there no difference between the cognition of a mere jar and the cognition of a mere floor?

There is indeed no difference from the perspective of the object (*viṣaya*), but from the perspective of its own nature (*svarūpa*), there certainly is a difference. This is what is stated by the words "and the cognition" (*jñānaṃ ca*).
The particle *ca* serves to aggregate another object of knowledge (*prameya*) by way of raising a doubt. [This applies] to the cognition under discussion, which functions as the agent (*kartṛ*).
The word "object" (*vastu*) and so forth are the words denoting the action. The phrase "thus indeed" (*evaṃ ca*) clarifies the subject matter of the sūtra.
"That perception" (*taddarśanam*) refers to the perception of the location (*pradeśadarśana*), acting as the agent. "Even though [the jar] is absent" (*asaty api*) refers to the jar.
Here, the non-existence of the jar will be established through the non-perception of its effect—so [it is argued].

He restates the opponent's position with the words "when the jar exists. According to the principle that "the term 'not appearing as both' excludes the other," this is established precisely through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), because that jar is an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*); and that which is its invariable effect—
"Because there is no cognition that has become a vessel for a portion of its own manifestation.
(Page 386) Having restated this, he refutes it with the words "And here... For he is terrified precisely by the contradiction with experience (*pratītibādha*).
The opponent maintained that the establishment of non-existence depends upon perception and conceptual construction; however, it has already been demonstrated that this is simply not tenable. || 9 ||

But surely, the cognition of a separate absence is well-known to everyone, and it does not occur at all times, but only during the state of the non-proximity of a jar. What, then, is the recourse here? In this world, that which is not distinct from something else cannot be treated as separate from it, just as the ground cannot be treated as separate from the ground itself.
And so it is with the absence of a jar. For in the case of the counter-example (vipakṣa), there would follow the consequence that such linguistic usage would be without a cause;

thus, there is the non-perception of a cause. Therefore, the very light which is distinct from the ground is itself to be treated as the absence of the jar by virtue of its being located upon the ground—this alone is the refuge in this matter.
This is stated by the Sūtra:
"However, for a blind person, there is a mass of light, or a touch such as warmth that is soft;
therein, one should establish his own cognition as having the nature of non-pot. (10)

However, in establishing the non-existence of a separate entity, there is a specific point, not previously observed by the ancients, which is worthy of inquiry. That is stated as follows: here, on the ground, there exists light—whether in the form of a mass of rays and its radiance—or touch, such as that of sunlight or moonlight, which is distinct from the touch of a hard jar and is soft.

[Having become subtle: For that long, it is designated by such kinship-terms as "the relation of cause and effect" or "belonging to the same causal complex," and thus it is not something unprecedented.
And that [absence], which is distinct from the well-known forms and tangibles constituting a jar, exists there on that ground in the form of their absence.

It is apprehended by its own cognition— that is, by the cognition of light and so forth, which consists of form and touch. When that [cognition] is conceptualized according to the previously stated reasoning, then there arises the discernment (*vijñāna*) that "on this ground, there is a mass of light-form distinct from the form of a jar," or [this occurs] when the eyes are not functioning.

The cognition that "this is a mass of touch characterized by being either cold or hot and soft, distinct from the touch of a rough jar," excludes [the object] from other things, such as its luminous color and its soft touch; thus it is observed.

(Page 387) One ascertains the absence of the color and touch of a jar; thus, it is that very light or its touch which is conventionally designated as the "absence of a jar" on that ground— this much alone follows from reason.

The worldly person's recourse to the absence of a distinct object succeeds in establishing non-existence; however, for the omniscient one, the cessation of knowledge is itself of a different nature from [ordinary] knowledge. Therefore, even during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), his cessation of non-existence consists solely of self-cognizing awareness (*svasaṃvedanajñāna*). Of that [cessation]:

For this is the meaning of the Sūtra: that knowledge becomes all-pervasive with respect to the objects of cognition (*jñeya*). He establishes this nature of light through a gross analogy: "in some places" means that the cognition of a bare ground is not a factor for the ascertainment of the absence of a jar (or, according to manuscript *kha* and *ga*, it is not the cognition of its presence).

Regarding the term "without interval" (*nirantara*): the cognition that there is an absence of a jar on a portion of ground even when a stone is placed upon it is simply the cognition of that stone itself. "Its existence" (*tadbhāva*) means the being of the stone; by the inclusion of the word "etc.
(*ādi*), wind and so forth are meant, and for some, even darkness is merely a form of color. For instance:
The Abhidharmikas [state]: "At that time, form is of twenty kinds... (Abhidharmakośa 1.10).
The phrase "wherever" (*yatrāpi*) and so forth is connected with the subsequent "there also" (*tatrāpi*). However, in the intermediate [context]...

The commentary has been read and explained; the same applies hereafter. The connection is as follows: "that cognition of touch belonging to him (the blind man) brings about the linguistic usage of the absence of the jar.
The word "of the blind man" (*andhasya*) is connected with the preceding term "not perceiving" (*anupalabhya*); the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent.

"Non-obstructive" means that it lacks that quality of resistance (*pratigha*)— namely, the property of touch— which constitutes an impediment to emergence from objects such as walls or partitions. "Determined" means that we,
who maintain the doctrine of the reality of appearances (*ābhāsavastuvādin*), accept non-existence as being strictly distinct from existence.

As for what was stated—that even non-existence (abhāva), when being cognized, is the Lord himself, whose nature is consciousness—that is logical; the intention is that this serves to establish non-existence as distinct [from the Lord]. It is "utilized" (upayujyate).
For the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). "At present" means that at another time, when there is the utility of a cloth and so forth,
that very same light is designated by a different form of conventional expression, such as "the cloth does not exist."
And this is not merely a matter of logic; rather, experience itself is the witness here, as he says: "the state of affairs" (*vastusthiti*).

"Manifests" (*āvirbhāvayati*) means "ascertains. For at that time, it does not depend on the ground alone, but rather on the space consisting of the cloth situated above it. (Variant readings: *bhūtalam eva* [kha]; *paṭāvakāśamayaṃ* [ga]).

But surely, on this view, only the absence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*) is the single thing to be conventionally designated, not a separate absence (*vyatiriktābhāva*); and consequently, just as the conventional usage of the "absence of a jar" is triggered by the ascertainment of that [light] in a location— on the grounds that "the light is the absence of the jar"— in the same way...
Lest one should suspect that even the conventional usage of the "absence of a piśāca" would apply to light itself— since light is of the nature of the absence of a piśāca— the Sūtra states:
"A piśāca might exist even in the absence of light, just as [it exists] within light."
Being invisible, it cannot be negated in any way within the interior of the earth.

Although a *piśāca* is distinct from light and is indeed non-luminous by nature, nevertheless, like [the absence of] a jar on the ground, it cannot be conceived within the light itself. Consequently, even if there is light— which is not a *piśāca*— one might nonetheless say that "being light, the *piśāca* is not present."

Nevertheless, its non-existence is not established in every respect (*sarvātmanā*). The phrase "in every way" (*sarvathā*) must be applied in three ways: as a restriction (*niyamena*), with reference to the ground and the light, and as far as the range of perception extends (*yāvadgati*). For it is not merely the absence of a *piśāca* that is to be proven, but rather its absence as a rule (*niyamena*).

Moreover, this [non-existence] is indeed possible even within another level of the earth, and it will be investigated as far as its limit extends. Thus, when there is the suspicion that it might exist anywhere within the range of light, one must insist— by means of a restriction— that it exists only in the specific location intended [to be specified].

The meaning of the sūtra is that such [cognition] does not constitute a certainty regarding the absence of that [object]; thus, as in the systems of other schools, there is no fault whatsoever even in the system described here. He explains this briefly with the words "And not" (*na ca*), and the word "thus" (*evam*) refers to the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
(Page 389)

The undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) regarding the non-existence of a piśāca that is suspected [by the opponent] does not apply even to our own position; the word "ca" (and) serves as the reason for this suspicion of the consequence. The intended meaning is that this consequence is suspected because light, being of the nature of a piśāca, would lack the form of illumination.

But the reason for the negation of the doubt is "of that which is internally latent," and so forth. And that—namely, the "otherness" (anyatva) ending in the locative case which was mentioned in the commentary regarding the position of internal latency—is explained as follows:
it has been stated that in that light, even a piśāca who is internally latent cannot be suspected of being negated because of its invisibility. And that...
The resolution is not prompted by an objection; for in this way, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) has been raised:
that if there is light in a certain location, it would follow as a consequence that "there is no *piśāca* here.
With this intention, he begins otherwise—saying "or rather"—in order to instruct those of coarse vision.

However, from the perspective of subtle analysis, since the affirmation and negation of light necessarily result in the determination of the location [of the absence], the first explanation is not inconsistent. Alternatively, although the absence of a *piśāca* is indeed apprehended when light is apprehended on the ground, nevertheless, in a specific part of a house where there is intense light...
Just as the absence of a jar, even when apprehended,
does not serve as a factor in the practical activity regarding the absence of a jar suspected throughout the entire interior of a house—
because its presence is still possible in another part of the house enveloped in deep darkness— so too [is it with the case at hand].
Because a *piśāca* might be suspected of existing in the midst of the light situated in a particular location,

it does not— so long as it remains in that portion of space— become a factor for the linguistic convention based on the absence of a *piśāca*; therefore, even in that case, the ascertainment of its absence must indeed be made, yet that [ascertainment] is not established.

"Or else," he provides another interpretation by way of this formulation: "because, in that central portion of light which is subject to being overrun by *piśācas*, we do not perceive any other being similar to a *piśāca* who does not depart from that light."

The word *tatra* is explained in three ways: as denoting the locus (*ādhāra*) of both light and space, and as having the sense of an inseparable concomitant absence (*nāntarīyaka-vyatireka*). Now, if it is possible to negate a piśāca by means of its absence even in a location (*pradeśa*), then—

(Page 390) Even in the case of light, why can it not be negated in that same way? He says: "Because of the location. For it would be negated in the location through identity with the light. What, then, is being considered? Indeed, even there, [the object] exists in its entirety.

A negation is possible; however, one might even say this much regarding a specific location: "There is light here, and therefore the *piśāca* is not there. But as for the light itself, what else could be present such that one could say, "Even the *piśāca* is not there"? Therefore, it is considered that in this case, there is not even the slightest opportunity for such a statement. He demonstrates this very point with the words "for then" (*tadā hi*).

By the phrase "or in a location" (*pradeśe vā*), the possibility that a spatially discrete atom exists with an interval between its own constituent atoms is refuted; this is the ultimate [view], explained according to the Sūtra as being like the invisibility of the interior of the earth. Nor is there even invisibility.
It is not merely otherness that is the reason for the impossibility of negating a *piśāca*, but rather otherness accompanied by invisibility.

He clarifies this very point through a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "for of that" (*tasya hi*). The word "of which" (*yasya*) refers to that which does not remove light, such as space, time, the self, atoms, and so forth; "somewhere" (*kvacit*) means in the presence of light.
Or, in a particular location, he who perceives that which is beyond the senses might exclude a *piśāca*.

For he is one who perceives the *piśāca* and other such beings beyond the senses. That space for a *piśāca* which is conceivable—namely, that which is generally the interval between the ground and the light—is distinct from [space] itself, as well as from direction (*dik*), time (*kāla*), and so forth.

It is conceivable and appropriate that one who perceives the world as being pervaded by atoms in the form of specific visual appearances— which cannot endure the form of a *piśāca*— and who thus treats those [atoms] and so forth as the absence of a *piśāca*, is able to negate the *piśāca*; therefore, it is not [the case that...].
In this case, there exists the capacity and so forth of one who does not perceive that which is beyond the senses. He clarifies the very subject at hand with the words "for it is not," etc.;

by the inclusion of the word "etc.," [he refers to] direction, the self, and so on. For this very reason, even for an omniscient being, when a *piśāca* appears, its form is nothing other than that of the constituent parts of light, namely the atoms of light.
"Space" (*avakāśa*) means location; having abandoned—that is, having excluded—that [space], [consciousness] shines because entities (*bhāva*) possess mutually unmixed forms.
For that reason, this suspicion also should not be entertained. He reflects upon that very point:

"Yathā" up to "iti" [is the end of the previous section]. He applies the same logical principle with the words "na hi. If this is the case even for a *piśāca* (a ghost), where this movement is not considered to remove light, then what need be said regarding a jar, which is the opposite of that?

This is precisely the doubt [in question]. With the intention that, in that case, it is the jar alone—which excludes light—that must be negated, and not the *piśāca*, he says "athāpi" (even so). "Anāloka" means by means of the perception of a single, solid mass of light devoid of any internal interval; this has already been stated here.

"It causes one to remember the samādhi in order to clarify it, even in this case"—this is the connection: because this statement is anticipated, for that reason this is made to be remembered. Now, if they are of the nature of one another, how can there be the expression "even when situated in one place"? He says: "And therefore..."

Thus: in whichever part of the light there must necessarily be proximity to a *piśāca*, whatever else is seen there is not a *piśāca*. [Objection: But apart from its own nature (*svarūpa*), what other "place" (*deśa*) could there be? To this he replies with the words "of those consisting of the elements" (*bhūtamayānām*). This refers to external things whose forms consist of the fivefold [objects] beginning with sound.

Even that which is external, such as the ground and so forth— which is connected to space by way of the nature of form (rūpa) belonging to earth and other elements distinct from cognition, either because it depends on the same causal complex (ekasāmagryadhīnatva) or because of the relation of cause and effect— that too indeed appears as "space. Therefore, it is simply the proximity of space itself [that constitutes the object].

Regarding the non-distinctness of location: since the self, time, and so forth consist of what is unreal (*abhūtamaya*), let them indeed occupy a single location. For in whichever philosophical system those [entities] exist, they are all connected with everything because of their omnipresence (*vibhutva*);
however, it is another matter that they are not connected with one another. Furthermore, none of them—such as sound and the rest—exist at all.

And consciousness—thus the universe consists of merely these six categories. Among them, sound and the other [objects] are composed of the elements (bhūtamaya) alone; hence the inclusion of the term "composed of the elements. Or, by the phrase "of cognitions," it is meant in contrast: for cognition, apart from its own essential nature (svarūpa), no other location (deśa) appears.
Whether it be the cause or the object, it appears as being dependent on the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīna*) and as lacking a substratum (*anādhāratvena*);

for, since there is an absence of parity (*samakakṣyatva*), there is no joining of them—this has been demonstrated many times in the section establishing [the nature of] place, time, and non-existence (*adharmadeśakālasamarthana*). [Regarding] another place...

A location other than the location of its own nature—that which is the delimitation by that [other location]—is the connection with being contained therein; and if there were an absence of that [connection], then...
(page 392)

The meaning of the word "otherwise" (*anyathā*) is as follows: "in that manner" (*tathāca*). Since the location is distinct [from the object], it is by that mode that this is another object of cognition; this is the sense of the particle *ca*. A particular light and a particular warm touch—just like a *piśāca*—are its very nature (*svabhāva*).

That very region which is conceived as the locus and support of a *piśāca* by those of limited vision is itself, when perceived in the absence of a *piśāca*, designated by the Omniscient One as "there is no *piśāca*. Now, one might object: where nothing is seen in the middle, forms and other qualities do indeed exist there.

—Why is this so? How then was it stated that "that very place, consisting of a specific form of light, is the absence of a piśāca"? To this he replies: "For color-forms and so forth... [even] though something situated in the middle might be invisible; for even if nothing is perceived in the middle, nevertheless...

In that regard, form and the other [sensory objects] exist there as atoms (*paramāṇu*) in such a way that they are not seen by people like us, yet they are indeed seen by the Omniscient One. By the words "and therefore," he shows that there is no unprecedented variety among the atoms. "Not in that way" means that even those things which possess resistance (*pratighātin*) are not [seen by us].

"Extremely so" means "just so. Regarding "more distant": just as a shadow is seen there, by means of darkness—that is, by being separated through an interval—those things which have an interval consisting of a distinct gap that is barren of homogeneity are called "separated by intervals" (*sāntaravyantarāṇi*); or, they are "separated by intervals" (*sāntarāṇi*) because of the darkness in between.

The *vyantarāṇi* (intermediate spaces) have their middles made variegated by the absence of darkness in the center, or by being interspaced, or by being separated. "Simultaneously" means they cause [the atoms] to turn back in their respective places, driving them away from their own locations; they are turned back through a process of producing moments of incapacity.

They are driven away from their own country in exactly the same way. "In this manner" means that for the Omniscient One, the atoms of *piśāca*s are equal to the atoms of other entities, beginning with those most visible to us. However, in the absence of a *piśāca*, that which [was done] by the *piśāca*...

The intervening space was previously occupied; therein, only the atoms of light being perceived become the object of the omniscient one’s conventional usage regarding the absence of a piśāca. But [one might object]: even while perceiving various other entities such as the self (ātman) and so forth, how could the omniscient one negate a distinct piśāca?
Whether a piśāca exists or not, because their own essential nature remains unimpaired,
the non-existence of a separate piśāca is established by this [reasoning].
(Page 393)

This is indeed difficult to establish even for an omniscient being by way of such a method. To show why this effort is thus futile, he says "Alternatively": if there were anything at all [to be seen], it would have to be seen by him; therefore, if he does not see a *piśāca* there, that *piśāca* simply does not exist, and in that case, every object located there [is likewise absent].

That [absence] is to be known by another cognition that is distinct from the cognition of the presence of the *piśāca*; or rather, that very same cognition is the object of the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding the absence of the *piśāca*. Thus, there is no need for the investigation of intervening atoms. But surely, the same would apply to us and others as well?

Why does it not occur? It is said: "Because it is prior. For one who perceives [reality] as limited, the thought arises that "there is no object of knowledge"; by means of this cognition, which is characterized by the knowledge of conjunction, the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāva*) is established. However, where there is the certainty that "[it] arises," [non-existence is not applicable].

Because there is the necessary possibility of cognitions of odor and so forth— as if smelling, as if tasting, as if attending, and as if touching— the cessation of those cognitions of odor and so forth is itself the absence of distinct odor, taste, sound, and touch, consisting in the cognition of the entry of breath and so on.

It is precisely the cause for conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, although the absence of a *piśāca* is apprehended by this [perception] when it apprehends either light or a specific location— since these two are distinct from the *piśāca*— nevertheless, even though it is apprehended, it is as if unapprehended because it is partial (*prādeśika*) with respect to either the location or the light, being distinct from that [absence].

Since there is no cause for the cessation of such presumption, even though the matter has been stated in so many ways; well then, if invisibility is the reason for a *piśāca* not being negated, then in the case of a jar or similar objects being negated—
"...one's own cognition [perceives] the state of being non-pot. (1.7.10).
In such introductory statements (*uddeśa*), "visibility" (*dṛśyatva*) should be indicated as the reason (*hetu*). [The opponent objects: "No," he says: "It is established" (*siddham*).
For every negation now [proposed] results ultimately in the negation of identity (*tādātmya*); and in that case—
Visibility is non-deviant [with respect to being perceptible]. For instance, the *Hetubindu* states: "The qualification must be stated.

Having thus spoken by way of an incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*), he returns to the subject at hand and maintains that even for one who perceives only what is near (*arvāgdarśin*), a *piśāca* cannot be denied, even if it is invisible.
(Page 394) If light were visible as individual atoms, then for one counting atom by atom, there would arise at this spot the cognition of a "piśāca-atom" due to their being without interval.

It is conceivable that this atom of light, being distinct from those [other atoms], has the very nature of the absence of the atoms of a *piśāca*; and since the same would apply to other atoms as well,
the atoms of a *piśāca* could be perceived in a location just like a jar.
This is to refute [the objection that] light-atoms themselves are the absence of piśāca-atoms there;

for there is no perception [of them] atom by atom, because what appears is a gross, single, dense, and extended manifestation, and because within that [manifestation], there are atoms of limited darkness and so forth, just as there are atoms of piśācas.

Because even the atoms of a *piśāca* are subject to doubt; thus, if light were visible down to its atomic constituents, the non-existence of a *piśāca* would be established even for one of limited vision— this has already been stated, and it must be investigated as far as possible (or "investigation alone," according to the Kha manuscript), but this is not so.

He says "or else" (athavā) to explain that the form of the object remains as it is. Even though atoms are invisible, if one were to imagine that there exist *piśāca*-atoms which obstruct their lack of interval (*nairantarya*), then—given the absence of any intervening space—that [obstruction] might be negated; however, this is not the case.

For just as atoms of taste, smell, and touch, though existing, do not produce the cognition of a single solid form due to their invisibility, so too the *paiśāca* atoms, although consisting of form (*rūpamaya*), remain entirely beyond the range of the eyes of beings such as ourselves.

Therefore, by the very non-perception of the forms existing between them, their state of being unaggregated is apprehended; this has been demonstrated in detail by the teacher Dharmottara in the *Bāhyārthasiddhi*.
In the same manner, the impossibility of negating a *piśāca* even within a specific location should be understood.
And thus, by this much analysis of the movement, the word *sarvathā* from the Sūtra has been explained as "within the surface of the earth" (*bhūtalasya antaḥ*),

and the word *sarvathā* itself has also been fully interpreted. He concludes with the words "And thus" (*tataśca*), signifying that through this entire investigation of motion, the term from the Sūtra has been completely elucidated.

This sutra is intended primarily to pacify incidental faults in order to establish the immutability of the meaning of the preceding sutra; therefore, it connects directly to that very point with the words "And necessarily... and "This very same...
[and so forth] up to "...for the blind, a mass of light or a touch... (1.7.10).

Thus, by way of introduction, the absence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*) has been stated. "The cognition of which" (*yatsaṃvedanam*) means the cognition of that [object], which stands in the place of the cognition of the ground (*bhūtala*). "Of that" (*tasya*) refers to that cognition.

There is no such cognition whatsoever that could function as a perceiver of the ground [of consciousness]—by means of which the absence of the cognition of form is said to be established through direct perception;
this is the meaning. Now, one might object: since there is a self-reflexive perception (*svasaṃvedana*) of the cognition of touch, by that...

Only the cognition of touch is apprehended, not the cognition of form; therefore, from that which is equivalent to the cognition of a bare floor, there would follow the negation of any other cognition capable of being associated with it.
This would be true, if that very [cognition] were present even when the cognition of form occurs.

The self-awareness of the cognition of touch might bear a different form from the self-awareness of the cognition of color; however, it is established that this is not the case even in a dream—this is explained by the intention to show the dissimilarity [of the dream state] with waking states such as "a jar" and so forth. He states the reason for this: "because of the duality of cognitions," and so on.

The unity of cognition, which grasps the nature of knowledge, is not tenable. Now, if there were two cognitions existing as objects of cognition—like a jar and a floor—what would that have to do with the cognition of them? He replies: because of the nature of knowledge, which is characterized by being the knower of the object to be known.
There is no difference between them. Here too, the reason is precisely self-awareness (*svasaṃvedanatva*).

Having thus demonstrated that the association with a single cognition lacks pervasion over the conventional usage of the absence of all [other] things, he shows the pervasiveness of the principle regarding the object by saying "it has been stated."

It indicates a specific distinction.
