The very existence of that [cognition], namely the existence of the cognition of form (*rūpa-jñāna*) characterized by such a restriction, appearing within a self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) that excludes [other objects], is the basis for the conventional usage of the absence of the cognition of form.
Now, it may be granted that by this much the identity of the cognition of form with the cognition of touch (*sparśa-jñāna*) has been refuted; however—

At that time, however, how is the absence of a second, distinct cognition of form established? It is said: "Because of the absence of its effect. If there were a cognition of form at the moment of the cognition of touch, then that conceptual construction which arises from the cognition of touch—[that would be the effect].

Even if it were produced from the cognition of form, conceptual cognition—which functions through the dual conceptualization of both form and touch—would have to be self-cognizable; yet such a thing does not exist. Regarding this very point, he provides an example with the words "even in the case of a lamp," just as previously [stated] regarding the perception of form.
Furthermore, because there is no occurrence of obstructing causes, one ascertains the existence of one's own eyes in the dark;
likewise, due to the absence of the effect—namely, the cognition of form—one ascertains the absence of a lamp. Thus:
Since there is no effect consisting of a specific conceptualization and since there is an absence of the cognition of form, by this very same logic—

even in the theory that the nature of non-existence consists in the absence of being accompanied or unaccompanied— the absence of the cause, the jar, would be established through inference from the location where it is absent; it would not be the case that "that very thing is that," so enough of this.

With these many words, he says "only this much," meaning that no other course is possible for these [objections], as he has scrutinized the systems of others to the best of his ability; thus, he shows that even here there might be the possibility of further objections, such as: "Let even conceptual construction (vikalpa) exist as something distinct, self-cognized."

By accepting the theory of a single cognition (*ekasaṃvedana*), he indicates that this [objection] is also of no consequence; for this very reason, he says "But it is logical," and so forth. By this, even the non-existence of sound, taste, and smell is established—despite the presence of the complete causal complex—by means of the absence of their effect, which is cognition.
And the absence of that [external] cognition occurs through the absence of its self-cognition;
however, by means of the internal perception of the sound (nāda), the touch of the body, the taste of the water in the mouth, and the scent of the tripuṭikā,
there may indeed be the exclusion of external sounds and so forth, but for one who has attained the meditative concentration on the element of space (ākāśa-dhāraṇā).
How can there be a cognition of the absence of all those [objects] when, at that time, there is no scope for the absence of all sound and so forth to be ascertained by the yogi?

This is because we have already established that the determination of the absence of one of two things—which are capable of being associated within a single cognition—is dependent upon the cognition of the other. Enough of this prolixity. || 11 ||

But surely, by the very same logic established by you, the very cognition of the validity of either the cognition of a real mother-of-pearl shell or the cognition of silver— which is its absence— is itself established as the cognition of the absence of validity for the other, namely, the cognition of silver. This is true.
[Objection: It is established; [Reply: Nevertheless, he shows by means of a sūtra that what was to be proven is not yet established:
"In this way, the cognition of mother-of-pearl would consist in the absence of the manifestation of silver;
however, it would not be the indicator of the invalidity of the initial cognition of silver. (12)

For by this, an investigation into the nature of the cognition of mother-of-pearl or the cognition "this is not silver" has been conducted, but not into that of the initial cognition of silver which is distinct from them.

"Neither diminished nor enhanced": for even when the invalidity of the prior cognition of a cloth—consisting in the validity of the cognition of a jar—is recognized, nothing at all is done to that prior cognition of the cloth; such is the meaning of the sūtra. "The state of having a non-existent object" means invalidity.

"It is accepted" means by the followers of the Sugata (Buddhists). "And that" refers to the invalidity of the former [cognition]. "Only this much," however, is the intended meaning: there certainly exists this kind of cognition in the world, but it must be considered what its nature as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is.
If it consists of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then our own view alone is victorious; but if...
That it consists of inference is not tenable; this will be stated by the Sūtra immediately hereafter.
But surely, by the word "this" (idam), that very object is referred to where the cognition of silver occurred;

and it is precisely there that the cognition "this is not silver" or "it is mother-of-pearl" has now arisen. And since a single [object] cannot possess two forms at one time, these two cognitions do not constitute valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

"It ought to be so"—thus there will be a sublation based on inference (*ānumānika-bādha*). In that regard, first of all, it is not established by this [statement] "this is that very thing," and an inference such as "it is that very thing" is not tenable. Furthermore, since the conventional usage of sublation (*bādhavyavahāra*) exists, it is only in our own system that it is logically consistent—such is the Sūtra.
Even if the property-subject (*dharmin*) were not established, there would be no sublation by means of inference;
rather, it is logical that [the subject] is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), being born from a single cognizer.

The word "api" (even/also) is to be applied in many ways: even by means of inference there is no sublation (*bādhā*) of the subject (*dharmin*), and furthermore, because the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*). Nor does this cognition of sublation arise through a remote process of investigation; rather, it occurs through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) itself. Therefore, [the reasons] must necessarily be established.

"But since there is a single cognizer, that [cognition] arises from him as its independent source"—this is the meaning of the aphorism. He introduces it with the words "inference also," and because there is so much more to be explained, only this much has been introduced; the remainder, however, is merely a conclusion of the preceding matter. [The phrase] "the cognition of mother-of-pearl" [is used].
While explaining the non-establishment of the reason (*hetu*), he establishes the non-establishment of the locus (*dharmin*) as being necessary for it,
by means of proving the first characteristic [of a valid reason], namely its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).

This is with the intention that the property-possessor (*dharmin*) is employed for the sake of the reason (*hetu*). Otherwise, someone might suspect: "The probandum (*sādhya*) is established by the reason; what is the use of the property-possessor there? [This is said] when the reason is "because it is a cognition of silver" in the case where the probandum is "the invalidity [of the cognition]. Now, why is this not called "unestablished in its own nature" (*svarūpāsiddha*) in the case where...

Fearing that [the reason] might not be taken as an objective support because it looks toward the non-establishment of its own property (*dharmyasiddhi*), he explains the logical principle [by stating], "its own nature" (*svarūpa*). Here, "own nature" refers specifically to the nature of the reason itself,

and not to the nature of the real entity (*vastu*)— for if it were the latter, even a rabbit's horn would be considered "unestablished in its own nature" (*svarūpāsiddha*)— and [this applies] to the reason as well.

The very nature of being a probans for a probandum, which consists in the exclusion of non-connection with a restricted place and time, is dependent upon a locus (*āśraya*). Consequently, that [probans] whose locus is not perceived from the statement—
such as "sound is impermanent because it is visible"— becomes, by its very nature, devoid of a substratum and thus [invalid].

It is only partially established because that [property] residing in sound is absent, and because there is no contact with the cognition of other forms and so forth. Therefore, this is called "unestablished in its own nature" (*svarūpāsiddha*). As for the reality of the cognition of the mother-of-pearl, although it is not established elsewhere, [it is established here].
Nevertheless, it indeed shines forth by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), because that which is independent of anything else is the locus of the final resting point of cognition (*pratītiviśrāntipada*).

[Objection: Even so, although truth is established in the substrate (*adhikaraṇa*)—namely, in the mother-of-pearl—by means of the cognition of the mother-of-pearl when the cognition [of silver] is true, it is not established in another substrate, namely, in the present cognition of silver.

This [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*) because it resides in a different locus (*vibhinnādhikaraṇatvena*). To the question, "Let it be so; what is the fault?", he says: "It is *vyadhikaraṇa* (residing in a different locus). However, if the word "of the crow" (*kākasya*) were not supplied, this should be considered simply as *svarūpāsiddha* (unestablished in its own nature). Now, why was *āśrayāsiddhatva* (unestablishedness of the locus) mentioned in this way? It is said: that...
Even for that which is unestablished due to being in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*), connection with another locus is not a fault;
rather, it is precisely the connection [of the property] with its own substratum by means of that [other locus]. [Objection: Let the crow itself be the substratum. [Response:
No—thus he says, "in the context at hand" (*prakṛte*). [He adds] "by its own nature" (*svarūpeṇa*), meaning that the property does not have another substrate as its locus.

Even though the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is established as suchness and the phenomenon-bearer (dharmin) is established as suchness by virtue of being the substratum for other properties, the nature of phenomena exists with that phenomenon-bearer as its support, and the status of being a phenomenon-bearer belongs to that [bearer] by virtue of that supported property— thus it is.

That which is the non-establishment of a conjunction (*saṃyojana*) is designated as either a non-establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) or a non-establishment of the substratum (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddhi*). Such is the manner of the unestablished (*asiddha*).
Having explained the diversity [of error], he now demonstrates the specific, unestablished mode in the present context with the words "But here.
"Previously" means at the time of the sublation. The cognition of the mother-of-pearl occurs even before the cognition of the silver that is to be sublated;
for it is precisely that [cognition of the mother-of-pearl] which, through the relation of opposition, serves as the reminder of the cognition of the silver. That alone—

When the silver-cognition is intended as the subject (*dharmin*) for the purpose of proving its invalidity, it is certainly not established at the time of experiencing the reality of the cognition of the mother-of-pearl, which is what is being proposed as the reason (*hetu*). Now, one might argue that the silver-cognition will not be made the subject, but rather the mother-of-pearl itself. This too cannot be maintained... [fragmentary].
The intention is "at that time. This very point establishes the status of the proven as being [already] established, by means of the phrase "for it is not," and so on.

For that which is now the object of the cognition of mother-of-pearl was not even now the object of the previously arisen cognition of silver; indeed, who but fate could dye the *kiṃśuka* flowers? But surely—
What is this so-called *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) as a refutation? For the probandum (*sādhya*) is indeed already established;
however, he shows that the inference would merely be redundant and nothing new would be established by saying "nor is it the case" (*na ca*).
Now, one might object: just as after seeing a mountain and the smoke upon it, [one infers fire] with haste due to some other business...
Just as one who has not previously inferred fire, having departed and now standing on a mountain, establishes for the first time— within the subject (dharmin) that is the remembered mountain—
the possession of fire, which occurred at a previous time; likewise,
[the cognition] establishes for the first time within the remembered silver or its cognition, its non-existence or its lack of external validity.

One might accomplish [the goal]. One might accomplish it if one were to recollect the cause as if it were smoke; and one would recollect it if there were an experience of it, but there is no such experience—thus he says "and not" (na ca). This might be so: just as one now infers past smoke from a particularity such as the soot on a wall that is currently being seen...

The inference of fire is pervaded by that very reality which is the primary probandum; the property intended as the reason (*hetu*) for its cognition will now be inferred from another reason, and from that, the inference of existence will follow. To this, it is replied: "It is a mother-of-pearl shell. For indeed—
There exists another probans that establishes the property (*dharma*) which serves as the means for such a state; for at that time, there is indeed the mother-of-pearl and the cognition thereof.

Its validity and its self-awareness—all of this exists elsewhere, in their respective substrata; thus, they are indeed *vyadhikaraṇa* (residing in different loci). Thus, having accepted that the remembered object possesses the status of a subject (*dharmin*), the refutation was stated; now, [the author] does not even tolerate that very [status] in the case of the silver.
And thus: for when the mountain is being remembered, there is actual reality (*vastutā*) in it, but not in the silver; rather, the cognition of silver is merely determined (*adhyavasīyate*).

That which is effective regarding what has been so determined becomes something established as a real entity by the cognition. For the external object of perception is [the basis] for conceptualization.

Let it be said that "determined" (*adhyavasita*) means touched by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), either through the determination of non-difference or through the non-determination of difference; and there exists a threefold object of words as the substratum (*dharmin*), which is based on existence, non-existence, or both.

Inference concerning such objects as the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and so forth, which are accepted by outsiders, cannot take that [primordial matter] as its subject (*dharmin*); however, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is not like this, because it is non-conceptual (*avikalpa*). And this has been established by you yourselves while demonstrating the non-conceptuality of self-awareness.
For the nature of pleasure and the like is such that it cannot be associated with linguistic convention, as it does not partake in anything else;
therefore, their self-awareness is not accompanied by verbal expression. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.249)

This has indeed been established by those who say thus. But surely there is this realization: "That cognition of silver was not valid at all; it is only now that I realize this through the experience of the cognition of mother-of-pearl. Certainly there is such a realization, but in your view, it cannot be accounted for in any way whatsoever.
It is logical; however, it is logical only according to our own view. He says this with the words "But for us" (*asmākaṃ tu*).

By the word "but" (*tu*), he indicates that although the subjects under the influence of *māyā*—whose hearts are inclined toward the objective aspect—imagine a temporal distinction in consciousness caused by the coloring of objects, [consciousness] is therefore [in fact] non-different from them.

Although they are conventionally designated as "cognitions," nevertheless their ultimate nature is indeed non-different; thus, at the limit of the self-reflexive awareness of the cognition of mother-of-pearl,
the self-reflexive awareness of the cognition of silver also remains present, once the connection with the veil of *māyā* has been removed.
For this conventional practice, whose essence consists of both illusion and ignorance, does not proceed by means of a single definitive conclusion; therefore, regarding that cognition of silver—
That which is the property of the subject (*dharmin*)— namely, its being non-cognitive in nature and its lack of investigation into recurring properties—
is established by the truth of the cognition of mother-of-pearl;
for even now, the states of recollection and self-awareness persist within the cognitions of the mountain and of smoke.

The establishment of the mountain— the locus (*dharmin*)— which exists as something manifested by that [inference], as possessing fire, can be successfully demonstrated precisely from the previous manifestation of smoke, which was already present; for otherwise, what would the mountain be, and what [would the fire be]?
Smoke. For there is no manifestation of those two in memory; for that [memory] is devoid of an object [and devoid of reflective awareness].

Consequently, for that which does not manifest in any way whatsoever, its status as a subject (*dharmin*) and its status as a reason (*hetu*) is like a painting of a rabbit’s horn on a bedsheet in the sky. That is something unprecedented (*apūrva*).
That which has as its nature another property (*dharmāntara*) characterized by invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), already established and to be cognized—
the state of being that [property], namely, the connection with that other property of invalidity;
that very thing is the "distinction" (*viśeṣa*), which is the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) consisting of the cognition and designation of that [object].

The cognition of silver is invalid; thus, at the time of establishing that [invalidity], it is logically consistent for the cognitions of silver and so forth—though existing at different times—to function as the subject (*dharmin*).
This is established only for us, but not for you in any way whatsoever.
Having established what was indicated by the word "tu" (but), he returns to the subject at hand—the refutation of the opponent—stating "and not...

The phrase "in this way" means by following the method of inference (*anumāna*). The reason for this is given as "instantly. For in inference, there is an infinite regress in the search for examples; thus, even at the end, this [objection] remains.
The sense is that its establishment through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) must be accepted. He concludes this with the word "thus" (*evam*):

the cognition of mother-of-pearl is not the awareness of the invalidity of the cognition of silver by way of perception, nor by way of inference; therefore, there is neither the sublation (*bādhyatā*) of the cognition of silver, nor...

Showing that the sublation of the cognition of mother-of-pearl is established, and that it is logically consistent within his own system, he explains the intermediate sūtra with the words "as long as" (*yāvat*). A single substratum is the "this" (*idam*) present before one; resting upon that, they manifest without abandoning it, being thus objects of cognition.
In that [state], such an illumination— the activity of manifestation— exists only so long as there is the conceptualizing mind.

The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the pair of mutually contradictory cognitions which, being externally opposed to one another, establishes the sublater (*bādhaka*); and by implication, the second is the sublated (*bādhya*). However, since the status of being the sublater has not yet been definitively established, it is not explicitly called "the sublated. And this applies everywhere.

"This very rule is all-pervasive," he says, "regarding existence, non-existence, and so forth. Now, with what intention was it said, "externally"? He replies: "But conceptual construction... For even at that very moment, there occurs the appearance of a conceptual construction such that for that very same thing, blue is [simultaneously] non-blue; yet in that case, there is no sublation, because that is precisely its cause.

In that case, there is no characteristic of contradiction; therefore, what possibility is there for sublation here?—this is the meaning of the word "vā" (or). Now, an objection is raised: since there is a conventional distinction between "that which is not falsely conceptualized" (*asatya-vikalpita*) and "that which is falsely conceptualized" (*satya-vikalpita*), how can it be said that there is no sublation here, and so forth? To this, it is replied:

The contradiction or opposition consists in mixing, through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the manifest perception—which is indeed the visible external form—with that [notion]; or, if it is conceived as "that" (*sā*), the meaning is that it might be so, it could possibly be so; in that case, it is simply the power of conceptual construction itself.
When [the object] is sublated, it burns away; and if a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises from experience (*anubhava*), then what is the point of a subject who is merely imagined?

Thus, he expels the Buddhist position with the words "conceptual construction. Now, one might object: we also accept that experience is a cause of conceptual construction, and the sovereignty of the subject (*pramātṛ-svātantrya*) resides therein.

The word *mātra* (only) is used to show that [the object] is employed in an excessive manner. Therein—that is, in the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which operates solely with respect to two distinct appearances differentiated by their respective temporal positions—as for the phrase "when, however," it refers to one's own system. Regarding the term "autonomous" (*svatantra*): for even a Naiyāyika...

Even if one were to accept two qualities of cognition belonging to different times as inhering [in something], one would still be unable to establish a single substratum for them; for if, in that very same space, there was first the roar of the ocean and subsequently the sound of a drum, what contradiction would that entail for anything?

By what cognition could the identity of their objects even be grasped? Even a conceptual cognition, though it may be valid, would establish only its own object and not the object of another cognition; for even if one cognition were cognizable by another cognition, [the same problem would persist].
"Let there be another cognition of cognition whose object is precisely that [first] cognition"—
this is possible only by accepting the reality of the autonomous cognizer (*pramātṛ*), which consists of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
There is the accomplishment of all desired goals, and the cognizer perceives the object, the conch, as something contradictory within conceptual cognition. In what manner is it contradictory?
He says: ... by way of its whiteness. How does he know that? It is said: "white," and so forth. That is the object, the conch.
"When was this manifested? He says: "At that time, it appeared as such. [Objection:

But since it appeared so through a difference in time, what contradiction is there between these two? [Response: Contradiction arises from having a single simultaneous appearance as its cause; here, the suffix -śat denotes the cause. [Objection: But the experience occurred at different times; therefore...
Now, from where does this simultaneous manifestation arise? He says:

That pair of manifestations which serves as its medium manifests in mutual dependence. If one asks why, it is because they are in fact one. That very thing which manifests as yellow manifests as white.

For this reason: having raised the objection, "But how can there be a contradiction even with this much?", he states the reason for its justification in the passage beginning with "yatraiva" and ending with "virodhāt. Now, [one might ask: "Is there not a contradiction here merely by this much?
In the case of sublation (*bādha*)... and in the case of contradiction (*virodha*), both arise based on the support that these two share a single locus (*ekāśrayatva*)."

Anticipating the objection that by revealing the contradiction, nothing further has been shown regarding the activity of a single subject, he says: "This [is so]. The cause of the contradiction is its having a single locus;
this must be understood to exist when there is one subject, but not when there is none. It is precisely here [that this is established].

He states two examples with the words "yathā" (just as). A single location, such as a house, belongs to both a jar and a cloth; therefore, even when they are perceived together, it is the mere nominal stem-meanings that are grasped.
Thus, when the relationship characterized by the vital force of the case-endings is known, it is solely the power of the cognizer [that determines it]—even in the case of light.

In the case of the [cognition] "there is no jar here on this ground," there is no other way [to account for it] except through the power of the subject (*pramātṛ*). Now, one might object: "By this much, contradiction has been established; nevertheless, what determines the restriction that only a certain thing is the sublater (*bādhaka*)? To this, he says: "And thus," referring to the cognition of mother-of-pearl.
Since the cognition "the mother-of-pearl has performed a causal function" arises as something fallen within self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*),
therefore the cognition of the mother-of-pearl is powerful;
whereas that [cognition of silver] is weak, being devoid of entry into a cognition of causal efficacy and lacking the presence [of such efficacy].

It sublates the cognition of silver—which has fallen within the scope of self-awareness—by uprooting its reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). But what is the use of the force of corroboration (*saṃvāda*) here? He replies: "Certainly not."
"Of the variegated" means [of that which is] variegated by the oscillation of cognitions of snow, silver, lac, tin, fragments of wood, and so forth.
"Precisely for this reason" means because the corroboration occurs subsequently and not at that very moment;
therefore, even that [corroboration] is dependent upon the principle of a single subject. "Therein" refers to the subject, within whom the appearances of entities [occur].
For the two characteristics of the mother-of-pearl shell are not contradictory; indeed, they find their rest there in this way:
"That very mother-of-pearl shell which was seen by me is this one now engaged in causal efficiency.
Thus, while there is contradiction at the outset, there is correspondence at the conclusion.

The relationship between the sublated and the sublator depends, first of all, upon a contradiction that is rooted in the unity of the cognizer; it is established that this [contradiction] is likewise dependent solely upon the cognizer.
Whatever other state of being is dependent on the existence of something else occurs only when that [other thing] is present.

Just as smoke is dependent on fire, which in turn depends on a causal complex such as wood and other factors; likewise, the conventional usage of "sublation" (bādhavyavahāra) is dependent on a cognition of contradiction that is itself dependent on the unity of the cognizer.
This is the inherent nature [of the case], and it would also apply in the case of distraction (*vipakṣe*).
The pervasion [is established] because of the consequence that [the effect] would be accidental. || 13 ||

Concluding this, he shows by means of a sūtra that another conventional transaction (*vyavahāra*) also occurs only when the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) exists, because it consists of a state of conformity (*samanvaya*), and not otherwise: "Thus,
in the all-pervasive [consciousness] which is inlaid with the manifestation of objects that appear as exceedingly distinct..."
Whether stained or stainless, worldly activity is experienced.
By means of the method of reasoning (*upapatti*) consisting of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as shown in the two sūtras beginning with *tattadvibhinna...* (1.7.2),
and by means of the manner of illustrating the relationship between cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and so forth as described in other sūtras.

This follows: for indeed, in the case of the Lord— who is omnipresent, whose essence is consciousness unconditioned by space and time, and who is autonomous— the ultimate reality consists merely of differentiation, which has as its essence the non-apprehension of the non-difference between consciousness [and objects] as fashioned by the power of *māyā*.

Everyone rests in that which is inlaid with objects such as blue or pleasure— which, though not distinct [from consciousness] because they are like reflections, appear as if distinct— and which is colored by them without any alteration of its own nature.
(page 405)
Worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is determined by firm experiential evidence (*anubhavapramāṇa*); it is twofold:

stained (*samala*), consisting of disputes over buying and selling for those blinded by *māyā*; and stainless (*nirmala*), belonging to those who have recognized the supreme reality of the Self, due to their attainment of immersion into the nature of the Supreme Lord.
In the vision of distinction (*viśeṣadṛśi*), there is the designation of "Vīreśas" [for those who have attained a specific state], but not for the bound souls (*paśus*) such as the Lākulas; rather,

it refers to the pure selves (*śuddhātman*) beginning from the Vidyeśvaras down to the initiated (*dīkṣita*), whose conventional activities consist of instruction, initiation, the performance of obligatory and occasional rites, meditation, meditative absorption (*samādhāna*), and so forth.

Even there, as long as a residue of impurity remains, the activity of Māyā does not cease; therefore, that state which constitutes the nature of empirical transaction— being essentially a synthesis animated by both difference and non-difference— is indeed obscured when difference is entirely concealed.

Nevertheless, that worldly activity, performed by those who have recognized as many supreme selves as there are, is indeed appropriate as being purely stainless, because it consists solely in the purification and awakening of impurities within one's own and others' selves. Thus, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), the word "of the knowers" (*jñāninām*) is a compound; whereas in the commentary, it is stated that [this] is possible for the deluded.

This is shown to demonstrate that even when such a conceit (*abhimāna*) does not arise instantaneously, this very reality shines forth by way of the repeated cultivation of the aforementioned instruction. As it is said in the *Śivavijñānopaniṣad*:
"The consciousness of the grasped and the grasper is common to all embodied beings."
"But for yogins, this distinction is vigilance regarding the connection" (Vi.bhai.
106). The word "only" (*kevalam*) means that even though the operation of *māyā* is universal, this [distinction] is additional.
The "perfected ones" (*siddhas*) range from the initiates (*samayins*) up to the gurus; they are pure souls (*śuddhātmanas*), partless (*niṣkalās*), and lords of knowledge (*vidyeśvarās*).

The Great Lords of Mantra (mantramaheśvaras), such as Ananta-bhaṭṭāraka and others; the Lords of Mantra (mantreśvaras), beginning with Aṅguṣṭhamātra and the rest; and by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," the Mantras themselves—these should be understood as having realized the true nature of the Supreme Self upon obtaining the instruction of the Supreme Lord.
As it has been said: "...

[they arise] from the Supreme Self, which is beyond the terrible [state]," and not, as in the Lākula and other systems, having the form of bound souls (paśu). For that very reason, the term *siddha* is applied to them.

That is the qualification; and in that case, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) itself, the partless Self is grasped, for the venerable Lord Śiva has no other separate agency apart from all worldly transactions.
(Page 406)

That is determined to be the state of rest (*viśrāntipada*). But those blinded by *māyā*—namely the *sakala*, *pralayākala*, and *vijñānākala*—their worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) is accompanied by impurity (*samala*). As the scripture says: "In all three of these states, [the power] whose nature is to conceal [reality]..."
"Overcome by the power of Śiva, they perform their various activities" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.36).
With the words "merely," etc., he explains the phrase from the commentary, *saṃbhāvyate* ("is conceived"). Thus all is auspicious. 14.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, the investigation into the single locus of the group of powers, in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, the great devotee of Maheśvara. 7.
Now begins the eighth reflection: I bow to that Amṛtāṅga, the supreme bliss, who, having previously reached the unsurpassed ground of nectar— the seventh stage of manifestation— rests therein.

Thus, it has been established in detail that He alone possesses the powers of knowledge, memory, and the removal [of ignorance], having internalized within Himself the infinite forms of the universe. Now, it must be determined what is meant by "Maheśvara.
In this regard, the state of being Maheśvara consists of both the domain of knowledge and the domain of action; of these, the former is addressed here.

This is determined in the section on knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*). Thus, the knower is determined both from the perspective of *prakṛti* (nature) and from the perspective of *pratyaya* (condition). In this context, what is called "knowledge" is that which is the self-awareness of "I"; it is said to be uncontracted by the coloring (*uparāga*) of the manifestation of diverse appearances (*bhedābhāsa*), even though it is [inherently] differentiated. And therefore—

That very sovereignty which resides within the group of manifestations is the Maheśvara-nature that constitutes the object of knowledge; in order to determine this, [the author employs] the temporary sense-organ... [etc.]
With these words, beginning with "ityādinā" and ending with "yataḥ śuddhe jñānakriye," a new reflection is commenced through these eleven verses. Therein:
Having stated in one verse that "some manifestation requires another manifestation while some do not," it is then stated in another verse that "nevertheless,
that manifestation is indeed one," and by means of two [verses] that "the manifestation of causal efficacy is likewise determined by manifestation"; in which manifestation does it [reside]?

The [concept of] causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is [explained] by two [verses]; the internal nature [of the Self], which serves as the foundation for the variety of other appearances, is [explained] by one verse; externality, both in terms of essential nature and division, is [explained] by two [verses];
and the summary of that which is the substratum of powers such as knowledge is [given] by one [verse].
The intended meaning is that by concluding the state of Maheśvara, there is a single [sūtra] that introduces the section concerning future activity.

Now follows the determination of the meaning of each sūtra. It has been stated that all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) rests solely upon the Supreme Lord. In this regard, a doubt might arise: what is the single life-force (*anuprāṇaka*) of worldly transaction?
Thus, there is no intrinsic reality to worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) apart from that [emptiness]; and therefore,
due to its clarity—
(page 408)
In the investigation of the discussion regarding the abundance and variety of what is generally perceived as manifest, no underlying cause is found; therefore,
it is said that one should set that aside,
[recognizing that] in some cases there is merely a dependence on the immediate sensory perception of the faculties.
Elsewhere, however, there are appearances [of light] in places such as blind darkness; but in other cases, there is nothing but blindness and thick darkness. || 1 ||

It is true that all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) rests upon the Blessed Lord; however, another point regarding this is stated—namely, the term *kevala*. That which is produced at that time, situated nearby, perceptible by the senses, and within the range of the organs, such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), is the basis for cognitions such as "this is a jar," which arise through the power of its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

The meaning is this: appearances (*ābhāsāḥ*) depend on whether they are present before the senses at the time of a conceptual-linguistic activity immediately following direct perception, or otherwise in the case of the linguistic activity of the blind and so forth; they do not require sensory presence at that very moment, for at that time those appearances are merely aroused by latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced long ago. This applies to one who is devoid of the faculty of sight.

Even the appearance as "form" arises solely from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of perceptions in previous lives, because it is remembered as such due to having occurred long ago; let it be granted that atoms possess independence,
but only insofar as it concerns the externalization of their own appearances.
[They are] the objects of conventional usage consisting of conceptualization. And "those very [ones]" refers to those who,

such as the Great Lords of Mantra (Mahāmantrēśvara) and others whose nature has been recognized through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), are always the objects of the manifestation of "I," and not any others whatsoever, by virtue of the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*).

They are restricted by having that [the "I"] as their object; and they, resting upon the ground of the subject in the state of "I-ness," exist for the sake of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)—this is the ellipsis. By the word "transaction" (*vyavahāra*), which occurs in the commentary (*vṛtti*).
"Primarily" (*prādhānyena*): for the supreme transaction, consisting of verbal expression, is dependent upon that [subject]. || 1 ||
And from this, the following is established; thus he says:

"There is no distinction whatsoever regarding the existence of the manifestation of an object, except in the case of conceptual constructions (vikalpa) which refer to objects that are yet to be, currently existing, or past. (2)
Even amidst such variety, although the appearance of objects falls within the domain of conceptualization regarding entities belonging to the three periods of time,
it nevertheless exists in its essence as nothing other than manifestation.

There is a certain distinction [of the subject] due to the constant luminosity of the reflective awareness "I am. Consequently, in acts such as seeing, there is only a single manifestation of blue—such as "I see blue," "I imagine blue," or "I remember blue. Thus...
Even the appearance of perception (*darśanābhāsa*) is one and the same in relation to yellow and other [colors]. Likewise are the appearances of imagination (*utprekṣā*) and so forth;

through the variety of their conjunctions and disjunctions, there is established among the subjects of *māyā* a variety of conventional usage—such as "clear" or "unclear"—which is fashioned by the power of the Lord.
"It has been said" refers to [the passage] beginning with "merely distinct cognizable objects... (1.5.21).
"Of these" refers to the objects that are subject to conceptual construction; their characteristic is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

The manifestation and appearance called "formative impression" (saṃskāra) certainly exists. And although this state of being a formative impression is not the ultimate state of "I-ness" (ahantā)—for it consists essentially of limitation—it is nevertheless said that for those in transmigratory existence, the "I-ness" of appearances becomes clearly manifest through its medium. Now, [one might object]:

"Why does this not shine? To which he replies, "It certainly shines," with the words "And of that" (*tasya ca*). "Previously" (*prāk*) refers to the introductory sections (*uddeśa*) beginning with "And of the Master" (*svāminaśca*) [in 1.5.80]. "To be excluded" (*bahiṣkāryaḥ*) means from that which is of the nature of pure I-consciousness (*ahantā*) yet acts as an obscuration.
The meaning is that this is what is to be manifested as "this" (idam) at the beginning. || 2 ||

Now, one might object: "What is the status of pleasure and the like? Since there is no external perception of them, and since at that time only the appearance of pleasure and its means remains, everyone would become entirely devoid of effort. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And even though the manifestation [of pleasure and so forth] exists in relation to pleasure and other such things, as well as in relation to the objects that cause pleasure and so forth,
it remains in that state because it has already passed away.

"But surely those manifestations, consisting of pleasure and so forth, exist as 'I-ness' (ahantā); how then can they be past? True; however, even while present, they do not exist within that [I-ness]. Thus he says: "unconditioned by time" (kālānavacchinna). But if this is so, why are even future things not said to be [past] when there is a requirement for "this-ness" (idantā)? He replies:

Regarding the word "previously": there is no appearance of pleasure or the like that did not exist previously, because it has occurred even at the end [of this life] in another birth; thus, when considering the nature of things, its status as "past" alone is appropriate. Now, (page 410)
Is that which exists on the ground of "I-ness" not itself presentness? True, this is so;

the reason for this is stated as "only of external things. This connects with what was said previously: "even though it has arisen, it says [so] in its activity. For by the word "then," it is shown that presentness resides solely in the external.

"Consisting of intellect" (*buddhimayaḥ*)—the word "grasper" (*grāhaka*) is to be supplied as the remainder. For it has been stated that if there is no entry into the form of the grasper, there is no connection with joy and so forth. Now, if the manifestation exists, what is the point of its being "present"?
He says: "By necessity" (*niyati*). "At another time" means when it is past by way of being external; "that very moment" (*tadātva*) is the state of being present. || 3 ||

The Sūtra demonstrates precisely this—that purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) arises from the appearance of the present—by means of the following verse: "But when pleasure and so forth are intensely delineated by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), their persistence will be exactly as it is [in reality], because they are clearly perceived as such. (4)

When that which has passed away, such as pleasure and so forth, is being contemplated without interruption, its persistence at the end in the form of extreme delight and so on occurs by means of that specific cause.
[The suffix] *liṅ* is used here to denote both the cause and the effect. For at that time, it is not being remembered; rather, it is indeed present.

It is an appearance of pleasure and so forth. For it is appropriate that what is being remembered has an indistinct appearance because it is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). As it is said in that regard: "Another distortion clarifies the conceptual construction..."

Thus [it is said]. And at that time, this [consciousness] indeed possesses a clear manifestation (*sphuṭābhāsa*). With the words beginning with "instruction" (*upadeśa*) and ending with "imposed" (*āhita*), he explains the meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) as being in a different grammatical relation (*vyadhikaraṇatayā*).
The entry into the root-center (*kanda*), the *suṣumṇā* channel, the plane (*pada*), and so forth, constitutes a specific instruction; "attachment" (*āsaṅga*) means passion (*anurāga*).

The other cause is the unseen [force] (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth. "Is presented" means it is made to appear as present, not by means of a garland or the like. The inclusion of the term "independent" is for the purpose of excluding memory; for even in the case of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), there is no contradiction for one who is clearly blind, because the state of consciousness has reflection (*vimarśa*) as its essence—this has already been stated.

[Objection: But if this is so, what is the use of memory there? [Response: It is said: "merely. The notion of pleasure regarding the past is not that previous [experience] itself; for this very reason, he says "experienced" and so forth. Of that conceptualization of pleasure...

(Page 411) The meaning is that that pleasure is primordial; it is not an object [of the senses]. Now, if one objects: "If its object has been presented by a conceptual construction based on memory, then why is it not a case of having a past object? To this he says: "And at that time..."

Thus: because the uninterrupted conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) clarifies precisely that which has the characteristic of a semblance of pleasure (*sukhābhāsa*) and has been presented by a general recollection (*sāmānyasmaraṇa*), it does not take into account previous factors such as place, time, or the assistance of another perceiver (*pramātṛ*). Therefore...

Even when the state of being a prior form (*pūrvarūpatā*) is brought to the fore, its dismissal has already occurred. As for that—let it be for now whether pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, when being delineated, perform a causal function or not; let there be non-reality (*asatyatva*) for things like the "earth-totality" (*pṛthivī-kṛtsna*) or the "unpleasant" (*aśubha*), even when they have been cultivated, as well as for pleasure and so forth.
To whatever extent purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is intended, that is entirely fulfilled; thus, one should not be led astray here even by the notion of unreality. || 4 ||

Regarding what was stated— that "the existent is always internal"— an objection from another [school] is raised with the intention that "existence consists precisely in the capacity for causal efficiency" (*arthakriyākāritva*).
Anticipating this and accepting it for the sake of refuting it, he introduces the aphorism (*sūtra*).
The appearance of existence and non-existence is held to have externality as its limiting adjunct;
their essence is not [external] existence, since they are always internal and real.

"Even though" (*yadyapi*)—and likewise "in that very way" (*tathaiva ca*) means by virtue of performing causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). "They might be" (*syuḥ*) indicates an admission that this is merely conceivable through worldly consensus and is not entirely unacceptable even to us. [This is said] in terms of the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*).
The word "also" (*api*) implies that even though they do not perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) when they exist;
for appearances, whether of the nature of existence or of the nature of non-existence, what is called "externality" is not their essence (*ātman*)—
that is, their own nature (*svarūpa*)— but rather, it consists in the nature of other appearances.

An *upādhi* is a limiting adjunct (*viśeṣaṇa*) that serves as the cause of coloring; because it is so, those manifestations (*ābhāsas*) possess an eternal existence by virtue of being internal. Now, one might object: "Let the manifestations exist as such;
but how can objects be so? To this he replies: "The manifestations themselves," which are possessed of differentiation.
On the level of externality, but not so internally;
those very appearances are the objects. The reason for this is that they are non-different from consciousness. Therefore, [if there were] a difference...

For it has been established that [if they were otherwise], they would not manifest. Now, one might ask: "In this way, how can the presence and absence of manifestations be described as objects within the mental state (*vṛtti*)? It is said: "Only" (*kevalam*). While it is true that there is no relationship of object and subject when there is absolute non-difference, such a relationship does not exist here, because of the awakening to the activity of the power of *māyā*.

Because exclusion (*vyatireka*) appears [in cognition]. Now, one might object: let this consideration apply to positive entities (*bhāva*); but how can it apply to a non-entity (*abhāva*), which is of the nature of a void? And how could these two—exclusion and non-exclusion—not exist in relation to consciousness? [We reply: Precisely because it is of the nature of a void. A non-entity is not a void by its own essential nature (*svarūpa*); for that [non-exclusion] belongs to the jar.

Emptiness (tucchatā) means that a jar is not [a jar]; that [emptiness] is the jar itself existing in such a manner. For this very reason, a cloth is not the being (bhāva) of a jar. Indeed, a cloth is nothing at all to the jar. [The opponent asks: But is emptiness also nothing at all to the jar? [The author replies: This is so. If it is nothing, then it belongs to the jar.
How, then, is a jar non-existent?

For we observe that people experience an extreme sense of distaste toward wealth, wives, household goods, and so forth, when they are subject to prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). That [distaste] would not exist [if those things were not non-existent].

Because no distinction can be applied to non-existence, which has the nature of being nothing at all. By this, one who asserts existence on the grounds of the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) should be considered as having already been answered. For if it is merely stated that "an entity does not perform causal efficiency there," then let it be that it does not perform it; but whence comes suffering?
If it is argued that this is because there is no causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) for that object, we remember this very point;
nevertheless, for those blinded by their own interests, an infinite blindness reigns supreme.

Thus, even non-existence (abhāva) is indeed a real entity (vastu). And so, even for those who maintain that the determination of objects is based on their capacity to produce effects (janakatā), regarding the claim that the cognition of a yogi has past and future things as its objects,
there exist therein various prior non-existences (prāgabhāva) and non-existences through destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva).

They should be considered as causes: "The destruction of the jar has arisen from this point onward," and "This prior non-existence of the cloth will last until that limit. For to those of limited vision, these entities cannot be apprehended without the mention of their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*).
(413) Just as a substance does not appear variegated in its first moment when it is devoid of qualities, so too,
whatever exists in its own form among all cognitions— whether that cognition be self-generated or generated by another— [is perceived].
That [it] is manifested is not at all surprising.

In our view, however, the very nature of entities consists in having manifestation alone as their essence; thus, because even blue, pleasure, and so forth are manifested in this manner, even that which has the nature of non-existence is not non-existent. For indeed—
A certain portion of his body is fixed; for this very reason, even in each single [aspect], there is the nature of the thirty-six [principles].
Thus it has been said. This is the intended meaning: assuming all forms from the external form onwards.
In the state of the void beyond the void (*śūnyātiśūnya*), having dissolved [all things], it manifests as the nature of Śiva, which is consciousness;
thus, it is indeed the expanded self (*vitatātman*). Therefore, even this appearance of non-existence is ultimately real.
[Objection: "In that case, these would be [mere] entities (*bhāva*). [Reply: They would truly be so if they were to appear in the form of becoming (*bhavana*). [For example,] a jar does not...
If entities were to appear in a form such as "it exists" and so forth, then why would blue, while appearing, not become yellow? Therefore, even non-entities are indeed objects;
it is simply that the positive form "a jar" exists in a state of conformity toward the light of consciousness.

The existence of entities is said to consist in their being and their manifesting; non-existence, on the other hand, reveals a lack of conformity toward manifestation, such that one says, "the jar does not exist" or "it does not manifest.

Yet this [non-existence] does not possess that [manifestation] independently, because it finds its rest in manifestation alone; thus, this very nature of the meaning of the negative particle is a play of consciousness.

Let it be for now that [the object] has been manifested as being determined to be "nothing. Even with the word "hare's horn," the word "non-existence" (abhāva) must be connected; for absolute non-existence is precisely of the nature "it is not a hare's horn. However, if the form "it is not" were inapplicable, then [the term would refer to] a jar or a cloth.

Just as in the expression "like a rabbit's horn," the rabbit's horn is merely a product of conceptual construction (*saṅkalpika*) and not a non-existence (*abhāva*). These [non-existences] manifest as such through the nature of a certainty whose essence is reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). And this is stated with regard to the commonality of experience among worldly people; for it is in that very place—

Thousands of prior, posterior, and absolute non-existences do not manifest at all times through being reflected upon; indeed, manifestation itself is existence. Alternatively, "those two" refers to both [prior and posterior non-existence].

Existents and non-existents are reflected upon. For even non-existents, like existents, belong to the same cognitive domain; yet, despite this shared domain, they are accessible only to subjects such as worms or omniscient beings. In this explanation, however, the word "tu" (but/however) is both not justified and justified. For he who [holds] that both [existence and non-existence] are indistinguishable according to the Buddhist [view]...
This specific distinction of his [the opponent] is illuminated when he thinks:
"If this non-existence is described as consisting of a determinative reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), then its essence is merely conceptual construction (*vikalpa*.
If that is so, then existence (*bhāva*) is exactly the same. He concludes this with the word *tat*, meaning "therefore."

"Even in the absence of externality" means even when that which constitutes "externality"—as understood through its separation—is absent. Even then, there is indeed manifestation in the form of "this is blue" or "this is pleasure. For, if the coloring agent—the blue object or the king—were not established, there would be no manifestation of the lotus or the person.

"This blue or this pleasure has now been produced by this"—this is the conjoining of the collection of manifestations (*ābhāsa*). Even when they are mutually separated, nothing occurs to the manifestations in terms of their own essential nature; thus, objects always exist as having the nature of manifestations.

And in this context, one should understand that "being a mere appearance" refers to its appropriateness to that particular state, and not to being residual to the "I-sense" (ahantā); for if it were so, he would not have said "as long as the latent impressions persist," since that [residuality to the I-sense] is indeed eternal. This is because [the object exists] as an object of apprehension.

The meaning is: "because of the removal of the obscuring darkness. As for the phrase "but of others," the remainder of the sense is that in the world, even for those things distinct from what is to be remembered—such as mental constructs in daydreams—which manifest to the subject as differentiated, their external form is nonetheless established. If one asks why this is so, he says:

"The three reasons are well-known," and so forth. Although cows and the like certainly produce pleasure and so on, they nevertheless perform other causal functions—such as satisfying hunger or pacifying bile—which result in a series of effects such as the body; these are not produced by what is commonly known as cow-milk and the like. However, as for pleasure and the rest...

Causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) consists solely in the nature of manifestation alone. But surely, the objects are manifestations, since they are what is grasped; how then can they be [the possessors] of that [manifestation] according to the *bahuvrīhi* compound in the commentary?
(page 415)

The state of being an object (*viṣayitva*) has been demonstrated. Regarding this, he says: "of those graspable by the mind. For these are forms adhering to consciousness, reflected in consciousness; although they appear as if distinct from it, they are not in reality other than consciousness.
Therefore, it is not appropriate for them to possess the status of an object (*viṣayitva*) by way of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but rather—
In their respective forms as external appearances, [the object] is like the blue in the manifestation of blue; as will be stated:
"That manifestation also, being its own, is a fresh arising" (2.3.1), and elsewhere as well.
"...it is to be cultivated (or: they are cultivated) by means of that nature...
Thus: "But in the cognizer, who is variegated by latent impressions (saṃskāra), let all subjects everywhere be of the single essence of 'I-ness'...
even though consisting of the appearance of blue."
The cognizer does not [perceive] yellow, green, and so forth as distinct from the object;
for even while conceptualizing one object, he perceives another as well.

According to this principle, there are here five stages of manifestation (*ābhāsadaśā*): the state of being composed of "I-ness" (*ahantāmaya*), the aggregate of latent impressions (*saṃskārapuñja*), the manifestation as a conceptualized blue (*vikalpyanīlābhāsa*), the manifestation as pure yellow to be reflected upon (*śuddhavimṛśyapītābhāsa*), and the yellow object (*pīto'rtha*). This is stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*). It is precisely this dependence...

He shows the form of worldly renown with the words "for from that" (*tato hi*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the causes of renown and its commonality among other subjects are included. Regarding "latent impression" (*saṃskāra*), it means they are veiled by darkness. "In every way" (*sarvathā*) means that they are not even cognizable as separate entities.

If they were external to the cognizer, they would be truly external by virtue of the "this" aspect; likewise, there would be a persistence of these [objects] across all time. However, if they consist solely of the "I-ness" (*ahantā*), there is no calculation of time, nor is there any state of being a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). But [one might object]: if this is so, [what of those things] being conceptualized through such autonomy?
What is the difference between those things being remembered? It is said: "by way of being objects of apprehension" (*grāhyatayā*) ... for the rest;

for in their case, the triad beginning with commonality to the cognizer is determined at the very time [of the original perception], and thus their extemporaneous externality does not fail to manifest. But as for those that are of the nature of error...

Regarding [the cases of] the double moon, silver, and so forth: although there is an ascertainment of their externality, they lack actual externality; however, in the case of mental fantasies (*manorājya*) and the like, that [externality] does not exist at all—this is the distinction.

"In both ways" means as the object of apprehension (*grāhyatā*) and as the external (*bāhyatā*). He states this briefly with the words "thus, therefore. Internality is twofold: as the "I-ness" (*ahantā*) and as residual impression (*saṃskāratā*); objectivity is twofold:
as the means of knowledge (*pramāṇatā*) and, in the case of blue, as the object of knowledge (*prameyatā*) precisely in the manifestation of blue.

In the case of independent conceptualization (*svatantravikalpa*), externality is sixfold, according to whether it is real or unreal and according to the distinction of time; this tetrad should be understood as being non-deviant from the preceding [category] and progressively leading to the succeeding one. "And its very nature" refers to internality, for that indeed consists in non-separation from manifestation (*prakāśa*).

The nature of entities is their non-conceptualized state of being manifest. And that—namely, the internal essential nature—is, as the case may be, delimited and colored by being either the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) or by the duality of objectivity and externality; it is at that time that this differentiation occurs. What is it? He says:

In cases such as error or independent conceptualization (*svatantra-vikalpa*), there is an object of apprehension (*grāhya*), but it is not external; this is because of the connection with that very time. This [statement] indicates three reasons, beginning with "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇya*). In memory—and by the word "etcetera," in intense mental construction (*saṅkalpa*) of pleasure and so forth—there is also externality, just as in the case of memory, it appears as if at its own time.

Because commonality and so forth are possible—[the variant *sadbhāvāt* is found in manuscript Ga]—and because pleasure and the like are manifest as external precisely through that much, namely, mere manifestation; and regarding the phrase "in perception," it refers to blue and so forth, for in that case the two reasons, such as commonality and so on, indeed exist. "That" refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*). "Because of the non-limitation by time" means...

The meaning is that because it is present at all times and is not delimited by time; "in that very way" means that its essential nature exists as such, in an unimpaired and pure state. Thus, while there is objectivity through externality, there is also the status of a means of knowledge through the state of being the apprehended, and through the state of latent impression (saṃskāra) within internality.

The state of being a subject is *māyīya* (pertaining to *māyā*); through pure *ahaṃtā* (I-ness), there is the state of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvaratā*) within; from that, there is an emanation in exactly that same manner—thus, consciousness has the universe itself as its body, consisting of manifestations. In that context, its "interiority" consists in its abiding at the level of the intellect (*buddhi*) while being veiled by *tamas*, of which...
In the state of *prakṛti*, there will be a clear recollection at a later time; whereas in the state of *māyā*, it is unclear, such that one thinks only "this belongs to someone.
(Page 317)

Moreover, even without the ripening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), because [the power] attains its functional state after being separated by an interval of time; yet on the level of mantra and so forth,
up to that of Sadāśiva, it does so through identity with the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃtā*) in a manner variegated by both equilibrium and disequilibrium.

Regarding the state of the venerable Śivabhaṭṭāraka, however, because of his being entirely immersed in the state of "I-ness" (ahantā), the specific internal distinctions will be explained in the section on the Āgamas. Those [distinctions] are merely indicated here by the general statement "in that state" and "in that very way.
Having thus examined the divisions, he concludes the subject at hand with the words "tadevam" (thus, therefore).

"It is to be suspected" means that it does not exist, because its own nature is not something to be negated—this is the intended sense. Here, the opponent begins to demonstrate that "externality" is not an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*), but rather the very essence itself: "Now," he says, "existence must be established by way of the opposite of non-existence."

He shows this with the words "manifestation" (*prakhyā*). And that [refers to] being the object of manifestation and so forth. "Of all"—the intention is that it is not only of external things. Now, if this is so, how is it that people employ the conventional usage of existence (*sattva*) only with respect to an external jar, and not with respect to the internal [object] and the grasper, which consist of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)? To this, he says:

And [this is] "externality. For this very reason: because it is agreed upon by the world that existence (*sattva*) consists precisely in the capacity to produce specific effects connected to a succession of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), even in the case of a son, the conventional designation of "non-son" applies when he fails to perform such an effect, despite being unreal.
Because it is accepted by others through its manifestation, for that reason, the appearance of the non-existence of a jar or the like—

which is the negation of the form perceivable by the external senses that performs worldly functions such as carrying water— is not an external jar; rather, in this form, that very appearance of the jar is the non-existence of the jar.

It has been stated: "But surely this is the case regarding prior non-existence (*prāk-abhāva*), posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsa-abhāva*), and mutual non-existence (*itaretara-abhāva*) because of the existence of the object to be negated;

however, how is it so in the case of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*)? To show that even in that case this method is indeed possible, he illustrates absolute non-existence in succession with the words "of a rabbit's horn," and so forth. For here:
The rabbit’s horn indeed appears in the intellect as something distinct from sky-flowers and the like.
He states another example with the words “in externality,” etc.; even there, existence would certainly be present, as if it were pure.
At the ultimate limit, that which is the consciousness "I" is itself— by virtue of being conceptualized—
the root of emanation consisting of the manifestation of all dualities, distinct from objective existence.

That which is created separately by *māyā* through all its aspects as forms such as the "graspable" (*grāhya*) and so forth, is indeed conceived in the intellect as being non-existent; for this very reason, because the ultimate internal form— which serves as the source for both manifestation (*prakhyā*) and description (*upākhyā*)— is [non-existent] in every respect.

It cannot be denied. He provides another example with the words "even in the sixth. "In some way" means that just as the mind (*manas*) is a sixth sense-organ distinct from the five [other] senses, so too there is an external sixth conceptualization (*vikalpa*) distinct from the fivefold external objects such as sound and the rest. For this very reason:

"Form" means that there exists something distinct from touch, smell, taste, and sound. For this very reason, it is shown in the Āgama that this very existence is non-existence—that which is non-empty is called "empty"... [etc.]
By such [statements] as this, || 5 ||
Now, is it not observed that in their various states— whether as internal, intermediate, or external— entities possess some specific causal efficiency appropriate to themselves,
just as the appearance of a beloved possesses [efficiency] such as memory, joy, or embracing, when characterized by identity with the subject?
Furthermore, if [the object] is internal, what kind of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) could there be? To this, he provides the answer in the Sūtra:

"Because they are internal and identical with the subject, their causal efficiency is not based on difference. Even when external, that [efficiency] exists through the differentiation of diverse appearances. (6)

Since these entities possess internality based on their identity with the cognizer, for that reason they possess no causal efficiency whatsoever. For such efficiency occurs only when there is a distinction between the cognizer and among the objects themselves;
how then could it exist when that distinction is absent due to non-difference? Indeed, [even so...]

[kha. That causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is indeed restricted to a specific manifestation (*ābhāsa-viśeṣa*). For even an external beloved woman does not lead to joy if she is devoid of the intermingling with other manifestations such as being embraced; and since causal efficiency resides solely in the manifestation, the manifestation itself is the reality—even for the opponent.
It is logical to accept that [the jar] arises from both; it is not the shape [that comes] from the clay, nor is the nature of the clay [that comes] from the potter.

For those who assert that the causal relation is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), their very appearances must be accepted as real entities, because positive and negative concomitance are restricted to conceptual exclusions (*kalpita-vyāvṛtti*).

Enough with this digression. Thus, regarding the intermediate state of transmigrating beings (*saṃsārin*), the reason for the Supreme Lord’s abiding within those transmigrating beings has been shown by way of illustration in the passage beginning with "in the subject of *māyā*. In that regard, in the state of the Blessed One, because of his identity with that [state], whatever...

The state of being the agent of all belongs to them alone; however, while they remain in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the subjectivity of Māyā, everything that is to be done by the subject of Māyā is said to be "all.
For the subject—from Brahmā down to a mere worm—is indeed variegated by such a diversity of latent impressions.
To that extent, it acts in various ways solely as is appropriate for its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). "From itself" means from the self, the cognizer.

That which is called the cause, being non-different from its effect, is the very essence (*ātman*) or nature (*svabhāva*) of those [things]. Thus, even the performance of a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), which was suspected to be based on difference, does not actually occur.

Having thus explained the word *api* as "even in the internal state which is devoid of differentiation," he explains [the verse] with the words "also when it is external" (*api bāhyatve*) and "that [state] is differentiated" (*sā bhinnā*). In this context, the phrase "when also" (*yadāpi*) and "of that" (*tasyāḥ*) refer to causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). The particle *ca* is displaced in its sequence; it means "not only... (*na kevalam*).

The manifestation (ābhāsa) possesses differentiation by way of being graspable, external, and so forth, as well as by way of location and other factors. He illustrates location with the words "location," etc., and time with the words "in memory," etc. Here, it should be understood that the object is indeed external and presently existing. Demonstrating the contrast with the aforementioned past time, he says: [the following].

He demonstrates the concomitance (*anvaya*) of the present time with another causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and therein he also introduces and illustrates the difference in form (*ākārabheda*) by the expression "clear manifestation" (*sphuṭāvabhāsa*).
This is done because of the other's doubt regarding the absence of a difference in manifestation— that is, the possibility of its non-existence.

There is a doubt; since that [doubt] does not apply when "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth are mentioned, those [terms] are employed. Now, one might ask: "Is this merely a suspicion? Why is there no difference in the appearance (*ābhāsa*) of pleasure (*sukha*) and the rest? Why is this not simply a real entity (*vastu*)? For they indeed possess the status of being objects (*viṣayatā*) only with respect to the intellect (*buddhi*)."

[This is] not with respect to an external object; so how can there be a distinction such as "clear" or "unclear"? Anticipating this objection, he provides the resolution: "But for those [cognitions] also... "In that very way" means "by way of distinction. (Verse 6)

In this regard, if someone were to say: "How could that internal nature—which is contradictory to the appearance of externality—belong to an entity that is being conditioned by that appearance? then how was it stated [as follows]?

"...therefore, because they are always existent within those [perceptions] that are themselves existent" (1.8.5); thus, by this aphorism, it is made known that these manifestations, being composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), always abide within [consciousness] itself.
Because those things appearing through illusion appear as external, that [consciousness] is also external.

The meaning is this: the manifestation of "this blue appears" is not the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the previously created object, but rather cognition itself; and since that cognition resides in the knower, objects are internal by way of this manifestation. The word "always" (*sadā*) refers to both when there is the manifestation of an orientation toward externality and when it is absent.
Since these manifestations—consisting of the appearance of blue and so forth—are composed of consciousness, they abide within [consciousness] itself;

otherwise, they would not manifest if they appeared as something separate. However, when their externality is projected by the power of *māyā*, which is characterized by absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), that [externality] consists of the act of manifestation itself.

That state which, by way of being the object, rests upon the nature of cognition—whether it be external or internal—is this very manifestation within [consciousness]. How could this manifestation within be contradictory to the manifestation externally, which is like a wall for the variegated painting of consciousness? It would be no more contradictory than the quality of blue, even though it possesses a non-momentary form.

Regarding momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*): here, indeed, the mutual exclusion of imagined [entities] exists merely through the exclusion of what is imagined; it is not ultimate. This is the meaning of the Sūtra. The intention [of the phrase] "in the case of internality" (*āntaratve*) is that it is a locus for the possibility of contradiction. As for "experience" (*anubhava*): although mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) are internal, they appear as if external.
Thus, they consist solely of the cognizer; otherwise, it has been stated that these [objects] would result in being devoid of their own nature.
"Objects" (*arthāḥ*) means that they are being sought as the forms of the objects of cognition (*prameya*). As for "appearance" (*ābhāsa*)...
(page 421)

Thus, although its essence is non-different from the cognizer, knowledge—which is in fact a property of the cognizer—is conventionally designated as "cognition" (*jñāna*) or "awareness" (*bodha*) because it appears, as it were, differentiated due to its coloring by the differentiation of those objects.
That which is manifested is divided; that which constitutes its functional aspect is what is called "knowledge."
It is divided; as for that part which consists of establishedness (*siddhatā*), he asks, "Does it arise? and answers, "The appearances of difference" (*bhedābhāsāḥ*).
By the word "and" (*ca*), he indicates that subjectivity (*jñānatā*) and objectivity (*arthatā*) manifest simultaneously—this is what he means by "of them" (*teṣām*):
those which previously did not appear separately as distinct from the subject (*pramātṛ*) due to non-difference.

Because they appear as their own limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), even though those appearances of blue and so forth are in reality not independent, they bring about, arouse, and lead to an independence whose essence consists solely in self-conceit (*abhimāna*). For instance, one engages in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) thus: "That which is this blue outside..."
"That very [object] appears"— for this very reason, even by the Buddhists,

the nature of the correspondence (*sārūpya*) is established through inference alone by virtue of its "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*), and not through direct perception; thus, the cognition of blue appears in the form of that correspondence.

Thus it has been stated. And the followers of Jaimini (the Mīmāṃsakas) declare that manifestness (*prakaṭatā*) is therefore a property of the object itself. "For this very reason" means that because the autonomy of these [objects] such as blue and so forth—which appear through *māyā*—has as its essence mere self-conceit (*abhimāna-mātra*), their dependence (*pāratantrya*) was described in the *Vṛtti*, but not their autonomy.

He shows that [the agent] is "touched" by saying "internally included" (*antarnīta*). For indeed, in the case of an independent [agent], the state of dependence—pertaining to other actions such as commanding, which serve to dispel the apprehension of obstacles directed toward that [primary action]—extends, as it were, even to the object in the form of the primary action; however, this is not so in an ultimate sense.
One who lacks independence with respect to the primary action would be connected by means of commands (*praiṣa*) and so forth.

Now, one might ask: "According to the Sūtra, when the commentary (*vṛtti*) is being presented, one should have said 'being manifested' (*ābhāsyamāneṣu*); what is the purpose of using the expression 'being revealed' (*prakāśamāneṣu*)? He replies: "By the word *prakāśa*..."
The intended meaning is that manifestation (*ābhāsana*) is nothing other than the nature of light (*prakāśa*),
as clarified by this term derived from a verbal root denoting the act of manifesting. However,
even in the case of independent mental constructs (*svatantra-vikalpa*), blue and other such objects do not appear as distinct from the light.
And even in that case, the operation of the power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*) must be admitted, and its ultimate nature as pure consciousness (*cinmātratva*) must be established;
on the contrary, for what purpose was it excluded by the term "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) in the *Vṛtti*?— this is the point in our hearts.

Having grasped [the object], one examines it; thus, the locative reading "in manifestation" (*prakāśane*) is clear, as it is possible [to say] "it exists.
