However, the word "manifestation" (*prakāśanam*) is to be cut off right after "is possible" (*saṃbhavati*); nevertheless, the remainder of the subsequent sentence must be supplied. Of those things directly perceived...

Since internality is not established for blue and other [objects], it must therefore be established for those very things through effort—that is, primarily—rather than for the appearances of conceptual construction (*vikalpābhāsa*), whose identity with consciousness is established without effort. He demonstrates this very point with the words "but in conceptual constructions... as follows: "whichever... refers to those which...
They maintain that only that which has the nature of a mental construct (*vikalpita*) is [the object], neither the external nor that which possesses both internal and external forms.

The phrase "adherence" (*abhiniveśa*) implies "for the purpose of establishing internality. It will be established [later] because their internality is well-known; therefore, on the contrary, externality must be proven with effort.
"Whatever this mental image (*ullekha*) is that will be established in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)"—by means of this sūtra [I.8.8].
Or else, according to the previous explanation: "Or else... [is the beginning of the next section].

The term "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) refers here to a manifestation (*ābhāsa*) that is the object of direct sensory apprehension by the external organs; however, in this context, all manifestations— whether within the domain of the internal or external organs—
appear directly in their own respective forms, ever-new in their nature.
Since they are each directly perceived according to their respective natures, although direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*) is non-deviant,
for one who considers some of them to be unreal— and therefore not directly perceived—
his very act of delusion is shown by the word "direct perception. Is it not the case that [these] are merely appearances?

He dispels the doubt—namely, "How could those [entities] which are being manifested possess differentiation, such that they are indicated by the locative case?"—with the words "of the one consisting of consciousness" (*cinmayasya*). The phrase "by way of differentiation" (*bhedena*) means by the intensification of the nature of activity, that is to say, the operation of manifestation directed toward objective entities. Now, [one might object]:...
Thus, it is logical that the appearance is internal; so how can there be an "external appearance"? To this, he says: "of blue and so forth" (page 423).

That manifestation is described as being "established in that" (tanniṣṭha) because of its separation—namely, its dependence on the subject of Māyā. He clarifies this very point by means of a reason: "according to the actual state of things. The phrase "of those" refers to those things which, although they do not actually differ from the Light, are nevertheless determined as such.

Grasping occurs through mere conceit (*abhimāna-mātra*)— which consists essentially of the activity of the primary illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*) produced by the power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*), and whose ultimate nature is exclusion (*apohana*)— and not as something separate from the Light (*prakāśa*),
because of the force of subsequent determinative cognition (*avasāya*). It is so called because it is "sought" (*arthyate*), and because it "binds" or "ties" the heart specifically.

They are designated by terms such as "objects" (*artha*) because they are connected with etymological definitions such as "they are measured" (*pramīyante*) or "they are apprehended" (*ālambyante*). To explain the word "also" (*api*), there is a commentary beginning with "that also" (*tadapi*);
in order to explain that, he says: "even though they are perceptible" (*pratyakṣatve 'pi*). The meaning of "also" (*api*) is in terms of mutual dependence.

With the intention that "it proceeds forth," he reiterates the conventional usage of externality while declaring its internal state; and even in that reiteration, he states by way of a subordinate restatement that it shines forth as non-different from the Light due to its being directly perceived (*pratyakṣatayā*). And this applies in both cases.
The construction is as follows: "it does so by means of the phrase 'thus' (*tadevam*), relying upon the reasons previously stated.

The phrase "connected with blue and so forth" means that consciousness, appearing in such a manner through the grasping of *māyā*, becomes identical with that very [object] when discernment (*viveka*) arises. It is "established" in its nature as knowledge through the distinction of objects.

He considers that the plural number is appropriate because differentiation is predominant. Now, if objects situated within [the self] are [perceived] by way of manifestation, then the heart would be perceived as crowded with thousands of entities such as blue and so forth, like a storehouse; why then is it said that it "would be perceived," when in fact it *is* indeed perceived? To this he says:

Regarding the phrase "within the wise": at that time, the entire manifestation of the universe shines forth as "I," having attained a state of non-differentiated oneness. Now, one might ask: "In that case, when there is the occasion of externality, from where does the manifold existence of blue and so forth arise?
To this he replies with the words "externalization" (*bahiṣkriyā*). By the word "that" (*yat*), the manifestation is being referred to.

Even in a verb expressing the agent, because the action alone is primary, that very manifestation of theirs which is thus [perceived] amounts to their being directed toward the object—that is to say, their being externally projected. Of the one consisting of consciousness...
(page 424)

Of that object whose sole nature is luminosity, this very state of being blue and so forth is its state of having mutually distinct forms, which is its difference from the subject. In this very context, as an incidental point, he also reflects on [the state] such as "desiring to create" and so on. By way of being the cause for this aforementioned object of knowledge (*prameya*),...

"Precisely for this reason, [it serves] as a means of subsistence. Now, one might object: "If, in this manner, there is an additional 'blueness' within luminosity, then that blueness must be of a non-luminous nature; if it is not, what indeed is called 'blueness'? To this, he makes the opponent understand by means of an example established for himself: "[of] luminosity... "Those" refers to blue and the other [colors].

He explains the very example with the words "paramāṇu" and so forth. "Of whom" refers to the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas. "From that" means from the accumulation of atoms (*paramāṇu*). "The object" (*artha*)—that is, the configuration (*sanniveśa*)—manifests the difference of objects such as jars and bowls; therefore...

The Vaibhāṣikas have stated that atoms, appearing in such a manner, are perceived as possessing the property of spatial arrangement (sanniveśa) when there is a manifestation; thus, they are described as having the nature of appearance. However, in the system of Kaṇāda, although there is no objective property called "arrangement" distinct from the dimension of magnitude (mahattva-parimāṇa),...

Since the differentiation of directions is non-ultimate, being merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), it cannot be the cause of the production of spatial arrangement, as it is undermined by the fallacies of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), circularity (*cakraka*), and infinite regress (*anavasthā*);
nevertheless, this much remains: the composite substance (*avayavidravya*) has indeed arisen in such a manner.

With the intention of avoiding the mode of flight [of the opponent], the proponent of the atomic aggregate (paramāṇupuñjavādin) has not been introduced. As for those Sautrāntikas who say that the property of configuration (saṃniveśadharma) resides within the aspect of consciousness (vijñānākāra) as its own manifestation, for them that [configuration] is a property of the manifestation itself; it is not [a property of external atoms].
Since this [cognition] is with respect to an object that appears, by the power of its identity with a single cognition, it is impossible to perceive it as having distinct parts;
according to this principle, when atoms appear as separate, because there is no continuity [of parts], there is only appearance.

"It is extended" is appropriate; this is what he means by "appearance. For appearance is not something additional to the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa), and thus it consists of consciousness alone. Anticipating the objection that "this may be either an error or merely conventional" (saṃvṛta), he refutes both possibilities with the words "nor even... (na cāpi).

(Page 425) Thus: that which is the property (*dharma*) of the manifestation (*pratibhāsa*) is not erroneous, nor is it merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), because the manifestation has the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), and consciousness is non-erroneous; and that aspect (*ākāra*) exists through identity (*tādātmya*) with that very [consciousness].

That which exists is real. Whatever is of the nature of something, it cannot, in its ultimate reality, be of the nature of an illusion or the like—just as a jar cannot be of the nature of redness. And thus, the arrangement [of the world] is of the nature of consciousness. That which is the opposite of being of the nature of an illusion or the like necessarily pervades what is called ultimate identity; otherwise, [it would not be so].

Indeed, identity itself is lost; by the perception of that [nature] here, the form of error and so forth—which is contradictory to its pervader—is negated. Alternatively, by the qualification "non-existent," the triad is negated.
He clarifies this very point with the example well-known [in the world], beginning with the words "clear" and so forth. The particle *ca* (and) has the sense of "also."

The intention is this: if even insentient things can achieve such a state through the power of their own transparency, how much more so for that which is of the nature of consciousness and autonomous? The word "explained" (*vyākhyātam*) was spoken in this way to indicate that this is the occasion for its explanation. || 7 ||
But has it not been said:
"Because they are internal and because the cognizer is one, there is no purposeful action for these [objects] based on their difference"? (1.8.6)

Thus [it is said]. Regarding this, one might raise the objection: "Since a conceptualized entity such as Garuḍa or a Piśāca lacks a common form perceivable by the external senses, how can there be an entry into specific causal efficiency—such as the neutralizing of poison or the instilling of terror—for that which is not external?
Anticipating this doubt, the Sūtra [states]:
This mental representation (*ullekha*) which occurs in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is also external, appearing as something distinct;
its internality consists in its identity with the subject (*pramātṛ-ekātmya*), and therefore even its difference [from other objects] constitutes externality.

In an independent or experience-based conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), that mental representation—the form being delineated through creative imagination (*utprekṣā*)—is also external; "external" does not refer solely to what is accessible to the external senses. For it appears as something entirely distinct from the nature of the cognizing subject (*pramātṛ*).

"This" means as something characterized by "this-ness" (*idantā*). Now, what follows from that? He says: "from that," meaning either from the difference that appears immediately after [the state] where there is already the identity of the knower (*pramātṛaikya*), or else, from the knower himself.

That differentiation which appears as such is called "external. External-ness is precisely the opposite of internality; internality, moreover, is identity with the subject (*pramātṛ*). That which is "within" is said to be the locus of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), whose nature is solely oriented toward itself; existence therein is internality, and external-ness is simply the opposite of that.
Externality: and that [externality] is indeed common to both the object that appears and the object that is conceptualized, such as pleasure and so forth;
this is the meaning of the Sūtra. He introduces it with the words "of those appearing through conceptualization," and so on.
Here, the introduction is made by way of an anticipated objection, rather than the meaning of the Sūtra being stated in brief.

Because it is perfectly clear. The intention [of the phrase] "it is established" (*upapannam*) is with respect to all people who seek the purposeful activity [of cognition]. The word "therein" (*tatra*) is a separate syntactical unit. It is connected with the subsequent passage beginning with "is experienced" (*anubhūyate*).
Its "externality" consists in its being cognizable by the external senses through the power of the prior operation of the eyes and other [senses].

He shows that even what has been established is not universal by saying "for thus" (*evaṃ hi*). He clarifies the expression "the reflective awareness of 'I'" (*ahaṃvimarśaḥ*) with the words beginning "the body" (*śarīra*). By the term "externality," he intends merely the absence of externality; thus, [this awareness] serves as the cause for internal discourse within the pure principle of consciousness (*śuddhacittattva*).

"The very externality of the self-reflection (*ahaṃvimarśa*). By the word "very" (*eva*), he states that here the externality is indeed complete. "Of that too" refers to the body. "Is conventionally expressed" as in "I am fair-complexioned; I see the jar. "Internally" means by way of internal contact, such as in hunger, satiety, and so forth.

Just as externality is conventionally designated as internality [in certain cases], so too internality exists even in the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties, which are objects of the reflective awareness of "this-ness" (*idantā*) despite being graspable (*grāhya*). The reason for this is that they consist of the activity of the subject (*pramātṛ-vyāpāra-mayatvāt*). Furthermore, in that case as well, the reason is their status as the subject (*pramātṛtva*) and so forth. This is the second [point].
The reason is "because of being an external counter-correlate. Here, the reason is "by virtue of being limited. Now, one might object:

intellect (*buddhi*) is characterized by ascertainment and is an expansion of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*); vital breath (*prāṇa*) also has the nature of breathing and belongs to the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*); and the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) is the life-force in both cases. Thus, this triad of powers— [Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the content up to that point.]

Because it is a power (*śakti*), it is not different from the possessor of power (*śaktimat*); so how can it be said to be limited by the reason that it consists of the activity of the subject (*pramātṛ-vyāpāra*)?
(Page 427)
It is not contradictory. To this it is said: for the operation of determination is indeed restricted to limited objects such as localized pleasure, pain, delusion, blue, yellow, and so forth;
and even the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), which is the act of breathing, is dependent upon the activity of a body measuring three and a half cubits.

The power of knowledge and the power of action, although they consist of the nature of these two [powers], possess limitation because their objects are the fivefold divisions of the vital breaths (prāṇa, etc. conceived through movement according to the distinctions of the elements and the directions; thus, their form is that of impulsion.
Therefore, since the contraction of these two is caused solely by their objects, those who disregard that contraction—
They abide there and do not grasp at the sense of "I," because they do not attend to external things such as the body—

which is the constrictor of the wind differentiated by the primary breaths of prāṇa and apāna— nor to external locations and so forth, which are the limiting adjuncts that constrict the expansion of consciousness regarding walls, mountains, and the like.

Therefore, for that reason, their vital breaths (prāṇa), exhalations (apāna), pleasure, pain, bodies, and so forth—whether appearing in the state of objects such as jars or elsewhere—have consciousness as their ultimate reality; they fulfill nothing other than the universal manifestation of that consciousness.
For this very reason, it is said in the Āgama:
"One should cast one's gaze upon a place such as a treeless mountain or a wall" (Vi.bhai. 60);
"Having abandoned concern for one's own body, one becomes pervasive within days" (107).
And so forth. Since there is no limitation when the substrate (*upadhāna*) is abandoned, it is therefore determined as follows:

by their very nature, these powers of knowledge and action are indeed unlimited; it is only when they are limited that they come to be designated as "intellect" (*buddhi*) and "vital breath" (*prāṇa*), while both forms remain essentially the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpatā*).

And there is the contraction of the object of cognition. Regarding the phrase "of that too," this refers to the manifestation of conceptual constructions, pleasure, and so forth. The reason for saying "one" is stated by the words beginning with "at that time," namely, that a second externality does not exist. The phrase "only one" means "always.
As for the phrase "even when residing in both," although it is cognizable by both the internal and external organs, it is not [dual] in an absolute sense.
"By way of distance and proximity...
(2.3.10), and so forth, according to external reasoning. Now, if a jar is cognizable by the internal organ, that is one [form of externality];
if it is cognizable by the eye, that is a second; therefore, this externality is of both forms.
As for what was stated on page 428,
how is that so? For it was just now [stated] that this single manifestation of a jar exists because of the unity of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "even though" (*yadyapi ca*).

The intended meaning is that duality is established through the intermingling of other appearances; thus, even though there is a unity between the appearance of the jar and the wall, duality arises due to the mixing of other appearances. Immediately after the word "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*), [the text continues].

The phrase "at the time of the arising of practice" (*pratipattyutpādakāle*) should be supplied, by which they believe that those appearances are fully cognized in their entirety. The term "the two" (*dvayam*) should be applied respectively to memory and direct experience; [it refers to] existence and non-existence by virtue of being capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Others read "samānapadam" (as a compound). In direct experience (*anubhava*), there is knowability by both external and internal organs; however, in recollection (*smaraṇa*), there is knowability by the non-dual internal organ alone. Since the internal organ is invariably concomitant with the external organ in direct experience, the internal organ need not be mentioned separately in that context.

Thinking thus, others read [the text] as "because it is cognizable by two instruments" (*karaṇadvayavedyatayā*). Now, if the object previously perceived appears in memory, and that [object] is of the very nature of being experienced (*anubhūyamānarūpa*), how can its distinction—such as its uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*)—be intended? Thus [they ask].
Anticipating this objection, he says: "At the time of recollection" (*smṛtikāle*), which means with reference to the time of remembering;

because it does not manifest to other subjects existing at that time of its recollection, but rather manifests together with those very same previous subjects, its uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*) has been stated.

And at that time, it does not perform a causal function (*arthakriyā*), nor is an external sense organ active therein; therefore, there is a lack of clarity. On this very point, he provides an illustration by way of a conjunction [reading *tathā* according to manuscript *kha*]: "In the same way," and so forth. He demonstrates the form as it appears at that moment through its aspect, saying: "I see this."

And it has been stated that "this is I" in order to clearly manifest the appearance as something external and on an equal footing with the subject; for in rites such as pacification (*śāntika*), [the practitioner acts] through the stalk of the lotus at the head of the one to be acted upon (*sādhya*), whether present before him or mentally visualized.

One meditates on [the goddess] entering, skillfully nourishing the entire collection of the internal network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) with a stream of supreme nectar flowing from a great crystal jar held simultaneously by the two hands of specific deities such as Garuḍa; in that case, the causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) is indeed manifest.
It is perceived. Anticipating the objection, "In that case, how is there no externality therein?
he provides the rebuttal with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). [The phrase] "in a quite different manner" means that even externality is indeed delineated therein. To explain:

"I am meditating thus," "this has been clearly meditated upon by me," "I have attained as if a direct realization"—thus he thinks. There is a word-break at *bāhya*. With the word *iti* and so forth, he concludes what was previously stated. Because of that which was previously stated with *iti*, this [state] remains as if established.

[It is] established that there is indeed a real unity between the manifestation of a jar as it is being experienced, as it is being remembered, and as it is being vividly delineated; and by virtue of its fitness, there is likewise a twofold externality, namely, [externality] as suchness and [externality] as being perceivable by the external senses. As for that which...

Due to delusion, one might not perceive identity here; for while identity is plausible between what has been experienced and what is being remembered, it is not so for that which is merely presented [in consciousness]. To address this, even regarding that which is presented, he establishes two kinds of externality by saying "either...
or... For even that which is presented as something unprecedented is not [internally real].

"Something other than form and so forth is delineated"—by means of this general principle, even in that case, a second kind of externality, characterized by being perceivable by the external senses, is indeed easily asserted. Now, if there is no insistence on this point, then why is such an extensive argument stated? It is said: [it is for the sake of establishing] its lack of substantial reality (*avastutva*).

One might object: "When the externality and duality [of objects] are being set forth, since it is necessary to demonstrate the classification of externality as stated in the Sūtra, what is the purpose of the qualification 'of jars and so forth'?
Anticipating this doubt, he explains the commentary beginning with "But of pleasure and so forth" by stating: "But of pleasure and so forth... [and so on].

The mention of the "subject" (mātra) following the term "without distinction" (aviśeṣa) is intended to reveal that even though there is no distinction in the case of a Garuḍa or similar being delineated in meditation— since it is not shared by other subjects— any other form of externality that might be delineated therein does not exist in the case of pleasure and so forth. || 8 ||

Now, one might object: "Granted that external objects such as a jar possess externality because they are produced by a potter and so forth; but what causes the externality of mental representations (ullekha), such as pleasure and the like? Anticipating this doubt, the Sūtra states:
"The manifestation of a representation, of pleasure, and so forth, occurs in the form of the external."
Just as [the Lord], by His will, is the presiding form over those things born of the eyes and other senses.

Of everything— including blue and so forth, pleasure and so forth, and the entire group of stable and transitory mental states (*sthāyivyabhicāri-cittavṛtti*) described by Bharata and others— which is reflected within the internal cognitive sphere (*antarbuddhibhūmi*), [there is a perception] by the subject (*pramātṛ*) through a distinct [mode].

That manifestation by means of the body occurs through the sovereign freedom (*svātantrya*) of manifesting external creation, which belongs to Maheśvara— who sustains internal appearances while simultaneously nourishing that external creation—
by His will characterized as absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), just as follows:

The manifestation of external objects such as blue and so forth— which are the domain of the external senses and consist of forms like those on the eye and other sense organs— whether by means of a cognition that is preceded by or for the first time designated by the term "perceptual knowledge," is also solely through the will of Maheśvara. Even in the case of a potter, it is supreme consciousness alone [that acts].

It consists primarily of the manifestation of the lump of clay, the staff, the wheel, and so forth, preceded by the movement of the body, the vital breath, and the specific cognition illuminated by His will; it is not some other thing whatsoever, as will be stated:
"For this potter... (2.4.9).

Thus it is said here. This is what is meant: even when the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) has no desire, whatever manifestations and so forth occur there, the Lord’s sovereignty alone is at work; and even where the desire of the bound soul (paśu) is involved, it is still the Lord’s sovereignty that must be relied upon for the arising of that very desire.
The meaning of the sūtra is that [the soul's agency] is due to the absence of any other cause and because it subsists upon the system of creation established by the Lord.
Regarding the phrase "and because it is not of that nature": shame, for instance, is neither pleasure nor pain, but rather a specific modification of the mind (cittavṛtti).
The same should be stated regarding longing and so forth. Regarding the phrase "because of being the Lord": this is because [the soul] participates in a limited degree of sovereignty.

"By that very [power]" means by the will of the Lord (*īśvarecchā*) alone. "It has been stated" refers to the sūtra (1.6.11): "...because of the manifestation of exactly what is intended. "Internally" means that it remains within the *ahantā* (I-consciousness) in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), its own nature being undissolved.

This is the meaning. He explains the illustration with the words "the eye and so forth. Now, an objection may be raised: "The mind (*manas*) is the grasper of those [states] such as the manifestation of pleasure; the intellect (*buddhi*) is that which determines them; therefore, one should say 'mental illumination' (*mānasaḥ prakāśaḥ*). Why, then, was it said to be 'intellectual' (*bauddhaḥ*)? To this [he replies]: "These... [iti]
With the words beginning with "bāhya," he dismisses this doubt;
for [the process] culminates in certainty.
(page 431)

The meaning is as follows: regarding that [object], when there is a mental ascertainment (*niścaya*), the Light (*prakāśa*)—whose body is resting within that [ascertainment]—is called "mental" (*bauddha*); yet, even so, it does not depend upon, nor does it entail, any distinction or alteration [of its nature].
In connection with this, another point is also investigated here, beginning with the phrase "and of the intellect (*buddhi*) etc."

The commentators on the Nyāya-bhāṣya have divided perception (*pratyakṣa*) into categories such as sensory, mental, yogic, intuitive, and so forth; however, the author of the Sūtras spoke only of sensory perception.
By the sūtra: "That which arises from the contact of a sense-organ with its object...

(Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.4). However, in systems such as Sāṃkhya, since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is considered distinct [from the senses], let it be regarded as mental (*mānasa*), or as belonging to the intellect (*bauddha*); or according to the Buddhist method.

The intention is this: let those mental impressions (*ullekha*), being non-different from self-luminous cognition, be designated as "perceptible by self-awareness" (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*); what is the point of this insistence on justifying a designation in an inappropriate place? But surely, by this same logic—

Recollection (*smṛti*) would also have to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). It would be so if it were to manifest a novel object, but it does not do so; this is what he shows with the words "and in recollection" (*smṛtau ca*). Now, one might object: "The manifestation of the object is vivid and indeed new; how then can this [recollection] be the apprehension of what has already been apprehended? To this, he replies: "the manifestation... and so forth.
He confirms that the determination [of objects] occurs solely by the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) with the words "when, however.
When one disregards the external object and reflects primarily upon the very form residing within consciousness—
thinking, "At this moment, my state exists in this manner as a form of manifestation"— then:

In the appearance—which has the nature of a reflection in the mirror of consciousness and is non-different from consciousness—consciousness itself is indeed directly perceived by virtue of its being self-awareness. Previously, it was deliberated that "the object was grasped by direct perception"; however, as for what exists of the object now...

"I exist as such a manifestation within the Light"— this is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) precisely as something unprecedented. When there is such an intention to speak— that is, when one wishes to intend and intends to grasp the very state of being a manifestation of consciousness, without regard for external form— one attends solely to the reflective awareness of that manifestation of consciousness.

Primarily, he provides an example with the words "just as. For the experience of two moons is erroneous only insofar as it involves the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an external form; however, with respect to the appearance of cognition itself, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is indeed non-erroneous.

(432) Therefore, even though certainty exists only in that [internal] manner, because an object— though itself devoid of variety— is established as "this is desired" or "this is undesired" according to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), it appears as if variegated; for this reason:
Self-awareness itself, culminating in the determination that there is awareness of an object,
has been described as the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) by way of another formulation. Having thus, by way of digression,
described the account of the experience of a jar [the account of the absence of a jar, according to manuscript *ga*].
He connects the very memory under discussion with the point that "it is something previously apprehended. The introduction here is as follows:
"But how can that same cognition of memory be both the apprehension of what has already been apprehended and yet have a novel object?
How are these two to be reconciled? To this, it is said:

This is not a fault because their objects are different: when the objectivity of that appearance with respect to the prior experience is what is being considered, then there is the grasping of what has already been grasped;
and even though this grasping of the already-grasped exists, it occurs while the prior experience, as conditioned by the manifestation of the object, remains present.
And since memory and its own nature are mutually non-distinct, it was stated previously regarding memory that self-awareness of memory itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):
"In memory, that which is... (1.7.5).

Thus [it is stated] in the Sūtra. Alternatively, having introduced the matter in this way, the application [of the argument] is as follows: that which was stated previously—that memory grasps only what has already been grasped—means that by taking a prior experience as its object, it acts in such a manner; and furthermore, that prior experience serves as the underlying permeating factor (anuvedhaka) in the form of memory. This is the case here.

Regarding the question of what the authority is for the three parts, he says "the former" (*pūrva*). The word "also" (*api*) serves to include this object of knowledge along with the previously mentioned objects of knowledge. The inclusion of all three parts, however, is expressed by the single particle *ca*. || 9 ||
Now, regarding what was stated— that there is "one Maheśvara"— the Sūtra concludes that very unity:
"Without that unity, the course of worldly consciousness would not exist."
Because of the identity of their manifestation, their oneness is established; thus, it is settled that the cognizer is one. || 10 ||

Therefore, from the aforementioned object of cognition (*prameya*), this follows as a logical reason (*hetu*): namely, that without the unity of cognitions (*saṃvid*) or knowledges (*jñāna*), no worldly path or entire conventional transaction (*vyavahāra*) could exist; yet, such [conventional transactions] do exist.

Therefore, the unity of cognitions must necessarily be accepted, and this is not difficult to establish. For light alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of cognitions, and that is one because there is no duality. And that which is one is, in the ultimate sense, the subject (*pramātā*). Thus, that which is to be taught here is now firmly established.

It has become unwavering. By the phrase "the Supreme Self" (*paramātman*) in the commentary, he declares its status as the ultimate subject (*paramārtha-pramātṛ*). For thus says the *Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi*: "Even though the stability of objects... (20)
Thus [it is said]. By the words "and so forth," etc., it is stated that the distinction which is primary according to form—that is, existence—does not exist;
this is expressed by the apprehension of the essential nature (*svarūpa*). The reason for that very point is "because its nature is pure consciousness" (*cinmātrarūpatvāt*).
He states that there is no distinction even by way of space and time with the word "space. Although there is a manifold variety of distinctions...

Although conventional discourse has already been mentioned, nevertheless, because it is all-pervasive, the relationship between the one who communicates and the one who is communicated— which encompasses everything— is discussed here; for this relationship exists within oneself in the form of doubt, deliberation, and ascertainment, and with respect to others in the form of instruction, buying, selling, and so forth.

This is indeed possible; for without that, even linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) would be impossible to carry out. Anticipating the objection—"But is it not the case that in the self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of cognitions, there is a resting point characterized by their respective connection [to words]; so what is new about this?"—he says "And if... regarding those things whose nature is to be perceived (*saṃvedya*).

[This refers] to those [aspects] such as blue that constitute the very self of the object of cognition (*saṃvedya*). For the ultimate form of blue and so forth is indeed their manifestation (*prakāśa*).
And by this very fact, it has been stated that a real identity (*aikya*) is indeed appropriate. Now, one might ask:
"In that case, how can an coloring (*uparāga*) even by blue and so forth be produced, by virtue of which it was said..."

Regarding the phrase "of those [aspects] conditioned by their respective objects of cognition," it is said: that portion of the Light itself, characterized as the object of cognition— which has been differentiated by the power of *māyā*, which, though not separate from the Light, appears as if separated from it, and which is thus distinct from it and even differentiated from other such portions— is, by means of that [portion], [conditioned].
These [views] have been refuted. Regarding the term "manifestation" (*prakāśa*),
it is established that for the Sāṅkhyas and the followers of Jaimini, consciousness (*saṃvit*) is self-luminous (*svaprakāśā*).

Even according to the ancient Vaiśeṣikas, it has been stated in the commentary on this sūtra (1.2.7)— "Knowledge and the nature of consciousness..."— that the self (*ātman*) is indeed of the nature of consciousness (*citsvabhāva*). This is also the view of the Buddhists.
"And the cognition that grasps the cognition...
and so forth has already been demonstrated. "The establishment of all valid cognitions" means the determination of the object... (Aparapramāṇasiddhi 20).

Thus it has been said. [Objection: But is that differentiation which is manifested by the power of *māyā* not indeed a real difference? And if so, then the statement "of cognitions whose nature is the object of cognition" is incorrect. [Reply: He says: "And of those whose nature is the object of cognition"—even if this is so, it is nonetheless non-dual (*advaya*). If that is the case, then blue and other such objects are illusory.

[They] might [be so]. To this also he says: "nor even... The reason why duality does not result is given by the word "since" (*yataḥ*). Distinction arises from something other than the body and the objects of cognition, but not from the Light (*prakāśa*); for if there were distinction even from that [Light], then the very principle that "the distinct is manifested" would be lost. Here he states the reason for its being internal with the words "and that which... But surely this...

How can it be consistent that [objects] such as blue are both distinct and non-distinct? To this he says: "The object" (*grāhya*). Here, the "subject" (*grāhaka*) is the illusory body and so forth; the "one whose nature is light" (*prakāśātmā*) is the ultimate subject (*paramārthapramātā*). "Of those two" refers to the object and the subject. And this has been determined.

"...that is seen by me... (Sūtra 1.4.8). And thus, it is precisely by way of being like a reflection. Now, one might object: "If so, even the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell would be like a reflection; therefore, all instances of error would have ceased to exist in the three worlds. True.
This is in relation to that which is illuminated by another. If so, where does the conventional usage of "error" (bhrānti) apply? He says: "It is *māyā*.

Regarding the phrase "whatever it may be": every error well-known in the world is said to be real when one considers its sublation (*bādha*), and this will also be stated in the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*); however, this is with respect to the subject (*pramātṛ*) who is under the influence of *māyā*.
For it is only with respect to that [object] that correspondence and non-correspondence regarding purposeful action are possible. || 10 ||
(435) Having thus concluded the discussion on unity, he concludes the section on Maheśvaratva with the following sūtra:
"He alone, by virtue of his constant state of reflective awareness, is Maheśvara."
For the pure power of knowledge and action of the Lord is nothing other than reflective awareness itself. || 11 ||
That which is called "uninterrupted awareness" is precisely the state of being reflective in nature;

for this reason, its nature—characterized by luminosity or by the coloring of blue, pleasure, and so forth—is never at any time unreflected upon, like a crystal gem. Therefore, by virtue of its essence of not being directed toward anything other than itself...

The Great Lord is the supreme sovereign by virtue of the wonder of "I-am-ness" (ahamiti-camatkāra) whose nature is bliss; for, according to the reasoning already stated, these two— knowledge and action— are indeed the pure, ultimate powers of the Divine, which is called "reflective awareness" (vimarśa).
"...the nature of manifestation... (1.5.11).

Regarding this point: it might be argued that while manifestation characterized by consciousness may indeed exist in its primary form (*prakṛti*), when the suffix *kvip* is applied to the derivative term (*pratyaya*), only the state of being (*bhāva*) is denoted, and not reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). That [is not so].
How is it said "by means of the root and the suffix"? He thinks as follows:

first, the act of sensing, characterized by cognition, is expressed by the verbal root; however, suffixes such as *ghañ* are prescribed only for the action itself, and that action is indeed differentiated by another property called "accomplishment" (*siddhatā*).

That which is expressed by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is precisely the fitness for reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa-yogyatā*) regarding the state of being accomplished, as in "this is cooking" (*ayaṃ pākaḥ*). Here, the reflective awareness that occurs is not one that enters into the essential nature of the action of cooking itself, because such a reflective awareness arises for the subject (*pramātṛ*); however, this is so within consciousness, whose very essence is light (*prakāśa*).
Since the state of being reflected upon cannot logically exist by depending on anything else,

that which consists in the state of being reflected upon— which functions as identical with the act of consciousness— is precisely the nature of the reflective awareness whose form is establishedness.

"It rests in autonomy. And therefore, the combined root and suffix manifest that form which is characterized by fullness— that is, whose nature consists of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of knowledge and action, which brings about a distinction from the insentient.

By the phrase "of the nature of inquiry," the sovereignty [of the subject] within the means of valid cognition (*pramā*) has been demonstrated. "Of this" refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Now, if it is so, then consciousness...
(page 436)

In this regard, if cognition and action are already included [in the term "consciousness"], then since both the base and the suffix exist even in the word *jñāna*, those two are indeed already included there; so why is "action" mentioned again as something additional? To this it is replied: "even in the case of 'cognition' (*jñāna*). This is true, even though it is a single [term].
In this context, the word "also" (*api*) is used in the phrase "in this word. It is said [to be expressed] by means of the two parts, base and suffix.

Regarding the phrase "predominantly": although the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together, nevertheless, because that meaning of the suffix manifests as a property (*dharma*) of the meaning of the base, it is the property [that is predominant].

Because a property (*dharma*) exists only by way of making its substratum (*dharmin*) prominent, that property causes prominence to emerge within the substratum—which is characterized by cognition—as the aspect of awareness (*bodhabhāga*), namely as "action" (*kriyā*). Furthermore, the word "and" (*api ca*) serves as a conjunction;
even in cases where there is no other verbal component denoting the aspect of awareness, [the same applies].
The word "even" (api) is used in the sense of "thus. For this very reason, it was stated previously that [the Lord] "speaks," whereas here it is said that He "implies" (ākṣipta).

He states the reason for this implication with the words "of non-comprehension. And he shows that this alone is logical with the words "the reality is indeed one. Now, why is reflective awareness (vimarśa) the state of Maheśvara? He says: "by virtue of its directness" (āñjasyena).

For reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is indeed independence from anything else, and that itself is autonomy. Now, one might object: reflective awareness is the pervasive master of consciousness; for consciousness never deviates from nor ever abandons reflective awareness. Therefore, since it is never absent [from consciousness], how can it be described as the agent (*kartṛ*) when its status as the object (*karman*) ought to be expressed?
Anticipating this objection, he says that even when expressing two things that have equal pervasion (*samavyāptika*) in this manner, there is no fault:

"The reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of consciousness is always inseparable from it. The reflective awareness of consciousness is inseparable, and by implication, that consciousness is also inseparable from it.
Therefore, it is not improper for this non-deviating reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) also to possess agency.
He states the reason for their equal pervasion (*samavyāptikatva*) with the words "because of possessing non-deviation" (*avyabhicāravattvāt*), meaning that they are mutually [co-extensive].
Having thus established agency, he applies another etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) in connection with the recollection of the statement regarding the cause.

Even then, because of that which was stated—namely, the state of being non-deviant—from that very reason, the application of a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*) is justified; thus, this designation is indeed appropriate.
(Page 437)
[Objection: Is this not merely the self-reflective awareness "I," wherein the fullness of the object (*bhāva*) has indeed not been reflected upon?

[Reply: It is not so; thus he says, "And then... [Objection: But might even non-existent things manifest through the power of will? Anticipating this doubt, he says, "the desired object. For the reason that something does not manifest is precisely its lack of objective reality (*nirviṣayatva*).

An action that necessarily involves the undertaking of karma does not occur in the absence of that karma, just as life does not exist in the absence of the vital breaths; thus, the "act of impelling" (*iṣikriyā*) constitutes the perception of a contradiction with its own nature. [Objection: But if reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) depends upon such appearances of entities which are unstable, how can it be pure?

"It is said 'thus' (ittham), meaning 'in this way' (evañca). In this manner, that which is the abiding of entities in the form of the "I-notion" (ahamiti) is eternal and not distinct from the Supreme Self; and since that very [abiding] is the form of the "I-notion," there is no impurity whatsoever in it. For it is not something separate at that time.

There is something that must be considered. Now, he begins to explain what is excluded by the mention of "pure" with the words "that very [nature]," and he distinguishes between purity and impurity with the phrases "even though it is pure" and "because it is the cause of impurity. This impurity is merely superimposed; it is not...

Because of its absolute repose in the innate "I-ness" (ahantā), having thus explained the purity and impurity of this "I-ness," he explains its impurity with the words "that very same" (saiva). This "I-ness" is not something else; rather, it is that very same [I-ness] which, through the variety of its own powers, by this...
It shines through various forms within the manifestations of reality, worlds, entities, elements, and so forth, in the spheres of appearance.

Amidst these diverse appearances, this "I-ness" (ahantā) exists in reality as their pervader and animator, by means of incorporating those other appearances within itself. That which is thus constituted is the "I-ness."

When their manifestation is concealed by the power of *māyā* through the fitness for the reflective awareness of "this-ness" (*idantā*), then that state of "I-ness" (*ahantā*) is appropriate and fit for transmigrating beings;
the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃ-vimarśana*) that occurs in that state is said to be impure.
The connection is remote. He demonstrates the nature of the self-reflection (*ahaṃvimarśana*):
although it consists of both the form of light (*prakāśa*) and the form of action (*kriyā*), it is likewise of the nature of power (*śakti*).
(Page 438)
From that, knowledge—which is designated as *sattva*—has fallen away; activity, which is designated as *rajas*, and the regulator *tamas* have entered into that middle state.
Consequently, the reflective awareness "I am composed of the three *guṇas*" arises, which is the cause for the fall from one's true nature.

That which exists as the state of "this-ness" (idambhāva), such as the intellect, the vital breath, and so forth, is differentiated; because it is [regarded as] the body and its attributes, the reflective awareness of "I" (aham-vimarśana) arises with respect to it, and consequently, its true nature falls away from that cause of arising. From where, then, does its such arising come? He says: "differentiated."

Since that which is the mere subject (*grāhaka-mātra*), distinct from the object (*grāhya*) upon which it depends, is precisely that part (*bhāgāṃśa*) which it penetrates, it arises in this manner. He shows the form of such a self-reflection (*ahaṃvimarśa*) with the words "I am this" and so forth, ending with "and I act."
[This concludes] with the aforementioned [passage]. Now, one might ask: "In this case, how can there be a distinction between the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*)?

He replies: "By means of their different loci (*vaiyadhikaraṇyena*). Now, the followers of Kapila (*kāpila*) maintain that the activities of knowledge and action, which consist of the fluctuations of *sattva* and *rajas*, belong to the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*), yet they are conventionally designated as "I" (*ahaṃ*) from the perspective of the Person (*puruṣa*). How is this so according to you?

This unprecedented process has been set forth. It is not at all unprecedented; for there is no such thing as a "Person" (puruṣa) distinct [from consciousness], but rather, that which is characterized by contracted awareness—whose very nature consists in the non-recognition of its own sovereignty—is what is called the "Person. Those two [powers] related to him...

"Cognition and action, whose nature is that reflective awareness of 'I'—and this very [awareness] consists in the non-recognition of one's own true nature; thus the individual person is manifold... (4.1.3).
This will be elaborated upon in this section. The term "reiterated" (*anūdita*) is used in the *Vṛtti*. And here, the repetition [of the point] is...
This is by way of a mere illustration, and not according to the logical principle that "wherever there is smoke [there is fire]. For if that were the case,

just as the possession of smoke would be the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the property to be established (*vidheya*), namely the possession of fire, so too would the self-reflection (*ahaṃvimarśana*) be the pervader of the ten states— the pure, the mixed, and the impure.

However, that restatement which occurs by way of a wall-like [support], as an already established fact, expresses the pervasiveness (*vyāpakatā*) of the object to be restated. And the particle *eva* (only/just) serves to illuminate this meaning, as in the example: "Only that which possesses fire possesses smoke. Now, it may be asked: has not the threefold reflective awareness (*ahaṃvimarśana*) been stated?

(On page 439) Regarding the division into pure (*śuddha*) and so forth: therein, has the triad of internal states (*daśāntara*), characterized as "mixed with another" (*paravyāmiśra*) and "other" (*apara*), which is established by scripture (*āgama*), been abandoned at all? It has not been abandoned; rather, it has been included. Thus he says:
"And these very [states]..."—it will be stated here that the posteriority of entities [is established] by the sūtra (3.1.5): "In this case, posteriority [belongs to the later]. || 11 ||

Thus ends the eighth reflection on Sovereignty (*māheśvarya*), contained within the section concerning the single locus of the group of powers, in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, the great devotee of Maheśvara. || 8 ||
And thus concludes this first chapter on Knowledge.
